## A69. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, October 3, 1746 069.JE-J.Bellamy 10-3-46

Jonathan EdwardsA069. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 10/3/46. BRBL, f. 1271. Addressed on back "To / Mr. Joseph Bellamy / at Bethlehem."

Northampton Octob. 3. 1746. dear sir,

I have been for some Time past in Expectation of seeing you here: And tho' you are not yet come, I hope it will not be long first. I want to see you very much.

We had some talk with you the last year, concerning buying & letting out some sheep for us: And you was so kind as to put your self to some Trouble for us, & to send us word of an opportunity there was. But having then engaged my Brother Wetmore,[^083-note1] I could not accept the offer that you gave us an account of. But Br. W.---has fail'd of procuring for us such a number of sheep as we expected. I should therefore be glad to procure and let out a score of sheep your way; and so would desire you to make some Enquiry, and take some Pains to know whether any sheep are to be bought, & at what Lay, and send me word by the first opportunity.

I have the money Ready to lay down, and would have inclosed it in this Letter, If I were sure of an opportunity of buying your way. but upon an intimation from you, will send the money directly, that you may have it to lay down. I am sensible that in such Cases, it is a great Advantage for the Buyer to have money in his Hands; and therefore I am willing, if you buy for us, that you should have this Advantage. -I have of late made considerable Enquiry, & understand that good sheep are not Commonly sold for more than 25 Pound ascore. but I hope to have an opportunity soon to see [^083-note2] you in these Parts, not only on this, but on some other Accounts. And As I understand you have intended a Journey here so I hope you will not fail of it. I am dear sir,

Your Brother & Affectionate Friend,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^083-note1]: I.e. Seth Wetmore of Middletown, Conn., who married JE's sister Hannah.

[^083-note2]: **marginal.** [v.]

## A70. Letter to Philemon Robbins, November 3, 1746 070.JE-P.Robbins 11-3-46

Jonathan EdwardsA070. JE to Philemon Robbins, 11/3/46. CHS, Ammi & Philemon Robbins Corr., 1742-92.

Northampton Novem. 3. 1746.

Rev. & dear sir,

The Account you gave me in your Letter was very affecting to me; But I received it when it was too late for me to write an Answer that should reach you before the appointed meeting of the Consociation, being from home on a Journey to Long-Island when the Letter came to my House; so that I had it not till the day that the Consociation was appointed to meet; and dont know the present Circumstances of the Affair, only as I lately learn'd something from mr. Bellamy, who was here about a Fortnight ago.. From all that I can can learn of the Affair, it appears to me by no means adviseable for you to lay down your ministry if th at Branford, if the major Part of the People will stand by you[^084-note1] . and if there could be any Hope of obtaining a Council of Churches from towards Boston (including at least three or four of the Boston Churches) on representing the Affair to them, to come & give & you & your Church their advice upon it; I should think it would be richly worth the while; and to obtain as large a Council as you can.. I believe the ministers that way would be very loth to be at the Trouble; but If you should & your Church should apply to 'em, & fairly represent the Case, I can't see how they Excuse themselves to God and their own Consciences in Refusing, or how they could reconcile their so doing with many of the Rules of Gods Holy word, I mean Christian Rules of Equity, Charity, & Love to our neighbour as our selves & pity & Relief to the oppressed &c. . There are many of the ministers that way that can't but know the many oppressive measures that have been, & are, from time to time gone into in Connecticut: And shall we never hear the Cry of the oppressed, [^084-note2] when it is in the Power of our Hands to do something for their Help, but let 'em lie & sink under their oppressions without Remedy?. However, if this that I have proposed ben't feasable, I should can think of nothing better than w something that mr. Bellamy proposed, viz. that you & your Church should apply your selves to the two Associations or Consociations of Fairfield County, Laying your Case before them, & desiring th to give you their Judgment, whether you are properly under sea brook saybrook Platform or no, and whether you are bound to submit to the Acts & Proceedings of nei the ministers & Churches of the your County towards that have been Regulated by that Platform, since you have publickly renounced it, & also openly denied the Jurisdiction of sd ministers & Churches. And whether you take this or the other Course, it appears to me highly needful & a that a narrative of the whole affair should be published. --. But others that know more of the present state of your affair are under greater advantage to give you proper advice. However since you have been pleased to ask my thoughts, I desire my good will in what I have written. who am, dear sir, your Affectionate & Compassionate

Brother & Servant.

Jonathan Edwards

The Rev. Mr. Philemon Robbins

[^084-note1]: Because of his support of the awakenings, the New Haven Consociation found Robbins "criminally guilty" and sought his dismissal. However, Robbins' congregation ignored the verdict and retained him as their minister.

[^084-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

## A71. Letter to Esther Edwards, November 3, 1746 071.JE-E.Edwards 11-3-46

Jonathan EdwardsA071. JE to Esther Edwards (daughter), 11/3/46. Harvard College Library, Autograph Coll. Written to Esther and Sarah, who are at Easthampton, Long Island.

Northampton Novem. 3. 1746.

Dear Child,

we lately received a Letter from you dated Octob. 13. and another from Sarah dated Octob. 22. and were much refresh'd to hear from you. I not long since wrote a Letter to you both, and sent it to Mr. Potwine's for conveyance, & therewith your Mother sent an w[. . .]-p[. . .]oat[^085-note1] for Sarah, as she now with this sends one to you, to be conveyed in like manner.. We are all through mercy in a tolerable state of Health. Our House is now forted in, & a watch is kept here every night in the Fort: every night. But there has been no mischief done by the Enemy in this County, since the taking of Massachusetts Fort: I am ready to think the French & Indians have lately turn'd their Course another way, down towards Annapolis,[^085-note2] to join the French Fleet. but we have lately heard that That Fleet have lately been totally confounded by a remarkable Hand of God against them, in storms & sore sickness; so that They have been quite discouraged, and are gone back again, after the two Chief men had killed themselves, through melancholly & vexation. 'Tis exceeding wonderful & affecting that God should so appear for so sinful & unworthy a People; to de fend us from our Enemies & Confound Them. [^085-note3] we all give our Love to you . Give mine & your mothers Love to Mr. Osborn & his Wife. I would not have you be discouraged & melancholly, tho' you are far from Home; God is every where, & I hope you will walk closely with him, & will have much of his Presence. Your Circumstances at East-Hampton[^085-note4] are on some Accounts much more comfortable than of your sisters at Home, for you lie down & arise and have none to make you afraid; here we have been in much fear of an Armies suddenly rushing in upon the Town in the night to destroy i. . . we daily remember you in our prayers to God, who I hope will be with you continually & will in every Respect be Gracious to yo. I am. my dear Child

your affectionate Father,

Jonathan Edwards.

Mrs Esther Edwards

[^085-note1]: MS damage; "white petticoat"?

[^085-note2]: I.e. in Nova Scotia.

[^085-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^085-note4]: Esther and Sarah had probably gone to Easthampton, Long Island, with their father for the ordination of Samuel Buel on Sept. 19. 1746.

## A72. Letter to Robert Abercrombie, January 8, 1747 072.JE-R.Abercrombie 1-8-47

Jonathan EdwardsA072. JE to Robert Abercrombie, 1/8/47. BRBL, "Hebrew Idioms," f. 1211. Addressed on back "To the Rev / Mr Robert Abercrombie / minister of teh Gospel / at Pelham."

Rev. & dear sir,

I wrote to you, a Little while ago, desiring you, if you went speedily to Boston, to enquire of Capt. McCun, for some Pamphlets & Letters, that I understood were sent me from scotland, that I had not received, & to bring them with you: I hear you have been to Boston, & are lately returned. I shall be glad if you would write me word, by the first good opportunity, how you found; and if you brought me any Letters or Pamphlets, send them; for I want them very much. Please also to send me word how long it will be e're Capt. McCun & Capt. Scot retu set sail for scotland. Herein you'll oblige your Br. & servt,

Jth Edwards.

Northampton

Jan. 8. 1746, 7.

## A73. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, January 15, 1747 073.JE-J.Bellamy 1-15-47

Jonathan EdwardsA073. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 1/15/47. BRBL, f. 1272.

dear Sir,

I receiv'd your letter by Mr. Strong this day. Mr. Searl was here at my House presently after, and I gave your Questions to him, and told him the Bearer intended quickly to return.

(As to the Affair of sheep. I Am much obliged to you for the Pains you have taken. I believe you have acted the Part of a trusty Friend therein. I suppose it is Known by this time, whether the man that went to Newtown has succeeded. If he has, & the sheep are bought, we shall rest in what you have done; but if not, & you shall have found no opportunity 'till this Letter reaches you, It is so late in the year, that I desire you would keep the money 'till shearing Time is over, & then buy; when I suppose They may be bought much cheaper than now. But sen I would pray you to send us word by the first opportunity, that if we are not like to have any sheep this year, we may seasonably be looking out, & laying in for wool elsewhere, for the supply of the Famil. In the spring, If you can give us any encouragement, I should be glad to lay out 60£ more for sheep in those as soon as shearing time is over, besides the 30£ you have in your Hands. But only,[^087-note1] if you buy so many sheep for us, It might be perhaps expedient, On some accounts, for the present, not to let it be Known who the sheep are for)

As to wh the Books you speak of; Mastricht is sometimes in one vol. a very thick large Quarto; sometimes in two Quarto volumes . I believe it could not be had new under 8 or 10 Pounds . Turretine is in three vols in Quarto, and would probably be about the same Price . They are both excellent. Turretine is on Polemical divinity; on the 5 Points, & all other Controversial Points; & is much larger in these than Mastricht; & is better for one [^087-note2] that desires only to be thoroughly versed in Controversies. But take Mastricht for divinity in General, doctrine Practice & Controversie; or an unis universal system of divinity; & it is much the better than Turretine, or any other Book in the world, excepting the Bible, in my opinion. I have Thoughts of sending, my self this year to England, for a few Books; and have written to Mr. Quincy, a mercht in Boston, about it, to desire his Advice and assistance, as to the Course to be taken to obtain 'em. If I imploy Him to send for me, I shall be willing to serve you (as I desire you to serve me about the sheep. I am willing) to take your money, & put it with my own, & put your Books into my Catalogue & have the Books[^087-note3] all come as mine: or shall be willing to serve you, if I can in any Respect, by writing to my Correspondents in scotland.

I have been reading Whitby, which has engaged me pretty thoroughly in the study of the Arminian Controversy; and I have writ Considerably upon it in my private Papers . I must intreat you, if possible, to borrow for me dr stebbing, on the spiri. . I had rather pay something for the use of it, than not have opportuni some considerable opportunity with it. I am got so deep into their Controversy, that I am not willing to dismiss it, 'till I know the utmost of their matters.

I have very lately received a Pacquet from scotland, with several Copies of a memorial, for the continuing and propagating an Agreement for joint Prayer, for the general Revival of Religion; three of which I here send you . For my Part, I heartily wish it was fallen in with by all Christians from the rising to the setting sun. -- I have returned you you Mr dickinsons Book, but must pray you [to][^087-note4] let me have further [^087-note5] opportunity with dr Johnsons . If you could Enquire of dr Johnson, or Mr Beach, or some other, & find out what is the best Book on the Arminian side, for the defence of their notion of Free will; & whether there be any mo better & more full than Whitby, I should be glad; provided you have convenient opportunity . I don't Know but I shall publish something after a while on that subject. dear sir, we have so many affairs to Confer upon, I--that concern us both, that I would propose that you should come this way again in February or March. You han't a great Family to tie you at Home, as I have. But if you can't come I must desire you to write fully & Largely on the foregoing particulars of this Letter . Herein you will oblige,. you. Cordial & affectionate Friend & Brother,

Jonathan Edwards.

Northampton, Jan. 15. 1746,7.

P.S. It now comes to my mind that I heard that dr Pynchon of Long-meadow has Turretine, And that he lately offered to change them[^087-note6] away for other Books; so that in all probability you may there have those Books[^087-note7] at a moderate Price.

[^087-note1]: This word was crossed out by a later owner of the MS, probably in preparation for publication.

[^087-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^087-note4]: MS damage.

[^087-note5]: **marginal.** [3]

[^087-note6]: A later owner of the MS crossed out "them" and inserted "it."

[^087-note7]: A later owner of the MS cross out "those Books" and inserted "it."

## A74. Letter to William McCulloch, January 21, 1747 074.JE-W.McCulloch 1-21-47

Jonathan EdwardsA041. JE to William McCulloch, 1/21/47. ANTS, f. 1747, #6.

Northampton Jan. 21. 1746,7.

Rev. & dear Brother,

The Time seems long to me since I have received a Letter from you: I have had two Letters from each of my other Correspondents in Scot land since I have had any from you. Our Correspondence has been to me very pleasant; and I am very loth it should fail.

Great Changes have been, dear sir, since I last had a Letter from you; And God has done great Things both in Scotland and America; Tho' not of the same Nature with Those that were wrought some years ago, by the Outpourings of his spirit; yet those wherein his Providence is on many Accounts exceeding remarkable; In Scotland, in the suppression of the late Rebellion; And in America, in our Preservation from the great French Armada from Brest, and their utter disappointment & Confusion, by the immediate & wonderful Hand of Heaven against Them, without any Interposition of any Arm of Flesh[^089-note1] : The nearest akin to Gods marvellous works of old in defence of his People, in Moses's, Joshua's & Hezekiah's Time, perhaps of any that have been in these latter Ages of the world . I have been writing some Account of it to Mr. McLaurin; But since that, I have seen a Thanksgiving sermon of Mr Princes,[^089-note2] preached on that Occasion; in which is a much more distinct, particular & (I suppose) exact Account of the matter (which sermon you will doubtless see) Tho' there is something that I observed in my Letter to Mr. McLaurin, of the Coming of that Fleet its being overruled for our Preservation in this Part of the Land where I dwell; when eminently exposed, And when one we have all Reason to think our Enemies in Canada had formed designs against us, That Mr. Prince does not mention.

--In my last Letter to you, I wrote you some Thoughts I & Notions I had entertained concerning the pouring out of the sixth vial on the River Euphrates, and the approach of the Happy day of the Churches Prosperity & Glory, & the utter destruction of Antichrist, & other Enemies of the Church, so often spoken of in the Holy scripture. I signified it it as what appeared to me probable, that one main Thing intended by the drying up the River Euphrates, was the drying up the Temporal supplies & Incomes of the Antichristian Church & Kingdom; and suggested it to Consideration, whether Gods appearing so wonderfully for the taking Cape-Breton, and the American Fishery thereon depending, out of the Hands of the French, and theref thereby drying up so great a st Fountain of the wealth [^089-note3] of the Kingdom of France, might not be looked upon as one Effect of the 6th vial . I would now also propose it to be Considered, whether God's so extraordinarily appearing to baffle the great attempt of the French Nation to repossess Themselves of this Place, ben't some Confirmation of it ; and whether or no the Almost ruining French East-India Trade, by the dreadful Hand of Heaven, in burning their stores at Port L'Orient, & the Taking so many of their ships by Commodore Barnet, and also the taking so many of their south-sea ships vastly rich, & several other things of like nature that might be mention'd, mayn't probably be further Effects of this vial . But whatever be thought of these particular Events, and the Application of Prophecies to them: yet it Appears to me that of Gods late dealings both with great Britain and the American Plantations, be duly considered, as They are in Themselves and their Circumstances, Afford just Reason to Hope that a day is approaching for the peculiar Triumphs of divine mercy & sovereign Grace, over all the unworthiness & most Aggravated Provocations of men . If it be considered what Gods Past dealings have been with England & Scotland, for two Centuries Past, what obligations he has laid those nations under, and the Particularly the mercies bestowed more lately, & then well Consider the Kind, manner & degree of the Provocations & wickedness of those nations, and yet that God so spares Them, & has of late so remarkably delivered Them, when so exposed to deserved destruction; And if it be also considered what Gods dealings have been from with this Land, in its first settlement, & from its Beginning hitherto, and how long we have been Revolting & Growing worse; and what great mercy he has lately granted us, in the late remarkable strivings of his spirit with us, and how his spirit has been treated, his mercy & Grace despised, & Bitterly opposed, how greatly we have Backslidden, what a degree of stupidity we are sunk into , and how full the Land has been of such Kinds of wickedness, as have approached so near to the unpardonable sin against the Holy Ghost, & how obstinate we are still in our wickedness , without the least appearances of Repentance or Reformation ; and it be then Considered how God has of late made his Arm Bare, in almost miraculous dispensations of his Providence in our behalf, to succeed us against our [^089-note4] Enemies, & defend us from Them ; I say if these things be Considered, it appears evident to me, not only that mercies are infinitely above the mercies of men; but also that he has in these Things gone quite out of the Usual Course of his Providence, and manner of dealing with his professing People . And I confess it gives me great hope that Gods appointed Time is approaching for the Triumphs & displays of his Infinite, sovereign beyond all that ever has been before, from the beginning of the world . At least I think there is much in these things, considered together with other remarkable things God has lately done, to encourage and Animate Gods People to unitedly to cry to God that He would appear for the bringing on those Glorious Effects of his mercy, so often foretold to be in the latter days ; And particularly to continue that Concert for Prayer, lately set on foot in Scotland, & which it is now proposed to continue for seven years longer . -----My wife & Children join with me in Respectful Cordial salutations to you & yours. That we all may be remembered in your Prayers, is the Request, dear sir, of your most affectionate Brother

Jonathan Edwards.

The Rev. Mr McCulloch

[^089-note1]: A French fleet, intent on recapturing Louisbourg and conquering Annapolis, Nova Scotia, was decimated by storms and disheartened by the death of their commander, the Duke d'Anville; the remnant sailed home without taking any action.

## A75. Letter to Robert Breck, April 7, 1747 075.JE-R.Breck 4-7-47

Jonathan EdwardsA075. JE to Robert Breck, 4/7/47. Boston Public Library, Chamberlain MSS, Ch. A.3.50.

Northampton April 7. 1747.

Rev. & dear Sir,

Thomas Wait of this Town, having been judged by this Church to be guilty of the sin of Fornication, has desired Liberty of an Appeal to a Council of Ministers; which the Church has allowed Him . He desired that the Council might consist of Ministers without any messengers. . The ministers fixed on are Mr Hopkins & you, Mr A---y of d---d, Mr W--of Hatfield, & Mr W---ms of H---y.[^090-note1] The Time is Thursday the last day of April, to meet at the meeting-House, at one o'Clock in the After-noon. The Place where the Council is to be provided for and entertain'd is Asa Wrights . I desire you would come without fail, and be here before noon.

---The number of the chosen Council is but small, & if some should fail the design might fail. This with humble service to Madam is from your

Brother & servt

Jonathan Edwards.

[^090-note1]: Revs. Jonathan Ashley of Deerfield, Timothy Woodbridge of Hatfield, and Chester Williams of Hadley.

## A76. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, June 11, 1747 076.JE-J.Bellamy 6-11-47

Jonathan EdwardsA076. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 6/11/1747. BRBL, f. 1273.

Dear Sir.

I herewith send you Mastrict, & one vol. of Turretine. If have one of Mr. Beach'ss & dr. Johnsons last, I shal should be glad if you would lend me them to me, after you have Used em sufficiently your self, & send 'em by some safe hand. I also desire you would send me word what that man has done, that was depended on for buying sheep &c. -I have Thought since I saw you whether it would not be proper in the Bonds that are taken of the men that hire the sheep, instead of their obliging Themselves to deliver so much wool at Mr. Potwine's, at to say at Mr Potwine's, or such other House as in Hartford as I shall appoint. that in Case Mr. Potwine should die or remove from Hartford, the Bond may still oblige them to deliver the wool at Hartford. Give my service to your spouse.

--- And I hope you will think of what talk we had of your taking a Journey in the Fall, for the Interest of Religion. Mr. Brainerd has lately been at my House with Mr. Wheelock. Mr W. is very poorly & not able to preach, & so has been for some Time; Tis uncertain whether he was[^091-note1] ever preach more. Mr. Brainerd is far from being so Broken in his understanding, as I have heard. He is capable of conversing very agreably, and praying in the Family most admirably. He is now gone to Boston with my daughter Jerusha: she intends to stay in Boston about a Fortnight while Mr Brainerd goes to the Eastward: & then He is to return with her hither again. -- Mr. Brainerd is a very desirable man indeed; I am glad I have had such an Opportunity of Acquaintance with him. Physicians speak of the state of his bodily Constitution as very dangerous & difficult & dr Mather of this Town gives him over, but dr Pynchon is not so positive that he will not recover ; For my Part I cannot but have some Hopes of his Recovery. I think it is what all that know him should earnestly pray for,

I am dear Sir,

your obliged Friend & Brother,

Jonathan Edwards.

Northampton June 11.

1747.

P.S. Please to send me a few Lines by the man that comes for Mr. searl.

[^091-note1]: **[1].** MS sic.

## A76a. Letter to John Erskine, [c. Summer 1747] 076a.JE-J.Erskine cSummer47

Jonathan EdwardsA076a. JE to John Erskine, [Summer?] 1747. Described and briefly excerpted in Sir Henry Moncrieff Wellwood, *Account of the Life and Writings of John Erskine, D.D.* (Edinburgh, 1818), pp. 196-201.

P. 196, on Erskine's correspondents:

"The most distinguished of them all was Jonathan Edwards, who cannot be slightly mentioned in a narrative of this kind. As a philosopher and a divine, as well as a Christian minister, he held a staion of eminence, which, whatever respect has been shewn to his opinions, few of his contemporaries have denied him. His correspondence with Dr Erskine began in 1747; and it was continued without interruption till his death, which happened in 1758.

"His first letter is dated at Northampton in Massachusetts, where he was then minister of the first congregation with which he was connected. Dr Erskine had sent him The Remains of Mr Hall,' with which their correspondence began; and on this occasion Mr Edwards expressed, with great tenderness and delicacy, his sympathy with one who had lost his most intimate and estimable friend in the prime of life, the companion of his youth, and, for a considerable time before his death, the delightful and affectionate associate of his [^092-note1] studies and of his piety.

"In a postscript to this letter he mentioned his book 'on Religious Affections,' then just published, and at the same time sent his correspondent a copy of it,--a book, of which it is not too much to say, that it is not only worthy of the talents and sincerity of its author, but that, while it shews that he was neither forward in rash in estimating striking or sudden impressions of religion, it contains more sound instruction on its particular subject, and lays down more intelligible and definite rules to distinguish true from false religion, and to ascertain, by distinct characters, the genuine spirit of vital piety, separated from all fanatical delusions, than any other book which has yet been given to the world.

"It was immediately occasioned by the different aspects of what was then called '*the Revival of Religion*' in America, in which there were many of the same features and characters, which distinguished the events which have been adverted to in the west of Scotland; but in which Mr Edwards thought he perceived, [^092-note2] mixed with many demonstrations of the efficacy of preaching, many false appearances and counterfeits of religion, and many pretended conversions, with regard to which he felt it to be his duty to warn the individuals, and to disabuse the public.

"He intended in this publication, after ascertaining the nature and importance of religious affections, to make the distinction precise and definite, between true and false religion. He intended to shew, on the one hand, the specious appearances in the state of the affections, which may often be substituted for the spirit of religion, when they are equally remote from genuine conversion and from real piety; and, on the other hand, to point out the inseparable and intelligible characters of personal religion, in which its practical and permanent effects are conjoined with its powerful impressions within the breast.

"In point of language, this book is undoubtedly defective, like all the writings of Jonathan Edwards. Though his ideas are [^092-note3] always precise, his sentences are often embarrassed, and his reasoning, though it goes deep into the human character, and very successfully lays open the secret recesses of the human heart, is frequently more intricate and metaphysical than his subject required, or than is suited to the capacity of every reader. But with all its defects, his treatise on religious affections, though he had never written any thing besides, would have placed him in the first order of enlightened and practical divines. It requires an intimate knowledge of the human heart, as well as of practical religion, to enable a reader to appreciate its value. But the more attentively the argument contained in it is considered, and is applied to real characters, it will always appear so much the more interesting and conclusive.

"In the same postscript to Mr Edwards's first letter to Dr Erskine, he gave him a general sketch of a plan which he had then formed, and which he afterwards executed with so much ability in his book on the [^092-note4] Freedom of the Will;--a book which, whether his opinions be questioned or adopted, has certainly given him an eminent station both among philosophers and divines.

'I have thought,' he says, 'of writing something particularly and largely on the Arminian controversy, in distinct discourses on the various points in dispute, to be published successively, beginning first with a discourse concerning the freedom of the will, and moral agency; endeavouring fully and thoroughly to state and discuss those points of liberty and necessity, moral and physical inability, efficacious grace, and the ground of virtue and vice, reward and punishment, blame and praise, with regard to the dispositions and actions of reasonable creatures.'

"Such was the first idea of a work, from which Mr Edwards afterwards derived his chief celebrity as an author. But a considerable time intervened before he found it possible to make any progress in his [^092-note5] design."

## A77. Letter to Caleb Clark, [Before September 1747] 077.JE-C.Clark bef.9-47

Jonathan EdwardsA077. JE to Caleb Clark, n.d. [before 9/47]. BRBL, in "Efficacious Grace," Book #11, p. 97, f. 1206.

Mr Clark

If you are not like to be over-loaden in coming Home I should be glad if you could bring some Books belonging to mr. darling for me. If you will can bring 'em, & speak to Job strong about 'em He knows what They be & will Procure 'em for you.

## A78. Letter to Thomas Gillespie, September 4, 1747 078. JE-T.Gillespie 9-4-47

Jonathan EdwardsA078. JE to Thomas Gillespie, 9/4/47. ANTS, f. 1747, #1. Addressed on cover "To the Rev. / Mr Thomas Gillespie / Minister of the Gospel / at Carnock in / Scotland."

Northampton Septem. 4. 1747.

Rev. & dear Sir,

I received your Letter of Novem. 24. 1746. tho' very long after it was written. I thank you for it, & for your offering me a Correspondence with you: such an offeri I shall gladly embrace, and esteem it a great Priviledge; more especially from the Character I have received of you from Mr Abercrombie,[^094-note1] who I perceive was intimately acquainted with you.

As to the Objections you make against some Things contained in my late Book on religious Affections, I am sorry you did not read the Book through before you made Them; if you had, perhaps the difficulties would not have appeared quite so great. As to what you is contain'd in the 74 & 75 Pages, I suppose there is not the least difference of Opinion between you & me, unless it be concerning the signification & Propriety of Expressions. I am fully of your mind, and alwaies was, without the least doubt of it, "That every one, both saint & sinner, is indispensably bound, at all seasons, by the divine Authority, to believe instantly on the Lord Jesus, And that the Command of the Lord 1 John. 3. 23. That we should believe on the name of his son Jesus Christ, as 'tis a Prescription of the moral Law, no less binds the sinner to immediate Performance, than the Commandment not to kill, To keep the Sabbath day, or any other duty, as to the Present Performance of which, in way of duty, all agree the sinner is bound; -and that men are bound to Trust the divine Faithfulness, be their Case, with Respect to Light or darkness, sight &c. what it will; and that no Situation they can be in looses them from Obligation to glorify the Lord at all seasons, and expecting Fulfilment of his word"[^094-note2] And that while the sinner that is without spiritual Light or sight is bound to believe, & that it is a duty that is at that very Time incumbent on Him to believe. But I conceive that there is a great deal of difference between these two things, viz. its being a mans duty that is without spiritual Light or sight to believe, & its being a his duty to believe without spiritual Light or sight, or to believe while he yet remains without spiritual Light or sight ; Just the same difference that is between these two Things, viz. Its being his duty that has no Faith to believe, and its being his duty to believe without Faith, or to believe without believing. I trust there is none will assert the latter, because of the contradiction that it implies. As 'tis not proper to say 'tis a mans duty to believe without Faith, because it implies a contradiction, so I think it equally improper to say 'tis a mans duty to believe without [^094-note3] those things that are essentially implied in Faith, because that also implies a Contradiction. But a spiritual sight of Christ or Knowledge of Christ is essentially implied in the very nature and notion of Faith; & therefore 'tis absurd to talk of believing in Christ without spiritual Light or sight. 'Tis a the duty of a man that is without those Things that essentially belong to faith, to believe; and tis the duty of a man that is without those things that essentially belong to Love, to Love God ; because 'tis an Indispensable obligation that lies on all men, at all Times, & in all Circumstances, to Love God : but yet 'tis not a mans duty to Love God without loving him, or yet continuing without those things that essentially belong to his Love. 'Tis the duty of those that have no sense of the Loveliness of God, & have no Esteem of Him, to Love him; & they bent in the least excused by the want of this sense & Esteem, in not loving Him one moment ; but yet it would be properly nonsense to say 'tis their duty to Love him without any sense of his Loveliness, or any Esteem of Him ; Tho' it be his duty this moment to come out of his disesteem & stupid in wicked insensibility of his Loveliness, & Love Him. I made the distinction, I thought, very plainly, in the midst of those sentences you quote as exceptionable; I say expressly p. 74 "It is truly the duty of those who are thus in darkness, to come out of darkness into Light and believe; but that They should confidently believe and trust, while They yet Remain without spiritual Light or sight, is an Antiscriptural and absurd doctrine.["] The misunderstanding between us, dear sir, I suppose to lie in the different Application of the Particle without, in my use of it, and your Understanding of it, or what we understand as spoken of & supposed without spiritual Light or sight : As I use it, I apply it to the Act of believing, and I suppose it to be very absurd to talk of an act of Faith without spiritual ; wherein I suppose you will allow me to be in the Right of it. As you understand it it is applied to duty or Obligation; and you suppose it to be not at all absurd to talk of an Obligation to Faith without spiritual Light or sight, but that the Obligation remains full where there is no spiritual Light or sight ; wherein I allow you are in the right of it. I think sir, if you read what I have said in my Book on this Head again, it will be exceeding apparent to you, that 'tis thus that I apply the Proposition without, & not as you before understood it. I thought I had very plainly manifested that what I meant by being in darkness, was a being in [^094-note4] spiritual Blindness, & so in a dead, stupid, Carnal & unchristian Frame and way, and not what is commonly called a being without the Light of Gods Countenance, under the Hidings of his Face &c. we have a great number of People in these Parts that go on that supposition, in their Notions & Practice, that there really is such a Thing as a such a manner of believing, such a Kind of Faith as this, viz. a confident believing & firm Trusting in God in the dark, in the sense mention'd, That is to be sought after, and is the subject matter of divine Prescription, And which many Actually have. And indeed there are inummerable Instances of such as in are apparently in a most senseless, careless, Negligent, Apostate, & every way, unChristian and wicked Frame, that yet, on this Princi encouraged by this Principle, do retain an exceeding strong Confidence of their good state, & count that herein they do their duty, & give much Glory to God, under the notion of trusting God in the dark, & Hoping against Hope; & not trusting in their own Righteousness; and They suppose it would shew a legal spirit for 'em to do other wise. I thought it would be manifest to every Reader that I was arguing against such a sort of People.

You say "It merits Consideration whether the Believer should ever doubt of his state, on any Account whatever, because doubting, as opposed to believing, is absolutely sinful." Here sir, you seem to supposng that a Persons doubt ing of his own good Estate, is the proper opposite of Faith, & these & some other Expressions in your Letter seem to suppose that doubting of ones Good Estate and Unbelief is the same Thing, & so that being confident of ones good Estate and Faith are the same Thing ; which I acknowledge I dont understand ; I don't take Faith, and a Persons believing that They have Faith to be the same Thing : nor do I take unbelief, or being without Faith, & doubting whether They have it, to be the same Thing, but entirely different. ----I should have been glad either you had taken a little more notice what I say on this Head p. 76, 77 or said something to convince me that I am wrong in this Point. The Exercise of Faith is doubtless the way to be delivered from darkness, deadness, Backsliding &c. or rather is the deliverance; as Forsaking sin is the way to deliverance from sin & is the deliverance it self. The Exercise of Grace is doubtless the way to deliverance from a Graceless Frame, that consists in the want of the Exercise of Grace. But as to what you say, of a or seem to intimate of a Persons being confident of his own good Estate, as being the way to be delivered from darkness, deadness, & Backsliding & prevailing Iniquity, I think, whoever supposes this to be Gods method of delivering his saints, when sunk into an evil, careless, Carnal & unchristian Frame, first to assure 'em of their good Estate & his Favour, & by that means to [^094-note5] while they yet remain in such an Frame, & so to make that the means of their deliverance, does surely mistake Gods method of dealing with such Persons. among all the multitudes I had opportunity to observe, I never knew one dealt with after this manner. I have known many brought back from great declensions, that appeared to me to be true saints, but it was in a way very diverse from this. In the first Place Conscience has been awaken'd, and They have been brought into great Fear of the wrath of God, having his Favour hid; and They have been the subjects of a kind of new work of Humiliation, brought to a great sense of their deservings of Gods wrath, even while They have yet feared it, becau before God has delivered Them from the Apprehension of it, and Comforted Them with a renewed sense of his Favour.

As to what I say of the necessity of Universal obedience, or one way of known sin, being Exception enough against a mans salvation I should known better what to have said further about it, if you had briefly shewn how the scriptures that I mention, & the Arguments I deduce from them are insufficient for the Proof of this Point. I confess they appear to me to prove it as fully as any Thing concerning the necessary Qualifications of a true saint can be proved from scripture.

You object against my saying p. 276. "nor can a true saint ever fall away, so that it shall come to that this, that ordinarily there shall be no remarkable difference in his walk & Behaviour since his Conversion from what was before" what I say, I think implies no more that his walk & behaviour over the same Ground, in like Circumstances, & under like Trials, will have a remarkable difference. As to the Instances you mention of david & Solomon, I don't know that the scrip tures gives us any where so much of a History of their walk & Behaviour before their Conversion, as to put us into any proper Capacity of Comparing their After walk with their Former. These Examples are uncertain ; But I think those doctrines of the scripture are not uncertain, which I mention in the Place you cite, to confirm the Point which teach that Converts are new men, new Creatures, that they renewed not only within, but without, that old Things are pass'd away, and all things become new, that They walk in newness of Life, that their Members of their bodies are new, that whereas they before were the servants of sin, & yielded their members servants of Iniquity to Iniquity, now They yield Them servants of Righteous ness unto Holiness. [^094-note6]

As to those doubts & Cases of difficulty you mention, I should think it very needless for a divine of your Character, to Apply your self to me for a solution of [---------] difficulties, However since you are pleased to insist on my giving my mind upon Them, I would observe, as to the first Case you mention, of a Person incessantly harassed by satan &c. You dont say of what nature the Temptations are that Je is harassed with; Nut I think it impossible to give proper Advice and directions without knowing this. satan is to be resisted in a very different manner, in Case of different Kinds of Onsets. when Persons are harassed with those strange, horrid Injections, that melancholick Persons are often subject to, He is to be resisted in a very different manner from what is proper in Case of vio lent Temptations, to gratify some worldly Lust. In the former Case I should by no means advise a Person to resist the devil by entering the Lists with Him, and vehemently engaging their Minds in an earnest dispute & violent struggle with the grand Adversary ; But rather by diverting the mind from his frightful suggestions, by going on steadfastly & dili gently in the ordinary course of duty, without allowing Themselves Time & Leisure to attend to the devils sophistry, or viewing his frightful Representations, committing Themselves to God by Prayer in this way, without anxiety about what had been suggested. That is the best way of resisting the devil that crosses his design most; & He more effectually disappoints Him in such Cases, that treats Him with Neglect, than He that attends so much to him, as to engage in a direct Conflict, and goes about to try his strength and skill with Him, in a violent dispute or Combat. The latter Course rather gives Him Advantage, than any Thing 'tis what He would: if he g can get Persons thus engaged in a violent He gains a great Point : He knows that melanchollick Persons are not fit for it: By this He gains that Point, of diverting & taking off the Person which is one great Thing He aims at : and by this, having now having gain'd the Persons attention to what He says, He has opportunity to use all his Craft & subtilty: & by this struggle, He raises melancholick vapours to a greater degree & further weakens his mind & gets Him faster & faster in his snares, He increases the Persons Anxiety of mind, which is the very thing by which mainly He ful fils all his Purposes with such Persons.

Concerning the other difficulty you mention relating to the verifying of Rom. 8. 20. All Things shall work together for Good &c. in a saint that falls under Backslidings & spiritual decay &c. It seems to be a matter of some difficulty to understand exactly how this is to be taken, & how far it may from [^094-note7] hence be infer'd that the Temptations the saints meet with from satan & an evil world, and their own declensions & sins shall surely work for their Good. However, since you desire my Thoughts, I would express Them, such as They are, as follows'

In order rightly to state this <atter, there are two Things may be laid down, as {ositions of certain & indubitable Truth concerning this doctrine of the Apostle.

I. The meaning cannot be that Gods dispensations & disposals towards each saint are the best for Him, most tending to his Happiness of all that are possible; or that all Things That are ordered for Him, or done by God with Respect to Him, are in all Respects better for Them Him than any Thing else that God could have ordered or done, issuing in the highest Good & Happiness that it is possible He should be brought to. For that would be as much as to say, that God will bestow on every one of his Elect as much Happiness as he can, in the utmost Exercise of his Omnipotence. and this sets aside all these different degrees of Grace and Holiness here, & Glory hereafter, which He bestows according to his sovereign Pleasure.

All Things may work together for Good to the saints, All may be of Benefit to them, & may have concurring Tendency to their Happiness, & may all finally issue in it, & yet not tend to, or issue in the highest degree of Good & Happiness possible . There is a certain measure of Holiness & Happiness, that each one of the Elect is eternally appointed to; And all Things that relate to Him work together to bring to pass this appointed mea sure of Good. The Text & Context speaks of Gods eternal Purpose of Good to the Elect, predestinatingting Them to a Conformity to his Son in Holiness & Happiness; & the implicit Reasoning of the Apostle leads us to suppose that all Things will surely concur to bring to Effect Gods eternal Purpose. And therefore from his Reasoning it may be infer'd, that all Things will tend to, & work together to bring to pass, that degree of Good that God has purposed to bestow upon Them, & not any more. And indeed it would be in it self unreasonable to suppose any Thing else but this. Inasmuch as God is the supream orderer of all Things, doubtless all Things shall be so ordered, that with one consent, They shall help to bring to pass his Aims, Ends, & Purposes : But surely not to bring to pass what He does not aim at, & never intended. God in his Government of the world is carrying on his own designs in every Thing ; but he is not carrying on that which is not his design. And therefore there is no need of supposing that All the Circumstances, Means & Advantages of every saint, are the best in every Respect that God could have ordered for Him, or that there could have been no Circumstances or means that He could have been the subject of, that would, with Gods usual Blessing on means, have issued in his greater [^094-note8] Good. Every saint is as it were a living stone, that in this present State of Preparation, is fitting for the Place appointed for Him in the heavenly Temple. And in this sense all Things undoubtedly work together for the Good to every one that is called according to Gods Purpose, He is all the while he lives in this world, by all the dispensations of Providence towards Him, fitting for the particular mansion in Glory that is appointed and prepared for Him, or Hewing for his appointed Place in the heavenly Building . And

II. Another Thing which is no less certain & demonstrable than the Position that has been already laid down, & indeed follows from it, is this; when it is said All Things work together for Good &c. Thereby cannot be intended All Things both Positive & negative Or that it is so universally, that not only every Thing positive Thing that the saints are the subjects of, or are concerned with will work for their Good, but also that when any Thing is absent or witheld from Them by God in his Providence, that Absence or witholding is also for their Good, or better for Them than the Presence or Bestowment would have been. For this would have the same absurd Consequence that was mention'd before, viz. that God makes every saint as happy as possibly He can. And besides, if so, it would follow that Gods witholding greater degrees of the sanctifying Influences of his spirit is for the saints Good, & that it is best for Them to live and die so low in Grace as They do. which would be as much as to say, that 'tis for their Good to have no more Good, or that it is for their Happiness to have no more Happiness here and hereafter. If we take good notice notice of the Apostles discourse in Rom. 8. it will be apparent that his words imply no such Thing. All Gods Creatures, And all that God does in disposing of Them is for the Good of the saint. But it will not thence follow that all Gods Forbearing to do is also for his Good, or that it is best for Him that God does no more for Him.

Therefore the following Things I humbly conceive to be the Truth concerning the sins & Temptations of the saints being for their Good.

1. That All Things whatsoever are for the Good of the saints, Things negative as well as positive, in that sense, that God intends that some Benefit to Them, shall arise from every Thing. so that something of the Grace and Love of God, will be hereafter to be seen to have been exercised towards Them in every Thing; altho' at the same Time, the sovereignty of God will also be to be seen, with Regard to the measure of the Good or Benefit Aim'd at; & some other Things, if God had seen Cause to order Them, would have produced an higher Benefit. And with Regard to negative disposals, consisting not in Gods doing, but forbearing to do, not in giving, but witholding, some Benefit, in some Respect or other, will ever accrue to the saints, even from These : Tho' sometimes the Benefit will not be equal to the Benefit [^094-note9] witheld, if it had been bestowed. As for Instance, when a saint lives & dies comparatively low in Grace, There is some good Improvement shall be made, even of this, in the eternal state of the saint, whereby he shall receive a real Benefit; Tho' the Benefit shall not be equal to the Benefit of an higher degree of Holiness, if God had bestow'd it.

2. God carries on a design of Love to his People, and to each individual saint, not only in all Things that They are the subjects of while They live, but also in all his works & disposals, & all his Acts ad extra, from Eternity to Eternity.

3. That the sin of the saints in general, is for their good, & for the best in this Respect, That it is a Thing that, through the sovereign Grace of God, & his infinite wisdom, will issue in a high Advancement of their Eternal Happiness, that They have been sinful fallen Creatures, & not from the Benef Beginning perfectly innocent & holy, as the elect Angels; And that They shall obtain some additional Good on occasion of all the sin they have been the subjects of, or have committed, beyond what They would have had if They never had been fallen Creatures.

4. The sin & Corru of the saints in this sense cannot be for their Good, that it should finally be best for Them, that while They lived in this world, their Restoration & Recovery from the Corruption They became subject to by the Fall, was no greater, The Mortification of sin & spiritual vivification of their souls carried on to no greater degree, that They remained so sinfully desti deficient, as to Love to God, Christian Love to men, Humility, Heavenly-mindedness &c. And that They were so barren, and did so few good works; And consequently, that in general, They had They much sin & of the Exercises of it, & not more Holiness & of the Exercises of that & Fruits of that; (for in proportion as one of These is more, the other will be less, as infallibly, as darkness is more or less, in Proportion to the diminution or Increase of Light.) It can't finally be better for the saints, that in general, while They lived, They had so much sin of Heart & Life, rather than more Holi ness of Heart & Life. Because the Reward of all at last [-] will be according to their works, And He that sowed sparingly shall reap sparingly, & He that sowed bountifully shall reap also bountiful ly; & He that builds wood Hay & stubble shall finally suffer Loss, & have a less reward, than if he had built Gold, silver & precious stones, Tho' He himself shall be saved. But notwithstanding This,

5. In The sins & Falls of the saints may be for their Good, & for the better, in This Respect, That the Issue may be better than if the Temptation had not happen'd, & so the occasion not given, either for the sin of yielding to the Temptation, or the virtue of overcoming it ; And yet not in that Respect (with Regard to their sins or Falls in general) that it should be better for Them in the Issue, that They [^094-note10] have yielded to the Temptations offered, than if They had overcome. For the fewer victories They obtain over Temptation, The fewer their good works, and espe particularly of that Kind of Good works to which a distinguished in Reward is promised in Rev. IId. & IIId. & in many other Parts of scripture. The word of God represents the work of a Christian in this world by a warfare; and 'tis evident by the scripture that He that acquits Himself as the best soldier shall win the greatest Prize. Therefore, when the saints are brought into Backslidings & decays, by being overcome by Temptations, The Issue of their Backslidings may be some Good to Them, They may receive some Benefit by Occasion of it, beyond what they would have received if the Temptation & never happen'd; & yet their Backslidings may be a great Loss to them in that Respect, That They shall have much less Reward than if the Temptations had been overcome, & They notwithstanding had persevered in spiritual vigour & diligence. But yet this dont hinder but that,

6. T It may be so ordered by a sovereign & Alwise God, that the saints Falls & Backslidings, through their being overcome by Temptation may in some particular Instances, may prove best for Them; not only that the Issue may be greater Good to them than they would have received if the Temptation had not Happen'd, but greater, than in that Instance, than if the Temptation had been overcome. It may be so ordered that their being overcome by that Temptation, shall be an occasion of their having greater strength, & in the whole, obtaining more and greater victories, than if they had not fallen in that Instance : But it cannit be so that in the general, it should prove better for Them that They are foil'd so much, & overcome so little, in the Course of their Lives, & that Th finally their decay is so great, or their Progress so small. From these Things it appears,

7. That the saying of the Apostle All Things work together for Good to that love God, Tho' it be fulfill'd in some Respect to all saints, & at all Times, & all Circumstances, yet is fulfilled more especially & eminently to the saints continuing in the Exercise of Love to God, not faili falling from the Exercises, or failing of the Fruits of [-] divine Love in Times of Trial : Then Temptations, Enemies & sufferings will be every best for them, working that which is most for their Good every way ; And They shall be more than Conquerors over Tribulation, distress, Persecution, Famine, Nakedness, Peril & sword Rom. 8. 35-37.

8. As God is carrying on a design of Love to each individual saint, in all his works & disposals whatsoever, as was observed before, so the particular design of Love to them that he is carrying on, is to fit [^094-note11] them for, & bring 'em to their appointed Place in the Heavenly Temple, or to that individual, precise Happiness & Glory in Heaven that his eternal Love designed for Them, & no other; (for Gods design of Love, or of Happiness to Them, is it only just what it is, & is not different from it self;) And to fulfil this particular design of Love, every Thing that does, or in any respect disposes, whether it be positive, privative or negative contributes. because doubtless every thing that God does, or in any Respect orders, tends to fulfil his Aims & designs. Therefore undoubtedly

9. All the while the saint lives in the world, He is fitting for his appointed mansion in Glory, & hewing for his Place in the heavenly Building : And fo All his Temptations, Tho' they may occasion, for the present, great spiritual wounds, yet at last, They shall be an occasion of th his being more fitted for his Place in Glory. And therefore we may determine, that however the true saint may die, in some Respects, under decays, under the decay of Comfort, & of the Exercise of some religious Affections, yet every saint dies at the Time when his Habitual Fitness for his Place in the heavenly Temple is most com pleat. because otherwise, all things that happen to Him while He lives, would not work together to fit Him for that Place.

10 God brings his saints at the End of their Lives, to his greatest Fitness for their Place in Heaven, not by diminishing Grace in their Hearts, but by increasing it, & carrying on the work of Grace in their souls. otherwise that cannot be true, that where God has begun a good he will perform or it, or carry it on to the day of Christ. for if they die with a less degree of Grace than they had before, then it ceases to be carried on before the day of Christ comes. If Grace is finally diminished, then satan so far finally obtains the victory, He finally prevails to diminish the fire in the smoking Flax. and then is that promise verified, that God will not Quench the smoking Flax, till He bring forth Judgment unto victory? so that it must needs be, that altho' [-] saints may die under decays in some Respects, yet They never die under a real decay of the work of Grace in General. If They fall, They shall rise again before They die, & rise higher than before; if not in Joys, & some other Affections, yet in greater degrees of spiritual Knowledge, self-emptiness, trust in God & solidity & Ripeness of Grace.

If these Things that have been observed are true, then we may infer from Them These Corollaries.

1st. That notwithstanding the Truth of that saying of the [^094-note12] Apostle Rom. VIII. 28. The saints have Cause to lament their Leanness & Barrenness, & that They are guilty of so much sin; not only, as it is to the dishonour of God, but also as that which is like to their own eternal Loss & damage.

2dly. That nothing can be infer'd from the foremention'd Promise, tending to set aside, or make void the Influence of Motives to earnest Endeavours to avoid all sin, to increase in Holiness, & abound in Good works, from an view to aim at an high & eminent degree of Glory and Happiness in the eternal world.

3dly. That Tho' it is to the eternal damage of the saints, ordinarily, when They yield to, & are overcome by Temptations, yet satan & other Enemies of the saints, by whom their Temptations come, are alwaies wholly disappointed in their Temptations, & baffled in their design to hurt the saints, Inasmuch as The Temptation, & the sin that comes by it, is for the saints Good, and They receive no a greater Benefit, in the Issue, than if the Temptation had not been, & yet less than if the Temptation had been overcome.

As to Mr Boston's view of the Covenant of Grace, I have had some Opportunity with and I confess I did not understand his scheme deliver'd in that Book. I have read his fourfold state of man, & liked exceeding well. I think He therein shews Himself to be a truly great divine.[^094-note13]

Hoping that you will accept my Letter with Candour, & remember me in your Prayers, I subscribe my self, your affectionate & obliged Brother

& servt,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^094-note1]: Robert Abercrombie, pastor of Pelham, Mass., who was raised and educated in Edinburgh.
