## A79. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, September 14, 1747 079.JE-J.Bellamy 9-14-47

Jonathan EdwardsA079. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 9/14/47. CHS. Address on back "To the Rev. Mr. Joseph Bellamy at Bethlehem."

Northampton, Septem 14. 1747

dear Brother,

Having a direct opportunity, I could not let it pass without writing a Line. we are through mercy pretty well. My wife kindly salutes you & your spouse. Mr Brainerd is now at my House, and has been here a long Time, in a very low state, growing weaker & weaker; He is like to be here till he dies his Feet & Legs a few days ago began to swell, and that symptom is increasing. He gives his hearty Love to you; and desires you to write back by the Bearer of this, who says He shall return the week after next: when He went from Kaunaumeek, He left some of his Things Books & other Things at Mr. seargeants, to be sent to your House, & committed to your Care; He desires you to write and inform whether They are there, and what Things They are. what if you should come & seem Him before He dies? I should be very glad to see you Here. His Mr. John Brainerd came from the Jerseys hither the week before last, & is now here, & presents his Hearty & humble Regards to you. he is this week has Thoughts of returning this week to the Jerseys & returning hither again the next. If you don't come hither This Fall (as I would not have you put by going to the Eastward for it) please to write a little more fully about the Business I committed you. my kind Love to your spouse. I am

your affectionate Friend & Brother

Jonathan Edwards

## A80. Letter to William McCulloch, September 23, 1747 080.JE-W.McCulloch 9-23-47

Jonathan EdwardsA080. JE to William McCulloch, 9/23/47. ANTS, f. 1747, #4-5.

Northampton

Rev. & dear Sir,

I thank you for your Letter of March. 12. 1747. which I suppose lay a long while at Mr. Prince's in Boston, before I received it, through Mr. Prince's Forgetfulness. It seems He had forgotten that He had any such Letter; and when I sent a messenger to his House on Purpose to enquire whether I had any Letters lodged there for me from Scotland, He told him No; when I suppose this Letter had been long in his House; and I should probably never have had it at last, had not one of my daughters occasion to go to Boston, who made a visit at the House, & made more full Enquiry.

I am sorry to hear of your Affliction through your Indisposition that you speak of, & desire to be thankful to the God of all mercy, for his Goodness in restoring you again to Health.

I have, in my Letter to Mr. McLaurin, given a particular account of what I know concerning the Propagation of the Concert for united Prayer, in America; which you will doubtless have Opportunity to see. The Propagation of it is but slow, but yet so many do fall in with it; and there is that Prospect of its being further spread, that it is a great Encouragement to me. I earnestly wish & Hope that They that have begun extraordinary Prayer for the outpouring of the spirit of God, & the coming of Christs Kingdom, will not fail, or grow dull & listless in such an Affair, But rather that They will increase more & more in their Fervency. in I have taken a great deal of Pains to promote this Concert here in America, and shall not cease to do if God spares my Life, as I have Opportunity, in all ways that I can devise. I have written largely on the subject, insisting on Perswasives, & answering Objections; & what I have written is gone to the Press : The undertaker for the Publication encourages me there that it shall speedily be printed: I have sent to Mr. McLaurin a particular account of it.[^096-note1]

you desire to hear how it was with the People of New England, when we were threatend with an Invasion by the French Fleet the last summer. As to the particular Circumstances of that wonderful deliverance, the fullest & best Account I have ever seen of it, is in Mr. Prince's Thanksgiving sermon on that Occasion; which in all Probability you have seen long before this Time. Nor need you be informed by me of the repeated mercy of God to us, in confounding our Enemies in their renewed Attempt this year, by delivering up their Fleet, in its way hither, into the Hands [^096-note2] of the English[^096-note3]. In all Probability that Fleet was intended for the Execution of a very extensive design, against the English Colonies, together with in Conjunction with the French Forces in Canada. For there was an Army lay waiting at Nova-Scotia, which on the News of the taking of their Fleet, immediately left the Countrey & returned to Canada. And another Army came of about 3000, came from Canada, over the Lake Champlain, towards New-England and New-York. and They, or a Part of them, attacked the Fort at Saratoga, in New-York Government, and killed or took about 50 men that were drawn out of the Fort;[^096-note4] but desisted any further Attempts about the Time we may suppose They received the News of the defeat of their Fleet. And very soon after They received this News in Canada, The French there released most of our Captives; And sent one ship loaden with Them, to the number of 170, to Boston, & another ship with about 60, if I remember right, to Louisburgh. The Reasons that induced them so to do are not known, & can only be guessed at by us : But by their doing it in very soon after they received the News of the Loss of their Fleet, it looks as tho' that had great Influence in the Affair. New-England has had many other surprizing deliverances from the French & Indians; some of which I have given a particular Account of, in my letter to Mr. McLaurin; which it would be needless for me to repeat, seeing you have such frequent Opportunities with Him. ----These deliverances are very wonderful and affecting ; our Enemies own that the Heavens are on our side, & fight for us ; But there are no such Effects of these mercies upon us that are the subjects of 'em, as God requires, and most justly expects. The mercies are acknowledged in words, but we are not led to Repentance by them. -There appears no such Thing as any Reformation or Revival of Religion in the Land. Gods so wonderfully Protecting & delivering a People, whose Provocations have been so great, and who do so continue in Apostacy & Provocation, is very marvellous ; And I can think of no Account that can be given of it so probable as this, That God has a design of mercy to the rising Generation, And that there are a great many of the Elect among our Children, born & ensue & unborn , And that for these Elects sake, God will not suffer us to be destroyed , having a design to bring forth a seed of the Posterity of this People, to inherit & dwell in this Land, that shall be A Gene an holy seed, & a Generation of his servants. & so that those words [-] are applicable to us, Isai. 65. 8, 9. Thus saith the Lord, as the new wine [^096-note5] is found in the Cluster, and one saith destroy it not, for a Blessing is in it; so will I do for my servants sakes, that I may not destroy Them all. And I will bring forth a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah an Inheritor of my mountains ; And mine Elect shall Inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there. I am full of Apprehensions that God has no design of mercy to those that were left unconverted of the Generation that were on the stage, in the Time of the late, extraordinary religious Commotion & striving of God's spirit, unless it be perhaps a small Gleaning from among But it may be when their little ones, the Generation that was then in their Childhood, are brought fully on the stage of action, God will abundantly pour out his spirit, & revive and carry on his work here & elsewhere in the Christian world.

I thank you for taking the Pains of writing to me your Thoughts of the 42 months of the Treading down of the holy City, which are new and entertaining. The Chief Objection against what you propose, that I can think of, that the 42 months of the treading down the holy City, seems to be the same Period with the 1260 days of the witnesses prophesying in sackcloth, mentioned in the very next verse in Connection with this; And That the same with the 1260 days of the womans being in the wilderness, Rev. XII. 6. and that the same with the Time, Times & an half of the womans being in the wilderness, v. 14. & that the same with the Time, Times & an half of the Reign of the little Horn, dan. VII. 25 & with the 42 months of the Reign of the Beast Rev. XIII. 5. And that this is evidently signifies the duration of the Reign of Antichrist, which is a Thing entirely diverse from the Times of the City of Jerusalem's being under the dominion of Pagans, Saracens, Persians & Turks in as you represent. However 'tis possible that what you mention may be one way wherein that Prophecy. Rev. XI. 2. may be fulfilled. For God's word is oftentimes fulfilled various ways, as one way wherein the Prophetical Representation of the Beast with seven Heads is fulfilled, is in the seven successive Forms of Government that Idolatrous Rome is under ; and Another way that it was fulfil'd was by Rome being built on seven Hills. One way wherein the Prophecy of the 70 years Captivity of the Jews was fulfilled, was in its being 70 years from Jehoiakims Captivity, to Cyrus's decree: And another way, that it was fulfil'd was in its being 70 years from Zedekiahs Captivity to the Dec to darius's decree Ezra VI: and another way, that it was fulfil'd was, in its being 70 years from the last carrying away of all Jer. LII. 30, to the finishing & dedication of the Temple. -But I expect no certainty as to these Things, or any of the various Conjectures concerning the Time of the calling of the Jews, and fall of the [^096-note6] Kingdom of the Beast, 'till Time & Fulfilment shall decide the matter. However, I cannot think otherwise, than that we have a great deal of Reason to suppose that that glorious work of Gods spirit, which before it is finished, shall accomplish these Things, is not very far off. And there is very much in the word of God, and in the present Aspects of divine Providence, to encourage an us greatly in our begun Concert for extraordinary united Prayer for the coming of Christs Kingdom. Let us therefore go on with what we have begun in that Respect, & continue instant in Prayer with all Perseverance, & increase more & more in Faith & Fervency, & not keep silence, nor give God any Rest, till He establish, & make Jerusalem a Praise in the Earth. And remember in your Prayers dear sir,

yours in great Esteem & Affection,

Jonathan Edwards.

The Rev. Mr. William McCulloch.

[^096-note1]: *An Humble Attempt.*

[^096-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^096-note3]: In June, 1746, a French fleet of 66 ships sailed across the Atlantic, but on reaching the Azores an epidemic broke out and then, in September, a hurricane battered the fleet off Nova Scotia. Admiral D'Anville died, and in October the fleet went back to France without having fired a shot.

[^096-note4]: The French and Indian army actually totalled between five and six hundred. This attack occurred on June 30, 1747; the fort was relieved shortly thereafter.

[^096-note5]: **marginal.** [3]

[^096-note6]: **marginal.** [4]

## A81. Letter to Stephen Williams, October 9, 1747 081.JE-S.Williams 10-9-47

Jonathan EdwardsA081. JE to Stephen Williams, 10/9/47. Drew University, Rose Library.

Northampton, October 9th, 1747.

It has pleased God to remove by death that eminent servant of His, the Rev. Mr. David Brainerd, about 6 'Clock this morning. You may remember that you desired me, if I had opportunity, to give you notice of the Time of his Funeral. It is, God willing, to be the next Monday : The Lecture before the Funeral to begin at one o'Clock. ----when Mr Brainerd in his Life-Time was speaking of the Circumstances of his own Funeral, and desiring that the neighbouring ministers of his Acquaintance might be sent for, I mention'd what you had said, manifesting a disposition to attend his Funeral, if it might be conveniently. He seem'd to in a considerable degree to take a thankful notice of it ; and desired me to take some Pains to find an opportunity to give you notice. I mention these things to you Rev. sir, leaving it with you to conduct your self according to your own discretion. But if you can be present, I should be very glad,

who am, your Humble servt,

Jonathan Edwards.

The Rev. Mr Ste. Williams

## A82. Letter to John Brainerd, December 14, 1747 082.JE-JBrainerd 12-14-47

Jonathan EdwardsA082. JE to John Brainerd, 12/14/47. ANTS, f. 1747, #2. Addressed on bottom half of last page "To / Mr. John Brainerd / at Cranberry / In New-Jersey."

Northampton decem. 14. 1747.

Dear sir,

I have read through your deceased Brothers papers, containing his Life, and have determined to publish an Abstract of Them. I have with this sent to you a Letter to Gov. Belcher, desiring his Leave to dedicate the Book to him; which I desire you to wait on his Excellency with. If He should consent to have the Book dedicated to him, it might not only tend to make the it the more taken notice of, & so the more useful, But also may do honour to your Brothers memory, whom many in his Life-time strove to lay under disgrace. I have sent my Letter to the Governour open, that you may see it, but desire you handsomly to seal, & deliver it.

In writing your Brothers Life, it will be unavoidable but that mention must be made of your Brothers Expulsion from the College : And therefore I think it is necessary that a just and particular Account be given of that matter, so that I should be glad that when you come hither in the spring, you would come furnished to give me a just, exact & certain Account of that matter Affair, that the Rector may have no Cause, nor find any Room to complain of the least misrepresentation in any Respect. I should be glad also to know particularly what offer your Brother made to the Rector from Time to Time of satisfaction, in order to his being Restored to College. There is mention made in his private Journals of his making attempts to be reconciled several Times and particularly of a Confession He offered (or something of that Nature) to the Justice, at Hartford, the May after his Expulsion, at the Time of the Election but there is no Account what it was. There is included in his diary, a Copy of the Confession He offered at last, at the Time of that Commencement that his Class took their degrees, but no other. Perhaps Mr. Burr may be able to give a Particular Information of some of These Matters, and Mr. Mills.[^098-note1] I should be glad that when you are on your Journey hither you would inquire of Him, or any other that you think would be likely to inform. I think your Brother told me that the Rector acknowledged that the Confession He offered at last was Christian satisfaction. However I should be glad to be more fully informed of that matter. [^098-note2]

I want also to be more fully informed of some Things in your Brothers Life : something more particular concerning his Parentage, his Mother in particular, who she was, & whence descended : & if there was any Thing remarkable in his Childhood, any remarkable dangers, or deliverances, or Restoration, or any other Thing worthy to be noted in writing his Life : A particular Account of his Mission to the Indians ; How the society in Scotland came first to appoint a number of Commissioners in New-York & the Jerseys ; How the Commissioners came to hear of, & improve Mr Brainerd ; How They came first to send Him to Kaunaumeek ; How he came afterwards to be called thence & sent to the Forks of delaware. And perhaps Mr. Tennent[^098-note3] & some others that were well acquainted with Him, may be able to inform of some remarkable Things of Him, of his Character, Behaviour, or speeches that may be worthy to be inserted in his Life. And I want to be more particularly informed of your Brothers Illness last winter at Mr. dickinsons,[^098-note4] for there his Journal is very short. I want also to [be] informed whether your Brothers publick Journal[^098-note5] be continued till He left the Indians, or whether any Thing further was published by Him, or prepared for the Press, beyond what was printed at Philadelphia. If there was, I should be glad to see it, that I mayn't publish the same Thing over again out of his diary. I should be glad that you would bring me an Account of these Things when you come, in the spring. And also bring any other of your Brothers Papers that may Contain what may be worthy to be inserted. some of his Letters to his Friends that I have seen are remarkable, and well worth publishing, & I doubt not but there were among others that were, that I have not yet seen : I desire that you would bring some of Them, such as you think are most worthy to be taken notice of, to your self or others; and particularly I desire you would as you come along, in my name request of Esther Sherman,[^098-note6] that she would send me some of his Letters to Her . Your Brother in his diary often mentions her writing on divine subjects, and I perceive He spent abundance of Time in writing ; I don't know [^098-note7] how to think that all that He meant was writing sermons: I would be glad to see some of these his Composures on divine subjects.

on further considering your Brothers diary, since I wrote the preceding Part of this Letter, I find that I want to be informed of some further Particulars, in order to writing his Life, which probably Mr. Pemberton or Mr. Burr can give Information in.[^098-note8] There is mention made of a meeting of ministers that Examined Him at New-York, in Novem. 1742. I want to know what meet ing of ministers that was; whether a meeting of the Presbytery, or of the Commissioners.

Why the commissioners gave Him so long a space, after He was examined before at New-York Concerning his Qualifications for the mission, before They acturally sent Him on the Business, as from Novem. to the next April. whether it was because they looked on the winter season unfit to engage in such Business.

It seems by your Brothers diary, that when your Brother He was examined at the Time foremention'd, The design was that He should be sent to the Indians in Pennsylvania, and he [appeared][^098-note9] to have that Expectation all winter, of going to those Indians; I would be informed, how the Correspondents came to Change their minds, & when the spring came send Him to Kaunaumeek.

What your Brothers special Business to N. York & the Jerseys was when, the next spring, He went thither from E. Hampton, before He went to Kaunaumeek. & what meeting of ministers that was, that He, at that Time, met at Woodbridge; whether a meeting of the Presbytery, or of the Correspondents; & what Instructions He there received.

He took three Journeys from Kaunaumeek, in to N. York & the Jerseys; one in May 1743. Another in september following; when he went no further than N. York; another at the Latter End of March, the next year. I want to Know what was the special Occasion of these Journeys.

who his Interpreter was at Kaunaumeek, an Englishman or Indian.

what Encouragemt the Commissioners saw in the state of the delaware Indians, that should Incline them to send a missionnary to Them, rather than any other Indians. [^098-note10]

I suppose my funeral sermon on your Brother is by this time printed : Mr. Bromfield writes me word, in a Letter dated decem. 1. that it was then in the Press, & would be finished in about 10 days from that Time; & that Maj. Henchman had agreed to print it without any subscription, & to send me my Part of them; & also that He, with some other Gentlemen, had determined to send 50 of Them as a Present to you. ---I am sir,

your affectionate Friend

Jonath. Edwards

P.S. If I had receiv'd one of my sermons on your Brothers Funeral, I would Now send one to Gov. Belcher. If He consents that I should dedicate his Life to him, it may not be amiss, perhaps, for you to make a Present of one of yours to Him, when you receive Them.

Mr. John Brainerd

[^098-note1]: Isaac Burr, a Hartford physician, and Rev. Jedidiah Mills, pastor of Huntington, Conn.

[^098-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^098-note3]: Gilbert Tennent.

[^098-note4]: Jonathan Dickinson.

[^098-note5]: *Mirabilia Dei inter Indicos* (Philadelphia, 1746).

[^098-note6]: Esther Sherman was mentioned in the Diary as a correspondent with whom Brainerd felt close; she later married Brainerd's college friend Job Prudden.

[^098-note7]: **marginal.** [3]

[^098-note8]: Ebenezer Pemberton, pastor of the First Prebyterian Church in New York City, and Aaron Burr, pastor of Newark.

[^098-note9]: MS damage.

[^098-note10]: **marginal.** [4]

## A83. Letter to Ebenezer Parkman, March 4, 1748 083.JE-E.Parkman 3-4-48

Jonathan EdwardsA083. JE to Ebenezer Parkman, 3/4/48. National Library of Scotland, Edinburgh, MS #948. Partial address on back: "To the [Rev.] / Mr Ebenezer [Parkman] / of Westb[oro] / Pr the Rev. [Mr. John] / Brainerd." Shorn along left side; conjectures for lacunae provided in brackets.

[Dear] Brother

[It has] pleased a holy God of late sorely to [afflict our] Family, by taking away by death [our dau]ghter Jerusha. The Rev. Mr John [who is th]e Bearer of this (who lately was [appointed m]issionary to succeed his deceased Brother) [can tell y]ou of the Circumstances. This is [to ask your] prayers for us under our Great [affliction,] that it may be sanctified to us, & [that God w]ould fill up the melancholy vacancy [made] by death in this Family, with his [gracious] & Comfortable Presence my [surviv]ing Children join with me in [------] to you Madam & your Family: [begg]ing your sympathy & Prayers & [that] you would remember our youngest[^099-note1] [who i]s under threatning Circumstances [I am] dear sir, by your afflicted Brother

Jonath. Edwards

March 4. 1747/8.

[^099-note1]: Elizabeth Edwards, b. May 6, 1747.

## A84. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, April 4, 1748 084.JE-J.Bellamy 4-4-48

Jonathan EdwardsA084. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 4/4/48. BRBL, f. 1274.

Northampton April 4. 1748

Rev. & dear Brother.

I here send a Couple of Bags to put our wool into, to be sent to Hartford to Mr. Potwines, desiring you to take Care of that matter as you have manifested very kindly manifested your self willing to do: I trust entirely in your Friendship & Faithfulness in that matter.

I you have probably before now heard of sore Affliction in the death of our daughter Jerusha, who died after 5 days Illness, Feb. 14. I have great satisfaction concerning her state, from what I know of her in Life, & what appeared in her at death: Mr. d. Brainerd, who had much intimate Acquaintance with her, she having Constantly been with him as his Nurse, 19 weeks before his death, express'd great satisfaction concerning the state of her soul, & that He look'd on her not only as a saint, but as a very Eminent saint.

--I desire your Prayers for us that God would make up our great Loss in spiritual Blessings. Please to accept of one of my Books on Prayer for the Revival of Religion, which I here send you -& send me word whether the Proposal for United Prayer be complied with in your Parts.

I wrote you some Time since informing that I was about to publish Mr. Brainerds Life from his private writings, desiring you to send me any Letters of his worthy to be inserted; but have had no Answer. Please to I would now renew that Request, & also that you would send me word whether you will allow me to mention your name in the printed Proposals for subscription, as one that will take in subscriptions in your Parts. This with respectful salutations to Mrs Bellamy, is from dear sir,

your affectionate Friend & Brother, Jth Edwards.

## A85. Letter to Sarah Pierpont Edwards, June 22, 1748 085.JE-SPE 6-22-48

Jonathan EdwardsA085. JE to Sarah Edwards, 6/22/48. BRBL, f. 1285. Sheared along left margin.

[M]y dear Companion.

I wrote you a few Lines the last sabbath [da]y by Ensn dwight, which I hope you [w]ill receive. --- By this I would inform [y]ou that Betty seems really to be on the [m]ending Hand; a I cant but think she [is] truly better, both as to her Health & [he]r sores, since she has been at mrs Phelps's [T]he first two or three days, before she [w]as well acquainted, she was very un- [qu]iet; but now more quiet than she [us]ed to be at Home. --- This is Lecture [da]y morning, and your two eldest daughters went to Bed last night, both [si]ck; and Rose beat out, & having the [he]ad-ach. we got Hannah Root to [h]elp Them yesterday in the Afternoon, [&] expect her again to day. How Sarah [&] Esther do to day I can't tell, for they [ar]e not up. we have been without [yo]u almost as long as we know how to [b]e; but yet are willing you should obey [th]e Calls of Providence without with [re]gard to Col. Stoddard.

If you have money to spare, & it [is]n't too late, I should be glad if [yo]u would buy us some Cheese in Boston, & [put it][^101-note1] with other things [^101-note2] if it can be safely. ---

Give my humble service to mr. Bromfield & madam & proper salutations to other Friends.

I am your most affectionate Companion

Jonathan Edwards

Northampton June 22

1748.

[^101-note1]: Conjecture for where MS is torn away.

[^101-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

## A86. Letter to John Erskine, August 31, 1748 086.JE-J.Erskine 8-31-48

Jonathan EdwardsA086. JE to John Erskine, 8/31/48. ANTS, f. 1748, #6-7.

Northampton Aug. 31. 1748.

Rev & dear Sir,

I this summer received your Kind Letter of Feb. 9. 1748. together with your most Acceptable Present of Taylor on Original Sin, and his Key to the Apostolic Writings, with his Paraphrase on the Epistle to the Romans; together with your sermons & Answer to dr. Campbel.[^102-note1] I had your sermons before, sent either by you, or Mr. McLaurin. I am exceeding glad of Those two Books of Taylor's. I had before borrowed and read Taylor on Original sin ; But am very glad to have one of my own: If you had not sent it, I intended to have sought opportunity to buy it. The other Book his Paraphrase &c. I had not heard of; If I had, I should not have been easy till I had seen it, and been possessed of it. These Books, If I should live may probably be of great use to me. -such Kindness from you was unexpected : I hoped to receive a Letter from you, which alone I should have received as a special Favour.

I have for the present, been diverted from the design I hinted to you, of publishing something against some of the Arminian Tenets, that by something else that divine Providence unexpectedly laid in my way, and seem'd to render unavoidable, viz. publishing Mr. Brainerd's Life: of which the inclosed Paper of Proposals gives some Account.

It might be of particular Advantage to me here in this remote Part of the world, to be better informed what Books there are that are published on the other side the Atlantick, and especially if there be any Thing that Comes out that is very remarkable. I have seen many notable Things that have been written in this Century against the Truth, But nothing very notable on our side of the Controversies of the present day, at least of the Arminian Controversy : You would much oblige me, if you would inform me what are the best Books that have lately written in defence of Calvinism.

I have herewith sent the two Books of Mr. Stoddards you desired. The Lesser of the two was my own; and tho' I have no other, yet you have laid me under such obligations, that I am glad I have it to send to you. the other I procured of one of my Neighbours.[^102-note2]

I have lately heard some Things that have excited Hope in me that God was about to cause there to be a Turn in England, with Regard to the state of Religion there for the better; particularly [-] what we have heard one that One Mr. West, a Clerk of the Privy Council, has written in defence of Christianity, tho' once a notorious deist; & also what Mr. Littelton, a member of the House of Commons has written[^102-note3]. I should be glad if you would inform me more particularly in your next, concerning this Affair, and what the present state of Infidelity in Engl great Britain is.

It has pleased God, since I wrote my last to you, sorely to afflict this Family, by taking away by death, the last February, my second daughter, in the 18 year of her Age, a very pleasant [^102-note4] & useful member of this Family, & that was generally esteem'd the Flower of the Family. Herein we have a great Loss; But the Remembrance of the remarkable appearances of Piety in her, from her Childhood, in her Life, and also at her death, are very comfortable to us, & give us great Reason to mingle Thanksgiving with our mourning. I desire your Prayers, dear sir, that God would make up our great Loss to us in Himself.

Please to accept of one of my sermons on Mr. Brainerds death, & also my sermon on Mr. Buels Instalment[^102-note5]. --I desire that for the future your Letters to me may be directed to be left with Mr. Edward Bromfield Mercht in Boston, & not with Mr. B Prince, who is so forgetful, that his Care is not to be depended on. ---My wife joins with me in respectful & affectionate Salutations to you, & Mrs Erskine. -desiring that we may meet often at the Throne of Grace in supplications for each other, I am dear Brother,

your obliged Friend,

Fellow-Labourer & humble servt

Jonath. Edwards

P. S. I desired Mr. Prince to send to you one of my Books on the subject of the Concert for Prayer, for a general Revival of Religion, the last year; and He engaged to do it; but I perceive he forgot it, & it was long neglected. But I have since taken some further Care to have the Book Conveyed; so that I hope that 'ere this Time you have received it.

In the Conclusion of your Letter of Feb. 9. you mention a design of writing to me again by a ship that was to sail the next month for Boston. --That Letter I have not received. The Rev Mr John Erskine

[^102-note1]: John Taylor, *The Scripture-Doctrine of Original Sin Proposed to Free and Candid Examination* (London, 1740; 3d ed., Belfast, 1746), and *A Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans. To Which Is Prefix'd A Key to the Apostolic Writings* (London, 1745; Dublin, 1746); John Erskine, *The People of God Considered as All Righteous: in three Sermons preach'd at Glasgow, April 1745* (Edinburgh, 1745).

[^102-note2]: The books are identified in JE's duplicate letter to Erskine, Oct. 14, 1748 (No. 90), below, as Solomon Stoddard, *Benefit of the Gospel to the Wounded in Spirit* (Boston, 1713), and *A Treatise concerning the Nature of Saving Conversion* (Boston, 1719).

[^102-note3]: **[3].** Gilbert West, *Observations on the History and Evidence of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ* (London, 1747), and *A Defence of the Christian Revelation* (London, 1748); and George Lyttelton, *Observations on the Conversion and Apostleship of St. Paul* (London, 1747).

[^102-note4]: **marginal.** [2]

[^102-note5]: *True Saints, When Absent from the Body, are Present with the Lord* (Boston, 1747), and *The Church's Marriage to her Sons, and to Her God* (Boston, 1746).

## A87. Letter to Eleazar Wheelock, September 14, 1748 087.JE-E.Wheelock 9-14-48

Jonathan EdwardsA087. JE to Eleazar Wheelock, 9/14/48. BRBL, f. 1320. Other copies of this letter (in another hand though corrected by JE), which was widely circulated to other clergy to subscribe to the publication of *Life of Brainerd*, can be found in the Sermon on Acts 24:25 (Nov. 1749), BRBL f. .

New-Haven septem. 14. 1748.

Rev. & dear Sir,

Having understood that you was willing to take in subscriptions for the printing Mr. Brainerds Life, I have inserted your name in the Printed Proposals; some of which I have here inclosed to you, desiring you to take some Pains to promote subscriptions in your Parts. I can't but think that an Account of the Life of this extraordinary Persons, as taken from his own private writings, will not only have a very great Tendency to promote the Interest of true Religion in general; but in a peculiar manner, and vastly more than any Thing that has ever yet been published, to open the Eyes of the Common People with regard [to][^103-note1] that wild sort of Religion that has so much prevailed in your Parts of the Countrey.

I think the Book at the Price proposed will be very cheap, considering how Books are now sold; which I have lately had special occasion to know. And I believe there will be so many subscribers that there will be no Books left for non-subscribers.

I desire that the proper Titles of subscribers, together with their Place of Abode may be added to their Names. & that you would Collect the subscriptions & forward them to Boston as soon as may be: Herein I am perswaded you will much serve the Interest of Religion as well as oblige your

Friend and brother Jonathan Edwards.

[^103-note1]: JE's omission.

## A88. Letter to Moses Lyman[?], September 30, 1748 088.JE-M.Lyman 9-30-48

Jonathan EdwardsA088. JE to Moses Lyman[?], 9/30/48. MS Collection of John H. Edwards, Woodbridge, Conn. Possibily sent as an enclosure for a letter, the MS seems to have been prepared by JE for a council or an association meeting. The only evidence that it was sent to Moses Lyman, however, is that the MS was given together with the letter to Lyman of May 10, 1742, as part of the Pinneo deposit to Yale (eventually de-accessed).

Northampton septem 30. 1748

Question . Whether supposing a society or Congregation of People, who have been Educated in the doctrines & way of Worshipped, generally profess'd by the People of New England, are subject to the following Calamitous Circumstances; viz That They are under a minister who is wholly unqualified, & notoriously unfit for that sacred office, with regard both to natural & moral Qualifications; which has been made very evident by many uncontestable Facts, that have been properly & abundantly proved, in a publick proceeding: But still they are held under this minister, are not allowed to settle another, or statedly to enjoy any other publick means for the good of the souls of them & their Children; and are obliged, tho' small, & not of great Ability, to maintain this minister; and so to expend their money, wholly to no Purpose, but only, in Effect, to maintain a Publick nuisance and their own Calamity; And this People have long been grievously distressed by being held under this minister while they have been waiting & hoping for Redress in the Use of all possible means; & all in vain; and there is no Prospect of their ever obtaining any Help, unless by turning to the Church of England: whether or no it be al lawful or adviseable for such a People publick ly, to renounce a stated union with the Churches of the Countrey, & join themselves to the Church of England;

I Answer in the Negative, for the following Reasons.

There are many Ceremonies practised & established in the Church of England which are not lawful, and cannot be complied with, as established by the Laws & Canons of that Church, with a a well-informed and good Conscience; they being properly add human additions to the ordinances of God; and Those that worship of God in the use of Them, their Fear, or worship toward God is taught by the Precept of Men, which is unlawful, & provoking to [^104-note1] God, as is evident by Isai. 29 13. A People ought not to do any evil or unlawful thing that Good may Come, or to deliver themselves from Evil

If such a People subject themselves to the Church of England, They cannot have the Choice of their own minister; but but must be subject to such an one as shall be sent them. And as the state of the Church of England now is, They can't reasonably have the least Expectation of any other than minister, than one that is an Arminian, or worse than an Arminian; one Who in his Teaching shall wholly Neglect many of those doctrines that are most essential to be known in order to Salvation; & that shall teach and inculcate those doctrines that shall tend to corrupt & infect the Minds of their hearers with such principles as are directly contrary to the scheme of the Gospel, and tend especially to hinder their souls salvation. Which will be an infinitely terrible Calamity to themselves & their Children. And if They, under these Circumstances by their won Act, put Themselves under the Church they will be guilty of bringing this Calamity on Themselves and their Posterity, so far as in Them lies, to all Generations. They will not be meerly passive in it, but it will be their own doings : which They can never justify : They will be guilty of the Blood of their own souls, & the souls of their Children, & perhaps of their Posterity to the latest Generation; who, if they should eternally perish by this Means, They must expect to have all rising up in Judgment against them accusing them as the murderers of their souls.

And If such a People shall say their Calamity is as great now as They are, & it is like to continue; they are not taught the necessary doctrines of the Gospel now; [^104-note2] & it can't be any worse in the Church of England.

I answer If it be so indeed their Misery Now is not their own Act; they are purely passive in it; and are, or ought to be praying & waiting for deliverance from it. And tho' now there appears No Prospect of their deliverance; yet there aren are many ways that They may be delivered in divine Providence; which often very great & unexpected Changes in a short time. But by taking the foremention'd Course, They take the mattter a out of the Hands of Providence, and take it into their own Hands, and take a Course forever to preclude all deliverance, & & to prevent their receiving any Benefit that might be received by Providential Events & to fasten their Calamity forever on Themselves & their Posterity. withou. But if They had no hope that God in his Providence would ever appear for their help, & had Reason to think he would ever appear for their help, & had Reason to think He would not; yet that would not justify their making so great misery to themselves & Posterity, as was before mention'd, their own doings:

They may are guilty of no sin in being purely Passive in their mi Calamity, when they cannot help it; But it is a great sin, for men, by their own act, to make themselves miserable. As for Instance, if a man were in a miserable Captivity, under severe Taskmasters; & esteemed his Bondage worse than death, & had no Prospect of deliverance; It would not be Lawful, in such a Case, for a Man to kill Himself to free himself from slavery.

As to any temporal loss such a People may sustain, which by paying their money for nothing, which [^104-note3] They can't avoid any other Way than by turning to the Church of England. The gaining or saving of money ought not to come into Consideration in such an affair as this. The worship of God, the doctrines of the Gospel, & affairs of our Eternal salvation, surely ought not to be put into the scales with so many shillings or Pounds in Bills of the old Tenour, or in silver and Gold: It is a shameful thing even to mention it : It is madness indeed when men will sell their Religion for a little money, to do so to is to sell God & Heaven, & own own souls; & symbolize with Judas, who sold Christ for 30 Pieces of silver.

whereas some may possibly say, the Church of England had a divine Blessing in & after the Times of the Reformation. I answer, while Calvinistical doctrines were generally taught & professed among and the way of salvation thoroughly preach'd amongst which was once the Case; These things were attended with the divine Blessing. But the Case is now altered , these doctrines have long been almost universally exploded in the Church of England. and the divine Blessing has departed with them.

For these Reasons, & many others, I think a People in the foremention'd Circumstances, cannot be in Gods way, nor in the Way of Gods Blessing, to in seeking Redress of their Grievances by joining with the Church of England. But ought still to wait on God in they the way of importunate Prayer; tho' they have already waited long, & see nothing but the midnight darkness. And tis to be hoped no such People will act suddenly & rashly in an affair of such vast Consequence: But will first thoroughly Acquaint themselves with the present state of the Church of England, that they mayn't act Blindfold. and to that End I would recommend them the dissenting Gentlemans answer to Mr. White three letters.[^104-note4] Jonathan Edwards

[^104-note1]: **marginal.** [L. 1v.]

[^104-note2]: **marginal.** [L. 2r.]

[^104-note3]: **marginal.** [L. 2v.]

[^104-note4]: **[1].** [Micaiah Towgood], *The Dissenting Gentleman's Answer to Mr. White's Three Letters* (London, 1746), a response to John White, fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge, whose three Letters (one originally published in 1743, the other two in 1745) were bound together as *Three Letters to a Gentleman Dissenting from the Church of England* (London, 1748).

## A89. Letter to William McCulloch, October 7, 1748 089.JE-W.McCulloch 10-7-48

Jonathan EdwardsA089. JE to William McCulloch, 10/7/48. ANTS, f. 1748, #2-3.

Northampton, Octob. 7. 1748.

Rev & dear sir,

I thank you for your Letter of Feb. 10. 1748. which I received the week before last. I had also long before that received the Letter you speak of, which you wrote the spring before, dated March 12. 1747. which I wrote an Answer to,[^105-note1] & sent it to Mr. Prince of Boston, & committed it to his Care; and am very sorry that you never received it. I am far from being weary of our Cor respondence. I ever look'd on my self as greatly honoured and obliged by you in your beginning this Correspondence; and have found it pleasant & profitable : and particularly your last Letter that I have but now received has been very agreable and entertaining; especially on Account of the good News it contains. I cannot but think that many Things mention'd in your Letter, and the Letters of my other Correspondents in Scotland which came with yours, are great Things, worthy to be greatly taken notice of, and to be an Occasion of much rejoycing & Praise to all that love Zion; viz. The remarkeable Change in one of the Clerks of the privy Councel, Gods stirring up Him and Mr. Littelton to write in defence of Christianity, The good Effect of This among men of Figure and Character ; The Good dispositions of the King, the Prince & Princess of Wales ; The late Awakening of two of the Princesses, Amelia and Caroline, and the hopeful Conversion of one or both of Them; The hopeful real Piety of the A. Bp of Canterbury, and his good disposition towards Calvinism, Experimental Religion & the dissenters; Several of the Clergy of the Church of England their lately appearing to preach the doctrines of Grace ; several of the Magistrates in various Counties in England their Exerting Themselves with uncommon Zeal to put the Laws in Execution against vice; And the eminent Piety of the Prince of Orange, now Stadtholder of the seven united Provinces. These Things (at least some of Them) are great in Themselves, and are of that nature that They have a most promising Aspect on the Interest of Zion, and to be happy Presages and Forerunners of yet better & greater Things that are coming. They look as if the Tide were turning, and glorious Things approaching by the Revolution [^105-note2] of the wheel of Gods providence. I think we and all others that have lately united by explicit Agreement in extraordinary Prayer for a general Revival of Religion and the Coming of Christs Kingdom, may without Presumption be greatly encouraged and Animated in the duty we have engaged in, by the Appearance of such a dawning of Light from such great darkness ; and should be ungrateful if we did not acknowledge Gods great Goodness in These Things, and faithfulness in fulfilling the Promises of his word ; such as those If any two of you shall agree on Earth as touching any Thing you shall ask, it shall be done of my Father which is in Heaven ; & Before They call, I will answer; & while They are yet speaking, I will hear.[^105-note3] I have already communicated these Things to some in belonging to These Town & other Places. some have appeard much affected with Them: And one that belongs to another Town has taken Extracts of these Passages. I design God willing to communicate These things to my Congregation, before the next quarterly day for Prayer ; and also to the neighbouring ministers, who, according to our stated Agreement will be met together on that day, to spend the former Part of the day in Prayer among our selves, & the latter Part in publick services in one of our Congregations : And shall also probably communicate these Things to some of my Correspondents in New-Jersey & else-where. And I can't but think it a They will tend to do a great deal of Good in various Respects; and particularly will tend to promote the Concert for Prayer in these Parts of the world. I desired Mr. Prince of Boston to send you one of my Books on the Concert, soon after it was publish'd; who engaged to do but long forgot it, as I perceived afterwards to my surprize: but since that more thorough Care has been taken about that Matter; & I hope you, & each of my other Correspondents in Scotland, have before now received one of those Books.

I thank you, dear sir, for sending me your Thoughts on some Things in the Prophecies of the Revelation of St John, and for being at so much Trouble as to send it twice (supposing the first Letter had miscarried) This I take as a particular mark of Respect, for which [^105-note4] I am obliged to you. I received, as I said before, your former Letter (which contained the same Observations) and sent an Answer to it, wherein I gave you my Thoughts, such as They were, on those subjects. But if you if you have received my Book on united Prayer &c. therein you have seen more fully some my Thoughts more fully on some Things in the Revelation, that have a near Relation to the same Matters that you write about ; The substance of which I before had written to you in a large Letter, desiring your Opinion of what I wrote. The Letter I think you received, By some Intimations contained in yours of March. 12. 1747. But you was not pleased to favour me with any Thing at all of your Thoughts of what I had so largely communicated to you, to that End, that I might have your Opinion. But I am not the less willing again to communicate my Thoughts of your Remarks.

As to what you observe concerning the number 666, and that Number being found in the name of the present King of France: It is indeed something remarkable that that Number should be found in both in his Latin & French Names, as you observe ; And I don't know but that the Omniscient spirit of God (who ha doubtless in his Predictions has sometimes his Eye on several Things, in which He knows They will be fulfilled) might have some Respect to his Name in the Prophecy : But yet I can hardly think that this individual King of France, or any other particular Prince in Europe, is inte what is chiefly intended by the Beast, so largely described in the XIII Chapter of Revelation, whose Number is said to be 666. Of all the Conjectures concerning the Number of the Beast, that I have lit on in my small Reading, That of Mr. Potters seems to me the most ingenious, who supposes the true Meaning is to be found by extracting the Root of the Number. But after all I have ever suspected that the Rhing chiefly aimed at by the holy spirit was never yet found out, and that the discovery is reserved for later Times. The chief Cause why Mr. Potters Conjecture don't fully satisfy me is the difficulty about adjusting the Fractions in the Root, when extracted.

with Respect to your very ingenious Conjectures concerning the [^105-note5] Period 42 Months or 1260 days of the Outer Court & holy Citie's being trodden under Foot of the Gentiles ; You know sir that That 42 Months, or 1260 days spoken of Rev. XI. 2. has been universally understood, as being the very same Period with the 1260 day[s] of the witnesses prophesying in sackcloth, spoken of in the next verse, and the 1260 days of the womans being fed in the wilderness, Chap. XII. 6. and the Time, Times & half a Time, of her being nourished in the wilderness ver. from the Face of the serpent, ver. 14. and the 42 Months of the continuance of the Beast, Chap. XIII. 5. But it does not appear to me probable that this Forty & two months of the Continuance of the Beast, means the Summ of the diverse Periods in which the Plot of Ground whereon the Antient literal Jerusalem stood, was under the dominion of the Romans, saracens, Persians & Turks ; But the space of Time during which the Reign of Antichrist, continues or the Popish Hierarchy continues. And as to the particular Time of the down-fall of Antichrist, you see my Reasons in the foremention'd Pamphlet, why I think it certain that it will not be known 'till it be accom plish'd : I cannot but think that the scripture is plain in that Matter, and that it does in Effect require us to rest satisfied in Ignorance 'till the Time of the End comes.

However, I should be very foolish If I were dogmatical in my Thoughts concerning the Interpretation of the Prophecies; especially in Opposition to Those who have had so much more opportunity to be well acquainted with Things of this Nature : But since you have insisted on my Thoughts, I conclude you will not be displeased that I have mention'd Them, Tho' not alto gether agreable to yours. I am nevertheless greatly obliged to you for your Condescension in Communicating your Thoughts to me: If we don't exactly agree in our Thoughts about these Things, yet in our Prayers for the accomplishment of these glorious Events in Gods Time, and for God['s] gracious Presence with us & his Assistance in Endeavours to promote his Kingdom & Interest in the mean Time, we may be entirely agreed & united. That we may be so is the earnest desire of, dear sir, your obliged & affectionate Brother & servt

in our common Lord,

Jonathan Edwards.

Mr. McCulloch

[^105-note1]: Neither McCulloch's letter of Mar. 12, 1747, nor JE's answer to it, are extant.

[^105-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^105-note3]: Matt. 18:19, Is. 65:24.

[^105-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

[^105-note5]: **marginal.** [4]

## A90. Letter to John Erskine, October 14, 1748 090.JE-J.Erskine 10-14-48

Jonathan EdwardsA090. JE to John Erskine, 10/14/48. ANTS, f. 1748, #4-5.

Northampton Octob. 14. 1748.

Rev. & dear sir,

A little while ago I wrote a Letter to you, wherein I acknowledg'd the Receipt of your Letter, & the Books that came with it, viz. Taylor on Original sin, & on the Romans; with your sermons, & Answer to Mr. Campbel[^106-note1]. for which most acceptable Presents I would now renewedly thank you. I sent my Letter to Boston, together with one of Mr. Stoddard's Benefit of the Gospel to the wounded in spirit, and his Nature of Saving Conversion, with a sermon on Mr. Brainerd's death,[^106-note2] & some Account of a History of his Life now in the Press, to be sent to Scotland by the first Opportunity. whether there has been any Opportunity or no, I cannot tell. I have very lately received another Letter from you, dated April 6. 1748. which was indeed exceeding Acceptable, on by Reason of the remarkable & joyful Accounts it contains of Things that have a blessed Aspect on the Interests of Christs Kingdom in the world : such as the good Effects of the writings of Mr. West & Mr. Littelton on some at Court, [--------]

[-----------------------------], The Religious Concern in Mr. Randy's & Mr. Gray's Parishes, The hopeful true Piety of the A. Bp. of Canterbury; His & the Kings disposition, not only to tolerate, but comprehend the dissenters, & their Indifference with Respect to the Liturgy, Ceremonies & episcopal ordination; The Piety of the Prince, who is now advanced to the stadtholdership, & has it established in his Family forever ; The Awakening of the Princess Caroline; and the good dispositions of the Prince & Princess of Wales. I think it is very fit that Those who have lately entred into an Union for extraordinary Prayer for the coming of Christs Kingdom & the Prosperity of Zion; should inform one another of things which they know of that pertain to the Prosperity of Zion, & whereby their Prayers are in some degree Answer'd; that They may be united in Joy & Thanksgiving, as well as in supplication; and that they may be encouraged & animated in their Prayers for the future, & engaged to Continue instant therein with all Perseverance.

I think those Things foremention'd, which you have sent me an Account of, are worthy greatly to be observed by those that are united in the Concert for Prayer, for their Comfort, Praise & Encouragement. I intend to communicate these Things to my own People [^106-note3] before the next quarterly season for Prayer, and to the neighbouring ministers, who are united in this Affair; and also to my Correspondents in this Province, & other Provinces in America. I doubt not but They will have an happy Tendency & Influence in many Respects. I hope, dear sir, you will continue still to give me particular Informations of Things that appear relating to the state of Zion & the Interest of Religion, in great Britain or other Parts of Europe. In so doing you will not only inform me; But I shall industriously communicate any important informations of that Kind, and spread them amongst Gods People in this Part of the world; and shall endeavour to my utmost to make such an Use of Them as shall tend most to promote the Interest of Religion. And among other things I should be glad to be informed of any Books that come out, remarkeably tending, either to the Illustration, or defence of the Truth, or the promoting the Power of Godliness, or in any Respect peculiarly tending to Advance true Religion.

I have given an Account of some Things which have a favourable aspect on the Interest of Religion in these American Parts of the world, in my Letters to Mr. Robe and Mr. McLaurin sent with this; which you will have Opportunity to see.

In your last Letter you desire to be particularly informed of the present state of New-Jersey Colledge, and of Things remarkable of a religious Nature respecting the Indians. --As to the former viz. the state of New-Jersey College; By the last Aaccounts I had, it was s in something of an unsettled [--------] state. Governour Belcher had a Mind to give Them a New Charter, that he thought would be more for the Benefit of the society. Accordingly a draught of a new Charter was drawn ; wherein it was proposed to make considerable Alteration in the Corporation of Trustees; and some to leave out some of the former Trustees; and that Governour for the Time being to be a Trustee, & three or four of the Council of that Province. Those two Things made considerable uneasiness, viz. leaving out some of the former Trustees, and making it a Part of the Constitution that the Governour & so many of the Council should be members of the Corporation. & this some feared that this would not [^106-note4] be for the Health of the society ; because the Men in Chief Authority in that Province have for the most Part [been] men of no Religion, and many of them open & profess'd contemners of it. How this matter has been settled, or whether these difficulties are got over, I can have not been informed. As to Governour Belcher Him self, He appears thoroughly engaged to promote vertue & vital Religion in Those Parts : which already has had some good Effects: vice & open Profaneness by the means is become less fashionable among the great men, & vertue & Religion more credible. The disposition of Governour Belcher may be in some measure by the following Extract of a Letter from Him, in Answer to one I wrote to Him on a special Occasion:

Burlington, New-Jersey, Feb. 5. 1747/8.

---"You will, sir, be sure of me as a Friend and Father to the Missio naries this way, & of all my weight & Encouragement for spreading the everlasting Gospel of God our saviour, in all Parts and Places where God shall honour me within any Power or Influence.

--As to myself sir, it is impossible to express the warm sentiments of my grateful Heart, for the Mercies without Number with which I have been loaded by the God which has fed me all my Life-long to this day. and my Reflection upon his Goodness covers me with Shame & Blushing. for I know my utter unworthiness, & that I am Less than the least of all his Mercies. I would therefore abhor my Self, & repent in dust & Ashes. You are sensible, my good Friend, that Governours stand in a glaring Light, & their Conduct is narrowly watch'd by Friends & Enemies : The one often undeservedly applaud them, while the other perhaps too justly censure Them. Yet in this I am not anxious ; But to approve my self to the searcher of Hearts, from whose mouth I must "hear pronounced, that the great and general Audit, those Joyful words Enter Thou &c-or that terrible sentence depart from me &c. Join with me then in Thankfulness to God for all the Blessings & Talents He has intrusted me with, and in Prayer that I may imploy Them to his Honour & Glory, to the Good of the People over whom He hath placed me, & so to the Comfort of my own soul ; That I may alwaies remember that He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the Fear of God."

In another Letter which I since receiv'd, dated Burlington N.J.

May 31. 1748. He says as follows.

"I will prostrate my self before my God and saviour; and on the bended Knees of my soul (abhorring my self in every view) I will beg for a measure of divine Grace & wisdom; that so I may be honoured in being an Instrument of advancing the Kingdom of the blessed Jesus in this world, and in that way be bringing forth Fruit in old Age.* I bless God my heavenly Father, that I am not ashamed of the Cross of Christ; And I humbly ask the Assistance of sovereign Grace, that in Times of Temptation, I may never be a shame to it : I mean that my Conversation may always be as becometh the Gospel of Christ. And I tell you again that all such as minister at the Altar, and in the Course of their ministry approve Themselves faithful to the great Head of the Church, will not only find my Countenance and Protection, but my Love and Esteem. -----As to our Embrio College, it is a Noble design; and if God pleases, may prove an extensive Blessing. I have adopted it for a daughter, and hope it may in Time become an Alma Mater, to this & the neighbouring Provinces. ---I am getting the best Advice and Assistance I can in the draught of a Charter, which I intend to give our infant College. and I thank you sir, for all the kind Hints you have given me for the service of this excellent Undertaking. And, as St Luke says of Mary, she kept all these Things & pondered Them in her Heart; so you may depend, what you have said about the College will not be lost with me; But, as far as God shall enable me, I shall exert & lay out my self in every way to bring it to maturity, & then to Advance its future wellfare and Prosperity : for this I believe will be acceptable in the sight of God our saviour ; a Relish to for true Religion & Piety being great strangers to this Part of America. The Accounts I receive from Time to Time, give me too much Reason to fear Arminianism, Arianism and even socinianism, in destruction to the doctrines of free Grace, are daily propagated in New-England Colleges. How horribly & how wickedly are these poisonous Notions rooting out those noble pious Principles on which our excellent Ancestours founded those seminaries! And how base a Return is it of the present Generation, to that God who is constantly surrounding Them with Goodness & mercy! and how offensive is it in the Eyes of that God, who is jealous of his Glory, and will take vengeance on his Adversaries, and reserveth wrath for his Enemies! And

"from these Things I am led to thank you for your Book wrote in Consequence [^106-note5] of the memorial from Scotland for promoting a Concert in Prayer. I am much pleased with this Proposal and Invitation to all good Christians, & with your Arguments to encourage & corroborate the design. ---The two missionaries you mention Messrs Spencer & Strong, I am told are at present at Boston. I have once and again desired Mr. Brainerd to assure 'em of my Kindness & Respect : But their Affairs have not yet led Them this way. I rejoyce in their being appointed to carry the Gospel in its Purity to the Six Nations. And when Mr. Brainerd, and They, proceed to Susquahannah, They shall have all my Assistance and Encouragement; By Letters to the Kings Governours where They may pass, and my Letters to the Sachem or Chief of those Indians."

With regard to the two missionaries Governour Belcher mentions;

The Commissioners in Boston of the Corporation in London for the Propogation of the Gospel among the Indians in N. England and Parts Adjacent, Had a little before Mr. david Brainerd went to Boston, the summer before his death, had received a sum of money from the Estate left by the famous dr. Williams, for the maintenance of two missionaries among the Six Nations : And having entertained a very great Esteem of Mr. Brainerd, from the Opportunity They had of Acquaintance with Him, while in Boston, They committed to Him the Affair of finding & recom mending the Persons proper to be employed in this Business. According ly He, after much deliberation, recommended one One Mr. Spencer belonging to Haddam, his Native Town; & Mr. Strong belonging to this Town, North-ampton : who are undoubtedly well qualified Persons, of good Abilities & Learning, & of pious dispositions.

The Commissioners on his Recommendation accepted these Persons; & after Mr. Brainerds death, sent to 'em; and They went down to Boston, and accepted the mission. But the Commissioners did not think proper immediately to send 'em forth among the Six Nations; But Ordered to go & live, during the winter, in New-Jersey, with Mr. John Brainerd, among the Christian Indians, there to follow their studies, & get Acquaintance with the Manners & Customs of Indians ; & in the spring to go with Mr. Brainerd, to Susquahannah, to instruct the Indians on that River, before They went to the Six Nations. Accordingly They went & lived in New-Jersey; but were discouraged as to their intended Journey to Susquahannah; [^106-note6] for They understood that the Susquahannah Indians greatly objected against entertaining Missionaries without the consent of the Six Nations, (to whom They are subject and of whom it seems they stand in great fear;) and insisted that the Missionaries should go to the Six Nations first. Therefore in the spring Messrs Spencer & Strong returned to Boston for new Orders from the Commissi oners : who saw Cause to order Them to come & live at my House, 'till the Time of an Appointed Interview of the Governours of Boston & N. York with the Chiefs of the Six Nations at Albany, in the latter Part of summer : when it was proposed that the some that should go to Albany with Gov. Shirley, should, on the behalf of the Commissioners, treat with the Six Nations concerning their receiving Missionaries. Messrs Spencer & Strong did according ly : They lived with me in the summer, & went to Albany in the Time of the Treaty : And the Nation of the Oneidas in particular were dealt with concerning receiving these missionaries; who appeared free and forward in the matter. Mr. S--r & S--ng at that Time some Acquaintance with the Chiefs of the Tribe; who appeared fond of Them, & very desirous of their going with Them. But the grand difficulty then in the way was the want of Interpreter ; which occasion'd their not going with the Indians at That Time, but returning again to New-England. Mr. Strong also was taken much out of Health, which discouraged Him from entertaining any Thoughts of throwing Himself into the Fatigues & Hardships of this Undertaking 'till the next spring. But the difficulty of the want of an Interpreter is now got over; a very good one has been found ; And Mr. Spencer was ordain'd on the the 14 of the last month, and is gone with the Interpreter, to go to the Countrey of the Oneida's, about 170 Miles beyond Albany, & about 130 Miles distant from all settlements of the white People.

It is a Thing that has a favourable Aspect on the design of Prop Propagating the Gospel among the Indians, that many of late have been remarkably spirited to o promote it, & liberally to open their Hands in order to it. Mr. Brainerd's going to Boston before his [7] death, and People there having some Acquaintance with Him & with his Labours & success among the Indians, [-] gave Occasion to a considerable number in Boston, men of good substance & of the best Character, & some of them principal men in the Town, to form Themselves into a charitable society, [----] that by their joint Endeavours & Contributions They might promote the Instruction & who & spiritual Good of the Indians : who have done some very liberal Things for the Indians in N. Jersey & also the Six Nations . The People of Northampton have also had their Hearts remarkably open'd to contribute to the maintenance of Mr. Spencers Interpreter. And a particular man at Springfield, has been moved to devote a considerable Part of his Estate to promote the Propagation of the Gospel among the Six Nations.

As to my writing against Arminianism; I have hitherto been remarkably hindred ; so that probably it will be a considerable Time before I shall have any Thing ready for the Press: But do intend, Goll God allowing & assisting, to prosecute that design : and I desire your Prayers for the divine Assistance in it. ----The Books you sent me will be a great Help to me; I would on No Account have been without 'em.

I condole with you & your dear spouse, [on] the Loss of your Noble & excellent Father[^106-note7] : which is doubtless a great Loss to the Church of God. But the glorious King of Zion, who was dead, is alive & lives forevermore, and can raise up others in exalted stations to favour Zion ; and seems to be so doing at this day, By things you give an Account of in your Letter. -----I have been the subject of an afflictive dispensation of late, tending to teach me how to sympathize with the afflicted ; which I think I mentioned in my last Letter to you; viz. the death of my second daughter the last February.

Please to present my most affectionate & respectful Salutations to your dear Consort. That I and mine may be rememberd in your & her Prayers, is the Request of your affectionate & obliged Friend & Brother,

Jonathan Edwards.

Rev. Mr. Erskine.

[^106-note1]: John Taylor, *The Scripture-Doctrine of Original Sin Proposed to Free and Candid Examination* (London, 1740; 3d ed., Belfast, 1746), and *A Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans. To Which Is Prefix'd A Key to the Apostolic Writings* (London, 1745; Dublin, 1746); John Erskine, *The People of God Considered as All Righteous: in three Sermons preach'd at Glasgow, April 1745* (Edinburgh, 1745).

[^106-note2]: Solomon Stoddard, *Benefit of the Gospel to the Wounded in Spirit* (Boston, 1713), and *A Treatise concerning the Nature of Saving Conversion* (Boston, 1719). Edwards, *True Saints, When Absent from the Body, are Present with the Lord* (Boston, 1747); according to his letter to Erskine of Aug. 31, 1748, JE had also sent a copy of *The Church's Marriage to her Sons, and to Her God* (Boston, 1746). * He was 66 years old the 8th day of January last.--JE's note

[^106-note3]: **marginal.** 2

[^106-note4]: **marginal.** 3

[^106-note5]: **marginal.** [5]

[^106-note6]: **marginal.** [6]

[^106-note7]: Erskine's father-in-law, George Mackay, third Baron Reay, who died in 1748.

## A91. Letter Joseph Bellamy, January 9, 1749 091.JE-J.Bellamy 1-9-49

Jonathan EdwardsA091. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 1/9/49. Hartford Seminary, Bellamy Papers, Doc. Box #187, f. 2929, item #81175.

Rev. & Dear Sir

I received your Letter dated Jan. 1. by Mr. Strong: but as to your other Letter you mention, that you sent by the way of Hartford about a Fortnight before, I have not received it. Mr. Searl is not in these Parts:

I suppose He is at a Norwich, a Place as far distant from Hence as Bethlehem is. He was here about a month or six weeks ago: and I perceive that the ministers in the neighborhood of the Place where he has been at Norwich, are desirous of his staying longer there, which is a Pla large Congregation, and where has been great & long continued difficulty & division ; and the People in general, of different Parties, greatly united in Him; excepting the separatists, & They are friendly to Him, and have pass'd Him for a good man. He is earnestly desired by the People of Quabbin, and has been applied to lately by the People of Ellington & of Old-Windsor. And, for my Part, I am wholly at a Loss at present where He can serve the Interest of Religion ; And if He should ask my Advice, should not know what Advice to give Him without further Information from Him or others.[^107-note1]

If I live till the spring I shall probably have Occasion for Mastict & Turretine,[^107-note2] being engaged in studies on the Arminian Controversies and preparing to write something upon Them. I hope you [^107-note3] will come and bring the Books your self for I should rejoice to see you here.

I have here sent a sermon directed to by madam stoddard to her Brother at Woodbury; I desire you take Care of the Conveyance of it : You will have Opportunity to read it by the way if you see Cause.[^107-note4]

I am exceeding sorry you did not go to Long-Island as you proposed : But I wish you Contrive to make out a Journey there still, & travel as you proposed from one End of the Island to the other. My wife & one of my younger Children have lately been in very dangerous Circumstances, but through mercy are now all moving about. Give my Love to Mrs. Bellamy.

I am sir your Brother & most affectionate Friend

Jonathan Edwards.

Northampton Jan. 9. 1748/9.

[^107-note1]: John Searl, a Northampton native, was preaching in Sharon, Conn., at this time, where he was ordained on Aug. 2, 1749.

[^107-note2]: Peter van Mastricht, *Theoretico-Practica Theologia*, and Francois Turretin, *Institutio Theologiae Elenctiae*.

[^107-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^107-note4]: Madam Stoddard is Col. John Stoddard's wife, and her brother is Anthony Stoddard, pastor of Woodbury.

## A91b. Letter to Northampton Church Committee (Drafts), April 13, 1749 091b.JE-NtonChhComm 4-13-49

Jonathan EdwardsA091d. JE to Northampton Chh. Comm., 4/13/49. Three drafts. BRBL, Sermon on Jer. 23:29 (4/49), f. 361 (one draft); f. 1323 (two drafts).

[f. 361:]

I make this offer to this I the subscriber That I will resign m make the following offer to this Chh the Committee of this Chh. _________

That if the People will wait till what I have prepared for the Press relating to the admission of members to the Chh. is published I will resign the ministry over this Church if the Church insists desires it upon it, provided that after they have had opportunity pretty generally to have read my said Book prepared & after they have first asked advice of a Council mutually Chosen * provided viz that none shall of the Brethren be admitted to vote in this affair but such as have or heard what I have to say from the Pulpit mind either read my said Book *+ [-] & the desire of the Major Part of such [-] Brethren only shall be looked upon as the m on the Mind of the Chh in this matter provided also that the society will engage that I shall be free from Rates. provided that also I am allowed by a regular Council thus to resign my ministry over this Church

* & followed their Advice with Regard to regular steps to be taken previous to their vote.

*+ or have have heard from what I have to say from the Pulpit in defence of the doctrine which is the subject of the said Book.

[f. 1323, draft 1:]

I the subscriber do hereby Signify & declare to such as it may Concern, that If my People will wait 'till the Book I am preparing for the Press, relating to the Admission of members into the Church, is published, I will resign the Ministry over this Church, if the Church desires it, after They have had Opportunity pretty generally to read my said Book, and after they have first ask'd Advice of a Council mutually chosen, & followed their Advice with Regard to regular Steps to be taken previous to their votes:[^109-note1] the following things also being provided, viz. That none of the Brethren be admitted to vote in this Affair But such as have either read my said Book or have heard from the Pulpit what I have to Say in defence of the doctrine that is the subject of it, and that the society will engage that I shall be freed from all Rates , And also that a regular Council do approve of my thus resigning my Pastoral office over this Church.[^109-note2]

[f. 1323, draft 2:]

I the subscriber do hereby Signify & declare to such as it may Concern that if my People will wait 'till the Book I am preparing for the Press relating to the Admission of members into the Church is published I will resign the ministry over this Church if the Church desires it after They have had Opportunity pretty generally to read my said Book & after They have first asked Advice of a Council mutually Chosen The following Things being provided. viz that none of the Brethren be admitted to vote in this Affair But such as have either read my said Book or have heard wha from the Pulpit what I have [to][^109-note3] say in defence of the doctrine is the subject of it. and that the society will engage that I shall be free from all Rates And also that a regular Council [do] approve of my thus resigning my Pastoral office [over] this Church.

J. E.

Northampton April. 13. 1749.
