## A92. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, May 12, 1749 092.JE-T.Foxcroft 5-12-49

Jonathan EdwardsA092. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 5/12/49. BRBL, f. 1287.

Rev. & Honoured sir,

I received your Letter of May 3d the day before yesterday, since I wrote to Mr. Bromfield by Mr. Alvord: I humbly thank you for your Letter. My warning now is exceeding short, & I have but Just Time to send a draught of Proposals for subscription, intending very shortly to write largely to you and send an abstract of your Former Letter to be added to my Book as an appendix, if you please, & an Answer to three more Objections, taking up about a sheet & an half in M. S. But now I must break off w by subscribing myself your obliged Brother & humble servt

Jonathan Edwards.

Northampton

May. 12. 1749.

## A93. Letter to John Erskine, May 20, 1749 093.JE-J.Erskine 5-20-49

Jonathan EdwardsA093. JE to John Erskine, 5/20/49. ANTS, f. 1749, #5-6.

Northampton May 20. 1749.

Rev. & dear Sir,

The day before yesterday I received your Letter of Feb. 14, with the Pacquet, containing the Pamphlets you mention in your Letter : for which I am greatly obliged to you. I have not yet had Opportunity to read these Books, But promise my self much Entertainment by Them, from the Occasions on which They were written, & the subjects They are upon. The last Letter I received from you before This was dated April. 6. 1748. so that I suppose the two Letters you say you sent wrote to me since Those which I acknowledge the Receipt of; have miscarried. which I much regret, as I much value what comes from your Hand.

In one of your last Letters which which came to hand, you desire to be particularly informed concerning the State of Religion in these Parts of the world, and particularly concerning the Mission to the Indians, & the infant College in N. Jersey. As to the Affair of preaching the Gospel to the Indians, Mr. Spencer went the last Fall, far into the western wilderness; to the Oneidaes, one of the Tribes of Indians called the six Nations, living on Suscohannah River, towards the Head of the River, to a Place called by the Indians Onohouhquauga, about 180 miles southwest from Albany on Hudsons River. where He continued almost through the winter; and went through many difficulties & Hardships, with little or no success, through the failing of his Interpreter; who was a woman that had formerly been a Captive among the Caghnawauga Indians in Canada, who speak the same Language with Those Oneidaes, excepting some small variation of dialect. she went with her Husband, an Englishman, and one of the People we here call separatists[^111-note1] : who shewed the spirit He was of there, in that wilderness, beyond what was known before. He differed with and opposed Mr. Spencer in his Measures, and had an ill Influence on his wife; who I fear was very unfaithful, [^111-note2] refusing to interpret for Mr. Spencer more than one discourse in a week, a sermon upon the sabbath; and utterly declined assisting him in discoursing & conversing with the Indians in the week Time. And her Interpretations on the sabbath were performed very unfaithfully as at last appeared. so that Mr. Spencer came away in discouragement in the spring, and returned to Boston, and gave the Corporation there, who employed Him, an Account of his unexpected difficulties & disappointment ; and became obliged to them to waith three months, to see if They could procure a Fellow-missionary, & another Interpreter, to go with Him to the Indians; which I believe is not much expected. If these are not obtained within the limited Time, Mr. Spencer is from free from any further to Engagements to Them. Mr. Spencer is now preaching at Elizabeth-Town in New Jersey, in the Pulpit of the late Mr. dickinson; and I believe is like to settle there[^111-note3]. He is a Person of very Promising Qualifications; and will hopefully in some Measure make up the great Loss that People have sustain'd by the death of their former Pastor.

As to the Mission in N. Jersey, we have from Time to Time had comfortable Accounts And Mr. John Brainerd, who has the Care of the Congregation of Christian Indians there, was, about Three weeks ago, at my Acc House; and informed of the Increase of his Congregation, and of their being added to from Time to Time by the coming of Indians from distant Places, and settling in the Indian Town at Cranberry, for the sake of hearing the Gospel ; and of something of a work of Awakening being all along carried among the Indians to this day; and of the some of the New-comers being Awaken'd; and of there being Instances from Time to Time of hopeful Conversion among Them ; and of the general good & pious Behaviour of the Professing Indians. But He gave an Account also of some Trouble the Indians meet with from some of the white People; and particularly from Mr. Maurice, [^111-note4] the chief Justice of the Province, who is a profess'd deist; who is suing Them for their Lands, under Pretext of a deed from will made by their former King; which was undoubtedly forged. However He is a man of such Craft & Influence, that it is not known how the matter will Issu Issue.

I have heard Nothing New that is very remarkable concerning the College in N. Jersey. It is in its Infancy. There has been Considerable difficulty about settling their Charter. Gov. Belcher, who gave the Charter, is willing to encourage and promote the College to his utmost ; But differs in his Opinion concerning the Constitution, which will tend most to its Prosperity, from some of the principal ministers that have been concerned in founding the society. He insists upon it that the Governour, for the Time Being, & four of th his Majes ties Council for the Province, should alwaies be of the Corporation of Trustees ; and that the Governour should alwaies be the President of the Corporation. The ministers are all very willing that the present Governour, who is a religious man, should be in this standing : But their difficulty is with Respect to future Governours, who They suppose are as likely to be men of no Religion and deists, as otherwise. However so the matter is settled, to the great uneasiness of Mr Gilbert Tennent in particular, who it is fear'd will have no further concern with the College on this Account. ----Mr. Burr their President is a man of Reli gion & singular Learning, and I hope the College will flourish under his Care.

I have taken a great deal of Pains in communicating to others, in various Parts, The pleasing Accounts you, & my other Correspondents in Scotland, gave me last year of Things of promising Aspect on the Interest of Religion on your side of the Ocean : which have been very affecting to pious ministers & People in N. England, and also in the [^111-note5] Provinces of N. York & N. Jersey ; and hope some considerable Good has been done by such Tidings ; particularly in Animating animating many in the duty of extraordinary Prayer for a general Revival of Religion, and promoting the Concert for Prayer proposed from Scotland ; which prevails more & more in these Parts of the world ; which together with some other things in some Places, are Cause of Thankfulness, & bode well to the Interests of Zion, (of which I have given a more particular Account in my Letters to Mr. McLaurin, & Mr. Robe, sent with this)[^111-note6] Tho' it be in general a very dead Time as to Religion, and a Time of the prevailing of all manner of Iniquity.

I shall send orders to Boston, that one of my Books on Mr. Brainerds Life may be sent to you, with this Letter, if any of them are ready, as I hope they are or will be very speedily.

I have nothing very comfortable to inform of concerning the present state of Religion in this Place. A very great difficulty has arisen between me & my People, relating to Qualifications for Communion at the Lords table. My honoured Grand-father Stoddard, my Predecessour in the ministry over this Church, strenuously maintain'd the Lords supper to be a converting Ordinance ; and urged all to Come who were not of Scandalous Life, tho' they knew Themselves to be unconverted. I formerly conformed to his Practice ; But I have had difficulties with Respect to it, which have been long increasing; till I dared no longer to proceed in the former way : which has occasioned great uneasiness among my People, and has fill'd all the Countrey with noise. which has obliged me to write something on the subject, which is now in the Press.

---I know not but this affair will issue in a separation between me & my People --I desire your Prayers that God would guide me in every step in this affair . my wife joins with me in respectful Salutations to you & your Consort.

I am sir, your obliged & affectionate Brother & servt

Jonathan Edwards.

The Rev. Mr John Erskine.

[^111-note1]: Rebecca Kellogg Ashley and Benjamin Ashley.

[^111-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^111-note3]: Spencer was installed at Elizabethtown in Feb. 1749 and served there till 1756.

[^111-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

[^111-note5]: **marginal.** [4]

[^111-note6]: Presumably the letters to McCulloch and Robe of May 23, 1749; the one to McLaurin is not extant.

## A94. Letter to William McCulloch, May 23, 1749 094.JE-W.McCulloch 5-23-49

Jonathan EdwardsA094. JE to William McCulloch, 5/23/49. ANTS, f. 1749, #3-4.

Northampton May 23. 1749.

Rev. and dear Brother,

The last Letter I received from you was dated Feb. 10. 1748. to which I wrote an Answer the latter End of last summer; which I suppose you received. because I perceive by Letters sent me this spring by some others of my Correspondents, your Neighbours, They had received Letters I sent to Them at the same Time, and in the same Pacquet. Your Letters to me have been very acceptable; I should be glad to receive 'em oftener.

---The Letter I last received from you, and others that came with it were peculiarly agreable, on the Account of the good news They contained concerning Mr. West & Littelton, the A. Bp. of Canterbury, some in the Royal Family, the Stadtholder &c-These Things I have taken a great deal of Pains to communicate to others : and They have been very entertaining, & I hope profitable to many. I was at the Pains to extract those Things from all the Letters I received at that Time those Things which appeared with a favourable Aspect on the Interest of Religion in the world, and to draw various Copies to send to different Parts, to such as I suppose would be most likely to be entertained & improved by Them, and to do good with Them. and I believe They have been of great Benefit, particularly to excite & encourage God's People in the great duty of praying for the coming of Christ's Kingdom, & to promote the extraordinary united Prayer in the method proposed in the memorial from Scotland. I sent one read these Articles of good News to my own Congregation, and also to the Association of ministers to which I belong, when met on one of the quarterly seasons for Prayer ; and read them occasionally to many others ; & sent one of the forementioned Abstracts to Connecticut, which carried into various Parts of that Government, and shewn to several ministers there. I sent one to [^112-note1] Mr. Hall of Sutton,[^112-note2] a pious minister about the middle of this Province ; who, according to my desire, communicated it to other ministers, & I suppose to his People . I sent a Copy to Mr. Rogers of Kittery,[^112-note3] I suppose about 70 miles to the Eastward of Boston ; who in Reply wrote to me, and in his Letter says as follows " Yours of the 22d of decem. came not to my Hand 'till the 19 of this; with which I was well-pleased, and had some sweet sense of the sovereign free grace of God in the Instances you mention'd, with some going forth of Heart after further displays of it in the mighty & noble of our Nation, and the great ones of our own Countrey; and indeed that the Kingdom of our exalted Redeemer might prevail in all the world. And, dear sir, I am full in the Belief that so many of the Lords People agreeing upon a Time to unite in Prayer for the pouring out of the holy spirit, and the coming of the Redeemers Kingdom, is from the Lord : and can't but Hope the day draws near, when He will pour out of his waters upon the thirsty, and his Floods upon the dry Ground ; as also that all his ministers & People who are engaged in so delightful a work for so noble an End, will give him no Rest 'till He shall make his Jerusalem a quiet Habitation &c. Name & Praise in the Earth."

I sent another Copy into New-Jersey to Mr. John Brainerd, missionary to the Indians there, with a desire that He would communicate it to others there as He thought would be most serviceable . He writes in Answer March 4. 1748. as follows. " I received yours of Jan. 12. on sabbath morning Feb. 5, and desire to acknowledge your Kindness with much Thankfulness & Gratitude. It was a great Refreshmt, as well as Encouragement to me ; and I trust has been so to many others in these Parts, who are concerned for the Prosperity of Zion. The next Tuesday after (as perhaps sir, you may remember) was the quarterly day appointed for extraordinary Prayer : upon which I called my People together, and gave Them Information of the most notable things contain'd in your Letter. And since I have endeavoured [^112-note4] to communicate the same to several of my neighbouring ministers, and sundry private Christians, as I had opportunity. I have also thought it my duty to send an Extract, or rather a Copy of it to Gov. Belcher. ---I have likewise (for want of Time to transcribe) transcribe) sent the original to Philadelphia by a careful Hand, that the Rev. Mr. Gilbert Tennent might have the Perusal of it ; where a Copy was taken, and the Original safely returned to me again. --I can't but Hope that this Letter (as it contains many Things wherein the Power & Goodness of God do appear in a most conspicuous manner) will be greatly serviceable in stirring up the People of God in these Parts, and encouraging their Hearts to seek his Face & Favour, and to cry mightily to Him for the further outpouring of his gracious Spirit upon his Church in the world. For my Part I think the remarkable Things which your Letter contains might be sufficient to put New-Life into any one who is not past Feeling ; And as a means to excite a spirit of Prayer & Praise, in all Those who are not buried in Ignorance, or under the Power of a lethargick stupor. And 'tis look'd upon by those whom I have had opportunity to converse with, whether ministers or private Christians, that what God has done is matter of great Thankfulness & Praise, and might well encourage his People to lift up the Hand of Prayer, and be Instant therein."

Mr. davenport,[^112-note5] minister of a Part of Elizabeth-Town in N. Jersey, writes thus upon it, in a Letter dated March April 1. 1749.

"I thank you for sending your Letter to Mr. Brainerd open, that I might see it, which I took a Copy of ; and have found it again & again refreshing & animating. I read it to the ministers who met at my House for Prayer, on the first Tuesday of Feb. ---and sent it to afterwards to Long-Island : Mr. Buel took a Copy of it and read it in his Congregation on the Island."

I hope dear sir, these Things will encourage you to continue your Correspondence, and to go on to give me Information of whatever appears in your arts of the world, favourable to the Interests of the Kingdom of Christ. It will not only be entertaining to me ; but I shall endeavour, whenever I receive such tidings, to communicate it for the Entertainment & Profit [^112-note6] fit of Gods People as I have opportunity.

I must refer you, dear sir, to my Letters to other Correspondents in your Neighbourhood, for other particulars relating to the state of Religion in these Parts of the world. and hope when you are before the Throne of Grace you will not forget your very affectionate Friend & Brother & servt

Jonathan Edwards.

P.S. I hope some of my Books on Mr. Brainerd's Life will be ready, so that one of them may be sent from Boston to you with this Letter: I shall send orders to my Friends in Boston accordingly.

The Rev. Mr. McCulloch.

[^112-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^112-note2]: David Hall, pastor of Sutton, Mass., 1728-1789.

[^112-note3]: John Rogers, pastor of the 2nd Church in Kittery, Maine, 1721-1773.

[^112-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

[^112-note5]: James Davenport, after renouncing Separatism in 1744, served various churches in New Jersey; at the time of this letter, he was at Connecticut Farms.

## A95. Letter to James Robe, May 23, 1749 095.JE-J.Robe 5-23-49

Jonathan EdwardsA095. JE to James Robe, 5/23/49. ANTS, f. 1749, #8-9.

Northampton, May 23. 1749.

Rev. & dear sir,

Mr McLaurin, in a Letter I received from Him the last week, dated March. 10. 1749. informs me of a Letter you had written to me, sent to Him; which He had taken Care of. This Letter, by some means or other has fail'd, and has never reach'd me. I intend to make Enquiry after to see if it ben't left at Boston, & forgotten to be sent. I have Reason to hope (tho' I have not received your Letter) that you & your Family are well; because Mr. McLaurin, & Mr. Erskine (the only correspondents from whom I have received Letters this Time) inform of nothing to the Contrary.

As to the present state of Religion in these Parts of the world, it is in the general very dark and melancholy. But yet there are some Things which appear comfortable and hopeful. Particularly, the Concert for extraordinary Prayer for the coming of Christs Kingdom, is Spreading & prevailing. and we hear of Awakenings & Revivals of Religion in some Places. we have had Accounts from Time to Time of Religion being in flourishing state in the Indian Congregation in N. Jersey, under the Care of Mr. John Brainerd, of the Congregation's increasing, by the Access of Indians from distant Parts, of a work of awakening carried on among the unconverted, and Additions made to the number of the hopefully converted, and the Christian Behaviour of Professours there. Mr. Brainerd was at my House a little while ago, and represented this to be the present State of Things in that Congregation.

I had a letter from Mr. davenport[^113-note1] (who is settled now as a minister over a Congregation belonging to Elizabeth-Town in N. Jersey) dated April 1. 1749. wherein He says as follows; "Mr. Lewis[^113-note2] told me that there has been a remarkable work of Conviction prevailing in his Place, ever since last december. I think He spoke of about 40 under soul Concern, a considerable number of 'em under strong Convictions, & some hopefully converted. --I heard lately a credible Account of a remarkable work of Conviction & Conversion, [^113-note3] among whites & Negroes, at Hannover in Virginia; under the ministry of Mr. davis,[^113-note4] who is lately settled there; and has the Character of a very ingenious & pious young man; whose support in his Preparation for service, Mr. Robinson*[^113-note5] contributed much, if not mostly to; & on his death-bed gave Him his Books &c." Mr. Buel of East-Hampton on Long-Island,[^113-note6] was here last week, & gave Account of a very considerable work of Awakening at this Time in his Congregation, especially among the Young People ; and also a yet greater work at Bridg-Hampton, under the ministry of one Mr. Brown,[^113-note7] a very pious & Prudent young young man lately settled there: These Congregations are both pretty large. He also gave an Account of Religions continuing in a very prosperous state at a Part of Huntington, where another Town on Long-Island, where was a great & general Awakening last year.

An Association of ministers belonging to the County of wo between this & Boston, seem of late to have applied Themselves something earnestly to invent means for the promoting Religion. The following is an a Copy of something They have agreed upon for this End, as it was put to me by a minister that lives that way.

" The summ & substance of the Answers given by the Association to this Question. what shall be done in our several Flocks for preventing the awful Threatning degeneracy and Backsliding in Religion, in the present day?

These we apprehend may be reduced to the following Heads, viz. Those that Respect our selves personally, and those which concern the Association as such, and those which relate to our People in our respective Churches & Congregtions.

I. As to what respects our selves personally;

1. we ought surely to get a deep and affecting sense of this; whether there is not in our selves defection, and great danger of further degeneracy : for otherwise we shall with little Heartiness undertake, [^113-note8] or Earnestness endeavour Reformation.

2. we are not to think it amiss that we our selves be excited to look, with a proper Attention & concern, into our own state, into our own Experiences in the divine Life, and into what little Proficiency we make, or declension we fall into, our selves.

3. we must by all means see to it that we be sound and clear in the great doctrines of the Gospel, which are the Life of our holy Religion : (we here intend those doctrines which are exhibited in our excellent westminster Catechism & Confession of Faith) and that we all boldly & impartially appear in the defence thereof. at the same Time we must take Heed and beware of the dangerous Errours which many have run into; particularly the Arminian & Neonomian on the one Hand, and the Antinomian & Enthusiastical on the other.

4. we must be very faithful in every Part of our ministerial works and make Conscience to magnify our office. In a particular manner, we must take good Heed to our Preaching; that it be not only sound, but instruc tive, savoury, spiritual, very awakening and searching, well adapted to the Times and Seasons which pass over us; labouring earnestly herein. we must therefore dwell much upon the doctrine of Repentance and Conversion ; the Nature, Necessity & Evidence thereof; & much urge the duty of Self-Examination, and open the deceits of the Heart : bringing the unconverted under the work of the Law, that They may be prepared to embrace the Offer of the Gospel. Moral duties must be treated of in an evangelical strain; and we must give unto everyone his Portion, and not shrink from it, under the Notion of Prudence ; In special, in the important duty of reproving sinners of all sorts, be They who they will. Again we must not be slighty in our private Conference with souls, and examining Candidates for the Communion, or other special Priviledges. and we must carefully & wisely suit our Endeavours to the several Ages & Conditions of Persons, the Elder & younger. And in a very particular manner, we must get our selves to promote Religion among our young People. And in a word we must see whether we are animated to all these Things by the Grace of God in us.

5. we are impartially to see what Evils are to be found among our selves, and remove 'em. Let us be seriously thoughtful whether (among our defects) we have not been, in some respect or other, the blamable means of discouragement to those who have been under [^113-note9] religious Concern ; or whether we have not given strength & Boldness to the ungodly, when we have been testifying against Extravagancies and disorders of the late Times.

6. we must conscientiously be exemplary in our whole Behaviour & Conversation. Tis necessary that we be serious & grave, as what highly becomes gospel-Bishops. And especially, we must be very watchful over our Frame and Conduct on the Lord's day. we must therefore look well to our sabbatizing. both at Home and abroad, both before our own & other People. Our Example is of vast Consequence in magnifying our office, before recommended.

7. we ought to stir up the Gifts which are in us, and to grow more & more, according to the sacred Injunction, 2. Tim. 1. 6.

8. we should follow all our Endeavours with fervent Prayer to God; especially our Labours in Preaching & Teaching : The seed of the Word is to be steep'd in Tears.

II. As to what concerns the Association as such.

1. We must lay aside disgust one with another, and study brotherly Love, that it may revive and continue. we must endeavour to be as near as we can of one mind, and go on harmoniously : and then we shall be the more strongly united in all, but especially in our present Proceedings. There must be respectful Treatment one of another, the Persons & Characters one of another; And be careful of ministerial Characters; which is of greater Consequence than at first sight may appear. And when we have occasion to dispute, let it be under a very strict Guard, avoiding all censuring Reflections.

2. That we manifest our Approbation of the Westminster Assemblies Catechism, as containing an excellent system of divinity : and we Purpose to preach agreable to the doctrines of the Bible exhibited therein.

3. we must be very careful of our Conversation in general as abovesaid, so especially must be respecting our Conduct while together in Association.

4. It is proposed that a Course of our Associations be turned into Fasts, upon this great Account.

5. We agree to be more especially fervent in continual Prayer for the Advancement of the Kingdom of Christ.

6. some special new & prudent Care must be taken to guard our Pulpits.

7. 'Tis proposed that we agree to endeavour to introduce the publick Reading of the holy scriptures. the Manner & Time to be left to dis cretion.

III. with Regard to what may be done among the People we stand related [^113-note10] to.

1. we conceive that whatever publick Exercises are to be agreed on, or whatever concerns the publick, the People are to be informed of, and Acquainted with our design.

2. That it be earnestly recommended to the People to consider the worth of their Priviledges, and the danger of being deprived of 'em; which They are parti which there is partly by the spreading of evil doctrines among 'em, and partly by the Conduct of too many people towards their ministers.

3. Let pragmatical factious spirits, fomenting division, be duly frowned upon.

4. we must guard Them against the Temptations of their several Employments, and the special seasons wherein They are most exposed.

5. we must consider what Evils there are to be found among Them, which do especially need reforming; as the Profanation of the Lord's day, which is enough to destroy all Religion; Tavern-haunting, Company-keeping, Chambering, Uncleanness, Profaneness &c. And we ought loudly to testify against 'em. And that what we do may be effectual, let us endeavour to convince their Consciences of the Evil of sin, and of these Sins. we are not to fail to warn People solemnly against the dreadful Guilt of Unthankfulness under Gods signal mercies, and of incorrigeableness under heavy & sore Judgments. Could we in wisdom do it, we should also warn 'em against their Oppressing the Lords Ministers in their Maintenance.

6. Let us endeavour to revive good Customs & Practices among 'em; particularly, the antient good Practice of Catechizing, Family Order, worship & Government, religious societies under good Regulation, godly Conference and Conversation among Christians; and in brief whatever is laudable and of good Tendency.

7. Church discipline should be revived; brotherly watchfulness & Admonition. Nor are we to forget to take special Care of the Children & youth of the Flock.

8. we may do well to engage, as far as we are able, all Persons of distinction & Influence to unite with us in this work of Reformation; e.g. Justices, school-masters, Candidates for the Ministry; and especially to assist us by their Example.

9. Solemn Renewal of Covenant hath been advised to as very useful upon this Occasion; (vid. Synod. 1679 for Reformation.)[^113-note11] but we leave this to each ones discretion.

Finally, in these Things we should think our selves bound to exert our selves, & use uncommon Fervency to preserve what remains of Religion & prevent further decay." Thus far [^113-note12] Octob. 1748. Thus far this Association.

The members of this Association, as their names were sent to me, are as follows.

The Rev. Messrs. Loring of Sudbury. Cushing of Shrewsbury. Parkman of Westborough. Gardiner of Stow. Martyn of Westborough. Stone of Southborough. Seecomb of Harvard. Morse of Shrewsbury. Smith of Marlborough. Goss of Bolton. Buckminster of Rutland. Davis of Holden.

I must refer you dear sir, for other Particulars relating to the state of Religion in these Parts of the world, to my Letters to my other Correspondents in your Neighbourhood.

My wife and Family join with me in very affectionate & Respectful salutations to you & yours . desiring an Interest in your Prayers for us all, and th for this Part of the Zion of God I remain,

dear sir, your Loving Brother,

& obliged Friend & servt,

Jonathan Edwards.

P.S. I intend to send order to Boston with this Letter, that one of my Books on Mr. Brainerds Life may be sent to you with it; hoping that some of 'em are ready, or will be speedily. I crave your acceptance of it.

The Rev. Mr. Robe[^113-note13]

[^113-note1]: James Davenport, pastor of Connecticut Frarms, N.J.

[^113-note2]: Thomas Lewis, pastor of the Bethlehem Church in Union, N.J.

[^113-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^113-note4]: I.e. Samuel Davies, pastor of Hanover County, Va.

[^113-note5]: *This Mr. Robinson was a young minister of eminent gifts and grace; I think, belonging to Pennsylvania, but had sometimes preached with great success in Virginia in various parts; but died three or four years ago, in his youth.-JE's note. [Robinson ended his career as an itinerant minister in Va., dying in 1746.]

[^113-note6]: Samuel Buel, pastor of East Hampton.

[^113-note7]: James Brown, pastor of Bridgehampton, L.I., 1748-1775.

[^113-note8]: **marginal.** [3]

[^113-note9]: **marginal.** [4]

## A96. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, May 24, 1749 096.JE-T.Foxcroft 5-24-49

Jonathan EdwardsA096. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 5/24/49. BRBL, f. 1288. Foxcroft underlined some words and phrase, but only JE's underlining is indicated.

Northampton May 24. 1749

Rev. & honoured Sir,

I have herewith sent an Answer to three other Objections against the doctrine maintained in my discourse now in the Press; which objections I find by further Consideration & Conversation, there is a Necessity should be answer'd. I have also sent a short Preface, and an Abstract of your Letter to me on this subject. I have taken such Things from the Letter as I desire may be published. If They are published as something that I add to my own Book, as an Abstract of a Letter which I received from you (in the Form wherein I have here sent it) It may be best to be as an Appendix : But if it be so published as something that you add in your own Name, I should think it would be better to be in a Preface. I should chuse the latter, viz. that you should add these Things in a Preface in your own name: But I must leave it with your Judgment. I should be glad that something may be observed concerning the late & Opinion of the late & present divines in England & Scotland. Some things I have observed, that lead me to suppose that their opinion is generally agreeable to Mr. Baxters. --In my Narrative of the work of God wrought here 14 years ago, which was sent to dr. Watts and dr. Guyse, I observed something of the manner of our Church to admit members without a Profession of Conversion: They, in some of their Letters written to dr. Colman, appeared much offended at it. I have a sermon of dr. Guyse, preached at the Ordination of Mr. Gibbons in London, wherebyin He plainly manifests his mind with regard to the Qualifications of the members of a Christian church.

And I have seen a practical discourse of Mr. Willison's of dundee, wherein He is much in warning graceless persons not to presume to approach the Lords table. But you have vastly greater Opportunities of full Information concerning the present Principles & Practice in England & Scotland, than I. And an Account of this would be more likely to have Influence on some, than an Account of what was in the last & preceding Centuries ---You speak in your last Letter, as tho' Mr. Stoddards Opinion was far from being the prevailing Opinion in your Parts. If it be so, I should be glad if this also might be inserted, for People in general here are not sensible but that their Opinion is become the established Opinion almost all over NEngland. You say, you believe the generality of the Churches & elderly ministers, your way hold to the first Principles of New-England in this matter : If you mean not only with respect to Qualifications for the Lords supper, but also Baptism, 'tis what I was by no means aware of and quite otherwise than I supposed. I did supposed it to be the universal, and long established Custom of the Countrey to admit to Baptism on lower Terms than to the Lords supper; excepting those Churches where Mr. stoddards Principles were established; [^114-note1] And particularly that it was the Custom to admit Parents who desired Baptism for their Children into the Church, in a state of Education, on their owning the Covenant, as it is called: which They do, not as professing or pretending to saving Faith and Repentance, or regenerating Grace. I should be glad to be more particularly informed as to that matter. And if it be otherwise than I have conceived, I think it had best by all means be published in the Book; for 'tis undoubtedly very diverse from what is universally received to be true Fact in these Parts.

The greatest difficulty of all relating to my Principles in is here, respecting Baptism. I am not sure but that my People, in Length of Time, and with great difficulty, might be brought to yield the Point as to the Qualifications for the Lords supper (tho' that is very uncertain;) But with respect to the other Ordinan sacrament there is scarce any Hope of it. And this will be very likely to overthrow me, not only with Regard to my Usefulness in the work of the Ministry here, but every where; If the Case be, as I supposed it was in the Countrey. ---The ministers in N. Jersey & Pennsylvania are many of Them Strict with Regard to Qualifications for the Lords supper; But I understand they are not so with Regard to Baptism; but do admit all, on owning the Covenant, not under the notion of a Profession of true Godliness. ---If I should be wholly cast out of the ministry, I should be in many Respects in a poor Case : I shall not be likely to be serviceable to my Generation, in a Business of a different nature. I am by nature very unfit for secular Business; and especially am now unfit, after I have been so long in the work of the ministry. --I am now Comfortably settled, have as large a Salary settled upon as most have out of Boston and have the largest & most Chargeable Family of any minister, perhaps within an hundred miles of me.

--I have many Enemies abroad in the Countrey, who hate me for my stingy Principles, Enthusiasm, rigid Proceedings &c. that now are expecting full Triumph over me. I need the Prayers of my Fathers & Brethren who are friendly to me, that I may have wisdom given me by my great master, & that I may be n enabled to conduct with a steady Faithfulness to Him, under all trials, & whatever may be the Issue of this Affair. I seem as it were to be casting my self off from a Precipice; and have no other way, but to go on, as it were blindfold, i. e. shutting my Eyes to every thing else but the Evidences of the mind & will of God, & the Path of duty; which I would observe with the utmost Care. --This western Part of N. England is exceeding full of Noise about this Affair; and few are indifferent. some of the ministers in Connecticut, that have been [^114-note2] chief Favourers of the & Promoters of the late work of God, have a spirit of opposing Zeal excited on this Occasion (from whom I should have least expected it,) And appear strangely ready to entertain groundless Jealousies & receive false Reports & misrepresentations concerning me, which the Countrey is very full of.

As to the three objections to which I have now sent Answers, I think the first of Them may properly be placed the first of all the Objections. as to the placing of the other two, I must leave it to your discretion, who have the Book before you, & see the Order of the Objections, and can better judge where they will most properly come in, than I, who don't fully remember their Order.

If you see Rector Williams at Boston, I hope you will endeavour to disswade Him from writing against me, as He has given out. not that I am afraid of the strength of any fair Arguing against the doctrine I maintain; But such are my peculiarly disadvantageous Circumstances, that he doubtless has it in the Power of his Hands to do me a great deal of Hurt, let his Arguments be never so weak; yea if they should be far worse than Nothing in the esteem of the observing & discerning Readers, yet its only being said that Rector Williams has written an Answer to me, will do me great Hurt with my People. A very likely way to discourage Mr. williams from writing, if He could be made to believe that it would not be for his Honour; and particularly if He could be artfully Led to think that my Books would go to great Britain, to England & sco scotland; & that his opposing me in this matter would be offensive to learned men there, and not for his Honour in that Part of the world. ----I should be glad if his writing might be prevented, not only on the for the Reason already mention'd, but also on this account, that it would save me a long and perhaps almost endless labour of Replying. For tho' I have been with great Reluctance brought to begin to write, yet since divine Providence has compelled me, & I have put my Hand to the Plow, I shall look upon it my duty to pursue the matter to the End; and to write as long as I see there is any need of writing in order to defend this important doctrine, if God gives me Ability & opportunity.

If you observe any Expressions in my M. S. not respectful enough to my Grandfather, I would pray you to inform me of it. I would in no degree be guilty of the sin of Canaan, in his disrespect to his grandfather.

I desire you to inform Messrs Kneeland & Green, that Capt Church & Mr. Potwine of Hartford, when I lately saw 'em together there, desired me, if there we should be Occasion for it, that They would jointly take off an Hundred of the Books, & send Him the money: & Mr. John Brainerd of N. Jersey has engaged to take 50; & Mr. Bellamy of Bethlehem in Connecticut, has engaged to take 50 or more, provided the Undertaker will wait for the money till the Fall of the year.

I thank you for the Pains you have taken to forward the printing of this Book, & your Readiness to take Pains to get subscriptions, & Readiness to take Care of & Correct the Impression. Under these obligations, & in hope of your future Friendliness to me, & Prayers for me under my present difficulties, I subscribe my self. Hond sir, your respectful & most obliged

Brother & servt,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^114-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^114-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## A97. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, June 5, 1749 097.JE-T.Foxcroft 6-5-49

Jonathan EdwardsA097. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 6/5/49. BRBL, f. 1298. Foxcroft underlined some words and phrases, but only JE's underlining is given here.

Northampton June 5. 1749.

Rev. & honoured sir,

I observe that dr Mather in his Ratio Disciplinæ speaks of the Churches of Christ in all Ages and the greatest Lights in the Churches both Ancient & modern, as concurring in this Principle, that Baptism is of larger Extent than the Lords supper, And that many within the visible Church may have the former for their Children, when they Them yet want some Actual Fitness for the latter (p. 81) And if I remember right the synod in New-England that first introduced the Custom of half-members, say to the same Purpose, as the same dr Mather gives an Account of their Proceedings, in his Magnalia. so that I believe what Mr. Baxter says to the Contrary will be disputed. And tho' I don't know but that, notwithstanding this, it may be well to mention mr what mr. Baxter says with Relation to this in a Prefix or Appendix, Yet I don't think tis best for me to Assert (who am so little read in Chh History.) in the Body of my discourse, to assert, the and say any Thing that implies an Assertion, that it has been the current Opinion of the Reformed Churches, that what Qualifies for one sacrament, does for the other sa also, as I think I have done in a Clause of my Answer to one of the last Objections which I sent by my wife, which therefore perhaps had best be left out.

In my Answer to that O the Objection from the Perplexity of Communicants, through their doubting of their state [^115-note1] I desire that these words may be asserted some where in a proper place in my Answer to that Objection. viz

"Mr. Stoddard often taught his People that Assurance was attainable, & that Those who are tr true saints might know it if they would, i. e if They would use the proper means & Endeavours in Order to it. and certainly it is not just to Charge those Perplexities on Gods Institutions, which arise through mens Negligence; and would not be just, if Gods on the supposition of Gods Institutions being such as I suppose Them to be."

I don't know but that In my answer to the Objection from the Passover, I said to this Purpose: that while the Israelites were in Egypt, sacrifices had not as yet been instituted. If I did say so, I desire (if it ben't too late) it may be altered, Thus; The People offered offered no sacrifices to the true God in Egypt; as is evident by Exod. VIII. 25, 26. or words to that Purpose, if they can be added with Good Connection. [--]

Excuse, for being so many ways troublesom, your

most obliged servt,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^115-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## A98. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, July 18, 1749 098.JE-J.Bellamy 7-18-49

Jonathan EdwardsA098. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 7/18/49. Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia, MS copy by Richard Webster. Printed in "Letters to Joseph Bellamy. .. 1739-1787," MS, 2 vols., 1:55.

Northampton, July 18, 1749.

Dear Sir,

I will take care of your proposals for Subscription for your Book[^116-note1] & send 'em by the first opportunity, with a letter or letters, recommending the affair. Mr. Searle[^116-note2] will give you an account of the reasons why I cannot come to his ordination. I am very sorry it happens so, for I have found a great inclination to go; & much the greater because I believe Mr. Searle & the people are oppressed.

I hope you will go & talk with Mr. Sergeant[^116-note3] & wish you would cultivate an acquaintance with him. I should be glad to talk with you about your going to Boston & about several other affairs. If my wool is not yet sent to Hartford, I desire you would take some care about it. Give my love to Mrs. Bellamy[^116-note4] & remember me in your prayers; you know my difficult circumstances. The printer in Boston told me my book on the sacrament[^116-note5] would be done in about three weeks, i.e, now next week; But I understand their language & dont Expect it till the beginning of September.

I am, sir,

Your Brother & entire friend

Jonathan Edwards.

[^116-note1]: Bellamy, *True Religion Delineated* (Boston, 1750).

[^116-note2]: JohnSearle, JE's student, who was to be ordained at Sharon, Conn.

[^116-note3]: Rev. John Sargeant of Stockbridge.

[^116-note4]: Frances Sherman Bellamy.

[^116-note5]: I.e. the *Humble Inquiry*, which was actually available in Northampton the week of Aug. 21.

## A99. Letter to Mary Edwards, July 26, 1749 099.JE-M.Edwards 7-26-49

Jonathan EdwardsA099. JE to Mary Edwards, 7/26/49. ANTS, f. 1749, #7.

Northampton, July 26. 1749.

Dear Child,

You may well think that it is natural for a Parents to be concerned for a Child at so great a distance,[^117-note1] so far out of view, and so far out of the Reach of Communication; where if you should be taken with any dangerous sickness that should issue in death, you might probably be in your Grave before we could hear of your danger.

But yet my greatest Concern is for your souls Good. Tho' you are at so great a distance from us, yet God is every where. you are much out of the Reach of our Care, but you are every moment in his Hands. we have not the Comfort of seeing you, but He sees His Eye is alwaies upon you. And if you may but be sensibly nigh to Him, and have his gracious Presence, 'tis no Matter tho' you are far distant from us. I had rather you should remain Hundreds of miles distant from us and have God nigh to you by his spirit, than to have you alwaies with us, & live at a distance from God. And if the next News we should hear of you should be of your death (tho' that would be very melancholy) yet if withal we should hear of that which should give great Grounds to hope that you had died in the Lord; How much more comfortable would this be (tho' we should have no Opportunity to see you, or take our [^117-note2] leave of you in your sickness) than if we should be with you in all your sickness, & have much Opportunity to tend you, & converse & pray with you, and take an Affectionate Leave of you, and after all have Reason to apprehend that you died without Gods Grace and Favour ! 'Tis comfortable to have the Presence of earthly Friends, especially in sickness & on a death-Bed ; But the great Thing is to have God our Friend, and to be united to Christ, who can never die any more, and whom our death can't separate us from. --my desire and daily Prayer is that in Gods due Time you may, if it may consist with the holy will of God, meet with God where you be, and have much of his divine Influences on your Heart wherever you may be, and that in Gods due Time you may be returned to us again in all Respects under the Smiles of Heaven, and especially in prosperous Circumstances in your Soul ; and that you may find all us alive. But that is uncertain ; for you know what a dying Time it has been with in us in this Town, about this Time of year, in Times years Past. There is not much sickness prevailing among us as yet : But we fear whether mortal sickness is not beginning among us : Yesterday Eliphaz Clap's remaining only son died of the Fever & Bloody Flux, and is to be buried to day. May God fit us all for his will. [^117-note3]

I hope you will maintain a strict & Constant watch over your self, & against all Temptations; that you don't forget & forsake God ; & particularly that you don't grow slack in Secret Religion. Retire often from this vain world, & all its Bubbles & empty Shadows & vain Amusements, and Converse with God alone ; And seek that divine Grace & Comfort the least drop of which is more worth than all the Riches, Gayety, Pleasures & Entertainments of the whole world.

If Madam Stoddard of Boston, or any of that Family should send to you to invite you to come there & remain there on your Return from Portsmouth, 'till there is Opportunity for you to come Home, I would have you accept the Invitation. I think it probable They will invite you. But if otherwise I would have you go to Mr. Bromfield's. He & Madam Both told me you should be welcome. After you are come to Boston, I would have you send us word of it. Try the first Opportunity, that we may send for you without delay.

we are all through divine Goodness in a tolerable State of Health. The Ferment in Town runs very high concerning my opinion about the Sacrament ; but I am no better able to foretell the Issue than when I last saw you.[^117-note4] But The whole Family has indeed much to put us in mind & make us sensible of our dependence on God's Care & Kindness, and of the vanity of all human dependances. and we are very loudly called to seek his Face, trust in Him, & walk closely with Him . Commending to the Care & special Favour of an heavenly Father, I am

your very affectionate Father

Jonathan Edwards

Your mother & all the Family give their Love to you.

[^117-note1]: During the summer of 1749, Mary Edwards was in Portsmouth, N.H.

[^117-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^117-note3]: **marginal.** [3]

[^117-note4]: JE preached Job Strong's ordination sermon in Portsmouth on June 28, 1749, and left in early July.

## A101. Letter to Ebenezer Parkman, September 11, 1749 101.JE-E.Parkman 9-11-49

Jonathan EdwardsA101. JE to Ebenezer Parkman, 9/11/49. AAS, Curwen Family Papers, box 3, f. 2.

Northampton septem. 11. 1749.

Rev. & dear Brother.

I doubt not but you very much wonder that I did not call to pay my Respects to you in my late Journey to Portsmouth. And indeed you have Reason to wonder at it. for truly it was very Strange that Circumstances should so happen as to afford a sufficient excuse for such a Neglect. However when you have heard the Circumstances, I doubt not but your wonder will be lessen'd.

when I set out from home, It was what I had in view to spend a Night at your House in my Journey down. when I set out from Home I intended to go to Brookfield the first day, and the next to Westborough & lodge at your House. But I met with a great deal of difficulty with my Companion, Mr. Lyman[^119-note1]. After we came to Cold spring, He was so terrified with Accounts we there met concerning the drought in the Parts below, that He was very loth to go forward; I had hard work to perswade yea He was so discouraged that we actually rode Back three miles : and I could get Him no further than Cold-spring that By the next morning He was perswaded to go forward, and we went as far as Worcester that day. And understanding that the way to Portsmouth was through Concord, & supposing your House to be much out of the way thither, and being loth to put Mr. Lyman out of [^119-note2] his way with whom I had met with so much difficulty to get Him along, I determined to leave my visit at your House 'till my Return. And accordingly laid out my Affairs : and hoped to set out from Boston on Wednesday, so as to be sure of having Time enough afore me. But when in Boston, I found I could not finish my Business so as to Begin my Journey before Thursday. However [I] intended to come & lodge at your House on Thursday night. But when Thursday came it proved a very rainy day: It began to rain in the Night, and continued raining pretty freely & plentifully most of the day. which tho' a very merciful & happy Event after so extreme a drought, yet gave some Exercise of mind concerning my Journey. I had publickly told my People that I hoped to return to 'em after two sabbaths. And I concluded they would be destitute if I was absent. and I was especially loth to leave 'em destitute at this critical time & difficult Time with me & my People I therefore resolved to strive to perform the Journey in the two remaining days of the week. And accordingly laid out my self very much in order to it. I disturbed Mr. Bromfield's Family between 3 & 4 in the morning, & called up his son to send Him for my Horse to Roxbury. My Horse I found was become poor & dull by being so long kept in Pastures burnt up [^119-note3] with drought. But by the way I happily fell in with Company, which seemed to encourage & help forward my Horse. And with their Help just made it out to reach Worcester that night without being much exposed to the malignant Influence of the Evening Air. My Company were strangers, & had their way through Marlborough : and if I had forsaken Them for the sake of coming through Westborough, I could have had no Time at all with you, and should at last have found my self unable to reach Worcester, and so wholly have defeated my design of getting Home that week. However it proved unhappy that I strove so much for it, for I almost ruin'd my Horse (He has not got over it yet) & worried my self exceedingly, & the next day was again hinder'd by the Rain, so that after all I could not get Home.

I not long since received a Letter from you (dated May 18.) a long Time after it was written. However I thank you for it. ---I had heard before of the Endeavours of your Association for a Reformation; Mr. Emerson of Groton sent me a Copy of the Ar Articles you agreed upon ; And I sent a Copy of them to Scotland to some of my Correspondents there.[^119-note4]

-- It has been a Time of great Ferment among my People for a long Time among on account of Principles relating to the Qualifications for Christian sacra ments. My Books on that subject have been among [^119-note5] them about three By which the Fermentation seems to be much quell'd for the present. They seem not to know what to say to my Book ; But are waiting to see what some Body else will say to it in some Answer They suppose will be written to it. ---It is uncertain what the Issue of the Affair will be.

---However, there has of late appeared some degrees of awakening on the minds of some of young People, more than has been in five years before. which I look upon very remarkeable, at so unlikely a Time of great uneasiness of the People with their Minister. I desire, dear sir, your Prayers both for me & my People in our present difficult Circumstances. And I desire we may from Time to Time remember one another according to your kind Proposal, formerly made. My wife joins with me in Respectful & Cordial salutations to you & Mrs. Parkman, I am dear sir,

your obliged & very respectful

Friend & Brother,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^119-note1]: Possibly Isaac Lyman, who had been called to the church of York, Maine, and was to be ordained in Dec. 1749.

[^119-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^119-note3]: **marginal.** [3]

[^119-note4]: **[2].** ISee letter to James Robe of May 23, 1749, for a copy of the Worcester County Association's covenant.

[^119-note5]: **marginal.** [4]

## A102. Letter to Northampton Precinct Committee, November 9, 1749 102.JE-N'tonPrec 11-9-49

Jonathan EdwardsA102. JE to Northampton Precinct Committee, 11/9/49. ANTS, Dwight MS copy; Dwight ed., 1:322-23.

[1. ANTS, Dwight MS copy of "Narrative," pp. 18-20:]

Dear friends & brethren

"I never heard that any such thing was proposed or thought of by the Committee of the Precinct as is proposed in their Report[^120-note1] untill yesterday; their determination was shewn me last night by a messenger from them, one of their number; & I have had no objection opportunity to confer with the Committee about it or to offer any objection to them against their proposal. I therefore think it requisite that I should at this time signify to you the reasons why the thing proposed by them appears to me not to be regular or reasonable.

1. As the proposal of the Committee is expressed they desire that a church meeting should be warned to see if the Church will not call a council or meeting of ministers to advise to measures to be taken by the church in order to issue the dispute between the minister of the Precinct & the Precinct, which I think is not proper. If the Church call a Council, it will doubtless be in order to be assisted with regard to some controversies or difficulties of its own, & not to remedy the disputes of the Precinct. The business of a Precinct meeting is to manage the affairs of a Precinct; & the business of a Church-meeting is about the affairs of a church & not about the affairs of civil societies. It is not yet certain that there is any dispute or difference [^120-note2] between the Pastor & the Church, for this has never been properly tried.

"2. If I do not misunderstand the Report of the Committee, it is therein proposed that the church meeting should in the warning be limited to a particular method of managing the business they meet upon viz. to consider whether to call a council of neighbouring ministers to advise to measures &c. I am not against warning a church meeting, if you desire to consider of proper measures to be taken to secure & promote the interests of religion, & the church's own welfare under its present circumstances. But I do not know why the Church should be limited to any certain method of proceeding which the Precinct has thought of The Precinct has no more business to limit or direct the Church to a certain method in managing its affairs, than the Church has to direct & limit the Precinct in the management of its Affairs. It is not yet known, that the Church will not themselves agree on some measures to bring their own difficulties to an end, & they will not think proper to choose a Committee of their own to that end, who may be successful [in contriving][^120-note3] a method, to which the Church may agree, which may supersed the need of a Council.

"My end in sending this writing to you is not to perplex you nor clog any reasonable proceedings, but to do my [duty][^120-note4] to you as your guide in religious matters & that I may do what is proper to prevent any just blame that you or I myself might hereafter fall under; & therefore I hope that what I have said will be taken in good part, from your affectionate pastor, who desires that you may go in the way of your duty, & in the way of God's blessing & may be happy in God's favour.

"Jonathan Edwards"

Northampton, Nov. 9, 1749.

[2. Dwight ed., 1:322-23:]

Dear friends and brethren,

I never heard that any such thing was proposed, or thought of by the Committee of the Precinct, as is proposed in their Report, until yesterday ; their determination was shown me last night, by a messenger from them, one of their number; & I have had no opportunity to confer with the Committee about it, or to offer any objection to them against their proposal. I therefore think it requisite, that I should at this time signify to you the reasons, why the thing proposed by them appears to me not to be regular or reasonable.

1. As the Proposal of the Committee is expressed, they desire that a church meeting should be warned, to see if the Church will not call a Council, or meeting of ministers, to advise to measures to be taken by the Church, in order to issue the dispute between [^120-note5] tween the *minister of the Precinct* and the *Precinct*, which I think is not proper. If the *Church* call a Council, it will doubtless be in order to be assisted, with regard to some controversies or difficulties of *its own*, and not to remedy the disputes of the *Precinct*. The business of a Precinct meeting is to manage the affairs of a Precinct ; and the business of a Church-meeting is about the affairs of a Church, and not about the affairs of civil societies. It is not yet certain, that there is any dispute or difference between the Pastor and the Church, for this has never been properly tried.

2. If I do not misunderstand the Report of the Committee, it is therein proposed, that the Church-meeting should, in the warning, be limited to a particular method of managing the business they meet upon, viz. To consider, whether to call a Council of neighbouring ministers, to advise to measures, etc. I am not against warning a Church-meeting, if you desire it, to consider of proper measures to be taken, to secure and promote the interests of religion, and the Church's own welfare, under its present circumstances. But I do not know, why the Church should be limited to any certain method of proceeding, which the Precinct has thought of. The Precinct has no more business to limit or direct the Church to a certain method, in managing its affairs, than the Church has to direct and limit the Precinct, in the management of its affairs. It is not yet known, that the Church will not themselves agree on some measures, to bring their own difficulties to an end, or that they will not think proper to choose a Committee of their own, to this end, who may be successful in contriving a method, to which the Church may agree, which may supersede the need of a Council.

My purpose, in sending this writing to you, is, not to perplex you, nor clog any reasonable proceedings, but to do my duty to you, as your guide in religious matters, and that I may do what is proper, to prevent any just blame, that you, or I myself, might hereafter fall under ; and therefore, I hope that what I have said, will be taken in good part, from your affectionate pastor, who desires that you may go in the way of your duty, and in the way of God's blessing, and may be a people happy in his favour.

Jonathan Edwards.

*Northampton, Nov.* 9, 1749.

[^120-note1]: The Precinct Report of Nov. 6, 1748, printed in Dwight ed., 1:322: At a meeting of the Committee, chosen by the first Precinct of Northampton, to concert what measures are proper for said Precinct to take, in order to issue the dispute, between the Rev. Mr. Edwards, minister of said Precinct, and the Precinct, respect- ing the admission of persons to complete standing in the Christian Church; said Committee determined to report, that they judge that it is expedient, that the Precinct endeavour that there may be a meeting of the Church in said Precinct, to see if the Church will apply to some of the neighbouring ministers, for their advice and coun- sel, respecting measures to be taken by the Church in the said af- fair; which application to the ministers aforesaid, said Committee jdge the best expedient in the present difficulty ; which conclu- sion the Committee came into unanimously, having previousl con- ferred with Mr. Edwards, that they might the better determine what would conduce to the end aforesaid. Ebenezer Pomeroy, John Clark, Joseph Wright, Noah Cook, Samuel Mather, Noah Wright, Ebenezer Hunt, Seth Pomeroy, Joseph Hawley.*Northampton, Nov.* 6, 1749."

[^120-note2]: **marginal.** [19]

[^120-note3]: Supplied from printed version (Dwight ed., 1:323).

[^120-note4]: Supplied from printed version (Dwight ed., 1:323).

[^120-note5]: **marginal.** [323]

## A103. Letter to Northampton Church, November 13, 1749 103.JE-ChhComm. 11-13-49

Jonathan EdwardsA103. JE to Northampton Church Committee, 11/13/49. Williams College Lib., Williamsiana Collection, vol. 9, p. 27.

That a Council be called, mutually Chosen, to consider of the present Circumstances of this Church, relating to the Controversy subsisting between Pastor & People, concerning the Qualifications of Communicants; & to give their Advice what Course we shall take to bring this dispute or Controversy to an Issue: And in general, what is to be done in our present Circumstances in Order to the Churches Peace & Prosperity. Proposed by

Jonathan Edwards

[*on verso, action of church committee:*]

The Comttee of the first Church in Northampton Appointed by the Church to Consider the within proposal & report to the Church what is best to be done, report as follows viz that the Church do Join with Mr Edwards According to the within proposals of having A Council & the Committee Agree to the Number of five & would not be A greater Number if the Church think fit to be Mutually Chosen & to Appointed to Meet in this Town four weeks hence from next thursday

Comttee Timo Dwight

Joseph Hawley

Increase Clark

Noah Wright

## A104. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, November 21, 1749 104.JE-T.Foxcroft 11-21-49

Jonathan EdwardsA104. JE to Foxcroft, 11/21/49. BRBL, f. 1290.

Northampton Novem 21. 1749.

Rev & honoured Sir,

I condole you on the awful Breach God has made in your Family, Since I last Saw you, in the death of Mrs Foxcroft. By what I have heard of the the amiable Qualities & Endowments she was possessed of, your Loss, & the Loss of your whole Family must needs be exceeding great. The Breach made in a Family by the death of such an one, in such a Place and Relation, must be great, & as it were wide as the Sea. Yet those excellent Qualifications that render your Loss very great, must in a peculiar manner yi afford you Comfort in your Affliction; as They give you confidence that death has been an happy Change to Her, and that now she is in blissful Circumstances, tho' she be taken from you, & her Body moulders in the dark & silent Grave. so that altho' your sorrow be great, yet you mourn not for Her, but for your self; And in mourning for your self, as left by her alone in this evil world, your sorrow has this alleviation, or rather blessed Consolation attending it, that your separation from her is not final & perpetual; for those that sleep in Jesus will God will bring with Him; And then you shall again meet her in joyful Circumstances, & be caught up together with her to be meet the Lord in the Air, and shall both together be ever with the Lord. In the mean Time, dear sir, may you have much of the Presence of her G & your God [^122-note1] & saviour, who is all in all; and who is the unfailing Fountain of all that is amiable and comfortable & profitable in the most desireable of Creatures.

My Afflictions & Troubles are also very Great; Tho' of another Kind. The Difficulties in this Church relating to my opinion about the Qualifications of Communicants are come to great Height indeed. Our Circumstances are not easily conceived by those that are at a distance. On the Sabbath in Octob. 15 15 I proposed that a day should be set apart by the Church for solemn Fasting & Prayer, to seek to God for his direction & help under our present difficulties, and that the services of the day should be carried on by the neighbouring ministers; which I proposed, as supposing that their services would be more acceptable than mine: and it seemed to be unanimously agreed to. And there being several Persons in the Town that desired to come into the Church, who are hopefully converted, and stood ready to make a Profession of Godliness, who had hitherto been kept out because a Committee of the Church had refused to consent That They should make any publick Profession of Godliness, & co & chose rather that They should not come in at all, than come in in that way; I proposed that the neighbouring ministers that assisted at the Fast should be applied to for advice in that matter to see if They could not direct us [^122-note2] into some Method wherein These Persons might be admitted consistent with a good Conscience in both Pastor & People. This was objected against. then it was proposed by one of the Brethren that these ministers should be applied to for Advice with Respect to a Method of the Churches being informed of the Reasons of my opinion; because it was said the People had not generally read my Book, nor were like to; & that great Part of the Church were never like to be informed Unless they were directed into some other way by ministers. There was then considerable discourse of the Peoples hearing my Reasons delivered from the Pulpit, seeing it was confessed that a very great [part] of the Church had not read, [JE's om.] & were not like to read my Book. But this also was objected against, & nothing was determined. Therefore the Meeting was adjourned 'till the next Sabbath for further consideration of these Matters; & the Fast was appointed to be on the Thursday following that Sabbath. The People went away, as appear'd, many of Them in a great Ferment of Mind. On Monday, the next day, a Considerable number of Them met together, & subscribed a writing, directed to the Committee of the Parish or Precinct, demanding a Precinct Meeting, the next Thursday, to take into consideration my Opinion respecting Qualifications of [^122-note3] Members of the Church; and to apply to me, and desire me to recede from my Principles; and if I refused, to see if the Precinct would not use Endeavours for a separation between the Pastor & People. Accordingly the Precinct Meeting was warned and Convened on the next Thursday. But some At the meeting it was moved and insisted upon by (I suppose) two or three Persons that I should be desired to it should be put to vote whether I should be desired to deliver the Reasons of my Opinion from the Pulpit, and it pass'd in the negative. Then some of the more considerate objected against the Precincts proceeding to the Business for which the meeting was warned before the Fast, which we had appointed to seek direction & help from God, accordingly the meeting was adjourned for a Fortnight.

The next Sabbath the Church was stayed according as had been determined the Sabbath before; & we entered on some further discourse on things that had been discoursed on the sabbath before; And it was in the first Place put to vote whether the Church would consent that such amongst as were able & willing to make a publick Profession of Godliness should be admitted into the Church with such a Profession fo (rather than not be admitted at all) for the present, 'till our unhappy Controversy could be brought to an Issue: and there was but a very few votes for it. Then it was put to vote whether the neighbouring ministers that were expected at the Fast should [^122-note4] not be sought to for their Advice in this matter, to see if they could not find out a way that these Persons whom all agreed to be qualified, should be admitted in some way that might be safe & satisfying to both sides. for this also there was but very few votes. Then it was put to vote whether the Church would not consent to hear the Reasons of my Opinion from the Pulpit on Lectures appointed for that End (for They would look upon it Profaneness to hear 'em on the sabbath) seeing it seemed to be a thing beyond dispute, that a great Part of the Church had not been informed, nor were like to be informed of my Reasons any other way. But this also pass'd in the negative. Then I proposed that it should be refer'd to the neighbouring ministers whether It was not reasonable that I should be thus heard, all things considered. very much was said against it, [-] with much warmth, and some injurious Reflections; and when it was put to vote and passed in the negative.[^122-note5]

The next Thursday we had our Fast. And the Thursday following Novem 2. The Precinct met according to adjournment, and Chose a Committee of nine men to consider what Course to take, and confer with me, & make Report to the next meeting; & then adjourned Themselves for a week. The Committee chosen were many of them some of those that were most violently engaged in this Controversy. The [^122-note6] next day this Committee came to me, and told me that They had all agreed to make me this Proposal or offer; which if I would consent to, they would endeavour to bring the Precinct to yield to; viz. that the People should hear me preach in defence of my Opinion, provided I would first draw out my sermons at Len each sermon at Length, in a legible Character, & give it to Them, and give Them opportunity to carry it to some minister, that He might see it, & prepare an Answer to it, before I delivered it; and that then I might deliver it, provided I would consent that He should deliver his Answer immediately after it. I told Them that at present I could not think it to be my duty to comply with this Proposal, unless it were also provided that I should also see the discourses of my Antagonist, as He was to see mine. I then told Them what I thought of the Irregularity of the Precinct's taking this Ecclesiastical affair into their Hands. but they strenuously justified it. And after long continued then the Committee went away without concluding any Thing, after long continued uncomfortable disputing, and some harsh Reflections & injurious Charges. And several of Them afterwards did very industriously endeavour to make me appear in the highest degree ridiculous by much misrepresenting my talk at that Time. --This Committee met afterwards at another House, by Themselves; and drew up a Report, Wherein they declare their O it to be their Opinion that the Precinct should endeavour that there should be meeting of the Church to see if the Church would not apply to some of the [^122-note7] neighbouring ministers, for their Advice what was to be done to Issue the dispute between me & the Precinct, respecting the Admission of members into the Church.

On Nov. 9. the Precinct met to receive their Report & having understood what the report was, I sent a Letter to the Precinct, informing Them that if I was not against warning a Church meeting if They desired it, to consider of proper measures to be taken secure & promote the Interest of Religion & the Churches wellfare under its present Circumstances; But did not Think it was proper for me to call the Church together, to take measures to issue disputes of the Precinct*,* as was proposed ; and that I did not think the Church should be limited to an or directed by the Precinct in the management of its affairs. But my Letter was taken in very ill Part, and wholly disregarded. They therefore Accepted the Report of the Committee, & appointed two of the deacons to come to me to desire a Church meeting, 1 to determine a vote whether the Church were of my mind with Respect to Qualifications &c. 2 To see if the Church will apply to some neighbouring ministers for Advice what Course to Take. & then proceeded to add ten more to the Precinct Committee, but without g giving them any Instructions, or appointing Them any Business; B which I suppose was an oversight. But I conclude their design that was that this large Committee of ni 19 should in general take care of their affairs, & see that they were managed effectually. Then They adjourned their meeting for four weeks.

The next day, the two deacons came to me with a Copy of the vote of the Precinct, desiring me to warn a Church meeting &c as aforesaid.

The sabbath following I warned a Church meeting to be the next day, to consider what Course ought to be taken by this Church under its present difficulties, with Respect to the Admission of members into the Church. The Church accordingly met. The meeting was open'd by Prayer. Then one of the Principal Brethren shew'd Himself greatly displeased that I had used such general Terms in my warning of the meeting, and had not warned it in such Terms as the Precinct had directed me; and uttered several very injurious Reflections & Charges; and declared that If I would not warn a Church meeting for the Purposes the Precinct directed, They would warn Them Themselves[^122-note8]. After I had given some Reasons of my Conduct, I told the Church that I thought the state of the Church did greatly demand the assistance of a Council; and that we needed the advice of a large Council, that should look into our Circumstances and give us Advice in general, what we should do for our Peace and wellfare; and insisted that I should be allowed to nominate half the Council. After much debate upon it the meeting was adjourned for a week; and a Committee of five Persons chosen to consider of the Matter, & confer upon it with the Pastor, & report their Opinion at the next Meeting. The Committee ag all excepting one agreed to my Proposal of a Council mutually [^122-note9] chosen.

Yesterday the Church met according to adjournment, and after Prayer, the Report of the Committee was read; & then the dissenting Committee-man got up, & gave the Reasons why he did not agree to it, with some very reproachful charges on me. And suggested that there was some snare laid to entrap The People in my Proposal of a Council mutually Chosen. which seemed to alarm the People and They greatly insisted that the Council should all be of neighbouring ministers. and a very uncomfortable meeting we had. after long debating They a determined to add ten to the Church Committee & Chosen the warmest spirited men They could find, & would accept no others: when men of Calm Tempers were nominated, They would not vote Them. this Committee are further to consider what to do, and the meeting is adjourned for a Fortnight; after They had voted That the sacrament of the Lords Supper should be discontinued, & no more administer'd during the Continuation of the present Controversy.

Thus Things have gone on. The Alienation of the People is exceeding great. They have had, not a little to increase the Flame from some Gentlemen abroad; and particularly from Col. Wms of Weathersfield & Mr Ashley of deerfield. A great Part of my People seem to be industriously engaged to reproach me at Home & abroad; [^122-note10] & represent all that I say & do in the darkest Colours. and seek my separation from 'em very much as a man would strive to gain his Point, in a great Law-Suit. And indeed I have not the least Expectation of continuing their minister; tho' I believe my People think I am struggling to my utmost for it. I think the People seem to be in awful Circumstances, and in the high way to Ruin, for the Present & future Generations; And I durst not leave them without first using all proper Endeavours that They may be saved from Ruin, in the Use of suitable means, As by the Advice of an able & proper Council &c. And then besides, since I am in so many Respects reflected upon and reproach'd for my Conduct, I t & so many misrepresentations are continually carried abroad in the Countrey, I think it greatly concerns me, before I leave this People that our Affairs should be looked into & Judged of by an Impartial Council. And indeed I greatly need the Advice of such a Council to know how to conduct my self in so difficult a situation. I earnestly desire your Prayers, & desire you would lay my Case before other ministers, as that you think are friendlily disposed, & desire their Prayers for me, that I may be have Gods Presence & be guided by his Counsel in these great trials [^122-note11] w & Temptations. And wish you would write me your Thoughts.

And I desire you would lend me Mr Baxter, & Langley & any other[^122-note12] good Book you have on this Controversy, & commit Them to the Care of Col. dwight; who will convey Them safely.

And There is another affair I would say something of, and that is concerning the Indians

& stockbridge[^122-note13]. ---I wish that the Commissioners would now take Care that there may be a man sent Them of sound Principles, & a pious Character. There has been so much contributed towards an Indian school there, that if the affair may be under the Care of a Missionary of Good Character, there there seems to be the best door for gradually propagating the Gospel among the Indians that is open'd at Present. If the school flourishes 'tis very likely some of the six nations would send their Children there to be instructed, & that the good Effects would be very extensive : I hope sir you will accept these Hints with Candour and ever remember with Christian Charity & Compassion before God,

your Respectful son & ser obliged servt

Jonathan Edwards.
