I declare I have no disposition to continue in the Pastoral Relation to this Church They retaining & manifesting their present settled aversion to it after such a Council as I have insisted on have had fair opportunity on a view of our state to judge whether it dont admit of some other Remedy to our Calamities & to give us their own Judgment & Advice in order to a Reconciliation & ag to your Consenting to continue longer under my ministry. (if They shall think fit to use any). I say if after this you appear still fix'd in an aversion to my being any longer your minister my private Inclination & judgment is that you should be gratified by an [-] Immediate separation. Tho' at the same Time I don't think it proper to bind my self by any Promises or come to any absolute determination before I have had the Advice in of a Council in so great & Important an affair. Because for us either of us to do thus & then send for a Council to advise us would be preposterous & inconsistent.

I declare that as the above mention'd is my private Inclination & Judgment so I verily believe that it will be the Judgment & advice of su the Council provided such a Council be called as I insist on

I declare I have no scheme or secret design in view to bring in the Chh into any snare to oblige Them to so that They should at last be obliged to continue in under my ministry contrary to what shall finally appear to be their fix'd Inclination after any means the Council may think fit to use to reconcile Them to it & if the Council advise to any such Thing it will not be unexpected to me & will not in the least owing to any design [^131-note1] or Contrivance of mine & will be altogether unexpected to me i. e. It will be unexpected to me if they advise to my finally continuing contrary to the Chhs fix'd Inclination &c-*

I declare that I have no desire that the Time should be lengthen'd out before a Council is called in order to bring our matters to some but that on the Contrary I desire it may be be spe speedily that the ma Calling such a Council may be hastened.

I declare that I decline setting aside the vote passed the last monday. not because it was my own draught or because I desire to get the my will the victory & my will & or obtain any victory over others but because nor because I am fond of those very words or Phrases but because I insist on the things therein contained whi They being only Essential things I studied when I drew the vote to only barely to insist such Things as the nature of our Case requires the Judgmt & Advice of a Council in upon And I think to set aside the vote of when passed after so long Consideration and debating upon it unless it w be with a view so to some material Alteration would be tri nothing but Trifling & to & to no pur other purpose but to open a door for [ ] a long Continued frivolous Jangle Jangling

And whereas many of the Church have intimated expressed a fear or suspicion that if the Couns Council had so large a Liberty of advisin Judging & Advising as is expressed in the forementioned vote They would perswade me to comply so far with the Chh as again to admit members in our former man into the Chh in our former manner leaving Pe every one to his own Ju act fo tho not fully brought off from my opinion. & some have intimated a suspicion that I expected it my self & acted with this view in I now declare that I have never taken one step with this Ex view or Expectation And Particularly that it is not any s & that I have not such Expecta tion & never had any such Expectation & that it is not because I would make a Reserve for such an Event that I insist on such Liberty of Judgment & advice as is ex in the Council [^131-note2] as is express'd in the forementioned vote and oppose their being Limited as is proposed in Maj. Pomroy's draught. But because I am not willing to have any Hand in a Thin what I judge to be in its own Nature unfit & preposterous for which I am satisfied I should be much blamed abroad & lay my self under disadvantages & should not be able to vindicate my self. & also because I doubt whether members of a Council will be willing to come from a distance if tied up in such a manner from giving advice & acting their own Judgmt.

As I declared to this Purpose before in the Chh meeting so I now renew the declaration and know of nothing further I can do at present to convince my Brethren that I these Things declared are true than saying that I have declared them by declaring that I have spoken uprightly & in the simplicity of my Heart.

If there remains a fix'd Resolution the either that the Chh Council Ccalled shall not have Liberty of advising giving advice for a Remedy of our Calamity according to their own Judgmt & Judges for thems. whether it be a separation an immediate separation be best or to confine me wholly to this County t in my choice I dont think it will tend to any Purpose to call another Chh meeting unless it be to repeat fruitless wrangling & strife. but if there is be a disposition further to Consider of these matters I stand ready to call the Chh together on at any Time I shall be desired.

N. H. March. 30. 1750.

[JE to Noah Cook, 3/30/50. BRBL, f. 1283 (fair copy)]

To Deac. Cook of Northampton.

Dear Brother,

I now make the following declaration, which I am willing you should show to any of the Members of this Church, whom you please, as you have Opportunity.

I declare I have no disposition to continue in the pastoral Relation to this Church, They retaining their present Settled Aversion to it, after such a Council as I have insisted on have had fair Opportunity, on a View of our calamitous state, to judge whether it don't admit of some other Remedy, & to give their own Judgment & Advice, & use their own Means (if They shall think fit to use any) in Order to a Reconciliation, & in Order to your consenting to continue longer under my Ministry: I say, if after this you appear still fix'd in an Aversion to my being any longer your Minister, my private Inclination & Judgment is that you should be gratified by an immediate separation. Tho', at the same Time, I don't think it proper to bind my self by any Promises, as or come to any absolute determination, before I have had the Advice of a Council in so great & important an Affair; Because for either of us to do thus, and then send for a Council to advise us, would be preposterous and inconsistent.

I declare that as the above-mention'd is at present my private Inclination & Judgment, so I fully expect that it will be the Judgment and Advice of the Council when They come; provided such a Council be called as I insist on.

I declare I have no scheme or secret design in view, in any step I take, to bring the Church into any Snare, so that They should at last be obliged to continue under my ministry, contrary to what shall finally appear to be their fix'd Inclination, after any means the Council may think proper to be used. And if the Council advise to any such Thing, it will not be in the least owing to any design or Contrivance of mine, And will be altogether unexpected to me: that is it will be unexpected to me, if They advise to my finally continuing contrary to the Churches fix'd Inclination &c.

I declare that I do not decline Setting aside the vote pass'd the last Monday, because it was my own draught, or because I desire to get my will, or obtain any victory over others, or because I am fond of those very words or Phrases; but because I insist on the Things therein contain'd, They being only essential things. I studied, when I drew the vote, barely to express such Things as the Nature of the Case absolutely requires the Judgment and Advice of a Council in. And I think to set aside the vote, when pass'd, after its being so fully and particularly debated and considered, unless it be with a view s to some material Alteration, would be to open a door to lengthen out our Controversy for the lengthening out our Controversy with frivolous Jangling & strife.

I declare that I have no desire that the Time should be lengthen'd out before a Council is called, in Order to bringing our matters to some Issue: but on the contrary, I desire that the calling such a Council may be hasten'd.

And whereas many of the Church have expressed a Fear or suspicion that if the Council should have so large a Liberty of judging and advising as is express'd in the foremention'd vote, they would perswade me to comply so far with the Church, as to go on to admit members in our form into the Church in our former manner, tho' not fully brought off from my opinion; And some (one at least) intimated a suspicion that I expected it my self, and had long acted with [^131-note3] this view; I now declare that I have never taken one Step with this view or Expectation; and that I have not, & never had any such Expectation; And that it is not because I would make a Reserve for such an Event that I insist on such Liberty of Judgment and Advice in the Council as in is express'd in the forementioned vote, and oppose their being limited as in is opposed in Maj. Pomroys draught; but because I am not willing to have any Hand in what I Judge to be in its own Nature unfit & preposterous; for which I am satisfied I should be much blamed abroad, as laying my self under disadvantages, and should not be able to vindicate my Self; And also because I doubt whether Members of a Council will be willing to come from a distance, if tied up in such a manner from giving Advice and acting their own Judgment.

As I declared Things to the same Purpose with These above before in the Church meeting, so I now renew the declaration, And know of Nothing further I can do at present to convince my Brethren that These things a[re][^131-note4] true, by declaring that I speak uprightly, and in the simplicity of my Heart.

If there remains a fix'd Resolution, either that the Council called shall not have Liberty of giving Advice for a Remedy of our Calamities according to their own Judgment (not that I desire the Church to bind Themselves to stand to their Advice) & judging for Themselves whether an immediate separation be best, or to confine me wholly to this County in my Choice; I don't think it will be to any Purpose to call another Church meeting, unless it be to prolong fruitless wrangling & strife. But if it be thought there is a disposition further to consider of these matters, I stand ready to call the Church together to that End at any Time I shall be desired.

Jonathan Edwards

Northampton March 30. 1750.

## A114. Letter to Thomas Gillespie, April 2, 1750 114.JE-T.Gillespie 4-2-50

Jonathan EdwardsA114. JE to Thomas Gillespie, 4/2/50. ANTS, f. 1750, #2. Printed in *Edinburgh Quarterly Magazine* 1 (1798).

Northampton April. 2. 1750.

Rev. & dear Sir,

I received your Favour of Septem. 19. 1748. the last summer. and would now heartily thank you for it. I suppose it might come in the same ship with Letters I had from my other Correspondents in Scotland, which I answered the last summer ; But it did not come to Hand till a long Time after most of the other and after I had finished and sent away my Answers to Them, and that Opportunity for Answering was past. I have had no Leisure or Opportunity to write any Letters to Scotland 'till now from that Time 'till now, By Reason of the my Peculiar & very extraordinary Circumstances, on Occasio Account of the Controversy that has arisen between me & my People concerning the Profession that ought to be made by Persons that come to Christian sacraments, which is likely speedily to Issue in a seperation between me & my Congregation. This Affair, in the Progress of it, has proved not only a Controversy between me & my People, but between me and a great Part of New-England ; There being many far & near that are warmly Engaged in it. This Affair has unavoidably engaged my Mind, & fill'd up my Time, and taken me off from other Things. --I need the Prayers of my Friends that God would be with me, and direct & assist me in such a Time of Trial, & mercifully order the Issue. As to the Epistolary Controversy, dear sir, between you & me, about Faith & doubting, I am sorry it should *seem* to be greater than it is, through misunderstanding of one anothers meaning, And that the real difference between us is so great as it is in some Part of the Con troversy.

As to the dispute about believing without spiritual Light or sight, I thought I express'd my meaning in my last Letter very plainly : But per I kept no Copy, and it might perhaps be owing to my dulness that I thought so. However I perceive I was not Understood. I cannot find out by any Thing you say to me on this Head, that we really differ in sentiments, but only in words. I acknowledge with you that "all are bound to be lieve the divine Testimony & trust in Christ, --and the want of spiritual Light or sight does not loose from the Obligation one is laid under by the divine Command to believe constantly on Christ and at all seasons, nor excuse Him in any degree for not believing; -Even when one wants the Influence and Grace of the spirit, still He is bound to believe : Ability is not the Rule of duty " I believe the obligation to believe lies on a Person at th who is remaining without spiritual Light or sight," or being in the darkness: No darkness, no blindness no carnality, or stupidity excuses him a moment from having as strong [^132-note1] & lively a faith & Love as ever was E exercised by the Apostle Paul. or rrenders it not sinful in Him that he is at that same moment without such a Faith & Love. And yet I believe it is absurd, and of very hurtful Consequence to urge Persons to believe in the dark, in the manner & in the sense in which many hundreds of done have done in America ; who plainly intend a believing strongly with such a sort of strong faith or great Confidence as is consistent with continuing still, even in the Time of these strong Acts of Faith, without spiritual Light, carnal, stupid, careless & senseless. Their doctrine evidently comes to this, both in sense & Effect, That it is a mans duty strongly to believe with a Lightless, sightless Faith, or to have a Confident but yet a blind, dark & stupid Faith. And such a Faith has indeed been promoted exceedingly by their doctrine ; and has prevailed with its dreadful Effects answerable to the Nature of the Cause. We have had, & have to this day, multitudes of such strong believers, whose bold, proud & stupid Confidence, attended with a very wicked Behaviour, has given the greatest wound to vital Religion the Cause of Truth & vital Religion that ever it suffered in America.

As To what follows, in your Letter, concerning A Persons believing Himself to be in a good Estate, Its being properly of the Nature of Faith ; In this there seems to be some real difference between us. But perhaps there would be none, if distinctness were well observed in the use of words. If by a mans believing that He is in a good Estate, be meant no more than his believing that he does believe in Christ, does love God, &cI think there is nothing of the nature of Faith in it. Because I knowing it or believing it depends on our own immediate sensation or Consciousness, & not divine Testimony. True believers, in the Hope they entertain of Salvation, make use of the following syllogism; He that whosoever believes shall be saved. I believe. Therefore &cAssenting to the major Proposition is properly of the nature of Faith; because the ground of my Assent to that is divine Testimony. But my Assent to the minor Proposition, I humbly conceive is not of the nature of faith, because that does not is not grounded on divine testimony, but my own Consciousness. There The testimony that is the proper Ground of Faith is in the word of God. Rom. 10. 17. Faith cometh by hearing, & Hearing by the word of God. There is such a Testimony given us in the word of God, that He that Believes shall be Saved ; But there is no such Testimony in the word of God as that such an Individual Person, in Scotland such a Town in Scotland or N. England, believes. There is such a Proposition in scripture as that Christ loves those [^132-note2] that love Him ; and therefore that every one is Bound to believe; and a firm believing it on divine Testimony is properly of the nature of Faith; and for any one to doubt of it is properly the heinous sin of unbelief : But there is no such proposition in scripture, or that is any Part of the Gospel of Christ, that such an Individual Person in Northampton Loves Christ. If I know I have Complacence in Christ, I know it the same way that I know I have Complacence in my Wife & Children; viz. by the Testimony of my own Heart, or inward Consciousness. Evangelical Faith has the Gospel of Christ for its Foundation ; But that I love Christ is a Proposition not contained in the Gospel of Christ.

And therefore, that we mayn't dispute in the dark, 'tis necessary that we we well explain what we mean by a Persons believing He is in a good Estate. If thereby we mean only believing the minor of the foregoing syllogism. I believe, or I love God, 'Tis not of the nature of faith; But if by a man's believing Himself to be in a good Estate, be under stood not only the minor, but the Consequence. Therefore I shall be saved, or Therefore God will never leave nor forsake me, then a mans believing his good Estate partakes of the nature of Faith ; for these Consequences depend on divine Testimony in the word of God & Gospel of Jesus Christ. Yea I would observe farther, that a man's judging of the Nature h the Faith or Love he finds in Himself, whether that sort of Faith which He finds, be saving, may depend on his Reliance Reliance on scripture Rules & marks, which are divine Testimonies But his judging that He has those Individual inward Ex arises Acts of understanding & Exercises of Heart that he has, depends on Con inward sensation, & not on the any Testimony of the word of God: The Knowing present Acts depends on immediate Consciousness, & the knowing past acts depends on Memory. And therefore the Fulness of my satis faction that I have now have such an Inward Act or Exercise of mind, depends on the Strength of the Sensation; and my satisfaction that I have had heretofore, depends on the Clearness of my memory, and not on the strength of my Reliance on any divine Testimony. And so my doubting whether I have or have had such individual inward acts is not of the nature of unbelief ; tho' it may arise from unbe lief indirectly ; because if [-] I had had more faith, the Actings of it would have been more sensible, and the memory of them more clear, & so I should have been better Satisfied that I had them.

God seems to have given Abraham's servant a Revelation that The damsel in whom He found such [-] marks, should be Isaacs wife viz. coming to draw water, to with a Pitcher to that well, Her readiness to give Him & his Camels drink &c. should be Isaacs wife. And therefore his Assenting to this was of the nature of Faith, having divine Testimony for its foundation. But his believing that Rebekah was the damsel that had those Individual marks, [^132-note3] his knowing that she came to draw water, & that she let down her Pitcher &c. was not of the nature of Faith ; His knowing this was not from divine Testimony, but from the Testimony of his own senses.

you speak of a saints doubting of his good Estate, as "Part of unbelief," & the opposite of Faith considered in its full compass & Latitude, as one Branch of unbelief, one Ingredient in Unbelief;" And of Assurance of a mans good Estate, as "one thing that belongs to the Exercise of Faith;" I don't know whether I take your meaning in these Expressions ; If you mean that a Persons believing himself to be in a good Estate is one thing that Appertains to the Essence of saving Faith, or that saving Faith in all that belongs to its Essence, yea & Perfection, can't be without it I must humbly ask leave to differ from you. That it a believing that I am in a good Estate is no Part or Ingredient in the Essence of saving Faith, is evident by this ; That The Essence of saving Faith must be compleat in me before it can be true that I am in a good. If I han't as yet acted faith, yea if there be any thing wanting in me to make up the Essence of saving Faith, then I am not as yet in a state of salvation, and therefore can have no ground to believe that I am so. Every thing that belongs to the Essence of saving Faith is prior in the Order of Nature to a mans being in a state of salvation, Because 'tis saving Faith that brings him into such a state : And therefore believing that He is in such a state, can't be one Thing that is Essential or necessary in order to his being in such a state ; for that would imply a Contradiction ; It would be to suppose a mans believing that He is in a good Estate to be prior in the order of nature to his being in a good Estate. But a Thing can't be both Prior & Posterior, Antecedent & Consequent, with Regard to the very same Thing. The Real Truth of a Proposition is in the order of nature first, before its being believed to be true. But 'till a man has already all that belongs to the Essence of saving Faith, that Proposition That He is in a good Estate, is not as yet true. All the Propositions contained in the Gospel, all divine Testimonies that we have in Gods word, are true already, are already laid for a Foundation for faith, and were laid long ago ; But that Proposition I am in a good Estate, not being one of them, is not true 'till I have first believed: & therefore this Proposition can't be known to be true ti believed to be true 'till saving faith be first compleat Therefore the Compleatness of the act of saving Faith won't make it take in a beliefve of this Proposition. nor will the strength or Perfection of the Act cause it to [^132-note4] imply it. If a man in his first act of Faith has ever so great a Conviction of Gods sufficiency and Faithfulness, & let his Reliance on the divine Testimony in the Gospel be never so strong & perfect, all will have tendency to make Him believe, this proposition I am in a good Estate, to be true, 'till it be true; which it is not till the first act of Faith is compleat, & has made it true : -H A belief of divine Testimony in the first Act of Faith may be to any assignable degree of strength & Perfection, without believing that Proposition; for there is no such divine Testimony then extant; nor is there is [sic] any such Truth extant, but in Consequence of the first act of faith. Therefore, (as I said) saving Faith may be with all that belongs to its Essence, & that in the highest Perfection, without implying a belief of my own good Estate. -I do not say it can be without having this immediate Effect; But 'tis rather the Effect of faith, than a Part, Branch, or Ingredient of Faith. And so I don't dispute whether a mans doubting of his good Estate may be a Consequence of unbelief (I doubt not but it is so in those who are in a good Estate) Because if men had the Exercise of Faith in such a degree as They ought to have, It could not but be very sensible & plain that They had it. But yet I think this doubting of a good Estate is entirely a different Thing from the sin of unbelief it self, & has nothing of the nature of unbelief in it ; i.e if we take doubting ones good Estate in the sense in which I have before explained it, viz. for doubting whether I have such individual Principles & Acts in my soul. Take it in a complex sense, & it may have the sin of unbelief in it : As thus; If, altho' I doubt not I have such & such Qualifications, I yet doubt of those Consequences for which I have divine Testimony as if when a Person that doubts not that he loves Christ, yet doubts whether He shall receive a Crown of Life. The doubting of this Consequence is properly the sin of unbelief.

You say, dear Sir, " The Holy Ghost requires us to believe the Reality of his work in us in all its Parts just as it is." & a little before, " The Believer his doubting whether or not He has Faith is sinful, because it is belying the Holy Ghost, denying his work in Him ; so there is no sin to which that doubting can so properly be reduced as Unbelief."

Here I would ask leave thus to express my Thoughts in a diversity from yours. --I think if it be allowed to be sinful for a Believer to doubt whether he has faith such That doubting is not the sin of unbelief on any such account as you mention, viz. as belying [^132-note5] or denying any Testimony of the Holy Ghost. There is difference between doubting of a the being of some word of the Holy Ghost, and doubting denying the Testimony of the Holy Ghost. as there is a difference between doubting concerning some other words of God and denying the Testimony of God. 'Tis the work of God to give a man great Natural Abilities; And if we suppose God requires such a man to believe the Reality of his work, in all its Parts, just as it is; and so that 'tis sinful for Him to at all to doubt of his Natural Abilities being just as good as They are; yet this is no belying any Testimony of God (tho' it be doubting of a work of God) and so is diverse from the sin of unbelief. So if we suppose a very eminent Saint is to blame in doubting whether He has so much Grace as He really has, He indeed dont believe the Reality of Gods work in Him, in all its Parts, just as it is ; Yet He is not therein guilty of the sin of unbelief, against any Testimony of God, any more than the other.

I acknowledge that a true saint, in a carnal & careless frame, to doubt of his good Estate, is sinful, as it were mediately & indirectly, as the Cause of it is sinful, viz. the Lowness & Insensibility of the Actings of Grace in him, and the Prevalence of carnality & stupidity. 'Tis sinful to be without Assurance, or (as we say) 'tis his own Fault, he sinfully deprives Himself of it or foregoes it. As a servants being without his Tools is his sin, when He has carelessly lost 'em, or as 'tis his sin to be without strength of Body, or without the sight of his Eyes, when He has deprived Himself of These by Intemperance ; not that weakness or blindness of Body in their own Nature are sin, for they are Qualities in of the Body & not of the mind, the subject in which sin is inherent. ---'Tis indirectly the duty of a true saint alwaies to rejoyce in the Light of God's Countenance, because sin is the Cause of his being without this Joy at any Time And therefore it was indirectly david's sin that He was not rejoycing in the Light of Gods Countenance, at that Time when He was in the Bed of Adultery with Bathsheba. But yet 'tis not directly a believers duty to rejoyce in the Light of God's Countenance when God hides his Face, But it rather then becomes Him to be troubled and to mourn: so there are perhaps many other Priviledges of saints that are their duty indirectly, & the want of 'em is sinful not simply but complexly [^132-note6] Considered. of this Kind I take the want of Assurance to be of ones good Estate to be.

I think no words of mine either in my Book or Letter implied that a Persons deliverance from a bad frame don't begin with renewed Acts of Faith or Trusting in God : If They did, They implied what I never intended. doubtless if a Saint comes out of an ill frame, where in Grace is asleep it mus & inactive, it must be by renewed actings of Grace : 'Tis very plainly impossible That Grace should begin to cease to be inactive in any other way than by its beginning to be active : It must begin with the renewed actings of some Grace or other : And I know nothing that I have said to the Contrary, but that the Grace that shall first begin sensibly to revive shall be Faith, and that this shall lead the way to the renewed acting of all other Grace, and to the farther Acting of Faith it self. But a Persons coming out of a carnal careless dead frame, by the reviving of Grace in his soul, is quite another Thing from a saints having a strong Faith strong Hope exercise of Faith, or strong hope, or strong Exercise of any other Grace, while yet remaining in a carnal Careless dead frame ; or in other words, in a Frame wherein Grace is so far from being in strong Exercise, that tis asleep & in a great measure without Exercise.

There is a holy Hope, a truly Christian Hope, that the scripture speaks of, that is reckon'd among the Graces of the spirit : And I think I should never desire or seek any other Hope but such an one ; for I believe no other Hope has any holy or good Tendency. Therefore this Hope, this Grace of Hope only, can properly be called a duty : But 'tis just as absurd to talk of the Exercise of this holy Hope, the strong Exercise of this Grace of the spirit, in a Carnal, stupid, secure fr careless Frame, such a [-] frame yet remaining, as it would be to talk of the strong Exercises of Love to God, or Heavenly-mindedness, or any other Grace in remaining in such a Frame.

--Tis doubtless proper earnestly to exhort Those who are in such a Frame to come out of it, by the strong Exercises of all Grace; But I should not think it proper to to press a man earnestly to entertain maintain strong Hope, a strong Holy hope (that Grace of the sp.) NOTWITHSTANDING the prevailing & continuance of great carnality & stupidity (which is plainly the sense of the People I opposed) For this is plainly to press People to an unholy Hope, a strong Hope that is not a no Christian Grace; and that is strong wicked Presumption. And the promoting of this has most evidently been the Effect of such a method of dealing with souls, In innumerable multitudes of awful Instances. [^132-note7]

You mean sir, to suppose t p. 6 & 7 of your Letter that 'tis Gods manner of dealing with his saints, while in a SECURE CARELESS Frame, first to give em Assurance of their good Estate, while They remain in such a Frame, and to make use of that assurance as a mean to bring 'em out of such a Frame. Here again I must crave leave to differ from you, and to think that none of the Instances or Texts you adduce from scripture do at all prove the Point. I think it is Gods manner first to awaken their Consciences, & to bring 'em to reflect upon Themselves, and bring 'em to feel their own Calamity which They have brought upon Themselves by so departing from God, (by which an End is put to their Carelessness & security) and again earnestly & carefully to seek Gods Face, again before They find Him, and before God Restores the comfortable & Joyful sense of his Favour. And I think this is abundantly evident both by scripture and Experience.

You much insist on Jonah as a Clear Instance of the Thing you lay down. you observe that He says Chap. 2. I said I am cast out of thy sight; yet will I look again towards thy holy Temple & v. 7. when my soul fainted within me, I remembered the Lord, and my Prayer came in unto Thee, even into thine Holy Temple. you speak of these words as "demonstrating an assurance of his good Estate and of Gods Favour" (I will not now dispute whether They do or no.) And you speak of this Exercise of assurance &cas his Practice in an Evil Frame, and in a careless Frame; for He slept securely in the sides of the ship , manifesting dismal secu rity, awful Carelessness, in a carnal Frame. That Jonah was in a careless frame secure Frame when He was asleep in the sides of the ship, I don't deny. But, dear sir, does that prove that he was remained still in a careless secure Frame when He uttered Those words Chap. 2. v. 4, 7. in his Heart He said Those Things in the Fishes Belly Chap. 2. v. 4, 7? does it prove that He remained Careless after He was awaked, & saw the terrible storm, & owned it was the Fruit of Gods Anger towards Him for his sins? & does it prove that He still Remained Careless when after the Whale had swallowed Him, when He seem'd to Himself to be in the Belly of Hell? when the waters compassed Him about, even to the soul; & all G as he says, all Gods waves & Billows passed over Him, & He was ready to despair; when he went down to the Bottoms of the mountains,[^132-note8] was ready to think God him had [-] cast him out of his sight, & imprisoned [^132-note9] in a Prison that He could never escape (The Earth with her Bars was about me forever) And his soul fainted within Him.[^132-note10] He was brought into this Condition after his sleeping securely in the sides of the ship, before He said I will look again towards thine Holy Temple &c-He was evidently first awakend out of carelessness & security, before & brought into distress, before He was comforted.

The other Place you also much insist on, concerning the Church of Israel, is very much like This : Before God comforted them Church with the Testimonies of his Favour, after their backslidings, He first, by severe Chastisements, together with the awakening Influences of his spirit, brought 'em out of their Carelessness & carnal security. It appears by many scriptures that this was God's way of dealing with that Pleople. so Hos. 2 Chap. 2. God first Hedged up her way with Thorns, and made a wall that she could not find her Paths. ---And took away her Corn & wine & wool & Flax, destroyed her vines & FigTrees, & Caused her mirth to cease, & b by this means brought her to her self, brought out of her security, carelessness & deep sleep, very much as the Prodigal son was brought to Himself; God brought her first into the Wilderness, before He spake Comfortably to her, & by gave opend to her a door of Hope; By her distress first brought her to say, I will go & return to my first Husband : & then when God spake Comfortably to Her, she called him Ishi, my Husband.[^132-note11] and God did as it were renewedly betroth her unto Him. That 2 of Hosea is very parallel with Jer. 3d One serves well to illustrate & explain the other, And that it was Gods way of dealing with his People Israel, after their Apostacy & carnal security, first to awaken it Them, & under a sense of their sin & misery & before He gave Them sensible Evi- dence of his Favour and not to awaken em ou to bring them sollicitously to seek his Face, before He gave Them sensible Evidence of his Favour, & not to awaken out of security by first making manifest his Favour to 'em, is manifest by many scriptures as Levit. 5 26. 40---42. deut 32. 36---39. 1 King. 8. 47---51. Jer. 29. 12, 13, 14. Chap. 30. 12---22. Chap. 50. 4--8. Ezek. 20. 35, 36, 37. Hos. 5. 15 with Chap. 6. 1---3. Chap. 13. 9, 10. Chap. 14. throughout. [^132-note12]

And besides I would Observe concerning that in Jer. 3. The Prophecy is not concerning the Recovery of backsliding saints, But or the mystical Church, which tho' she had corrupted herself, still continued to be Gods wife ; But concerning Apostate Israel, that forsaken and renounced her Husband, and gone after other Lovers, & whom God had renounced, put away & given her a bill of divorce (v 8) so that her recovery could not by giving her assurance of her good Estate, as still remaining his wife, and that God was already married unto Her; for that was not true, and is not consistent with the context. And whereas it is said v 14. Return O backsliding Children, saith the Lord, for I am married and I will take you one of a city &c. Indeed I am married, in the Hebrew, is in the preterperfect Tense ; But you know sir, that in the Language of Prophecy the præterTense is very commonly put for the future. And whereas it is said v 19. How shall I put Thee among the Children? ---& I said Thou shalt call me Father. I acknowledge this here, my Father, & that Rom. 8. 15 Is the Language of Faith; 'Tis so two ways. 1. 'Tis th such Language of the soul as is the immediate Effect of a lively Faith : I acknowledge that the lively Exercises of Faith do naturally produce satisfaction of a good Estate, as their immediate Effect. 2. 'Tis Language which in another sense does properly & naturally Express the very Act of Faith it self, yea the first act of faith in a sinner, before which He never was in a good Estate ; As thus, supposing a man in distress, pursued by Enemies that sought his Life, should have the Gates of several Fortresses set open before Him, and should be called to from each of Them to fly thither for Refuge, and viewing Them all, & seeing one appearing to Him strong & safe, but the othe rest insufficient, He should accept the Invitation to that one, & fly thither with this Language, This is my Fortress : this is my Refuge : In vain is salvation looked for from the other : Behold I come to this. This is my sure defence. Not that He means that He is already in the Fort within the Fortress & so in a good & safe estate, But this is my chosen Fortress, to which I betake my self for safety. so if a woman were at once sollicited by many Lovers, to give her self to Them in a married state, and beholding the superiour Beauties & Excellencies of one far above all the Rest, should betake her self to Him, & cast her fly into his Arms with this Language ; This is my Husband : behold I come unto Thee : Thou art my spouse. Not that she means [^132-note13] that she is already married to him, but that He is her chosen Husband &c-Thus God offers Himself to sinners as their saviour, God & Father ; And the Language of the Heart of Him that accepts the offer by a true Faith, is, Thou art my saviour; in vain is salvation hoped for from others that offer Themselves Thou art my God & Father. Not that He is already his Child, but He chooses Him, & comes to Him that He may be one of his Children. as Jer in Jer. 3. 19. Israel calls God F her Father, as the way to be put among the Children and be one of Them, and not as being one already. & in v. 21, 22, 23. she is not bou brought out of a careless & secure state by knowing that the Lord is her God ; but she is first brought to consideration, & sense of her sin & misery, weeping & supplica tions for mercy, & conviction of the vanity of other saviours & Refuges. Not only before she has assurance of her good Estate, but before she is brought to fly to God for Refuge that she may be in a good Estate.

As To the Instance of Job; I would only say that I think He, was far f while in his state of sore affliction, Tho' he had some great Exercises of Infirmity & Impatience under his extreme Trials, yet was very far from being in such a Frame Frame as I in tended, when I spoke of a secure, careless, carnal Frame &cI doubt not, nor did I ever question it that the saints hope & Knowledge of their good Estate, is in many Cases of excellent Benefit to help Them against Temption, & Exercises of Corruption.

with regard to the Case of gre extraordinary Temptation & Buf feting of satan, which you mention, I don't very well know what to say further. I have often found my own Insufficiency as a Counsellor in such-like Cases, wherein Melancholy & bodily distemper have so great a Hand, and give satan so great Advantage, as appears to me in the Case you mention : If the Lord do not help, whence should we help? If the Christian Friends of such afflicted, and (as it were) possessed Persons, would from Time to Time pray & Fast for them, it might be a proper Exercise of Christian Charity, and the likeliest way I know of for Relief. ---I kept no Copy of my former Letter to you, & so don't remember fully what I have already concerning this Case. But this I kno have often found with such Melancholy People, that the greatest difficulty don't lie in giving Them good advice, but in perswading [^132-note14] them to take it. One thing I think of great Importance, which is that such Persons should go on in a steady Course of a the Performance of all duties, born of the general & Particular calling , without suffering Themselves to be diverted from it by any violence of Satan, or specious Pretence of his whatsoever, properly ordering, proportioning & Timing all sorts of duties, duties to God, publick, private & secret, & duties to man, relative duties, of Business & Conversation, Family duties, duties of Friendship & good Neighbourhood, duly proportioning Labour & Rest, Intention & Relaxation, without suffering one duty to croud out or Intrench upon another. If such Persons Could be perswaded to this, I think in this way they would be best guarded against the devil, & He would soonest be discouraged, and a good state of Body would be most likely to be gained, & Persons would be act most as if They trusted & rested in God, and would be most in the way of his help & Blessing.

with Regard to what you write concerning immediate Revelations, I have thought of it, & I find I can't say any thing to any Purpose, without drawing out this Letter to a very extraordinary Length : And I am already got to such Length, that I had need to ask your Excuse : I have written enough to tire your Patience. -It has indeed been with great difficulty that I have found time to write so much : And if you knew any extraordinary Circumstances, I doubt not you would excuse my writing any more. I acknowledge the subject you mention is very important : Probably, If God spares my Life, and gives me opportunity, I may write largely upon it. --I know not how Providence will dispose of me: I am going to be Cast on the wide world, with my large Family of 10 Children. ----I humbly request your Prayers for me under my difficulties & Trials.

As to the state of Religion in this Place & this Land it is at pre sent very sorrowful & dark. But I must for a more particular Account of Things refer you to my Letters to Mr. McLaurin of Glasgow & Mr. Robe. so asking a Remembrance in you Prayers I must Conclude by subscribing my self with much Esteem & Respect your obliged Br. & servt

Jonathan Edwards

P. S. July. 3. 1750.

Having had no Leisure to sir finish the Preparation of my Letters to Scotland till before this Time, by Reason of the extraordinary Troubles, Hurries & Confusions of my Unusual Circumstances; I can now inform you that the Controversy between me & my People, that I mention'd in the Beginning of my Letter, has issued in a seperation between me & my People. an ecclesiastical Council was called on the Affair ; who sat here the week before last; who, by a Majority of one voice, determined an immediate seperation to necessary ; and accordingly my the Pastoral Relation to my People was dissolved on June 22. If I can procure the printed Accounts from Boston of the Proceedings of the Council, I will give order to my Friend there to inclose them with this Letter, & direct them to you. ----I desire your Prayers that I may take a suitable Notice of the Frowns of Heaven on me & this People, (between whom was once so great an union) in the bringing to pass such a separation between us; and that these Troubles may be sanctified to me; that God would overrule this Event for his own (which doubtless many Adversaries will rejoyce & Triumph in) that God would open a door for my future Usefulness, & provide for me & my numerous Family, in our present unsettled, uncertain Circumstances, being cast on the wide world. J. E.

## A115. Letter to Samuel Hopkins of Springfield (Draft), April 3, 1750 115.JE-S.Hopkins 4-3-50

Jonathan EdwardsA115. JE to Samuel Hopkins of Springfield, 4/3/50. Draft. BRBL, f. 1313.

To mr Hopkins of springfield

dear B I understand that there wa our People had on yesterday a Precinct meeting for the managing our ecclesiastical affair (as They have had a great many such the w fall & winter past) And that at this meeting it was not determined to Chuse a com a messenger was appointed to a Committee was Chosen to write to the Association in the lower Part of the County to desire their advice concerning in some things concerning the Controversy subsisting between me & this Chh. & have the appointed a Messenger to carry the Letter. The whole meeting as I was informed consisted of 44. and Persons & the majority that voted this was 26. as I was informed by one that Counted 'em They gave me no notice of the desi meeting or their design in it so that I had no opportunity either to concur or remonstrate. They have given me notice of what They have done or what particulars They intend to ask the Judgmt of the Association in It was proposed by one in the meeting that They as I was was in Informed that I should be notified of what They determined that I might have opportunity to send also if I thought fit but it the motion was rejected with much dislike. why They chuse rather to send to the mini be your association rather than our own I dont know. unl unless only as I am informed that maj. Pomroy sai Jun. said he had conversed with several of the ministers & that by their conversa. he was perswaded They stoo that association would give advice take Cognizance of * their affairs. ** I conjecture that one main Thing that They are would have your Judgmt in in is whether is a controversy between me & the Chh. whether The I ought not to be allowed a Choi to chuse two of the members in Ten of the Council that shall decide our affairs have powers to d Issue our affairs I am p satisfied I am that if you knew all Circumstances you would be fully perswaded we needed no previous Council to decide this Controversy than our or any further advice than we have had or if we did that there could be no occasion it was proper that this previ I should have some hand in this previous Council in calling them & Refering Representing things before [--] & that tis especially needless for them in if they will have this controversy judged by a council in which they only have a hand that there is no need of having their this association to go to yours or if even all These But if you judged all these things were proper. yet I am perswaded you would not Judge it very unreasonable that in Them not think the the offer properly [-] brought to you when Referred only by about 26. of the precinct at a precinct meeting instead of being Referred by the Chh which Consists of about 300 male members But if you would allow of em all those forementioned things yet you doubtless you would not think it proper to [-] pass undertake undertake to Judge this matter of C [--] verify or or anything Else that has become matter of Controversy between me & the Chh only concerning our mutual Rights only as being the Representations of one side. It would be impossible you should have a Just view of our affairs without a very long Rehearsal & corr cor so as to put you into a proper Capacity to Jud Judg to Judge of my The Points or advise in matters relating to our controversy. & to be sure cant expect at of em only on the Re Representation of a those that ans of one side. we have In the winter The Chh and Pastor have already by joint agreemt the w mutual choice called a Council of Chhs the winter Pa chiefly to decide this point in controversy between us viz. whether I had a Right to go out of the County for a part of the Council that shall have Power to Issue in our affairs who were so far from thinking that there was no need of hearing both parties in order to decide it That they at their first sitting spent about two days in hearing & considering what each had to say. & sin then being at a loss what to determine adjourned Thems. for about 6 weeks to take Time to Consider of it and at their second meeting spent another day in further hearing Each party & in deli & in deliberation & finally were at a loss being equally divided as to Question whether I had a Right which was all They had Power to Judge of as a Council but as to its being Prudential that I should be allowed to go out for a minor Part. they did (to all appearance * with a concurring) judge * & advise that it should be allowed. &

About 50 of my People did once since this subscribe a Por Request to the ministers of this association to come together to [-] give em advice what They should do under present Circumstances & in their draught made such a Representation as moved the ministers that They met & actually passed a vote that they would give advice but some of them thought it necessary to hear my Representation of things before They proceeded to act & accordingly came over hither & having heard my Representation more [------] altered their minds & determined that it was best to act nothing & accordingly the[y] broke up & did nothing.

But I believe sir I need say no more to make you sensible (& probably needed not to have said any thing) to make you sensible how far you are from having a proper Call to Judge of any matters in Controversy between me & this Chh. I am your Loving Br.

J.E.

N. April. 3. 1750.

## A116. Letter to Peter Clark, May 7, 1750 116.JE-P.Clark 5-7-50

Jonathan EdwardsA116. JE to Peter Clark, 5/7/50. MHS, Bostonian Society Deposit, Colburn Autograph Coll., v. II, 35. MS extract in BRBL, f. 1280 (see below). *NEQ* 29 (1956), 228-233.

Northampton May 7. 1750.

Rev. & honoured Sir.

There having been Application made to you from Time to Time by my People, in an Affair that most nearly concerns me occasioned (I suppose) by Intimations They have received from Some of the neighbouring Ministers of what they knew of your Abilities, And Something They had hear'd you had Said particularly relating to this Affair; and there having been an Intercourse by Letters between you and my People, and also the neighbouring Ministers about this matter ; I thought it not amiss for me also to write to you, & say Something for my Self. I don't know what has been said to you by Those who have applied to you, nor what Representations They have made of my Principles & Conduct : But I know some of Them have been greatly engaged in Opposition to me in this Affair, and have been apt to view Things which I say & do in a most disadvantageous Light ; and therefore I have Reason to expect they will make an answerable Representation of Them to others. I know by your Letters, which I have seen, you have had some great misrepresentations made to you; and know not how far your mind may be prepossessd with such Prejudices as Mankind in general are very liable to in Cases of Controversy, by receiving Accounts from Time to Time, from such only as are on one side only. But nevertheless am encouraged to write on my own behalf, from the Esteem I have long entertain'd of your Judgment, from some of your writings, particularly your defence of Infant Baptism against my Class-mate Walton,[^134-note1] and also by the appearances I saw of Candour in your Late Letters to Maj. Pomroy & Mr. Billing.[^134-note2] And my writing appear'd to me the more requisite from what you signify in your Letter to Maj. Pomroy of your Thoughts of writing & sending to my People your Opinion of my Book lately publish'd, after you should have had Opportunity to read it. -----I have taken a great deal of Pains to explain my self both in what I have written & spoken ; But yet I am so unhappy as to be misunderstood by many. notwithstanding all I can say for my self, There appears (as seems to me) a strange disposition to take me wrong, and to entertain uncharitable and injurious Thoughts of my meaning, & also concerning the Principles & dispositions I act from, and the Ends They suppose I secretly aim at. By which means many at a distance have conceived very disadvantageous & injurious notions of me. -----I am far from pretending to a discriminating Judgment of men's spiritual state, so as infallibly to determine who are true Converts & who are not, or imagining that I, or any Body else is sufficient for the Execution of any such design as the setting up a Pure Church consisting only of true Converts. Nor do I claim any Power above my Neighbours in that Respect. I have seen enough of my own fallibleness, & of the uncertainty of my own Judgment in things of this nature, I think, forever to guard me from such folly, as to assume to my self the divine Prerogative in this Respect. I have constantly born [^134-note3] a full Testimony in Preaching, writing & Conversation against the Assuming & Arrogance of such as set up Themselves to be discerners of mens Hearts, and have promoted separations under a Notion of setting up pure Churches. I have ever been an Enemy to all Pretences of knowing mens spiritual state, & other secret Things, not revealed in the word of God, or manifested the Events of Providence, by any supposed immediate Revelation, Impulse or Suggestion. or I have always nauseated the Presumption & folly of such as appeared forward to be quick & peremptory in their decisions concerning the state of mens souls, from a pretended extraordinary skill in the m secret methods of the spirits operation. And the older I have grown, the more & more has Experience and Observation of the Event of Things taught me the contemptibleness & Folly of such Pretences. I have much disliked the Tyranny of of Those who set up their own Experiences as a Rule to judge others by, and of such as insist ond a particular Account of the Time of Conversion, and of the order & method of their Experiences, in order to a cordial Embracing Persons, who Profess the main Principles or vertues wherein Godliness consists, & are of answerable Conversation, in the arms of Charity as true Christians & Brethren in Christ. I have long born Testimony against these Things. I have ever been an Enemy to a separating, divisive, Factious, uncharitable spirit; and have exerted my self in many ways against such Things, as They have abundantly appeared in the Countrey of late years. I have not set my self to oppose ministers, or to Encourage a diss disaffection between ministers & People, under a Pretence of their not being Converted, not being lively Preachers &c. I have heretofore lived in a happy Union with the Ministers of this Neighbourhood; which I have industriously cultivated, and look'd upon as one of the special Blessings of my Life : But I fear this Controversy has in some measure interrupted it, or at least the happy Fruits of it. A state of Controversy is peculiarly disagreable to me ; And I look upon it & as my great Calamity, & desire to take it as a Frown of Providence that should deeply humble that I am obliged to enter into such a Controversy even with my own People : I dreaded it greatly before it began, & nothing could make it tolerable to me, But that I have the Testimony of my Conscience that I could not avoid it, and so that 'tis an Affliction that God lays upon me and calls me to bear.

I am often (and I don't know but pretty generally in the Countrey) represented as of a new & odd opinion with Respect to Terms of Christian Communion, and that I am for introducing a peculiar way of my own; whereas m I don't perceive that I differ at all from the dr. Watts in his Book entitled The rational Foundation of a Christian Church, & the Terms of Christian Communion,[^134-note4] which he says is the common Sentiment & Practice of all reformed Churches. I had not seen this Book of dr. Watts's when I published what I have written on the Subject ; But yet I think my sentiments, a s I have there express'd Them, are as exactly agreable to what he lays down, as If I had been his Pupil. nor do I at all go beyond what dr. doddridge plainly shews to be his Sentiments in his [^134-note5] Rise & Progress of Religion, & his sermons on Regeneration, & in his Paraphrase & Notes on the N. Testament.[^134-note6] Nor indeed Sir, can I perceive when I consider the sentiments you have express'd in your Letters to Maj. Pomroy & Mr. Billing, can I perceive but that They come exactly to the same Thing that I maintain. You suppose The sacraments, are not converting ordinances ; but that as seals of the Covenant They presuppose Conversion, especially in the Adult ; And that 'Tis visible Saintship, or in other words a credible Profession of Faith & Repentance, a solemn Consent to the Gospel Covenant, Joined with a good Conversation, and competent measure of Christian Knowledge, is what gives a Gospel Right to all Sacred ordinances : but that it is necessary to those that come to these ordinances, & in those that profess a Consent to the Gospel Covenant, that They be sincere in their Profession or at least should think Themselves so.

The great Thing which I have Scrupled in the established method of this Churches Proceeding, & which I dare no longer go on in, is their publickly assenting to the form of words rehearsed on occasion of the Admission to the Communion, without pretending thereby to mean any Thing as an hearty consent to the Terms of the Gospel Covenant, or to mean any such Faith or Repentance as belong to the Covenant of Grace, & are the grand Conditions of that Covenant ; It being, at the same Time that the words are used, their known & established Principle, which They openly Profess & proceed upon, that men may & ought to use these words & mean no such thing, but something else of a nature far inferiour, of which I think they have no distinct determinate notions, but something consistent with their knowing that they don't chuse God as their Chief but love the world more than Him, and that They do not give Themselves up entirely to God, but make Reserves ; and in short, knowing that they live still under the reigning Power of the Love of the world, and Enmity to God and Christ. so that the words of their publick Profession, according to their openly established use, cease to be of the Nature of any Profession of Gospel Faith & Repentance, or any proper Compliance with the Covenant ; for 'tis their Profession that The words as used, mean no such Thing. The words used under these Circumstances do at least fail of being a credible Profession of these Things. I can conceive of no no such vertue in a certain set of words, that 'tis proper, meerly on the making these sounds, to admit Persons to Christian sacraments, without any Regard to any meaning of those sounds : nor can I think that any Institution of Christ has establish'd any such Terms of admission into the Christian Church. It don't belong to the controversy between me & my People, how particular or large the Profession should be that is should be required. I should not chuse to be confined to exact Limits as to that matter ; But rather than contend, I should content my self with a few words, briefly expressing the cardinal vertues of the Covenant, made (as should appear by enquiry into the Persons doctrinal Knowledge) understandingly, & there were an external conversation agreable thereto. Yea I should think that such a Person solemnly making such a Profession, had a Right to be received as the object of a publick Charity, however He Himself [^134-note7] self might scruple his own Conversion, on account of his not remembering the Time, not knowing the method of his Conversion, or finding so much remaining sin &c. And if his own scruples did not hinder his coming to the Lords Table, I should think the minister or Church had no Right to debar such a Professour, tho' He should say He did not think Himself Converted : for I call that a Profession of Godliness, which is a Profession of the great Things wherein Godliness consists ; & not a Professing his own Opinion of his good Estate.

when I say in my Book that a positive Charity is requisite, my meaning has been misunderstood by some, as tho' by positive, I had meant peremptory. whereas I meant no more bu than positive, in opposition to a meer negation of a contrary determination. I think there should be not only be no evidence against a man, but some positive exhibition or visibility implying Probability, or some worthiness of a real act of the charitable Judgment of the Church in a Persons Favour as a true Christian, agreable to his Profession. I think you express the very same Thing, when you speak of a Credible Profession as what entitles a man to Admission. Credible is that which is worthy of credit or belief.

Sir, If you write to my People your Opinion of my Book, I desire you would do it before the Council that is to meet here J on June 19. to judge whether or no I ought t immediately to be dismiss'd from my Pastoral office. and I ask the Favour of you, of yo either sending me a Copy of your Letter to Them, or specially directing Them to let me see what you otherwise 'tis probable I may never know what you write It was not without some difficulty that your last letter to Maj. P--was communicated even to the Precinct, tho' you directed that it should be communicated. -------The state of this people is very unhappy.--I would not speak to their dispa ragement : I know it is a day of great Temptation with Them; and allowances must be made for Them on many accounts. ---In your Letter to Mr Billing, you say, Rev. sir, that He speaks as one that knows the Heart of a minister : But there but few that Know the Heart of a minister under my Circumstances. ------But It would be tedious, & would tire your Patience for me to give a particular account of the state of Things. But if you had fully known Them, & how ready a People in such a state are to catch at every word, from a man They have received such a Character of, and to make much of little Things, you would probably have forborn, only on so uncertain a Report of my Principles, to say to them, They might easily be reduced to an absurdity, tho' it was only on Condition you had been rightly informed. --some Things which you have said have been improved to my disadvantage, both by ministers & People; tho' I confess without your having given them much occasion.

I conclude with asking your fervent Prayers to the God of all Light & Grace for me under my great Troubles I am

Honoured sir, with much esteem & Respect,

your son & servant,

Jonathan Edwards.

The Rev. Mr. Clark

[2. JE to Peter Clark, 5/7/50 (extract). BRBL, f. 1280:]

Extract of a my Letter to Mr. Clark of salem

I am o village of May 7. 1750.

I am often (& I dont know but pretty generally in the Countrey) represented as of a new and odd Opinion with Respect to Terms of Christian Communion & as being for introducing a peculiar way of my own whereas I don't perceive that I differ at all from the scheme of dr. Watts in his Book entitled the rational Foundation of a Xtian Chh & the Terms of Xtian Communion which He says is the common sentiment & Practice of all reformed Chhs I had not seen this Book of dr Watts's when I published what I have written on the subject But yet I think my sentiments as I have there express'd them are as exactly agreable to what he lays down as if I had been his Pupil. Nor do I at all go beyond what dr. doddridge plainly show'd to be his sentimts

In his Rise --------& his sermons on Regeneration & in his P--& Notes on the N. T. Nor indeed sir when I consider the sentmts you have expressed in your Letters to Maj. P. & Mr. B. can I perceive but that they come exactly to the same thing that I maintain you suppose the sac.--ts are not converting Ord--but that as seals of the Cov. they presuppose Conversion especially in the Adult And that 'tis visib. saintship or in other words a Credible Faith & Repent A solemn Consent to Gosp. Cov. join'd with a good Conversa. & Competent Measure of Xtian Kn. is what gives a gosp. Right to all sacred Ord -But that it is necessary to those that come to these Ord& in those that Profess a Consent to the Gosp. Cov. or to mean any such Faith or Repentance as belongs to the Cov. of Grace and are the grand Conditons of that Covent It being at the same time that the words are used their known & established Principle which they openly profess & proceed upon that men may & ought to use these words & mean no such thing but something else of a nature far inferiour of which I think They have no distinct determinate notions but something consistent with their knowing that they don't Choose G. as their chief good but love the world more [^134-note8] than Him & that they do not give Thems. up Entirely to God but make Reserves & in short knowing that they don't heartily consent to the Gospel Cov. but live still under the reigning Power of sin the Love of the O & Enmity to God and Christ. so that the words of their publick Profession according to their openly established use cease to be of the nature of any Profession of Gospel Faith & Repentance or any proper Compliance with the Covent for 'tis their Profession that the words as used mean no such Thing. the words used under these Circumstances do at least fail of being a credible Profession of these things. I can conceive of no such vertue in a certain set of words that 'tis proper meerly on the making these sounds to admit Persons to Xtian sacraments without any Regard to any pretended meaning of those sounds nor can I think that any Institution of Christ has established any such Terms of Admission into the Christian Chh. ## A116a. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, June 25, 1750 116a.JE-J.Bellamy 6-25-50

Jonathan EdwardsA116a. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 6/25/50. No MS. Published in *The Evangelical and Literary Magazine* 5 (July 1822), 365-69. The anonymous preface to the letter (signed "H.") states that "the following papers" are in JE's "own hand writing," which, along with the passage of only three days since the final council, suggests that JE copied out the Result of the Council and the Protest of the Minority for Bellamy from a manuscript copy (see Result of the Council at Northampton, June 22, 1750).

*Northampton, June* 25, 1750

DEAR SIR,--I here send you an account of the doings of the council that sat here last week.

The council consisted of 19 members, which came to pass through one of the churches that I chose, refusing to send a delegate; viz. the church of Cold-Spring, which there is reason to think was through the practices of some of the Northampton people, privately with the people of Cold-Spring. So that I had one less of those that I chose in the council than the people, and the event was accordingly. The vote for my separation from the people was passed by the majority of one voice. When the question was put, the ministers were equally divided upon it, 5 on the one side and 5 on the other; but of the messengers (among whom I had the least interest) 5 were on the one side and 4 on the other, so that thus the vote was carried. Of the five ministers, and four delegates that dissented, four ministers and three messengers entered their protestation against the result. Mr. Reynolds, being a very timorous, cautious man, he and his delegate, though they dissented, yet did not join in the protest.--I have here enclosed a copy of the result of the council, and also of the protestation against it.--There were about 23 of the church that voted for my continuing their minister. Some staid away from the meeting, because they would not appear to act either way, but most of the rest voted for my being dismissed with great alacrity.--Sir, I desire to hear from you at all opportunities; we are now thrown upon the ocean of the wide world, and have nothing to depend upon but God who is all sufficient; I desire your prayers for us in our present circumstances.

I am, sir, your peculiarly obliged loving brother,

JONATHAN EDWARDS.

THE RESULT OF THE COUNCIL.

AT a Council of Nine Churches, viz:--

The Church of Enfield, Rev. Mr. Peter Reynolds, *Pastor*; Mr. Edwards Collings, *Delegate*. Sheffield, Jonathan Hubbard, *Pastor;* Mr. David Kellog, *Delegate.* Sutton, David Hall, *Pastor;* Mr. Jonathan Hale, *Delegate.* Reading, William Hobby, *Pastor;* Mr. Sam'l Bancroft, *Delegate.* First Church in Springfield, Robert Breck, *Pastor;* Mr. Thos. Stebbins, *Delegate.* [^135-note1] First Church in Sunderland, Joseph Ashley, *Pastor;* Mr. Sam'l Montague, *Delegate*. Hatfield, Timothy Woodbridge, *Pastor*; O. Partridge, Esq. *Delegate*. First Church in Hadley, Chester Williams, *Pastor;* Mr. Enos Nash, *Delegate.* Pelham, Robert Abercrombie, *Pastor;* Mr. Matthew Graw, *Delegate.*

Convened at the call of the first Church in Northampton, together with the Elder of the Church in Cold-Spring, added by the consent of both the Pastor and Church in Northampton; in order to advise to a remedy from the calamities arising from the unsettled, broken state of the first Church in Northampton, by reason of a controversy subsisting about the qualifications for full Communion in the Church.

The Rev. Mr. Hubbard was chosen *Moderator*, and the Rev. Mr. Williams, *Scribe.*

The Council, after seeking the divine presence and direction, had the matter in controversy laid before them: and finding the sentiments of the Pastor and Church, concerning the qualifications necessary for full Communion, to be diametrically opposite to each other; the Pastor insisting upon it as necessary to the admission of Members to full Communion, that they should make a profession of sanctifying Grace; whereas the brethren are of opinion that the Lord's Supper is a converting ordinance; and consequently, that persons, if they have a competency of knowledge, and are of a blameless life, may be admitted to the Lord's Table, although they make no such profession; and also finding that, by reason of this diversity of sentiments, the doors of the Church have been shut for some years, so that there has been no admission; and not being able to find out any method, wherein the pastor and brethren can unite, consistent with their own sentiments, in admitting members to full communion. The council did then, according to the desire of the church, expressed in their letters missive, proceed to consider of the expediency of dissolving the relation between pastor and people, and after hearing the church upon it, and mature deliberation of the case, the questions were put to the members of the council severally;

1. Whether it be the opinion of this council, that the Rev. Mr. Edwards persisting in his principles, and the church in theirs in opposition to his, and insisting on a separation, it is necessary that the relation between pastor and people be dissolved? Resolved in the affirmative.

2. Whether it be expedient that this relation be immediately dissolved? Passed in the affirmative. [p. 368]

However we take notice, that notwithstanding the unhappy [^135-note2] dispute which has arisen and so long subsisted between the pastor and church of Northampton, upon the point before mentioned, that we had no other objection against him, but what relates to his sentiments upon the point aforesaid, laid before us; and although we have heard of some stories spread abroad, reflecting upon Mr. Edwards's sincerity, with regard to the change of his sentiments about the qualifications for full communion; yet we have received full satisfaction that they are false and groundless. And although we don't all of us agree with Mr. Edwards in our sentiments upon the point, yet have abundant reason to believe that he took much pains to get light in that matter, and that he is uprightly following the dictates of his own conscience; and with great pleasure reflect upon the christian spirit and temper he has discovered in the unhappy controversy subsisting among them; and think ourselves bound to testify our full charity towards him, and recommend him to any church or people agreeing with him in sentiments, as a person eminently qualified for the work of the gospel ministry. And we would recommend it to the Rev. Mr. Edwards and the first Church in Northampton, to take proper notice of the heavy frown of divine Providence in suffering them to be reduced to such a state, as to render a separation necessary, after they have lived so long and amicably together, and been mutual blessings and comforts to each other. And now recommending the Rev. Mr. Edwards and the Church in Northampton to the Grace of God,

We subscribe, JONA. HUBBARD, *Moderator, in the name of the Council.*

*Northampton*, June 22d, 1750.

PROTESTATION AGAINST THE COUNCIL'S RESULT, BY SOME OF THE MEMBERS.

WE cannot agree to a dismission of the Rev. Mr. Edwards, at least for the present, for the following reasons; previous to which we observe, that though we presume not to infringe the rights of other consciences, yet we beg leave to enjoy our own, and being sought to offer advice and counsel at Northampton, are constrained to say to this church,

1. That we disapprove of the separation of the Rev. Mr. Edwards from his people, because that in the nature of the thing there is no just cause therefor, his sentiments being, as we apprehend, perfectly harmonious with the mind of the Lord Jesus Christ, and strictly conformable to the practice of the apostles, and that of the reformed churches in general. [^135-note3]

2. Upon the supposition that Mr. Edwards were in the wrong in the present controversy, yet there is, as we apprehend, no proportion between the importance of the controversy, and that of his dismission.

3. It appears that there have been no proper essays, in the way of fair reasoning, with or before the parties, to convince either of them of the truth or falseness of their principles, which love to the truth itself, and their souls requires.

4. Because the Church, or at least its committee, while they offer us reasons for separating them from their pastor, yet will not suffer us so to enter into the grounds of those reasons, as to offer them that light which the word of God affords; which we esteem an imposition on our consciences, and does but tend to keep them in the dark.

These, brethren, are some of the reasons, for which we can by no means approve a separation, at least at present, but if such separation should eventually come on, we bear a free and cheerful testimony in favour of our dearly beloved brother, and your once dearly beloved Pastor; though now esteemed your enemy, because (as we apprehend) he has told you the truth. He needs not indeed any recommendation of ours, which is more properly commendation of ourselves than of him, nor need we say much to others, for that his praise is in most of our churches through the land. Yet we are constrained to say to the world, that God has furnished him with those ministerial gifts and graces, by which he has hitherto shone as a burning and shining light, and though his people in general cease to rejoice in his light, yet we hope and trust others may rejoice in it for a long season. So wishing that the dear people of God in this place may take the point in controversy into a meek, calm, serious and prayerful consideration; and that so truth with holiness may greatly prevail in this place, we subscribe,

Yours in the bond of the Gospel,

DAVID HALL, EDWARD BILLING, ROBERT ABERCROMBIE, JONATHAN HALE, MATTHEW GRAY, SAMUEL BANCROFT.

*Northampton*, June 22, 1750.
