## A117. Letter to John Erskine, July 5, 1750 117.JE-J.Erskine 7-5-50

Jonathan EdwardsA117. JE to John Erskine, 7/5/50. ANTS, f. 1750, #3-4.

Northampton July 5. 1750.

Rev. & dear Brother,

I now acknowledge the Receipt of three Letters from you since I last wrote to you; one of Septem. 12. another of Septem. 20. another of decem. 22, all of the year 49 1749. The two first I received in the winter, with Mr. Glas's Notes on scripture Texts, Ridgley on original sin, Wheatley's Schools of the Prophets, davidson's sermon occasion'd by the death of Mr. Harrison, and Mr Mckailes sermon.[^136-note1] Your Letter written in decem. I received a little while ago. I have greatly regretted the want of Opportunity to answer you 'till now: But such have been my extraordinary Circumstances, the multitude of distracting Troubles and Hurries that I have been involved (which I can't easily represent to you) that I have had no Leisure. I have been very uneasy in neglecting to write to my Correspondents in Scotland; & about two months ago I set my self to the Business; but was soon broken off; and have not been able to return to it again till now. And now sir, I thank you for your Letters & Presents. The Books you sent me were entertaining to me, and some of them will be of Advantage to me if God should give me Opportunity to prosecute the studies I had begun on the Arminian Controversy. There were various Things pleasing to me in Glass's Notes, tending to give some new Light into the sense of scripture. He seems to be a man of Ability; tho' I can't fall in with all his singularities.

The account you say Mr. davidson gave of the Absurdities of the Moravians are not very surprizing to me : I have seen so much of the Tendency & Issue of such Kind of Notions & such sort of Religion as are in vogue amongst Them, and among many others in many Respects like 'em, that I expect no other than that sin, Folly, absurdity & things to the highest degree reproachful to Christianity, will forever be the Consequence of such things. It seems to me thate has been enough of the & enough of this Kind has lately appeared, greatly to awaken the Attention of Christian divines, and make 'em suspect that the devils devices in the various Counterfeits of Exper vital Experimental Religion, have not been sufficiently attended to, And the exact distinctions between the saving Operations of the spirit of God, and all its false Appearances, not sufficiently [^136-note2] observed. ----There is something now in the Press in Boston, largely handling the subject.[^136-note3] I have had Opportunity to read the M.S. and, in my humble Opinion, it has a Tendency to give as much Light in this Matter or as any thing that ever I saw. Minister It was written by Mr. Bellamy, minister of Bethlem in Connecticut ; The minister which Mr. Brainerd sometimes speaks of as his peculiarly dear & intimate (as possibly you may have observed in reading his Life. He was of about Mr. Brainerds Age, And it might have been well if He had more years over his Head. But as He is one of the most intimate Friends that I have in the world, and one that I have much acquaintance with, I can say this of Him ; That He is one of very great Experience in Religion, as to what has pass'd between God & his own soul ; one of very good Natural Abilities, of Closeness of Thought, & extraordinary diligence in his studies, and Earnest Care exactly to know the Truth in these matters. He has long applied his mind to the subject He has wrote upon, and used all possible Helps of Conversation & Reading. And tho' his stile is not such as to please the polite World ; yet if his youth, & the Obscurity of his Original, & the Place that He lives in &c. don't prevent his being much taken notice I am perswaded his Book w might give serve to give the Chh of God considerable Light as to the nature of true Religion, and many impor tant doctrines of Christianity. from the knowledge I have of Him, I am fully Satisfied his aim in this Publication is not his own Fame & Reputation in the world ; but the Glory of God, and the Advance ment of the Kingdom of his Redeemer.

I suspect the Follies of some of the Seceders, which you mention in your Lett both your Letters of sept. 20 & decem. 22. arise in considerable measure from the same Cause at least in with the follies of the Moravians, & the Followers of the Wesleys, & many extravagant People in America. viz. false Religion, counterfeit Conversions, & the want of a genuine Renovation of the spirit of their minds. The spirit seems to be exactly the same with what Appears in many, who apparently, by their own Account have had a false Conversion. -----I am a great Enemy to Censorious ness, & have Opposed it very much in my Preaching & writings; But yet I think we should avoid that Bastard mischievous Charity, which by which satan keeps men asleep, and hides [^136-note4] their Eyes from those snares & crafty works of his, which it is of the utmost Consequence to the Church of God to discern & be aware of; [-] and by which, for want of their being discovered, the devil has often had his greatest Advantages against the Interest of Religion. The scripture often leads us to judge of true Religion, and the si gracious sincerity of Professours, by the spirit Genius, The Temper & spirit of it Jam. 3. 17. Eph. 5. 9. Gal. 5. 19----25. 1 Cor. 13. 4. &c ---Rom. 8.9. 1 Joh. 4.16. Joh. 13. 35. 1 John 2. 10. 1 Joh. 3. 14. & 18, 19. & 23, 24. Chap. 4. 7. v. 12. 13. & m very many other Places. ---I have been greatly grieved at the a spirit of censoriousness ; But yet I heartily wish that some sorts of Charity were utterly abolish'd.

The Account you give of A. Bp. Herring, and The moderate, generous, truly catholick & Christian Principles appearing in Him & some others of the dignified Clergy, & other Persons of distinction in the Church of England, are very agreable. 'Tis to be hoped that these Things are Forerunners of something good and great to be brought to pass for the Church of God.

I have seen some Accounts in our publick Prints publish'd here in America, of those Conversions & Baptisms in the Russian Empire, which you mention in your last Letter ; and should be glad of further Information about it. we have had publish'd here an Extract of a Letter, written by dr. doddridge to Mr. Pearsall of Taunton in somersetshire, and transmitted by Him to Boston, in a Letter to Mr. Prince[^136-note5] ; giving an a surprizing Account of a very wonderful Person, a German by Nation, a Preacher of the Gospel to the Jews, lately in London ; whom He (dr. doddridge) saw and conversed with & heard preach (or rather repeat) a sermon there ; who had had great success in preaching to those miserable People in Germany, Poland, Holland, Lithuania, Hungary & other Parts, God having so blessed his Labours in that in the various Parts through which he had travelled, He had been the Instrument of the Conversion of about Six Hundred Con- verts many of whom are expressing their great Concern to bring others of their Brethren to the Knowledge of the great & blessed Redeemer, & beseeching Him to instruct their Children, that They may preach Christ also. I should be glad, if you hear any Thing further of the Affair, to be [--] informed of it by you. --I think such Things may well be improved to animate and encourage those who have engaged in the Concert for Prayer for a the Reviving of Religion.[^136-note6] ---I rejoyce to hear what you write of some Appearances of con awakening in Mr. Gillies's Chh in Glasgow, & if it continues should be glad to be informed.

I am very glad to hear what Mr. McLaurin informs of the Encouragements likely to be given from scotland to N. Jersey College ; a very hopeful Society ; And I believe what is done for that Seminary is doing Good in an eminent manner. -Mr. McLaurin tells me of some Prospect of your being removed to a Congregation in Edinburgh; which I am pleased with, because I hope there you will act in a larger sphere, and will have more opportunity to exert the disposition that appears in you, to promote good publick designs for Zions Prosperity.

I thank you for the Concern you manifest for me under the presen my difficulties & Troubles, by Reason of the Controversy between me & my People, about the Terms of Christian Communion. -------

This Controversy has now issued in had that Issue which I expected; it has ended in a separation between me & my People. -many Things have appeared that have been exceeding unhappy & uncomfortable in the Course of this Controversy. The great Power of Prejudices from Education, established Custom, and the Traditions of Ancestours & certain admired Teachers, and the exceeding unhappy Influence of Bigotry has remarkabl remarkably appeared in the manage ment of this Affair. The spirit that has actuated and engaged my People in this matter is evidently the same that has appeared in your own People in their opposition to winter Communions, but only risen to a much higher degree ; And some of the Arguments that have been greatly insisted on here have been very much of the same sort with some of those urged by your People in your Affair. There have many Things said & done during our Controversy that I am willing should be buried in Oblivion ; and therefore shall not now declare 'em.

But would only say in the general, that there has been that Prejudice, & spirit of Jealousy, and increasing engagedness of spirit, & fixedness of Resolution to gain the Point in view viz. my dismission from my Pastoral office over Them, upheld and cherished by a Perswasion that herein They only stood for the Truth & did their duty, That it has been an exceeding difficult Thing for me to say or do any Thing at all, in Order to their being enlighten'd, or brought to a more Calm & sedate Consideration of Things, without [^136-note7] its being misinterpreted, and turned to an occasion of increasing Jealousy & Prejudice ; even those Things wherein I have yielded most, and done most to gratify the People, and asswage their spirits, & win their Charity. I have often declared to the People, and gave it to 'em under my Hand, that if after all proper means used & regular steps taken, They continued averse to continuing under my ministry, I had no Inclination to do any Thing as attempt ing to oblige Them to it. But I looked on my self bound in Conscience before I left ( Them, (as I was afraid They were in the way to Ruin) to do my Endeavour that proper means should be used to bring em to a suitable Temper, & so to a Capacity of proceeding considerately & with their Eyes open, properly & calmly exa & prayerfully examining the Point in Controversy, & also weighing the Consequences of Things. To this End I have insisted much on an Impartial Council, in which should be some of the Elderly Ministers of the Land, to look fully into our state, & view it with all its Circumstances, and with full Liberty to give both me & Them such advice as They thought requisite & proper. And to this End I insisted that the Council should not wholly consist of Churches ministers & Churches that were professedly against me in the Point in Controversy ; & therefore that it should not consist wholly of ministers & Churches of this Neighbourhood, who were almost altogether in opposition to me ; but that some should be brought from abroad. This I also insisted on as I thought it most likely an impartial Council would do me justice in the publick Representation They would make of our Affairs in their Result. About this The People insisted that the Council should be wholly of the neighbourhood ; undoubtedly because They supposed Themselves most sure that their Judgmt & Advice would be favourable and agreable to them. I stood the most more against it, because in this Countrey we have no such Thing as appeals from one Council to another, from a Lesser to a larger ; as ti and also because the neighbouring ministers were all youngerly men. These Things were long the subject matter of uncomfortable Troubles & Contests. & many were the Proposals I made. At last They complied with this Proposal (after great & long continued Opposition to it) [--] viz. that I should nominate two Churches to be of the Council, who were not within the Bounds of this County. And so it was [^136-note8] agreed that a Council of Ten Churches should be called, mutually Chosen, & that two of my half should be called from abroad. I might have observed before that there was a great & long dispute about the Business of the Council, or what should be left to Them: and particularly, whether it should be left to Them, to or They should have Liberty to give us what Advice they pleased for a Remedy from our Calamities. This I insisted on, not that I desired that we should bind our selves beforehand to stand to their Advice, let it be what it would ; but I thought absurd to ti so tie up & limit the Council, that They should not Exercise their own Judgment, & give us their Advice according to their own mind. The People were willing the Council should make proposals for an accomodation ; But that if They did not like Them, the Council should be obliged immediately to separate us, & would not have our 'em have any Liberty to Advise to wait longer, or use any further means for Light, or take any further Course or other Course for a Remedy from our Calamities. At last a vote was pass'd in the Church in these words. "That a Council should be called to give us their best Advice for a Remedy from the Calamities arising from the present unsettled broken state of this Church, by Reason of the Controversy here subsisting concerning the Qualifications for full Communion in the Church : And, if upon the whole of what they see and find in our circumstances, they judge it best that Pastor & People be immediately separated, That They proceed to dissolve the Relation between 'em." [-] Accordingly a Council a was agreed upon to meet here on this Business on June 19. I nominated two out of this County of which Mr. Foxcrofts Church in Boston was one. But others were nominated provisionally, in case these should. Those that came were Mr. Halls Church of sutton, & Mr. Hobby's Church in Reading. One of the Churches that I nominated within the County refused to send a delegate, viz. Mr. Billing's Church of Cold-spring. However Mr. Billing Himself (tho' with some difficulty) was admitted into the Council. The People in managing this Affair on their side, have made Chief Use of a young Gentleman of liberal Education, and notable Abilities & a fluent speaker, of about seven or eight & twenty years of Age , my Grandfather Stoddard's Grandson, being my mothers sisters son[^136-note9] a man of lax Principles in Religion, falling in in some essential Things with Arminians, & is very open & bold [^136-note10] in it. He was improved as one of the Agents for the Church, & the was their chief spokesman before the Council. He very strenuously urged before the Council the necessity of an immediate separation. and I, knowing the Church the maj most of them to be inflexibly bent on this Event, I told the Council that I should not enter into the dispute, but should refer the matter wholly to the Councils Judgment : I signified that I had no desire to leave my People on any other Consideration than their Aversion to my being their minister any longer ; But They continuing so averse, had no inclination or desire that They should be compell'd. but yet should refer my self to their Advice. when the Church was not convened in order to the Councils knowing their minds with Respect to my Continuance, about 23 appeared for it, others staid away chusing not to act either way : But the generality of the Church, which consists of about 230 male members, voted for my dismission. My dis mission was carried in the Council by a majority of one voice.

The ministers were equally divided ; but of the delegates one more were for it than against it. And it so happen'd that every member of the Council that were of the Churches of the Peoples chusing voted for my dismission, but every one that were of the Churches that I chose were against it. And there happening to be one of these fewer than the other, by the Chh of Cold-spring's not sending a delegate (which was through that Peoples Prejudice against my Opinion) the vote was carried that way, by the vote of one delegate. However on the 22d of the last month, I the Relation between me & this People was dissolved. I suppose the Result of the Council, together with the Protestations of some of the members are printed in Boston by this Time.[^136-note11] I shall Endeavour to one of the printed Accounts to be sent with this Letter to you, together with one of my Books on the Point that has been in Controversy between me & my People. ----Two of the members of the Council who dissented from the Result, yet did not sign the Protestation, viz. Mr. Reynolds & his delegate. which I suppose was owing to Mr. Reynolds's extraordinary cautious & timorous Temper. ---The last sabbath I preach'd my farewel sermon. many in the Congregation seem'd to be much affected & some are exceedingly grieved. [^136-note12] some few I believe have some Relentings of Heart, that voted me away. But there is no great Probability that the leading Part of the Church will ever Change. -besides their own fixedness of Resolution, there are many in neighbouring Towns to support their Resolution ; both in the ministry & Civil magistracy ; without whose Influence I believe the People never would have been so violent as they have been.

I desire that such a Time of awful Changes, dark Clouds & great Frowns of Heaven on me & my People may be a Time of serious Consideration, thorough self-reflection & Examination, & deep Humiliation with me. I desire your fervent Prayers for me & those who have heretofore been my People. I know not what will become of Them : There seems to be the utmost danger that the younger Generations will be carried away with Arminianism as with a Flood. The young Gentleman I before spoke of is high in their Esteem, and is become the most leading man in the Town; and is very bold in declaring & disputing for his opinions ; and we have none able to Confront Him & withstand Him in a dispute : and some of young People already shew a young disposition to fall in with his notions.

And 'tis not likely that the People will obtain any young Gentleman to of the Calvinistical Perswasion to settle with Them in the ministry, that will have courage & Ability to make Head against Him.

And there as to the older People, there never appeard so great an Indifference among Them about Things of this nature. They will at present be much more likely to be thorough in their Care to settle a minister of Principles contrary to mine, as to Terms of Communion, than to settle one that is sound in the doctrines of Grace. The great Concern of the leading Part of the Town at present will probably be, to come off with flying Colours in the Issue of the Controversy they have had with me, & of what They have done in it ; for which they know many condemn them.

An End is put for the Present by these Troubles to the Studies I was before engaged in, and my design of writing against Arminianism. I had made considerable Preparation, and was deeply engaged in the Prosecution of this design, before I was rent off from it by these difficulties. And if ever God should ever give me Opportunity, I would again resume that Affair. But I am now as it were thrown upon the wide Ocean [^136-note13] of the world , And know not what will become of me & my numerous & chargeable Family ; nor have I any particular door in view, that I depend upon to be opened for my future serviceableness. most Places in N. England that want a Minister would not be forward to invite one with so chargeable a Family, nor one so far Advanced in years, being 46 the 5 day of last October. I am fitted for no other Business but study : I should make a poor Hand at getting a Living by any Secular Employment. we are in the Hands of God : and I bless Him. I am not anxious concerning his disposal of us. I hope I shall not distrust Him, nor be unwilling to submit to his will. And I have Cause of Thankfulness, that there seems also to be such a disposition in my Family. -You are pleased dear sir, very kindly to ask me whether I could sign the westminster Confession of Faith, & submit to the Presbyterian Form of Church Government; and to offer to use your Influence to procure a Call for me to some Congregation in scotland. I should be very ungrateful If I were not thankful for such Kindness & Friendship. ---As to my subscribing the to the substance of the westminster Confession, there would be no difficulty : and as to the Presbyterian Governmt, I have long been perfectly out of conceit of our unsettled, independent, Confused way of Chh Government in this Land: And the Presbyterian way has ever appear'd to me most agreable to the word of God, and the Reason & nature of Things. tho' I cannot say that the Presbyterian Government of the Chh of scotland is so perfect that it can't in some Respects be mended. But as to my Removing with my numerous Family over the Atlantick, it is, I acknowledge, attended with many difficulties that I shrink at. Among other Things, this is very considerable, that it would be an uncertaintie whether my Gifts & Administrations would suit any Congregation that should send for me without Trial. And so great a Thing as such a removal had not need to be on some certainty as to that matter. If the Expectations of a Congregation were so great, and They were so Confident of my Qualifications, as to call me at a venture, having never seen or heard me, Their disappointment might possibly be so much the greater & the more uneasy, after Acquaintance and Trial. ---My own Countrey is not so dear to me, but that if there were an evident Prospect of being serviceable to Zions Interests elsewhere, I could forsake it. And I think my wife is of fully [^136-note14] of this disposition.

I forgot to mention that in this Evil Time in Northampton, there are some of the young People under awakenings; and I hope two or Three have lately been converted : two a very lately, besides two or three hopefully brought Home the last year.

My wife & Family join with me in most respectful & Cordial salutations to you, & your Consort. and we desire the Prayers of you both for us under our present Circumstances. --My youngest Child but one has long been in a very infirm, afflicted & decay ing state with the Rickets & some other disorders : I desire your Prayers for it. ---I am, dear Sir,

your most affectionate & obliged

Friend & Brother

Jonathan Edwards.

P. S. For Accounts of the state of Religion in America and some Reasons of my Conduct in this Controversy with my People, I must refer you to my Letters to Mr. Robe & Mr. McLaurin.

[^136-note1]: John Glas, *Notes on Scripture-Texts* (Edinburgh, 1747-60); on JE's use of this work, see *Works, 13*, 137, n. 9. John Harrison* (London, 1749); Hugh McKaile, *The Last Publick Sermon, Preached by Hugh MacKaile upon the Sabbath Immediately Preceeding that 8th of September 1662, the Day Affixed for the Removal of the Ministers of Edinburgh from Their Kirks, and Themselves and Their Families from the City in the Days Thereafter with the Last Speech and Testimony Delivered by Him on the Scaffold* (Edinburgh, 1749).

[^136-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

## A118. Letter to William McCulloch, July 6, 1750 118.JE-W.McCulloch 7-6-50

Jonathan EdwardsA118. JE to William McCulloch, 7/6/50. ANTS, f. 1750, #7-8. Addressed on back "To the Rev / Mr. William McCulloch / Minister of the Gospel / at Cambuslan in / Scotland. / To the Care of the Rev / Mr. McLaurin of / Glasgow."

Northampton July 6. 175 1750.

Rev. & dear Sir,

'Tis now long since I have received a Letter from you ; The last was dated March 10. 1749. However, as you having heretofore manifested that our Correspondence was not unacceptable to you, I would not omit to do my Part towards the Continuance of it. Perhaps one Reason of your neglecting to write, may be the failing of such agreable matter for Correspondence as we had some years ago, when Religion was flourishing in Scotland and America, And we had joyful Informations to give each other of Things pertaining to the City of our God. 'Tis indeed a so now a sorrowful Time on this side the Ocean : Iniquity abounds, & the Love of many waxes Cold: multitudes of fair & high Professours, in one Place and another, have sadly backslidden: sinners are desperately harden'd: Experi mental Religion is more than Ever out of Credit with the far greater Part : The doctrines of Grace, and those Principles in Religion that do chiefly concern the Power of Godliness are far more than Ever discarded : Arminianism & Pelagianism have made a strange Progress within a few years : The Chh of England in New England is, I suppose, treble of what it was seven years ago : many Professours are gone off to the heigh great Lengths in Enthusiasm & Extravagance in their notions & Practices : great Contentions and separations & Confusions in our Religious state prevail in many Parts of the Land: some of our main Pillars are broken ; one of which was Mr. Webb of Boston,[^137-note1] who died in the latter Part of last April: much of the Glory of the Town of Boston is gone with Him: And if the Bereavements of that Town should be added to by the death of two or three more of their remaining older ministers, That Place would be in a very sorrowful state indeed, like a City whose walls are broken down, & like a large Flock without a shepherd, encompassed with wolves, & many in the midst of it.

These are the dark things that are appear : But on the other Hand, there are some Things that have a different Aspect. There have in some Places appeared Revivings of Religion. some little Revivings have been in some Places towards Boston. There has been some Reformation not long since in one of our Colleges. Besides [^137-note2] And by what I hear, there has been much more of this nature in some other Parts of the British America than in New-England : something Considerable in several Towns on Long-Island; and in also in some other Parts of the Province of New-York near Hudsons River ; something in several Parts of New-Jersey, particularly through the Labours of Mr. Greenman,[^137-note3] a young Gentleman educated by the charitable Expenses of the pious & eminent Mr. david Brainerd, mention'd in his Life ; which I think I sent to you the last summer. And since I last wrote to scotland I have had Accounts of the prevailing of a Religious Concern in some Parts of Virginia.

And I must not forget to say inform you, that altho' I think it has of late been the darkest Time in Northampton that ever was since the Town stood, yet there have been some of late some awakenings o on the minds of some of the young People here, & two or three Instances of hopeful Conversion the last & as many very lately.

when I speak of its being a dark Time here, I have a special Rerence to the Great Controversy that has subsisted here, for about a year & half between me & my People, about the Terms of Communion in the visible Church ; which has now at Length Issued in a separation between me & my People. for a more particular Account of which, I must refer you to my Letters to Mr. Robe, & Mr. John Erskine. besides I shall endeavour to procure the printed Copies of the Result of the Council, that sat here the week before last, with the Protestation of some of the members, that these may be sent to you with this Letter, together with one of my Books publish'd on the Point in debate between me & my People; of which I crave your Acceptance.

I am now separated from the People, who we between whom & me there was once the greatest union. remarkable is the Providence of God in this matter. In this Event, we have a great Instance of the Instability & uncertainty of all Things [^137-note4] here below ---The dispensation is indeed awful in many Respects, calling for serious Reflection, & deep Humiliation, in me & my People. -The Enemy far & near will now triumph : but God can overrule all for his own Glory. I have now nothing visible to depend upon for my future usefulness, or the subsistence of my Numerous But I hope we have an all-sufficient faithful Covenant God to depend upon. I desire that I may ever submit to Him, walk humbly before him, & put my trust wholly in Him. --I desire dear sir, your Prayers for us under our present Circumstances. I am [-] sir,

your respectful & affectionate Friend

& Brother,

Jonath. Edwards.

P.S.

My wife & Family join with me in cordial salutations to you & yours.

The Rev. Mr McCulloch

[^137-note1]: John Webb, pastor of the New North Church, d. Apr. 16, 1750, a. 66.

[^137-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^137-note3]: Nehemiah Greenman (c. 1724-1779), who at this time was pastor of Madison, N.J.

[^137-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

## A119. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, July 31, 1750 119.JE-T.Foxcroft 7-31-50

Jonathan EdwardsA119. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 7/31/50. BRBL, f. 1292.

Northampton July 31. 1750.

Rev. & Honoured Sir,

I am sorry that the Result of the Council that Sat on my Affair, with the Protest against it, was not publish'd in the news-Papers; as I think it would be to my Advantage that They should be known & made publick in all Parts of the Countrey; And if They had been published in the publick Prints that would undoubtedly have made Them much more publick, and generally known; so that in that case, probably 20 would have seen Them, where one will see Them as they are now printed by Themselves. I can't but still desire that They may be so publish'd, and therefore desire you to pu perswade some or other of the Publishers of news-papers to put Them into their Papers; as I suppose As They are not so long, but that They may conveniently do it; and I suppose They will be no disadvantage to their Papers.

There is no manner of Prospect at present of this Peoples altering their minds. The Committee for supplying the Pulpit have got me to preach three Sabbaths since I preach'd my Farewell sermon; But it is with great Reluctance. They from week to week do their utmost to get the Pulpit otherwise supplied : They have taken much Pains to get the neighbouring ministers to take their Turns to preach here ; but meet with difficulty: They have talk'd of hiring some Body for the present, that They have no thoughts of settling, 'till They can hear of [^138-note1] some likely Candidate to hire on Probation; but they don't know who to get. And therefore they have determin had of late, both a Precinct & Church meeting, And have determined with all possible speed to get a Candidate for settlement; and have sent deac. Pomroy to Cambridge, to consult the President concerning a Candidate; and I suppose hope the deac. will bring one with Him, who may supply the Pulpit next sabbath, that they maynt be obliged to aske me to preach any more.

I should be glad of a Line from [-] you by mr Graves[^138-note2] who brings this. And desire you will still remember in your Prayers

your most obliged

Friend & Servant

Jonath. Edwards.

[^138-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^138-note2]: Nathan Graves.

## A120. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft (Enclosure), [After June 1750] 120.JE-T.Foxcroft aft.6-50

Jonathan EdwardsA120. JE to Thomas Foxcroft[?], n.d. [after June 1750]. BRBL, f. 1325.

I would intreat you Sir, before you Seal up the Pacquets to dr Guyse & dr doddridge, to procure of Mr. Kneeland, two of the printed Copies of the Result of our Council, with the Protest; & put one into each Pacquet. I have an Account with Mr. Kneeland, & I desire him to set them down to my Account.

yours

J. Edwards.

## A121. Letter to William Russell, September 14, 1750 121.JE-W.Russell 9-14-50

Jonathan EdwardsA121. JE to William Russell, 9/14/50. BRBL, f. 1317.

Rev. & dear Sir,

You may remember that when I was at

your House the last week, I was at your talking with you concerning my opinion, with Regard to the visible Qualifications for Christian sacraments; and that you signified that you agreed with me in supposing that, by the Institution of Christ, it was a saving Faith or a cordial Reception of Christ & self-dedication to Him, should which should be professed. I then mention'd what mr. Williams of L--g M--w[^140-note1] had told me that you said to Him, viz, that you thought that altho' this, you supposed, was the Truth; yet if my People, and Candidates for my Communion at Northampton, continued to be of another mind, after I had declared to Them my opinion with the Reasons of it, And they declared to me me their conscientious desire to be admitted to full Communion without any such Profession, I might with a good Conscience take 'em in according to their Judgment. But you said mr. W---s was mistaken & had misrepresented you, &c And that the next morning, I brought on the discourse again, and desired you plainly to tell me your real sentiments as to that matter, viz. whether I being of the forementioned Opinion with Respect to the Institution of Christ, appointing A po profession of saving Faith, &c (which you also supposed He had appointed) I could with a good Conscience, acting as a minister of Christ and one Appointed and sent by Him, to e in the service of his His[^140-note2] House to execute his Institutions, be active in receiving such to a sacraments, & administering sacraments to them, who in the Profession They made did not pretend to signify any thing of that a nature as [^140-note3] a saving Faith, or a cordial Reception of X Christ, and entire selfdedication to Him, but that They meant something of a vastly different Nature, and acted on those Principles, that Persons might & ought to make such a Profession as They made, who was intended no such thing, but were unde Conscious to Themselves that They were real Enemies to Christ, & loved the world better than Him. I desired to know your mind, and have your Advice as to that matter, as it was an affair that it highly concerned me to be well informed in, and because I look'd on you as a Person of Judgment, and I thought it very natural under such difficult Circumstances and having such an Opportunity to consult so near a Friend and Relation. And I thought you then complied with my desire, and told me your mind, very plainly expressing your sentiment. You may Remember what you said to th what I proposed concerning a stewards attending his masters orders, in giving the Portion of meat appointed to each member of the Houshold, & the Comparison you yourself brought concerning the Kings officers admitting Persons to the Priviledges of subjects, their attending the Kings Instructions as to the Qualifications that should appear & the Profession they should make. In the Time of it I thought you spoke plainly. -But since that something has pass'd, which has made me suspect, that after all, I never understood you, & that indeed you held concealed from you your real sentiments. [^140-note4] this suspicion arose in my mind in my Journey from N. Haven hither.

My Request therefore, dear sir, is that you would write to me, and informe me whether I rightly understood you or not, and express your mind with plainness in this matter. The Reasons why desire it are these two. viz 1.I truly desire to Know your mind for my own benefit, an for which Reason I ask'd[--] at first. 2. Misunderstandings often tend to weaken & Interrupt Friendship; & tis doubtless desireable that Friendship & good understanding should be maintain'd & Chu cherished between Brethren. I am sir,

your Affectionate Brother

Jonathan Edwards.

Middletown

Septem. 14. 1750.

P.S. I desire your Prayers for me & my Family under our great difficulties & Trials.

Mr. Russel.

[^140-note1]: Stephen Williams of Longmeadow, Mass.

[^140-note2]: MS sic

[^140-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^140-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

## A122. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, November 5, 1750 122.JE-J.Bellamy 11-5-50

Jonathan EdwardsA122. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 11/5/50. BRBL, F. 1276. Address on back, "To the Rev / Mr. Joseph Bellamy / at Bethlem."

Rev. & dear sir,

My wife seems to be very unwilling that our sheep should be sold They she Chuses rather that They should be let out at a lower Rate, if none will still hire Them at the Rate of a Pound of wool a sheep. -I should be glad (if They cant be let out so) They may not be sold, any of Them, as yet. if I should settle any where in this western Part of the Countrey possibly I may find some way to dispose of 'em my self.

I am sir, your

affectionate & grateful Friend & Brother

Jth Edwards.

Canaan Nov. 5.

1750.

## A123. Letter to John Erskine, November 15, 1750 123.JE-J.Erskine 11-15-50

Jonathan EdwardsA123. JE to John Erskine, 11/15/50. ANTS, f. 1750, #5-6. Northampton Novem. 15. 1750.

Rev. & dear Sir,

Some Time in July last I wrote to you, and ordered one of my Books on the Qualifications for Communion in the Church, too to be sent to you from Boston with the Letter. In my Letter I informed of what had come to pass, in the Issue of the late Controversy between me and my People, in the dissolution of my Pastoral Relation wi to Them ; and ordered the printed Result of the ecclesiastical Council that sat on our affairs, and the Protest against the said Result, to be put up with the Letter: and also, at the same Time, sent Letters to my other Correspondents in Scotland, with the Books &c. I have as yet had no Call to any Stated Business elsewhere in the ministry, altho' of late, there has been some Prospect of my having Invitations to one or two Places. This People of Northampton are hitherto destitute of a minister. They have exerted Themselves very much to obtain some Candidate to come & preach to Them on Probation, and have sent to many distant Places ; but have hitherto been disappointed, and seem to be very much nonpluss'd. But the major Part of 'em seem to continue without any Relentings or misgivings of Heart concerning what has been done ; at least the major Part of the leading men in the Congregation. But there is a number whose Hearts are broke at what has come to pass; and I believe are more deeply affected than ever They were at any temporal Bereavement. It is thus with one of the principal Men in the Parish, viz. Col. dwight. And another of our principal men, viz. dr. Mather, adheres very much to me : and there are more women of this sort than men. And I doubt not but there a is a number, who in their Hearts are with me, who durst not appear, By Reason of the great Resolution, and high Hand with which Things are carried in the Opposition, by the prevailing Part. such is the state of Things amongst us, that a Person cannot appear on my side, without greatly exposing Himself to the Resentments of his Friends & neighbours, and being the object of much Odium.

-----The Committee, that have the care of supplying the Pulpit, have asked me to preach the greater Part of the Time since my dismission, when I have been at Home ; But it has seem'd to be with much Reluctance that They have come to me, and only because They could not get the Pulpit supplied otherwise: and They have asked me only from sabbath to sabbath; in the mean Time They have taken much Pains to get some body else to preach to 'em.

Since I wrote to you in July last, I received your Letter, dated 30th of April last, with your generous pr & acceptable Presents of Frasers Treatise of Justifying Faith, Mr. Crawfords manual against Infidelity, Mr. Randals Letter on frequent Communicating, Mr. Blairs Sermon before the Society for propogating Christian Knowledge [^142-note1] with an Account of the society, And the Bp. of London's Letter to the Cities of London & Westminster.[^142-note2] The view, the last mentioned gives, of the wickedness of those Cities, is very affecting; and the Patience of God towards such Cities, so full of wickedness, so heinous & horrid in its Kinds, and attended with such Aggravations, is very astonishing. That these Cities, & the nation, & indeed Christendom in general, are come to such a Pass as They are, seems to me to argue that some very remarkable dispensation of divine Providence is nigh, either of mercy of[^142-note3] Judgment; or perhaps both ; of great mercy to an elect Number, & great wrath & vengeance[-] towards others : And that those very Things you take notice of in Isai. 59. are approaching, appears to me very probable. However, I cannot but think, that at such a day, all such as truly Love Zion, and lament the wickedness that prevails in the Earth, are very loudly called upon to united and earnest Prayers to God, to arise and plead his own Cause, that He would make bare his own Arm, that That may bring salvation, that now when the Enemy comes in as a Flood, the spirit of the Lord may lift up a Standard[-] against Him. when the Church of Christ is like the ship wherein Christ & his disciples were when it was tossed with a dreadful Tempest, and even Covered with waves, and Christ was asleep, certainly it becomes Christians (tho' not with doubting & unbelief) to call on their Redeemer, that He would awake out of Sleep, and &[^142-note4] rebuke the winds & waves.

There are some Things that afford a degree of Comfort and hope in this dark day, respecting the State of Zion. I can't but rejoyce at some Things which I have seen, that have lately been publish'd in England, and the Reception They have met with in so corrupt a Time & nation. some Things of dr. doddridges (who seems to have his Heart truly engaged for the Interest of Religion) particularly his Rise & Progress of Religion, & Col. Gardeners Life, and also Mr. Herveys Meditations[^142-note5]. And I confess, 'tis a Thing that gives me much Hope, that there [are] so many on this side the Ocean united in the Concert for Prayer proposed from Scotland ; of which I may give a more particular Account in a Letter to Mr. McLaurin, which may be sent with This. ----I had lately a Letter from Governour Belcher ; and in the Postscript He sends me the following Extract of a Letter he had lately received from dr. doddridge.

" Nor did I ever know a finer Class of young Preachers, for its Number, than that which God has given me this year, to send out into the Churches. yet are not all the supplies here or elsewhere, adequate to their necessities : for many Congregations in various Parts of England remain vacant. But I hope God will prosper the Schemes we are forming for their assistance. --- I bless God, that in these middle Parts of our Island, [^142-note6] Peace and Truth prevails in sweet Harmony : and I think God is reviving our Cause, or rather his own, sensibly, tho' in a gentle & almost unobserved manner."

This which the doctor speaks of I hope is a Revival of Real Religion ; Tho many Things, in many Places, have been Boasted of as glorious Revivals, which have been but Counterfeits of Religion. so it has been with many Things that were intermingled with, & followed our Late happy Revival. There have been in New-England, within this 8 years past, many hundreds, if not Thousands of Instances very much like that of the Boy at Tiptry-Heath, mention'd By Mr. Davidson,[^142-note7] as you give account in your Letter.

We ought not only to praise God for every Thing that appears favourable to the Interest of Religion, & to pray earnestly for great a general Revival, but also to use means that are proper in order to it : and one proper means must be allowed to be a due administration of Christ's Ordinances : One Instance of which is that which you & Mr. Randal[^142-note8] have lately been striving for, viz. a restoring the primitive Practice of frequent Communicating. I should much wonder (had it not been for what I have lately found my self of the Force of Bigotry, & Prejudice arising from Education & Custom) how such Arguments and Perswasives as Mr. Randal uses, can be withstood. But however, They may be resisted for the present, yet I hope those who have begun will continue to plead the Cause of Christs Institutions. And whatever Opposition is made, I should Think it would be best for Them to plead for nothing at all short of Christs Institutions, viz. the Administration of the Lords supper every Lords day. It must come to that at Last; & why should Christs ministers & People, by resting in a partial Reformation, Lay a foundation for a new struggle, and an uncomfortable Labour & Conflict, in future Generation, in order to a fi full Restoration of the primitive Practice.

I should be greatly gratified dear sir of the continuance of your Correspondence, and by being informed by you of the state of Things relating to the Interest of Religi on in Europe, and specially in great Britain; and parti cularly whether the affair of a Comprehension[^142-note9] is Like to go or whether the Test Act is Like to be taken off, or if there by any Thing else done or published or done in England or Scotland, that remarkably affects the Interest of Religion.

I have with this Letter sent Mr. Bellamy's True Religion, of which I ask your Acceptance, as a small Testimony of Gratitude for your Numerous Favours to me.

I ask a Constant Remembrance in your Prayers, that I may have the Presence of God under my unusual Trials, and that I may make a good Improvemt of all Gods dealings with me. My Wife joins with me in most Cordial Salutations to you & Madam. I am dear sir,

your affectionate & obliged Friend & Brother,

Jonathan Edwards.

Mr. Erskine.

[^142-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

A Sermon Preached before the Society for Propagating Christian Knowledge. .. To Which is Subjoin'd a Short Account of the Present State of the Society* (Edinburgh, 1750); and Thomas Sherlock, *A Letter from the Lord Bishop of London to the clergy and people of London and Westminster; on the occasion of the late Earthquakes* (London, 1750).

## A124. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, [c. April 1751] 124.JE-J.Bellamy 4-51

Jonathan EdwardsA124. JE to Joseph Bellamy, n.d. (date missing at upper right corner) [c. 4/51]. Diedrich Collection, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan.

Northampton

Rev'd & dear sir,

I much desire to see you here this spring, and should be glad you would come so to be here on the third thursday in May, when it is agreed to desire a Council to meet here, to Look into the state of Things, & give me advice with Regard to my duty in my Circumstances ; and also to give Advice to the People here that have adhered to what Course They shall take under their very difficult Circumstances. I hope sir, you will not fail. I shall think it of great Importance that some ministers should be here that give a fair Representation of Things relating to Canaan & stockbridge. I suppose that the ministers that will be called will be M dr. sewal, Mr. Prince, Mr. Clark, Mr. Hobby, Mr. Wigglesworth, Mr. Walley of Ipswich, Mr. Hall of sutton, Mr. Billing, & Mr. Abercrombie.[^143-note1] I am sir

your Friend & Brother

Jth Edwards.

Mr. Bellamy.

[^143-note1]: **[1].** Joseph Sewall and Thomas Prince of Old South Church, Boston; Peter Clark of Danvers; William Hobby of Reading; Edward Wigglesworth of Harvard College; John Walley of Ipswich, David Hall of Sutton, Edward Billing of Cold Spring, and Robert Abercrombie of Pelham.

## A125. Letter to Joseph Sewall and Thomas Prince, April 10, 1751 125.JE-Sewall and Prince 4-10-51

Jonathan EdwardsA125. JE to Joseph Sewall and Thomas Prince, 4/10/51. AAS, Curwen Papers, Box 2, f. 2. Cover letter for no. 125a, Northampton Minority to Sewall and Prince.

To the Rev. dr. Joseph [-] Sewall & the Rev. Mr. Thomas Prince Pastors of the third Church in Boston, to be communicated.

Reverend, honoured & beloved,

My Brethren in this Place, who now apply to you for your Advice under their distressing Circumstances, being Those whom I think my Self obliged to be tenderly concerned for, They having long been under my pastoral Care, and having adhered to Me when most of their Neighbours have been alienated from Me and have renounced my Ministry, and have manifested Themselves especially friendly under very great Trials; I do concur with Them in desiring that They, under their present difficulties, may have the Advice of a wise and judicious Council, which I am sensible their Case greatly requires. And tho' my Settlement in the pastoral Office, over so small a Number, under their Circumstances, appears to Me to be a Thing attended with great difficulty & darkness; Yet I am willing to resign my Self in that Affair, to the direction of a Council of such Ministers & Churches as They now apply Themselves to. And if I should finally leave Them, my Obligations to Them and Affection for Them make me unwilling to leave Them in such extremely difficult Circumstances, without some Advice from such as may be confided in as Persons of the best Ability & Integrity, to direct Them what to do and which way to turn Themselves. I also desire an Opportunity to lay my own Case before such a Council, to ask their Judgment of it, and to be advised by Them how to conduct my Self with Regard to my Settlement in the work of the Ministry; there seeming at this Time, through a merciful Providence in the Time of my great Troubles, to be divers doors opening for my Improvement & serviceableness in that great work. ---Hoping for an Opportunity to lay before you my Circumstances, and to receive your Advice in these important Concerns, at the Time & Place specified in my Brethren's Letter, in Conjunction with the Rev. Elders & Messengers of such other Churches as They apply to; and asking an Interest in your Prayers for me and Them, and for the whole Church & Congregation in this Place in their present dark state, I am

with much Honour & Respect,

your brother and servant,

Jonathan Edwards.

Northampton

April 10. 1751.

## A126. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, April 23, 1751 126.JE-T.Foxcroft 4-23-51

Jonathan EdwardsA126. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 4/23/51. BRBL, f. 1293.

Newberry April 23. 1751.

Rev. & honoured sir,

It has been suggested to me by several ministers, since I came from Boston, that there is great danger of dr Chauncey's influencing m dr. sewall & mr. Hubbard to oppose their Chh's sending to the Counsel at Northampton. And if their Chh fail I think mr. Clark & mr. Wigglesworth will not go, & so all will fail. This therefore is humbly to request of you that you would take an Opportunity this week to confer with dr. Sewall mr. Hubbard the secretary & Maj. Henchman about it; the matter being to be determined the next sabbath.

I think the matter is of great Importance & therefore I hope you will excuse

your obliged Brother & servt

Jonath. Edwards.

## A127. Letter to William Hobby (Draft), [June 1751] 127.JE-W.Hobby 6-51

Jonathan EdwardsA127. JE to William Hobby, 6/51. ANTS, f. 1751, #2-3, 14. This letter came after a series of pamphlets following the Final Council that voted to dismiss JE. The majority published in response to the Protest of the Minority, [Robert Breck,] *An Account of the Conduct of the Council which dismissed the Rev. Mr. Edwards from the pastoral care of the first church in Northampton* (Boston, 1750). Hobby answered with *A Vindication of the Protest against the Result of the Northampton Council* (Boston, 1751), which the majority countered with [Breck et al,] *A Letter to the Rev. Mr. Hobby, in answer to his Vindication* (Boston, 1751). See Dwight 1:453ff., who says the following by JE was published, though there is no evidence of that.

sir I think myself obliged to in the most publick manner I am able to correct a a mist great mi & very injurious Representation made a very publick fact con cerning me in a Late Pamphlet Entitled a Letter to the Rev. Mr. Hobby in Answer to his Vindication of the Protest against the Result of the Northampton an ecclesiastical Council met at Northampton &c--

signed by R. B./ J. A./ T. W./ & C. W.[^146-note1]

These Gentlemen in this Pamphlet gives an account of gave to the giving an Account for this Pamphlet what declaration those gave in p. 16 of their Pamphlet what declaration both the Chh & I made before that Council of our Principles say[-] that M I Mr. E. declared that he He could not in Conscience be active in admitting any into the Chh unless I They first made a Profession THAT THEY WERE INDEED SANCTIFIED. whereas I declared the Reverse of this openly & publick in ly & very particularly open before that very the Council in the meeting House a great multitude being present. I For that Reason because I had heard that such Reports had been made abroad of my opinion but expos but carefully corrected em or expressly denied & Contradicted em but told the Council very ex that there was no truth in such Reports that the thing I insist on was not that a Person should say SAY THEY WERE CONVERTED OR WERE GODLY that that was not what I called a ever intended by that a Person making a Profession of Godliness & that I should not think it became Persons to [--] come a Chh & make such a Profession as this But what I [--] insisted on as a proper Profession of Godliness was [-] his Professing that the great Things wherein Godliness consists or that He found these the great things by in his Heart wheri which tho He might think them not to be Godliness yet were in truly such things as the SS. represents as the Essentials of true Piety. This writing I was obs Informed was handed round among the members & read by Them was read by the members of the Council. ## A128. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, June 28, 1751 128.JE-J.Bellamy 6-28-51

Jonathan EdwardsA128. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 6/28/51. Hartford Seminary, Bellamy Papers, Doc. Box 187, f. 29-30, item #81191. Addressed on back "To the / Rev. Mr Jos. Bellamy / at Bethlem."

Dear Brother:

I have been to Boston, and have agreed with the Commissioners; They engage 70£ sterl. Pr annum, besides the small matter that stockbridge People Engage. The Instalmt is appointed on the 2d Thursday in August, when I hope to see you here. I came hither the last week. I am sir

your most affectionate

Friend & Br.

J. Edwards.

stockbridge

June 28. 1751.

P.S. I met in Boston many very kind Letters from scotland, with a present of 60 sterling in Goods, which will come to perhaps a third more as it may be disposed. it came free of all Charge, Freight & Insurance being Paid. 10£ sterling more is coming. -Thus it proves that we need not fear to trust God in the way of duty. -Admiral Warren has appropriated 700£ sterling for the use of the Mohawks here, & Mr. Hollis has engaged 180 sterling yearly for the same use. ------

## A129. Letter to John Erskine, June 28, 1751 129.JE-J.Erskine 6-28-51

Jonathan EdwardsA129. JE to John Erskine, 6/28/51. ANTS, f. 1751, #8-9.

Stockbridge June 28. 1751.

Rev. & dear Brother,

I have lately received a Treatise of the Restoration of the Jews, and a Pamphlet entitled a Serious Address to the Church of Scotland, with a sermon on the Qualifications of the Teachers of Christianity, [-] preached by you before the synod, an with Glas's Notes On scripture Texts N. 5.[^148-note1]. These Pamphlets were inclosed in a Wrapper superscribed by your Hand. There was also in the Pacquet a brief Advertisement concerning one of the Pamphlets, written in your Hand tho' without any date or name, or any Letter in the Pacquet. But yet I conclude those these Pamphlets were pro sent by you. And accordingly I now thank you for Them. Your discourse on the Qualifications of Teachers of Christianity is a very Acceptable Present. Glas's Notes on scripture Texts contain some Things things[^148-note2] that are very Curious, & discover Close Study, & a critical Genius. The Treatise of the Restoration of the Jews, if written by a Christian divine, is a strange and unaccountable Thing: By Reason of their being nothing at all said or hinted about the Jews Conversion to the Christian Faith; or one so much as one mention of Jesus Christ ; and his supposing that the Prophecies of Ezekiel are to be literally fulfilled, in the building such a Temple & City as is there described, and the Issuing of such a River from the threshold of the Temple, & running into the East sea, and the Jews offering Sacrifices, and observing other Rites spoken of in Ezekiel; and that the Messiah is yet to come & to Reign in Jerusalem as a temporal Prince &c. And I am wholly at a Loss as to the Authors real design, whether it was to promote Judaism or deism; or only to amuse his readers.

Since I received these Pamphlets, I have received Letters from all my other Correspondents in Scotland; but none from you. Mr. McLaurin speaks of your writing, or designing to write; but suggests that possibly your Letter would not arrive so soon as the Rest. so that I hope I shall yet, ere Long, receive a Letter from you. The Letters I have received from my other Correspondents make mention of a great Revival of Religion in Holland and Mr. McLaurin has sent me print ed Accounts of it, publish'd, as I understand, by Mr. Gillies, his son in Law, being Extracts of Letters from Holland. [^148-note3] I had some Notice of it before in a Letter from Mr. davenport, who for the most part resides in N. Jersey. The account He wrote was brought over from Holland, by a young Dutch Minister whose name is John Frielinghousen, born in N. Jersey, son to an eminent du & successful dutch [^148-note4] His elder Brother is settled at Albany & by all Accounts and able & faithful Minister there. This second son had been in Holland two years, I suppose to perfect his Education in one of their Universities, where his Brother at Albany had his Education. He came over into America the last summer having first been married, and ordained in Holland in order to take the Pastoral Charge of some of the Places that had been under his Father's Care. The Accounts Mr. davenport[^148-note5] gives from Him are not so particular as Those that are publish'd by Gillies. But there is one Material & Important Circumstance which He mentions, not taken notice of in the Accounts from Scotland, viz. that the Stadtholder was much pleased with the work. [^148-note6]

At the same Time that we rejoyce in this w glorious work, and Praise God for it, it concerns us earnestly to pray that Gods ministers & People there may be directed in such a State of Things, wherein wisdom and great discretion is so exceedingly needed, and great Care & skill to distinguish between true & false Religion. or those inward Experiences which are from the saving Influence of the spirit of God and those that are from satan transforming Himself into an Angel of Light. without this it may be expected that the great deceiver will gradually insinuate Himself ; acting under disguise, He will pretend to be a zealous Promoter assistant in Building the Temple, yea the mo chief Architect, when his real design will be to bring all to the Ground, and to build Babel instead of the Temple of God: finally to the great Reproach & Grief of all true Friends of Religion, and the haughty Triumph of its Adversaries. If I may be allowed my Conjecture in this affair, There lies the greatest danger of the People in Gelderland who are concerned in this work. I wish they had all the Benefit of the late Experience of this Part of the Church of God here in America. Mr. McLauring informs, that dear sir, that you have a Correspondence in the Netherlands, And as you know something of the Calamities we have suffered from this Quarter, I wish you would give 'em some kind Admonitions. They will need all the warnings that can be given them : For the Temptation to religious People in such a state of Things is to countenance the Glaring Counterfeits of Religion, without distinguishing Them from the Reality what is true & genuine, is so strong, that they are very hardly indeed broug restrain'd from it. They will at last find the Consequences not to be good of an abundant declaring & proclaiming their Experiences on all Occasions & before all Companies, if they get into that way, as They will be likely to do without special Caution in their Guides. I am not so much concerned about any danger the Rev Interest of the Revival of Religion in Gelderland may be in from violent open Opposition, as from the secret subtil undiscerned Guile of the Old serpent. --I perceive pious abiding Effects of the late awakenings in scotland and America. I think it is fit They should know the very Truth of the Case, and that Things should be represented neither better nor worse than They are. If They should be represented worse, that would give Encouragement to unreasonable Opposers. If better, that might prevent a most necessary Caution of the true Friends of the Awakening. I could There are undoubtedly very many Instances in N. England, in the whole, of the Perseverance of such as were thought to have received the saving Benefits of the late Revival of Religion, and their continuing to walk in New-ness of Life, & as becomes saints; Instances which are uncontestible; and which men must be most obstinately blind not to see. But I believe the Proportion here is not so great as in Scotland. I cannot say that the greater Part of supposed Converts, give Reason by their Conversation to suppose that They are true Converts. The Proportion may Perhaps be more truly represented by the Proportion of the Blossoms on a Tree which abide and come to mature Fruit, to the whole number of Blossoms in the spring. [^148-note7]

In the formentioned Letter which I lately had from Mr. davenport, mentions some degrees of Awakening in some Places of N. Jersey. The following are Extracts from his Letter.

" I returned last Month from Cape May, where I had been labouring some Time, with little or no success, as to the Unregenerate; except Somewhat encouraging the last day of my Preaching among Them. Yet, blessed be God, I hear of the Success of Several Ministers in the Jerseys, & the Revival of Religion in some Places, tho' it is a very dull Time in most. Mr. Read[^148-note8] of Bound-brook has, I hear, some Encouragement by Reason of some souls in his Place being under Conviction. Mr. Kennedy,[^148-note9] who is likely to settle at Basking-ridge, I hear has more Encouragement in this way. & Mr. John Frielinghuysen, more yet among the dutch. He is the second son of that Frielinghuysen you speak of in your Narrative, who died a few years ago. This second son came over from Holland, where he had been two years, & was ordain'd a Little before He came over last summer. ----Pious ministers among the dutch our way I think increase faster of late than among other People. I was at the House of such an one, Mr. Varbryk,[^148-note10] as I came along in this Journey; who was ordain'd last Fall about 5 miles beyond dobbs's Ferry, in N. york Government. ---Mr. William Tennent told me that Mr. John Light,[^148-note11] a pious young dutch minister in New Jersey, was translating Accounts from Holland into English. ---Mr. Brainerd[^148-note12] has had some special success lately through Mercy; so that 9 or 10 Indians appear to be under Convictions, as He tells me; and about 12 of the white People near Them, that used to be stupid like the very Heathen; and many others more thoughtful & serious. Mr Sacket has lately been favoured with particular success in reducing a number drawn away & infected by the Separatists. and some endeavours I have used since that, & with Him, have I trust not been altogether in vain. The good Lord grant that false Religion may cease, & true Religion prog prevail through the Earth."

This letter of Mr. davenport's was dated April 26. 1751.

The dutch People in the Provinces of N. York & N. Jersey have been famed for being generally exceeding Ignorant, stupid & Profane, little better than the savages of our American deserts. But 'tis remarkable that things should now begin to appear more hopeful among Them, about the same Time that Religion is reviving among the dutch in their Mother Countrey. And certainly the Revivals of Religion which do have very lately appeared, especially that among the dutch in Europe, do verify God's holy word, which gives such great Encouragement to his People to pray for such mercies. And I must think these Things not only afford great Encouragement to those who have engaged in the Concert for united Prayer, begun in Scotland, to go on in with that Affair, but binds it strongly upon Them so to do; and that it will be an aggravated Fault, if, after God does such glorious Things, so soon after we have begun in an extraordinary manner to ask Them, if we should grow cold & slack & begin to give o fail. And I think what God has now done may well be Cause those who seemed at first with some Zeal to engage in this affair, but have grown careless & about it, & have left off, to reflect on Themselves with blushing & Confusion.

---what if you dear sir, & other Ministers in Scotland who have been engaged in this Affair, should now take Occasion to inform Ministers in the Netherlands of it, and move to them to come into it, & Join with us in our united & extraordinary Prayers for an universal Revival of Religion? -----------

As to my Present Circumstances, I came the last week to this Place, bein having undertaken the Business of a Missionary to the Indians Here, my Instal having been chosen the Pastor by this Church, and chosen Missionary by the Co Commissioners for Indian Affairs in Boston. My Instalmt is appointed to be on the 2d Thursday [^148-note13] in the next month. I don't expect to get ready to remove my Family 'till winter. -- But I must refer you dear sir, to my Letters to Mr. McLaurin & Mr. Robe, for a more full account of my Circumstances, and of the Things which have pass'd relating to 'em. I have with this sent you the Gazette containing the Result of a late Council at Northampton[^148-note14] & intend to Order one of my Farewel sermons to be put up for you. -My Family were in their usual State of Health when I left 'em, excepting my youngest who had something like an Intermitting Fever. ---Please to present my cordial Respects & Christian Love to your dear Consort. And remember me in your Prayers, with Regard to the Trials & Changes I am called to pass through, & the new & important Business I have undertaken.

I am dear sir,

your most united & obliged Friend & Brother,

Jonathan Edwards.

Mr Erskine Notes

[^148-note1]: Samuel Collett, *A Treatise of the Future Restoration of the Jews and Israelites to Their Own Land* (London, 1747); *A Serious Address to the Church of Scotland, with Relation to the Growth of Deism and Immorality* (London, 1739); John Erskine, *The Qualifications necessary for teachers of Christianity* (Glasgow, 1750); John Glas, *Notes on Scripture-Texts* (see *Works, 13*, 137, n. 9)
