## A130. Letter to Thomas Gillespie, July 1, 1751 130.JE-T.Gillespie 7-1-51

Jonathan EdwardsA130. JE to Thomas. Gillespie, 7/1/51. ANTS, f. 1751, #6-7.

Stockbridge July 1. 1751.

Rev. & very dear Sir,

I am very greatly obliged to you for your most kind, affectionate, comfortable and profitable Letter, of Feb 2. 51. I thank you sir for your sympathy with me under my Troubles, so amply testified, and the many suitable & proper Considerations you suggest to me for my comfort & Improvement. May God enable me to make a right Improvement of Them. 'Tis not to be wondered at dear sir, that you are shock'd and surprized at had what has happened between me and the People of Northampton. 'Tis very surprizing to all impartial and considerate Persons that live near, and have the greatest Advantage to know the Circumstances of the Affair, and the Things that preceeded this Event & made way for it : But no wonder if it be much more so to strangers at a distance. I doubt not but that God intends his own Glory, and the Prosperity Safety & Prosperity of Zion, and the Advancement of the Interest of Religion, in the final Issue of this Event ; And, I trust also, my Good. But it is best that the true state of the Case should be known, and that it should be view'd as it is, in Order to receiving that Instruction, which divine Providence holds forth in it, & in order to the proper Reflections & a right Improvement:

As There are is a difference among particular Persons as to their natural Temper, so there is some difference of this Kind to be observed in diffe rent Countreys, and also in different Cities & Towns. The People of Northampton are not the most happy in their Natural Temper. They have, ever since I can remember, been famed for a high-spirited People, & close, & of a difficult turbulent Temper. However, tho' in some Respects they have been a stiffnecked People, yet the God has been pleased in Times past to bestow many special & distinguishing Favours upon. The Town has stood now near an 100 years. Their first Minister Mr. Eleazar Mather (Brother to dr. Increase Mather of Bother,[^149-note1] & Mr. Samuel Mather of dul dublin in Ireland) was a very eminent man of God. After Him came Mr. stoddard, my Grand father; a very great Man, of strong Powers of Mind, of great Grace, and great Authority, of a Masterly Countenance speech & Behaviour. He had great success in his ministry. there being many seasons in his day of general Awakening among his People. He continued in the ministry at Northampton about 60 years. But God was pleas'd especially to manifest his Power in the weakness of his sucessor; [^149-note2] there having been a [--] more remarkable Awakening since his death that Ever had been before that. Altho' since that also, a greater declension, and more awful departures from God in some Respects than Ever before : and so the last minister has had more to humble Him than any of his Predecessours. May the Effect be answerable to God's just Expectations! ---The people fr having from the Beginning been well Instructed ; have had a Name, for a long Time, for a very knowing People ; And many have appeared among Them Persons of good Abilities ; and many that have been born in the Town have been promoted to Places of publick Improvement: They have been a People distinguished on this Account. -These things have manifestly been abused to nourish the Pride of their Natural Temper . an which has made made[^149-note3] 'em more difficult & unmanageable. There were some mighty Contests & Controversies among Them in Mr. Stoddards which were managed with great Heat & violence ; some great Quarrels in the Church, wherein Mr stoddard, great as his Authority was, knew not what to do with them.

In one Ecclesiastical Controversy in Mr. stoddard's days, wherein the Church was divided into two Parties, The Heat of spirit was raised to such a Height, that it came to hand-Blows ; a number of one met [--] the Head of the Opposite Party, and assaulted Him and beat Him unmercifully. In later Times the People have had more to feed their Pride : They have grown a much greater & more wealthy People than formerly, and are become more extensively famous in the world, as a People that have excelled in Gifts & Grace, and had God extraordinarily among them. Which has insensibly nou ingendered & nourished spiritual Pride, that grand inlet of the devil into the Hearts of men, and Avenue of all manner of Mischief among a Professing People. spiritual Pride is a most monstrous Thing. If it ben't discern'd and vigorously opposed in its firs Beginning, it very often soon raises Persons above their Teachers, & supposed spiritual Fathers, & sets 'em out of the Reach of all Rule and Instruction ; as I have seen in innumerable Instances. And therein this Inconvenience attends the publishing of Narratives of a work of God among a People. such is the Corruption that is in the Hearts of men, and even of Good men, that there is great danger of their making it an Occasion of spiritual Pride. --- There is great Reason to think that Northampton People have provoked God greatly against them by trusting in their Priviledges and attainments; & the Consequences may well be a warning to all Gods People far & [^149-note4] near, that hear of Them. ---- Another Thing Which probly has contributed in some measure to the unhappiness of the Peoples Manners, was that Mr. stoddard, tho' an eminently Holy Man, was naturally of a dogmatical Temper ; and the People being brought up under Him, and with a high veneration for Him, naturally were led to imitate Him : Especially their officers & leading men seem'd to think it an excellency to be like Him in this Respect.

--- It has been a very great wound to the Church of Northampton that there has for fourty Forty or fifty years been a sort of settled division of the People into two Parties; something like the Court & Country Party in England (if I may compare small Things with great) There have been some of the chief men in the Town, of Chief Authority & wealth, that have been great Proprietors of their Lands ; who have had one Party with Them. And the other Party, which commonly has been the greatest, have been of Those who have been Jeasou Jealous of them, apt to envy 'em, and afraid of their having too much Power and Influence in Town & Church. This has been a Foundation of Innumerable Contentions among the People from Time to Time ; which have been exceeding grievous to me ; and by which doubtless God has been dreadfully provoked, & his Spirit grieved & Quench'd, and much Confusion, and many evil works have been introduced. --Another Thing that Evidently has contributed to our Calamities is, that the People we had got so Establish'd in certain wrong notions & ways in Religion, which I found Them in and never could beat them out of. Particularly it was too much their Method to lay almost all the stress of their Hopes on the particular steps & method of their first work, i.e. the first work of the spirit of God on their Hearts in their Convictions & Conversion, & too look but little at the abiding sense & Temper of their Hearts, and the Course of their Exercises & Fruits of Grace, for Evidences of their good Estate. Nor had They learn'd, and many of Them never could be made to learn, to distinction between Impressions on the Imagination, and truly spiritual Experiences. And when I came among Them I found it to be a Custom among Them without discretion or distinction of Occasions places or Companies, to declare & publish their own Experiences; and oftentimes to do it in a light manner, without any air of solemnity. This Custom has not a little contributed to spiritual Pride, and many other Evils. when I first settled among the People, being young & of [^149-note5] but little Experience, I was not thoroughly aware of the Ill Consequences of such a Custom ; & so allowed it, or at least did not testify against it as I ought to have done. ---And here I desire it may be observed that I would be far from so laying all the blame of the sorrowful things that have come to pass to the people, as to suppose that I have no Cause of self-Reflection & Humiliation before God on this Occasion. I am sensible that it becomes me too look on what has lately happen'd, as an awful Frown of Heaven on me, as well as on the People. God knows the wickedness of my Heart and my great & sinful deficiencies and offences which I have been guilty of in the Course of my ministry at Northampton. I desire that God would discover them to me more & more, and that now He would effectually humble me & mortify my Pride and self-confidence, and empty me entirely of my self, and make me to know how that I deserve to be cast away as an abominable Branch, and a vessel wherein is no Pleasure. and if it may consist with his holy will sanctify me, & meet make me a vessel more meet for my masters Use, & yet improve me as an Instrument of his Glory & the good of souls the souls of mankind.

One Thing that has contributed to bring Things to such a Pass at Northampton, was my youth & want of more Judgment & Experience, in the Time of [-] that extraordinary awakening above sixteen years ago. Instead of a Child, there was want of [a] Giant in Judgment & discretion among a People in such an extraordinary state of Things. In some Respects doubtless my Confidence in my self was a great wrong to me ; But in other Respects, my diffidence of my self injured me. It was such that I durst not act my own Judgment, and had no strength to oppose received notions & established Customs, & to testify boldly against some glaring ap false appearances of Reli & Counterfeits of Religion, 'till it was too late. And by this means many things got Footing which have been a dreadful source of spiritual Pride, and other things that are exceeding contrary to true Christianity. If I had had more Experience and Ripeness of Judgment & Courage, I should have guided my People in a better Manner, and should have guarded Them better from satans devices, and prevented the great spiritual Calamity of many souls, and pl perhaps the eternal Ruin of some of Them, and should have done what [^149-note6] would have tended to lengthen out the Tranquility of the Town. ---- However, doubtless at that Time there was a very glorious work of God wrought in Northampton, and there were numerous Instances of saving Conversion ; tho' de undoubtedly many were deceived, and deceived others ; and the number of true Converts was not so great as was then imagined. many may be ready from things that are lately come to Pass to determine that all Northampton Religion is come to Nothing, & that all the Famed Awakenings & Revivals of Religion in that Place prove to be nothing, but strange Tides of a melancholy & whimsical Humour. But They would draw no such Conclusion if they exactly knew the true state of the Case, & would judge of it with full Calmness & Impartiality of mind. -- There are many things to Considered in the Case of Northampton.

1. That many of those who have been most violently engaged, and have chiefly led[-] & excited others in it, Tho' they have been Leading men in the Town, and have been esteemed considerable for their Knowledge, Estate and Age, and have been Professours of Religion, yet have not been the most famed for Piety.

2. The leading men, who have been most engaged in this matter, who have taken vast Pains to stir up others that are inferiour have had this great Advantage in their Hands, That the Controversy was a Religious Controversy ; That which I opposed was what They alwaies had supposed to be a Part of divine Truth, a precious & important doctrine of the word of God, & that the Cause of my opposers was the Cause of God. This has led the more ignorant & less considerate People to look on their Zeal against me a vertue, & to giv Christen even their Passions & Bitterness in such a Cause with sanctified names, & to let 'em loose, & prosecute the views of their Bitterness & violence without Check of Conscience.

3. They have also had the great Advantage of the vast veneration the People had for Mr stoddard's ministry memory; which was such that Many of Them looked on Him as a sort of deity. They were all (i.e. the except the young People) born & brought up under his ministry, and had been used from their Infancy to esteem his sayings all as Oracles. And He, they knew, maintain'd that doctrine which I oppose, with great Positiveness & Zeal, & opposed the Contrary as which I maintain, as an exceeding pernicious doctrine. Under these Cir cumstances I naturally appear as a dangerous opposer of the Cause of God, [^149-note7] and my teaching & insisting on the doctrine which Mr. stoddard opposed appears to 'em a sort of horrid Profaneness.

4. Crafty designing men have abundantly fill'd the Ears of the more ignorant with suggestions that my Opinion tends to overthrow all Religion, and to ruin the present & future Generations, and make all heathen, shutting them out of the Church of Christ.

5. Not only many of the Leading men in Northampton have used their utmost Endeavours to engage the minds of the Common People in this Controversy ; But They have also been put forward by the neighbouring ministers all round. my [--] opposers have also been assisted and edg'd on by some at a greater distance, Persons of Note ; And some great men in Civil Authority have had a great Hand.

6. It is to be considered, That the Contrary opinion to mine had not only long been established in Northampton, without so much as one opposer to it, but it had also been fully & quietly established for a long Time, in all the neighbouring Churches & Congregations, & in all the Countrey round, even to a great distance. so that my opinion, when first broach'd, appeared to the People exceeding singular. Their views being very narrow, It appeared to Them that all the world do almost was against me. And my most crafty Opposers have improved this advantage, and have abundantly im Represented me, as ex all alone in my opinion.

7. many of the People, who at length came to have their spirits much raised, and were brought to join in violent measures, yet came slowly into it, after beving long Practiced with, & indefatigable Endeavours used to engage and inflame 'em.

8. There about 20 Heads of Families, who besides others, that were women & young People, ever appeared openly against the Proceedings of the Town ; & many others have appeared friendly to me. And there is not a little Reason to think, that there are many more, especially women & youth, that would appear so, if They dare. For a Person, by appearing my Friend at Northampton, so much as to discountenance my being turned out of the Pulpit, exposes Himself to Immediate Persecution of his neighbours, and perhaps of his nearest [^149-note8] Friends. I mean He is falls under their Great Resentment, looses all their Friendship, is every where the Object of Reproach. & ________________

9. Tis to be Considered that these things have happened, when God is greatly withdrawn, & Religion was very low, not only at Northampton but all over N. England. _________

10. I believe the devil is greatly alarmed by the Opposition made made to Mr. stoddards doctrine, & a Practice the agreable Practice, which had been so long established at Northampton, & so extensively in the Countrey : In which He found his Account, & hoped for greater Consequences, mo & more agreable to Him. And God for wise Ends, has suffered Him to exert Himself in an extraordinary manner in Opposition, as God ordinarily does when Truth in is in the Birth.

But I am drawn out to an unexpected Length in my observations on these Things, and have not left my self Room nor Time for some other Things, that I would willingly write . & must therefore refer you to my Letters to my other Correspondents in scotland, particularly Mr. McLaurin, Mr Robe, Mr. McCulloch, & Mr. John Erskine. To some of Them I have been sending a particular Account of my present Circumstances, & things which have lately pass'd relating to 'em. In a I would only say in general, that I have had a Call to settle at stockbridge, a place in the western Borders of New-England, next to the Province of N. York, about 36 miles from Albany, & The Place where Mr. sergeant was minister & missionary to the Indians. I am both called by the Church here constituted partly of English & partly of Indians, and am appointed missionary to the Indians by the Commissioners for Indian Affairs in Boston : Agreable to what you suggest in your Letter, as tho' you had been able to foresee future Events, when you Perhaps you are to be employed where the Gospel has been little understood,

or attended to. I suppose this Place will for the future be the Place of my Ordinary abode. Tho' it will be some months before I can remove my Family.

I have no Leisure at present to write on that subject you speak of, viz. Impressions & im supposed immediate Revelations ; [^149-note9] tho' I own the vast Importance of the subject. I had begun to write something against the Arminians, before the late Controversy broke out with my People ; which broke me off from it, and obliged me to write on that Controversy. & now lately Mr. Williams of Lebanon has wrote a Book in answer to mine on that subject, which I think my self obliged to answer, if God gives opportunity.

I have much to p teach me to behave as a Pilgrim & stranger on the Earth. But in the midst of Troubles & difficulties, I receive many mercies. Particularly I have great Reason, with [-] abundant Thankfulness, to take Notice of the great Kindness of Friends in Scotland. Blessed be God who never forsakes those that trust in Him, and never wants Instruments for the Conveyance of his Goodness & Liberality to those who suffer in his Cause.

- I shall take Care that there be conveyed with this Letter to you, one of my Farewell sermons, and the Result of the Council, that sat at Northampton the last may.

Remember me dear sir, at the Throne of Grace, with Regard to all my Trials. and with Regard to the important my new Circumstances, & the important service I have un undertaken in this Place. --And please in your next to inform me of what Family you & of their state.

I am sir.

your most affectionate Friend & Brother, Jonathan Edwards. Mr. Gillespie

## A131. Letter to Isaac Hollis (Draft), Summer 1751 131.JE-I.Hollis Summer51

Jonathan EdwardsA131. JE to Isaac Hollis, Summer 1751. Draft. ANTS, f. 1751, #4-5.

stockbridge To Mr. Hollis

Rev. & honored sir.

Having seen your late Letter to Mr. Fox Prince of Boston and another written to Capt Kellog ofschool master in this Placeto the & having lately been chosen & appointed missionary to the Indians in this Place, I thought my self obliged to take the first Opportunity to write to you who have exerted your self in so extraordinary a manner to promote our Interest here to serve which I am now devoted Partly to off my Thanks to you for what you have done h & have lately offered to do with so fervent & enlarged a Heart & bountiful a Hand for the El Advance mt & Enlargemt of Xs Kingdom of Grace among these Poor people & the eternal wellfare of their souls which excite the Joy & Admiration of all Good Xtians & deserves the Thanks of all that make the Interest of Zion their own & especially of Him who has the Care of the souls of the Indians in this Place more especially Committed to his more immediate Care.

And partly to ob inform you of what I have have had opportunity to observe of the state of Things here relating to the affair of the Instruction of the Indians which you have a Right to know seeinghave pleased so gratly to interest you selfin this affair it being an affair which you have been pleased so greatly to Interest your self in and on which depends [^150-note1] so much on the Fruits of your Generosity I have had s Considerable opportunity to see the state of Things for tho tis but about a month since I came here after I had undertaken the mi work of the ministry here as the stated missionary yet I had been here before two months in the winter & p spent much time with the Indi ans particularly the Mohawks under Capt Kellogs care.

There are two here schools for the Instruction of the Indian Children one under M the Care of Mr. Timo W.-- which both subsisted very began soon after Mr. sergeant began to preach to these Indians thwha His school Consists wholly of the Chil. of the proper Housatonnock Indians The in other under the Care of K Capt Kellog which began he began with Stockbridge Indians on the plan which Mr. sergt projected But in the Changeable unsettled state that things have been in since Mr. sergeant death has altered from that form & it now Consists wholly of mohawk Children ha that have been brought down from the hither from their own proper Countrey about 80 miles distant, to that End that they might be Instructed taught to read & write & Instructed in the Xtian Relig.

That There are some things give a very hopeful Prospect with Regard to these Indians particularly the forward Inclination of the Children and their aptness to learn But that which has evidently been the greatest defect from the Beginning in the method of Instruction [^150-note2][^150-note3] here is that no more proper & effectual measures have been taken to bring the Children that are here taught to the Knowledge of the English Tongue*[^150-note4] for want of this all the Labour & Cost that has been expended here in schools here for near to years has been consequentially to but little Effect when The Childen are taug when the Children are taught to read the Book but many of them for want of the English Language they know nothing what They read (The Books are being all in the English Tongue) They Learn to only Learn to make such sounds for such marks but dont knowthe meaning of thte sounds so that veryfew of them know any Thing the meaning of the sounds & so have neither profit nor pleasure in reading. & will therefore be apt soon to Loose even what they have learned having no Benefit or entertainmt in the use of it.

Tis of on many accounts of great importance that they should be brought to the English Language. as this would greatly tend to theirbeg begin to int acquantin forward their Instruction their own Barbarous Languages being very unfit exceeding Barren & very unfit to express moral & divine Things & their being brought to English would above allthings tend to their being brought to civility that civility which is to be s thought as tis would tend bring into into to in would open their minds & bring em into acquaintance & Conversation with the English & would tend above all things to bring to that Civility which is they find among the English.

some Pains has been taken to teach the Chil. the English tongue But nothing Considerable has been o can bedone without accomplished if the Chil.were put out to English Fa dispersed intoEnglish Families And I can think of but two ways that th it can be Effected either the Introducing a number of English Children into their schools to Learn with them & be their mates or the disposing the Indian Chil. into English Families to live there a year or two where they must be obliged to speak the English & nothing & then Return un into the Indian school to perfect them in Knowl reading writing & other useful Knowl. the Latter (if their Parents can be perswaded to it as probably they may) will be much the most Effectual. & found Effectual I would therefore humblypropose this thins in the the English here all seem acknowledge the necessity of one of those methods. In order to the moneys not being spent in vain that is Laid out for their Instruction as Long as they keep together & their Company & they are ever spent only with Indians unless Just in what they lay to their school master they never will learn the English [^150-note5] Tongue

I would honourable sir humbly propose that some such method should be taken with Regard to the Children that have the Benefit of your Benefaction & Liberality & that part of your Benefaction should be expended in that way under the Care a number of prudent & faith ful Trustees for in Order to the mana Business being managed thoroughly & effectually a Great deal of Care & activity will be necessary [--] vastly more than the schoolmaster can have Leisure for There are many Things pertaining to the Regulation of the affair of the Instruction of the Indian Chil Children that seem greatly to require the Care of an number of Trustees Persons who shall be intrusted to dispose things according to the best of their discretion giving a part sending from time to Time a particular & exact account of the manner in which they have laid out your money.

---I thought my self obliged to give you these Intimations you being at a great distance & not capable of Knowing the exact state of things any otherwise than by the Informa tion of those that see them& are on the spot and it beingnecessary that you you thus areenabled Right to know s those circumstances that are such im portance in the affair that without a proper Regard to 'em what the Great Expence you are at willbe li is liable to spewh in a great measure in vain. I Re humbly Request your prayers to fountain of all Light & Grace for his dir direction & assistance in that Important service I have lately undertaken in this Place [-] I am honoured sir

your B most humble servt & Broth affectionate Brother in the Gospel Ministry

J. E.

which I would suppose has been owing the Fault of the Teachers who I suppose have done what They could in the Business to which They have been appointed & in the Improvemt of the means & Advantages which have been put into their Hands However

To Mr. Hollis in the

summer. 1751.

## A132. Letter to William Hogg, July 13, 1751 132.JE-W.Hogg 7-13-51

Jonathan Edwards132. JE to William Hogg, 7/13/51. Yale Manuscripts and Archives, Anson Phelps Stokes Autograph Coll., MS 402, Series I, B. 3, f. 178. Hogg's notation on back, "Answered 8th May 1752 / to Mr. Prince's Care."

Stockbridge July 13. 1751

Dear Sir,

The Accounts which I have lately received from Correspondents in Scotland, of the Respect to me & my Family, which you have, in various ways, testified both by word & deed, may well deeply affect us with Gratitude, and excite our Admiration. And in the first Place, we have Reason to admire, and be most gratefully affected by, the Providence of God, which in the Time of our peculiar and uncommon Troubles, has appear'd for us in so wonderful and unexpected a manner; when -according to an human view of Things, Nothing was to be expected but difficulties and Straits; and Friends that were near at Hand, which we formerly should have expected most from, stood at the greatest distance, and seem'd to rejoyce at our Trouble, and to be ready, on every occasion, to increase Them -others who are perfect strangers, that we never so much as heard of, and at so great a distance, are raised up, have most friendly Affections excited, & hearts enlarged towards us, to extend their Kindness to our Relief and bountiful supply, even beyond the Ocean. How true, in this instance, appear to be, that God is, as He declares himself in his word to be, and Alsufficient and faithful God, and that his Promise never fails; That we need not fear to trust Him in the way of Obedience to Him; tho', according to an human Appearance, we seem to run the greatest ventures by cleaving to him.

In the next Place, our Gratitude is due to his People, to whom He has given so much of his Spirit of Love and Kindness, and made the Instruments of his Bounty. -I would by this dear Sir, in particular render Thanks to you; to whom They are due, in some Respects, in peculiar manner.

I with my Family, have for this two years past gone thro' many Troubles: But I hope the Lord has not forsaken us, nor suffered us to sink under our Trials. He has in many Respects exercised a Fatherly Care of us in our distresses. A door seems to be open'd for my further Improvement in the work of the ministry, in this Place; which is situated in [^151-note1] the northwestern Frontiers of New-England, about 150 miles west from Boston, and about 36 miles south East from Albany, on Hudsons River, in the Province of New York. It is a place where an Indian mission has been for Some Time established, and a Church Settled, made up partly of English and partly of Indians, formerly under the Pastoral Care of Mr. John Sergeant; who died the Summer before last. I have been invited to take the Ppastoral Charge here, and desired by the Commissioners for Indian Affairs, to undertake the Business of a Missionary. And this hence-forward is like to be the Place of my Settled Abode. There are some Things remarkable in divine Providence, that afford a Prospect of good things to be accomplished here for the Indians, and give Reason to hope that God has mercy in store for Them. particularly God so enlarging the Hearts of some Gentlemen in England to contribute of their Substance for this End. Sir Peter Warren has given lately given 700 £ Sterling, that the Annual Interest of it may be improved to this End, and particular ly that to promote the Instruction of the Mohawks here, (one of the chief Tribes of Indians in North-America, about 50 of which, old & young, came down hither the last Fall to live for the sake of Instruction, at 80 miles distance from their proper Countrey). And the Rev. Mr. Isaac Hollis of High-Wycomb in Buckinghamshire, in Letters lately sent, haswhich I have [been][^151-note2] sent, has offered 180 Pounds Sterling Pr annum, for the support & Instruction of Indian children (boys) in a Boarding School here. And also desires that if any Boys can be found of forward Genius, that They may be put to Learning, and have a Liberal Education, to fit Them for the work of the ministry; and promises to be at the Charge of it, over & above the forementioned 180 £ sterling Pr annum. [^151-note3] And Besides, Mr. Coram of London[^151-note4] (who had been a correspondent of Mr. Sergeants) in his Life Time had laid a Plan of a Boarding School for the Education of Indian Girls here; and gave great Encouragement as to a sufficient Subscription to be obtain'd in London for the building & supporting it. But He dying the last spring, committed the Care of the Affair to the Rev. Mr. Chandler of London;[^151-note5] who has undertaken it. And also the society in London, for the propagating the Gospel among the Indians in N-England and Parts adjacent, have lately manifested a disposition to expand liberally, to promote the Gospel here, as there shall be occasion. And the Governments of Massachusetts & Connecticut have done considerable for the Encouragement and support of the mohawks here. perh and among other things done, by this Gover Province of the Massachusetts they have appointed a Committee to provide them a sufficiency of Land to settle on.

I shall have Reason, dear Sir, much to value the Prayers of one who has so much of a Christian spirit, as you have manifested towards me, and who has given so much Evidence of a disposition to unmerited, disinterested benevolence. I particularly desire your Prayers with Regard to this important Business, which I have now undertaken.

I conclude with fervent Prayers to the God of all Grace and Love, and Fountain of all Good, that He would abundantly reward you with the Blessings of his Goodness spiritual & temporal. And am Sir

Your most obliged Friend

& humble servant,

Jonathan Edwards.

P.S. I have here inclosed a copy of a Result of a late council at Northampton: and shall order one of my Farewell Sermons preached at Northampton to be put up at Boston, & conveyed to you. a very small Testimony of Gratitude.

[^151-note3]: **marginal.** [3]

[^151-note5]: Dr. Samuel Chandler (1693-1766), English Presbyterian minister.

## A133. Letter to Thomas Hubbard, August 31, 1751 133.JE-T.Hubbard 8-31-51

Jonathan EdwardsA133. JE to Thomas Hubbard, 8/31/51. Draft, ANTS, f. 1751, #13, f. ND1, #12.1-3; extract printed in *Boston Weekly Newsletter*, Oct. 3, 1751; MHS *Collections* 10 (1809), 142-53. The significant disparities between the draft and the printed version, evident in almost every sentence, indicate that a fair copy was once available; the MHS version is underwritten, "From the original MS." Only major differences between the draft and printed version are noted here.

[1. JE to T. Hubbard, Aug. 1751, draft.]

Honoured sir.[^152-note1]

when the Commissioners of the General Assembly were going to albany to treat with the six to the Treaty with the Indian They came by the way of stockbridge being directed so to do to in order to Treat with the mohawks here Concerning their settlemt in this Place (being so directed by the Assembly). But th when they came hither th Mohawks Hendrick & almost all the Heads of Families were gone to their own Countrey Nicolas was the only Pers man of Influence among Them that was left behind so that they had no Oppor. for any such Treaty at that Time & theref when They met Them at albany They proposed to em to return with Them that They might have opportunity to treat with them here on those matters. I being then at Albany with the Commissioners having been invited thither by them. I by their allowance talked with Hendrick & Nicolas alone about this affair using arguments with them to perswade Them to endeavour to get as many of their Chiefs to come to stockbridge & Treat of this affair with em the commissioners of the massachusetts. & this matter was further urged afterwards by the Commissioners themselves thems. The Hendrick made answer that it was necessary [^152-note2] according to their manner before they determine to meet with the English to treat about so publick a Concern first & to hold a Council among thems. & to have some time of Consideration. & then to hold a Council among Thems. therefore they would [-] Return to their own Countrey & and after Consultation The They would send word of their determin to stock bridge & give notice of their determination in 20 [days] accordingly in about 20 days Nicolas & several others came down & brought word that Hendrick & others of their chiefs would be here in about a week to treat with the English about the affair of Religion & the Int & a proposed. & by Nicolas's account They seemed to expect or to at least to desire to here to meet not only T with the General Courts Committee formerly Chosen to provide [^152-note3] em with Lands but al also with the same Commissioners that They saw at albany & mentiond Co. d. of Brookfield[^152-note4] in Particular. upon this I desired the Principal Inhab. of the Town to meet together to Consider what was to [be] done on this occasion & mo considering that it this was a very critical Juncture. & tha perceiving that the Tribes of the Mohawks were expected to Come to a decisive Conclusion whether to go on with the design of seeking Instruction & care at stockbridge or no we looked upon we all were of one mind that it was necessary forthwith to give notice to the Committee of the Assembly formerly appointed & also to [the] Commissioners that were at albany & give em notice & Represent to em this & signify The what appeared to us of the Importance of their coming to meet the Indians [^152-note5] on this Occasion with Capt. Kellogg of suffield[^152-note6] as an Interpreter on this Occasion. & accordingly send one messenger to albany for Coll. Wendell[^152-note7] not Knowing he was gone from there and another to springfield & Brookfield to to Col. Py d Brig. dwight for Brig. D. Coll. P Col. B Capt. d. & Capt. Kellog & another to sheffield to Capt Ashley.[^152-note8] on saturday. Aug. 10 arrived here Brig d. & Col. P. Capt. d. & Capt. K. & Capt ashley came the at the Beginning of the next week. when on Tuesday arrived 13. of the Chiefs almost all the Chiefs of the Tribe of the Mohawks. [--] from their two Towns Con Conneh Connanjóhhaury & Tewawnitarrógo They came with a great Train so that together with what were here before. They were 92. in all In the Fre The Gentlemen present had many Interviews with Them & much discourse from day to day on the next Col.

These Chiefs when they and the Commissioners Those Gentlemen impowered to [------] the General assembly signified that the Committee had heretofore proposed to em the affair of settling here & sending the in N. England & sending [^152-note9] their Chil. to the school here. but that they were but few here but now & Could come to no de decision & could give no & therefore had not Power to act in behalf of their nation but now They were come the Council of the nation were present & they had full Power to act. But in the first Place put em in mind how the English had faild of their those Things that They had been encouraged with the Hopes of here[to]fore & desired that now nothing might be said but what should stand & be made good. & that therefore they we should thoroughly consider wh what Previous & diffi what we determined & Let every Thing be fully setled. & after this & some

Last Col. after the Committee had made their first speech to them & generally proposed the affair They would meet with Them about. & they had taken time to Consider of it the matter Last Col.

thanked them for their offer & They signified their falling in with whatever Propos the Proposal that had been made Them of Coming a number of them to come here & of sending their Chil. here & coming to be Instructed & coming a number of them to live here & declared gave a belt of wampum in Confirma. of it. & declared [^152-note10] that They said that then here th what They did in this matter not only as done for on their own behalf for for all nations of Indians tha that by this They opened the door for all nations that they might come & bring their Chil. hither to be Instructed. & as a Confirmation that They would do what they could to perswade other nations to send their Chil. hither.

after this the Gentlemen of the Commission free had much free discourse with the Indians for Nine them a from d. to day & made them a Present th till they went away They went away on Thursday Aug. 21. The day They a appeared in Good Humour & were very well & seemingly well satisfied [--] & came away seemingly well satisfied so far as [--] appeared. The day before they went away a present was made Them in the behalf name of the Province I was sorry it could be no greater. never was there an occ perhaps never was there an occasion more requiring a Present & and whereon a very Liberal Present might have been mor to better purpose.[^152-note11] some dissatisfaction has about 50 old & young staid behind & others that went away declared a design some of coming Thems. others of sending their Children in the Fall & winter.

some considerable uneasi ness has arisen since the Chiefs of the mohawks went away concerning the distribution of the pre sent which was left entirely to the Indians Thems. The Chief their Chiefs gave out distributed the present Chiefly among those that went behind away & told those who staid behind that the English would provide for them but since they understand that there are no promises of clothing only for those that belong'd to the school & They are gone a away some of them went several of them are gone away in a disgust & I dont know what the Consequences may be but in general the aspect of divine Provid. appears fa exceeding favorable on the design one of the Chiefs of the some of the Chiefs of the mohawks that we seemd [--] to be much engaged in the design especially [^152-note12] Abraham Hendricks Elder Brother. who I cant but Look upon as a remarkable man. & in many many Things he has done seems to shew the solidity Prudence Humility & & Xtian real selfdenial & Humili ty and acts very much as a Person endowed [with] the Humility selfdenial & Zeal of a true Xtian The Chh of England seem to be very Jealous of the Mohawks becau and greatly against their Coming hither and Effectu (so far as I can learn) effectually to engage Abraham against it & to induce Him to do what in Him lies to keep em in their own Countrey They have made advanced him to an office & have made Him a Reader in the Chh of England to carry on divine service in the Absence of their minister but Abraham this Abraham instead of improving this to the design They int The Effect upon Abraham the Chh in of England intend Abraham to his utmost improves it to a Contrary Purpose & while He officiates among his People He from sabb. [to sabbath]

Exhorts the People to come down hither tells for instruction tells them that there they live in darkness but here in Light He knows but very little & can teach them but little but here are those that can give em vastly greater degrees of knowledge[^152-note13] he suffers a sort of Persecution from some opposers among his People Besides the Tribe of the [^152-note14] Caunéen Cauneehangthey's or proper mohawks. there are some hopeful appearances among some of the Tribe of the Oneyutas Oneíyutas. a number of these who live at Onohquaúga about 200 miles from albany where Mr. spencer went manifested a religious disposition to our Commissioners at Albany[^152-note15] .

One of Their Chief men of that Place have have since that been to visit the Pla have been to visit this Place He appeared a so very solid sober Conscientious man & returned with messages f from us to his Brothers at Home & I am sorry we had not wherewith to make Him an Hand som present. Abraham told me of divine Providence as it appears to me now opens the door wider than ever it has done before for the Introducing

God in his Providence divine seems now to be opening the door for the Introducing the Light of the Gospel among these nations beyond what ever has been more than ever it has done before And [^152-note16] if we the English dont fail in any our [part] there is a hope prospect of great Things being done and probable this very season is our . Col. Lydius & Col. Johnson & Maj. in the said in the Time of the Treaty at Albany one said spoke of it as undoubted Thing that those a Thing beyond all doubt or dispute that those nations were lost to the British Interest unless something very extraordinary was done that was never like to be done

*who are above all others acquainted with the state of the Indians

By all accounts about one half of the Nation of the Onantaúgoes Onaontaúgaes [^152-note17] are actuyla actually left their old Habitations & are gone to live in Canada The French having provided Land for them & many others are resorting th to settld settle there. Abraham told me that the Quiuquuh's & the Onoontaugaes & the Chonuntoowaunees are generally in the French He says they come to albany & flatter the English & speak pleasant words but their Hearts are with the French. The last of these nations viz the Chonun toowaúnees who are vastly the greatest of the six that the Gov. of Canada was alwai (meaning by his Emisarries) was alwaies there --Indians Four of Caghnawaúgaes have lately been in this Town from Canada among the Caghnawaúgaes in Canada two of them related to Capt Kellog . & two of them the Kinsmen of Capt Carter of Norwalk. two of these especially appeared to be uncommonly [^152-note18] intelligent men. These had told th me that the Indians that used formerly to appear on in the on the side of the English are in g continually in great multitudes flocking to Canada . & informed in what manner the French particularly the Priests dealt with. They said all the Far[-] nations have that [-] used to be our Friends had lately Left us & had entred into League with the French

& we have very lately from time to time had credible Informa. from the mohawks that the French are now Gone with an Army of 600. into the south western Parts of North America to strengthen their Interest in 400 French & 200 Indians intending to augment their Army to a 1000 as they go along . in order to strengthen their Interest there & particularly to Kill a certain Virginia Trader who lately has gained the affections of the Indians that way & drawn their trade that way & to d cut off the nation of the Tooweéhtooweeys that are very Friendly to the English & that Col. Johnson [^152-note19] having had undoubted intelligence of this partly by m a French deserter man who deserted the army & some of others se had sent a Belt of wampam to all the Five Nations to alarm Them .

Thus great are that Politick nation [^152-note20] who Know which side of the where their Temporal Interest lies as well as in their Endeavours to establish their Interest among Interests among all the Indians in North America. & to alienate them from the British Interest. I was credibly informed while at Albany that the Indians there in the Time of the Treaty gave that as one Reason why they Chose to deserted the English & Clove to the French that the English gave em so much Rum that they had could not live with them or near them as they had found by long Exp. it was an occasion of their being greatly wasted .

Now tis remarkable that in this situation of things the only remaining Method that divine Providence has left us to regain & secure these Indians in the British Interest is this very thing viz to our out utmost to Prosecute the design of Instruc Ins Xtian Instructing thoroughly in the protestant Relig. Them & Educating their Chil. at here at stockbridge Col. Johnson tho I suppose a man of not much Relig. even t tho says he knows owns this & says he knows that it will be for the British Interest to for them to bring their Chil. to stockbridge & therefore He will promote it to his utmost And now G. seems to be opening this door to us in an unusual manner.

This opportunity may easily be lost by our negligence[^152-note21] There is a party among the Mohawks at home that violently oppose the Indians coming hi that are pursuing the design of their going [for] Instruction here. & Abraham has suffers a sort of Persecution Concerning the necessity of Trus [^152-note22] great Convenience of Trustees with Regard to the difference here amongst the English

They ridicule Him & others that are no religiously disposed & tell em. the English will fail all their pretences of Kindness to em will come to nothing & stand ready to insult em on our disappointing Them There are many Things in which in the Present situation of this Affair tho we which greatly need to be done without delay. I would also humbly propose that a young Gen tlem. a scholar a man of good Genius & a fe of fervent Piety be sought for [-] & sent hither as soon as possible. to assist in instructing be learning the Mohawk Language to fit Him to be a missionary & if ne (if need be to go into amongst the six Nations) in their own Countreys) in the mean time to be assisting in Instructing the Indians here & their Chil. in all necessary Knowledge & that a salary be offered Him sufficient to encourage Him. & also that a Couple of Likely Boys be sent hither to be under the Care

to be learning the Mohawk Language to fit em to & also trained up in other useful Learning to fit him Them to be Interpreters for the Countrey & also to be employed as school masters or missionaries this would be of excellent service as it would tend to introduce the English Tongue This I [^152-note28] suppose may be done without any additional Charge or but a small matter for as excepting the Charge of their Board . There is also a necessity of another master to be employed to teach the Indian Boys to work at certain Hours.

And there is another thing which is most appa rently of absolute necessity in order to th the prosperity of the Indian affair in this Town yea indeed to the keeping it alive viz. a that there should [be] some Persons of wisd. & Integrity here on the spot or very near who should be appointed by the Commissioners & the Gen. Assembly as a sort of Curatours to have the Immediate Inspection & direction of who affairs relating both to the Mohawks & stockbridge who shall in a [-] considerable degree be in trusted with moneys & should be thems. paid for extraordinary Labours going Journeys & the Like. The Indian affair here does as much need the immediate continual Care of a Number of Tr Persons who are impowered to Inspect it as a College or great Hospital & in some Respects much more Things have heretofore gone into vast Confusion for want of it & & Now the necessity of it is greatly increased as the objects of Care in creasing & multiplie No person that has any Tolerable view of the affair Can imagine it to be sufficient to answer its necessities t that it is a Corporation that has the Care of it 150 miles off if there are some Gentlemen here more intr They may Probabl what renders it more necessary that things here should be under the immediate Care of some Trustees here is the [^152-note29] mi great misunderstandings & Jealousies that are between some of the chief of the Pres. English Inhab. of the Town which is one of our greatest Calamities. Things on this account do much more need Constant Inspection & therefore G the Gentlemen intrusted ought to be such as are perfectly impartial no way Interested or related to in related to these contending Parties.

Tis very probably that Gentlemen might be found very properly Qualified that would be willing only on some Intimation from the honble Commrs & the gen. Assembly to Come & live here[^152-note30] as dr. Ashley of westfield a Gentleman of great dis discerning & activity in Busi ness. & of an upright & pious Character & Col. d. of N-n who tho he has a rough way of talking Talking yet not of acting is of a very publick sp of g is very [-] relig. con scientious man of a publick sp. of great Activity & Resolution in publick affairs & very discerning & there is some Hope that Brig. d. & Col. P. of Brook field would if desired be willing to live he Come & live here who are excellently Qualified for the Business which needs to be done here The Mohawks great insist that these two Gentle These Trustees might men should be improved to treat with Them for the future The assembly & Commissrs mi for the greater safety might if They saw fit to intrust these curatours for a limited time for Requiring an exact & parti cular account of their acts & expenses to be laid before their Constituents from time to time

I have recom one of the greatest defects in the method of Instruction & most hurtful defects in the method of Instruction in the schools here is that no more Effectual measures are taken to teach the Chil. the English Tongue The Instructions that have been given in th at school for 15 years Past have been in a great measure in vain for want of this The Chil. Learn to read to make such sounds on the sight of such marks but Know nothing what they [^152-note31] say & having neither profit nor entertainmt by what they read They neglect it when they leave school & quickly Loose [it] there are but two ways to remedy this mischief either the bringing in a number of English Chil. into the school with the Indians or the putting the English Chil. into English Families. to be there a year or two where they might hear where they should hear nothing but English. & then return em into the school here. this would be far the most Effectual way & there is no doubt but most of the Indians might be perswaded to it th some of the Mohawks have moved it of their own Accord. But this method cant be gone into without the Care of a number of Trustees to manage it. to take [care] to find proper Places to ride from time to time to visit the Children & see how they are looked after & the Like I have strongly recommended it to Mr. Hollis that his money should be com mitted to the boarding school so far as he is concerned in it should be committed to the Care of a number of Trustees. For want of these it happens from time to time that the Mohawks & their Instructors are run out of provisions & have nothing to Eat & Now this week they have had nothing to Eat but squash & Indian Corn & Bread something must also be done at providing Clothing for others of the members of the school. when the Indians have their Lands Laid out there will be a necessity of a great deal of Care to be taken of em at their first settlemt by [--] helping them at first in bringing to their Land &c& innumerable new Things Constantly occur requiring the Care of some body that has some Powers

[-] In the Time of the Treaty Hendrick manifested a desire to go to Boston which was was fallen in with & it was proposed that his Br. Abraham should go with him & be there in the time of the sitting of the General assembly. and it was thought it would be a satisfaction to the assembly & Commissioners to see em & converse with them about those religious & affairs & might tend to greatly to [^152-note32] promote the grand design & tis they insisted that nicolas should Go with them as they supposed because he was the first to Come & live here & would be very much offended if He was neglected. so that I suppose they will come at the Beginning of Novem september October.[^152-note33]

I desire sir that you would excuse my troubling you with so long a Letter. I thought it of Great Importance that you should have a particular Informati Knowl. of the state of Things here I am Hon sir Please to give my duty to the Commissrs I am Hond sir

your honours

most humble & obedient

servt

J. E.
