## A137. Letter to Timothy Edwards, January 27, 1752 137.JE-TE 1-27-52

Jonathan EdwardsA

A137. JE to TE, 1/27/52. No MS; Dwight transcription only, with lacunae. ANTS, 1752B, #2. Dwight, 1:485-87.

To the Rev'd Timothy Edwards East Windsor

Stockbridge, Jan. 27, 1752.

Honoured Sir,

We have lately heard the sorrowful tidings of the death of two of Sister Backus's[^157-note1] children, as we are informed both at your house; which is the occasion of Cousin Eunice returning from Stockbridge at this time; she having a desire to see her mother & surviving sisters at Windsor, on this melancholy occasion. We are much affected with sister's great & heavy afflictions, & lament the death of two such likely promising children in their early youth. It is my earnest desire that it may be sanctified to us of this family. I desire your prayers, that it may be so; particularly to those that are young in the family; that they may be awakened by it to diligent preparation for death; & that we all may take notice of our distinguishing mercies, with a becoming thankfulness to God. I look upon it as a great favour of Heaven that you, my Parents, are still preserved in the land of the living to so great an age. I hope, by the leave of Divine Providence to make you & sister Backus a visit in the Spring. We are, through mercy, in our ordinary state of health, except that little Betty don't seem of late to be so well, as she was in the summer. If she lives till spring, I believe we must be obliged to come again to the use of the Cold Bath with her. My wife & children are well pleased with our present situation. They like the place far better than they expected. Here, at present, we live in peace; which has of long time been an unusual thing with us. The Indians seem much pleased with my family, especially my wife. They are generally more sober & serious than they used to be. Beside the Stockbridge Indians, here are above sixty of the Six Nations, who live here for the sake of instruction. Twenty are lately come to dwell here, who came from about 200 miles beyond Albany. We expect our son & daughter Parsons[^157-note2] will remove hither in a short time. Many of their goods are already brought up. Cousin Eunice has nothing [^157-note3] sabbath.I hope some of her friends will be kind to her in that respect. There are perhaps none of her uncles but are much better able to help her than I am at this time; who, by reason of lately marrying two children, & the charge of buying, building & removing, am, I suppose, about 2000 Pounds in debt, in this Province money.[^157-note4] I should be glad if sister Mary would suggest it to Br. Ellsworth[^157-note5] to do something for her. If she don't care to do it in her own name, let her do it in mine, as coming doing the errand from me. Please to give my duty to my mother, & love to sister Mary. My wife is at this moment from home. My children give their duty to their Grandparents, & aunts, & love & affectionate condolence to their mournful surviving cousins.

I am, honoured Sir,

Your dutiful son, Jonathan Edwards[^157-note6]

[^157-note1]: "Mrs. Backus was the fifth sister of Mr. Edwards. Her husband, the Rev. Simon Backus of Newington, (Weathersfield,) was designated by the Connecticut Legislature, as chaplina to the exedition against (troops sent to) Louisburg in 1746, to prevent its recapture by the French. He died there soon after his arrival. in [---] 1746. The vessel, containing his effects & a considerable (sum) contributed by the gentleman of the army for his family, was cast away on its return, & the family left in very indigent circumstances."-Dwight's note.

[^157-note2]: Elihu and Sarah Edwards Parsons.

[^157-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^157-note4]: "I suppose that this means £2000 old tenor, as it was then called; the value of which, continually varied, but has been commonly estimated at 6s. 8d. sterling to the pound."-Dwight's note.

[^157-note5]: Capt. John Ellsworth, the husband of JE's sixth sister, Ann.

[^157-note6]: Dwight wrote then deleted three lines of annotative material after the signature.

## A138. Letter to Joseph Dwight, February 10, 1752 138.JE-J.Dwight 2-10-52

Jonathan EdwardsA138. JE to Joseph Dwight, 2/10/52. RIHS, Ms. v. V, 1128, p. 160.

Stockbridge Feb. 10. 1752.

Honoured Sir

I have some Apprehensions, from some Things I have lately heard and observed, that there is a design of dismissing Mr. Ashley & his wife[^158-note1] from their Business at the Boarding school, very speedily & suddenly. If it be so, I Intreat your Honour to give me Opportunity to speak with you concerning that Affair, before it be put in Execution. Appoint me a Time and Place, and I will wait upon you. --- If my Apprehensions are Groundless, I ask Pardon. I am Sir,

your very humble servt

Jth Edwards.

[^158-note1]: Benjamin and Rebecca Kellogg Ashley.

## A139. Letter to Andrew Oliver (Draft), February 18, 1752 139.JE-A.Oliver 2-18-52

Jonathan EdwardsA139. JE to Andrew Oliver, 2/18/52. Draft. ANTS, f. 1752, #6-7. Partly written on back of Yale College commencement broadside for 1750.

To And. Oliver Esq. Feb. 18. 52.

Sir. I think it is absolutely necessary that I should let you into some of the secrets [-] of our affairs In your Honour may Remember Remember your Honour may Remember si

In my Letter that I wrote to Your Honour he last fall & also Latter End of Last after the Interview with the Mohawk Chiefs the last August I earnestly & also in my Letter to Mr. speaker Hubbard I earnestly insisted on the necessity of some Persons being on the spot or very near appointed by the Commissrs & Gen. assembly. a sort of Curatours to have the immediate Care & Inspection & Care of our affairs -& in those Lett & concerning this affair I wrote That used those words " What renders it more necessary that things here should be under the Care immediate Care of trustees is the misunderstanding & Jealousies that here subsist between some of the Chief of the Pres. English i Present English Inhabitants of the Town which is one of our greatest Calamities. Things on this account do much more need Constant Inspection & theref the Gentlemen intrusted ought to be such are as are perfectly impartial no way interested in or related to those Contending Parties." In I then re commended Col. d. of Brookfield. But then knew not of what now appears that He would be the furthest of any Gentleman whatsoever of from having that most necessary Qualification I mentioned by his being about like to be the son-in-Law of one of these Contending Parties. which match by his marrying his daugher Mrs sergt. which match I there now appears the is Reason (as now abundantly appear if not Reason to apprehend (from what already appears plainly appears) will be extremely hurtful Conseq. to the impor tant affairs of stockbridge. There are already very hurtful Consequences of this new Alliance & many things that shewedly forbode those that that will be much more hurtful. This There was the last year a very formal & solemn Pacification between Col. W. & deac. Woodbridg. [-] with solemn Promises made by Col. W. that He would henceforward live quietly & friendlily with deac. W & no more attem speak ill of him or attempt any thing against him or in any wise molest Him but this new alliance. with with the News of Col. wof W---ld being yet alive and & his daughters being the mistress of the female school & & Col. W. of W-d's being yet alive & He [-] hims. being [-] now joined with the Commissioners in the Care of that school have so el elevated Him that He has now very much thrown off all appearances of Peace with deac deac. W. & in a very open manner revived the misunderstanding with Him by strangely affronting Him in a very open manner. And there appears of late a very sudden & strange alteration in Col. d. the temper & Conduct of Col. d. who has had ever since the appointmt of the Committee by the general assembly the sole managemt of all our affairs so that nothing has been done but He is the doer of it as for Col. P. he is hardly to be seen Here he stays at Home: & this is much the Case with Capt. Ashly & when He is here he leaves things wholly with Brig. d. I know not what the late alt great alteration in Him can be owing to unless it [be] female Counsels together with the Influ ences of his He now appears to approve that which Col. W. & Mrs. S. approve which a little while ago he greatly condemned & to Condemn that wh what they condemn (in some Instances) which which before He approved. and things [^159-note1] are carried on in [in] a very strayge strange manner.

The Indians here have a de very ill opinion of Col. W. & the deepest Preju dice against Him. He having often molested em with Respect to their Lands & other affairs and as they think done very unjustly to 'em & Mad. s--t Partakes of no small degree of the same Prejudice. This has been app appeared by things they have said of her at my House of their own accord without any Body saying any thing to lead em to it They say that Mr. s. did very well till He married her but after h afterwards there was a great Alteration of in Him & He became quite another man They speak of her as Proud & Cove tous & not to be trusted There is affection of the Indians in the latter part of his Life this among other Evid. of their Prejudice against M. s that tho great Pains have been taken she to get Chil. for her Boarding female school. she has not been able to get above 4. Chil. 3. stockbridge Indians & 1 Mohawk. And there are already have already been loud Complaints by which justly or not I will not determine But if one of the Parents of their T her not it shews the Effect of their Prejudice and what Treatmt of her Children it may be expected will be the Effects of it. [^159-note2]

Mrs. sergt is undoubtedly a woman of very Considerable Abilities and her natural Temper disposes her much more to dominion than subjection she loves mu to have a Hand in the managemt of publick affairs & she had a vast Ascendant over Mr. sergeant & it to act appearance is but to have as great over Col. d. and she had very much the disposal of Mr. Hollis' monies. at least in she made bold with them in some Instances to dispose of em according to her own discretion in some In stances. as to the Justice of her manner of disposing Them I will not Assert that she is not [-] at all wronged in Representations that are made by some that know but this is a witho past doubt with me that she made more bold with his money than I should have dared to have done & with the publick Benefactions of some others than I should have dared to have done. or if she is wronged in the Representations that are made I could wish that they

And I could wish that the manner of spending Mr. Hollis's money since Mr. sergeants death by another Person into whose Hands They have fallen were thoroughly known. The longer I continue here & the more insight I get into the managemt of such affairs These affairs in stockbridge the more am I filled with astonishmt. when one Considers the noble sp. of Charity Mr. Hollis has shewn & the Large Benefacti ons that have been made by hi Remittances [which] have been made by Him to [JE om.][^159-note3] this Place & to how little Good Purpose at least of late especially of late & how ignorant of He is of the true state of his affairs here & how far his conceptions of them probably are from the Truth it is enough to make one sick. I would say every Thing in Capt. K---gg's Favour that is his Just dues I believe He has done good service by his Endeavours the summer before last to perswade the Mohawks to come hither. & that his Letters Mr. sergts Letters in his Life Time seconded by Capt. Kellogs after his death was the first means of perswading the Mo some of the Mohawks to come hither to visit this Place and the last winter tho He kept no school. yet I believe he took a great deal being animated with the Mohawks Coming took a great deal of Pains in his t to teach em to Read in his way to teach em to read. But He could be perswaded to turn out of his own disord set up a school or turn out of his own disorderly way. no Governmt was maint was maintained nor man very little manners taught but all su was suffered to go on in wildness & nastiness & great Confusion to the Great offence of such as have visited the Place. & tho He has been much urged He never could be perswaded to keep any exac particular accounts of his expenses to the satisfaction of the Θ. I never have seen any of his the accounts which He sent to Mr. Hollis. But was informed by one of the late Committee from another of the same Committee that had seen one of them that He was extremely dissatisfied with it. and as to th Mr Hollis's Boys or those that He has pretended to teach & maintain at Mr. Hollis's Cost Mr. Hollis's T the particular design that Mr. Hollis had in view by his in his most generous Benefaction & which he supposes is pursued to good & Happy I mean the Educating the Boys that Capt. Kellogg has pretended to teach & maintain at his Cost T this money has been entirely lost at least it has been so if his way of managemt before was as it has been since I have been here I dont mean that his scholars have learned nothing at all by Him. But I mean they have had no better Education nor near so good as they might and probably m would have had without [^159-note4] any of this Cost. so that in Effect I believe Mr. Hollis's money has rather prevented & Clog'd his great design & prevented it. Capt. Kellogg has enticed away a number of stockbridge Boys from deac. Woodbridges school where they were regularly taught & governed Instructed & governed & taught good manners for the sake of making up [--] number of Mr. Hollis Boys by which he might draw his Pay for the Boarding school where they were much more neglected & have have grown more wild & disorderly & vicious. which is a mere Cheat to Mr. Hollis. [-] a perfect wasting of his money & doing mischief with it. That He taught the Boys nothing more than deac. Woodbridge ta would have taught the Boys were not taught to wash as Mr. Hollis [directed] [^159-note5] nor any thing at all done towards it & other Commendable things which deac. Woodbridge taught were neglected. & then He has been absent near half his time since the begin ning of Last August leaving the Care of his Boys to one body or the other. And none The Irregularities and disorderly manner of [-] Capt. Kelloggs managemt of the B Boys has been a great what the Mohawks have found Great fault with & has been a chief discouragemt to em

And now another school master is come that the In & has set up a Regular school & has suddenly made a great & happy alteration in the state of things & which the Mohawks are greatly taken with. & it now it is Known that the Indians will send all the Chil. to Mr. Hawley & none to Capt. Kellog yet Capt. Kellog is there still & not calling th the Boys He formerly had his Boys still & looking upon hims Them as under his Care & looking on hims. a superintendent with Respect to them than has been no & whether He intends to draw the Mr. Hollis's pay others can judge as well as I. He has nothing to do there as a master or teacher. tho He may t still take some Care of their Clothing & in some measure do the Part of a steward. In the way we are in we are like to have sup superintendents multiplied here drawing great salaries & [ ] & expecting great honours & having but little Business Capt Kellogg looks on Hims. a sort of su a superintendent of the whole school & mad. s. expects to be s. of the Female school.

Brig. d. had his Eyes opend as open to see Capt Kellogs defects as any Body & used to be abundant in speaking of his useless [-] ness his exceeding unfitness for the Business he he was in The disorder & nastiness in which things were kept under his Care & how that it was high time He was gone &c &cbut now hi suddenly his Tone is turned. Col. W. & Mrs. s. were alwaies in the same Box with Capt. Kellog & have ever appeared his great Friend. But still Col. Pynchons Eyes are open who tho He has been but little here can inform Your Honour something of these Things if H enquired of [he] should be enquired of. [^159-note6]

The managemt has been something strange with Respect to Mr. Hawley. Before He [^159-note7] Came Representating most [ ] were carried Representations were carried to him from some misrepresentating of things tending greatly to discourage his meddling at all with the Business. for what Reason I know not unless because it was supposed He was one of my Nominating & so it was supposed he would he would would naturally fall under my Influence & not be governed by them. when Col. d. came the Condu which was soon after Mr. Hawley [--] had begun his school the Conduct was as if He was at a loss whether to smile or Frown upon it whether to discourage or en& it was given out by some that are Conversant with Col. W & courage H & if it had not been for his daughter that it was doubtful whether Mr. Hawley would not soon Mr. Hawley's courage, prudence, and steadiness be removed. of temper He w in so difficult a situation He would undoubtedly have been laid under some lasting unsp unspeake & I feel still it will be the Endeavour of some to make his able disadvantages. finall it Just bework difficult to that End that they may discourage Him fore Col. d. went away He discourses unless they can draw Him over to such an attachment to em with Mr. Hawley in Capt. Kelloggs Presence. & [ ] him Come as Mr. Hawley Hims. informs me and warns Him [ ] Him to Mr. Hawley to be use a great deal of Caution on becoming to any [ ] & not to have his dependency too much on me & to be very Cautious in [ ] taking advice of me & offeres his own friendship & Assistance tells Him He is able that he might see Cause hereafter to alter his opinion of some Persons & assures him that he is nothing able to support him & assist Him than I two to one that He had Authority had Authority to direct him and order how he should conduct in the school. & that I had no Authority at all to intermeddle in his Concerns in the school & that when I introduced him into the school I did it without Authority that the Commissioners had no authority to order the in the affair but that the Authority was all vested in the Committee of the General Assembly & he had their Authority for they expected He should act for the Rest. & conti adds repeated Charges that He should not tell me what He had said by no means tell me of these Things that he had said to Him but without getting any promise from Mr. Hawley.

Now I Never Here appears a sudden wonderful Change in Col. d with Respect He has Constantly for many years professed the highest Respect for me esteem of me & Respect to me [ ] far beyond what I could with any modesty expect. He expressed an Esteem of me beyond any other Minister in N. England & has very lately expressed his great desires of Living under my ministry & I never have had one word with Him nor with Mad. sergt & Col. W. n or Capt Kellogg. Tho they greatly opposed my Coming to stockbridge before I came [^159-note8] But since have all manifested themselves to me well pleased with it tho I have heard They have said Contrary things behind my B Back. Mrs. Serg. has been proceeded to a great Extravagance in her testimonies of Esteem & Regard to my Face. tho from time to time I have found by what she has said to others her heart was not at all in it.

I suppose Col. W. of W---d has greatly Established the Character of his uncle & [ ] Cous. sergt in London & also the Cha and also that he has established the Confirmed my [ ] raised & Confirmed Mr. Hollis's good opinion of Capt. K. who has alwaies been his great Friend. And it may be expected that when Col. W. comes he will be exceeding Busy & active in our affairs agreable to his natural Temper. but I cant think his Influence on our affairs will be very happy. The society in London if they had any true view of the Case would never have appointed Mserg. to be the mis tress of the Girls school. & her own Father & near Kinsman the m Commi to receive & tee to Look after her & her Accounts. But things are like to [be] situated more preposterously still. if they according to the Course Things are in are as tis Expect viz. that Mad. sergt should be the mistress & her own own Husb. & if in Effect the whole Committee of the General Assembly to to receive her accounts make Representations to his Constituents & to [be the] ma [-] sole m & sovereign manager of that affair & all all other affairs here or rather this Power will be in Mad. sergts Hands with the here As he intends to settle here Family of the Williamses for her Counsel & her husband her Instrufor the sake of his wife's being the ment to execute her designs [-] mistress of the female school. as wish the Governmt of all our affairs are have to be in the Fam one Family of the Williams's tis the more Col. W. is a was that the of Go to Elisha W. Col. E. his daughter & Husband & I confess I have no hopes of seeing the affair Prosper if things are carried thus I expect nothing but perpetual [ ] or [ ] which probably wi & dissensions undermining and counterworking between one Family among the Inhabitants of the Town. which probably will & probably They will think themselves so strong that they will atsoon bring all to the Ground. I shall appear tempt nothing short of Purging the Town of all that stands in their no other than as they will soon go to work way. For my part, I have no reason to expect that they do thus [ ] because they [ ] except me from such an attempt the Issue to purge the Town of me as a nuisance as They well know & know already that I am not for & They doubtless & [ ] only Think me a great nuisance here their Turn. The affair at stockbridge being great & being much taken notice of in the Θ makes some People very fond of having a Hand therein and eager to engross the whole manage engross the managemt of it to Thems. and so impatient of every Person & thing that stands in their way. The Brigd is exceedingly engaged about his wifes being the mistress & therefore pushes that affair with great vigour. has already pur bought a great number of Boards & brought em on her Land to Build a school-House there. But [^159-note9] how imprudent will it be to set up a publick Building on a particular Persons Property.

I write these things Honoured sir because I am satisfied you have not heretofore been enlightend in the true state of Things as you ought to have been. It was my knowl. of some of these matters tho' but little in comparison that [-] occasioned me when last in Boston so earnestly to press the Commissioners frequently visiting the Place. I have been slow to speak. my disposition has been entirely to have suppress'd what I know that would be to the disadvantage of any of the People here. But I dare not hold my Tongue any longer. you doubtless will own sir that tis but doing you Justice for those that have been some body or other to Let you know the true state of things in a matter of such vast importance that is under your Care which you, being at so great a distance never can know but by the Information of some that live here. And I know of none you can more reasonably expect it from than from your missi the missionary you have have put here to have a the special care of the religious affairs of the care of the Interest of Relig. among the Indi ans. I did not intend to have intermeddled with the Affair of Mrs. S. being the mistress or to say any thing that should tend to hinder it. & therefore avoided every thing of such a Tendency in my Letter to sir WP.[^159-note10] but being now applied to again by the honble Commsrs & seeing the Tendency of her Influence more & more Evidently appearing I thought this was the Time that G. called me to speak & that if I should hold my Tongue now I should perhaps Lay a Foundation for Great [--] uneasiness of Conscience to my Conscience all my Life after when I might groan under a contin the view of the Continued[--] in C Consequences of any silence & when it might be too late to speak.

[leave it] with you to Judge whether [^159-note11] I think things things which I have mention'd together with Col. W---'s Laying out his 500 to [-] produce so very small an Effe an Effect so very small may be a sufficient warning to you not to take Care who you intrust with the money of the selfish designs & Intrigues for private Interest are the Ruin of our affairs society. Tis of the utmost Consequence that Persons improved here should be of the most proved & approved Character for faithfulness & simplicity.

tis necessary that it should be known whether the Comittee of the General Assembly here act as your Committee as well as the Committee of the General Assembly as things are often carried in the Assembly by Particular Parties & Interests. It will not be likely to be for the Health of the affair for the Assembly to take the matter entirely out of the Hands of the Commissrs. It must needs be a great defect if you have no Instruments here at your under your direction that have any Power to dispose of your money to your minds & put your [^159-note12] orders in Execution. But that all should fall into the Hands of others that dont look on Thems. at all accountable to you.

And now sir I leave it to your discretion how to use this Letter. you are sensible of the difficult situation I am in & how much Trouble it might be an occasion of to me if my this Letter should be made publick especially if Brid Brig. d. should settle as he is resolved to do if Mad. S. be the sc mistress of the Girls school & which there is no probability of if she be not. However I am not afraid that some of the Commissioners should be that I am acquainted with & Know to be my Friends should see this Letter as Mr. Bromfield & Mr. Foxcroft. and as to others you are better able to Judge of their disposal in such an affair than I. --and if you Judge it to be absolutely necessary for the publick Good that it should be shewn to all it the Commissrs I will not forbid it If [ ] is provided and Tho I should suffer greatly by it if mrs. sergt if you are satisfied that mrs. sergt is not like to be established as the mistress there may be no need of it. But I will Lay Your Honour under no absolute Restriction but trust my self in your Hands & Leave the affair to your wisdom [ ] your in the first Place to do depending that in the first Place you will do the part of a Friend to the X the Interest of Relig. & Xs Kingd. & in th after that the Part of a faithful Friend to me

[fragment with additions:]

It is of great importance in order to the flourishing of the design that the Person that is to be the Mistress is one against whom the Indians have no Preju. & ill opinion Their Prejudices are hardly eradicated. Tis pretty easy to get their Friendship but when once they get a notion a Person as dishonest They will hardly ever trust em again

They now strive to the utmost to confine my usefulness to as narrow a sphere as possible They find fault behind my Back. with my Preaching to the Mohawks & instructing their Chil. as an intermeddling where I have no Business Things are now so situated that they think the day is their own & therefore are less & less Cautious in their Conduct & seem Resolved to have all in their own Hands This is but too agreable to a Temper & Conduct which I have long been acquainted with in many of thea certain Family

## A140. Letter to the Indian Commissioners in Boston (Draft), February 19, 1752 140.JE-Ind.Comm. 2-19-52

Jonathan EdwardsA140. JE to Indian Commissioners, 2/19/52. ANTS, f. 1752D, #5, E, #4.

stockbr. Feb. 19 1752.

To the Honble A. Oliver Esq. Treasurer of the Commiss Commissrs &c- to be Communicated .

Honoured & Rev. sirs

Honoured sirs

according to your desire I se Honoured sirs. I received your

Thank you for your Favour of the 31 of decemb immediately after the Receipt of it I sent wrote to Mr. Hawley & sent that Part Him an extract of your Letter that part of it that Related to Him - It was some Time before the letter Reached him But the week before last Mr. Hawley came I call whereupon I called the Moh several of the sachems of the Mohawks were then present & Abraham who is Chief among them in religious affairs. I went with Mr. Hawley to the Boarding school & told called the Mohawks & Onohquanga's together & told em what was designed with Mr. Hawleys services among them They appeared very highly pleased I [ ] they declared that they had been very uneasy at the Confusion things had been in that there had been no Regular school kept & their Chil. not taken Care of and this was what they [had] long been waiting & wishing for. I never say saw such marks of satisfaction & well pleased- ness among them on any occasion whatsoever & they have since appeared highly pleased with Mr. Hawley & very forward to assist Him & strengthen Him in Ordering & governing his school. He appears to [be] a young man of uncom- mon Prudence & steadiness of mind spirit of Governmt & faculty of Teaching & has his Heart much in the affair & seems disposed greatly to exert Hims. in it. I had heard Him much recommended but his Qualifications appear to beyond my Expectation. He has about 36. scholars in his school a large school about 36 in all yet desires me to employ Him on the best Terms I can & [-] to inform you what allowance He would expect if continued in the service. He has left Good business that he was in as a Candidate for the ministry , where he had 20s a week y.m.[^160-note1] besides his Board a week & a prospect of a very comfortable settlement if he had continued. & His services here are extraordinary & doubt besides teaching his scholars to read & write teaching them them the English Tongue & to instruct em in Religion & also tw instructing two English boys that a by the order of the Governmt are put into the school. & He Hims. taking pains to learn the Mohawk Language & sometimes preaching to 'em as They have desired Him I should think He ought while stantly preach to em once a week every sabbath & go once a week He is here upon probation to have as much as Candidates for the ministry have for while preaching on Probation. for his service is mu has his service is much greater than theirs & he has left such Business for this and if He settles in the Business I should think he ought to have as much as mi enough for a Comfortable & Honourable maintenance for a minister

Tis of absolute necessity that Mr. Hawley should bef be informed what to Authority the Commissio- ers have with Respect to him & whether they have any authority to appoint or those that act by their Order to orde introduce Him or order his Business in the school or at all to determine His authority or order his Business in the school for this is disputed and denied here & this strenu- ously asserted that none meerly on the desire [-] & appointmt of the commission have any authority at all to intermeddle but that th all those matters are entirely in the Hnds of the General Committee of the Assembly.

or who he is to looked to for acc [ ] order [ ] Look to for orders from time to time your Honour in your late Letter says no- thing whether the Commissrs have agreed to what I proposed in one of my Letters Concerning. what I proposed of Things to be allowed as for Premiums to encourage & Engage the Children in their Learning which was proposd for deac. Woodbridges school - I would now [^160-note2] humbly request the same for Mr. Hawleys school where they will be no less useful & necessary.

But then tis necessary that Mr. Hawley should know what authority the Commissrs have with Respect to him & who he has is to Look to from or for orders with the Respect to the affairs of his Business in the school disposing of Rewards Premiums & other Thing wherein He will need orders from on Emergencies from time to time [-] for this is a matter of dispute here for Mr. Hawley has been informed by a Gentleman of no inferiour Character that the Commissioners have no managing that act by their Order have any authority have no Authority at all to dir in such matters & that when I introduced Him into the school I acted By the com your Order I acted wholly without Authority But that all Au Authority relating to the affair is vested entirely in the Committee of the Assembly.

I gratefully Acknowledge the unmerited honour the Commissrs have done me in desiring me after con to draw up a plan for a female school after conferring with Col. d. Col. W P - & Col. W - to be trans- mitted Hence. I have yet had no opportunity for the proposed Conference. for Confer Conferring with those Gentlemen about the matter Col. d. has lately been here but neglected Conferring with him & Col. W about the affair because I was [in] daily expectation of Col. P. when I hoped to have opp. to confer with em all together. but the last week Col. d. suddenly went away & I had no information of it but the night before tis tis now wholly uncertain when I shall have opportunity to But I am still in expectation of Col. P. & Capt. d. [-] If opportunity should be Present & we should have a Conference, tis expected in about a Fortnight fo when I hope to have Opp. to for the desired Conference. But I have appre apprehend a probability of difference of sentiments about the affair. Mad. sergt with whom who is Col. Wms own daughter & with whom Col. d. is entring into the nearest Relation strictest Engagemts & nearest Relations in has notions of the affair very [-] wide from mine & when I wrote by the thought concerning [ ] sch Her notions of the manner of the [ ] of its Buildings appearance & attendants the state and employ Busi- ness of the Chief Mistress appear to me to be such as it would be hardly prudent to put in Execution at present little Chimerical when I wrote my Letter to General Pepperel sir W. Pep.-- concerning the manner a female school I purposely avoided mentioning my thoughts concerning those things fr from because I was not willing to give offence But since I was agains again applied to by [-] vote of the Commissrs I looked upon it [-] that I was called in Providence to take matters into th my most deliberate consideration & speak my mind freely. Officers Building Tenements officers & servants should not be mul- tiplied needlessly at every to save because the Charge will be hereby needlessly Enhansed Charge but the Care of the affair will be the Greater & more difficult attended with Greater difficulty It will be more difficult ap The Affair will be more apt to run into the Confusion & it will be more difficult to keep em in order. It would to be at great Pains & cost to make a [-] machine that is very complex when one that is much more simple will reach the End as well as [-] [----] [---]. I humbly conceive that the Beginn the Beginnings should be moderate Tis easier to add what is on Experience is found to be wanting than to undo or remove what is is found may be found too much. Things with Respect to the Mohawks are at present in a great measure unsettled & uncertain And if Great and therefore I humbly conceive that & there will be some venture & therefore & moderation at the Beginning is the more Requisite as there will be the less venture in in it Mrs. sergt seems to expect to not to have much not to be much concerned have little to do in the immediate instruction of the Chil. teaching them to read & the Like &c- & to have litt & only to do the Part of a super Kind of superintendent over the affair. But it appears to me necessary that the mistress of the Female school as well as the male should be should devote her self to the Business of teaching The affair if it be well don the Business if it be well done will Require all the Care & strength & Ki skill of a woman of superiour Abilities & Education [^160-note3] The art of teaching & more little Children at the first opening of their understanding requires sup superior Talents. & the cultivating their minds & bringing them & new forming the minds of those that come out of such great wildness will require consid great Prudence faith- fulness & Constant application &

The Cost that is expected it is expected to be expended to maintain a female superintendent will be wholly thrown away. & perhaps [-] Laid out rather than Clog than help the affair & the Committee of Capt will be sufficient for superintendence and therefore the committee mistress should be one whose circumstances will allow her to devote her self to the Business not having any very Great care upon her & then it will be a hard thing to find a gentlewoman of sufficient ta- Hands besides. | lents [-] for the Business of teaching in this school that will be willing to serve under Mrs. sergt & be subject to her.

But I am sensible these sentimts will be very disagreeable & I fear pro voking to some that you have directed me to consist with. as tis Known that Mad sergts Circumstances Late it will as she has is about marrying to Col. d. - & so will immediately have the Care of th two families of her own & probably & afterw after a while must have the Care of a third & she is a weakly P very weakly Per- son & not used to a Laborious way of living & it will be wholly impossible for her to do any thing neverthe the the Part of a school mistress in this school by her self to give any Constant attendance to the Business & I know by what she has said to me she does not Expect it

However I intend to d conf confer with those Gentlemen you mentiond as soon as I can get Opp. I have no Private Interest [ ] particularly in view nothing in the affair to [ ] my I have no Interest of my own or of my Friends to serve in this Affair.

I have nothing but my Conscience that should dispose me to Expose my self displeas say or do any thing [which] will probably be displeasing to any of these and to expose my self to new Troubles & diffi my Parishioners culties after my so lately emerging from those in the Place wherein I am now settled after I have so lately emerged from diff those that were so great & larger in the Place where I was formerly was.

However if you ins [-] still desire me that I should Confer with those Gentlemen & draw up a plan for the Her But I desire some new Instructions from you. Respecting this affair. If it be desired that I should draw up a plan my thoughts Res send my thoughts Respecting a Plan for I am ready to do. & if nothing t notwithstanding there being the no less Probability of an agreement he being the highest Probability of a wide disagree mt it be desired that I should Confer with [-] the forementioned Gentlemen I will do it.
