## A141. Letter to Joseph Paice, February 24, 1752 141.JE-J.Paice 2-24-52

Jonathan EdwardsA141. JE to Joseph Paice, 2/24/52. Draft, ANTS, f. 1752B, #6a-b, 7; Paice copy, London, Lambeth Palace, MS 1123, Pt. 1, no. 60.

[1. Draft]

Sir

I have I have been so favoured & honourd by some the Commissioners of the honourable at Boston of the Honble society for propagating Xtian Knowl. in N. E. & the Parts adjacent that they have sent me copies of three of your Letters to Sir W. P. one dated 9th of April another 8 of June the last 13 of Aug. all of the year 1751. together with three other Papers y on drawn up on the subject of the female school for the Instruction of Indian Girls with Letters sent to me by the Commissrs on the same subject. proposing to me to write to you on our affairs Indian affairs & encouraging me that probable a letter would from me would not be taken amiss. which together with the sp. which appears in your Letters & the Hope very Hop as hope that by my writing to one so all & so of such capacity & disposition I mi might serve to promote the great & important design of the settlemt of the place is what encourages & induces me to write & is all that what I have to offer in excuse for my troubling you with this and to begin with what should be uppermost in my Heart I thank G. that has excited such a Concern in an uncommon Concern in some at so great a distance that are so able to for the enlargemt of the Kingd. of X in america in some at so great a distance so able to help us among the poor Indians in some at so great a distance so able to [-] help us who are immediately concerned in their Instruction and I thank you sir for so exerting yourse so they that affair so near to your Heart and so exerting your self in it for which you deserve th for taking the Interest of Relig. among the ameri can Indians & the British Interest in America so near to your to your Heart & so Exerting yourself so much in it for which you des merit the thanks of all Bri British subjects in these Parts of the O & Xtians in these Parts & especially of ministers engaged in missionaries to the Indians. If we the Inhabitants of the British America had no Concern I think [...] that is manifested by some in great Britain about those things & the Zeal & activity that appears in them to promote sp spread the Gospel in the dark Parts of this Continent may well shame us that are the inhabitants of the British America [-] If we regard only our temporal Interest & safety [-] without any Respect to the Enlargemt of Xs Kingd. it certainly greatly concerns us to do our utmost to propogate the Protestant Relig. among the Indians. --I [-] [--] rejoyce to see such Just that a Gentleman in London such Just sentiments on this Head in a Gentleman in London to find in your Letters [-] & Papers sent to sir William such just sentiments on this Head The English have not only greatly faild of their duty in so neglecting the instruction of the Inst Indians but we have been extremely impolitick as we began & say our negligligence in this matter has brought have brought the whole British Empire in in this america into very difficult & dangerous Circumstance. for while we have been asleep our old inveterate Enemies the French have been awake & have which I am the much more sensible of sin since my being he I have been in this Place & have been Advanced b where I have been now for about a twelve-month during which space I have been had much acquaintance with the same many of the Iroquois or six nations as they Call Thems. & have had frequent Conversation with some of their Chiefs. while we have been asleep our most dangerous & inveterate Enemies the French have been awake They have discerned & taken the advantages which we have over lookd & neglected (& which we might much more fully made our own than they) to our unspeakable & as tis to be feared irreparable Loss damage we have the English had vastly Greater advantages in their Hands to gain the six nations & most of the other nations of North america & Establish them in the British Interest their Interest than the French. as the British settlements are most po abundantly more populous & numerous & Popu lous & better situated as we Possess the sea Coasts & the more powerful Indian nations are much [^161-note1] Nearer to us, & could be supplied have a Better market for their Commodities & be bet supplied with with such goods as they need at & at a much Cheaper Rate

[-] And the Six Nations or Iroquois have been much ever since the settlemt of America. till of which are the powerful Body of Indians. in these Northern Parts of the Continent have b ever since the settlemt of america. been much more till of late been much more inclined to the English than the French. & tho the French have been Labouring Indefatigably Labouring to draw em over to their Interest for this perhaps a whole Century pa past yet they have h made but slow & we all the while very negligent yet they have made but slow progress till of late. we instead of improving the Advantages P divine Providence has put & so long left in our Hands to to consult our own safety by using means to secure these Nations in our Interest w we have on the Contrary been constantly taking Courses to alienate Them. Tis true we have traded a great deal for most of our trad our Trade has been carried on with them in a way as has tend naturally tended to alienate beget in them a Prejudice distrust of us & aversion to us them most of our Indian Traders being persons of little Conscience They have the Indians have been abundantly defrauded It c and commonly that is has been given em in exchange for their skins & furs that has done [-] em no good but been their greatest Plague viz vast Quanti Rum in vast Quantities. which tho pleasing to their appetites they are sensible is their undoing & serves nothing to gain their affections .

but the Contrary. They gi Thems. give it as a Reason why they are under a necessity of deserting us. that we that destroy them --n nothing has been more common than for our Traders first to make them drunk & then to trade with them & defraud em of their Goods when they have lost the Use of their Reason & are as in unable to defend themselves. Tho the K. annually gives 500 sterling to as a Present to the I six nations. yet there is all Reason to think the [----] mony is advanced & that the Indians have [...] is embezzeld & [-------] used for the private Gain advance the private gain of those into whose hands it falls & of that part thatis given tis bestowd in such a manne it is given in that which af answers no Good End viz in Rum to make em drunk

And as to Instruction in Relig. very little has been done any these People by the missionaries of the society for propagating the Gosp. in foreign Parts And the society have been vastly imposed upon (as appears by Printed act accounts of the society which come over) by their Representations of the society. The moneys of that society instead of being used to propagate the Gospel among the Heathen are almost wholly spent chiefly spent to prop promote the Chh of England faction against Presbyterites & Congregational those of the Presby terian & Congregational Perswasion in N. England The Chh of England here is among those of the Chh of England here especially their Clergy being grea almost wholly high Chh. men & great Bigots watch using all manner of methods to promote their particular Party & & to incre to engross & every Thing to them to incroach upon & molest dissenters & engross every thing to themse. wherein they are no less active and the than the Papists are to advance the French & papist Intrest in america against the Protestant & British Interest on on the Ruins of the Protestant & Brittish Interest which is a Thing worthy to be Considerd. in any Projection for a Coalition of the Chh. of England & dissenters in this affair the affair of t the Instruction of the Indians. & establishmt of school in the Establishmt of schools for the Education of their Chil. & youth. The French here have been more Governmt has been more faithfull to the have here in america have been more faithfull to those by whom they have been Intrusted than the English The French Governmt in Canada have been more faithful to their King. & the french missions more True to the Interest of their Religion.

They have had their Missionaries for many years constantly amongst the most Powerful of these nations who by all accounts have been great in their Labours [^161-note2] among them using all the arts & subtil devices th of the Clergy of the Chh of Rome prejudicing the them against the Protestants and English by innumerable Jesuitical falshoods and as the French fail not as the Mohawks tell me to make great use of our negligence as an advantage to Prejudice the Indians against us telling Them that tis apparent that the English Care not for their Good as they take no Pains to Instruct em in Religion at the same time offering their own assistance & Labours for the E salvation of their souls if they will be their Friends. The vast difference of the temper of the French & English nations as it has appeard in the different Conduct towards these People has been very strange while they have been so exceeding vigilant we have been like men in a Lethargy as to make us the objects of the mirth of the Fr which the Indians are of which even so as to make us the m objects of the Mirth of the French. & of late the Contempt of the Indians. for they often in my hearing have made mention of this remarkable difference & have told me how the French Laugh at us. we have stood by & seen the Advantages the French [-] were taking & have stood stood by & Let em go on quietly in their molesting of em when we might easily have prevented em till it has been too late & then we lament it Thus when they were about building their Fort at Crown Point on B our own Land (which has been our Greatest annoyance in the Late war) it was known before of & our anti pr anticipating & preventing Them talked of but nothing all Ended in talk & nothing was done & in a Little time we most severly suffered for our sloth. besides the loss of our Great Troubles & Loss of Blood & dimi diminution of our Bounds. the that [-] Fort has Cost us to defend our selves against it perhaps ten times so much as building & maintain the Charge of Building & maintaining a fort there our selves.

The Great Advantage the French have by their Interest [^161-note3] in the Indian Nations never so sensibly appeard as in the Late war. for by means of them in the total They were much too Hard for the Bri these Brittish Colonies tho The the French in Canada are but a handful in Comparison of them. The Things we sufferd in the war have go raised the Indians opinion of the [-] strength of the French & given a notion of our Impotence & several many Things that happened in the war served to Render us Contemptable in their Eyes & to disincline em more & more to a strict alliance with and especially our make such a Pretence of our Invasion of Canada & making such great Preparations for it & treating with Them so much about it & at last failing without putting any Thing in Execution and so greatly disappointing those of the Indians that we had engaged & were ready to assist us. & then after that making another Pretence of Besieging the Fort at Crown point & also making Great Preparations for that & engaging doing much to Engage their Assistance & finally dropping that also without ever going against the Place besides some flagrant Instances of unfaithfulness to the Mohawks who proved thems. our faithful Allies of which They have loudly & often Complaind. when these things are considerd tis no wonder they have been followed with h such sad Effects to the in so great an alienation of most of the Northern Tribes from the British Interest especially when it is also Considerd that the French stand ready to aggravate these things to the Indians to put their own Interpretations Constructions upon them & to heighten the Contempt & Resent & blow up the Resentmt which they saw naturally rising in their minds on these Occasions

The French have been mightly encouraged by these Things & this Encouragemt they we together with the late Experience they have of the Advantage of their other Alliance of the Indians. & to them & its disadvantage have exceedingly exceedingly engaged them to Lay out thems. to [^161-note4] to finish the Business of alienating from the English all the nations of Indians in North America & fastning Them in their F from us & fixing them strongly in a Friendhip with them. I believe the People of England are in no measure sensible how much the Court of France have exerted thems. to that End since the last war & what Cost they have been at to this End since the last war. The Presents that are made Them at the French Kings Cost are very large & such as we can have little hope to vie with them in and the Mohawks tell us of Great Things they have been doing the in the two Past years to the west of us in building forth forts at the Carrying Places between the Lakes & Rivers & in the most Important Places in Treaties they have had with the nations the Presents they have made them. They have so extended their Forts ssettlemts & fortified Places that they have now in effect Joind their settlemts in Canada & those on Missisippi River. & hem'd us all in and have had by which they are become very formidable to the few Indi and have had great success in gaining over almost all the nati the Greater Part of the Iroquois & almost all the nations of about the Great Lakes. by which they are become very formidable to the few Indians that are yet our Friends. who t blame the British Governours for their negligence & Commend the Governour of Canada for his wis superiour wisdom The French have left no method measure stone unturnd no method neglected to Gain their Purpose they have not only sent forth their Emissaries missionaries & other Emissaries but they have of late gone with armies to make sure of the Effect do their Business the more thoroughly their way is when they have gaind the friendship of a nation to perswade some of em to Come & settle in Canada & inveigle em to b permit their building forth forts in their Countrey. whereby they in Effect become some of the French dominions so they are constantly enlarging the French Empire in America and curtailing the British dominions more & more In time of war they are far more active & thorough than we & E dont I they are no less active in to establish & enlarge their Interest t in time of Peace to when we are soundly asleep in war they drives us in. tis fo found by experience we cant maintain our Frontiers against them & but when t where they once get footing they never get Back. they hold their own & never give Back.

what will be the Consequences of these things in future times G. only knows But there is n if another war should break out unless the most high should remarkably interpose in our defence there is a great Probability of the B our being brought into before unexperienced distress Indeed sh as things are now situated there is a great Prospect of the French Kings having the greatest Part of North-America in his Possession Tho the K. of Great Brit. has much the greatest number of subjects here and has had vast s heretofore vastly the Greatest Advantage to Enlarge his dominions here yea it would have been an easy thing in the Time of the Late war with the naval force of Great Britain to have taken the Possession of the whole. certainly the French in the like Case would not have neglected the take opportunity But we must Look to God & not to earthly Princes for defence That things are brought to this Pass is but both the Natural Conseq. & also a Just Punishmt of our so much neglecting the Eternal welfare of these People.

divine Providence seems now to have left us but one way to help our & regaining the by to repair the s nations to the British interest to do any Thing consider able towards regaining these Nations to the British Interest & that is applying our selves now at Length (tho it be Late in the Day) in good [^161-note5] earnest to our Duty, in Instructing them in the Principles of the true Relig. cultivating the minds of their Children & storing them with t useful Knowledge : There seems still to be an Opportunity for us to do good Things much towards attaching them to our Interest as well as promoting their own true Happiness if we have but a heart to improve it prudence sufficient know how to man Prudence sufficient to manage the affair wisely. The Indians have some sense of the worth of knowledge if one is able to read & write they look upon a considerable Attainmt and they

value shamefulness of vice & of the value of Order vertue Order & Civility & They have some sense of the Worth of Knowl. if any one among them is able to read & write it is Look'd upon as a great attainment. and he and they esteem it a Thing much to be valued to be able to read & understand the Bible and therefore many of them are fond of their Childrens Learning the English Tongue to that End that they may understand what they Read. Therefore herin we can outdo the French. For they however Great Expence they are at in bestowing Presents upon them yet agreable to the Genius of their Religion keep & maxims of Their Chh. keep the Indians in Ignorance They without Let me have They forbid em the Use of the Bible nor do They teach em to [...] write & read & write. If we should go on & many among Them by our means should have these Attainmts. & it was seen by the Nation that there was such a difference between Those that have been under our Care & those under theirs it would naturally see that the greatest Benefit was obtain'd by those on our side & af & it would n & the favour & seeing the difference would naturally excite those Indians Minds [...] by being together the most at te supposed seeking of their Good & taking notice of the French that the French keep their Indians in Ignorance & Re refuse to te enable to read the Bible would naturally excite their Jealousy of the French as not truly seeking their Good but as having some ill design in all their in their pretences of Kindness to em. & that the Rather because they Have so much discerning that they are sensible that the French are a designing Crafty treacherous People. And tho our Presents to them should of Cloathing Arms & Ammunition should not equal those of the French. yet if we vigourously prosecute that design of Instructing Them they would soon see that the Benefits they receive from us are more substantial & of Greater value than those they receive from the French for they are a discerning People and we have t also this Advantage that our Relig. would recommend it self more to their Reason & to the n Light of Nature in em tho not so much to their Corruptions. --There is probably no way [^161-note6]

This wa In this way of our dealing with these Nations we would be the most Xtian in it self the most Xtian & benevolent & in this might we might hope that his Gods Anger would be turnd away which we has been provoked by our past negligence which & from whence we have Reason to fear we shall suffer the Punishment of [...] and Cruel m our avoiding our cruelty to their souls & Bodies by neglecting to [...] them cheating them [ ] prejudicing them against the Gospel by our wi wickedness & Killing m Killing multitudes of em with strong drink & vastly diminishing their numbers with strong drink.

And this method would not only be the most becoming Xtians & so most pleasing to the great Governour of the Θ but if we look only to the natural tendency of things in the it in the Present situation of things. I am perswaded there is no Course in the Θ that can be devised by any Policy or art that would be so likely to [-] g gain & attach these Nations unto us. I [-] think this is the voice of Providence in the P & what G is & the Intimation which G. gives us in the Present state of Things that if every ever North America is regaind from AntiXtian Powers an subjection to Antichristian Powers it must be more by the spreading of the Light of the Gospel than by the Policy Wealth or Arms of the British K Empire If the Kings Annual Bounty of 500 sterling the Greater Part of which it is to be feared is imbezzeled and Great Part of the remainder spent to make the Indians drunk were Laid out in for their Instruction it would be ten times so Effectual to gain the designed End.

And divine Providence seems now in a remarkable manner to be opening a door in for the Prosecuting this design of Instrucing the Indians to Effect that design of Instructing the Indians here in stockbridge the Indians & to give us a better opportunity for it than perhaps was at least in some Respects than ever was given before. Here they have before their Eyes the Congregation of the Houssatunnuck Indians consisting of above 200 souls above 250 souls who have sat under the Care of the English above 16 Years and have been constantly well treated by us & see in them many happy Effects of the our Care of em & Kindness to em in their things that Concern their Temporal Interest And have in them they have a & none of those Ill Consequences which They Indians are ready to fear. They have before their Eyes a Confutation of the Greatest & that which Commonly the Greatest Objection of the Indians against putting un thems. under the Care their Children under the Care of the English viz that the English will make slaves of em and the Eyes of many of Them seem to be turnd this way. and there seems to be some thin special Influence on the minds of many of them at this time inclining them to seek greater degrees of Light than they have heretofore lived in. besides those that are of the Tribe of the Cauneeyenkeys or proper Mohawks. There lately is come to us above 20 old & young. of the Oneiuta (another of the six Nations) from O a place Called Onohquanga a Place about 200 miles south-west from Albany on susquehannah [^161-note7] River near the Head of it on an Invitation that was sent to em from Hence the Last summer. There is some thing remarkeable in these Onohquange Indians of late years through some remarkable Influence on their minds they have had a strange turn of mind they have Reformed several of them that have notorious drunkards have reformed. and they have Generally left their former inclination to war & bloodshed shed. & turned their minds to Religi on. & have been seeking after instruction & have the & they appear & those of them that are come hither shew the best disposition of any of our Indians. they seem above all other sober & serious & delight in lea & shew a thirst after Knowledge -delight much in Instruction They are well pleased with wh with what they find here & the Chief of em intends to come in the spring & invite others of his People hither & thinks it probable that He shall bring many with him. And we begin now to get into more happy Circumstances as to the method & means of Instruction than heretofore Their Instruction ha Things have been in no small degree of Confusion for want of a Proper Person to be the school [master]. we [^161-note8] have by been in quest of a proper Person for this Business at length one is obtaind. who I hope is well qualified for it his name one Mr Gideon Hawley. a young Gentle man [---] of Liberal Education of about 24 years of age. who is now here & has set up a Regular school here for the Instruction of the Iroquois greatly to to the satisfaction of the Indians He in appears to be a person of Remarkable prudence stead Piety Prudence in & steadiness of Temper. of Good Resolution & sp. of Govern of a happy Talent in Te teaching & of of a good sp. of Governmt is one that has Long had an special Inclina tion to the Business of Instructing Indians & has an opportunity for it tho He has been here but about He applies yet he has Hims. w He has a school of about 36. He applies Hims. with great Zeal & diligence to teach the Chil. to Read & read write to regu Le instruct em in the English Language. & in the Principles of Relig. to Regulate their manners & Hims. to Learn the Iroquois Language and to teach tw a Couple of English Boys who are put into the school by the Govern mt to fit em to for serviceableness to the Indians in due time. He has al There is already a happy alteration apparent amongst these Indians since he Came & He tho He has been here but about ---

& He th he has got a Considerable interest in the Indians affections. & their Chiefs apply them have diligently applied thems. to assist Him & strengthen his Hands in Governing their Chil. & bringing them to good order. some of their sachems were [^161-note9] the Chiefs of the Mohawks were here when have been here of late who doubtless manifested great satisfaction & will doubtless carry home a good Report of what they have seen.

Another thing that appears very favourable to our design and that is that the Housatunnuck & stockbridge Ind the uni happy union that appears between those Iroquois & the stockbridge Indians who the latter making the other welcome & doing all that they can to encourage them so that now if the English dont fail of their duty & if private views & designs & some unhappy misunderstandings between some of the Chief English Inhabitants of stockbridge dont which is our the greatest Calamity that attends the Affair.

I say if these Things dont prevent there is a most hopeful Prospect of much good being done to those Interests & also mu g much being done for the British Interest in America. If things go on under a Wise Conduct tis to be hoped that instead of one male school & one female there may after some [time] be many schools several schoools [^161-note10] for each sex & means here found for giving some of the Chil. of Best Genius a superiour Education to fit them fo to be Instructors to their school masters or missionaries to their own People & here might be created in time a kind of Academy to this End. and if this should take Effect & I see not at present it may not it will be probably be found necessary in with these People not to go out [of] the usual methods of a scholastick & Academical Education. and particularly not to begin with teaching the schol the that Boys the Learned Lan guages. but after that unless it be some that [-] have a peculiar Genius for Learning of Languages. but to begin with infinitely m those more rational studies. which will better suit the Genius of these People.

Instructing them in Geography & something in Geography & History & then perhaps to proceed to something of Mathema easier Parts of the Mathematicks the first Rudiments of Astronomy. the and after that something of Grammar & Logic &cB withal perfecting them in the study of divinity. But no particular method can now be fixed i the d must be left to be found by the united est help of discretion & experience in such as have the Care of the Business doubtless more happy methods might be found for the instructing both the Girls & Boys than are commonly gone into among the English a Couple of Good [--] Terrestial Globes If such things as these should use go forward (as I know nothing why they may not if we don't hinder by our [-] own negligence or folly & private designs) this might have in draw probably wold have a powerful Influence to draw the draw the nations of Indians to us & Engage them in our Interest [^161-note11] This would by degrees open the Eyes of the Nations & Convince them that Great Benefits were to be received from us than the French *

Not that I suppose that Instructing the Indians is all we should do to secure em in our Interest with the undoubtedly many other Things might be done that might be joind done which joind

possibly it may be thought I am in too much haste some of the young men Boys & young men among the Iroquois have made pretty swift progress in Learning the English tongue. & tis to be hoped Mr Hawley will be able in Time to get a Good Acquaintance with their Language. & when H He is disposed assoon as he has any Considerable Knowledge of it to take some of to go up into their Countrey & Endeavour to taking some of the best of the Indians with Him to assist Him to perswade & the People there to bring their Chil. hither for Instruction which it is to be hoped will have an Happy Effect

with this might serve Greatly to forward the design. Kindness may be besides the Kindness in maintain bestowed on their Chil. in Boarding & Cloathing them at school Kindness may be shewn to those Parents that bring their Chil. & presents may sometimes be made to those of their Chiefs that assist in the Affair & still Forts might be built by the Governmt in some important Places not yet possessed by the French but yet which if we neglect em much longer we may Expect they will not be neglected by them they if our old ne obstinate negli gence be continued much longer we may expect the french will Come near Closer & Closer upon us with their Fortifications Trading Houses might be Er[^161-note12] [^161-note13] before the Trading houses might be erected & Care might be taken that they should be be dealt with it with an inviolable Honesty & faithfulness which would have a mighty Influence upon hi em

dear sir. Before the full Copies of your three Letters to sir W were sent to me by some of the Commissioners of I in Boston th Mr Oliver the Honble Andrew Oliver Esq. their secretary & Treasurer was pleas'd to send me an extract of the first of those Letters & & to propose that I should send my thoughts concerning a female school to sir W --accordingly I did so. which may recieve improvemt & perhaps b be corrected by your thoughts in one of the Papers sent with your Letters. I think that [-] one school should of Girls should not Consist of more than 15 or 20. And that Each school mistress should be allowed one female assis only I humbly conceive it is necessary for the schoo as to the Chil. of the Iroquois at Least that m whose Parents no Lands or Tenements in that Place that they should be boarded night & day & taken in C & Lodged at the publi Expence of the Charitable Fund which give the mistress much greater Advantage to have Influence upon them to be g form their manners & Lay an their Minds Change their manners & bring them to a civil orderly & Xtian way of Living. I agree with you sir that one mistress with a Female Assistant wi who shall be subject to her will be sufficient for one school But then there will be need that the mistress de be generally present in the school & devote her self to the Business of teaching & from which in order to be done with Good Effect with Respect to those those that are taken up out of such wildness & Barbarity will Require the Constant Application of a woman of superiour Talents & therefore I humbly differ from You in supposing that missionaries wives should be [^161-note14] preferd for this Business women it being impossible that women that are married and have the Care of families of their own should be sufficiently devoted to this Business.

But I fear I have quite tired your Patience & th I ask Pers Pardon for troubling you with so large a tedious a Letter. I have al drawn on to so great a Length. by the multit great Importance of the subject & what wi the view of your pious & Charitable concerns about it tho you are at so great a distance & have far less to excite your Concern than we I He who is sir

your with Respect & Gratitude

your most humble servt

Jonathan Edwards.

hoping[^161-note15] that some Good improvemt may be made by one so able & willing of the particular Informations I have given by one so able & willing. the which I have hope to your wisd. hoping for your candid Aceptance of what I have written with an honest intention I am sir

[2. Copy by Joseph Paice for Abp. Thomas Secker (see no. 153a)]

Stockbridge in N England Febry 24. 1752.

Sir:

I have been so favor'd & honor'd by some of the Commissioners (in Boston) of the Honble Society for propagating Christian Knowledge in N England and Parts adjacent, that they have sent me Copies of three of Your Letters to Sir William Pepperell, written chiefly on the Subject of Schools for the Instruction of Indian Girls, with three other Papers drawn up by You, & Sent to him on the same Subject, with Letters sent me by the said Commissioners, proposing to me to write to You on our Indian Affairs, encouraging me, that probably a Letter from me would not be taken amis Sir William himself has also Honour'd me with a Letter, proposing my Writing to You which, together with a hope that my so doing might serve to promote the Great & Important Ends & designs of the Settlement of this place, is what Encourages & Induces me to write, & is what I have to offer in Excuse for my Troubling you with this.

And to begin with what should be uppermost in my heart -I thank God that has excited such Concern for the Enlargement of the Kingdom of Christ in America among the Poor Indians in some at so great a Distance, so able to help us who are immediately concern'd in their Instruction; I think the concern that is manifested by some in Great Brittain about these things, & the Zeal & Activity that appears in them to Spread the Gospel in the Dark Parts of this Continent, may well Shame us that are the Inhabitants of the Brittish America If we regard only our Temporal Interest & Safety, without any Respect to the Enlargement of Christ's Kingdom & of the Good of the Souls of those unhappy People, it certainly greatly Concerns us to do our utmost to Propagate the Protestant Religion among the Indians. The English have not only greatly failed of their Duty in so Neglecting the Instruction of the Indians, but we have been Extremely Impolitic, & by our Negligence in this matter have brought the whole Brittish America into very difficult & Dangerous Circumstances, which I am much more sensible of since I have Lived in this place, where I have been now for about a Twelvemonth, during which Space I have had very frequent Conversation, & much acquaintance with many of the Iroquois or Six Nations (as we Call them) I have often had free & Large Conversation with some of their Chiefs, who have a great acquaintance with the State of those Nations, & Nations beyond them --Whilst we have been asleep, our most dangerous & Inveterate Enemies the French have been awake; they have discerned & taken the advantages which we have overlook'd & Neglected, to our unspeakable, & it is to be feard, Irreparable Damage. The English have heretofore had vastly greater advantages in their hands to gain the Six Nations, & most of the other Nations, & Establish them in their Interest, than the French, as the Brittish Settlements are abundantly more numerous & populous than the French, & Better Situated.

as we Possess the sea Coasts, & the more powerful Indian Nations are much Nearer to us, & might have a Better market for their Commodities, & be much more Easily Supply'd with such Goods as they need, & at a much cheaper rate from us than from the French; & the Six Nations or Iroquois (which are the most Powerful body of Indians in these Northern Parts of the Continent) have ever since the Settlement of the European Colonies, 'til of late, been much more inclined to the English than the French; & though the French have been Indefatigably Labouring to draw them over to their Interest for perhaps a whole Century past, & we all the while very Negligent of them, yet they have made but slow Progress 'til very Lately. Instead of our Improving the advantages Divine Providence has put, & so long continued in our hands, to consult our own Safety & Strength, by using proper means to secure the Friendship & Alliance of these Nations, we have on the Contrary been constantly taking Courses to Alienate them -Tis true we have traded with them a great deal, but our trade has been carried on in such a way as has naturally tended to Beget & Establish in them a Distrust & Aversion to us. most of our Indian Traders being Persons of little honesty or Conscience, the Indians have been abundantly Defrauded, & commonly that has been given 'em in Exchange for their Skins which has done 'em no Good, but has been their Greatest Plague viz Rum in vast Quantities, which, thô Pleasing to their Appetites, they are Sensible is their Bane, & serves nothing to gain their Affections, but the Contrary -they themselves give it as a reason why they are under a necessity of deserting us that we destroy them --

Nothing has been more common than for our Traders first to make 'em Drunk, & then to [^161-note16] trade with them & defraud them of their Goods, when they have lost the use of their Reason and are unable to defend themselves. Tho the King annually gives £500 Sterling as a Present to the Six Nations, yet (I suppose it to be very apparent) that the Greatest Part of the money is Embezzel'd, & used to advance the Private Gain of those into whose hands it falls; & as to that part of it which is bestow'd on the Indians, much of it is given in Spirituous Liquors, which not only does 'em no good, but is the occasion of their more foolishly Squandering away the more valuable goods that are given them immediately after they have received them so that very little is Carried home with them --And as to Instructions in Religion, but little has been done by the Missionaries of the Society for Propagating the Gospel in Foreign parts. That Society have been vastly imposed upon by the Representations of their Missionaries, as appears by the Printed accounts Published by the Society which come over hither ---The Iroquois themselves have often in my hearing Complain'd greatly of the Negligence of those Missionaries --the money of that Society, instead of being used to Propagate the Gospel among the Heathen, is Chiefly spent to Promote the Church party in opposition to those of the Presbyterian or Congregational persuasion in N England; those that are of the Church of England here, especially their Clergy, being almost universally wholly High Church men, & great Bigots, using all manner of methods to promote their own party, & to encroach upon & root out the N England Churches, & engross every thing to themselves; wherein they are perhaps no Less active, than the Papists are to build up themselves here upon on the Ruins of the Protestant & Brittish Interest in America, which is a thing worthy to be Consider'd in any projection for a Coalition of the Church of England & Dissenters in the Affair of the Instruction of the Indians, & the Establishment of Schools for the Education of their Children & Youth.

The French here in America have been more faithful to those by whom they have been intrusted than the English --the French Government in Canada have been more faithful to their King & the French Missionaries more True to the Interest of their Religion they have had their Missionaries Constantly for many Years amongst the most powerful of these Nations of North America, who have been great in their Labours among them, using all the arts & Subtile Devices of the Romish Clergy, prejudicing them against the Protestants & English by Innumerable Jesuitical Falsehoods; & by Accounts we have from the Mohawks, the French fail not to make great use of our Negligence as to their Instruction, as an advantage to fix an Ill opinion of us in their minds; Telling them it is Apparent that the English care not for their Good as they take no Pains to Instruct 'em in Religion; at the same time offering their own Assistance & Labours for their Eternal Salvation, if they will be their friends.

The Vast difference of the Temper of the French & English Nations, as it has appear'd in the Conduct of each towards these People, is very Strange while they have been so Exceeding Vigilant, we have been like men in a Lethargy, so as to make us the objects of the Mirth of the French, & of late of the Contempt of the Indians -they often, in my hearing, have made mention of the Remarkable Difference, & have told me how the French Laugh at our Sluggishness & Stupidity ---We have seen the Advantages the French were Taking, in one instance & another & have stood by, & let 'em go on Quietly 'til it has been too late, & then we have Lamented that we did not seasonably bestir ourselves to prevent them Thus, when they were about building their Fort at Crown Point on our own Land (which has been our greatest annoyance in the Late War) it was known of before, & our anticapating them talk'd of, but all Ended in Talk, & nothing was done; & in a Little time we most severly Suffer'd for our Sloth & Neglect -Besides our Grievous Distress from thence, & Loss of Bloud, & Diminution of Territory, that Fort has already Cost us more to Defend ourselves against it, perhaps Ten times so much as the Charge of Building & maintaining a Fort there ourselves would have been.

The Great advantage the French have by their Interest in the Indian Nations never so [^161-note17] sensibly appear'd as in the Late War, for by means of them they were much too hard for these Brittish Colonies, tho the French in Canada are but a handful in comparison of us. The things we Suffer'd in the War have rais'd the Indian's Opinion of the Strength of the French, & fix'd in 'em Notion of our Impotence; many things that happen'd in the War served to render us Contemptable in their Eyes, & to disincline 'em more & more to a Strict Alliance with us; especially our making such a Pretence of our Invasion of Canada, & such great preparations for it, & treating with them so much about it, & at last Failing without putting any thing in Execution, & so, greatly disapointing those of the Indians that we had Engag'd, & who had prepar'd to assist us -& then after that, making another Pretence of Besieging the Fort at Crown Point, & also making Great Preparations for that, & doing much to Engage the Indian's Assistance, & finally dropping that Design also, without going against the Place -Besides some Notable instances of unfaithfulness in the English toward the Mohawks, who proved themselves our Faithful Allies in the Late War, of which they have Loudly & often Complain'd -When these things are Consider'd, 'tis no wonder they have been follow'd with such sad Effects, in so great an alienation of most of these Northern Tribes from the Brittish Interest -Especially when it is also Consider'd, that the French stand ready to aggravate these things to the Indians, to put their own Constructions upon them, to heighten the Contempt, & Blow up the Resentment which they saw naturally rising in their minds on these occasions.

The French have been mightly Encouraged by these things; & this Encouragement, together with the Experience they have lately had of the advantage of the Alliance of the Indians to them & the Disadvantages which they have seen us Suffer by it, have Exceedingly Engag'd them to Lay out them selves to finish the Business of Alienating from the English all the Nations of Indians in North America, & fixing them strongly in a Friendhip with them & Dependance upon them I Believe the People of England are in no measure Sensible how much the Court of France have Exerted themselves, & what Expence they have been at for this purpose since the Conclusion of the Peace. The Presents that are made them at the French King's Cost are very Large, & such as we can have little Hope to Vie with them in; and the Mohawks here tell us of Great things they have been doing in the Two Past Years to the West of us; in building Forts at the Carrying Places between the Lakes & Rivers, & in the most Important Places; In Treaties they have had with the Nations; Messages that have been sent to them, & presents that have been made 'em -They have so Extended their Plantations & Fortify'd Places, that they have now in Effect join'd their settlements in Canada & those on the Missisippi River, & hemm'd us all in; & have had Great Success in gaining over the Greater Part of the Iroquois, & almost all the Nations about the Great Lakes, by which they are become very Formidable to the few Indians that are yet our Friends, who Blame the Brittish Governors for their Negligence, & commend the Governor of Canada for his Superior Wisdom. the French have Left no stone unturn'd, no method neglected to gain their Purpose they have not only sent forth their Missionaries & other Emissaries, but they have of Late, on several occasions, gone with Armies to do their Business the more thoroughly --Their way is, when they have gain'd the Friendship of a Nation, to persuade some of em to Come & Settle in Canada with presents & many fair promises, & to Inveigle 'em to Permit their Building Forts in their Territories, whereby their Countrys are in Effect Annexed to the French Dominions -So they are constantly Enlarging the French Empire in America, & more & more Curtailing the Brittish Dominions ---In time of War they are far more active & thorough in their Business than we; & they are no Less Active to Establish & Enlarge their Interests & undermine ours, in time of Peace, when we are soundly asleep -In time of War they Drive us in 'tis found by Experience that we cant maintain our Frontiers against them & their Indians; but where they once get Footing, They hold their own, & never give back.

What will be the Consequences of these things in Future times God only knows but, if another War should Break out whilst things are in their Present situation, we may well Cry The Lord have Mercy on us! unless the Most High should remarkably appear for us, there would [^161-note18] be Great Probability of our being brought into unexperienc'd Distress -Indeed, if Things continue in the Course they are now in, there is a Great Prospect of the French King's having the Greatest Part of North America in his Possession --Tho the King of Great Brittain has much the Greatest Number of Subjects here, & has had heretofore vastly the Greatest advantage to Enlarge his Dominions in these parts of the World --It would have been an Easy thing in the Time of the Late War (unless Heaven had remarkably appear'd against us) to have taken Possession of the whole of this Northern Continent --Certainly the French in the Like Case would not have Neglected the opportunity -But we must Look to God, & not to Ministers of State for Defence --That things are brought to this Pass is both the Natural Consequence, & also a Just Punishment, of our so much Neglecting the Eternal Welfare of the Indians.

Divine Providence seems now to have Left us but one way to help ourselves, or to do any Thing considerable towards regaining these Nations, & that is applying ourselves now at Length (tho it be Late in the Day) in Good Earnest to our Duty, in Instructing them in the Principles of True Religion, cultivating the minds of their Children, & Storing them with the useful Knowledge -There seems still to be an Opportunity for us to do much in this way towards attaching them to Our Interest, as well as promoting their own True Happiness, if we have but a Heart to improve it, & a Prudence Sufficient for the Conduct of the Affair ---The Indians, Wild as they are, have some Sense of the shamefulness of Vice, & of the Value of order Virtue, Order & Civility -they are also in a Degree sensible of the Worth of Knowledge -If anyone among them is able to Read & Write, it is look'd upon as a Great attainment, & they Esteem it a thing much to be Valu'd to be able to Read & Understand the Bible --------& therefore many among them are fond of their Children's Learning the English Tongue to that End, that they may understand what they Read ---Therefore, herin We have an advantage to out do the French -For how =ever Great Expence they are at in the Presents they bestow upon 'em, yet, agreeable to the Genius of their Religion & Maxims of Their Church, they keep 'Em in Ignorance, they Forbid em the use of the Bible, nor do they teach 'em to Read & Write If we should go on & prosecute the Design of Instructing them to Good Effect, & many among them by Our means should have these Attain =ments, & it were seen by the Nations that there was such a Difference between such as have been under Our care & those under Theirs, it would be seen that the Greatest Benefit was receiv'd by those that are on Our side; & their observing the Difference, & taking notice that the French keep Their Indians in Ignorance, & refuse to Enable them, or allow 'em to read the scriptures, would naturally Excite in the Minds of this Jealous People a Suspicion of the French, as not truly Seeking their Good, but as having some Ill design in their pretences of Kindness to 'em; & that the rather, because they have so much Discerning as to be sensible the French are a Designing, Crafty Treacherous People; & thô our Presents of Cloathing, Arms & Ammunition should not Equal those of the French, yet they would see the Advantage they receive from Us to be more substantial, & of Greater Value than any thing the French bestow upon them --we should also have also this Advantage, that our Religion would recommend it self more to their Reason & the Light of Nature in 'em, thô Less to their Corruptions. As This way of dealing with these Nations would be in itself the most Christian & Benevolent, so therein we[should have most Reason to Expect God's Blessing, & might hope that his Anger for our Past Neglects & Ill Treatment of them would be Turn'd away, from whence we have otherwise Reason to fear that he will use them as a sore scourge, to inflict on us a just Punishment of our Cruelty to their Souls & Bodies, by our withholding the Gospel from them, Defrauding them of their Goods, Prejudicing them against Christianity (the Religion we profess) by our Unchristian Behavior, & more than Heathenish Wickedness; & our Killing multitudes of them, & Greatly wasting their numbers with Strong Drink --And not only would this method be most becoming Christians, & so most Pleasing to the Great [^161-note19] Governor of the World, but if we look only to the Natural Tendancy of it in the present Situation of things, I am persuaded there is no Course in the world that can be Devised by any Policy or art, that would be so likely to Gain these Nations & attach them to us I think this is Evidently the Voice of Providence, & the Intimation which God gives us in the present State of things, that if Ever North America is regain'd from an Adherence to our Antichristian Enemies, it must be more by Spreading the Light of the Gospel, than by any Policy, Wealth or Arms of the Brittish Empire ---If the King's Annual Bounty of £500 Sterling (the Greater part of which it is to be feared is Embezzel'd, & great Part of the remainder Spent to make the Indians Drunk) were Lay'd out for their Instruction, it would be Probably ten times so Effectual to gain the End that is Aimed at. There now seems to be a Door opened in a Remarkable manner in This Place

for the successful Prosecution of this method of making the Indians our Friends by Instructing them; giving us better opportunity than we have had for it many Years. Here they see the Congregation of Houssatunnock Indians, now consisting of above 250 souls,

who have been some of them under the Care of the English above 16 Years, & have been constantly well Treated by us -they see the many happy Effects of our Care of them, & kindness to them in things which Concern their Temporal Interest, & none of those Ill Consequences which those Suspicious People are Exceedingly apt to apprehend. -They have before their Eyes, in these Indians, a Confutation of that which commonly is their Greatest Objection against putting their Children under the Care of the English, viz that the English will make Slaves of 'em, & the Eyes of many of the Iroquois seem now to be Turned this way; & there appears some special influence on the minds of many of them at this Time, inclining to such Greater Degrees of Light than they have hitherto Lived in --Besides those that are of the Tribe of the Cayreeyenkeys or proper Mohawks, there are Lately come to us above 20 Old & Young of the Oneiutas, another of the Six Nations, from a Place called Onohquanga, (about 200 Miles South West from Albany, on Sasquehannah River near the head of it,) on an Invitation that was sent to 'em from hence the Last summer -There is something wonderful in these Onohquanga Indians -of Late Years, thrô some Remarkable Influ=ence on their minds, they have had a Strange turn of mind; several of their Chief men, that have been Notorious Drunkards have wholly Reformed; & they have Generally left their former inclination to War & Bloudshed, & Turned their Minds to Religion, & have been seeking after Instruction --Those of 'em that are Come hither Shew the Best Disposition of any of Our Indians -they are peculiarly Serious, Disposed to Civility, & manifest a Thirst after Knowledge and Delight in Instruction: they are Well Pleas'd with what they find here, And the Chief of 'em, who is a very Serious man, intends to go home in the Approaching Spring, & invite others of his People hither, & thinks it probable that he shall bring many with him. We begin now to get into more happy Circumstances as to the method & means of Instruction -Heretofore, Things have been in no small Degree of Confusion, For want of a Proper person to be the Schoolmaster of the Iroquois; after many abortive Endeavors, one at length is obtain'd, who appears well Qualify'd for the Business Mr Gideon Hawley; a young Gentleman of Liberal Education, about 24 Years of Age; he has now set up a Regular school, Greatly to the Satisfaction of the Indians -His Character is that of a Person of Good Abilities, solid Piety, remarkable Prudence & Steadiness of Temper for one of his Years, a happy Talent in Teaching, Good Resolution & Spirit of Government and has Long had an Inclination to the Business of Instructing Indians.

He has a School of about 36 Iroquois Children & Youth, which indeed is too Great for One [^161-note20] Master, considering the manifold Business he has to do: he applies himself with Great Zeal & Diligence to Instruct the Children in reading & writing & the English Tongue, & in the Principles of Religion & Good manners; himself Labouring at the same time to Learn the Iroquois Language; Besides teaching a Couple of English Boys, who are put into the School by the Government to learn the Indian Tongue, & other things necessary to fit them to be serviceable to the Indians, either as Missionaries, or school Masters in Due time There is already a happy Alteration among the Indians since Mr Hawleys Coming, tho he has been among them but about 3 Weeks; he has already got a Considerable Interest in the Affections of the Indians, & their Chiefs have Diligently apply'd themselves to assist Him, & Strengthen his hands in Governing their Children, & Bringing them to Good order -Some of the Chiefs of the Mohawks having been here of Late, who have manifested Great Satisfaction in these New Regulations, & will Doubtless, carry home a Good Report of what they have seen. Another thing That appears very Favorable to our Design, which is the Happy Union that Subsists between those Iroquois & the Stockbridge Indians the latter making the other Welcome, & doing all that they can to Encourage them in seeking Instruction & coming hither for it --The Stockbridge Indians had a Meeting the Last week, of their own accord, without any Motion from any English Person, to consider whether they had done all that it was Proper for them to do to Encourage the Iroquois coming hither, & to Promote the Design of their Instruction; and Determined that they had not yet done their Duty, but that something farther was incumbent on them & after Consultation they concluded & did as follows ---They gave Notice to the Iroquois that are here present, that they Desired a Conferrance with them, & after all were Convened, they Told them, that they observed the English had done a Great Deal to Promote their being Instructed in the Christian Religion, which made them to Reflect on themselves, & Consider whether they had not failed of doing their part; they told them, that as to themselves, they now for sometime had Experienc'd the Great Benefit of the Instructions of the English that once they were in a State of Great Ignorance & Darkness, but now were brought into the Light, & knew that it was Good; & therefore Earnestly Desir'd them to give heed to the Instructions the English gave them, & Not to Listen to any objections against them; & Particularly not to give way to any Suspicions or Jealousies of any Ill Design in the English, fearing that they intended to make slaves of them or their Children, or any thing of that Nature; & told em, that they themselves at First were full of such Jealousies, but now they had been so many Years under the Care of the English, & found that there was no thing at all in their Suspicions, no Foundation for 'em & told them for their Encouragement, they might have the use of those Lands that were round about the Boarding School where their Children were Instructed as long as they pleas'd & concluded with observing, that Time in this World is but short, saying to this Purpose, "we have but a Little Time to Continue here; we had therefore Best to Improve our time, Give Diligent heed to the Instructions we have, & do our utmost to Practice accordingly; & it may be, if we Do so, we may hereafter meet together in Heaven" -I had this Account of the Conferrance from Abraham Caunaugh stansey, who is the Chief man of the Nation of the Mohawks in all Matters of Religion, a very serious Devout & Upright man

So that now if the English dont fail of their Duty, & if Private Views & Designs, & some unhappy [^161-note21] misunderstandings which Subsist between the Principal English Inhabitants of Stockbridge, (which is the Greatest Calamity that attends the Affair): I say if these things don't Prevent, there is a most hopeful Prospect of much Good being done in Promoting the Truest Welfare of these People, & also much being done for the British Interest in America If things go on under a Wise Conduct, it is to be hoped, that instead of one Male School and one Female, there may, after some time, be several Schoools for each sex, & means found for giving some of the Children of Best Genius (for there are some very Forward Genius's among 'em) a superior Education, to fit them to be Instructors, School Masters or Missionaries to their own people -and here might be Erected in time a kind of an Academy to this end.

and if this should take Effect (as I see not at present why it may not) It will probably be found necessary with these People to go out of the Usual methods of a Scholastic & Academical Instruction, & particularly not to begin with Teaching the Boys the Learned Languages, but to begin with more Entertaining & Rational studies, which will better Suit the Genius of these People, instructing them something in Geography & History, & some of the Easier parts of the Mathematics, & the First Rudiments of Astronomy & after that, something of Logic & Natural Philosophy withal setting apart a fit Proportion of Time every Week for the Study of Divinity -& perhaps some that have a peculiar Genius for Learning Languages may soon be initiated in the study of the Learned Languages == but no Particular method can be fix'd on before some Trial -The Best method must be Left to be found, by the United help of Discretion & Experience, in such as have the Care of the Business == Doubtless more happy methods might be found for instructing both the Girls & Boys than are commonly gone into among the English in New England -----I should think it were no matter how soon a Couple of Good Terrestial Globes, & some Good Maps of Places mention'd in the Holy Scriptures, were procured for the use of the school here. If such things as these should take Effect, as I know nothing why they may not if it be Judg'd Best that they should & we Properly Exert ourselves in order to it, & our Misunderstandings & Private designs dont Prevent; it probably would have a Powerful Influence to Draw & Unite the Nations of Indians to us Possibly it may be thought I am in too much haste too forward in my Projections; & that it is time Enough to talk of an Academy &ca: many years hence --But certainly, if we Consider how active the French are, & what Amazing Progress they have made of Late, & are daily making, it may be Sufficient to convince us that we had need not to be Dilatory == not that I suppose the State of Things is already Ripe for the putting all these things in Execution --Things are not Sufficiently settled & Certain with respect to the Iroquois but, if Things remain with their Present Good appearance one Twelvemonth longer, I should think it high time to begin to Lay New Foundations for a more Enlarged Design --Some of the Boys & Young men amongst the Iroquois have made Pretty Swift Progress in Learning the English Tongue; & it is to be hoped Mr Hawley in time will be able to get as acquaintance with Their Language & he is disposed, so soon as he can get any Considerable Knowledge of it, to go up into the Countrys of the Six Nations, taking some of the Best of the Indians with him, to Endeavour to persuade the People there to bring their Children hither for Instruction; Abraham Caunaugh Stansey has notify'd himself willing to go with him, which it is to be hoped will have an Happy Effect

I dont suppose that instructing the Indians is all we should do to secure em in the British Interest -[^161-note22] undoubtedly many other things might be done, which Join'd with this might serve greatly to forward the Design. Beside the Kindness shewn to their Children, in Boarding, them Cloathing & Instructing them, Kindness might be shewn to those Parents who bring their Children, & Presents might sometimes be made to some of their Chiefs that assist in the Affair --And still Forts might be Built & maintained by the Government, in some Important Places not yet Possess'd by the French, which if we Neglect much Longer, we may Expect will not be long Neglected by them. If our Old Obstinate Indolence be Continu'd still, we may Depend upon it that our Enemies will come Closer & Closer upon us with Their Fortifications; our supineness will not only Embolden them, but as it were Tempt & Draw them on ---We might to Good Effect set up Trading houses, from whence the Indians might be Supply'd with Goods at a much Cheaper Rate than the French can Afford them; & care might be taken that they should be Treated with inviolable Honesty & Fairness, which would have a mighty Influence upon 'em; and no Rum should be sold to 'em. Before the Full Copies of Your Three Letters to sir William were sent to me by some of the Commissioners in Boston, Andrew Oliver Esqr. their Secretary & Treasurer was pleas'd to send me an Extract of the First of those Letters, & to propose that I should send my Thoughts concerning a Female school to sir William, accordingly I did so. what I Drew up may recieve Improvement from Your Thoughts Contain'd in one of the Papers sent sir William with Your Letters ----I think with you that one school of Girls should not consist of more than 15 or 20, only I Conceive it to be Necessary, as to the Children of the Iroquois at Least, whose Parents at present have no Lands or Tenements in New England, that they should be Boarded & Lodg'd under the Care of their Mistress, in an house built for that purpose -which wil give the Mistress much greater advantage to change their manners, & Form their minds, & bring 'em to a Civil, Orderly & Christian way of Living -I agree with you sir, that one Mistress, with a Female Assistant who shall be subject to the Mistress, will be Sufficient for One school -But then there will be Need that the Mistress be generally Present in the school, & Devote herself to the Business of Teaching, which, in order to be done with Good Effect with respect to such as are taken out of such Wildness & Barbarity, will require the Constant Application of a Woman of Superior Talents & therefore I Differ from you in supposing that Missionaries Wives should be Preferr'd for the Business, it being ordinarily Impossible, that Women who are married, & have the Care of Families of their own, should be sufficiently Devoted to this Business.

But I fear I have Quite tired your Patience --I have been Drawn on to so Great a Length in my Writing by the Vast Weight of the Subject, & the many Important things Pertaining to it which present themselves to the view of one in my Situation together with a View of your Concern about the Affair, tho' you are at so great a Distance, & have so much less to Excite & Oblige your Concern than we that are on the spot -Hoping, that some Good Improvement may be made of the Particular Informations I have given, & for your Candid Acceptance of what I have written, I remain

Sr

Your most huml Servt

Jonathan Edwards.

Copy To Mr Joseph Paice in London

## A142. Letter to Timothy Dwight, February 27, 1752 142.JE-T.Dwight 2-27-52

Jonathan EdwardsA142. JE to Col. Timothy Dwight, 2/27/52. ANTS, f. ND1, #9, 1752E, #3. Addressed on cover "To / Col. Tim0 Dwight / In Northampton."

Stockbridge Feb 27. 1752

dear Sir,

I thank you for your Letter, for your Care of us Re-specting the Sale of my Homestead, and in sending me thoseten dollars. I send you such a Note for it as you desire.Please to return my hearty Thaks to Deac. John Smith, for thedollar He sent me when you have Opportunity. I shallneed a great deal more Joinery work done this spring or sum-mer ; But am as yet uncertain when I shall have stuffprepared. If John Pomroy or some other Good & prettyquick workman could be engaged, I should be glad.

Mr. Hobby's Copy of the Remonstrance was thro' mistakesent to me, and I have sent it to you by Capt. Shelden.You desire me to give a few Hints from the minutes I tookof the Objections justly arising from the Tenour of the Re-monstrance ; But seem to have forgotten that I drew upthose minutes & gave 'em to you when at Northamptonlast. I beseech you not to patch up a mock Reconcilia-tion with the Church, accepting of something from Themthat is Nothing but a meer Sham. Nothing ought to beaccepted but proper Christian satisfaction made to you &me, and made as the offence committed. And I desireyou never will would consent to the settlement of a minister thatis of a Principles contrary to yours, you thereby will bringyourselves into a great shame. I can't believe that Mr.Stoddards Principles will ever have a quiet establishmtagain at Northampton, or that that People will everprosper again in that way ; but 'tis probable that the smallCompany that adhered to me, if They hold their own, willprosper & prevail. I believe there will be two societiesthere. yours may be the smallest at first ; But if you are steadfast, [^162-note1]& act prudently, I believe at last they will be the Biggest &will get the Meeting-House. I have been extremely hinderdof late ; otherwise should have near finished my the firstdraught of my Answer to Mr W-----[^162-note2] However I hope to get itinto the Press this summer. I am, sir,

your affectionate and obliged

Brother & servt

J. Edwards.

[^162-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^162-note2]: I.e. *Misrepresentations Corrected*, published in 1752.

## 143. Job 36:22 143.JE-J.Mauduit 3-10-52

Jonathan EdwardsA143. JE to Jaspar Mauduit, 3/10/52. Draft. ANTS, f. 1752F, #3-4.

To Mr Jasper Mauduit

March. 10. 1752

Sir. It has been proposed to me by some of the Honourable Commissrs of Indian Affairs in Boston to write to you giving you a particular Account of the state of Things relating to the Instruction of the Indians in this Place & the Prospects there are of success in that that attend that affair as making what may have a great Tendency to promote the design. I readily fall in with a Proposal by wh in which by which I esteem my self much honoured by those that made it & because I think no other thin fit & Reasonable & what the nature of what would probably tend to your what is fit & Reasonable & what sh would tend to your satisfaction to have a just & full account of the state of things relating to this affairs of this Place (which is the ali principal affair your Honble Commissioners have under their Care) by some Person that lives on the spot & so is may be supposed to be under the best advantage to see the state of affairs with all its attending Circumstances And this is the more Requisite at this time as there is some a Probability of Greater an Incre a Consi derable Increase of supplies for the support of this Affair and as our supplies come Chiefly from your Treasury And since our dependence for supplies is so much on the Charitable Fund under your Care the nature of the Case requires that you have as just Idea of the affair as can be given you by such as are have opportunity for the most full Acquaintance with it both with Regard to those things that Circumstances that are prosperous and appear with an hopeful and promise[^163-note1] & also the difficulties & dark Clouds that attend. I am perswaded from long Observation that tis a former common [^163-note2] fault of accounts that are sent home to England by missionaries & other Persons involved in such affairs to be laid before missionary societies & Employers or those from those who Employ [-] em or support em that in their accounts they men th almost wholly ne take little notice of any thing Else but things Pertain that as b pertain to the Post Prosperity & success & of their the affair they are em employed in omitting difficulties Those Things that are of a Contrary nature so that those that are informed by em never have a no any sense & Just notion of the true state of their affairs. This has been notoriously the Case with Regard to the accounts sent him by & home from time to time by the missionaries of the society [-] for the Propagating the Gospel in foreign Parts.

There are many Things that appear with a hopeful and Promising aspect on our affairs with Regard to the Houk Houssatunnuck or stockbridge Indians who are a Part of the Tribe of the River Indians (as They are Called because they used heretofore have Chiefly lived near Hudsons River on Each side of the River) when Mr sergt first came hither there was but about 50 of them young & old. but they have been gradually increasing by others of the tribe coming from in to settle here for the sake of Instruction so that now there are about 250 so that there are here a This Town may now be looked upon as the Head Quarters of the Nation of the River Indians There being many more here than are together in any other Place. Therefore And these Indians. have now entirely got over all their [--] Jealousies & suspicions of of some ill design of the English upon Them in perswading Them to submit to Instruction & that and particularly that the English wanted slaves of Them & their Children. They are [--] much more civil & civilized than formerly & of late there seems to be some an increasing seriousness among Them. There has [been] from the Beginning a [---] school maintained for the Instruction of their Chil. & many are [] under the Care of Mr. Timo Woodbridge a man [^163-note3] of very good Abilities and a Gentleman of a manly upright & Generous disposition. and by an agreeable Conduct has gained a Great Ascendant in the Ind ians aff affections and established a Great int Hims. very much in the Affections & Confidence of the Indians but th his school til of late has not been in happy Circum so happy Circumstances as might be desired. which is has been very much owing to great difficulties He has been under being greatly s much straitened in his Circumstances & under great Ad disad many discouragemts by Reason of some Things peculiar Circum unhappy Circumstances in the state of things amongst th some of the English Inhab. of stockbridge  but of late hap his school is brought into much better Circumstances [-] he has now the promise of a bett encouragemt of a better support & is m seems to be much animated & engaged to serve in his Business He has a large school. and an Indian for his usher whose name is John Wonwaunonpequunnonnt [-] who is also my Interpreter an an[^163-note4] extraordinary man whe he und on some Accounts understands English well a good Reader & writer an ex & an & is an excellent Interpreter & as to as to Knowl. in divinity & understanding of the SS. perhaps there was never an Indian educated in America that exceeded Him in Knowl. in divinity and understanding of the SS.  But He heretofore has not been so strictly in temperate as he ought to have been but there seems now to be an alteration in Him in this Respect & He is much more Careful. & the things of Relig. seem to lie with much weight on his mind. [-] He seems to be very diligent & faithful in his Business.

As to the Iroquois or Indians of the six nations (as we call them) tho of Late the Greater Part of them lately been much alienated from the English & have been drawn over to the French Interest yet others of em have particularly most of the senecas & Quinquuhs some of the Oneiutas & all the Onoontaugaes yet many of the Rest have of Late have there has of late years appeared [-] in them a growing inclination to Xtianity & desire of knowl & Instruction many of the Rest as among the Mohawks Conneenchees or proper Mohawks in the some of the Oneiutas & Tuscaroras a growing Inclination to Xtianity Religion & desire of Kn. & Instruction. The nearest of these nations viz. the Conneenchees when [^163-note5] at Home are in their own Countrey are about 80 miles from us being about [   ] 40 miles beyond albany wheras stockbridge being about 40 miles south-East from Albany & their nearest Town about 40 miles beyond Albany on the other side of Albany. mr. S. in the latter part of his Life sent Letters to the Mohawks to invite em to bring their Chil. hither for Instruction

Mr. serg. in the latter part of his Life had proposed another school after he had been settled here some years projected another school wh[       ] of Indian Chil. might be b for the effectual cultivation of the minds & Change of the manners of the Indians. His design was that a House should be built in which the Chil. be boarded & maintained at the Expence of the English & be constantly day & night under the Instruction of their master & Governours. & that they should not only be Instructed in reading writing & Relig the Principles of Relig. & the English but be brought up to work. & that that their should be two masters one to Instruct em in Learn & the other to oversee Time should be divided between study & work & under different masters [---]   But he never met with many difficulties which Clogd his design . & particularly was very much put by hindered by the Late war so that he lived [not] to see his [^163-note6] design put in Execution. indeed something was done at mr the Expence of mr I the Revd mr. Isaac Hollis He first took a number of Boys & under his own Immediate Care & Boarded & Clothed & Instructed em Hims. at Mr. Hollis Cost. & then some of those afterwards were sent abroad & put to English Families there to be maintained & Instructed at & maintained at mr. Hollis's Expence.  After that mr. s. procured Capt. Martin K.for the presnt Exigency to take Care for the present Exigency till a House could be built the foundation of a Boarding school could be properly laid & a proper Person a man of Learning Could be obtained to be the school master. Capt. Kellogg being not a man of Learning but of pretty good underst. for one that was being an illiterate man & a man in years & thought [^163-note7] to be the fitter for such Business. & the more easily but the more easily obtained being Lame & not well ab so well able on this account to attend follow other Business that required more action.

Capt K. was a lit a little while   here before the Beginning of the war. & when the war broke out He s took a number of his Boys with him the stockbridge Boys with Him to Newington about 70 miles from Hence. who still were maintained at mr. Hollis's Cost.

when the war Ended mr. sergt applied Hims. anew to the Prosecution of the design of a his design of a Boarding school and went about building a House which He left but in its Beginnings He also wrote Letters to the Mohawks inviting Them to bring their Chil. Hither to be instructed in his Intended school. but he did & not live to see any thing brought to Effect. Capt. K. still His     boys   were left in Capt. K-gs Hands -who continued to take Care of them some time after h & after mr. sergts death

Capt. Kellogg wrote to the Mohawks shewing mr. sergs Letters that He wrote in his Lifetime & the year before last in the year [--] a number of the Mohawks came down about 20 & old & young which was a little before I came to this place. It had then been long since any thing had been heard from Mr. Hollis & many supposed he was probably dead. & Therefore Capt. K. dismissed his Boys that he had before taken Care of at mr. H-s's Cost & a applied Hims. wholly to the Care of the Mohawks who were soon taken Notice of by the Governmt & taken under their Care & mr Capt. K. went on to Instruct em at the Governmts Expence but not in so happy a manner as was to be desired he He never set up a school any school but very much left the Chil. to their Liberty to come to him to read their Books when He s they pleased. & He being under a vexatious never Could He never could be perswaded to go out of this way in a more Regular Method of teaching. the Chil. were very much neglected in as to instruction in Good manners Civility & Good manners [^163-note8] & were thus thus Things continued in Great Confusion. which is not so much to be wondred at considering Capt Kellogs Age Lameness & age he being about 65 years old & the Business new to him. They

soon after they arrived the great defect [-] which had been so discouraging to the Mohawks was supplied a schoolmaster was obtained whom One Mr. Gideon Hawley a young Gentleman of Liberal Education & about 24 years of age who appears to be well Qualified for the Business He [--] came hither th & set up a regular school greatly to the Joy of the Iroquois. I never saw so great marks of satisfaction in them on any Occasion. Mr Hawley has a school of about 36 Iroquois Chil. & youth. which indeed is too Great for Him considering the manifold Bus. He has d to do. for besides his teaching the Chil. to read & write & teaching the English Tongue the Principles of Relig. & Good manners He & teaching a couple of English Boys who is are put into the school by the Governmt to learn the Iroquois Tongue & other things necessary to fit em to be serviceable to Indians as missionaries or school masters in due time. He Hims. is Labouring to Learn the Indian Tongue. There is already a happy Alteration among the Indians since He came. He has gained a Considerable Interest in their affections & their Chiefs have diligently applied Thems. to assist Him & strengthen his Hands in governing their Chil. & bringing Them to Good Order.

Another thing appears very favourable to our design viz. the happy union that there is be subsists between these Iroquois & the stockbridge Indians The latter having lately had of their own own accord had a meeting to to see what they could do to Encourage the Consi on their Part to Encourage the

Encourage the mohaw Iroquois in coming hither for Instruction. I have given a particular [^163-note15] account in a Letter to Paice of Lon to Mr. J.
