Mr. Hawley ind intends assoon as H some time in the approaching summer to go up into the Countrey of the Iroquois & take with Him some  of the best of the Indians to Endeavour to perswade em to bring their Chil. hither to be instructed Abraham Conaughstansey encourages Him in the design & offers his Assistance. This   Abraham is indeed an extraordinary man for   his Uprightness & Prudence & Xtian   Zeal & selfdenial.  Things now in many   Respects seem to be in prosperous Circumstances   the Chil. in both schools each school both   of the stockbridge Indians & Iroquois are   making sensible advances in their Learning & reading Learning. & Increase in their knowl. of the Principles of Relig. & the English Tongue & are more & more inured to order  & Good manners.    But still they are far from being brought into such These things together with Gods so wonderfully the forward disposition that appears in the Governmt to promote their design & Gods so wonderfully opening the Hearts of some at a Great distance to in England to Contribute so to the d so liberally to that desig & Engaging some th so many there to of such ability to exert thems. for to promote for our help give us R Reason to hope that G. has something d a design of doing some Great Thing for these unhappy People.

and As to difficulties that arise from within they are also of two sorts. arises There are some that arise from among the Indians with whom we have to do. ## A144. 144.JE-T.Hubbard 3-30-52

Jonathan EdwardsA144. JE to Thomas Hubbard, March 30, 1752. Parts of draft in two locations: ANTS, f. 1752E, #6, and BRBL, f. 1314. Dwight transcript (partial), 4 quarto leaves.

[ANTS (folio leaf):]

MR. HUBBARD OF BOSTON. March 30. 1752.

sir. I would pray you not to Let any Know any thing of this Letter till you have sir read it through. and And Present circumstances seem to require my giving you particular account of [-] of the great affair of the Instruction of the Indians here seem to require my giving you a particular account of our state Mr Sergt before his death had In order to your having a right view of just understanding of things tis necessary that I should give you some history of Things which perhaps you may not have been perfectly acquainted with.

Mr. Sergt in his Life Time exerted hims. Considerably in order to the Esta pro to promote the putting in Execution his Pl Prized plan of a Boarding school. He used many Endeavours to find a proper master a man of Learning for He alwaies supposed such an one would be necessary. But meeting with disappointmts & the war Coming [-] on the affair Lay dormant for several years But near its End before the End of the war Mr Isaac Hollis urged that the matter should be no longer deferred & sent made Considerable Re having made considerable Remittances to dr Colman urged that his money should not be unimproved. whereupon Mr Sergt in the year l748 agreed with Capt M. K. of N. near W. in Con --[^164-note1] a good Friend of Col. Elisha Williams for the present Exigency.

ti to take the Care of both a House [^164-note2] Could be built and the Founda. of his designed boarding school properly laid & a proper Person could be obtained for a school master & 12 Boys were put [ ] three to N. to be put into their Care of by Capt K. at Mr H --'s Charge Capt K. being Lame a man in years above [-] 62. & being Lame & not well able to follow other Business was the more easily obtained. & so 12 Boys were carried down from Here to N. to be taken Care of by Capt K. at Mr H--s Charge where they continued a year In the spring of the Y. l749 the Business being concluded Capt K. brought his Boys hither when Capt Mr S. came to re The [ ] when he Mr S. came to reckon with Capt K. as Agent for Mr. H He was extremely uneasy at some things in his Conduct & Accts & Expressed a Resolution to set things on some other Foot that more Effectual Care might be taken that Mr H. should have Justice done Him in the Expence of his money. But that summer on July 27. [-] Mr S. died before he had Executed his design & left the Boys in Capt K---g Hands in the House intended for the B. sch.

But in its first Begin. & Just suffic. to shelter them from the W. where a Kind of B. sch. was kept but in a very broken Confused manner & nothing was taught the Boys more than they might have been taught in a much better manner in the regular school that is maintained by the Commissioners & under the Care of Mr. W---[^164-note3] & no Bene fit Received by th Benefits received by them But what they would have had without any of Mr that Extra ordinary so that 'tis beyond dispute that Mr. Hollis' money was entirely thrown away.

The winter following began an exceeding [^164-note4] that Great misunderstanding between Col. W.[^164-note5] & & Capt K. on one side & Mr. W. on the other which was concerning first began Concerning Capt K. & his manner of spending Mr. H---s money.

The Parents of the Capt K--gs Boys & the Indians of the Town in general were extremely uneasy & the Indians of the Town in general at Capt K.Conduct & have often Loudly complained in my hearing of Capt K--gs ill treatmt of their Chil. his neglecting them as to their Board & Clothing & Instruction & why he little Cares that their Chil. should be kept Clean & orderly. & By this means the Indians of the Town in general have imbibed a deep Prejudice against Capt K ---

In that Confused state things conti nued till the Fall of the year 1750 when about 20 of the Mohawks came down hither and it having been & it then having been a Considerable time since Capt K. had heard any thing from Mr. Hollis & Capt K. supposing that He was dead & that no further supplies were to be expected from Him dismissed all his Boys. & some of the Mohawks being lately come He applied Hims. wholly to the Care of Them expecting his Pay from the Governmt.

In this state things were when I first Came hither which was in the Begin. of Jan. 1750/l. Capt K. at first seemed much animated by the Mohawks coming & took a great deal of pains with them to teach em to read but his method was unhappy He set up no school but left the Chil. to thems. to come & read & go when they pleased He never could be perswaded to go out of this way into a more regular Method of Teaching tho much Pains has been taken with Him to perswade Him & seemed by degrees to grow more & more negligent as the Influence of the newness of the Mohawk affair diminished. The Chil. have the Chil. under his care have all along been most wofully neglected as to Instruction in Civility in Good manners or any manner of Care of their Cleanliness & decency in their manner of living as an ill husband in his ** see Paper at the End.

The Mohawks have been very uneasy at his negli at this Negligent & Confused state of things relating to the Instruction of their Chil. & have grown more & more so being desirous of a regular school & some proper method to bring their Chil. to [-] order & an amendmt of manners Nevertheless the work

The last summer Capt K. received a Letter from Mr. H-directing Him to increase the number of Boys maintained & Instructed by Him from 12 to 24. seeming to suppose that Capt K. had then 12 maintained & Ins then then under his Care at his Cost

In Aug. Last was that notable Interview with of the Co Chiefs of the Moh. & the Committee of the assembly which I gave you a particular Account of in a former Letter when The Indians then manifested [--] exceedingly well disposed to th what we proposed relating to the [^164-note6] Instruction of their Chil. & promised to promote it to their utmost not only among their own People but among other nations yet objecting the Co n neglected Confused state they observed things to be in their Chiil. much Neglected the no regular school maintained nor those measures taken for the Instructing their Chil. which they had observed the English looked upon necessary in teaching their own Chil. But were encouraged by the Committee of the P.[^164-note7] & by Brig. D. who was also present at all the in all Transactions) that they would endeavour that there should be an alteration in that Respect The Committee being all of one mind that Capt K. was very unfit for the Bus. He was in & Brig. D. who tho not one of the Comtee at that time yet was present at in all Transactions. He then very often in my House spoke with much my wife was much in speaking in my Hearing of Capt K. unfitness &how it was necessary He should be removed & high time He was gone &c ---He then was exceeding

The Brig. was at that Time exceeding Friendly to me as indeed he had been my Great Friend for 20 ye pe perhaps more 20 years past expressing an high opinion of me and far beyond what I Could with any modesty expect. often sent as tho he Esteemed me above all other m -s in N. E. & th &c -& [--] under my Late difficulties at N.H.. has often expressed great

∏ Before I cam when the People here [-] [--] [. . . ] to get me to be were seeking after me Col. W. & Capt & Mad. Sergtshewed thems. extremely averse to expressed thems with much Engagedness & exerted thems to their utmost to hinder it after I came they saw th [ ] to so strong & [. . . ] no hopes of preventing dians that I should be their minister. and among [--] airs of well pleasedness & [ ] Professed Great satisfaction Md Sergt in particular [...]said Things to some Persons that manifested great uneasiness at the Prospect of my settling after my Call whether it was through some sudden Change of mind I will not determine [----] Mad. S. also from time to time has uttered things to one and another that manifested that she was far from being well-pleased & Capt K. has also manifested the [--]Calamities utmost aversion to my settled ministry in this Place

The Commissioners very soon [ ] in Boston understanding the great need of a school master for the Mohawks endeavoured to find a proper Person & treated with Mr. Forbush of west borough[^164-note8] for whom we long waited but he finally fail'd.

Things continuing long in their former neglected Confused state the Moh. many of them were much discouraged some of em took their Chil. away giving this negligence as a Reason of it & the affair of the M. seemed to be under a dark Clould Cloud through great part of the last winter.

But yet in the midst of this darkness some New things appeared which seemed to be remarkable smiles of Heaven on our de sign.

There had been here the last summer an Indian from Onohquaga on the susquehanna River near the head of it about 200 miles southwest from Albany, whose name was Joh Jonah [^164-note9] Tonaughquunnaugus : who hearing of Things that were doing here Came to visit the Place that He might make Report to his People. Letters were sent from Here by Him to the Inhab. of O--to invite to come & bring their Chil. hither for Instruction in Conseq. of which 21. of them young and old came hither [-] though so long & tedious a Journey in the depth of a most severe winter & arrived in the latter part of december something very remarkable has of late appeared among these Onohquagas who are some of the Nation of the Oneita's a strange turn or Change of disposition & Reformation from dr the the drunkenness & Bloodthirstiness to to vertue & Relig. & a Thirst after Instruction of which Abraham the Mohawk[^164-note10] gave me a particular account agreeing with the Accounts we have from others These Onohquagas are the best by far disposed Indians we have. [-]

In the Beginning of Feb. Last the great defect of a schollmaster which had been so discouraging to the Moh. was supplied a schoolmaster was obtained one Mr. G. H.[^164-note11] a Gentlemen of lib. Educa. of about 24. Y. of Age. who appears excellently qualified for the Business both as to abilities & moral & Relig. Endowmts He has set up a regular school. greatly to the Joy of Iroquois Mohawks & Onohquagas I never saw such appearance of satisfaction in em on any occasion. Their Chiefs have much exerted Thems to assist Him & strengthen his Hands in governing their Child. & bringing them to order last page

another thing that look like seems to shew a remarkable Hand of heaven in favour of our disign. is this in the later p the last February. the [-] st. Indians of their own accord met together to Consid what we had don whether they [-] had doen their duty in Every order to promote the Iroquois Coming hither for Instruction in th Xtianity and what remained for our parts to do and in the Issue of their Consultation desired a Conference with the Moahawks Iroquois & when met with Them they told em that they observed that the English had done a great deal that they might be Instructed in Relig. which made to Reflect on thems. as not having done their Part that as to Thems. they now for some Time had had Experience of the great Benefit of the Instructions of the English. that once they were in a state of Great darkness but now were brought into Light & Knew that it was good & theref earnestly desired em to give Heed to the Instructions of the English & not to listen to Objections particularly to give way to no suspicions of the English as though they intended to make slaves of them or their Chil. that they Thems. at first were full of such suspicions but now had been so long under the Care of the English & found that they were wholly without Grounds & to encourage em offered em the use of some of their Lands near the Boarding school

He is a man of some peculiar unhappiness of Temper very assuming & of high & great Resentmt that renders it exceeding difficult to manage with Him.

There now began to appear a very large & universal alteration in Brig. d. a strange Turn of mind & Change of sentiments as was to many things & a new w and particularly an Unaccountable alteration as to his friendship toward me without ever any thing Conduct. great Endeavours were used to alienate Mr. Hawley from me & to beget in uneasiness & Jealousy towards me. [-] discoursing with Mr. H. in Capt Kellogs Presence He warns him not to have his dependence

Now the Old misunderstanding between Col. W. & Mr. W-ge for th By the former [--] too much upon me & offers hi tells Him that He might see cause hereafter to alter his Opinion of some Persons & assures H offers Him [-] his own Friendship & assures Him that He is much more able to support Him and assist Him than I two to one h that He had authority to direct Him & order how he should conduct Hims in the school & that I had no authority to inter meddle in his Concerns & since then in discoursing with Him a long Time alone about me He endeavoured to perswade Him that I intermeddled with that which I had no Business with in by the Express vote of the Commissioners) till some other Person had learned the language & was fitted to preach to em in their own Tongue) that I had herein did him an injury & incroached on his Province over Mr. Hawleys saying & that it might Insight them as an affront to Him. on Mr. Hawley's replying that He rejoyced in it & that He was glad th of the advantage He had by his words that he then said his his words I dont Remember but it seemed to hearing me Preach the Replied Brig. replied with an air of Contempt as though it was beneath Him to learn of me in preach. all this was before ever He had expressd the least dissatisfaction at any Part of my Conduct.

Another dark Cloud that has lately risen is th a late great Increase of uneasiness in the Indians here with Col. Wthey have long had a rooted & perhaps im universal Prejudice against Him but it has lately risen to a great Height by some things that have happened so that They have talkd of breaking up & leaving the Town & seeking Habitation elsewhere because of Him.

Another thing that threatens Ruin of the affair of the Mohawks is this & the boarding school is this. Capt K was not here when Mr. Hawley neither Capt. K. nor Mr. H were here when Mr. Hawley first set up his school among the Mohawk (I introduced him him by order from the Commissrs) But they bo they both came soon after. when He came it appeared that He was resolved not to quit his station tho it was a very apparent that the Indians would insist on Mr. Hawleys being the schoolmaster that should have the Care of all their Chil Boy Children so that his setting up a distinct school was doubtless impracticable apparently yet He Claimed the Boys He formerly had which I suppose was the greater Part of Mr Hawleys school calls them his Boys clai Challenges a superiour authority over em and still pr and a Kind of superintendence under the Brigadie's Countenance & Encouragemt to the unspeakable embarrassing very great Embarrassing & Confounding of the Affair. whether He intends to draw Mr. Hollis' Pay other I will leave you sir to judge whether He intends to draw Mr. Hollis' pay. He is away from his Family & Business & Newington & and is at the Boarding school [ ] with a daughter & son and doubtless expects to be paid [ ] by somebody But certainly that Business he is now, if it can be called a Business is not that for which Mr. H. has spends his time here which heretofore he has set a high price upon.

design Mr. Hollis and the government have in view, spending his time here now is of no service to the bus but very much the Contrary. He pretends in some to do the Business of a steward but is very unfit for it being naturally very slack & negligent & his greatly increased by his age b his Lameness & age being about 66. The stewardship under his Care is managed in a very miserable manner greatly to the wasting of the Countreys money wh (for he has the care of the Provision for not only for Mr. H-s's boys but for the Mohawk & Iroquois Families that are maintaind by the Governmt) The Gov [...] but steady Care th He ought to maintain things [...] to go to the Care & Lay out for themselves & [^164-note12] there is sad Harvests & wast of Things made there in the General observa to the general observation of such as have opportunity to see how things are managed.

prov such provision poor provision th is made that the school master cannot live there in when it is very necessary he should as the master of a Boarding school in order to sustain his Children in a civ an orderly civil way of living . as agreable to the design of that school. and Capt K.has been exceeding slack as to his Accts and has appeared very obstinate in this slackness tho he [ ] has been much ex tho there has been much Reasoning & Expostulating with him about the matters. And he is now a great Impediment to Mr Hawley in his Business. His Lordly disposition together with [-] the notion he has of his g authority here Keeps every Thing uneasy & unsettled. Tis apparent that Capt K. is not pleased in Mr. H- Hawleys being there and evidently Counteracts Him in his measures in many Respects. when he pleases he [...] out of the school [-] & also from the Business to serve Him in his Occasions & sometimes calls em off pointedly to take the Care of them Hims & instruct 'em Hims. & that He He maynt have the Trouble of the Constant Care of thems them Hims. sends away from him into another Room to study . where they sometimes sit on the Bed[--] others get get up a dance about the Room. so some tis such man a way of managemt keeps Things in [] a broken Confused state tis impossible for Mr. H-y in such a state of things to maintain any steady order & Governmt. tis in vain to pretend to care keep some of the Boys in order while others can attend in disorder. Mr Mr. Hawley has a disposition to invent methods for a Happy Reputation of the school & seems to have a Genius for it for tis wholly in vain for Him to pretend to [^164-note13] any such Things. The boys are so [...] that they Know not who to submit to as their master. & nothing goes on successfully. Mr. H-y is so discouraged that He would by no means continue were it not for the Hopes of an alteration. & while things Remain

Mr. Hollis' money & the Countreys to[o] is spent in great measure in vain; & if there be no Remedy it all will prove to be worse than in vain Tis never to be hoped that any Gentleman fit for the Business will be moved to keep the school under such Circumstances Be te unhappiness of the state of things at the Boarding school by Reas. of Capt K--gs being there is too manifold for me to to be fully declared in next paper

# next paper Circumstances are more lamentable than can easi be All these Things are [...] manifest are things I ha Our Circumstances are more Lamen table than can be con easily be conceived of in many Respects & all seems in great measure to spring that from one source viz. that great & new Qu B Quarrel between Col. W--& deac. W. whi which is a breach wide as the sea that cannot be heald. I have not the Least Expecta. that ever Col. W.will be reconciled to deac. W-The Brig It need not th be wondred at that the Brig. shews Hims entirely on that side in this Contention which and me between of considering his Circumstances. t and there is no other Cause that I can conceive of I can conceive of no other Cause of the strange alienation from me mind has [...] to one that informed me of informed me of I having alwaies been looked upon with a suspicious Eye because deac. W---e had a main Hand in getting me to be a missionary here & Col. W. & Capt K. were Known to oppose it mad

[continued in BRBL, f. 1314:] [NB. Pp. 8-9 do not appear in edited version of this letter; do they go elsewhere, or were they accidentally omitted?]

mad. S. was heard to say has said to me that [^164-note14] informed me of it that it was only to serve a tw in Justification of one that spoke in the strongest Terms of against me as utterly unfit for the place. that t it was only to serve a tw that the designs of some particular Persons that I was p got here. & the Brig. has lately in discourse with me insisted upon as just as what Gave just Cause to others to suspect me that deac. W---e was so often at my House. which he is easy to be accounted for seeing He goes by by my door every day in his way to school school. And that Capt K. is more Has a very great Prejudice against me as the Brig. Confessed to me in late discourse with me. And there is great Reason to think the & that He is encouraged by Col. d. to continue here under present Circumstances is certainly owing to some new Cause something that has qui greatly Changed his mind

last paper sometimes Capt K. & the Br Col. d. talk as tho they would make us believe that Capt. K. will speedily go away. & but there are other things that plainly shews are plain Indication of thoughts of his Continuance in both. Capt K. has often declared that He intends to continue here till Col. EW. comes Hence & then to be determined by his Advice as to a further Continuance. He not long since proposed to Mrs Ashley to teach undertake to teach Him the Mohawak Tongue which plainly shews He has thought of abiding. The Col. speaks of it as of great Importance that He should be continued here now because He has a scheme for the getting over from the French. the Forts they have lately built between us & the mississippi. which if it be a Business that He can be supposed equal to & that t worth the while to Pay him for his time here for. & were the Business Mr Hollis sent him his money[?] for yet certainly is an would be a Business that would require a great deal of Time. # Last page

The Affair of a Female school is in many Respects under a dark Cloud & th in the way things are in there is not the least probability of its coming to any thing. Md S. is entring into Circumstances wherein she is like to be utterly un incapable of a any Cons doing the Bus. of a school-mistress she is a very weakly[?] Person & she has already one Family of her own & is like presently to have Brig Col. d---ts Family to take Care of. besides a probability of a Third Family besi between them for her to breed & bare & Educate. [-] & in by Conversation I have had with she plainly she do not expect to have much to do in tea in the immediate Instruction of the Chil. to read in reading &c-But a large salary given to maintain a female superintendent will be money thrown away a Committee would be sufficient for superintendence The mistress should be one whose Circumstances will allow [^164-note15] her to devote her self to the Business of Teach. which wa in order to be done to any Effect requires the skill prudence & Constant application of a woman of superiour Education. & one that has no other Great Care or Business on her Hands Besides M-S. is a Person that the Indi ans have a general disrelish of & prejudice ill opinion of as appears by what they are often saying of her. & also by this that altho she with the Brig assistance of Brig. d. has been by [-] endeavouring to get Chil. for her school. she with has never been able to get but three stockbridge Indians (which are put out at Brookfield) & not one of the mohawks she pursued & would never have obtained them but for deac. W---ges assistan Help. she had has not been able to she obtained one or two mohawk Girls to live with her for a little while but they soon were weary of living with her & went away & there is little prospect of her ever obtained obtaining any of them & Great Complaints have already been made among the Indians of her conduct towards those three that that she has sent to Brookfield next p.

whether the vote of the Assembly in which is this Clause [-] "It being expected that that the Girls will be boarded by at mrs S--ts in Case that she undertakes to keep the school" to me I say which this is implies that she shall be the mistress & be continued so to be if she becomes mrs. mrs dwight or however she Changes her name & Circumstances &c & incapacitates her self by new Circumstances I will not undertake to Judge.

In my Letter that I wrote to you sir the Last summer[^164-note16] I had this Passage. " what renders it more necessary necessary that things here should be under the immediate [pinned-in frag.] Care of Trustees is the misunderst. & Jealousy here subsisting between some of the Chief of the present English Inhab. of the Town which is one of our Greatest Calamities things on this Acct do much more need Constant Inspection & theref. the Gentlemen intrusted had need ought to be such as are perfectly impartial no way interested in or related to those contending Parties" Indeed I then recommended Col d. but Knew not of what now appears that he was like to be ne very nearly related

[end of frag.]

Indeed I then R The Chief of those Contending Parties Its happening so must [-] evidently proves a great Calamity to our affairs If the Assem bly had any Idea of the state of our affairs they would be sufficiently sensible that tis very unfit that all things here should be so such [--] has been the state of things for Event since the Ch appointmt of the gen. Courts Committee that all our affairs have been in the Hands of one man nothing that is at all that is material has been done but He has been the sole doer of it as & if He settles here as He is determined to do if his wife should be the mistress of the Girl's school so things are henceforward to be as for Co the Col Pynchon he the other two of the Committee they stay at Home and h and are very little here but Tis certainly very unfit that all our [^164-note17] affairs should be at the Arbitrary dispo sal of one only & he onely so greatly engaged in that Q with a Party in that Quarrel Contention which has its [--] Influence in every Thing that is done here.

If things are continued in this situation This Countrey the Countrey had as good throw their money into the sea.

There is indeed now a glorious opportunity given in divine Provid. for doing good amongst the six Nations. But tis in vain

last p. I have heard that it has been suggested that I have a mind that one of my own Family should be mistress of the Girls school but tis a meer surmize perfectly without Founda. I have not the least Inclination to any xx Last p

to expect any Good if Things Go on in this Course Tis not difficulty to foresee what will soon be the Consequence. Mr. Ashley & his wife are fully determined to go away & to go & live among the mohawks in their own Countrey. whom the mo all the Iroquois love & especially the Onohquaugas are exceeding fond of and have manifested it in from their publick speeches from Time to Time I am very apprehensive that their going away without any other Event a & going to live in the Iroquois Countrey would entirely break up the mohawk affair The In will would that it would at once draw most of those that are here away & keep others back & greatly disgust give em a very great disun disgust to the English. They have long shewn thems. very Jealous for mr Ashley & his wife that they are not well treated by those that have the C managemt of things & have public very publickly Complained of it And then Mr Haw ley also is in the forementioned Case fully deter mined to Go Go away. which would be another Fatal stroke under our Circumstances.

if a few mohawks should after all Conti nue whi yet (which I much doubt of) yet the affair would have a mortal stroke & would doubtless languish to death. The design of making a settlemt of em in the Hoplands which the Countrey has bought for em would be would entirely fail. for none now appear willing to settle there but the Onohquaugas. who are above all attached to mr. Ashley & his wife & & if they Lead the way probably a few Mohawks would follow em. but a they are above attached to Ashley & his wife & tis beyond all doubt they will not settle here if mr. Ashley & h Those Persons are not with 'em. The & that the fairest Prospects & mo will be dashed. the most glo [---]. the Glo. opportunities divine Providence is giving us will be lost next p.

Tis probable sir you ha may have very different Repres Representa. made of Things very different from these. cant as my Representa These things may be called very extravagant Representation of things Account [--] of things [^164-note18] the Fact I ha Represent I am able to Confirm the most material of them by the Representa. I have made they are such as suffi can be warranted by sufficient Testimonies if En Enquiries should be made & such as you sir if will see (if things go on as They are) Confirmed by the Issue future Events & Consequences of things

& so all that we have done will prove worse than in vain [-] for the Consequence will be the future prejudi establishing a Prejudice in the minds of the six Nations against any such attempts of the future & putting all designs of this nature more Effectually out of our Reach it may be for two or three Generations & according to the Genius of the People they will never Trust

[---] Yea I apprehend more danger in than this the stockbridge Indians are in such a Rustle & in so uneasy & future Passions by Reason of the state of the th by Reason of the the Pres. situation of things that th I think there is real danger that most of them that if the there be no alteration they will break up & last Col.

I expect he by Reason of our Those difficulties to be Represented by some of the Family of the W---ms's & those that are related to em to be represented as very unfit for the Place of I am in. & should not wonder A mischief maker &c & should not wonder if they should strive to Remove me However I will discharge in a good Consc. tis necessary here shou those whom have the Governmt of the state of things which they never can know but by information from some here. I have no Col. D. [---] notwithstanding all his past the forementioned Conduct Professes still to be my Hearty Friend Friend. that often men dont Know their own Hearts that the the one of those things I think is certainly true as viz. that he of his Est Affection are the same that they were him his He is greatly changes as to his Esteem or if He be my Cordial Friend as He says it Happens so strangely that Friendship in Him acts like the Enmity in other Persons --I have no Interest to make for myself or any of my Friends. It has of late been abundantly given [-] out that I am seeking the female school for some of my Family which is perfectly a groundless surmize. I have not the least inclination to any such Thing.

I entirely trust your Honours wisdom as the use you make of this Letter that you will make such an use of this Letter as to do good & not [any][^164-note19]hurt with it. Laying you under no Restraint Lay no Limitation but such as shall be set by your own disgression.

[small leaf:[^164-note20]]

whom they know to be no fit matter to be made a Tool to serve their designs. However I will endeavour alwaies to discharge a good Consc. at the same Time endeavouring so far as may be consistent with this to live peaceably with all men. we are here in a remote & hidden Corner where a vast deal of publick moneys & moneys given for Charitable & pious Purposes have expended & I am satisfied that the O is in no measure sensible after what manner much of it has been spent. Tis absolutely necessary that those that are first in the ordering & Governmt of our affairs should know the state of things which they never Can know but by Information from some that live here which never would be given if fear of incurring the displeasure of particular Persons must alwaies be sufficient to prevent

---Col. d. notwithstand all that has been forementioned professes still to be my Hearty Friend and declares that what He has said & done has not been from disaffection but Judgmt to which I have nothing to say. but only that if He is not mistaken through ignorance of his own Heart (as many times Persons are) It strangely happens that Friendship in Him acts like Enmity in other Folks.

I shall prescribe to your Honour no Limitations in the Use you shall make of this Letter but what are set by your own discretion entirely trusting your wisdom to use it so as to do good & not hurt with it.

I am y sir

your most humble servt

& obliged servt

J. E.

## A145. Letter to Andrew Oliver (Draft), May 1752 145.JE-A.Oliver 5-52

Jonathan EdwardsA145. JE to Andrew Oliver, 5/52. Draft in ANTS, 1752D, #8 and #9.

To Mr. Oliver. May. 1752.

sir. Things have gone on affairs amongst us have gone on in great Confusion since I last wrote to Honoured sir your Honour. we have one difficulty & disturbance after another & every Thin The Mohawks who were quite weary of th Confus a long continued state of Confusion seemed greatly pleased with mr. Hawleys Coming & Every thing for a little while seemed to appear put on the most Pleasing promising aspect. But this appearance soon [...] & Con vanished Confusions Returning & to a greater degree than Ever has had t a tendency. more to discourage them much more than In half the Mohawks went away. And there is little probability of as to most of them that they will Return any more some of went away in a great disgust with Capt. K. for hi especially for his Conduct in diffe disposing of as a steward after thi other things happened one after another greatly to dis turb the minds of such as were left. mr

mr. Hubbard[^165-note1] of sheffield a great Friend of Capt. K. & hi Friend with Capt. K. & his Party be being at the Boarding school [ ] struck [a child of t]he Chief sachem [of the][^165-note2] Onohquaugas on his Head with his Cane without any manner of Provocation which put the Indians into a terrible Ruffle so that they seemd to so that they seemed to Resolved all of them immediately to pack up & be gone. Mr. Hawley & mr. Ashly[^165-note3] came to me to inform me of it to ask my advice what to do in to Pr calm their minds & to prevent its proving the utter Ruin of the affair. I told them I did not Care to return that Col. d. had often blamed m do had blamed me much for inter meddling with the Affairs of the Mohawks & told me that herein I meddled with what was none of my Business. & I theref. advised em to go to Him & L declare the whole affair to Him that he might use proper mean Re means to prevent the fatal Conseq. on my advice they went to him but their coming was not well ill Resented it was taken as the fruit of a disposition to find fault with Persons on that side [-] & supposed it were little thing was supposed by the Brig. to be a trifle & that indeed there was no such great uneasi remaining uneasiness among the Mohawks in which He was greatly mistaken to my Knowl. The Chief of those that were here came that day to my House & to Complain of the treatmt & mr. Hubbard happened at the same time to be present & shewed very Great uneasiness. mr. Hubbard was perswaded to give some money to pacify em. However the Brig. was provoked & his Passions aroused in for In the afternoon He went down to the Boarding school in the afternoon & Came into the school in school [time]. & fell upon mr. H. [^165-note4] in the Presence of the sc whole school in a ma very fervent manner & Continued so as & Continued his him under th his his Chastisemt for 3 Hours together by the watch so as it b wholly to break up the school & alarm all the Mohawks. He told mr. Hawley He was of No Judgmt of no prudence that He was unfit for the Business He was in there that if He had any Regard to [the] prosperity of it He [^165-note5] would quit it immediately. that He was a mischief-maker. when mr. Hawley [col. 2] desired that his conduct might be then examined & looked into He told him he should not take so much notice of Him. that H Him th He would inform of his ill Con duct & that my Recommendation should would not do his turn.

The Mohawks in generally heard it the Brig. talk was very loud st & he did not endeavour to conceal it from 'em. for They were greatly alarmed & very much concerned about it & said they did not Know but that great man would kill their schoolmaster & were much afraid mr. H. would go away. They had several meetings about the affair. the Chief of em went to Capt. Kellogg & express'd their great uneasiness to Him & desired to have opportunity to [---] speak to the Brig. about the Affair were & told im they were afraid that Mr. H. would go away. Capt. K. told em He hoped they would get another as good. they told im they n did not that they new wi they were acquainted with Mr. H. & [did not like new things][^165-note6] th mr. Hawley that very [day was going a jour-] ney into Connecticut but the Indians insisted on opportunity to speak with him about this Affair before He went. & when they met him They entreating him not to be discouraged [-] nor to leave them & said that if H He went away they would go also.

The Brig--s End seemed to be to discourage Mr. H& drive him [off] & indeed He was [^165-note7] greatly his sp. very much over Come for th a while after this severe Ch strange treatmt The Indians seemed t Mohawks seem to have imbibed a great disgust toward the Brig. from this & some other thing.

The Col. Brig. has made Him[self] [--] disagreeable to the Mohawks & to all the Indians in the town by this & some other Conduct of his. The stockbridge Indians have had several the s things that have put [them] into a great [^165-note8] Ruffle this winter past & this spring. They were considerably Ruffled by [-] what they perceived to of [-] a great opposition made to something that was done which they had i about a seat in the meeting House which they had a hand in & much insisted on insomuch that they had a meeting about it it among thems. of their own Accord. every thing is kept in a Tumult & uneasi ness through a high-Handed way of managing affairs. Col. Pynchon has seems entirely long ago entirely to have forsaken the Business [which] I suppose is through his dislike of the sp. & Conduct of one that is Joined with Him a fellow as of the same Committee Capt. ashley exprest expresses a great dis like of st. managemt & I cant perceive that He will any thing more than assist in has any Hand in the managemt of affairs He is discouraged declares He will do his utmost that the af mohawk that affair shall be thrown up by the Governmt Capt thus all things are left to the arbitrary disposal of one man who seems Resolved to He of the has done every thing of im portance without taking the voice of the Rest of the Committee if we may Credit Capt ashley as to the following particulars as to the following particulars. [^165-note9]

[1/3 col. blank]

Every thing that Gives the Least that Lays any Clog or brings the least Clog to d designs seem to provoke to a high degree. Capt. K. has lately given out that he has had it from a certain Great man that [I] [^165-note10] was not like to be here 4. years Hence The like has also been it also has been said by Gentlemen of the Party of Hatfield[^165-note11] that I was wholly unfit for the Business I was in & was not like to continue in it Long.

Col. E. W El--a W.[^165-note12] is now come Home which probably gives new spirit to those menaces. However sometimes

However sometimes what they see among the Indians seems to convince em that the affair is Languishing & like to come to an End & then they lay [-] the blame to us & say we as the Causes of its Ruin doubtless we shall all be th all that are concerned that ben't tools h Tools will have many things laid to their Charge.

But there is no immediate necessity of the affairs breaking up unless Col. d. & Capt. K. are Resolved to have it so and are determined when they leave it to Leave it to in Ruins believe the Life of the affair depended on them. & they are determined to have their wills that in that that if they have not the managemt No body else shall. but undoubtedly if they don't leave the Business soon they will leave in Ru the affair in Ruins & the affair by going to Ruin will leave them for mr Hawley & mr ashley & his wife to be will leave it [ ] Those on whom [^165-note13] The dependence of the affair as to Continuance & Prosperity is chiefly on the Onohquaugas who are much best disposed & most likely to come in Considerable Number & have not been here so long to see so much to discourage 'em & who are alone are willing to settle at the Hoplands. The affair is not at all desperate as to them if there by a speedy alterati & some of the [--] Mohawks if there be a speedy alteration But if the Brig. & Capt. K. ## A146. Letter to Aaron Burr, May 6, 1752 146.JE-A.Burr 5-6-52

Jonathan EdwardsA146. JE to Aaron Burr, 5/6/52, Princeton, Firestone Lib., Edwards Coll., AM 2298.

Sheffield May 6. 1752.

Rev. & dear Sir,

I thank you for your Favour by Williams your Pupil, and also for your other Letters, received before. my not answering Them before now was not in the least owing to want of Respect, or any disposition to uphold any misunderstanding ; But partly from the multitude of Affairs which have continually press'd my Mind; which yet would not have prevented my writing if I had hadknown of any good Opportunity. I heard nothing of Mr Josiah Williams's going in the winter, 'till after He was gone: If I had, I should doubtless have wrote by Him. ----- As to the Affair of the Report of what you said concerning my Book on the Terms [o]f[^166-note1] Communion &c from the Credit I give you, in [you]r Representation, I fully believe you have been [misr]epresented: and therefore don't think it worth[whil]e to make an Uproar in tracing the mat[ter to th]e original. I would pray you to give your [self no fur]ther uneasiness about that matter, as tho' [an]y thing remain'd with me to occasion dissaffdisaffection: I assure [you] there is Nothing of that Nature.

you are pleased to ask my Thoughts concerning your proposed voyage to great Britain for the sake of N- Jersey College. You have Those nearer to you that [kno]w ten times as much of the Circumstances & necessities of the College, that are vastly more able & in fitter Circumstances to advise you; Gov. Belcher & the Trustees in particular. There doubtless might great advantages be obtain'd by your going to England & Scotland; & spending about a year in great Britain, more than by all Letters that can be written. The only doubt is whether the College [^166-note2] won't extremely suffer by your being so long absent. But of that I am not a fit Person to Judge. One Thing I will venture to give you my Thoughts in viz. That since you have not had the small Pox, If you can find a skillful prudent Physician, under whose Care you can put your self, you would take the small Pox by Inoculation before you go, after properly preparing your Body for it, by Physick & diet: -- If you go, it will be necessary you should take some Companion with you. I know not who you have there : But I have been favoured with some Acquaintance with Mr. Wright, whom I should think would be a very suitable Person to go as your Companion on such a design. If I were going, He would be very agreable to me; I should not expect to find one more agreable or fitter for that Purpose.

I heartily thank you for your Kind offer with [res-]pect to the Education of my son. 'Tis prob[able that] I shall send Him before long: I have des[ired Mr] wright to take Care to provide a good & [he is] obliging & ready to Helpful. and from th[e kind] and generous disposition y[ou] have manifested, I shall have somedependance on your Fatherly Care of Him.

If you go to great Britain, I shall be ready to do my utmost to forward the design of your going in my next Letters to Scotland. -- Mr. wright can inform you something of the state of Things in stockbridge. You may perhaps do much to promote our Affairs in London. But I hope to write to you again about these matters before you go. In the mean time, asking your Prayers I am dear sir,

your Friend & Brother,

Jonathan Edwards.

## A146a. Petition of Stockbridge Inhabitants to Spencer Phips, May 27, 1752 146a.JEetal-S.Phips 5-27-52

Samuel BrownA146a. JE et al to Spencer Phips et al., 5/27/52. Petition. Mass. State Archives, Columbia Point. Written by Samuel Brown, but signed by JE.

To His Honour Spencer Phips Esqr Lieutenant Gover nour and Commander in chief in and over his Majties Province of the Massachusetts Bay in New England. And to the Honourable his Majties Council and House of Representatives in general Court Assembled at Concord the Twenty seventh Day of this Instant May. The petition of us the subscribers Inhabitants of Stockbridge; humbly shewth That it will be greatly for the intrest, and benefit of the Inhabitants of this Town; that there should hereafter, when there shall be occation; be proper encouragement for an able & well qualified minister to Settle here. That therefore it appears manifest to us, that it be will be much for the benefit of the people of this Town, and of the Indian Mission here, that a convenient dwelling house & barn, with a Suitable quantity of Land for a home lot, be Sequester'd to the use of the Ministry, which with a hundred acres of land that the Town have provided by the advice & direction of the general court, will be Sufficient for the use & improvment of any minister that may here after be settled among us. That the present pastor by reason of his advancement in years, cannot be expected according to the ordinary course of nature, to continue in the Ministry near so long; as Ministers who are Settled in their youth. We therefore expect that a Settlement will the sooner be needed for another. And your petitioners apprehend that this; unless a personage be provided Seasonably cannot be done without great cost, & difficulty, by reason of the peculiar circumstances of the Town: which allows of but few english families, and there being but a small part of the lands in their hands, which renders it difficult to obtain lands for the above Said purpose, And the Indian lands being in such circumstances that it cannot be had without application to and approbation of the general assembly

And by reason of lands rising it will become more and more [^167-note1] difficult hereafter, to obtain a convenient Settlement for a minister Suitably Scituated for his calling. Your petitioners have been inform'd, that when the pastor of this church prefer'd a petition to the general assembly the last year; for liberty to purchase lands of the Indians in Stockbridge, near the middle of the Town, that his petition was granted and in consequence of Said grant the pastor afore Said did purchase of the Indians, an house, and a small barn, with about eight acres of land conveniently Scituated.

Your petitioners have been further inform'd, that when the Said petition was under consideration in the general assembly, there appear'd a disposition in the court, to purchase part of Said granted lands, and to be at the expence of building an house for the use of the present pastor: and his Successors in the mission founded here. And in as much as the present pastor has been at great expence in removing his family, and purchasing Necessary accommodations for his numerous family; and that the Town of Northampton from whence he remov'd, being under difficulty circumstances; puts the pastor of this church under disadvantages respecting the disposal of what he has there: on this account he is willing that the house and lot afore Said, that he has purchased of the Indians, might be Sequester'd to the use of the Mission founded here. Your petitioners viewing themselves perticularly intrested in those things that tend to the support and encouragement of the present pastor, & they that may Succeed him in this great work. Therefore your petitioners humbly request, that it would please your Honour & the honourable court if in your wisdom you Shall think fit, to grant that the Said house barn & lot of land may be purchased for the above Said ends & uses And that the same may be put into a tenantable condition for the comfort of the pastor of the church and his family and your petitioners Shall as in duty bound Ever pray &c Sam Brown Jonathan Edwards Joseph Woodbridge David Pixley Josiah Jones

[^167-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

Mr. stod. in his Book Called a Guide to X is much in directing minesters to incalculate th incalculate in Persons under Convictions things directly contrary to these things which Mr. W teaches you -There These forementioned doctrines of mens Enmity total Corruption & Gods absolute sovereignty &c But in following this Book of Mr. W--s's one that is not such a Guide to X but you will follow quite another sort of Guide to X

It is what a doctrine that has ever been taught you and used made use of for the aw warning awakening & humbling of Gospel sinners that they had greater Guilt & were exposed to a more terrible Punishmt than the very Heathen. England. Thus you are at once deprived all the Chief Texts in the Bible that hitherto have been made use of among you to teach you the distinguishing Qualifications & priviledge of the truly pious & the nature & Benefits of a true Conversion naturally Leading to all the Rest of Taylors notions about Religion who utterly explodes & Expunges scheme of Relig. which utterly expunges your former the doctrines you have been formerly taught concerning eternal Election con saving Conversion Adoption Justification & so of a natural death in sin & the whole doctrine of original sin & the mighty change made in the soul by the Redemption of X

This And this taken with those preceding things which I have observed in Mr. W--ms's Book. naturally tends to lead you & & especially the young People among you apace into a liking to the [^168-note8] new fashionable Lax notion schemes of divine as remote that so greatly prevail in N. England of late as wide from what you have been taught in from alwaies been taught & embraced & has been esteemed your Glory by [-] you & esteem Justly esteemed your Glory as the east is from the west by others.

An *APPENDIX*.

BEING A LETTER to the People of the first Church and Congregation in NORTHAMPTON.

*Dear Brethren*,

HO' I am not now your Pastor, yet having so long stood in that Relation to you, I look on my self obliged, notwithstanding all that has of late pass'd between us, still to maintain a special Concern for your spiritual Welfare. And as your present Circumstances appear to me very evidently attended with some peculiar dangers, threatning the great Wounding of the Interest of vital Religion among you; which probably most of you are not well aware of: I look on my self called to point forth your Danger to you, and give you Warning. What I now especially have Respect to, is the danger I apprehend you are in, from the Contents of that book of Mr. *W*. of *Lebanon,* to which the foregoing Performance is a Reply; which I perceive has been written and publish'd very much by your Procurement & at your Expence; and so (it may naturally be supposed and expected) is dispers'd in your Families, and will be valued, and much made use of by you as a Book of great Importance. What I have Respect to is, not so much the Danger you are in of being established by that Book in your former Principles, concerning the Admission of Members (tho' I think these Principles are indeed very opposite to the Interest of true Piety in Churches;) But what I now mean is the Danger there is, that while you are making much of that Book as a Means to maintain Mr. *Stoddard*'s Doctrine concerning the Terms of Communion, You, and especially your Children, will by the Contents of it be led quite off [^168-note9] from *other* religious Principles and Doctrines, which Mr. Stoddard brought you up in, and always esteemed as of vastly greater Importance, than his particular Tenet about the Lord's Supper; and be naturally led into Notions and Principles, which *He* ever esteemed as of fatal Tendency to the Souls of Men.

By the Way, I would have it observed, that when I take Notice of these Things in his Book, my Aim is not to beget in you an ill Opinion of Mr. *W*. as tho' he were as corrupt in his settled Persuasion, as one would be ready to think, if we were to judge only by Things delivered in *some Parts* of this Book; and especially if it should be supposed, that he embraced all the *Consequences* of what he here maintains. Men often don't see or allow the plain Consequences of their own Doctrines. And therefore, tho' I charge very pernicious Consequences on some *Things* he says, yet I don't charge *Him* with embracing these Consequences: Nor will I undertake to explain how it could come to pass, that he should maintain Things now in *this* Book, in Opposition to me, which are so contrary to the good and sound Doctrines he has formerly delivered in *other* Books. Let that be as it will, and however orthodox the Principles may be, which he more ordinarily maintains; yet the *ill & unsound* Things he delivers here, may do never the less Hurt to you & your Children, who may read this Book without having in View the more wholesome Doctrines of his other Writings.

For Instance, You have ever been taught, that *unconverted Men don't really believe the Gospel, are never truly convinced of its Truth*; and that 'tis of great importance[^168-note10] that Sinners should be sensible of the Unbelief and Atheism of their Hearts. But contrary to this, Mr. *W---ms*'s book abundantly teaches you and your Children this Notion, *That unsanctified Men may really be convinced of the divine Truth of the Gospel, and believe it with all their Hearts.*

You have been ever taught, that Christless Sinners, especially when under some more slight Awakenings, are very ready to flatter themselves that they are willing to accept of Christ as their Saviour; but that they must be brought off from their vain Imagination, and be brought to see that the Fault is in their own Wills, and that their not being interested [^168-note11] in Christ is owing to their Obstinacy and Perversness, and wilful wicked Refusal of God's Terms; on which Account they are wholly inexcusable, and may justly be cast off by God. But contrary to these Things, this Book of Mr. *W.* abundantly teaches you, that Men, in an unconverted State, may indeed *cordially consent to the Terms of the Covenant of Grace, may comply with the Call of the Gospel, may submit to it's Proposals, may have Satisfaction in the Offer God makes of himself as our God in Christ, may fall in with the Terms of Salvation propounded in the Gospel, and renounce All other Ways, and may sincerely and earnestly desire Salvation in this Way; and that some unconverted Men are not wilful obstinate Sinners.*

(P. 21. *b.*) Which doctrines, if embraced and retain'd by your Children as true, will tend forever to hinder that Conviction of the Opposition and Obstinacy of the Heart, which Mr. *Stod*. ever taught you to be of such Importance in Order to the Soul's Humiliation, and thoro' Conviction of the Justice of God in it's Damnation.

You have ever been taught, that the Hearts of natural Men are wholly corrupt, entirely destitute of any Thing spiritually Good, not having the least Spark of Love to God, and as much without all Things of this Nature, as a dead Corpse is without Life: Nevertheless, that 'tis hard for Sinners to be convinced of this; that they are exceeding prone to imagine, there is some Goodness in 'em, some Respect to God in what they do: Yet that they must be brought off from such a vain Conceit of themselves, and come to see themselves utterly depraved and quite dead in Sin.--But now this Book of Mr. *W.* leads you to quite other Notions; it leads you to suppose, that some natural Men are *above Lukewarmness in Religion*, that*they may truly profess to be the real Friends of Christ, and to love God, more than his Enemies, and above the World.*

It was a Doctrine greatly inculcated on you by Mr. *S.* as supposing it of great Importance for all to be convinced of it, That natural Men *are not subject to the Law of God, nor indeed can be*; that they never do truly serve God, but are wholly under the Dominion of Sin and Satan.--But if Sinners believe Mr. *W---ms*'s Book, they won't be convinced of these Things; nay, will believe quite contrary Things, *viz.* [^168-note12] That Sinners, while in a State of Nature, may *have a cordial Subjection to Jesus Christ*, and may *be subject to him with all their Hearts* and may *be so devoted to the Service of Christ as to be above those that serve two Masters* may *give up themselves to be taught, ruled, and led by him in a Gospel-Way of Salvation* and may *give up all their Hearts and Lives to him.*---

And is it likely, while Sinners believe these Doctrines of Mr. *W.--* that they will ever be brought to a thorough Humiliation, in a Conviction of their being wholly under the Power of Enmity against God? Which Mr. *S.* taught you to be of such great Importance.

You know it was always a Doctrine greatly insisted on by Mr. *S.* as a Thing of the utmost Consequence, that Sinners who are seeking converting Grace, should be thoro'ly sensible of God's being under no Manner of Obligation, from any Desires, Labours, or Endeavours of theirs, to bestow his Grace upon them; either in Justice, or Truth, or any other Way; but that when they have done all, God is perfectly at Liberty, whether to shew them Mercy, or not; that they are wholly in the Hands of God's Sovereignty. (See *Guide to Christ,* p. 75. *c, d.* & *Benef. of the Gosp.* P. 64. and P. 75, 76.)--Whereas, if a Sinner seeking Salvation believes Mr. *W---ms*'s Book, it will naturally lead him to think quite otherwise. He (in P. 28.) speaking of such Sincerity and Earnestness of Endeavours as may be in natural men to qualify 'em to come to the Sacrament, and of the great Encouragement God has given, that he will bestow his saving Grace on such as use such Endeavours, adds these Words (near the Bottom of the Page) "God never will be worse than his Encouragement, nor do less than he has encouraged; And he has said, *To him that hath shall be given.*" Naturally leading the awakened Sinner, who is supposed to have moral Sincerity enough to come to the Sacrament, to suppose, that God is not wholly at Liberty; but that he has given so much Encouragement, that it may be depended upon he will give his Grace; and that it would not be reasonable or becoming of God to do otherwise; because if God should do so, he would *be worse than his Encouragement*[^168-note13] and would not fulfil that Word of his, *To him which hath shall be given*. And how will this tend effectually [^168-note14] to prevent the Sinner's looking on God as absolutely at Liberty, and prevent his resigning himself wholly into the Hands of God, and to his sovereign Pleasure?

It is a Doctrine which has ever been taught you, & made Use of for the warning, awakening and humbling of GospelSinners, That they have greater Guilt, and are exposed to a more terrible Punishment, than the *Heathen.*---But this is spoken of by Mr. *W.* as an unsufferable Treatment of *visible Saints:* Naturally tending to alleviate and smooth the Matter in the Consciences of those that are not scandalous Persons, tho' they live in Unbelief and the Rejection of Christ under Gospel-Light and Mercy.

If you will believe what Mr. *W.* says (P. 56.) Those blessed *Epithets* and *Characters* in the Epistles of the Apostles, which you always, from the first Foundation of the Town, have been taught to be peculiar and glorious Expressions and Descriptions of the blessed Qualifications and State of true Saints, and Heirs of eternal Happiness; such as *being elected, chosen before the Foundation of the World, predestinated to the Adoption of Children through Jesus christ; quickened, and made alive to God* tho' once dead in Trespasses & Sins; *washed, sanctified, justified;---made to sit together in heavenly Places in Christ; begotten again, to an Inheritance incorruptible, undefiled*; --with innumerable others the like:--I say, if you believe Mr. *W.* you have been quite mistaken all your Days, and misled by all your Ministers; these Things are no more than were said of the whole Nation of the *Jews,* even in their worst Times! Which is (as I have observed) exactly agreable to the strange opinion of Mr. *Taylor*, of *Norwich* in *England,* that Author who has so corrupted Multitudes in *N. England.* Thus you are at once deprived of all the chief Texts in the Bible, that hitherto have been made Use of among you, as teaching the discriminating Qualifications and Privileges of the truly pious, and the Nature and Benefits of a real Conversion; too much paving the Way for the rest of *Taylor*'s Scheme of Religion, which utterly explodes the Doctrines you have been formerly taught concerning eternal Election, Conversion, Justification; and so, of a natural State of Death in Sin; and the whole Doctrine of Original Sin, and of the mighty Change made in the [^168-note15] soul by the Redemption of Christ applied to it.

And this, taken with those other Things which I have observed, in Conjunction with some other Things which have lately appear'd in *Northampton,* tend to lead the young People among you apace into a Liking to the new, fashionable, lax Schemes of Divinity, which have so greatly prevail'd in *New-England* of late; as wide as the East is from the West, from those great Principles of Religion, which have always been taught, and have been embraced, and esteemed most precious, and have justly been accounted very much your Glory by others.

If this Book of Mr. *W.* with all these Things, is made much of by you, and recommended to your Children, as of great Importance to defend the Principles of the Town, how far has your Zeal for that one Tenet, respecting natural Men's Right to the Lord's Supper, transported you, and made you forget your Value and Concern for the most precious and important Doctrines of Jesus Christ, taught you by Mr. *Stoddard*, which do most nearly concern the very Vitals of Religion!

I beseech you, Brethern, seasonably to consider how dark the Cloud is that hangs over you, and how melancholy the Prospect (especially with Regard to the rising Generation) in many Respects. I have long been intimately acquainted with your religious Circumstances, your Notions & Principles, your Advantages & Dangers; having had perhaps greater Opportunity for it than any other Person on Earth.--Before I left you, it was very evident, that *Arminianism,* and other loose Notions in Religion, and Mr. *Taylor*'s in particular, began to get some Footing among you; and there were some Things special in your Circumstances, that threaten'd a great prevailing of such like Notions: which if they should by Degrees generally prevail, will doubtless by Degrees put an End to what used to be called saving Religion.

Therefore let me intreat you to take the friendly Warning I now give you, and stand on your Guard against the encroaching Evil. If you are not inclined to hearken to Me, from any remaining Affection to one whose Voice and Counsels you once heard with Joy, and yielded to with great Alacrity; yet let me desire you not to refuse, as you would act the Part of Friends to yourselves & your dear Children.

I am,

Dear Brethern,

He who was one (as I hope through Grace)

*Your faithful Pastor, and devoted Servant for Jesus sake,* J. E.
