## A148. Letter to Timothy Dwight, June 30, 1752 148.JE-T.Dwight 6-30-52

Jonathan EdwardsA148. JE to Col. Timothy Dwight, 6/30/52. ANTS, 1752B, #3. Addressed on back "To / Col. Timo Dwight / In Northampton." With enclosure.

Stockbridge June 30. 1752.

dear Sir

I request of you the Favour of endeavouring to sell my Land at Winchester. My deed of the Land, together with a Plan of it, is in the Hands of your son. I shall be in great need of money, and therefore must endeavour to procure it that way, or some other. The Town of stockbridge [-] sent in a Petition by deac. Woodbridge, to the general Assembly, that they would buy my House & House-lot for a a Parsonage. But it was not granted : tis supposed the granting it was prevented very much by Capt. Ephraim[^169-note1] who was at Concord the whole Time of the sitting of the Assembly, constantly busy with the Re- presentatives, with his Lime-juice Punch & wine. Objections were made against the Petition, which could come from None but He. By this means I shall be in greater need of money than I expect- ed.

I have wrote a Letter to Capt. B. sheldon, another to Charles Phelps, another to Capt. Leavitt of suf- field, desiring Them to endeavour to obtain some more subscriptions for the printing of my Book[^169-note2] & to send what They got to you, to be forwarded to Mr. Foxcroft. which I now desire you to do, if any subscriptions are sent to you. Herein you will oblige your affectionate Brother

Jonathan Edwards.

Give my love to sister dwight.

Sir [^169-note3]

I have sent the Copy of my Answer to Mr. Williams, by my son Parsons, to be conveyed by you to Mr. Foxcroft. I need not tell you that extraordinary Care had need be taken in the Conveyance. There are many Enemies who would be glad to destroy it. I know not how in the world it can be well got to Mr. Foxcrofts Hand, especially by Reason of the small pox. but I trus desire you would do the best you can.

J. E.

Col. dwight

[^169-note1]: Ephraim Williams.

[^169-note2]: *Misrepresentations Corrected* (1752), also referred to in the enclosure.

[^169-note3]: **marginal.** [encl.]

## A149. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, June 30, 1752 149.JE-T.Foxcroft 6-30-52

Jonathan EdwardsA149. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 6/30/52. BRBL, f. 1294.

Stockbridge June 30. 1752.

Rev. and honoured Sir,

I have now at Length sent you my Answer to mr. W[^170-note1] And must request the Favour of you, added to all your other condescending & most obliging Favours, to correct the Press. A little while ago, I wrote you a Letter from Northampton, & sent a draught of Proposals for subscription to be printed, and sent a few subscriptions. since that Mr. Hazard[^170-note2] of N. York has desired me to set Him down for 4 dozen. I expect many more subscriptions. There are but few of the written Proposals I have sent abroad yet come 3 or four have appear'd willing to subscribe in this Town. whi I should be glad that the printed Proposals when done might be forwarded to Col. dwight of Northampton, with all convenient speed.

I should be glad that you would endeavour that this Book may be printed in a pretty good Paper & Character, & may be printed correctly. And if the Bookseller can be agreed with to let me have a Number for the Copy ---If not, I must go without. With Respect to any Alterations that you may think needful to be made; It becomes me much to prefer your Judgment to my own : But it is very difficult, & almost impossible for another to enter into all the Views of a Writer, or to know what he every thing He has in View in all that He says; And therefore a little variation of sentiment, may much thwart and disappoint his design, insensibly to another. But this, I should take as a very friendly Part, & much desire, that if you observe, that in any Instances I have mistaken mr. Williams' meaning, & misrepresented Him, or in any Respect injured Him, or des deliver'd my self unhappily in any other Respect, you would inform me via Col. dwight of Northampton, who has often opportunities to send to me. I have another copy by besides this I me,[^170-note3] much like that I Now send to you, and can make needed alterations and send 'em to you: -I desire you would use some Endeavours to promote subscriptions be in other Places, where you think it feasible, and that, to that End, you would speak or write to the Rogerses, to mr. Hobby, Mr. Hall, Mr. Eaton, Goddard &c-One I think If have not erred in my Calculation, this Book [-] will be considerably less than my former, which may be some Encouragemt to subscribers. A I thank you for your Late letter of June 4[^170-note4] and the Care you took of the Pacquet from mr. Erskine. He mentions another Pacquet sent before, which never came to Hand. If you hear of it, I sh desire you would send it. Asking your continued prayers, & presenting Humble Respects to your Family, & mr. Bromfield & his Family,

I am sir your obliged Brother & servT

J. Edwards I will hereafter send the Table mention'd in the Preface.[^170-note5]

[^170-note1]: The MS of *Misrepresentations Corrected, and Truth Vindicated*.

[^170-note2]: Nathaniel Hazzard.

[^170-note3]: Probably the draft in two quarto booklets in the Yale Collection, f. 1200-1201.

[^170-note4]: Not extant.

[^170-note5]: This postscript is written in the left margin perpendicular to the text of the letter.

## A150. Letter to Thomas Prince, July 2, 1752 150.JE-T.Prince 7-2-52

Jonathan EdwardsA150. JE to Thomas Prince, 7/2/52. MHS, John Davis Coll, 161.G.76. MS damage on first page. Addressed on back "To the / Rev. Mr. Thomas Prince / Pastor of a Chh / in Boston / To the Care of Col. Dwight / of Northampton."

Stockbridge July 2. 1752.

Rev. & honoured Sir,

We have lately heard of the death of your daughter Mrs. Mercy; and the Report seems to be credible; Tho' We have heard very little of the Circumstances: We live now at so great a distance from Boston, that we are not [at an Advantage for to seek] [^171-note1] certain & speedy Information from thence, as we used to be.

dear Sir, the dispensations of Heaven have indeed, in Some Respects, been distinguishingly afflictive toward you and your Family. So is God often wont to deal with his People before they leave the world, the Enjoyments of the world gradually leave Them, and the world, while They continue in it, is made more and more an empty Place to 'em. But your Comfort, sir, may be that in God is a Fulness that don't diminish, and is subject to no variableness, through the dark and gloomy Clouds that pass over us. I trust that God's design in thus dealing with You, is to fit you to be more and more fill'd with that Fulness, and so to bring forth more Fruit to Gods Glory in this World, and perfectly en-[^171-note2] [...]at world where [.. .] where all Tears [...] Eyes of Gods Peo[...] shall flee away; [...]ct with pious de[...]ndearment, & in Perfect & glorious Prosperity and a more perfect Enjoyment [^171-note3] of 'em than in this world; and yet such an Enjoyment as will be no Temptation to any Withdrawment of the Heart from God; but so as to draw the Heart to God, and give an Enjoyment of God in them. May God grant [that][^171-note4] this may be the Issue of your sore Afflictions, which are such as call for the Condolence of your Friends, especially such as have been laid under such special Obligations as I have been.

Please to present my most affectionate salutations to Mrs. Prince, and your only surviving Child, as from a cordially condoling Friend. I hope they will not sink under their Affliction, or give way to melancholy. My desire is that the God of all Comfort would be your & their support & Light in your darkness. --May God make me thankful for all distinguishing Mercies, which I have received in the Midst of many Troubles & difficulties which have in some Respects been distinguishing.

My wife and daughter Esther & oldest son are gone to N. Jersey, have been gone a Fortnight. My son & daughter are gone to abide there. she was married to President Burr on ye 29 of last month.

desiring a Remembrance in your Prayers I remain, dear sir

your obliged Friend

& humble servt

Jonath. Edwards.

Rev. Mr. Prince

[^171-note1]: Conjecture for MS dam. along a fold.

[^171-note2]: The bottom left-hand portion of the first page is missing.

[^171-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^171-note4]: Conjecture for MS. dam. along a fold.

## A151. Letter to John Erskine, July 7, 1752 151.JE-J.Erskine 7-7-52

Jonathan EdwardsA151. JE to John Erskine, 7/7/52. ANTS, f. 1752A, #2, C, #10.

Stockbridge July 7. 1752.

Rev. & dear Brother,

The last spring I received a Letter from you, dated at the Beginning July 17. & at the End Septem. 5. 1751. And the week before last, I received Another Letter dated Feb. 11. 1752. with a Pacquet containing Arnauld de la frequente Communion, Goodwins sermon at the Ordination of Mr. Pickering, Mr. some's sermon on the Methods for Reviving Religion, Reasons of dissent from the sentence of the general Assembly, Edwards on Christ God-man, Mr. Hartleys sermon, Parrish on the Assembly's Catechism, & dr. Gill's serm. on Isaiah 11:12.[^172-note1] I heartily thank you for these Letters & Pamphlets. Arnauld on frequent Communion will not be very profitable to me, by Reason of my not understanding the French. But several of the Rest have been very agreeable to me. That Letter which you mention in your Last, dated Feb. 11. as sent about a Twelvemonth before, containing some Remarks on the decay of the Power of the Papal Clergy, & an abstract of Venema's Reasonings, to prove that Judas was not present at the Lords supper,[^172-note2] I never received And regret it much that I miss'd of it. And request that you would still send me those Remarks on the decay of the Papal Clergy.

I am obliged to you for the particular Informations you have given me concerning Mr. Adams of Falkirk's Affair.[^172-note3] Tho' it is Pity so deserving a Person should suffer at all from his brethren, only for not acting Contrary to his Conscience; yet 'tis matter of Thankfulness that the Assembly of the year 51 shewed a so much better Temper than that of the preceding year. I shall be glad to hear concerning the Temper & Conduct of the Assembly of this present year 52.

I am sorry to hear that there is so much Reason to fear that the Revival of Religion in the Netherlands will be hindered and brought under a Cloud thro' the prevailing of Imprudences. It is what I was afraid I should hear. I should be glad to see the pastoral Letter you mention against Fanaticism, tho' written by one disaffected to the Revival. I wish I could see a History of Enthusiasm, thro' all Ages, written by some good Hand, a hearty Friend of vital Religion, a Person of accurate Judgment and large Acquaintance with Ecclesiastical History. such a History, well written, might doubtless be exceeding useful & Instructive, and of great Benefit to the Church of God ; especially if there [be] united with it a proper account and History of true Religion. let I should therefore Chuse that the work should be a History of true vital & Experimental Religion & Enthusiasm; bringing down the History from Age to Age; Judiciously & Clearly making the distinction between one and the other; observing the difference of source, Progress & Issue; In each remarka properly so pointing out the Limits, and doing Justice to each, in every Age, and in at each remarkable Period. I don't know that there is any such thing extant, or any Thing that would in any good measure answer to the same Purposes. If there be, I should be glad to hear of it.

I thank you for the Account you give me of Mr. Taylors writings, & the Things which He is doing to propagate his Opinions. It now appears to be a remarkable time in the Christian Θ world ; perhaps such an One as never has been before. Things are going down Hill so fast; Truth and Religion, both of Heart & Practice, are departing by such swift steps, that I think it must needs be, that a Crisis is not very far off. And what will then appear, I will not pretend to determine. [^172-note4]

The last week, I sent away my Answer to Mr. Williams.[^172-note5] If I live 'till it is publish'd, I will endeavour to send one to you, and some other Friends in Scotland. -I hope now, in a short Time to be at Leisure to resume my design of writing something on the Arminian Controversy. I have no Thoughts of going through with all Parts of the Controversy at once: And But the subject which I intended, God willing, first to write something upon, was Free-will & moral Agency ; endeavouring, with as much Exactness as I am able, to consider the Nature of that Freedom of moral Agents, which makes them the proper subjects of moral Government, moral Precepts, Counsels, Calls, Motives, Perswasions, Promises & Threatnings, Rewards & Punishments: strictly examining the modern Notions of those Things, endeavouring to demonstrate their most palpable Inconsistency & absurdity ; endeavouring also to bring their great Objections & Outcries against the Calvinistic divinity, from these Topics, to the strictest Reasoning. and particularly that grand Objection, in which the modern writers have so much gloried, & triumph'd, with so great a degree of Insult towards the most excellent divines, that the Calvinistic notions of Gods moral Government are contrary to the common sense of mankind. In this Essay, I propose to take particular notice of the writings of dr. Whitby & Mr. Chubb. And the writings of some others, who tho not properly Arminians Pelagians, nor Arminians ; Yet, in their Notions of the Freedom of the will, have, in the main, gone into the same Scheme. But if I live to prosecute my design, I shall send you a more particular Account of my Plan after it is perfected.

I suppose there has been a Trial before now whether a national Collection can be obtained in scotland for N. Jersey College; unless it has been thought prudent, by such as are Friends of the Affair, to put it off a year Longer; as some Things I have heard seem to argue. There was a design of Mr. Pemberton's[^172-note6] going to England and scotland. He was desired by the Trustees, and it was his settled Purpose to have gone the last year : but his People and his Colleague Mr. Cummings[^172-note7] hindred it. His Intention of going Occasioned great Uneasiness among his People, and created some diss disaffection towards Him in the minds of some of 'em. since that, President Burr has been desired to go, by the unanimous voice of the Trustees. Nevertheless, I believe there is Little Probability of his consenting to it; Partly on the Account of his having lately entred into a married state. One the 29 of last month, he was married to my third daughter.

What you write of the Appointment of a Gentleman, to be Lieut. Governour of Virginia,[^172-note8] who is a Friend of Religion, is an Event, that the Friends of Religion in America have great Reason to rejoice in : By Reason of the Late Revival of Religion in that Province, and the Opposition that has been made against it, & great endeavours to crush it, by many of [the] Chief men of thet Province. Mr. davies,[^172-note9] in a Letter I lately received from Him, dated March 2. 52. mentions the same Thing. His words are, "We have a new Governour : who is a Candid, condescending Gentleman. and as he has been educated in the Church of Scotland, has a Respect for the Presbyterians : which I hope is a happy Omen." --I was in the latter Part of the last summer, applied to with mu with much Earnestness & Importunity, to come and s by some [^172-note10] of the People of Virginia, to come and settle among Them in the work of the Ministry ; who subscribed very handsomely for my Encouragement & support. and sent a messenger to me with their Request & subscriptions.

But I was installed at stockbridge, before the messenger came. I have written some Account of the state of Things at Stockbridge to Mr. McLaurin, which you doubtless will have Opportunity to see. Northampton are still destitute of a Minister, and in broken, sorrowful Circumstances. They had the last winter One Mr. Farrand,[^172-note11] a young Gentleman from N. Jersey College : but contended much about Him, so that he has left Them. They are now in a state of Contention ; my warmest Opposers are quarrelling among Themselves. -I hear they have lately sent for a young Preacher, one Mr. Green of Barnstable,[^172-note12] who is soon expected : but I know nothing what his Character is.

Another Minister has lately been dismiss'd from his People, on the same account that I was dismiss'd from Northampton, viz. Mr. Billing of Cold-spring. Many of Cold-spring People were originally of Northampton, were educated in the same Principles, and have followed their Example of the People there.

I heartily thank you for the Account you have from Time to Time sent me of New Books, that are published in great Britain. I desire you would continue such a Favour. I am fond of knowing how Things are going on in the learned world.

Mr. John Wright, a Member of N. Jersey College who is to take the degree of Bachelor of Arts the next september, is now at my House. He was born in Scotland ; has lived in Virginia ; is a Friend and Acquaintance of Mr. davies; has a great Interest in the Esteem of the religious People of Virginia. and is peculiarly esteemed by President Burr : has been admitted to special Intimacy with Him ; and is a Person of very good Character for his Understanding, Prudence and Piety. He has a desire to have a Correspondence with some divine of his Native Countrey, and has chosen you for his Correspondent, if He may be admitted to such a favour. He intends to send you a Letter with this, of which I would ask a favourable Reception, As He has Laid me under some special Obligations.

My wife joins with me in affectionate salutations to you & Mrs. Erskine. -Hoping that there we shall continue to remember each other at the Throne of Grace, I am

dear sir,

your affectionate & obliged

Br & servt,

Jonath. Edwards.

Mr. John Erskine

## A154. Letter to Elisha Williams, August 15, 1752 153.JE-J.Willard 7-17-52

Jonathan EdwardsA154. JE to Elisha Williams, 8/15/52. BRBL, f. 1321.

To Col. Elisha Williams now in Stockbridge

Stockbridge Aug. 15. 1752.

Honoured Sir,

The more I think of it, the more I am confirmed in it,

that it will answer no good Purpose, either for the forming a

right Judgment of our Affairs, or the bringing them to an

happy Issue, to take Accounts of 'em from particular Persons,

of contrary Judgments, privately & separately. I think it is

high Time that the Affairs of Stockbridge, which have been

Matter of Misunderstanding & Controversy, should be tho-

roughly examined, even from their first Foundation, and

search'd to the very Bottom; and that it should be done here

on the spot, all Parties being Face to Face, and the Inhabi-

tants of the Town in general Present: and that this is the only me-

thod that will tend to any Good. But then I humbly conceive

that the Persons that should make this Enquiry, either as Judges

or Mediatours, should be such as may justly be looked upon

as wholly impartial, and in such Circumstances as have not a vi-

sible Tendency to bias them on one side or the other. This cer-

tainly is requisite in the nature of Things, and in Order to the

just Confidence of Persons concerned, and the Satisfaction of

the world. Now sir, I trust you will not take it as any

Reflection upon you, or any Evidence of want of due Respect,

that I Say you cannot justly be esteem'd such a Person; being

nearly related to the Family chiefly concerned in these

Controversies, and being known to have been long united

to Capt. Kellogg, in a peculiar & very intimate Friendship.

As to my Judgment on these Affairs, it is the Reverse of that

which I have Reason to think You are fix'd in. I own that

I am full in it, that for Mrs. dwight to undertake the Care

of the female boarding School will in no wise answer the [^175-note1]

design or Expectation of the society in London, with Regard

to such a school. And tho' I would maintain the utmost

Care not to injure her in any Respect, yet I think a publick

important Interest ought not to be Sacrificed for her Sake.

And I think that Capt. Kellogg's staying here, at Mr.

Hollis's Charge, while He is not in the Business that Mr. Hol-

lis appointed Him to (and for the support of which Busi-

ness alone He makes his Remittances hither) and without

any Stated visible Employment whatsoever, which has

been the Case ever since the Beginning of last February,

is a just & great offence to all Christians that observe it; And

must, if it Continues, become more a scandal in the Eyes of the

whole Countrey, and all far & near that know of it.

Now sir, if I should submit the Reasons of my Opinion &

Conduct, in these and other Things relating to our affairs,

to your Judgment, and we should give you the desired Op-

portunity to enquire into, and judge of Them our Affairs,

I have the greatest Reason to think that the Judgment you

would pass on Them, on such a Hearing, would be the Founda-

tion of a Representation You would make of Them home

to England. And you will not be offended if I think

that it concerns Me, as I regard my Reputation in the World,

that the Judgment which is made on our Affairs for such

a Purpose, should be a true and impartial one. I

have Reason to stand on my Guard in this Matter: for I

know many of your Friends here have their spirits great-

ly engaged in these Affairs, and that I am look'd on by

Them as a Person not a little obnoxious; that some of Them

have not spared my Character; that one of Them, who has

lately spent much Time with you at Weathersfield, is in Effect

no other than my open and avowed Enemy. And I have

good Evidence that another of Them has drawn up a Letter [^175-note2]

to Mr. Hollis, in which I am not a little reflected upon,

and various Things are said to my disadvantage (I

don't say this by meer Conjecture) and I have reason to

think that others are privy to the Contents of that Letter.

Therefore, I hope sir, that you will excuse me that I

wholly decline having any Hand in such an opening of

our Affairs before you as you have proposed: which I pro-

fess I don't refuse from any disrespect to you, whom I ever

desire to treat with Honour, with your excellent Consort

now with you : On the mention of whom, I cannot but renew-

edly congratulate my Self and my Countrey, on her becoming

one of its Inhabitants; as I hope she brings no small degree

of the Blessing of Heaven into N. England with her.

But that the good End which you propose by enquiring

into our Affairs may not fail of being obtain'd, with the

best Advantage, I would now humbly make you this of-

fer; viz To join with you in an earnest Application to

the Body of the Commissioners, that They would appoint a

Committee, to come on the spot, and make thorough En-

quiry into our present difficulties, and the management

of Stockbridge Affairs, from the very Beginning, by all the living

Inhabitants or Residents in the Town that have had any

Hand in Them in any Respect. In which Case, I am ready

to promise freely to open my self, and declare openly the Rea-

sons of my Judgment concerning the Affairs of the two board-

ing Schools, and give all the Light in the State of our Af-

fairs, in every Respect, that lies in my Power. And it shall

be no Objection, if you are present, & hear all that is

said. I am willing that all Affairs should be determin'd

and settled by the Judgment of such a Committee, &

that

the Commissioners should make such a Representation [^175-note3]

to England, as they think proper, on their Report.

This with the most cordial Respects to Madam

is, honoured sir, from

your respectful &

most humble servt

J. Edwards.

## A155. Letter to Elisha Williams, August 18, 1752 155.JE-E.Williams 8-18-52

Jonathan EdwardsA155. JE to Elisha Williams, 8/18/52. BRBL, f. 1322. MS copy at RIHS, ms. 1129.

To Col. Elisha Williams now in Stockbridge

Stockbridge Aug. 18. 1752.

Honoured sir,

An Indian lately pick'd up a Letter in the street, directed to me,

not knowing what, nor from whom it was. However, it is come to my

Hands. I have had some doubt in my Mind whether I had any

Right to it, coming to Me in such a manner: for it seems it went out of

the Hands of the Possessour of it accidentally, & not designedly. However,

seeing it inscribed to me, I open'd it, and found it a Letter from you; and

presuming You intended I should have it, I would now make some Reply

to it.

In the Beginning of your Letter, you speak of an Interview with Col. d--t,

your Uncle, and Captain K--gg, in your Presence, as what I my self had

mention'd. In which you seem to have taken the Matter very wrong.

When you mention'd the Misunderstandings here subsisting, and de-

sired some Account from Me of them, I Signified as much, as that if I

did at any Time give an Account, I should chuse that all Parties concerned

in these Misunderstandings should be Face [to][^176-note1] Face: but mention'd the

Name of no one Person: much less did I single out these Names; which

would have been to exclude others concerned in our Controversies. And I spake

of the Thing in general, and not as being at this Time, or in any parti-

cular Persons Presence. But it was you sir, that did this in your Reply,

as near as I can remember, in these Words, Well, why can't that be

now? After taking the matter into Consideration, I have given you my

Reasons why I think it is not best to be done now as a Judge or Media-

tour. You seem to think yourself injured; and particularly in my not

giving you the Reasons why I think it will not answer the design and

Expectation of the society for Mrs dwight to undertake the Care of the fe-

male school ; And are pleas'd in your Letter to tell Me once and again,

That you have a Right to know my Reasons, and therefore that you in-

sist on my giving you the Reason why I Judge &c. To which I

would say, If you are truly vested with this high Authority, I was not

aware of it; And therefore, if I have erred in not submitting to you

in this Manner, I have transgressed ignorantly. However, I am willing

to be informed, if I have had mistaken Notions concerning the Com-

mon Rights of mankind, as well as ignorant of the extent of your

Commission. I should think it might be a Matter of doubt whether

the society themselves have so great Authority. If they should de-

sire to know my sentimts concerning such an Affair, and I in Compli-

ance with their desire should tell Them my Judgment, then to insist

on my Reasons as what They have a Right to demand, not allowing

me to judge for my self whether it be best to suppress Them, but to de-

termine for me that I can have no sufficient Reason for my silence.

Without doubt the society would have a Right to pay as little Regard

as They please to my Judgment, and as much less as They please for

my not giving the Reasons of it, and to establish a mistress & maintain

any one Person They think best in the school, without Regard to my

Judgment. But this will by no means amount to a Power to demand

the secrets of my Heart in this matter; which for ought They know

I have good Reason to conceal. ---- But whatever Power of this [^176-note2]

Kind the society has, I suppose They have committed it to no single Person

in America. It is known that there is a Body of Commissioners, to whom they

have committed their Authority in many Respects; who are able to exercise

it, acting jointly, but not singly. If they have committed their Authority

to any Single Person, acting alone, in any particular Affair, in that Affair

they have made Him their sole Commissioner. And if there be any such

Commissioner in the Affair of establishing a Mistress of the female school,

who therefore has Power to demand and judge of all Reasons pro & Con

in this Affair, I may be excused for not supposing it in my Conduct hitherto,

the Commission not having been publish'd, or at least not made known to

me. I have acted according to the best Light and Information I have had.

I know not who to look to for directions, with regard to my duty in my

present Station here, but (under Christ) to the Body of Commissioners that

have introduced me into it; who have signified to me that I am to receive

my directions from Them, and am accountable only to them, and not to

[be][^176-note3] dictated to by any here. I trust that They that sent Me hither are able

to inform me to whom I am accountable Therefore 'till Ihave further

Instructions I shall act accordingly better than others that are compara-

tively strangers to our Affairs. And therefore, 'till I have further Instruc-

tions, I shall act accordingly. To them I refer my self; to them I am rea-

dy to give my Reasons &c. at any Time when They shall ask for

Them. To their Judgment I refer all our difficulties and misunder-

standings so far as I have any Concern in Them; and so far as I have no

Concern in Them, I am willing to let Them alone. If our Affairs are re-

presented before any in Order to our receiving the Benefit of their wisdom, friend-

ly Interposition, and Mediation, in the Manner you proposed to have our

Affairs represented before you, I think They are the properest Persons,

much more suitable than a single Gentleman, nearly related to the Fa-

mily that from the Beginning have been chiefly interested in the lamen-

table Controversies which have been the Bane of the indian affairs.

With Respect to those that They employ, They may act authoritatively;

and as to others, let 'em hear our Affairs as you proposed to hear 'em.

I can see no more difficulty in their representing Affairs before Them for

their Advice and friendly Mediation, than in all Parties representing

Affairs before you for such a Purpose, which you proposed, and Seem'd to

think there was no difficulty in the Way of. To insist on this Objecti-

on of Some Persons concerned not being under the Authority of the Com-

missioners, will be in Effect to insist that none shall ever come hither,

either to judge or advise, or in any Respect to take knowledge of our

Affairs, to use their wisdom to put an End to our Confusions, because all the

Controverting Parties are not subject to the same Constituents.

As an Objection against my giving my Reasons, why I think it would not

answer the end for Mrs. dwight to be the Mistress of the school, before

a Committee appointed by the Commissioners, You suppose that this

would be to endeavour in an open Manner to hurt her Reputation.

To which I would say; It will be Time enough to mention & consider [^176-note4]

the Objection, when it is known that my Reasons are taken from Things that

would be to her Reproach. And if that be supposed to be the Tendency of an

open Hearing before some of the Commissioners, then I would humbly en-

quire, why you thought well of such an open Hearing now, [-] all Misunder-

standing Parties being present, while You are in Town? Certainly you could

not reasonably think all the misunderstanding Parties, better Friends to Mrs.

dwight than the Commissioners.

I mention'd some Things as Reasons why I should stand on my Guard.

you are pleased to speak of these Things as groundless surmises and Jealousies,

tho' I told you expressly I did not speak by Conjecture. It will be no

affront to you sir, that I say, that I understand the Affairs of Stockbridge

better than you can do. ---- And besides those Things that I mention'd

concerning your Friends, I might have added that even as to your

Self, I have, at least, some Reason to suspect that your Nind had been

So prepossess'd and prejudiced by means of Them, or by some other means,

that you did not come to Town with a Nind altogether calm and friendly

towards me and my Family, from your Treatment of my wife, at your

first coming to my House, in my Absence, after your having been so long

absent from N. England; When, as one of the first Complements, you did

in Effect peremptorily give her the Lie, in telling her before all the Company,

on he saying something which she doubtless supposed to be Fact

with an assured Air, that she knew better, on her saying something

which she doubtless supposed to be Fact, & wherein she asserted Nothing

injurious to you, and tho' she treated you, after her known manner, with

all possible Respect. Certainly this was charging Ger with asserting con-

trary to her own knowledge. I don't mention this because I desire to lay

it up against you, but as one Thing that will justify my Caution. And

for this Reason did I mention what has appear'd in the Temper of some

of your Friends towards Me. I have no disposition to any Thing else

but Peace and Friendship with Them. This I have sought hitherto

and this I am resolved to pursue hereafter, so long as there can be any

Hopes of it. Tho' I don't think our Meeting to represent the Grounds of

our Misunderstanding before you as a Mediatour, would be a proper

Expedient in Order to it. Indeed I need no Mediatour as to my own Part.

I am already fully disposed to Peace. I require no humble Confessions or low-

ly submissions, and insist on no Terms with Them, but only that henceforth

They don't act the inimical Part. As to your Kinsman, tho' it be a Mat-

ter of plain & known Fact, that He freely & openly, and without Re-

straint or Reserve, declares by words & Actions, his disesteem & great dis-

like of Me, and his Resolution to injure my Character, and this with-

out my ever having injured Him in the least degree; Yet I have not the

least disposition to be his Enemy, or to lay up any of these Things a-

gainst Him, but am ready freely to forgive him, & desire to live in Peace

with Him, and bury every Thing in Oblivion from this day forward:

And there has been no day wherein this has not been my disposition.

I utterly disclaim proceeding on the Foot of personal Resentment in these Af-

or any delight in Forbearing to comply with others desires. I wish with all

my Heart that all such Principles of acting, and all selfish Principles

whatsoever, were utterly & forever banish'd from Stockbridge; which

must necessarily be very provoking to God, and pernicious to the great [^176-note5]

design of enlarging the Kingdom of Christ here. If I know my own

Heart, I have for more than thirty years, set my Heart on the Ad-

vancement & enlargement of Christ's Kingdom on Earth, as a King-

dom of Light, Love and Peace, and have preferred these Things to

my chief Joy. If I am influenced, in any Thing I do, from Prin-

ciples contrary to these, my earnest Prayer to God, the searcher of

Hearts, is, that God would cleanse me from such secret Faults.

I remain sir, with all due respect,

your most humble servant,

J. Edwards.

[2. Second draft.]

To speaker Hubbard

Stockbridge Aug. 29. 1752.

Sir

The special End of my Writing to your Honour at this Time is humbly

to propose to you that you would use your Influence that deac. Wood

bridge may be added to the general Courts Committee for the taking Care of

the Mohawk Affair in this Place. Probably you will not wonder that

I should propose it, when you have understood the present State of Things

here, by which the necessity of it appears. I informed you something of the

Calamities which attend the Mohawk affair in my Letter of last spring;

which, as I then Signified, were owing very much to the affairs falling almost

entirely into the Hands of one man, who was entring into a strict Alliance

with Col. Williams's Family, by his Engagements with his daughter

Mrs. Sergeant, & who was almost constantly here, while the rest of the

Committee kept at a distance. Our Confusions continue, and grow worse &

worse, and from the same Cause. Col. dwight takes up his Constant

Abode here; and as we are informed was lately married to Mrs. Ser-

geant, and so is now become Col. Williams's son in Law, and appears in

all Respects to be strongly engaged attached to and engaged with that Fa-

mily. He claims, and has used a sort of sovereign arbitrary Power here

with Regard to the Mohawks, and both the boarding schools. He utterly

denies all Authority of the Commissrs in these Affairs, and says all is in the

Hands of the general Courts Committee; and that He only of the Commit-

tee being resident here, it must be look'd upon that They leave affairs

with Him. Accordingly, he has done many Things of Consequence of his own

Head, and according to his own Pleasure, without the voice of either of

the other Gentlemen of the Comttee since the Comttee were first ap-

pointed. And almost every Thing has been done in an exceeding un-

happy Manner. He of his own Head Instead of building two school

Houses, agreable to the vote of the Assembly, has framed two large

Houses with various Apartments, each of which will doubtless cost as

much as three school-Houses : For what Purpose, I know not. The state

of things is apparently such, as makes it very doubtful whether we

shall have any Occasion for for so much as school-House for the Mo-

hawks any where in N. England ; And if any where, probably not here,

but at the Hoplands. I think the Case required the mature Conside-

ration of the Committee [ ] first [ ] most Part before the Founda-

tion of any school House, school House or other House, had been laid,

and it should been Enquired of the Indians, whether, if They settled

in the Hoplands, They would be willing their Children should be

at school here. For I think there is little probability of this. The

Col. has determined the Place, as well as the Form of these Houses by

Himself alone[^178-note11] if I am rightly informed. He has of his own Head in

I think in a very precipitant Manner framed a large House for a

female boarding school, on his wifes Home lot, near her House; when

it remains yet undet undetermin'd whether she shall be the settled mis-

tress, and when indeed there is not the least Prospect of her ever having

a school. One would think They have made Trial enough to Convince them

that the Indians,[^178-note12] both stockbridge Indians & Mohawks, have such a Preju-

dice against her, that They will not let her have their Children. The

House is framed big enough, not only for a school-House, but to entertain &

Lodge all the schollars. Tho' the society in London granted 10L sterl. to

prepare her House for their Entertainment & Lodging. That House has [^178-note13]

been lately finish'd in a pretty sumptuous manner ; but not with Lodgings

for Indian Girls. But He nevertheless expects the 10£ Sterl. to help defray

the Charge of it.  He in the winter, of his own Head sent for some of

the Chiefs of the Mohawks to come hither from their own Countrey. And

sent for Capt. Jos. Kellogg of Suffield in Order to a Treaty with Them: which

Treaty He managed by Himself alone. And the chief Business of it

was to know what we should do to secure the six Nations in the Brit-

ish Interest : than which no Business could have been devised more un-

happy for m our great & important Affairs with them in this Place.

For they are exceeding apt to suspect, that in all we do for them, we

act from any Kindness to them, but from a Regard only to our own Inte-

rest, & because we need their Help. Which they have often express'd

since they have been here. I have laboured much to Convince 'em

that in this Affair we evidently acted the Part of Friends to them

& sought their real & best Interest : and They seem'd in some measure

convinced ; but such a Treaty as this, in the boarding school here,

By one They supposed acted & spoke in the Name of the Countrey,

tended fully to establish Them in their former suspicion, and so to de-

feat our own designs. The Col. singly, & according to his own dis-

cretion distributed the 200L O. T. the general Court granted in the

winter, to Onoh-quaugas, who were newly arrived ; not all to them:

but some to them, and some to the Chiefs of the Mohawks, in such

a manner as did more to create uneasiness among Them, so far as

I could learn, than to gain their Affections. And so far as it was used

to the last-mentioned Purpose, it was to gain their Affections to Him-

self, and to establish his own Interest with Them, & not to excite their

Gratitude to the Government, if the Onohquaugas understood Him

right, & speak true. For they all (i. e all their Heads of Families)

with one voice declared to me, that He deliver'd the Present to Them

in his own name, & as his own Kindness to 'em ; That He said to 'em

that He had gathered up a little in one Place, and a little in ano-

ther, till He had got so much for them, which He now gave them.

The Col. of his own Head did also again send for Capt. Jos. Kellogg,

& kept Him here about 10 weeks in the spring & summer,

without any visible Business & Employ whatsoever : And as to his

secret Business we can but Guess at no that. And many other

Things have been done of great Consequence, and which have had

a most unhappy Influence without the voice of the Rest of the

Comttee, if Capt Ashley may be credited. 'Tis Apparent that

this Affair cannot prosper under his Hands, if it be should [-] conti

nue to under his Management as it has been. And indeed it is

already brought to the very brink of Ruin, and will soon be past

Recovery, and all the Cost the Countrey & Commissrs will be lost

if there ben't some Alteration. He is The Col. is too sanguine & self-

sufficient & Confident in his too hasty & precipitant in his measures, too

unsteady, of too passionate & fiery a Temper, which tends to keep every

Thing in a Ruffle and Tumult ; Too sovereign & arbitrary. He He is

not of a disposition at a and manner that at all suits Indians, who don't

seem at all pleased with Him, but have shewn much of the contrary.

They dont Love a man of his sovereign & forbidding Airs, nor have

They at all liked his Conduct. Tho' he has taken Pains to gain an ascendant [^178-note14]

in their Esteem : He is of a very suspicious, Jealous temper; which was remarka

bly the Temper of the Family at Northampton, which He came from on

the mothers side. And He is too uxorious ; & has had too many Things

in view for the promoting his private Interest in the management of

our affair, to Consist with his being so free of Temptation, as those ought

to be who have the management of stockbridge Affairs.  He expec

His wife expects the salary of 30L sterling as Mistress of the Girls school, without

immediately doing the Business of a school-mistress, as she has manifested to

me : And whether the mistress under her was to be one of the Family

I cannot tell. Two of their Children They expect should be both boarded

& educated at the Countreys Charge. And He has had it in view, not only

to be a Comttee-man (and so chief manager of all affairs) But also steward

of both boarding schools, as He has signified to me ; which would have

been a great Profit to Him, as a shopkeeper & otherwise, besides what He would

Expect from the Countrey, as the Reward of his services. He had a design

that his son should be master of the male-boarding school, and actually

Sent Him up from Brookfield to stockbridge for that End, with a Letter

to me, desiring me to introduce Him into the school, tho' it was only un-

der the Pretence of a necessary present supply. I leave t it to others to Judge

whether He would not have been for continuing Him if he had been

introduced. But it happen'd, that before his son came, I had a Letter

from the Commissrs, to send for Mr. Hawley. so that his son was forced

to go back again. He has also had a Scheme for the getting Mr. Hol-

lis'S moneys into his own Pocket. Capt. Kellogg told Mr. Hawley in

the spring, that it was proposed that He should resign Mr. Hollis's

Affair into the Cols Hands, when things were ripe for it, or to that

Purpose. I suppose the design was, That He was to have the Care

of Mr. Hollis's Boys, and would see that they should be instructed

by his son, and would Himself take Care of 'em as steward, and so draw

the Pay for the whole. Besides his wife had a design, that the

Farm her House stands upon should be bought by the Countrey, for a

School Lot, for the female school (for she signified this to me)

And so they would have had the Advantage of selling it for good

Pay, & a good Price, and yet still to have lived upon it, & upon the

Incomes of it, as Officers concerned in the Business of the School ; and

the Family & the school being blended, the Provision of the school

would have been their Provision, And the servants of the school

to take Care of the School Farm, would have been their servants.

Besides all these Things, the Brigadier has had it in his Mind (as

He intimated to me) to turn the Channel of the Kings Bounty of 500£

sterl. to the six Nations, from going by the way of N. York. He did

not say that He intended it should come thro' stockbridge, and through

his Hands, as chi the resident Agent for the Government, and be dealt

forth to the Indians, out of his shop. -- If all these things could

have been brought to bear, the Profit to Him & his Family would

have been great indeed.

In the Course Things are now in, every Thing is going into such a Channel,

and forming into such a shape, as tends to establish a dominion of the Family

of the Williams' over stockbridge Affairs, and bring all Things in a great

measure into their Hands ; As tis apparent that this is what they are ea- [^178-note15]

gerly grasping at : By their natural disposition they are sufficiently apt to assume

& engross all Power Profit & Honour to Themselves. Col. W--ms of

Weathersfield, since his Arrival has been very busy about our Affairs.

Has been abundantly resorted to by his Friends in stockbridge : He has

lately spent near a Fortnight here ; and assumed more to Himself than

I thought He had a Right to do, in demanding Accounts concerning our af-

fairs.

These things shew the Necessity of some other Committee man, that

shall be resident here, and have a hand in the management of Af-

fairs, besides Col. dwight, for the Family of the Williams's for his Coun-

sil. Tis apparent the other Gentlemen of the Committee don't In-

cline to have any Thing to do with Col. dwight, without greater strength

on their side. Col. Pynchon has not been here since last October : &

I have [ ] the Re I have Reason to think the Cause is, He don't like

such a Companion in the Committee. And Capt. Ashley has said to me

several Times, that He don't care to have any Thing to do, without Col.

Pynchon. I know Col. P. would rejoyce to be Join'd in Commission with

Mr. Woodbridge. The Latter is a Person well capable of the Business, and

in some Respects better than any man in N. England ; for He has more than al

most any man in these western Parts of New-England, been acquainted with In-

dians, and has demonstrated that He has great Skill in managing Them,

by the vast Ascendant He has gain'd and constantly maintains over them. And

He has certainly the Character of strict Integrity, among all that have been

longest acquainted with Him. That He has no disposition to lay schemes

for his private Interest to the Prejudice of the Indians, He has demonstrated

by the best Proof, viz. long Trial. He has had the fairest Opportunities to

have made an Estate by the Indians, of any man in these Parts, But He

has not taken his Opportunities ; but on the Contrary, has often given up his

own Interest for their sakes. Much has been said against But if Reports

should be followed, all would probably [be] found to come from one Family to

whom He has been obnoxious ; as standing in the way of their particular

designs. He is known to be a Gentleman of good discerning, and there is no

great danger of his being wheedled, and made a dupe or Tool by such as

craftily built up Themselves on the Ruin of publick designs. Col. Pynchon is

acquainted with Him, & knows his Character. I would propose to your Honour

to discourse with Him about the Matter. Perhaps adding deac. W--ge to

the Comittee is the only Expedient that is feasable for the delivering stock-

bridge Affairs from present dreadful Embarrassments. It may be none will care

to move that Col. d. should be turned out ; But if Mr. W--ge is added,

it may be as effectual a Relief as if the other were dismiss'd. Then Col. P. &

Capt. A. will be encouraged to come to Stockbridge, & be active in the Busi-

ness of the Comttee : And in all Probability the Brigr will soon dismiss Himself

& have no more concern in the Business. But if we have no Redress at all, 'tis

past all doubt, the Mohawk Affair will soon be past Recovery.

I leave it to your Honour to make use of this Letter, as your Wisdom shall di-

rect. I asking your candid Interpretation of the Freedom I have used in

this Case of Extremity. ---- My wife joins with me in most respectful &

affectionate Salutations to you Madam & your Family. - I am

Honoured sir,

your obliged & most humble servt

Jonathan Edwards.

_____________________________________

P.S. Tho Capt. Ashley in talk with

me in a variety of Expressions signified

that the Building the female school house

on the Hill was against his mind, and that

He should never consent to it, yet I hear since

he has own'd He did Consent. -- Possibly it

may prove so concerning some other things. This I

observe that I may in nothing injure the Brigadier.

Octob. 14.

_________________________________________

The Honble Tho. Hubbard Esq.
