## A159. Letter to John Erskine, November 11, 1752 159.JE-J.Erskine 11-23-52

Jonathan EdwardsA159. JE to John Erskine, 11/23/52. ANTS, f. 1752D, #1-2.

Stockbridge Novem. 23 N. S. 1752.

Rev. & dear Brother,

In August last I wrote to you,[^182-note1] and sent away the Letter (with

Letters to some of my other Correspondents) to Boston, to be conveyed to

scotland. Therein I acknowledged the Receipt of two Letters from you,

one of July 17 -51, Another of Feb. 11. 52; with the Pamphlets sent

with the last Letter. And now acknowledge the Receipt of another

Letter from you of May 13. 52. and the Pamphlets you sent with the

Last. The Letter I received the latter End of september: the Pamphlets

I did not receive till very Lately: they were forgotten by Mr. Prince.

stinstra against Fanaticism[^182-note2] I shall have no Benefit by, because I am

not acquainted with the French Language. What the Jewish Con-

vert has publish'd of his Conversion[^182-note3] &c. is very agreeable. And I now

heartily thank you for this Letter and Pacquet. I am very glad to

see what you write Concerning the state of Religion in the Nether-

lands. But I believe there is more of a mixture of what is bad

with the Good that appears in that Land than Mr. Kennedy, & many

other ministers there, are aware of; and that they will find that

the Consequence of their not Carefully & Critically distinguishing

between the good and the bad, and guarding with the utmost Cau

Caution and diligence against the Latter, wi will prove worse

than they now Conceive of. By your 'tis now Exactly with

Mr. Kennedy, as it was with many pious ministers in America

in the time of the great Religious moving here. They looked upon cri-

tical Enquiries into the difference tr between true grace and its Coun-

terfeits, or at least [-] a being very busy in such Enquiries, & spending

Time in them, to be Impertinent & unseasonable, tending rather to

damp the work of the spirit of God than promote it, diverting

their own minds, & the minds of others, as they supposed, God at

such an extraordinary Time did loudly call 'em more especially to

attend. The The cry was, "O, there is no danger, if we are but

lively in Religion, & full of Gods spirit, and live by faith, of being

misled. If we do but follow God, there is no danger of being

Led wrong. 'Tis the cold, carnal & [-] lifeless that are most

likely to be blind & walk in darkness. Let us press forward

& not stay & hinder the good work, by standing & spending

Time in these Criticisms & Carnal Reasonings! &c &c!["]

This was the Language of many, till they ran on deep into

the wilderness, and were taught by the briars & thorns of the

wilderness. However, tis no wonder that divines in Europe will

not lay very much weight on the admonitions They receive from

so obscure a Part of the world. Other Parts of the Church of

God must be taught as we have been; and when they see &

feel them, they will believe. Not that I apprehend there

is in any measure so much Enthusiasm & disorder mixed with

the work in Holland, as was in many Parts of America, in

the Time of the late Revival of Religion here. But yet I

believe the work must be more pure, and the People more thorough- [^182-note4]

ly guarded from him his wiles, who beguiled Eve through his subtil-

ty, & corrupts the minds of zealous People from the simplicity that

is in Christ, before the work goes on to a general Conquest,

and is maintain'd in its Power & Glory for a great Length of Time.

But God will have his own -- who being his Counsellor hath taught

Him? We must expecti expect confusion & uproar before we have that Abun-

dance of Peace & Truth which the scripture speaks of. Many

must run to and fro, & Knowledge will be increased.

The dutch Ministers in America, which you speak of, which I have

Acquaintance with, are some of the Younger Ministers, & such as were

born in America (tho' several of them have had Part of their

Education in Holland). I have not Acquaintance enough with Them to

know their sentiments particulary about those corrupt mixtures above

mention'd, and the Care which is to be used in guarding against

Them. However, 'tis not very likely, if some of them should write to

their Brethren in Holland, that their Letters would have more In-

fluence upon Them than Letters from you, and some others of the Mi-

nisters of scotland. Nevertheless, there is a Prospect that there will in

Time be very happy Effects of the growing Acquaintance and Uni-

on there is between a very considerable number of very hopeful

& pious dutch Ministers in the Provinces of N. York & N. Jersey,

& many English & scotch ministers in America. The number of

well disposed dutch ministers in those Provinces has of late remarka-

bly increased: so that I think when they meet together in their Cœtus,

They make the major Part. some of the Elder ministers seem to be

of quite contrary sentiments and dispositions, not appearing friendly

as the other, to what They esteem the Power of Religion, nor approv-

ing of awakening, searching, strict & experimental Preaching; which

has occasion'd various Contests among Them. However, the stricter

sort, being the prevailing Part, are like to carry the day. The dutch

Churches in these Provinces have hitherto been so dependent on the

Classes in Holland, that whenever any among Them we have

been Educated for the ministry, among them, Th and any Churches

have been desirous of their Administrations, They could not receive

their Orders on this side of the water, but have been obliged to go

to Holland for Ordination: which has been a great Incumbrance

that has attended the settlement of ministers among Them, and has

undoubtedly been one Occasion of such multitudes of the Dutch, living

wholly without ministers. Application was made not long since,

through the Influence of the foremention'd serious younger ministers

to (as I take it) by the Cœtus here for their Consent, that they might

unite themselves to the synod of N. York, which now consists

of English & scotch. But the success of their Application was pre-

vented by a Letter written by one of their elder Ministers, re-

monstrating against it, & rep very falsely representing the N. York

synod, as no proper Presbyterian synod, but a Com rather a Com-

pany of Independents. On which, the Classis of Holland advised

Them by no means to unite Themselves with that synod.

The last september I went a Journey into N- Jersey and had op- [^182-note5]

portunity in my Journey of seeing some of these younger dutch mi-

nisters, and conversing with them on this subject. They seem

resolved by some means or other to disengage Themselves and their

Churches from the foremention'd great Incumbrance of being obliged

to cross the Ocean for the Ordination of every minister. I was much

gratified, during the little Opportunity I had, to observe the agreeable

disposition of these ministers. -- There were also many other Things

I had Opportunity to observe in those Parts which were very agreeable.

I was there at the Time of the publick Commencement in the College,

and the Time of the meeting of the Trustees of the College, the

Time of the meeting of the N. York syn Correspondents of the

society for propagating Christian Knowledge, and the time of

the meeting of the N. York synod. so that I had Opportunity to

converse with ministers from Long-Island, N- York, N- Jersey, Penn-

sylvania and Virginia. The College is in flourishing Circumstan-

ces; increases apace; and is happily regulated. The Trustees seemed en-

gaged to their utmost to promote Learning, vertue and true Religi-

on in it; & none more than Governour Belcher; who is the

President of the Trustees, and was at the Commencement & Trus-

tees meeting. But they very much want further supplies for

the convenient support of the College. --- I had considerable Op-

portunity with Gov. Belcher; was several Times at his House at

Elizabeth-Town. He labours under many of the Infirmities of

Age, but savours much of a spirit of Religion, and seems very

desirous of doing all the good He can while he lives. The New

York synod is in flourishing Circumstances : much more so than

the Philadelphia synod. They have the greatest Body of Ministers

now, and increase much more faster They are in higher Credit

with the people in almost all Parts, and are chiefly sought to for

supplies by destitute Congregations. With Respect to the Proceed-

ings of the Correspondents, They have dismiss'd Mr. Horton from his

mission on Long-Island,[^182-note6] and He is about to settle in a Congregation

in N- Jersey. He was dismissed by Reason of his very much failing

of Employ: in his Business many of the Clans of Indians He used to

preach to having dwindled away by death or dispersion, and there [being] [^182-note7]

but little Prospect of success among others that remain, and some

being so situated that they may conveniently ta be taken Care of

by other Ministers. The Correspondents have it in their view

to improve the money by which He used to be supported, to sup-

port a Mission among the six Nations, after they have found a

suitable Person to undertake the Business of such a mission, and he

is fitted for it by learning the Language. They used endeavours

to obtain a suitable Person for the Purpose in N. Jersey. But meeting [^182-note8]

with no success, They voted to impower Mr. Bellamy, Mr. Hopkins

of Sheffield, and myself, to procure a suitable Person (if to be we

can find such an one) in N. England, for the present to come and live

at stockbridge, to be here learning the Mohawk Language with

Mr. Hawley, our school-master for the Mohawks, to fit Him

for this Mission. Persons proper to be employed, and such as may

be obtain'd are very scarce; and 'tis doubtful whether we shall be

able to obtain one.

There is a very dark Cloud that at present attends the Affair, relating to

the Indians at stockbridge, occasion'd very much by the some of the gene-

ral Court's Committee (at least the Chief of them, who is a Gentleman that

has lately married Mrs. Sergeant, & has removed and lives at stockbridge)

pursuing measures very contrary to the measures of the Commissioners of

the society in London. The Opposition is maintain'd, not with a small degree

of stiffness & Resolution; and the Contest is become so great that it has brought

Things into very great Confusion. The foresaid Gentleman is a man of some

Note; and his wife's Relations earnestly engage with Him; & have & th

& many of these are Persons of considerable Figure in the Countrey. The

Commissioners all very much dislike this Gentlemans Conduct. This Contest

occasions no misunderstandings among the People in Stockbridge & in Gene-

ral ; all, excepting those nearly Related to that Family, are ha both

English & Indians, are happily united to me and my Family. To

It would be very tedious for me to write, and for you to read all the

particulars of this uncomfortable affair, and the more undesirable as

it would tend to hurt the Reputation of some Persons. The Commissio-

ners are exerting Themselves to relieve us of this Calamity, and it is

probable They will be successful.

I thank you for the Account you give of some valuable Books pub-

lish'd : I desire you would continue to favour me in this manner. ----

I began the last August to write a little on the Arminian Controversy,

but was soon broke off; and such have been my extraordinary Avoca-

tions & Hindrances, that have not had time to set pen to Paper about

this matter since. But I hope God in his Providence will favour me with

Opportunity to prosecute this design : and I desire your Prayers that God

would assist me in it, and in all the work I am called to, and enable

me to conduct myself to his glory & acceptance under all difficulties

& Trials. ---- My wife joins with me in most hearty & affectio-

nate salutations to you & Mrs. Erskine. I am, dear sir,

your most affectionate & obliged Br. & servt

Jonathan Edwards.

P.S. I propose with this to send you Mr.

Hobarts second Address to the members of the Episco-

pal separation in N. England, & my Answer to

Mr. Williams,[^182-note9] which I would desire you to give

your neighbours, my Correspondents, opportunity to

read if they desire it.

Mr. John Erskine

[^182-note1]: JE's letter was dated July 7, 1752, at the beginning, July 24 at the close, and may not have been carried to Boston before August.

[^182-note2]: Johannes Stinstra, *Lettre Pastorale, contre le Fanatisme* (Leiden, 1752).

[^182-note3]: No information on this publication has been found.

[^182-note4]: **marginal.** [2]

[^182-note5]: **marginal.** [3]

[^182-note6]: Azariah Horton (1715-1777), missionary to the Shinnecock Indians at Southampton, L.I., N.Y., who settled at Madison, N.J., in 1752.

[^182-note7]: **marginal.** [JE om.]

[^182-note8]: **marginal.** [4]

[^182-note9]: Noah Hobart, *A second address to the members of the Episcopal Separation in New-England* (Boston, 1751), and JE, *Misrepresentations Corrected*.

## A160. Letter to William McCulloch, November 24, 1752 160.JE-W.McCulloch11-24-52

Jonathan EdwardsA160. JE to William McCulloch, 11/24/52. ANTS, f. 1752F, #1-2.

Stockbridge Novem. 24 N.S. 1752.

Rev. & dear Sir,

I thank you for your Letter of March 3. 1752.[^183-note1] which I re-

ceived this Fall. I thank you for your friendly & instructive

Observations on Gods dealings with me and my Family.

Tho' God's dispensations towards us have been attended with some

distinguishing Trials, yet the End of the Lord has been very

gracious. He has ever manifested Himself very pitiful and of ten-

der mercy, in the midst of difficulties we have met with, in mer-

ciful Circumstances which They have been attended with, &

also in the Event of them. Our Circumstances here at Stock-

bridge are in many Respects comfortable ; we here live in

Peace and Friendship with the generality of the People : But

we are not without our difficulties & Troubles here. The Indian

Affair, which the last year was attended with so pleasing

& glorious a Prospect has since been unspeakeably embarrassed,

through the Particular schemes of some great men that have

had concern, who are divided and opposite in their Coun-

sels & measures from the Commissioners of the society in Lon-

don, and so are to their utmost striving to accomplish their

designs in Opposition to Them, and in this great Contest I

am looked on as a Person not a little obnoxious. There are

some of a certain Family of note, who vigorously abetted &

set forward my Opposers at Northampton, and were a

Chief Occasion of my Removal from that Town. to whom my

settlement at Stockbridge was very grievous, who now take

Oc Occasion to exert themselves to their utmost to weaken

my Interest & Influence : and I have all Reason to think,

would if it were possible undermine me, and procure my

removal far hence. Many Endeavours have been used

to disaffect my People towards me ; but all in vain ; They

are all firmly united to me, excepting a few who are of the [^183-note2]

forementioned Family, or nearly related to 'em. Endeavours

have been used also to disaffect some of the Commissioners,

but wholly in vain : They seem to have their Eyes very

wide open, t as to their particular designs & schemes,

& the true springs of their Opposition. We hope for

an End to this lamentable Contest before long : But it's

Effects hitherto have been very sorrowful, especially with Re-

gard to the Affair of the Mohawks. Some other Things have

happen'd which have much prejudiced the Cause of Religion

among the Indians parti and among other Things, the

late discovery of the famous Tartarian Root, described in

Chambers's dictionary,[^183-note3] called Ginseng : which was

found in our woods the last summer, and is since found

in the woods in many of these Western Parts of New-En-

gland & in the Countrey of the six Nations. The Traders

in Albany have been eager to purchase all that They

could of this Root to send to England, where They make

great Profit by it. This has Occasion'd our Indians of all

sorts, young & old, to spend abundance of Time in wandring

about the woods and sometimes to a great distance

in the neglect of the publick worship and of their Hus-

bandry; and also of their going much to Albany to all

which proves worse to them than their going into the woods,

to sell their Roots : where They are alwaies much in

the way of Temptation to drunkenness, especially when

They have money in their Pockets. The Consequence

has been, that many of Them have Laid out their

Money, which They have got for their Roots of Gin-

seng, for Rum, wherewith They have intoxicated them-

selves.

God has been very gracious to my Family of late, when some [^183-note4]

of them have been visited with sore sickness. My Wife

has lately been very dangerously sick, seemed to be brought

to the very Brink of the Grave, had very little Expecta-

tion of Life ; but seemed to be assisted to an unmoved Resig-

nation to the will of God, & unshaken Peace & Joy in

God, in the Expectation of a speedy departure. But God

was pleased to preserve Her, & mercifully to restore her to

a pretty good state of Health. My youngest daughter[^183-note5]

also (who has ever been a very infirm child) was brought

nigh unto death by a sore fit of sickness : but is now also

restored to her former state. My daughter Pas Parsons,[^183-note6]

my eldest daughter who with her Husband has removed

from Northampton and dwells in stockbridge, has also very

lately been very sick, but is in considerable measure restored.

My daughter Esther's marriage with President Burr,

of Newark, seems to be very much to the satisfaction

of Ministers & People in those and also our Friends

in Boston, & other Parts of N. England.

As to the State of Religion in America, I have but little

to write that is comfortable. But there seem to be better

Appearances in some other Colonies, than in N. England. when

I was lately in N. Jersey in the Time of the synod there,

I was informed of some small movings & Revivals in

some Places on Long-Island & in N. Jersey. I there

had the Comfort of a short Interview with Mr. davies

of Virginia.[^183-note7] From the little opportunity I had, I was much

pleased with Him, & his Conversation. He seems to be very

solid & discreet, and of a very civil, genteel Behaviour,

as well as fervent & zealous in Religion. He gave an

Account of the Probability of the settlement of one Mr.

Todd,[^183-note8] a young man of good Learning, & a pious disposition [^183-note9]

in Parts a Part of Virginia near to Him. Mr. davies

represented to the synod the great Necessities of the People

in the back-Parts of Virginia, where multitudes were

remarkably awaken'd & reformed several years ago, and

ever since have been thirsting after the Word and Ordi-

nances of God. The People are Chiefly from Ireland, of

scotch Extraction. The synod appointed two men to [go][^183-note10]

down & preach among these People, viz. one Mr. Henry,

a Scotch man, who has lately taken a degree at N. Jersey

College ; and Mr. Greenman, the young man who

was educated at Mr. david Brainerd's Charge.[^183-note11]

The People of Northampton are in sorrowful Circumstances,

yet destitute of a minister, have met with a long series

of disappointments in their Attempts for a Resettlement of the

ministry among Them. my Opposers have had warm

Contentions among Themselves. Of late they have been

wholly destitute of any Body to preach steadily among them:

sometimes [they] meet to read and pray among themselves ; & at [^183-note12]

other Times set travelers, transient Persons to person to preach,

that are hardly fit to be so employed : Not long since

They set one such to preach. whom Maj. Hawley, a

leading man, called down out of the Pulpit in the midst

of his sermon, as being unfit to be there.

My wife joins with me in most respectful salutations

to you & yours, desiring your Prayers, that God would be

with us in all our wandrings through the Wilderness

of this World. I am, dear sir,

your most affectionate Brother in

the Labours of the Gospel,

Jonathan Edwards.

Mr. McCulloch.

[^183-note1]: Not extant.

[^183-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^183-note3]: Ephraim Chambers, *Cyclopedia*, 1, 147-48.

[^183-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

[^183-note5]: Elizabeth Edwards (1747-62).

[^183-note6]: Sarah Edwards Parsons (1728-1805), married Elihu Parsons (1719-85).

[^183-note7]: Samuel Davies (1723-61), minister in Hanover County, Va., 1747-59, then succeeded JE as president of the College of New Jersey.

[^183-note8]: John Todd (1719-93), served mainly in Providence, Va., 1752-93.

[^183-note9]: **marginal.** [4]

[^183-note10]: **marginal.** [JE om.]

[^183-note11]: **[7].** Robert Henry, Presbyterian, settled Charlotte, Va., 1755-66, and Mecklenburg, N.C., 1766-67; and Nehemiah Greenman (c. 1724-79), who actually ended up serving churches in New York and New Jersey.

[^183-note12]: **marginal.** [JE om.]

## A161. Letter to Thomas Gillespie, November 24, 1752 161.JE-T.Gillespie 11-24-52

Jonathan EdwardsA161. JE to Thomas Gillespie, 11/24/52. ANTS, f. 1752C, #8-9.

Stockbridge Novem. 24 N. S. 1752.

Rev. and dear Brother,

In Letters and Pamphlets lately received from some of my Correspon-

dents in Scotland, I have received the affecting and surprizing Account

of your deposition, for not assisting in the settlement of Mr. Richardson at

Inverkeithing.[^184-note1] The Circumstances of which Affair seem to be such as abun-

dantly manifest your Cause to be good, at the same Time that They

plainly shew the persecuting spirit with which you have thus been

proceeded against. 'Tis strange that a Protestant Church should

Condemn and depose one of her Ministers for conscientiously declining

to act in a forced settlement of a Minister over a Congregation that

have not chosen Him as their Pastor, but are utterly averse to his Admi-

nistrations, at least as to a stated Attendance upon them. 'Tis to be

wondered at that such a Church should, at this Time of day, after the

Cause of Liberty in matters of Conscience has been so abundantly defen-

ded, should arrogate to herself such a kind of Authority over hum

the Consciences of both Ministers & People, and use it in such a

manner, by such severity to establish that which is not only so contrary

to that Liberty of Christians wherewith Christ has made them free, but

so directly contrary to her own profess'd Principles, Acts & Resolutions

enter'd on publick Record. The several steps of this Proceeding, and

some singular measures taken, and the hastiness & vehemence of the

Proceeding, are such as savour very strongly of the very spirit of Persecu-

tion. And must be greatly to the dishonour of the Church of God Scotland;

and are such as will naturally engage the minds of God's People abroad

in the world in your Favour, as suffering very injuriously. 'Tis won-

derful that a Church which has itself suffered so much by Persecution,

should be guilty of so much This Proceeding gives Reason to suspect

that the Church of Scotland, which was once so famous, is not what

it once was. It appears probable to me at this distance, that there is

something else at the Bottom, besides a Zeal to uphold the Authority

of the Church. Perhaps many of the Clergy of the Church of Scotland

have their Minds secretly infected with those lax Principles of the

new divinity, and have imbibed the generous Noti doctrines (as

they are accounted) which are so much in vogue at the present day,

and so contrary to the strict, mysterious, spiritual soul humbling

Principles of our Fore-fathers. I have observed that these modern

fashionable Opinions, however called noble and generous, are com-

monly attended, not only with a haughty Contempt, but an inward

malignant Bitterness of Heart towards all the zealous Professours

& defenders of the contrary spiritual Principles, that do so nearly con-

cern the vitals of Religion, & the Power of experimental Godliness.

This, be sure, has been the Case in this Land. I have known many

Gentlemen (especially in the ministry) tainted with these large

Principles, who, tho' none seem to be such great Advocates for Liber-

ty and freedom of thought, and condemn a narrow & persecuting

spirit

spirit so much as They ; yet it in the Course of Things have made [^184-note2]

it manifest that They themselves had no small share of a persecu-

ting spirit. They were indeed against any Bodies in restraining

their Liberties, or pretending to controul Them in their thinking &

professing as they please ; and that is what They mean w truly,

when they plead for Liberty : But they have that inward Enmity

of spirit towards those others mention'd that if They see an Oppor-

tunity to persecute Them under some good Cloak, and with some

fair Pretext, will eagerly embrace it, and proceed with great severi-

ty & vehemence. Thus sir, perhaps if the Truth were known, it

would appear that some of your most strenuous Prosecutors, hate

you much more for something else than for your not obey-

ing the Orders of the General Assembly. I don't pretend to know

how the Case is : I only speak from what I have seen & found

in here in America in Cases something similar. However

'Tis beyond doubt that this Proceeding will stand on the Records

of future Time for the lasting Reproach of your Prosecuters; and

your Conduct, for which you have suffered it, will be to your Lasting

Honour in the Church of God. And which is much more, that

which you has been condemned in you by man, and for which

you have suffered from them, is doubtless approved of by God;

& I trusted you will have a glorious Reward from Him : For your

the Cause you suffer in is plainlyless the Cause of God. And if God

be for us, who can be against us? If He justifies, what need we care

who condemns? Not only is the mercy of God, dear Brother, mani-

fested in it's being granted you to suffer for his sake, but in mercy

it is to be taken Notice of in many of the Circumstances of this

suffering. Particularly that He has excited so many to appear for

you ; That you had the major Part of the Presbytery which you

belong to, with you in this Affair, (tho' God has honoured you above

all the Rest in calling you to suffer for his name) The major Part

of the Commission of the general Assembly did in Effect approve of the

Conduct of the Presbytery, judging it no censurable That no greater

Part of the Assembly had a Hand in th your deposition ; That so

many of Gods People in Scotland have on this Occasion very boldly

& openly appeared y to befriend you, and as suffering in a Righ-

teous Cause, openly condemning the Conduct of your most bitter

Prosecuters and to testify an Abhorrence of their Conduct ; And

that many have appeared liberally to contribute for your out-

ward support, so that by what I understand, you are like to be

no loser in that Respect ; by which your Enemies will be,

perhaps, entirely disappointed ; and above all, that you have

been enabled through the whole of this Affair, to Conduct

your self with so much Christian Meekness, decency, Humility,

proper deference to Authority, & Composure and Fortitude of

Mind ; which is an evident Token that God will appear for

you, & also that He will appear against your Enemies.

Litt When I received your kind Letter, soon after my dismission from

Northampton, so full of sympathy Expressions of sympathy towards me [^184-note3]

under what I suffered, I little thought of your being brought your

so soon under sufferings so similar. But seeing God has so ordered it

in his Providence, my Prayer & Hope is that He would abundantly reward

your sympathy in my Case. --- Blessed are the merciful for they shall

obtain Mercy.

____________

As to my self, I still meet with difficulties in my new station which

arise Partly from private views (as it is to be feared) of some particular

Persons of some note and disposition, who are concerned with the

Affairs of the Mohawks here ; and partly from the same spirit, & the

same Persons some of Them (and others nearly related to Them) that

fomented C the Contention with me at Northampton. However the

People, all, both Indians & English, excepting TH a very few of the

above- mentioned Relation, are firmly united to me : And the Com-

missioners in Boston, and who are my Constituents, and from whom

I have my support, are altogether on my side; and are endeavouring

to their utmost to remove the difficulties that attend our Affairs,

by which the Cause of Religion here, especially among the Mohawks,

suffers, much more than I do, or am like to do, in my personal &

temporal Interest. These difficulties which have arisen have indeed

almost brought the Mohawk Affair to Ruin, which the last year

was attended with so glorious a Prospect : It would be very tedious to

relate the Particulars of this unhappy and undesirable as it would

tend to hurt the Reputation of so particular Persons. --- I think

God by these things calls me to expect no other than to meet with

difficulties & Trials while in this world. And what am I better

than my Fathers, that I should expect to fare better in the world

than the Generality of Christ Followers in all past Generations?

-- May all our Trials be for our purification, and being more & more

meet for our Masters use, & to enter & prepared to enter into the

Joy of our Lord, in ano a World where all Tears shall be wiped

from the Eyes of God's People. Let us, dear sir, earnestly pray

One for another, that it may be thus with us : And that, however [we]

may be called to labour & to suffer, we may see Peace on God's Israel,

and hereafter eternally glory & Triumph with his Inheritance.

God has of late mercifully preserved my wife and my youngest daugh-

ter, in Time of very sore and dangerous sickness, & restored Them again.

My us eldest daughter has also been sick and is restored in a Conside-

rable degree.

Northampton People remain in sorrowful Circumstances, destitute

of a settled minister, and without any Prospect of a settlement, having

met with many disappointments. -- But all don't as yet seem to be

effectual to bring 'em to a suitable Temper of mind.

I should I much desire to hear from you, & to be informed of your

present Circumstances. --I am, dear sir,

your Affectionate Brother in the Gospel ministry,

Jonathan Edwards.

Mr. Gillespie

P.S.

P.S. I intend to send to Mr. Foxcroft, of Boston desiring Him

to put up for you one of my Answers to Mr. Williams,[^184-note4]

which I suppose is now printed; of which I ask your

acceptance.

[^184-note1]: In 1752 the Scottish General Assembly ordered the settlement of Andrew Richardson at Inverkeithing despite the congregation's opposition. Gillespie supported the people and was removed from his position at Carnock.

## A162. Letter to William Hogg, November 25, 1752 162.JE-W.Hogg 11-25-52

Jonathan EdwardsA162. JE to William Hogg, 11/25/52. BRBL, f. 1311.

To Mr. Wm Hogg.

Stockbridge Novem. 25 N.S. 1752.

dear Sir,

I thank you for your kind Letter of May 8. 1752, added

to all the other Testimonies of your unmerited Respect &

Friendship. The Pamphlet you speak of entitled private Judg-

ment defended, which you speak of as what you had sent

to mr. Prince for me, is not come to Hand; probably through

mr. Prince's Forgetfulness, which often has been the Case with

Letters & Pamphlets that have been sent to Him for me from

Scotland. For tho' He be an eminently worthy man, and

one who has laid me under Obligations, yet He is

forgetful: and probably more so now, it being a Time of

Affliction with Him, by Reason of the late death of his

daughter. I intend at the first Opportunity to send to

Boston & enquire after this Pamphlet, and another sent

to Him for me by Mr. McLauring, which is not come

to Hand.

I have great Reason always to remember with much Gra-

titude your tender sympathy on occasion of the late great

Troubles I met with at Northampton, and the extraordi-

nary Respect testified since, not only by word but deed.

I have great Reason to remember the Kindness of friends, &

Friends at a great distance and unknown; But have

more special Reason thankfully to take notice of, & remem-

ber the Kindness of a gracious God, that has raised up

these Friends, and has made them his Instruments to

Convey his Bounty to us. God's dealings with me

and my Family have been mixed; Affliction & mercy

has been intermingled, formerly & lately, & is so still: God

has mercifully open'd a door for usefulness here at stock-

bridge: after & has given us a settlement, in many Respects

comfortable

comfortable, here at stockbridge after we were turned out [^185-note1]

at Northampton. But here in the with our mercies

we have our difficulties ; which are indeed much great-

er Calamaties to the important Affair of the Instruction

of the Six Nations, than Calamities to me or my Fami-

ly, tho' we suffer not a little by them. Our Calamities have

arisen from these sources. The last year, after so remar-

kable an appearance of Forwardness in the Mohawks to come

& settle in N. England, & submit to Instruction, not only

were the Commissioners in Boston of the society in London

for Propagating the Gospel in N. England & Parts adja-

cent, much animated by it , but the general Court took

much notice of it, and appointed a Committee of three Gen-

tlemen to take Care of, and promote this affair. The chief

of these three Gentlemen, has since fo contracted an Acquaintance

with a Gentlewoman in stockbridge, & has married And makes

this Town the Place of his Constant abode, having brought

his Family hither. He being a Person of a very sanguine &

enterprizing, and something of a sovereign Temper, has taken

the management of the Mohawk affair almost wholly into

his own Hands, and claims the whole Power of the

management of that Affair to the General Courts Committee,

exclusive of the Commissioners, who maintain all the

Instructors here, out of the Charitable Fund Committed

to them. And this Gentleman having designs & views,

very diverse from those of the Commissioners, & those that

are employed by them, this has led Him to measures

quite Contrary to theirs; which he has pursued with great

Resolution. And the commissioners having principally

intrusted me with the Care of their affairs here, this has

occasioned a first a misunderstanding & Jealousy in Him

towards me, & the two schoolmasters maintained by the Com-

missioners, & at length to an Open Opposition. [^185-note2]

Another source of difficulty is this. In the Case of the late

great Controversy at Northampton, There was a number of

Gentlemen belonging to other Towns, of a certainly Family

of considerable note in N. England, which had long mani-

fested a jealous & unfriendly spirit towards me, at least

some of them ('Tis needless for me to say what I think

were the first Causes of this unfriendliness) who on occasion of

the foresaid Controversy, set in on the side of my Opposers, were

their Chief Counselors during the whole Continuance of the

Controversy. One or two of the Inhabitants of stockbridge

were of the same Family; who when my coming to settle

here was first talked of, greatly opposed it. But when

they saw the stream was to[o] strong for them seem'd to concur

in it, & appeared very friendly. But since the foremen-

tion'd Gentleman of the general Courts Committee has mar-

ried into the Family, They have thrown off the Appearance

of friendship in a great measure, And act entirely in

Concert with Him in his Opposition, and are abetted &

upheld in it by the some Gentlemen of note in other Pla-

ces the same that fomented the Contention at Northamp-

ton. A third source of difficulty is this. Mr. Isaac

Hollis of High-Wycomb in Buckinghamshire in England

in Mr. sergeant's time, made large Remittances hither

for the support of a boarding school in stockbridge. Mr.

sergt took much Pains to find a suitable master, a

man of Learning. but being disappointed, He, the year

before his death, improved an Aged man, that was Lame

& not able to follow Husbandry, a man of pretty good

Abilities, but not a man of Learning, as a present supply,

till a suitable master Could be found; But grew

grew very uneasy at his Conduct, convinced of his utter

unfitness for the Business, & resolved to dismiss Him, & pro-

cure some fitter Person. But He dying be soon, this man

was

was left in the school, & continues in it still, others being [^185-note3]

loth to inform Mr Hollis of his unfitness. Means have

been used to perswade Him, but He all to no Effect.

And by what He has perceived of a dislike of his Conduct,

He is very much out of Temper, & sets Himself very much

against the other school-master, whom the Commissioners

have provided for the Mohawks: which keeps things in

great Confusion among Them. Thus sir, you see some-

thing of the unhappiness of the situation of Affairs here.

Endeavours have been used by my Opposers to dissaffect

the Inhabitants of the Town, towards & also the Commissrs

in Boston towards me; But hitherto all in vain.

The People all, both Indians & English, excepting those

forementioned, are firmly united to me. And the Com-

missioners seem to have their Eyes wide open with

Regard to our Affairs ; And are exerting themselves

to their utmost to extricate us out of these difficulties.

& 'tis to be hoped God in his Providence will appear for

us. I desire sir that you would be helping together by

your Prayers for us, & for the poor Indians, which suffer

most by these Contentions. ---- I have the more Reason to hope

for your fervent Prayers, from the Experience I have had of your Cordial

Friendship, and the Account you give me of your own Experience of af-

fliction. I por pray God abundantly to reward your Love & Bene-

ficence towards & bless you & your Family, & make you Blessings

yet more & more. My Wife joins with me in most cordial

& grateful salutations to you mrs Hogg & your surviving Children.

--- God has lately raised from sore & dangerous sickness, my wife &

youngest daughter. ---- I intend to give orders that one of my

Answers to mr. Williams, should be put up for you. which when

you have read I desire you would lend to Mr. davidson.[^185-note4] I have with

this sent a Letter to Him, desire Him to pardon my treating Him with

Common Civility, in giving him the Title of Revd. tho' he desires I

would not. I am dear sir. your most obliged & affectionate

Friend and servt, Jonathan Edwards.

## A164. Letter to Thomas Hubbard (Draft), March 19, 1753 164.JE-T.Hubbard 3-19-53

## A165. Letter to Esther Edwards Burr, March 28, 1753 165.JE-E.E.Burr 3-28-53

Jonathan Edwards165. JE to Esther Edwards Burr, 3/28/53. BPL, Ms. E.9.4 (65-14). Addressed on back "To / Mrs. Esther Burr / At Newark."

Stockbridge March 28. 1753.

Dear Child,

We are glad to hear that you are in any respect

better, but concerned at your remaining great Weak-

ness. I am glad to see some of the Contents of your

Letter to your Mother; and particularly that you have

been enabled to make a Free-will-Offering to God's ser-

vice, and that you have experienced some inward di-

vine Consolations under your Affliction, by the extream

Weakness & distressing Pains, you have been the subject

of. For these you ought to be thankful, and also for

that unwearied Kindness & tender Care of your Com-

panion, which you speak of. I would not have you

think that any strange Thing has happen'd to you in

this Affliction: 'Tis according to the Course of Things

in this World, that after the worlds smiles, some

great Affliction soon comes. God has now given you

early & seasonable warning, not at all to depend on

worldly Prosperity. Therefore I would advise, that if

it pleases God to restore you, to let upon no Happiness

here. Labour while you live, to serve God and do

what Good you can, and endeavour to improve

every dispensation to God's Glory & your own spiritual

Good, and be content to do and bear all that calls

you in this wilderness, and never expect to find

this world any thing better than a wilderness.

Lay your Account to travel through it in weariness

Painfulness

Painfulness & Trouble, and wait for your Rest & [^188-note1]

your Prosperity 'till hereafter. where They that die

in the Lord rest from their Labours, and enter into

the Joy of the Lord. You are like to spend the rest

of your Life (if you should get over this Illness) at a

great distance from your Parents; but care not much

for that. If you lived near us, Yet our Breath and

yours would soon go forth, and we should return to

our dust, whether we are all hastening. 'Tis of

infinitely more Importance to have the Presence of an

heavenly Father, and to make Progress towards an

heavenly Home. Let us all take Care that we may

meet there at last.

As to means for your Health, we have procured one

Rattle-snake, which is all we could get. It is a medi-

cine that has been very serviceable to you heretofore,

and I would have you trie it still. If your stomach is

very weak and will bear but little, you must take it

in smaller Quantities. We have sent you some

Ginseng. I should think it best for you m to make

Trial of that various ways: trie stewing it in wa-

ter, and take it in strength and Quantity as you

find suits your stomach best. You may also

try steeping it in wine, in good madera or Cla-

ret; or if these wines are too harsh, then in some

good white wine. And whether you stew or

steep

steep it, you had best to slice it very thin, or bruise [^188-note2]

it in an Iron mortar. And for a Cordial take

some spices steep'd in some generous wine that suits

your Taste, and stomach. And above all the

Rest, use riding in pleasant weather : and when

you can bear it, Riding on Horse-back; but never so

as to fatigue you. And be very careful to avoid

taking Cold. And I should think it best pretty

much to throw by doctors, and be your own Physician,

and hearkening to them that are used to your Consti-

tution.

I desire that Mr. Burr & you would be frequent

in counselling Timmy[^188-note3] as to his soul-Concerns.

Commending you to God, before whom we daily

remember you in our Prayers, I am

your affectionate Father

Jonathan Edwards.

P.S. Your mother would

have you use a conserve of

Raisins; A Pound of good sugar

to a Pound of Raisins, after

They are ston'd. Mix with

it, Nutmegs, Mace, Cinnamon, Cloves, ground in a spice-

Mill, with some Orange-Pill; One Nutmeg to half a

Pound of Conserve, and the other spices in the same Quantity.

take a little as suits your stomach, in the morning, & an

Hour before dinner, & in the After-noon. Try this

The same spices & Orange Pill to be put into your spiced

wine. But when you take this, you must omit taking the

wine. The only danger we apprehend in these

Things

Things is that possibly the heat of 'em may raise a [^188-note4]

Fever; therefore you must observe the Operation

of them as to that: And when you drink your

spiced wine you may mix some water with it

to abate the Heat of it. --- Your mother has

also an Inclination that you should sometimes try

a Tea made of the Leaves of Robins Plantain,

If it be known at Newark by that Name ; she

says she has found it very strengthening & Comfor-

table to her in her weakness.

The Family all unites in their Love to you.

[^188-note3]: I.e. Timonty Edwards, ho was stydying at Nassau Hall.

[^188-note4]: **marginal.** [4]

## A166. Letter to Timothy Edwards (Son), April 1, 1753 166.JE-T.Edwards 4-1-53

Jonathan Edwards166. JE to Timothy Edwards (son), 4/1/53. Dwight copy only. ANTS, f. 1753A, #9.

Master

To Mr Timothy Edwards, at New York

Stockbridge April 1753

To Mr Timothy Edwards

My dear Child,

Before you will receive this Letter, the matter will

doubtless be determined, as to your having the smallpox;

You will either be sick with that distemper, or will

be past danger of having it, from any infection taken in your

voyage. But whether you are sick or well, like to die or

like to live, I hope you are earnestly seeking your salva-

tion. I am sure there is a great deal of reason it should be

so, considering the warnings you have had in word &

in providence. That, which you met with, in your passage

from to New York to Newark, which was the occasion of yr.

fever, was indeed a remarkable warning, a dispensation

full of instruction, & a very loud call of God to you to be

to make haste, and not to delay in the great business

of religion. If you have that distemper, which you have

been threatened with, you are separated from your earthly friends:

none of them must come to see you; and if you should die

of it, you have already taken a final & everlasting leave

of them while you are yet alive; not to have the comfort

of their presence & immediate Care & never to see them

again in the land of the living. And if you have

escaped that distemper, it is by a remarkable Providence

providence that you are preserved. And your having

been so exposed to it, must certainly be a loud call of

God, not to trust in earthly friends, or any thing here

below. Young persons are very apt to trust in Parents

& friends, when they are sick, or when they think of being on

a deathbed. But this providence remarkably teaches you

the need of a better Friend, and a better Parent, than earth= [^189-note1]

ly parents are; who is everywhere present, & all sufficient,

that can't be kept off by infectious distempers, who is able

to save you from death or to make happy in death, to save

from eternal misery, & to bestow eternal life. It is indeed

comfortable, when one is in great pain, languishing under

sore sickness, to have the presence & kind care of near &

dear earthly friends; but this is a very small thing, in

comparison of what it is, to have the presence of a hea=

venly Father and a compassionate & almighty Redeemer.

In Gods favour is life, & his loving kindness is better

than life. Whether you are in sickness or health,

you infinitely need this. But you must know

however great need you stand of it, you dont deserve

it: neither is God the more disposed to bestow

it upon you, for your standing in necessity

of it, your earnest desiring of it, your cying

to him constantly for it, from fear of misery, &

taking much pains. Till you have savingly

believed in Christ, all your desirous & pains,

& prayers lay God under no obligation; and, if

they were ten thousand times as great as they

are, you must still know, that you would be

in the hands of a sovereign God, who hath

mercy on whom he will have mercy. Indeed

God often hears the poor miserable cries of sinful

vile creatures, who have no manner of true regard

to him in their hearts; for he is a God of infinite

mercy, & he delights to show mercy for his Son's sake,

who is worthy, though you are unworthy, who came

to save the sinful & the miserable, yea some of the

chief of sinners. Therefore, there is your only hope; & in [^189-note2]

him must be your refuge, who invites you to come

to him, and says, "He that cometh to me I will

in no wise cast out." Whatever your circumstances

are, it is your duty not to despair, but to hope

in infinite mercy through a Redeemer. For God

makes it your duty to pray to him for mercy;

which would not be your duty, if it was al=

lowable for you to despair. We are expressly

commanded to call upon God in the day

of trouble; and when we are afflicted, then to pray.

But, if I hear that you have escaped,--either that

you have not been sick, or are restored,--though I

shall rejoice, and have great cause of thankfulness, yet

I shall be concerned for you. If your escape should

be followed with carelessness & security, and forgetting

the remarkable warning you have had, & God's great

mercy in your deliverance, it would in some respects

be more awful than sore sickness. It would be

very provoking to God, and would probably issue in

an increasing hardness of heart, & it may be divine

vengeance may soon overtake you. I have known

various instances of persons being remarkably warned

in Providence, by being brought into very dangerous

circumstances and escaping, and afterwards death

has soon followed in another [-]way. I earnestly

desire, that God would make you wise to salvation,

and that he would be merciful & gracious to you

in every respect, according as he knows your circumstances

require. And this is the daily prayer of your tender

affectionate & tender father, Jonathan Edwards

P.S. Your Mother send their love to you, as being tenderly concerned for you.

## A169. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, April 13, 1753 169.JE-T.Foxcroft 4-13-53

Jonathan EdwardsA169. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 4/13/53. BRBL, f. 1285. Foxcroft did some underlining, but only JE's indicated here.

Stockbridge April 13 1752

Rev. & honoured sir,

I thank your[^192-note1] for your Favour of March 19 and for the

particular Informations you give me, tending to relieve my

mind with regard to the bold and vaunting manner of those

that seek my Overthrow. You say Gentlemen in Boston

seem to think that I am apt to magnify things with Respect to

the Attempts made for my Overthrow. Perhaps they

would not think so if They heard & saw all that is said and

done here. Brigdr D. has from time to Time, express'd

to our People, his Assurance that He should be successful in

his designs against me, and that I should undoubtedly

be removed in a little Time. To the like Purpose several

of the Williams's have express'd themselves, tho' I now

begin to think that these bold & great threats were designd

only to terrify us, & thereby to bring us to their own Terms.

I have herewith inclosed Proposals for printing by subscripti

on something I have been writing, with a Letter to mr. Knee-

land. I am afraid you will be sorry at the sight of these Pro-

posals, as They may give you a Prospect of a great Addition to the

Trouble I have already put you to. I am indeed concerned

about it, and ashamed to ask it of you to continue that Assis-

tance, with Respect to this Piece, which you have afforded

in Times past with Respect to former Publications -----

But I will venture at present to ask this of you, viz. to forward

the Letter to Mr. McLaurin, and about 30 of the Proposals

with it. It would also much oblige me if you use some

Endeavours to spread the Proposals and to forward sub-

scribing. This with my humble service to your Family

& Request of a Remembrance in your Prayers is from,

sir

your most obliged

son & servt,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^192-note1]: MS sic.

## A170. Letter to John Erskine, April 14, 1753 170.JE-J.Erskine 4-14-53

Jonathan EdwardsA170. JE to John Erskine, 4/14/53. ANTS, f. 1753A #7-8. Addressed on back "To the Rev. / Mr John Erskine / Minister of the Gospel / at Kirkintillock."

Stockbridge April 14. 1753.

Rev. & dear Sir,

After many Hindrances, delays & Interruptions,

divine Providence has so far favored me, & smiled on

my design of writing on the Arminian Controversie,

that I have now almost finish'd the first draught

of what I first intended. and am now sending the

Proposals for subscription to Boston to be printed, with a

Letter to Mr. Foxcroft to send 30 of those Proposals to

Mr. McLaurin to deliver half of them to you, as you

have manifested your self ready to use Endeavours

to get subscriptions in Scotland. The printing will

be delayed to wait for subscriptions from thence. I there-

fore request, that you endeavour to promote and expedite

the Affair.

Stockbridge Affairs relating to the Indians, are in many

Respects under a very dark Cloud. The Affair of the Iro-

quois or six Nations here is almost at an End, as I have

given a more particular Account to Mr. McLaurin.

The Commissrs in Boston I believe are discouraged

about it, and have Thought of sending & settling

a Missionary in their own Countrey. The Correspon-

dents of the society in Scotland, have also determined

to send a missionary there, and have Chosen Mr.

Gordon,[^193-note1] a Tutor of the College at Newark, for that

End. Mr. Gordon is expected here at the Beginning

of May, to live at my House with Mr. Hawley,

in order to Learn the Iroquois Language with Him.

Tis

Tis Probable that He & Mr. Hawley will go up & [^193-note2]

spend this summer in the Iroquois Countrey. The

Correspondents have also a disposition that Mr. Brainerd

should remove with his whole Congregation of Indians

to settle somewhere in the Countrey of the six Nations;

& Himself & his Indians are ready for it. 'Tis probable

something will be done to prepare the way for it,

or at least to see whether the way can be prepared

or any door open'd for it, this summer. some of

those Indians have a great desire that the Gospel

should be introduced & settled in their Countrey.

some of the stockbridge Indians, have of late been

under Considerable Awakenings, two or three elderly

Men, that used to be vicious Persons. --- My Family

is now in usual Health. My daughter Burr in N.

Jersey has been very ill all the winter past. we last

heard from her about five weeks ago ; when it was

hoped there was some Amendment.

My Wife joins with me in respectful & affectio-

nate Salutations to you & Mrs. Erskine, desiring

a Remembrance in your Prayers.

I am dear sir,

your affectionate Br.

& obliged Friend & servt

Jonathan Edwards.

Mr. Erskine.

[^193-note1]: Alexander Gordon (d. 1754), tutor of College of New Jersey, 1752-54; he went with Hawley to the Iroquois but did not remain, apparently because of poor health.

[^193-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

## A171. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, May 24, 1753 171.JE-T.Foxcroft 5-24-53

Jonathan EdwardsA171. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 5/24/53. BRBL, f. 1296. Foxcroft's notation on the back of the MS indicates the letter was "Recd Jne 8. 53 pr Mr. Allen Answ. July 13. 1753."

Stockbridge May 24. 1753.

Rev. & honoured Sir,

I thank your[^194-note1] for your Favour by Mr. Hawley.

He with Mr. Woodbridge, Mr. Ashley, and his Wife, went

away the last Tuesday in Order to go into the Countrey of

the Six Nations. Mr. Gordon that Mr. Hal Hawley expected

to go with Him fails. The Correspondents had at one meeting

appointed Him to go, but at a late Meeting, wherein some

Members were present who were absent before, They

determined that it was not best till they had sent to

Scotland to know the Minds of the society.[^194-note2] Mr. Pem-

berton in particular was earnest in Opposition to his

going at present.-- This is some discouragement to Mr.

Hawley.[^194-note3]

I humbly thank You for the Readiness you manifest to

assist in the Publication of what I have written against

Arminians, in promoting subscriptions, & in the care of the

Press. ---- with Respect to the Character, I should be

glad the Book might be printed in the best Character

Mr. Kneeland has, and that it should be done every

way in as handsom a manner as may be. I think

the Character in which my Answer to Mr. W---s is

printed is better than that of my Book on relig. Aff--ns.

But Mr. H--- tells me that Mr. Kneeland has sent

for new Types; perhaps they will be better than any He

now has.

I have had Thoughts of writing to some Gentlemen

your way to take some of the Proposals and endeavour

to

to promote subscriptions; But I did not know but I should be [^194-note4]

thought too troublesom. I should be glad if I knew any Body

that I could be so free with, as to desire 'em a little to exert

Themselves in the Time of the Commencement at Cambridge:

I had thought of writing to Col. Brattle, who kept at my

House at Northampton the biggest Part of a Week, once in the

Time of a treaty with Indians at deerfield. But I have

not Acquaintance enough to know it will do. -- I should

be glad of a word of Advice from you. -- With Respect to

the other two Colleges, N. Haven & Newark, I have no

difficulty. I know who to improve.

My wife joins with me in respectful salutations. desiring

continued Interest in your Prayers. I am sir,

your obliged Son & servt

Jonathan Edwards.

[^194-note1]: MS sic.

[^194-note2]: The Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge.

[^194-note3]: The Hawley biography in Sibley's *Harvard Graduates*, XII:395, states that Gordon did go and includes details of how Hawley and Gordon worked together. The decision to permit him apparently came after this letter was written.

[^194-note4]: **marginal.** [2]
