## A172. Letter to a Singing Teacher, June 4, 1753 172.JE-SingingTeacher 6-4-53

Jonathan EdwardsA172. JE to Singing Teacher, 6/4/53. Yale, Sterling Lib., Archives and Manuscripts, Samuel Rossiter Betts Autograph Coll., #603, B. 2, f. 137.

Windsor June 4, 1753

Sir,

There is very great need of somebody at

Stockbridge to teach the Indians to Sing. They have

good voices and many of them are apt to learn

and I should be glad if I could get you there the

next Fall or winter to that End if you could be

obtain'd on reasonable Terms. I desire that you

would inform me whether you would be willing

to come and on what Terms. Your Pay will be

good and the English People there are a very agrea-

ble sort of People I suppose you would expect to be

paid for not only for the time you should Spend at

Stockbridge but for your Journey at least in Part but

perhaps you might afford to Come if we should pay

for your Journey from Westfield It might not be out

of your way to come as far as Westfield on your own

Business, in it being in your way to deerfield

Please to Send me a letter as soon & order it to be

left either at my Fathers at Windsor or Mr. Hopkins

of Springfield or Capt. Dwights of Northampton

and that as soon as may be that if you cant come

I may get somebody else. I am Sir

your humble servant,

Jonathan Edwards

## A173. Letter to Joseph Dwight, July 5, 1753 173.JE-J.Dwight 7-5-53

Jonathan EdwardsA173. JE to Joseph Dwight, 7/5/53. RIHS, Ms. v. VI, p. 3. Addressed on verso "To the Honble / [J]oseph Dwight Esq / In Stockbridge."

Stockbridge July 5. 1753.

May it please Your Honour,

A considerable Part of the English Members of

the Church being together, and having heard your

[L]etter[^197-note1] of July 3. They desire me to inform you, that as

[th]ey long ago sent one of their Number to inform you

[t]hat They were disposed to Reconciliation, & stood rea-

dy fully to converse with Your Honour, with respect to

the Reasons of all Parts of their Conduct towards you,

if you would appoint Time and Place, and given em Op-

portunity; so what They did then is still in Force,

and their Minds are not altered. They also

think it requisite that Mrs. Dwight should give

the Church the Reasons of her openly turning her

back on the sacrament of the Lords supper, she

having united herself to this Church in Covenant,

& so bound herself to join with the Church in up

holding and attending the Ordinances of the Gos-

pel. We desire you to inform her that when

[sh]e can attend it the Pastor is Ready to ap-

[po]int a Church Meeting to that End. I am

Sir your most humble servt

Jonath. Edwards.

The Honble Jos. Dwight Esq.

[^197-note1]: **[1].** Holes in the MS affect the beginning of this and the following two lines, and the last two lines before the close.

## A174. Letter to Timothy Edwards (Son), July 17, 1753 174.JE-T.Edwards 7-17-53

Jonathan EdwardsA174. JE to Timothy Edwards (son), 7/17/53. Maine Hist. Society, Fogg Coll., 420, v. 4. Addressed on verso "To / Timothy Edwards / At Newark."

Stockbridge July 17. 1753.

Dear Son,

I rejoyce, and desire to do it with Thankfulness & Praise to God,

that we have heard from Time to Time of your being in Health,

wherein you have been distinguished from many of your near

Relations of late ; as particularly your Brother dwight, your

Brother & sister Parsons, your sister Burr, & your sister Eu-

nice[^198-note1]. I hope you will improve Life and Health while God conti-

nues them to prepare for sickness & death, which you must expect:

death will certainly come at its the Time which God has appointed,

whether you are prepared or unprepared.

I rejoyce to hear that you follow your Studies, and make good Profici-

ence. How con great your Proficience is I can't certainly tell, but

I hardly think it will be best for you to enter the College the next

Commencement. One of the Chief Things that is the Ruin of New-

England Scholars is their going to College before they have a thorogh

Acquaintance with the Languages : 'tis a wound they never get

over as long as they live; They never come to such a degree of Learn-

ing in any Measure as they might otherwise do. This you will

be sensible of hereafter, if your Life is preserved. --- If you don't

enter College this year, we should be willing to see you here in

the Fall with Mr. Burr & his wife. --- You may possibly re-

gret the putting off your Freshmanship a year longer, and so

serving some that now you are a Companion to, but that is a

little thing in Comparison of the forementioned disadvantage,

a thing not worth the Regarding. If you are brought up

to Learning, I would feign have you have good Learning, & be

a good scholar. A poor scholar is a poor Creature. above all

I desire that you may have Grace to make a good Improvemt

of Learning, & all other Talents, without while which they will

but aggravate your Condemnation. That God would give you

that infinitely important Blessing is the fervent Prayer of

your tender & affectionate Father Jth Edwards.

P.S. Your Mother, Brothers & sisters give their Love to you.

P.S. Your Mother desires you would [^198-note2]

send your old Coat in Sr Williams's[^198-note3]

Trunk or any other old Clothes you have

that you have done with which will be service-

able to your Brothers. -- give my service to

sir Williams & tell Him I beg that Favour of

Him to allow those Clothes a Place in his

Trunk.

[^198-note1]: Timothy Dwight, Elihu and Sarah Edwards Parsons, Esther Edwards Burr, and Eunice Edwards.

[^198-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^198-note3]: Elijah Williams, son of Maj. Ephraim Williams of Stockbridge, then a student at the College of New Jersey.

## A175. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, August 6, 1753 175.JE-J.Bellamy 8-6-53

Jonathan EdwardsA175. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 8/6/53. Pierpont Morgan Lib., New York. Addressed on verso "To / the Rev. Joseph Bellamy / In Bethlehem."

Stockbridge Aug 6. 1753

Rev. & Dear sir,

I have sent a Couple of Men for my

sheep Mr. Brown & Hinds[^199-note1]. This is to de-

sire that you would see to the delivery

of em, & see that Justice is done about

it --- I have but a moments Time ----

--- You say the sheep have been on

Charge. I suppose I shall see you

before long & then I will take Care of that

matter . pray come & see us.

I am sir

Your Loving Br

Jonathan Edwards

[^199-note1]: Samuel Brown and Phinehas Hinds of Stockbridge.

## A176. Letter to John Ely, August 27, 1753 176.JE-J.Ely 8-27-53

Jonathan Edwards176. JE to John Ely, 8/27/53. Princeton Univ., Firestone Lib., JE Misc. Papers. Addressed on verso "To / Lieut John Ely / at Sprinfield."

Mr Ely

Sir

Please to send us by Deac. Brown

five or six Yards of tow-Cloth and also

5 or 6 yards of Check that which is

good & serviceable & reasonable & if

you have any good Paper send me a

Couple of Quire. and take an Account

of these Things. herein you will

oblige your humble servt

Jonath. Edwards.

Stockbridge

Aug. 27. 1753.

P.S. Please also to send 3 sets

of Knitting needles of the com-

mon size.

## A177. Letter to Ephraim Williams, Jr. et al., September 11, 1753 177.JE-EWmsetal9-11-53

Jonathan Edwards177. JE to Ephraim Williams Jr. et al., 9/11/53. RIHS, Ms. v. VI, p. 4. Addressed on verso "To Maj. Ephm. Williams / Mr. Josiah Williams / Mrs. Abigail Dwight / Mrs Judith Williams / In Stockbridge."

To Maj. Ephraim Williams,[^201-note1] Mr. Josiah Williams

Mrs. Abigail dwight, & Mrs. Judith Williams, Mem-

bers of the Church in Stockbridge.

What I lately wrote to you signifying the Desire

& Expectation of the Church of your meeting them

the next Thursday, was not in my own Name, but

it was in Fulfillment of a vote of the Church which

I have no power to alter ; They have by their own

vote appointed a Meeting on Purpose to hear you, next

and desired me to inform you that they expected you

should then be present; and will doubtless then meet

& expect that you should appear; not the less for Col.

Dwights not being at home at that Time, if that is

like to be the Case, which the Church knows nothing

about. Col. dwight is not one of the Complainers,

nor one of the Church, and the Church are not

Sensible of any Concern they have with Him & know

not of any Reasons why they should first enquire

when He is like to be in Town , before they venture to

appoint a Meeting to hear those of their own Members

who have exhibited so high a Charge against their

Pastor & Brethren. The Church doubtless supposes

that the Complainers are, or should be able to give

the Reasons of their own Complaint. ---- It might

be very hard for the Church to accommodate all

their Meetings & Proceedings to the Convenience

& Leisure to such a Number of their disaffected

Members ; & besides that to the Convenience and

Pleasure of others that they are not concerned

with : An End is put to all Proceedings of the Church

for its own Regulation and Preservation if this be

reasonably expected. You have now an Opportu-

nity to offer your Reasons & Evidences to support your

Charge if you have any to offer, & to lay before the

Church the Reasons why you insist on a Council, &

to have 'em Considered ; which I hope you will

embrace, rather than to cast Contempt on the Church

(which you have obliged your selves in Covenant to

submit to) by refusing to appear before 'em.

I am your Pastor &

Servant for Jesus Sake,

Jonathan Edwards.

Stockbridge

Septem. 11. 1753.

[^201-note1]: I.e. Ephraim Williams Jr., newly commissioned in June 1753. Ephraim Williams Sr. had left Stockbridge prior to Aug. 14 to live in Deerfield.

## A178. Letter to Aaron Burr, September 17, 1753 178.JE-A.Burr 9-17-53

Jonathan EdwardsA178. JE to Aaron Burr, 9/17/53. Princeton Univ., Firestone Lib., JE Misc. Papers. Addressed on verso "To the / Rev. Mr. Aaron Burr / at Newark."

To the Rev. Mr. Aaaron Burr, Pastor of the

Church of Christ in Newark, to be Communicated.

Reverend & beloved,

By this I would inform you, that a meeting

of the Church of stockbridge on the 14th Instant,

It was unanimously voted, that whereas Mrs

Esther Burr, formerly Edwards, a Member of

this Church, has in divine Providence been removed

from hence to dwell at Newark, she be recommended

to your Stated Communion, as a Member in full

standing ; having heretofore been admitted in such

Standing in this Church, by Recommendation from

the Church of Northampton, and having so remain'd

without offence during her Continuance here.

Jonathan Edwards, Pastr of the Church

in stockbridge.

stockbridge

sept. 17. 1753.

## A179. Letter to Ephraim Williams, Jr. et al., September 18, 1753 179.JE-Ephraim Williamsetal 9-18-53

Jonathan EdwardsA179. JE to Ephraim Williams et al. RIHS, Ms. v. VI, p. 5, #1175. Addressed on verso "To Maj. Ephraim Williams / Mr. Josiah Williams / Mr. Jonathan Devreux, Mrs Abigail Williams, / Mrs Abigail Dwight & Mr[s] Judith Williams / Members of the Chh in Stockbridge."

To Maj. Ephraim Williams, Mr. Josiah Williams, Mr Jona-

than devreux, Mrs Abigail Williams, Mrs Abigail dwight,

& Mrs Judith Williams, Members of the Church in

Stockbridge. Stockbridge Septem. 18. 1753.

The following is a Copy of the Votes pass'd by this

Church, at their Meeting on the 14. Instant; which as they

concern you, I now send to you. I am your servt

for Jesus Sake,

Jonath. Edwards.

I. Whereas a Charge of Scandelous Offences has lately been

exhibited against this Church, & especially against the Pastor &

some of the Members, and laid before the Church in a Wri-

ting signed by Maj. Ephraim Williams & others ; And there

being some Reason to apprehend from the Tenour of the said Wri-

ting, together with the Conduct of the subscribers, that their

Intention is, that the Charges which they have exhibited in

this Writing should be directly carried to a Council, and the Evi-

dences by which they would support them be laid before them

in the first Place ; therefore voted, that whether ever their Com-

plaint be carried to a Council, or any others besides the Church them

selves, or no, Yet the Nature of things manifestly requires that the

Reasons & Evidences they have to justify their Charge ought first to be

laid before the Church, before whom they have laid the Complaint

and the Church has an undoubted Right to insist on this, & Au-

thority to require it ; and that whether it be supposed to be proper

that the Church should act as decisive Judges in the Affair or not.

II. As to what is (as we think unseasonably & preposterously)

desired, in the foremention'd Writing, viz. that the things they alledge

in the foremention'd Writing therein should be refer'd to the Judg-

ment & final Decision of a Council; Voted, that it appears to this

Church, that the peculiar state of this Church, and also the Circum-

stances of this Case are such, that if the Judgment of these things

be refer'd to any other Judges besides the Church themselves, 'tis proper

and necessary that the whole Affair be first laid before the ho-

nourable Commissioners for Indian Affairs, that they on a full Hear-

ing of it, may have Opportunity to use their own Wisdom in Endea-

vours to put an End to the Calamities which attend their Affairs

in this Place. This appears to us to be what the Nature of the

Case requires for the following Reasons.

1. The Circumstances of this Church & Congregation are very different

peculiar, much differing from those of most other Churches ; The Com-

missioners having the chief Care of the religious Concerns of this Town;

The very Being of the Church being owing to them, under God ; it being

brought about thro' their Care and Expence, and in pursuance of the Impor-

tant Ends of their Commission ; and the Settlement of the Town being to

accommodate an important religious Affair which they are Trustees of.

For which Reasons it must be supposed, that so far as the religious Concerns

of the Church come under the Care of any out of the Church, they [^203-note1]

Chiefly fall under their Care, and must most properly in the first

Place come under their Cognizance. And as the Difficulties

which now attend this to the highest Degree concern the Inte-

rest of the Commissioners here, threatning no less than the ut-

ter subversion of their Affairs, therefore we think they can't fitly

be refer'd to the Determination of others, without their Judgment &

Advice.

2. The forsaid Complaint exhibited by Maj. Ephraim Williams

&c. is in the first Place against the Missionary, as behaving Him-

self altogether unworthy of his Ministerial Character; & we think

we can't in Justice to the Commissioners by any Means, refer the

Determination of that Matter to the Decision of other Judges,

without their Cognizance and Advice ; because that we would be

referring it to the Judgment & final Determination of other Jud-

ges, whether the Missionary the Commissioners have appointed

is fit for the Business they employ him in, and so in Effect to

take the Affair of the Appointment of a Missionary out of their

Hands, and as much as in us lies, to give others Power, without

consulting them, to disannul & break their Establishment

of a Missionary here.

3. Not only is the Pastor complain'd of, but the whole Church,

which partly consists of Indians ; which must in a peculiar Man-

ner be look'd upon as under the Care of the Commissioners;

the grand Design of their Commission being to take Care of

the spiritual Concerns of the Indians.

4. Referring these things to an ecclesiastical Council in the

first Place, we think would not be effectual to bring these dif-

ficulties to an Issue.

Therefore voted by the Church, that considering these Things

& being willing to proceed in the fairest & most charitable Man-

ner with the Complainers, the Church make the said Complain-

ers this Offer : That the Affairs they desire should be refer'd to the

Judgment of a Council, should first be laid before the Commissio-

ners, either the whole Body of the Commissioners, or their Committee,

as they shall Chuse ; And that first Opportunity be first given to

them to use their Wisdom in Endeavours to put an End to our

Calamities, if they think fit; And that if They, after they have

had full Cognizance of the Affair, judge it necessary or expedient

that the Affair be refer'd to an ecclesiastical Council we are ready

to comply with it, and to refer our selves to such a Council in a

Manner agreeable to the Usage & Principles of Congregational

Churches : And we are willing to leave the Affair of calling a

Council wholly to the Advice of the Commissioners.

voted Unanimously,

Test. Jonath. Edwards Pastor.

[^203-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## A180. Letter to Edward Bromfield, October 16, 1753 180.JE-E.Bromfield 10-16-53

Jonathan EdwardsA180. JE to Edward Bromfield, 10/16/53. ANTS, f. 1753A, #4-5.

Stockbridge, Octob. 16, 1753

Honored and dear Sir,

As you have been pleased to mention to me the proposal lately made to the commissioners for Indian Affairs in Boston from the society in London, in which they say they were confirmed in the expedience of nominating nine persons in the provinces of Massachusetts, New York, and colony of Connecticut, that the society might choose six out of the members to be joined with the two Col. Williamses as commissioners for Stockbridge affairs, to act by correspondence with the commissioners in Boston, and to inform me what persons the commissioners have nominated, and to ask my thoughts of this.

I have considered of the matter with much deliberation. On being first informed that they speak of being partly led to this proposal by something I had written, I am very much at a loss [to know] what they could refer to. But on looking over my papers, by a rough draft of my letter to Mr. Mauduit which I have kept, I find I there referred to something I had said in letters I had once before written to the commissioners and another to the Speaker of the House of Representatives in these words: "What renders it the more necessary, that things here should be under the immediate care of trustees on the spot, is the misunderstanding and jealousy here subsisting between some of the chief of the present English inhabitants of the town, which is one of our greatest calamities. Things on this account do much more need careful inspection; and therefore the gentlemen entrusted ought be such as [are] perfectly impartial-- in no way interested in, or related to, these contending parties."

This I suppose must be what the society must have referred to in their late letter to you. But my meaning seems to be quite mistaken. What I then had in my mind, which I then supposed might have taken effect, was in being moved to some gentlemen of the best character and wholly impartial and disinterested and disengaged in the contention that had subsisted here, to come and settle here. And they should be entrusted in some degree with the care of our affairs.

But the thing which is now proposed by the corporation cannot answer in any measure the intention I had in view, and I supposed their making such a proposal must be owing to their unacquaintedness with the state of Stockbridge and the country around us. 'Tis probable that they supposed that Stockbridge was just in the corner of the province of the Massachusetts where it borders on the colonies of Connecticut and New York and that each of these colonies were so peopled originally that a number of persons of ability and character might be found in each of these provinces that might be well qualified to have the inspection and care of the important affairs of this place; who, by reason of their neighborhood, might have much greater advantage for a full and particular information on the state of things and the more frequent, easy, expeditious, and effectual interposition to direct and regulate them as the state [of] things requires on emergent occasions. But if they were as fully acquainted with our geography and the state of things here as we are, they would at once see that the appointing a kind of subordinate body of commissioners, out of those nominated to have the more immediate oversight and direction of our affairs, would have a contrary tendency to a very great degree; and that instead of expediting and making more easy the management of our affairs, it would unspeakably clog and embarrass them. Most of these gentlemen live at such a distance from us and so much more out of the way of communication with us than Boston and are at such a distance one from another, that it must render their proper inquiries and sufficient informations of our affairs and united acting in them and management of them infinitely cumbersome, and rendered so impracticable that it never can be expected to take place.

Boston being our metropolis and the chief center of business for the whole country, we have more frequent opportunities of reciprocal communication with Boston than with most of the places where these gentlemen live, taken singly. But how much greater still is the distance of these places, taken collectively. New York is nearly as far from us as Boston. Albany at nearest is 40 miles from us. Weathersfield is 70 miles. Hartford, the place of Mr. P. and L.,1 is near as far. Mr. Wolcott's habitation of Windsor is above 65. Mr. Lyman at Suffield is more than 50. Dr. Ashley at Westfield, above 40. Mr. Porter of Hadley, about 60. The communication of Stockbridge with Boston is more frequent and easy than even with Hartford and Weathersfield. And if the whole body of the commissioners lived at Weathersfield, they would not be under so good advantage to look after our affairs as they are at Boston, unless they should travel and from time [to] time come on the spot and view our affairs themselves. And how much more difficult must [be] the meeting of these persons to consult on our affairs than of the commissioners in Boston that live so near together. They often are called together in a few hours as occasions arise. But how otherwise will the case be with respect to the gentlemen nominated, who live at so great a distance one from another, Hartford and Weathersfield being about 130 miles distant from New York, and 110 from Albany. Hadley is about 100 from Albany, about 50 from Weathersfield, and about 180 from New York. Albany is about 170 from New York and there is nothing in the state of the country that gives occasion for any great communications from one of those places to another, unless from Albany to New York. As to Col. Ephraim Williams, who used to live at Stockbridge, his state of health is so exceedingly broken by many fits of the palsy that he has put all his estate out of his hands and is removed to live at Deerfield, which is about 200 miles from New York, about 70 from Weathersfield, about 120 miles from Albany on the usual road, and 80 from Stockbridge.

If we should take only the gentlemen in Connecticut alone, the commissioners in Boston can meet and confer and act unitedly with ten times the ease as they can. But general meetings from these distant places to confer on our affairs will be so difficult that there will [be] no reason ever to expect 'em. And indeed, if any such thing should be expected that our affairs should first come under the inspection and determination of those corresponding commissioners before they can properly fall under the cognizance of the commissioners in Boston, it must issue in that which will be little if anything short of laying a fatal block in the way of all further management of affairs and putting a final stop to all further proceedings in those affairs which are already sufficiently embarrassed.

There, sir, I have here represented my thoughts of this affair as they appear to me, humbly asking your candid acceptance of what I have written and pardon of the freedom I have used. I remain, sir,

Your most humble and obliged friend and servant,

J. E.

## A181. Letter to Thomas Gillespie, October 18, 1753 181.JE-T.Gillespie 10-18-53

Jonathan EdwardsA181. JE to Thomas Gillespie, 10/18/53. Probably a draft. ANTS, f. 1753A, #2, 10.

Stockbridge Octob. 18. 1753.

Rev. & dear Sir,

The last November I wrote a Letter to you, and de-

sired Mr. Foxcroft to put up with it for you one of my

Answers to Mr. Williams[^205-note1]. After that in the latter Part

of the Winter I received a Letter from you, dated June 15.

1752. with Milton on Hirelings, & duplicates of a Letter

from a Gentleman in Town &c. & Answers to the Reasons

of dissent &c.[^205-note2] I now return you my hearty thanks for

these Things. Since that I have received Letters from

Mr. Erskine McLaurin & Mr. Erskine, with various

Pamphlets & Prints relating to your extraordinary Affair.

I think dear that altho your sufferings are like to continue,

the General Assembly having neglected to restore you to

your former station & Employment in the Chh of Scot-

land[^205-note3]. yet your sufferings are attended with many mani-

festations of the Gentleness & fatherly Kindness & Favour

of the great Governour of the World, in the many alleviating

supporting Circumstances of your Persecution : In that so

many of God's Ministers and People have appeared to be

so much Concerned for you and have so zealously & yet

so properly exerted themselves in your behalf, and have

so many ways given their Testimony in your behalf

and to the Goodness of the Cause wherein you suffer,

& the unrighteousness of those Hardships which you have

been subjected to; And that even so great a Part of the

general Assembly themselves have in Effect given this Testi-

mony for you, in there being but a very small majori-

ty, but what openly appeared for the taking off the

Censure of the former assembly, without any Recantation,

or so much as Application from you desiring them so to do.

you

You have some peculiar Reasons to rejoyce in your suffer- [^205-note4]

ings, and to glorify God on the Account of them. They

having been so greatly taken Notice of by so many of the

People of and there being so much written concerning

them tends to render them, with their Circumstances,

and particularly the Patience and Meekness with

which you have suffered, so much the more extensively

& durably to the Glory of the Name of your blessed

Lord, for whom you suffer. God is rewarding you

by laying a Foundation, in what has been said & done

and written concerning your sufferings, for Glory to his

own Name, & [-] Honour to you, in his Church, in future

Generations. Your name will doubtless be mentioned

hereafter with peculiar Respect, on the Account of these

sufferings, in ecclesiastical History; As they are now

the Occasion of the Exercise of a tender Affection in

multitudes of Gods saints, that otherwise would perhaps

have never heard of you, and of their fervent Prayers

for you ; As they are doubtless an Occasion of the

Pe a peculiar Notice which saints & Angels in Hea-

ven take of you, and of their Praises to God on your

Account ; & will be the Occasion of a peculiar Re-

ward which God will hereafter bestow upon you,

when you shall be united to their Assembly.

As to my own Circumstances, I am still meeting

with Trouble, and expect no other as long as I live

in these this World. some great men have mighti-

ly opposed my continuing the missionary at stock-

bridge, and have taken occasion abundantly to re-

proach me, and endeavour my removal. But I

desire to bless God; He seems in some Respects to set me

out of their Reach. He raises me up Friends who [^205-note5]

are exerting themselves for me in Opposition to my

Enemies ; particularly the Commissioners for Indi-

an Affairs in Boston, with whom innumerable

Artifices have been used, to disaffect them towards

me, but altogether in vain. Governour Belcher

also has seen Cause much to exert Himself in

my behalf on Occasion of the Opposition made

to me. my People, both English & Indians stead-

fastly adhere to me, excepting the Family with

whom the Opposition began & those related to

that Family, which Family greatly opposed me

while at Northampton. Most numerous, con-

tinual & indefatigable Endeavours have been used

to undermine me, by alienating my People from

me : innumerable mean Artifices have been

used, with one and another, Young & old,

men & women, Indians & English ; but hither-

to they have been greatly disappointed. -- But yet

they are not weary. ------

As we, dear sir, have great Reason to sympathize one

with another, with peculiar Tenderness, our Circum-

stances being in so many Respects similar, so I

hope yo I shall partake of the Benefit of your

fervent Prayers for me. Let us thus endeavour to

help one another (tho' at a great distance) in travelling

through this wide wilderness. That we may have the

more joyful meeting in the Land of Rest, when we

have finished our weary Pilgrimage. I am dear sir,

your most affectionate Brother & fellow servt

Jonathan Edwards

My wife joins in most

affectionate Regards to you & yours.

[^205-note1]: *Misrepresentations Corrected*.

[^205-note2]: John Milton, *Considerations Touching the Likeliest Means to Remove Hirelings Out of the Church* (London, 1659); *A Letter from a Gentleman in Town to His Friend in the Country* (Edinburgh, 1752); *Answers to the Reason of Dissent from the Resolution of the General Assembly to Apply to Parliament for an Augmentation of Stipends* (Edinburgh, 1750).

[^205-note3]: In 1752 Gillespie had opposed the forced settlement of Andrew Richardson at Inverkeithing by the Scottish General Assembly and was removed from his own position as punishment.

[^205-note4]: **marginal.** [2]

[^205-note5]: **marginal.** [3]

## A182. Letter to Ephraim Williams, Jr. et al., November 19, 1753 182.JE-Williamsetal 11-19-53

Jonathan EdwardsA182. JE to Ephraim Williams et al., 11/19/53. RIHS, Ms. v. VI, pp. 6-7.

At a Meeting of the Church of Stockbridge, Novem. 19. 1753.

The Church having considered a Writing sent to the Pastor, to be

communicated to them, dated Octob. 26. 1753,[^206-note1] Signed Ephriam

Williams Jun Jonathan Devreux, Josiah Williams, Abigail

Dwight, Judith Williams; voted to send to the above-named

Persons the following Message.

Brethren & Sisters,

As you are Members of this Church, who have Subjected

your Selves to our Care and Watch, and as we are obliged to watch

over you, and Seek your spiritual Wellfare; we would propose

the following things to your Serious Consideration.

1. Whether you dont grossly abuse this Church, in saying The Church

intimates that they have a Right to determine & issue the Matters of

your Complaint themselves; And whether it ben't with the most gla-

ring Absurdity that you say that you think this is evidently hinted

in our first Vote in our saying these words; "WHETHER EVER

THEIR COMPLAINT BE CARRIED TO A COUNCIL, OR ANY OTHER

BESIDES THE CHURCH THEMSE[LVE]S, OR NO. ---- And again in the

second Vote in these words; " As to what is as we think unseaso-

nably & preposterously" (i.e. as beginning at the wrong End) "desired

in the foremention'd Writing, viz. that the things alledged therein

should be refer'd to the Judgment & final decision of a Council; Voted,

that it appears to this Church, that the perculiar state of the Church,

and also the Circumstances of the Case are such, that IF THE JUDG-

MENT OF THESE THINGS BE REFER'D TO ANY OTHER JUDGES

BESIDES THE CHURCH THEMSELVES, ---- When Nothing can be

more manifest, than that the Church in thus expressing themselves condi-

tionally, avoid Saying, or giving the least Intimation, whether they think

these things should be finally issued by themselves or no. Is it therefore

proper or becoming on such a Foundation, to go on in such a reflecting

reproachful Manner, to tell us, that this carries in it an Air of un-

reasonable stiffness, self-willedness, & also Guilt --- ? And then, in such

taunting Language to say, Now suppose the Pastor and Church should

meet, & gravely determine the Complaint to be groundless; & agree

That for the future they will view themselves in a good Light, and de-

cree that all other Churches should make the same Judgment, and

view them in the Same Light. &c?

2. Whether or no it becomes you, in this Application you make

to the Church, to which you have, in solemn Covenant, as in the Pre-

sence of God, united your selves, putting your selves under their Care

and Watch; to treat them in such an assuming Manner, inter-

spersing here and there, in invidious & supercilious Language,

such confusions Suggestions and Insinuations ; and that even be-

fore you give us any Opportunity to confer with you about those

things you find Fault with us for ; refusing to give us such an Oppor-

tunity, tho' it has been so much insisted on ; suggesting that our

votes carry in them an air of unreasonable stiffness, self-willedness

& Guilt, in not daring to venture the Affair on a proper Issue;

charging us with an unreasonable shyness, against bringing the

Matter

Matter of your Grievance, to a fair and impartial Trial ; and [^206-note2]

say, that our Votes appear manifestly calculated to relieve some

particular private Interest, rather than to serve a publick Cause,

notwithstanding the promoting the religious Interest of this Church

is the thing so much pretended to in our Votes ; & saying, there

is Ground to suspect Methods will be used to evade the Force of

Reasons, & tamper with Evidences : And again, saying, It ap-

pears to you, that under a Pretence of our paying a venerable Re-

gard to the honourable Commissioners, we are indeed Consulting

private Interest & artfully evading a proper & just Examination

& issuing the Matters of your Grievance ; adding that you must needs

think our Conduct a dark symptom of a bad Cause, and Conscious-

ness of the Danger and Consequences of a fair & impartial Trial:

And Again, suggesting, that what we have voted is a Fetch

& scheme to secure against a fair Trial, and thereby lengthen

out the Controversy, & protract Things, until there may be an

opening for Employment to the Destruction of the Churches

Peace &c.

We beseech you to reflect on the Temper you manifest in these

things, and consider whether this be a Conduct becoming Christi-

ans, and whether herein you han't given this Church Just & great

Cause of Offense ; and whether the tolerating such Treatment

of Churches by their Members, in their Application to 'em

in ecclesiastical matters, would not tend utterly to subvert

all Peace and Order in Churches.

3. Whether or no your saying, You think it evident by the Votes

of the Church that the Church claims a Power of determining

& Issuing Matters of Complaint against themselves, does con well agree

with your afterwords charging the Church with dishonesty & Incon-

sistence in taking upon them to do one ecclesiastical thing them-

selves, without Advice from others, even so much as suspending one

of its Members. Certainly if we claim a Power to do all our

selves alone, without any Advice from others ; then we may, at

the Same Time, claim a Power to suspend one Person, without

Inconsistence with our Pretences.

4. Is your now denying it to be proper that you should lay the

Reasons & Evidences of your Complaint before the Church, and as-

serting that the Nature of things evidently requires that you

should not, well consist with your past Pretences, when you was

cited by this Church to come & let them hear your Reasons & Evi-

dences, & you utterly disclaimed and disobeying the Church in this

Matter : not pretending to refuse ever to do it; and pleading

that your Affairs required sOne of you to be absent, that you could

not be all present at that Time ; and pleading that this Matter

might be defer'd 'till you could see Col. dwight & the Church

together.

5. In your Complaint you Say, your heartily desire, on your

Parts, to have the Matters of offence removed, and that we offer you

Christian Satisfaction on these Heads ; and say that in Case we decline

this, you desire we would join with you in calling a Council &c.

pretending

[^206-note3]

pretending not to desire a Council, but on Refusal of satisfaction.

Now we desire you to consider, whether if you are hearty in them Seeking

Satisfaction (and so to prevent Occasion for a Council) as you profess, you

are consistent in refusing fully to lay before us the Matters of Offence,

and plain Evidences thereof for our Conviction. It is not plainly setting

before guilty Persons the Evidences of their Guilt, a proper step to be

taken for their Conviction, that they may be brought to proper Humilia-

tion and Repentance? And especially, is not proper when publick Satis-

faction is required, that the Persons supposed to have offended, should be

shown not only, that they are guilty, but should be shown that their

Guilt is attended with that Visibility & Evidence, as properly to require

publick Satisfaction?

6. Some of your Charges are only general. Thus you charged the Pastor

with a Series of Actions, wherein He has behaved altogether unbecom-

ing his Character as a Minister, and his Profession as a Christian. But

you specify but one thing as an Offence in Him in particular, tho' your

general Charge implies a great Number of very heinous Offences.

We desire you to consider, whether it be reasonable to expect publick

Satisfaction of Him for such a Number of Crimes, when he is not so much

as informed what they are, or that the Church should refer their series

of great Offences, to the final decision of a Council, without his or

their knowing what the things that they refer, & are to [be] judged of.

7. Your Complaint not only contains Matters of Charges against the

Pastor, and Church in general, but against some particular Members,

Particularly against two of them aga as guilty of Forgery. Now we desire

you to consider whether you act reasonably, in refusing to give expecting

that this Matter, as well as others, should be carried directly to a Coun-

cil, without giving the Church any Opportunity to hear what Eviden-

ces there are of their being guilty of such a Crime ; or what they can

say for themselves ; or knowing but that these particular Persons would

be convinced of their Fault, and would give you Satisfaction, if you

should fully lay before them the Grounds & Reasons of your being of-

fended with them, and the Evidences of their Guilt. And have we any

Power to force these Brethren, that we have solemnly taken under our

Care, to refer this Matter, which you charge them with, to a Council,

which you and we should chuse for them ; without ever hearing

them our Selves.

8. How can the Church know whether[-] there will be any Occasion for

a Council, before they have heard particularly what the accused and the

Accusers will say, when they appear Face to Face? How can they know

but that, when they come to confer together, the Accused may offer that to

the Accuser, which may convince 'em that they have been misinformed

and that at least some of the Charges are grounded on plain Mistakes

of Matters of Fact, to their full Satisfaction that they have taken up

things very wrong, so that they themselves may be convinced that there

is no Occasion to trouble any Council with those things, or to carry such

groundless Accusations any where abroad, to the Injury of the good Name

of innocent Persons?

9. And besides all that has been already mention'd, let it be con-

sidered, that before ever you sent in your Complaint, most of you who

are Complainers, having openly withdrawn from the Communion of the

Church, the Church had voted to call upon you to appear to give the Rea-

sons of this Conduct. In which Vote one of your selves was concurring.

--- The Church then when they first took this Matter in Hand, had

doubtless

[^206-note4]

doubtless Power so to do. None, we presume, that this was not a

Matter that was proper for the Churches Enquiry & Examination. And

if they had Power to take it in Hand at all, they had Power at least

to cite you to appear before 'em, in order to hear you upon it. And

if it could be properly taken out of their Hands, to be carried before

other Judges, it must be in Consequence of Such an Appearance, and the

Church's first hearing your Reasons, and conferring with you upon

them Face to Face, & not by refusing to appear at all. And as by

your own declaration, Part of the Design of your Complaint is to give

the Reasons of your Said withdrawing Communion, therefore the

Church (as they have Power to demand Opportunity particularly to en-

quire of you, and confer with you shows these Reasons, before they

are carried to other Judges) have Power to require you to appear, more

particularly to explain your Complaint, and exhibit the Evidences

on which you ground the Righteousness of that Treatment of the

Church, and God's Ordinances in it; viz. openly rejecting Communion

with them in these Ordinances. ---- We pray you to consider how

strange and unexampled is the Method of your Proceeding. How

many Instances have there been in the Countrey of Persons absent-

ing themselves from the Communion in Churches to which they belong-

ed, from their being offended with the Minister or Church? And

when was ever any such thing advanced, that the Churches that had

the Care of them, had no Power to call 'em to an Account before

'em in such Cases? How unreasonable is that Rule of Proceeding

which is now in Effect advanced by you! viz. That Persons that

are cited before any Judicatory (in a Case in which they have

proper Power & Right to cite 'em to appear) may, without Com-

plying with the Citation, throw in a Complaint against that Judi-

catory ; and by that Means, not only claim Liberty of Appeal, but

also at once to divest that Judicatory of all Powers; & so entirely

to set 'em aside, as even to make void their Citation. Let it be

Considered, whether according to such Maxims as these, Persons in

all Cases whatever, mayn't set aside and disable all Judicato-

ries on Earth, and exempt themselves from even appearing before

any Judge, 'till the last Day.

We intreat you seriously & thoroughly to consider these things. If you

do so, we doubt not but you must be convinced that your Conduct to-

wards the Church is very unreasonable and injurious.

And as to our joining with you in referring the Matters of your Com-

plaint to other Judges besides the Church, 'tis time enough to talk fur-

ther of that Matter, when you have done your Duty with respect to your

appearing before this Church, as you have been required, & which we still

demand of you. You must first appear before this Church, to exhi-

bit your Evidences, & give the Church Opportunity to interrogate you

concerning the Reasons of your withdrawing from their Communion,

(those of you who have withdrawn) before any such Step can be taken

as you propose (if it ever be taken) without the plainest Irregularity &

Absurdity. And since you have refused to obey the Church, when cited

to appear before 'em, and persisted in it against the repeated Remon-

strances of the Pastor ; insisting on that Reason, that your Affairs

would not allow all the Complainers to be present; we may well

expect

expect now, that you should find a Time, when all of you that [^206-note5]

have signed the Complaint will be present; & inform us of it;

that a Church Meeting may be appointed to hear you all together.

which we will wait in Expectation for the present.

As to the Commissioners first having an Opportunity to use their

Wisdom, to see if they can't remove our Difficulties, before their

Affairs here are put into the Hands of others, that should have

Power, in Effect, to break 'em up, without their having any such Op-

portunity ; When you come to give us the Reasons & Evidences of your

Complaint, and so the Reasons of your withdrawment from our Com-

munion, We shall be willing more particularly to give our Reasons

why we insist on such a Method, so natural & rational, & evidently

necessary; and shall be ready to hear your Objections against any

thing the Church has voted in that Affair, if offered with Decency.

But you may assure yourselves, we shall never think ourselves obli-

ged to hear you, if in discoursing on this subject, you persist in treating

the Church in the Manner you have done, in your late written

message. or ever admit any to speak on your Behalf, that treats

the Church in such a Manner.

As the Church stands ready to meet you, and confer with

you ; so we would not have you expect that we should carry on

a Controversy with you by writing, or meet any more to hear

your written Messages, you your selves refusing to be present.

voted Unanimously

Test: Jonathan Edwards Pastor

## A183. Letter to Timothy Dwight (Fragment), December 10, 1753 183.JE-T.Dwight 12-10-53

Jonathan EdwardsA183. JE to [Col. Timothy Dwight], 11/10/53. Fragment. ANTS.

Stockbridge, December 10, 1753

dear sir,

This is to desire you renewedly to take

into your Consideration your removing &

settling in this Town. 'Tis probable that

Brigr D---t[^207-note1] and the Williams's would

be glad to exchange with you. And as

to your great objection against coming here

that here you will not have sufficient Busi-

ness to keep you employed, I am willing to

allow that there is something in it; But yet

I cannot but be of opinion, that it has

much more than its due weight with you;

especially considering how much there is

in the other scale to counterballance. On

the one Hand it is to be considered, that

tho' you will be more distant from your Business

at Enfield and Suffield, yet there will be no necessi-

ty of relinquishing it; and perhaps not

your Probate Business. But if you resign the

latter, you will not be out of Employ; you

will probably find, one way or other, more

Business here than you expect, & full as

much as will be for your Comfort. 'Tis

further to be considered, that you have

all

[.. .]

[^207-note1]: Joseph Dwight.

## A184. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, February 5, 1754 184.JE-T.Foxcroft2-5-54

Jonathan EdwardsA184. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 2/5/54. BRBL, f. 1297. In Foxcroft's hand on verso: "Revd Mr Edwards / Recd Feb. 27. 1754. / Answd ye Same day."

Stockbridge Feb. 5. 1754.

Rev. & honoured Sir,

I humbly desire you to [-] take the Care of this

Pacquet to Mr. McLaurin of Scotland. ---

Since I returned from Boston I have wrote

often to you, and sent many Letters & Pacquets

of Great Importance; but never have heard whe-

ther any one of them has arrived. I long since

sent to away my Book against the Arminians,

And want to know very much what is become of it.

--- I have here inclosed a number of subscriptions

which Mr. Bellamy obtained. I have not Counted

them. Mr. Bellamy told me that there was

about 170, And that He had obtained about 30

more, which He had in another Paper, which

He Could not very readily find. Please to inform

the Printer of this. I was the Week before last

at Mr. Bellamy's, at Bethlem; being sent for

by Him, to give Advice, together with some

other Ministers, on occasion of his being applied

to by the Presbyterian Congregation in N. York,

to be their Pastor. We did advise Mr. B. [not] to [JE om.]

leave his People at present, His People being great

ly united to Him, and it appearing doubtful

whether there would be an happy Union, & gene-

ral

ral Satisfaction, in the Congregation at N. York, [^208-note1]

with respect to Mr. B----y's Ministry, & Principles

concerning the Admission of Members. We tho't

that Congregation had been too hasty in their Proceed-

ing, and had so thoroughly considered the matter,

& sufficiently ripen'd things, for the giving Mr. B-

a Call. --- But I think it something probable

that they will Renew their Call. If they should,

and it should be united in it, and take proper

steps in their Proceeding, I don't know but they may

succeed. But it will depend much on the Opi-

nion of the Consociation of that County. --

For my Part, I wish they might succeed. For

mr altho Mr. B. is in some Respects a little

unpolished ; yet he is a Man of such Gifts & Grace,

such Activity Resolution, attended with sagacity

& Prudence, that I know of man in any measure

so likely to be a means of uniting that Congregation,

& maintaining its peace, of greatly increasing & very

much promoting the Interest of Religion in that

flourishing Town as He. He has the Happiest

Talents of managing in the midst of difficulties,

pleasing & influencing all sorts of People; and yet

suppressing & bearing down those things that are

bad; of any man I know of. He is of very

good Natural Abilities, benevolent, agreeable,

sprightly & sociable; as well as of extraordinary

Gifts for the Pulpit, & has the greatest Ability [^208-note2]

to Command the Attention of an Auditory,

& reach the Hearts of his Hearers, of any

Man I know of. And is yet an indefa-

tigable student. --- I should greatly re-

joyce to hear of his being settled in

that Congregation, & should think, if

it were brought about with general

Satisfaction, it was a Token of great

Good to that City.

I am hon'd sir

your obliged son & servt

Jonath. Edwards.

Rev. Mr. Foxcroft

[^208-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^208-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## A185. Letter to Joseph Dwight, February 25, 1754 185.JE-J.Dwight 2-25-54

Jonathan EdwardsA185. JE to Joseph Dwight, 2/25/54. ANTS, f. 1754, #4. Two letters of same date. No MSS; Dwight transcripts only.

[Letter 1:]

Stockbridge, Feb. 25, 1754

HoW[ ] Sir,

I have inclosed, & send to you, a copy of what

Mr Hollis has sent to me, signifying his desire, that I should take

the care of his school for the future. This is to ask the favour

of you, that, when you think fit to resign the care of that school,

you would give me seasonable notice of it; & likewise that you

would be pleased to inform me of the present state of the

school, how many boys belong to it, & who they are, & what

bedding & other household stuff, or utensils & tools for work,

or books, paper, ink [ ] or other implements for writing, or other

things, are now in being, which have now been procured for the

benefit of that school, at Mr Hollis' expence; that I may take

care of them. I also request, that you would give me a full

account of the state of the school, in all its present circumstances;

that I may the better know what needs to be done, in speedily

taking care of it, & ordering matters relating to it; so that the great

ends of it may be best promoted, & Mr Hollis' noble & christian

desires & just expectations may be best answered. I would pray

you to give me notice, when I may wait on you, in order to re-

ceive from you this information, so as best to suit your leis-

ure & convenience. Herein you will oblige

Your most humble servant,

Jonathan Edwards.

[Letter 2:]

Stockbridge, Feb. 25, 1754.

Honble Sir,

It is now late in the evening, & the evenings are

so shortened, that there can be no opportunity for the conference

proposed this evening. I should be glad to wait on you tomor-

row on this affair if you should be at home. But as you

say that you are like to be from home, I will wait on you

God willing the next day at or about 9 o clock in the morn-

ing. I suppose that Mr Hollis does not expect that I should

take the care of defraying the charges of his school, until I have

taken the affairs of the school in general under my care

Probably the General Court expects to bear the charge of the

school until some agent of Mr Hollis has opportunity for this. But

this must be left to your honour's judgement.

I remain, Sir,

your humble servant

Jonathan Edwards.

## A186. Letter to Joseph Bellamy, February 28, 1754 186.JE-J.Bellamy 2-28-54

Jonathan EdwardsA186. JE to Joseph Bellamy, 2/28/54. ANTS, f. 1756-59C, #6.

Stockbridge

Rev. and dear Sir,

'Tis wholly needless that I should come again on the affair of your going to N. York, and altogether improper, as I suppose now the affair will properly be referred to the association or consociation. And besides, I think I can do more good by writing than by coming.

I wish you had been a little more particular in your information. I desire you would write to me again as soon as possible. I have a mind to write a letter to the Moderator of your Association; but only I want to know much more about the matter, that I may know the better how to write. Please to inform me whether Lawyer Smith has received my letter, and what he writes to you. And what has been done at N. York, and at the Presbytery, and what and after what manner application has been made in this affair, and what is going to be done further. Probably I shall have mind to write to some others besides ministers about this affair. Therefore, I desire you to be particular and full and speedy in your writing to me. Particularly inform me when the Association meets on this affair.

By the will of God, Mr. Hopkins and I are going a journey to Deerfield the last week in March about the installment of Mr. Billing at Greenfield. I would also go to Windsor before I return; shall therefore be gone near three weeks.

If it should finally so come to pass that you should remove to N. York, my wife desires to buy your Negro woman, as she supposes she will do better for the country than the city. She will probably come along through your place some time in April, when she will talk with you about it.

The last week, I received a letter from Mr. Hollis in England, in which he commits his school wholly to my care, and makes me sole Trustee of all his affairs here. I am, Sir,

Your affectionate friend and brother,

Jonath. Edwards.

## A187. Letter to Joseph Dwight, February 28, 1754 187.JE-J.Dwight 2-28-54

Jonathan EdwardsA187. JE to Joseph Dwight, 2/28/54. ANTS, f. 1754, #5. No MS; Dwight trans. only.

Stockbridge, Feb. 28, 1754.

Hon'd Sir,

To prevent mistakes & future controversies, I would inform

you, that, when I came yesterday from your house, I went directly to

the boarding-school to inform Mr Smith of our conclusion, & get

some more certain information concerning the state of the school;

and that although Mr. Smith had before mentioned 10 boys as belong-

ing to the school, yet he now tells me that three of the largest had

left the school, & I understanding that they were men grown told him that I

would not have him take them any more. I also understand that another of the

ten boys has been gone from the school for some time to his father's house where he is sick

viz. Unkatunk's son Abraham; & that I therefore shall not expect to be accountable for the

boarding, for the time which I mentioned, of more than are actually in the school for

that time. When I was at the boarding-school, I observed several English children

of your Honour's family, that I suppose are there boarded & instructed. And

as these share in the labours of the schoolmaster & eat with those of whom

I have the care I think there should be some consideration of it

I will also signify that I have often been informed that the Mo-

hawks have long had the resolution, all of them both old & young to leave Stock-

bridge as soon as [sugaring][^211-note1] time is over. I have appointed a conference with

them to-morrow concerning the matter; & if I find that they stand to such a

resolution, I shall then suspend any farther expence upon them from that

time on Mr Hollis' account; & shall give you information accordingly.

I am, Sir,

Your most humble servant,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^211-note1]: Dwight leaves a blank in the copy; the supplied word, taken from other letters, is conjectural but probable, since making maple sugar occurred in the spring.

## A188. Letter to Joseph Dwight, March 2, 1754 188.JE-J.Dwight 3-2-54

Jonathan EdwardsA188. JE to Joseph Dwight, 3/2/54. RIHS, Ms. v. VI, p. 9, #139. Addressed on verso "To the Honble / Joseph Dwight Esq. / In Stockbridge."

Stockbridge March. 2. 1754.

Honble Sir,

Having confer'd with the Mohawks, they inform

me that they had all agreed & resolved the last Fall,

that they would all go away this Spring, And that

their doing So is agreeable to the determination of the

Council of their Nation, the Sachems of the Cannéen-

ghe Tribe, and can't be altered unless it be by a

new determination of their Sachems. --- Therefore

agreeable to what I signified before, I shall forbear

to expend any of Mr. Hollis' Money upon them so

long as they appear to persist in this Resolution. -

agreeably to this, I informed Mr. Smith the last

Night. I am sir,

your most humble servt

Jonath. Edwards.

## A189. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, March 6, 1754 189.JE-T.Foxcroft 3-6-54

Jonathan EdwardsA189. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 3/6/54, and enclosure. BRBL, ff. 1298, 1307. Foxcroft's note on verso of cover letter: "Revd Mr Edwards / Recd Apr. 9. 1754."

Stockbridge March. 6. 1754.

Rev. & honoured Sir,

In my great Fulness of Care and Business I have

forgot whether I had received your Favour of Jan.

3 before I last wrote to you or since. However I now

thank you for that Letter. With that I received a

couple of Letters from Scotland. I desire to be thank-

ful to God who has restored you from your late Ill-

ness.

I have here troubled you with another small

Addition to be made to my Book that is in the

Press with directions annex'd where to insert it

I think you will be at no difficulty to find the

Place.

I am about to write to the Commissioners and

Mr Prince about Mr. Hollis's school and what

I have done and about to do in Pursuance of

his desire that I should take the Care of his

school which Letters you will probably see

This with respectful Salutations to your Fa-

mily & desire of your Prayers is from

honoured sir

your greatly obliged

Son & Servant

Jonath. Edwards.

P.S. I would propose

whether it might not

be best to put the Addi-

tions Papers contain-

ing the Additions to be

made to my Book, into

the M. S. at the Places

where they are to be in-

serted, to prevent their

being overlook'd & for

gotten.

Honoured sir. I just now, (It being the 11th of March) received your Letter

of Feb. 27. after I had folded up this & all my letters. I thank you for your favour

---- I should prefer such a Page as that of my answer to Mr Williams rather than such

a small Page as you mention less than a Psalter. But yet I should insist on good white

Paper, and his best Types. --- N. York Congregation tho denied have not given over

seeking for Mr. B. they have sent up again after Him. But now take a new method, they

don't as yet make Application to Mr. Bellamy, but to the association to which He belongs. -- I am something inclined to think they will prevail. -- I wish the printing

of my Book might be hastend. I am sorry Mr. Kneeland has not yet begun it. I

am afraid the subscribers will be out of Patience. I am sir,

with greatest respect & Gratitude

your &c.

J.E.

The Rev. Mr. Foxcroft

189. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, n.d. [3/6/54], enclosure. BRBL, f. 1307.

N. B. I desire that what is written in th on the

Opposite leaf may be inserted, in the Body of the

discourse (not in the margin) in that section of the IId

Part. entitled Of Liberty of Will consisting in

Indifference. near the Beginning. after these words,

[-] or words like these. "But inasmuch as this

"opinion has been of such long standing in the World,

"and has been so generally received, and greatly insisted on

"by Pelagians, semi-Pelagians, Jesuits, Socinians, Ar-

"minians & others, It may deserve a yet more full Consi-

deration. & therefore I shall proceed to a more particu-

"lar & thorough Enquiry into this Notion." *

_________________________________________________________

In that section of the IVth Part that treats of the Ob-

jection about Stoical Fate, I mention the Epicureans

as maintaining a Doctrine of Contingence opposite to the

Fate of & Necessity of the stoics. This is the Notion

I have had: but on thinking further on the Matter

I am a little diffident of the sufficiency of my Evidence

of the Matter. I therefore would leave the Judgment

of that matter with you, who have greater opportuni-

ties to know; and if I am mistaken, please to make

the necessary Alterations. I am sir,

your humble servt

Jonath. Edwards.

## A190. Letter to Josiah Willard, March 8, 1754 190.JE-J.Willard 3-8-54

Jonathan EdwardsA190. JE to Josiah Willard, 3/8/54. MA Archives, vol. 32, pp. 476-78a. MS draft in ANTS, f. 1754, #6. Addressed on verso "To the Honourable / Josiah Willard Esq. / Secretary for the / Province of the / Massachusetts Bay / In Boston /These."

[2. Sent copy, Mass. Archives:]

Stockbridge March. 8. 1754

Honourable Sir,

Having lately received a Letter from the Rev. Mr Isaac Hollis

in England, concerning his school in this Place, desiring me to

take the Care of it, I thought it proper & just, by the first Op-

portunity, to give you Information of it ; as the Affair of this school

is what the general Court have interested themselves in, and

have been waiting to know the Mind of its pious and generous

Founder & Patron concerning. And not knowing whether

He has signified his Mind in any Letter to your Honour, or

any publick Committee, or any other way for the Informa-

tion of the honourable Assembly, I have with this sent an

Extract of Mr. Hollis's Letter to me, for you either to com-

municate to the general Assembly, or otherwise to dispose of,

according to your discretion.

After I received this Letter from Mr. Hollis, I speedily informed

Brigadier dwight of it : Who manifested Himself ready to resign

the Care of the school ; But offered to continue things in their

present Situation for a Week or Fortnight, 'till I could be pre-

pared to take the Care of it ; provided that I would engage to

answer the Expence from the day that I received Mr. Hollis's

Orders. I signified to him, that I supposed the general Court

expressed no other than to be at the Charge of the school 'till

some Agent for Mr. Hollis could possibly be in a Capacity to

take Care of it. But He insisting on the contrary, I did on Advice ac-

cept his Offer. The special Reason of my desiring Him to take Care

of the School, as he had done, for a little while, tho' it were at

Mr. Hollis's Expence, was this; The Mohawks had often in-

formed me and others of a Resolution they had taken of all

going away this spring, to return no more : And I was willing to

prevent their being broken up immediately, & all sent Home,

before I could have proper Opportunity to inform them of Mr.

Hollis's new Orders, and thoroughly to inform my self whether

they would all persist in their Resolution of going Home this

spring. The last Friday, I had a Conference with them all,

Men, Women & Children, at my House, many of my Neighbours

being present; when I open'd the Affair fully to them. They ap-

pear'd still to persist in their Resolution of going away ; And said

they had come to such an Agreement the last Fall all to go

away this spring, in Pursuance of a determination of the Coun-

cil of their Nation ; and that they could not act otherwise,

without applying renewedly to the said Council of the

sachems of their Tribe. I gave Col. dwight Notice of

what

what had pass'd ; and informed Him that I should forbear to [^214-note1]

expend any thing more upon them, so long as they persisted

in this Resolution. But since that, I have had the offer of

half the Boys that belong to the school, who are of the six Na-

tions; viz. three of 'em ; there being but six in all. Their Pa-

rents came to me, earnestly desiring me to take their Children,

manifesting themselves willing to take Care of their own main-

tenance, not expecting that the Province would maintain

'em any longer. I accordingly consented to take them : They

were just then going into the woods to make sugar, taking

their Children with them, as their manner is. And now I

wait for Nothing but their Return in Order to the taking

them under my Care. If any of the Rest should in like man-

ner change their Minds, as to the taking their Children away

to their own Countrey, I stand ready to provide for their main-

tenance and Education. And with the leave of the honoura-

ble Commissioners, whose servant (under God) I am, shall

take the Care of Mr. Hollis's School according to his desire.

I shall need sir, your Advice with respect to the House in

which the school has lately been kept, whether I may still

make use of it for the Benefit of the boarding school ; The House

having been built at the Charge of the Province, on Land

which our Indians have sequester'd for the Benefit of that

school. I am

Honoured sir,

with the greatest Respect

your most humble servt

Jonathan Edwards.

The honourable Josiah Willard Esq.

[^214-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

Sir

pay him out of it.
