## A201. Letter to Thomas Prince, April 14, 1755 201.JE-T.Prince, 4-14-55

Jonathan EdwardsA201. JE to Thomas Prince, 4/14/55. AAS, Curwen Papers, Box 3, f. 3. Addressed by JE on back "To the Rev. / Mr. Thos Prince / In Boston" with notation by Prince: "[From] Mr Jonathn Edwards / Stockbridg. April. 14. 1755. / Boston. [rec'd?] ---- 23."

Stockbridge April. 14. 1755.

Rev & honoured sir,

I have no Heart to propose to the Commissi-

oners any such Thing as maintaining Mr.

Hollis's School, while we wait to hear from

Him. I have observed an Aversion in 'em to

meddle in his affairs ; And then I cannot say

so much concerning the Advantage that that

school is like to be of, in this Time of war &

Confusion, as I think will be likely to induce

'em to run the venture of being at such a Charge:

But unless I hear very speedily from Mr Hollis

shall throw up his school.

I would intreat you very speedily to deliver

this Letter to Mr. speaker Hubbard.

We have some Thoughts of sending my

daughter Lucy to Boston to live at your House

this Summer, according to a former Invitation

from you, & repeated pressing Invitation from

Miss Sally. ---

My Wife Joins with me in respectful

Salutations to you Mrs Prince & Miss Sally.

Asking a Rememberance in your Prayers

I am Sir,

your obliged humble servt

Jonathan Edwards.

The Rev. Mr. Prince.

## A202. Letter to Joseph Hawley, [After January 1, 1755] 202.JE-J.Hawley aft.1-1-55

Jonathan EdwardsA202. JE to Joseph Hawley, n.d. [after 1/1/55]. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #31. Possibly accompanied JE's letter to Thomas Prince of 4/14/55.

Sir

I have sent a Letter to Mr. Prince by the Bearer,

to be committed to your Care. I request of you the Favour of

taking special Care of it, & delivering it with your own Hands,

assoon as ever You get to Boston. Pray don't fail. herein

you will particularly oblige. yours &c.-

J. Edwards.

To Maj. Hawley

## A203. Letter to John Erskine, April 15, 1755 203.JE-J.Erskine 4-15-55

Jonathan EdwardsA203. JE to John Erskine, 4/15/55. ANTS, f. 1755, #1, 4. Addressed "To the / Rev. Mr. John Erskine / Minister of the Gospel / at Culross in Scotland."

Stockbridge April 15. 1755.

Rev. & dear Sir,

The last year in the Spring I received, without a Letter, a Pacquet,

containing the following Books ; [------------------------------------],[^228-note1]

Casaubon on Enthusiasm, Warburton's Principles of natural & reveled

Religion, Merrick on Christ the true Vine, Campbell's Apostles no

Enthusiasts, discourse on the prevailing Evils of the present Time,

Remarks on Apostles no Enthusiasts, Moncrief's Review & Examina-

tion of Some Principles in Campbell's Apostles no Enthusiasts, Gilbert

of the Guilt and Pardon of Sin, Hervey on the Cross of Christ, An Ac-

count of the Orphan School &c. at Edinburgh, Memorial concerning

the Surgeon's Hospital, Gairdners Account of the Old Peoples Hospital, State

of the Society in Scotland for propagating Christian Knowledge, Abridge

ment of the Rules of Said Society, Regulations of the Town's Hospital

at Glasgow, Annals of the Persecutions of the Protestants in France.[^228-note2]

In the Beginning of last december, I received another Pacquet

without a Letter, The wrapper superscribed with your Hand. In this

were the following Pamphlets ; A sermon by a Lay Elder before the

Commission, A Letter to a Gentleman at Edinburgh, Resolution of the

gen. Assembly of May 22. 1736. Rutherford's Power of Faith and

Prayer, Enquiry into the Method of Settling Parishes, The Nature of the

Government and Constitution of the Chh of Scotland, Essay on Gospel

& Legal Preaching, Necessity of Zeal for the Truth, A vindication of

the Protestant doctrine of Justification against the Charge of Antino-

mianism[^228-note3]. The last week I received a Letter from you dated July 11. 54.[^228-note4]

which was found at Mr. Prince's by one that went to Boston from hence,

and had lain there Mr. Prince could not tell how long. In this

Letter you make mention of these last mention'd Pamphlets received

last december. I now return you my hearty thanks for this Letter,

& these generous Presents. I should have wrote to you long ago had

I not been prevented by the longest & most tedious sickness that ever

I had in my Life ; I being followed with Fits of the Ague, which came upon

me about the middle of last July, and were for a long Time very se-

vere and exceedingly wasted my Flesh & strength, so that I became

like a skeleton. I had several Intermissions of the Fits by the use

of the Peruvian bark ; but they never wholly left me 'till about the

middle of last January. In the mean time, I once several Times

attempted to write letters to m some of my friends about affairs

of Importance ; But found that I could bear but little of such writing.

Once in attempting to write a Letter to Mr. Burr, a Fit of the

Ague came upon me while I was writing; so that I was obliged

to lay by my Pen. when my Fits left me, they left me in

a poor weak state, all over bloated; so that I fear'd whether I

was not going into a dropsy. I am still something swell'd, & much

overrun

overrun with scarbutick Maladies. Nevertheless I have of late gradu- [^228-note5]

ally gain'd Strength.

I lately received a Letter from Mr. McLaurin, dated Aug. 13. 54.[^228-note6] which

Mr. Prince sent me with a Letter from Himself, wherein He informed

that the Captain of the same ship that brought the Letter also brought

an Account of Mr. McLaurin's death, that He died w very suddenly with

an Apoplexy, a little before He left Glasgow. since I received that Letter,

I sent to Mr. Prince desiring to know more of the Certainty of the Ac-

count : Mr. Prince writes back, that He sees no Reason to doubt of it.

---- This is an affecting Piece of News: It is an Instance of death which

I have much Cause to lament. He has long shewn Himself to be a

very worthy, kind & obliging Friend & Correspondent of [-] mine. And

doubtless the Church of Scotland has much Cause to lament his death:

There is reason to think that He was one of them that stood in

the Gap, to make up the Hedge in these evil Times. He was a

wise, steady & most faithful Friend of Gospel Truth, and vital Piety,

in these days of great Corruption. I wish that I may take warning

by it, as well as by my own late sickness to prepare for my departure

Hence.

I have nothing very comfortable to write concerning my own success

in this Place. The Business of the Indian mission, since I have been

here, has been attended with strange Embarassments, such as I

never could have expected or so much as once dream'd of ; ari of

such a Nature, and arising from such a Quarter, that I take no de-

light in being very particular & explicit upon it. But besides what

I especially refer to, some Things have lately happened that have occasion'd

great disturbance among the Indians, and have tended to alienate

'em from the English. b As particularly the killing of one of them

in the Woods by a Couple of Travelers, white men, who met

Him , And the contended with Him. And tho' the men

were apprehended & imprisoned, yet on their Trial, they escaped

without sentence of death ; One of them receiving a lighter Punish-

ment, as guilty of Man-slaughter : By which these Indians, and

also the Indians of some other Tribes, were greatly displeased and

disaffected towards the English. Since this, the last fall, some

Indians from Canada (doubtless instigated by the French) broke

in upon us on the sabbath, between meetings, and fell upon

an English Family, and kill'd three of them, which occasioned

a great alarmed in the Town & in the Countrey. Multitudes came

from various Parts for our defence, that night & the next ; and

many of these Conducted very foolishly towards our Indians on

this occasion, suspecting them to be guilty of doing the Mis-

chief, charging them with it, & threatning to Kill them, &

the like. After this, a Reward being offered by some private

Gentleman, to some that came this way as soldiers, if they

would bring them the scalp of a Canada Indian ; Two men w

ere so extremely foolish & wicked that they, [--] in the night, dug [^228-note7]

one of our Indians, that had then lately died, out of his Grave, to

take off his scalp; that by pretending that to be the scalp of a

Canada Indian, whom they had met & killed in the Woods,

they might get the promised Reward. When this was discovered,

the men were punished. But this did not hinder but that such

an Act greatly increased their Jealousy & disaffection towards the

English. Added to these things, we have many white People in

the neighbourhood, Many dutch & some English, that will at all

Times, without any Restraint give them Rum ; which is a Constant

Temptation to their most predominant Lust.

Tho' I have but little success, & many discouragements here at Stock-

bridge, yet Mr. Hawley, Missionary among the six Nations (who went

from N. England to Onohohquaughe, a Place more than 200 miles

to the westward from hence) has of late had much Encouragement.

Religion seems to be a growing spreading Thing among the savages in

that Part of America, by his means; And there is an hopeful Prospect

of way being made for another Missionary in those Parts. which

may have happy Consequences, unless the six Nations should go over

to the French ; which there is the greatest Reason to expect, unless

the English should exert Themselves vigorously & sucessfully against

the French in America, this year. They seem to be waiting to see

whether this will be or no, in Order to determine whether to

entirely to desert the English, and Cleave to the French. and if the

six Nations should forsake the English, it may be expected that

the stockbridge Indians, & almost all nations of Indians in North

America will follow 'em. It seems to be the most Critical

season with the British dominions in America, that ever was since

the first settlement of these Colonies. and all probably will de-

pend of the warlike Transactions of the Present year. what will

be done I can't tell. We are all in a Commotion from one End of

the British America to the other : one to and various Expeditions

are Projected, and preparing for, One to Ohio, another to the

French forts in Novatia Scotia, another to Crown Point. But

these affairs are not free of Embarrassments : great difficulties arise

in our Present most important affairs, through the disunited

state of the several Governments. 'Tis hard for them to g agree

upon means & measures. And we have no Reason to think

the French are behind us in their Activity & Preparations.

A dark Cloud seems to hang over us : we need the Prayers of all

our Friends, & all Friends to the Protestant Interest. stockbridge

is a Place much exposed, and what will become of us in the

struggles that are coming on, God only knows.

I have hear'd that Messrs. Tennent & davies are arrived in [^228-note8]

America, having had good success in the errand they went upon.[^228-note9]

Mr. Bellamy is not like to go to N. York, principally by Rea-

son of the Opposition of some of the Congregation, and also of some

of the neighbouring Ministers. I have heard they have lately

unanimously agreed to apply themselves to Mr. McGregore of

New-Londonderry,[^228-note10] alias Westfield in N-England, to be their

Minister ; who is a Gentleman that I think, if they can obtain

Him, will be likely to suit 'em, and well to fill the Place.

And I have heard that there has been some difference in his

own Congregation, that has lately made his situation there

uneasy : If so, he will be more likely to consent to the mo-

tion from N. York.

My wife joins with me in respectful & affectionate salu-

tations to you and Mrs Erskine. I am sir,

your affectionate & obliged Brother

Jonathan Edwards.

Sir,[^228-note11]

In a Journey I went to Northampton the last April, I carried the

foregoing Letter, with others for scotland so far, seeking an Opportunity to send

'em from thence to Boston: But there I met another Letter from Mr. Prince,

with a Joyful Contradiction of his former Account of Mr. McLaurin's death:[^228-note12]

which Occasion'd my bringing my Pacquet home again. Nevertheless, after I

had broke open & revised this Letter, I thought best to send it along, in-

closed in a Wrapper to Mr. McLaurin; who I hope is yet living,

& will convey this to you. I am dear sir,

your affectionate B. J. Edwards

st-ge. June 2. 1755.

Mr. Erskine

[^228-note1]: This title was irretrievably deleted by a later hand.

With a preface containing some reflections on a late book, entitled, Christianity as Old as the Creation; and on what Mr. Woolston alledges with respect to the resurrection of Jesus Christ* (London, 1730). No information could be found on "Discourse on the prevailing Evils of the present Time." *A letter to Professor Campbell, whereto is subjoin'd remarks on his vindication of the Apostles from enthusiasm* (London, 1731); Alexander Moncrieff, *An Enquiry into the Principle, Rule, and End of Moral Actions, wherein the Scheme of Selfish-love, laid down by Mr. Archibald Campbell. .. Is Examined, and the Received Doctrine Is Vindicated* (Edinburgh, 1735); Thomas Gilbert, *A learned and accurate Discourse concerning the Guilt of Sin, pardon of that Guilt, and prayer for that pardon* (London, 1695; rep. ## A204. Letter to Jonathan Edwards, Jr., May 27, 1755 204.JE-JEJr 5-27-55

Jonathan EdwardsA204. JE to JE Jr., 5/27/55. BRBL, f. 1284.

Stockbridge May. 27. 1755.

Dear Child.

Though you are a great way off from us,

& from yet you are not out of our Minds:

I am full of Concern for you, often think

of you, and often pray for you. Though you

are at so great a distance from us, & from all

your Relations, yet this is a Comfort to us, that

the same God that is here, is also at Onohoh-

quaughe; and that though now you are out

of our sight & out of our Reach, you are al-

waies in God's Hands, who is infinitely gra-

cious; and we can go to Him, and commit

you to his Care and Mercy. Take heed that

you don't forget or neglect Him. Alwaies set

God before your Eyes, and live in his Fear,

and seek him every day with all diligence:

for 'tis He, and He only can make you happy

or miserable, as He pleases; And your Life

and Health, and the eternal salvation of

your and your all in this Life and that

which is to come, depends on his will &

Pleasure. The week before last, on Thurs-

day, David whom you knew, & used to play

with, and who lived at used to live at

our House. His soul is gone into the eter-

nal World. Whether he was prepared

for death, we don't know. This is a loud

Call of God to you to prepare for death. You [^229-note1]

see that they that are young die, as well as Those

that are old: David was not very much older

than you. Remember what Christ has said,

that you must be born again, or you never can

see the Kingdom of God. never give your self

any Rest, unless you have good Evidence that

you are converted & become a new Creature.

We hope that God will preserve your Life &

Health, and return you to Stockbridge again in

safety; but alwaies remember that Life is un-

certain: you know not how soon you must die:

& therefore had need to be alwaies ready.

We have very lately heard from your Brothers

& sisters [--] at Northampton and at Newark,

that they are well. Your Aged Grandfather &

Grandmother, when I was at Windsor, gave their

Love to you. We here all do the same.

I am,

You[r ten]der[^229-note2] and affectionate Father,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^229-note1]: **marginal.** [v.]

[^229-note2]: MS damage.

## A205. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, June 3, 1755 205.JE-T.Foxcroft 6-3-55

Jonathan EdwardsA205. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 6/3/55. BRBL, f. 1301. Foxcroft's note on verso: "Revd Mr Edwards / Recd June 25. -55 / Pr Mr Brown."

Stockbridge June 3. 1755

Rev. & honoured Sir,

I thank for your Letter of March 31[^230-note1] by Mr. W---ge,

& for the kind Concern at the difficulties I meet with in

this Place. The People who have made difficulty here-

tofore are far from being yet at rest. I have heard

that They have lately conceived new Hopes of accomplish-

ing their designs: I imagine it to be from Col. Wil-

liams of Hatfield[^230-note2] his being chosen representative:

I suppose they depend on his Influence especially with

Gov. Shirley. ---- Mr. W--ge is not like to go to

Crown Point: But the Reason of it has been greatly misre-

presented by his Enemies, as tho' he was disliked by

the Indians as their Captain, and that they all refused

to enlist under him : whereas, on the Contrary, he is I sup-

pose the only Person they would be willing to go un-

der, and many of them shewed a Forwardness to go un-

der Him, and most of em would probably inlisted, if

He would have gone. But the true Reason of his not

going was the earnest solicitations of the Susquehanna

Company in Connecticut, further to assist them in their

Business.

I humbly desire you to take particular Care of the in-

closed Pacquet to Mr. McLaurin; and if any thing

be come from scotland for me, to forward it to stock-

bridge. --- I am yet in a low state as to my Health;

and the lower by Reason of a great Hurt I received

in a late Journey to Windsor, by a dangerous Fall from

my Horse; the Horse pitching Heels over Head with

his whole Weight upon me. But thr' mercy I

am much better than I have been. I desire you

to Pray for me, that God would be with me under

my various Troubles, and sanctify mercies & afflictions.

This, with humble Respects to your Family, is from

Honoured sir,

your obliged Friend & humble servt

Jonath. Edwards.

Rev. Mr. Foxcroft

[^230-note1]: Not extant.

[^230-note2]: Israel Williams.

## A207. Letter (with Stockbridge Inhabitants) to Israel Williams, Septemer 4, 1755 207.JEetal-I.Williams 9-4-55

Jonathan EdwardsA207. JE et al. to Israel Williams, 9/4/55. MA Archives, v. 54, p. 96.

Stockbridge Sept. 4. 1755

Sir,

Yesterday a Message was Sent to us from

Connecticut, by the Committee of War there, infor-

ming us that They had ordered all their Soldiers

Station'd here, and at Pantoosuck, to leave these

Places the next Monday. The Messenger informs

us that the Committee of War express'd it as their Opini-

on that Stockbridge still needs defence ; But that

this is no longer to be expected from Connecticut, seeing

they have very lately done so much for the defence of

the Countrey in general ; and that therefore they conti-

nued their men 'till next Monday, that we might

have a little Time to apply for Help else-where.

We think it manifest that, if the Town be left whol-

ly destitute of Soldiers, we shall be greatly exposed. If

this be understood by the Enemy (as probably it will)

It will invite them to us as their ready & easy Prey.

They would glory s much in destroying this Town, &

taking so many Forts ; and would be fond of embracing

such an Opportunity of dislodging the English Inhabi-

tants, and So breaking the Union between the English

and Indians, and drawing off this Tribe, among the

many others that are forsaking the English Interest &

joining with the French since the Ohio defeat.[^233-note1]

We therefore desire sir, that our Case be considered,

that a speedy supply of soldiers may be ordered, for our

defence this station, sufficient to keep our Forts & in

other respects to defend the People. we are sir

your most humble servts

Jonathan Edwards.

Josiah Jones

Samll Brown

Joseph Woodbridge

Stephen Nash

Elijah Williams

Tim0: Woodbridge

John Taylor

John Willard

P.S. There are 30 of our Indians, or more, gone with

Gov. Shirley; being urged by Him. they were very Backward,

making this Objection, that the Town, and their Wives &

Children would be left very defenceless on which the

Governour offered them, a sufficient Number of En-

glish soldiers should be kept here for the Defence of

the Town. of this On this Dependence our Indians

left the Town. of this we have undoubted Informa-

tion from many of our Indians that were present.

-- Besides we have just now word sent us by

Mr. Van Schaack of Kinderhook; That they have

received late Information, that two large Parties

of Indians are now come out against our Frontiers:

one designed for the dutch settlements, the other

for New-England. 'Tis very likely that They would

thus endeavour to cut out work for us at home,

while our Army is in distress, to prevent, if possible,

Col. Israel Williams

of our sending sufficient succour to our

Army. The Army at Crown Point, doubtless,

see that They shall have Time enough to make

Excursions.

[^233-note1]: On July 9, 1755, British forces under Maj. Gen. Edward Braddock were defeated, and Braddock killed, in a battle along the Monongahela River near Ft. Duquesne (Pittsburgh).

## A208. Letter to Israel Williams (Draft Fragment), September 5, 1755 208.JE-I.Williams 9-5-55

Jonathan EdwardsA208. JE to Col. Israel Williams, 9/5/55. ANTS, f. 1755, #7-8. Draft fragment, supplemented by Dwight trans.

Stockbridge 5 Sept. 55

Sir,

Yesterday the English inhabitants of this Town sent

away a Letter directed to you, to be conveyed to Hatfield,

representing the state of the Town, as left very greatly exposed

by the drawing off all the Connecticut soldiers, and Gov. shirley's

(by his urgency) perswading away almost all the Indian Inhabi

tants, fit for war ; who objected much against going, on that

Account, that the departure of so many, would leave the Town,

& their wives & Children defenceless ; And that the Governour

removed their Objection, by promising that a sufficient Number

of English soldiers should be maintained here during their

absence, for the defence of the Town : And also that we had

had Just Information sent us in writing from Mr. Vanschaak,

that Tw Two large Parties of Indians are lately gone

out from Crown Point against our Frontiers : And so in-

treating that soldiers may speedily be sent. But being

informed to day that you are gone from Hatfield, and

not knowing whether you will re seasonably receive the

foremention'd Letter, I now, on the desire of the People, give

you this brief Information of what was therein written;

earnestly desiring that we may not be left so easy & open a[^234-note1] [.. .]

[.. .] prey to our enemies, who, we have

reason to think, are not ignorant have the means of learning

our situation, & are certainly preparing to attack some

of the most defenceless of the frontier villages. We hope that

the troops may be forwarded immediately; for, having no ade-

quate means of repelling an attack, we have no security for

a single day. I am, with great respect respectfully,

Your obedient humble servant,

Jonathan Edwards.

[^234-note1]: With the exception of a few words on the next line, JE's original draft ends here; the remainder is supplied from Dwight's transcript. On the verso of the fragment JE made a few notes of a sermon to the Indians, apparently on their going to help fight against the French: now I have told you plain __ If you be [----] [-] sick or wounded & be going to die It may be then you would Remem- ber what I h said in this ser- mon ____ soon it may be you will be concerned for your soul Then I you will be far off ---- I cant come to you --- to give you advice and what I say now lay it up in your [col. 2] Heart ___ your own Hearts tell you what I say is right If you do as I say you will afterwards rejoyce

## A209. Letter to Thomas Foxcroft, September 15, 1755 209.JE-T.Foxcroft 9-15-55

Jonathan EdwardsA209. JE to Thomas Foxcroft, 9/15/55. BRBL, f. 1302. Foxcroft's note on verso: "Revd Mr Edwards / Recd Octo 4. 55.".

Stockbridge Septem. 15. 55.

Rev. & honoured Sir,

My son waits on you with this,

and with a Pacquet prepared and sent

away long ago, in Order to go to Boston,

to be conveyed to Scotland; but was

strangely neglected by the messenger who

was to have carried it, and at last came

back to me again.

I request your Prayers & Blessing for

my son, who is now a member of N. Jer-

sey College; and ask your Prayers for

me, and my whole Family, with re-

[spe]ct[^235-note1] to all the difficulties which attend

[ou]r Present Circumstances; and for two

of my Children, who are ill; of whose

Case my son the Bearer of this, can in-

form you. I am honoured sir,

your most obliged Friend

& humble servt,

Jonath. Edwards.

Rev. Mr. Foxcroft.

[^235-note1]: MS damage to this and following line.

## A210. Letter to Thomas Prince, September 15, 1755 210.JE-T.Prince 9-15-55

Jonathan EdwardsA210. JE to Thomas Prince, 9/15/55. Princeton Univ., Mudd Lib., Sesquicentennial Records, Coll. A141, MS tipped into *Princeton University Memorial Book of the Sesquicentennial of 1876*, p. 366. Addressed on back "To the Rev. / Mr. Thomas Prince / Minister of the Gospel / In Boston," with notation by Prince, "[From] Mr Jonathn Edwards / Stockbridg. Sep. 15. / Boston [rec'd?] ---- 19. 55."

Stockbridge sept. 15. 1755.

Rev. and hond Sir,

My son, a Member of N. Jersey College,

waits on you with this, if God permit, to pay

his, & my duty to you. For him, I ask your Prayers

& Blessing. --- I had dismiss'd Mr. Hollis's scho-

lars (not having heard any thing from him) about

the Middle of last July, agreeable to your Advice.

But soon after, I received a Letter from Him, dated

the last April ; wherein He desires me to increase

the Number of his Boys to sixteen. on which,

I restored his School, and increased it; so that it

now, in the whole, consists of 11. I have reserved

Room for four or five Mohawk Boys ; intend-

ing to try if I can obtain any thro' Mr. Haw-

ley's Influence : Tho' I have no great Ex-

pectation of it, so long as the war continues.

Mr. Hollis desires me to draw a Bill upon

him for what money I want. I have tho'ts

of going this Week to N. York and N. Jer-

sey, and propose to endeavour to sell my

Bill there. I have prepared a large Pac-

quet for Mr. Hollis, giving him a very large

and particular Account of his Affairs, and

intend to send it with the Bill. Two

of my Children are ill, which makes my

setting out this week on my Journey some-

thing uncertain. I desire your Prayers for them,

& for us all. My wife joins in most respect-

ful Salutes to you, Mrs Prince & Miss Sally.

I am Sir, your most obliged Son & Servt

Jonath. Edwards.

Rev. Mr. Prince.

disadvantageous Light. ** other

________________________________

If I am so ill a Person as you have Conceived I need your Prayers

I Condole with you the

Loss you have sustain'd in the death

of Col. W--ms your worthy & honou-

rable Consort I am That G. would

be your mighty support [---] & Comforter

in your des bereaved & desolate Circum-

stances & sanctify [-] the death of

your this your nearest Relation [ ]

& other Relations to you & me is

the [-] sincere Prayer of madam

& humble servt

[2. Fair copy:]

Stockbridge Octob 30. 1755.

Madam,

I have very lately seen a Gentleman,[^237-note10] who has, not long since,

been in London and Norwich in England, and conversed with

many Persons of Note in each Place, and with those of your parti-

cular Acquaintance in the latter: And from the Informations he

go has given me, concerning what he heard in both those Places,

especially in Norwich, I have Reason to think that you have wrote &

sent thither, that which has been much to the Disadvantage of my

Reputation : which is the Occasion of my Writing this Letter to you: the

design of which is not to demand Satisfaction, or to testify my Resentment;

but in Calmness & Charity to Say Something for my self, & in Meakness

to plead my Cause, with one whom (however she has thought & spoke

ill of me, and I have suffered much by her Means, without Cause)

I can embrace in my Charity, as a true follower of the Blessed Lamb

of God. I am so sensible of the exceeding Infirmity, we are the sub-

jects of in the present State, that what I have heard lately & formerly,

of what you have express'd with Warmth of spirit, to the disadvantage of

my Character (as I think unjustly) don't make it difficult with me to

make large Allowance, for what I know of the Circumstances you have

been in, since you came into this Part of the World, greatly tending to

prejudice your mind & to introduce, and fix in your Mind the most

disadvantageous Ideas of my Temper & Conduct, in many Respects. I sup-

pose I am well Sensible, what has abundantly Said of me, by Some Per-

sons, concerning my natural Temper ; and the Light in which my Behavi-

our, in many Instances of it, has been continually represented. Nor am I in-

sensible, what Parts of my Conduct, both before and since I have been at

Stockbridge, but especially since, have been looked upon as chiefly ob-

noxious to Censure, by those whose representations you have been most

in the way of. ---- 'Tis no Part of my present Aim, to detract in the

least from the Character of those Persons, or to endeavour to restore and

support my Character on the spoils of theirs ; But only to intreat you, Madam,

sedately to consider, what may come to pass, thro' the general great Infir-

mity of Mankind, in this present State of Imperfection, darkness & Con-

fusion; what diverse, and even Opposite Opinions of Persons & Things, Men,

even of good Character, often receive, and strongly & zealously maintain:

And especially, how often this happens in their Opinions of Persons that

have acted in a publick Character & very important Stations; & in the Pas-

sages and Incidents of whose Lives, have occurred Things that have

been extraordinary, and beside the common Course of Events, and which

have made much Noise in the World, unusually attracting the Observa-

tion, and engaging the Attention & Conversation of a Countrey ; And

that in this Case, it will be hard to form a right Judgment : and especial-

ly if such a Persons Conduct is so much, and so long the subject of Talk,

that in the Issue, there is a division into different Parties, of Opin Oppo-

site Opinions in the concerning the Matter, and the affair is clouded

with

with the dust of Controversy, managed with Zeal & Earnestness; as often [^237-note11]

is the Case: And that also sometimes things fall out exceeding unhap-

pily between Persons & Families, in the general of good Character; so that

Misunderstandings arise, Prejudices are strangely imbibed, and Strongly

fix'd : And tho' there be no real, or at least no great Foundation, still

the Prejudice subsists ; And by some Means or other, a Kind of Mist

of darkness is maintain'd, causing Things to be view'd on each side

in very false Colours : In which probably, the grand Enemy of the

Peace and Wellfare of Mankind has a great Hand. It is not hard

to conceive that in such Case, it may be next to impossible for a stranger,

that comes from a far Countrey, and falls wholly among one of these

opposing Parties, or misunderstanding Families, at the very Junc-

ture when the Controversy is at the greatest Height; to view things

in a true and clear Light, or to avoid being greatly blinded, and strong

ly prejudiced, in forming in the first forming & fixing a Judgment of

the Affair ; especially if it be fix'd soon, without Time nei for much

Circumspection, or any long deliberation. A Person, Madam, of your

discerning, & who has had your Opportunities, must needs have observed

much of this Kind in the World. Therefore I would intreat you to

consider whether this may not possibly be your Case, with respect to me.

So it has pleased God to order in his Providence, that my Life has

been attended with a succession of Such Incidents of various Kinds, as

have, for more than Twenty Years Past, as have been the subjects of

much Noise in the Countrey; about which others have been divided in

their sentiments, and men's spirits have been engaged, with no small

Warmth, especially in some Families. And I would pray you, Madam,

to consider that you are a stranger in the Countrey ; and therefore can-

not judge of Such Affairs, as if you had alwaies lived in the Countrey,

and had, been from the Beginning, been Acquainted with it's Affairs;

The Rise of different Parties, The Tempers, views, Interests & Manner

of different Combinations & Families; The first Original of Misun-

derstandings, which are subsisting between vari Persons of various

sorts and setts ; And that your Lot, from your first arrival hither,

or rather before your Arrival, was cast among, those who have

been on one side, with Regard to my Affairs; and that you never

have properly had any Opportunity to hear what I have to say for

my self, or to know how things would appear to you, if I were to have

Opportunity of free and full Conversation with you. If this had

been, and I had been heard with Candour, & you had a view of the

story of my Life, from the Beginning, with all the Circumstances of

those Passages of it, about which so much has been Said, and with Relation

to which I have been so much blamed by some; you might probably

have had quite other Thoughts ; and many things which now appear

very dark and mysterious, might have been explain'd, and have appeared

very intelligible to you ; and you might be convinced that you have

truly misapprehended Facts, and misconceived of the Principles & spi-

rit from which I have acted, in many Instances. Not that I am so

vain as to pretend that my Conduct has been so pure, that I have

no Cause of Self-reflection and Humiliation before God : But this

He knows, who searches my Heart; that I have long made it my

great

Care to approve my self to him, and to act in such a manner, & from [^237-note12]

such Principles, as have been prescribed in the excellent Rules which

have been given, & the amiable & perfect Example which has been set,

by him who is the Lamb of God, and Light of the World. And

this I know, that If, in the important Business I am employed in,

I have acted, as some suppose, from private Resentment, from impla

cableness of spirit, or stiffness & willfulness of Temper, or an assuming

disposition, and Fondness of Rule and Authority, or any Principle of a

like Kind ; I must have acted very contrary to the Spirit & Nature of

the Christian Religion, and extremely unbecoming the Character of

a Minister of Jesus Christ; & never can expect to be justified before

my great Master & Judge. ------ But I forbear; Perhaps any Ex-

pressions which may seem to denote a Confidence of my Integrity,

may be thought to arise from Ignorance of my own Heart. And I con

fess that Experience teaches me, the need of constantly maintaining of

a watchful and Jealous Eye over my own Heart, with humble Prayer

to God for Light to enable me to judge truly of my self. But this

I will venture to affirm with confidence, that if I have acted from such

unchristian Principles, and without an hatred of all Remains of 'em in

my self, and habitual earnest hungrings & Thirstings after that Righ-

teousness, & true Christian Piety & vertue, consistsng in the contrary

amiable Dispositions of Heart ; attended with earnest Cries to God,

with many Tears, as the Infinite Fountain & sovereign Bestower of

such precious Gifts Endowments ; It must be because I have been ex-

tremely & totally blinded concerning my self. My desire is, and has

long been, that God would search me, & prove my Heart, & see if there

be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the Way everlasting.

I desire to speak and Act at all Times, as having in View the Account

which I have shortly to give to that Omniscient & righteous Judge,

who is not liable to be blinded by vain Pretences and Professions,

nor misled by Prejudices and Misinformations.

I doubt not, Madam, but that you thought you had sufficient Grounds

for the Judgment you have formed of my Temper & Conduct, and the

Report you have made of them : But I would intreat that there may

yet be for Reflection, and Consideration, whether it is not possible that

you may have apprehended Things much worse than they are. If

you should still think it your duty to persist in the same Representations,

which you have heretofore made to my Disadvantage ; And it should

happen hereafter by divine Providence you should, by some Means, come

to be convinced, that you had wounded and greatly wronged an in-

nocent Person, and a Minister of Jesus Christ ; who notwithstanding

all that had been judged and said by others concerning him,

had indeed been acting in the Fear of God, with Tenderness of Consci-

ence, endeavouring in all Things to acquit Himself to the divine

Acceptance ; and was influenced by quite other Principles than you

imagined ; would not this deeply affect a mind endowed with a Truly Chris-

tian Humility, Candour & Benevolence of Heart, such as I charitably be-

lieve you are possessed of? However, if you never should have this

Conviction

Conviction in this World of darkness, as possibly you may not, I hope I [^237-note13]

shall alwaies feel to the same Readiness to forgive you, which hitherto

I have found ; tho' I know myself to be much injured, and may

perhaps greatly suffer thro' your Report to my disadvantage.

I shall comfort my self with the Time when all God's People shall

meet together in an unembarassed, unalloyed Charity, in th a World

of such clear & perfect Light which shall abolish all Misunderstand-

ings, and even the strongest Prejudices, and dissipate the thickest

Clouds, throu'gh which many of them now view one another

in a very false & disadvantageous Light.

I know not, Madam, what Construction you may put upon my

writing as I do. I know, when once Persons have imbibed a

deep Prejudice against anothers, It has a Tendency to cause them to look

on every thing they say or do, in quite another Light, than otherwise

they would do. But I ask your Candour ; And I ask your Prayers,

that God would take away what He sees amiss in my Heart. If I

am so ill a Person as you have conceived, I need your Prayers the more.

I condole with you the Loss you have sustain'd, in the death of

Col. Williams, your honourable Consort ; for whose sake your left

your dear native Land, and cross'd a vast Ocean, to dwell in a strange

Land ; and who doubtless, was under God, your c the greatest sup-

port & Comfort of your life. That God would now appear as your

mighty Support & Comforter, in your bereaved desolate Circumstances,

and sanctify the late Death of this your nearest Relation, and

other Relations, to you & me, is the sincere Prayer of

Madam,

your most respectful &

humble servt.

Jonathan Edwards.[^237-note14]

Mrs. Williams

[^237-note1]: Probably Rev. Samuel Davies of Virginia. Davies had traveled to England and Scotland in 1753 and 1754 on a fund-raising tour for the College of New Jersey; he visited Norwich from Sept. 3 to 17, 1754, and was in the company of a John Scott (Mrs. Williams was the daughter of Rev. Thomas Scott of that city). Davies and JE both participated in the meeting of the Presbyterian Synod of New York, held in Philadelphia, beginning Oct. 1, 1755.

## A212. Letter to John Erskine, December 11, 1755 212.JE-J.Erskine 12-11-55

Jonathan EdwardsA212. JE to John Erskine, 12/11/55. ANTS, f. 1755, #2-3. Addressed on cover "To the Rev. / Mr. John Erskine / Minister of the Gospel / at Culross / In Scotland."

Stockbridge Decem. 11, 1755.

Rev. & dear Sir,

I last wrote you in July 24. 55. Since that, in the latter

Part of last October, I received a Letter from you, dated June 23. 55.

together with the Essays on the Principles of Morality, from Mr. Hogg;

and the Analysis of the moral & religious Sentiments of Sopho, from

your Self.[^238-note1] I thank you for your Letter & Present: and shall write a

Letter of Thanks to Mr. Hogg, for his Present by your Hands, added

to former Instances of his Generosity. I had before read that Book of

Essays; having borrowed Mr. Bellamy's; and also that Book of Mr. david

Hume's which you speak of.[^238-note2] I am glad of an opportunity to read such Cor-

rupt Books; especially when written by men of considerable Genius; that

I may know have an Idea of the Notions that prevail in our Nation.

You say that "some People say that the Lord Kaims's being made a Lord of

session would have been prevented, if Chancellor Hardwick, & A. Bp.

Herring[^238-note3] had seasonably seen his Book." I should be glad to know

who this Chancellor Hardwick is, & and what his Character. By your

mentioning him in such a manner, I am ready to suppose he may be

in some Respects of Good. And it is a matter of Thankfulness, if a man

of good Character, and a Friend to Religion be Lord Chancellor.

As to our warlike concerns, I have not heretofore been very parti-

cular in writing about them, in my Letters to Scotland, supposing it high-

ly probable, that you would have earlier accounts from Boston, N.

York & Philadelphia, than any I can send you, living at so great

a distance from any of the sea-ports. Nevertheless, seeing you propose

my sending some Account of the present Posture of Affairs, I would

say, that it appears to me, that notwithstanding some remarkable

Favours of Heaven, of which we are very unworthy, It has in the gene-

ral been a year of great Frowns of Providence on the British Ameri-

ca. Notwithstanding our success at Nova Scotia, and our having the

Better in the Battle near Lake George, and taking the French General

Prisoner ; yet, considering the Advantages the Enemy hath obtained

against us, by General Bradock's defeat;[^238-note4] especially in gaining over

& confirming the Indians on their side, and disheartning & weakening

our Friends, and what we have suffered from our Enemies, and how

greatly we are weaken'd and almost sunk with our vast Expences,

especially in N. England, and the Blood as well as money we

have expended; I say, considering these things, and how little we

have gained by all our Cost & Trouble, our Case is no better, but

far worse than it was in the Beginning of the year. At least,

I think it certain that we have obtained no Advantages in any

wise to balance our Expence of Blood & Treasure. The Expedition

to the Eastward has been remarkably succeeded; But the other three

Expeditions, That against the French forts on the Ohio, That against

Niagara, & that against Crown Point, have all been unsuccessful

as to their main design. And tho' the Army under General John-

son[^238-note5]

son had a Kind of Victory over the French and took the Baron [^238-note6]

dieskeau, their General ; yet we suffered very greatly in the Battle;

and the taking of the French General, probably was the saving of

his Army; for by telling a lie to our Army, viz that the French

were in continual Expectation of being greatly inforced by a large

Body that marched another way, and had appointed to meet

them near that Place, Our Army was prevented from pursuing the

Enemy after they had repell'd them ; which if they had done, they

might have been under great Advantages to have cut 'em off, and pre-

vented the return of almost all of them to Crown-Point ; which could

be no otherwise than through the Water, in their Batteaus. Our

Army never proceeded any further than the Place of the Engagemt;

but having Built a Fort there, near Lake George, alias Lake St Sa-

crament, after they had built another near Hudson's River, about

14. Miles on this side, & left Garrison's, lately returned, as

also has the Army under General Shirley,[^238-note7] who went with a

design against Niagara, after having built some vessels of Force

in the Lake Ontario, & strengthen'd the Fortifications at Oswego

and sent for the Remains of Gen. Bradocks Army to Albany there

to go into Winter Quarters. The Governours of the several Provinces,

have in the latter Part of the last month, had a meeting to confer

together concerning our warlike Affairs, And to agree on a Plan

of Operations, to be recommended to the Government at Home, for

the next year. But I have heard nothing of their determinations.

The Indians have not done much mischief on the Frontiers of N. England,

since Our Army have been above us ; but have been dreadful in their

Ravages in the back settlements of Virginia, New & Pennsylvania.

It is apparent that the ministry at home miss it very much in

sending over British Forces to fight with Indians in America, &

in sending British officers to have the Command of Our American

Forces. Let them send them send us Arms, Ammunition, & money

& shipping ; & let N. England men manage the Business their

own way ; who alone understand it. And to appoint British officers

over them is Nothing a Hindrance and Discouragement to 'em. Let

'em be well supplied & supported and defended by sea, and

then let 'em go forth under their own Officers, and manage in

their own way, as they did in the Expedition against Cape

Breton. All the Provinces in America seem to be fully sensible,

that New-England men are the only men to be employed against

Canada : as I had Opportunity abundantly to obtain observe in

my late Journey to N. York, N. Jersey & Philadelphia.

However we ought to remember that neither N. England men

nor any other, are any thing unless God be with us. And when

we have done all at finding fault with measures taken & Instru-

ments employed wh we can't expect Prosperity unless the ac-

cursed Thing be removed from our Camp.

God has lately frown'd on my Family in taking away a faithful

servt

Servant,[^238-note8] who was a great Help to us. two of my [^238-note9]

Children have been under threatning Infirmities,

but are something better. I desire your Prayers for

us all. My Wife joins me in affectionate

& respectful salutations to you & Mrs Erskine.

I am, Rev. & dear sir,

your obliged Brother & affectionate Friend

Jonathan Edwards.

[^238-note1]: Henry Home, Lord Kames, *Esays on the Principles of Morality and Natural Religion* (Edinburgh, 1751); and John Bonar, *An Analysis of the Moral and Religious Sentiments of Sopho*[Lord Kames] *and David Hume, Esq.* (Edinburgh, 1755).

[^238-note2]: Titles by David Hume in JE's "Catalogue of Reading" (Beinecke Library) are *A Treatise of Human Nature* (2 vols. London, 1739;nd40), *Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding* (London, 1748), and *An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals* (London, 1751). See also *Works, 1*, 14, n. 1; and *8*, 604, n. 1.

[^238-note3]: Philip Yorke, Earl of Hardwicke, and Abp. Thomas herring.

[^238-note4]: On July 9, 1755, near Ft. Duquesne.

[^238-note5]: Sir William Johnson.

[^238-note6]: **marginal.** [2]

[^238-note7]: William Shirley.

[^238-note8]: Not further identified.

[^238-note9]: **marginal.** [3]
