## B115. Letter from Joseph Bellamy, May 31, 1756 B115.J.Bellamy-JE 5-31-56 edited

Joseph BellamyB115. Joseph Bellamy to JE, 5/31/56. ANTS, f. 1756-59A, #8. Addressed on back "To / The Rev. Mr Jonathan Edwards / at / Stockbridge."

Bethlem May 31. 1756.

Dear Sir,

I am in pain, fearing our army against Crown Point will be defeated - God only knows how it will be - but if it Should be - your own discretion will make you Sufficiently Speedy to Secure your Self & family &c - We Stand as ready to receive you or any of your family to all the Comforts our house affords as if we were your children - I am greatly interested in your Safety - I am Concerned for Mr. Hawley I fear he will be too Ventersome, & fling away his life for nothing - I wish, if you know how to get one along, you would Send him a letter - our youngest Child still remains unwell, but not bad. - the indian boys grow more & more easy & content - but they love play too well - are very ignorant - & very stupid as to things of religion - & in Arithmetick when I would teach them any thing that is a little difficult, they Soon are discouraged, & dont love to try - So I take them off & put them to writing again - designing by little & little to get them along - they will endure hardship & bend their minds to business like English boys - it Seems they were never [-] learnt their Chatechism; shall I learn them? I have got 3 bibles, but not given them to the boys, they are So ignorant. This is my 2nd Letter, I expect you will give me any instructions you think proper. And remain Rev. Sir your unworthy friend & sert.

J. Bellamy Compliments to Mrs Edw. & family

## B116. Letter from Jonathan Belcher, December 8, 1756 B116.J.Belcher-JE 12-8-56 edited

Jonathan BelcherB116. Jonathan Belcher to JE, 12/8/56. NJ Historical Society, Ms. Group 11, Bamberger Autograph Coll. JE’s endorsement on back of last page: "Gov. Belcher. decem. 8. 56." After Belcher’s signature appears the following notation: "This Letter was given me this Monday / 11th April 1831 by Mr. Joseph Woodbridge - the Endorsement is in / Edwards' hand - Stockbridge 11th April 1831 / Theodore Sedgwick Jr."

My very worthy and dear Friend,

Sir,

Had I not the necessary Dispatches of Government and the Infirmities of Age to plead my Excuse I shoud blush to say that your very kind and excellently good Letter of the 13. of March last lyes now before me to be answered, and I am coverd with Shame that I cannot lay a lean Claim to your mistaken Opinion of me (your sinful worthless Friend) however I take it as an admonition and instruction to be what I shou'd be, and yet I have a humble Hope that through some measure of Grace I have sincerely endeavoured to contribute what I cou'd for Building up the Kingdom of the great Redeemer in this World, and which I humbly pray may be the happy Fruit of the incorporation of New Jersey College - on which God seems to be pouring down his Blessings from on high, and for this I give Praise, Honour and Glory to His great Name. amen. -

I am glad, Sir, to tell you that Mr. President Burr with his Spouse and Family, and with the Students, have been fixt at Nassau Hall for about a Fortnight past and the Presidt. [^375-note1] was to see me last week and said all things relative to the College were thro' the Goodness of God in a comfortable & prosperous Way. My Prayer to the God of the Spirits of all Flesh is that the Governours and governed of Nassau Hall may be signal Examples of sincere Piety in their Lives and Conversations as well as excelling in the best Human Literature so shall Generations to come rise up and call them blessed. amen. - And now, Sir, allow me to say that in all the Veiws I can survey myself I must earnestly cry out God be merciful to me a Sinner and give me true Faith in Christ with a Repentance unto Salvation never to be repented of. - As I am arrived thro' the tender Patience and Forbearance of God to an advanced Age, yet I find myself growing weaker and Weaker. - & O then may my Path become that of just which is as the shining Light that shineth more and more unto the Perfect day, & thus I roll my Soul upon the Mercy of God in the Merits of his dear Son for eternal Life, and in these things I ask you to join with me in [^375-note2] your earnest Prayers at the Throne of Grace, where I shall always remember you in my sincere Addresses which I hope thro' the Powerful Mediation and intercession of the Lord Jesus Christ may find Acceptance with his heavenly Father - My Wife joins with me in kindest Respects to Mrs. Edwards, your worthy Consort -

I always am, Revd. Sir, Your Cordial Friend & Servant J Belcher

Eliza.Town (NJ)Decr. 8: 1756

Mr. Edwards- (also endorsed:) Gov. Belcher. decem. 8-56 (also endorsed:) Gov. J. Belcher to Revd. Jonathan Edwards

Eliz. Town 3 Dec. 1756 -

[^375-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^375-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## B117. Letter from Gideon Hawley, December 27, 1756 B117.G.Hawley-JE 12-27-56 edited

Gideon HawleyB117. Gideon Hawley to JE, 12/27/56. BRBL, "Defense of the Pentateuch," f. 1204. Addressed on back "To / The Rev / Mr Jonathan Edwards / Stockbridge."

Sheffield 27 Decr. 1756

Rev & Hond Sir

Mr. Ashly, I suppose, bro't you a line from me at Cherry-Vally; where I positively determined, not long after it left me, for the present to proceed no further towards Onohoquage. And as soon as I had dispached some Business and ye Roads wou'd

admit, I turned my Course and arrived at Mr. Hopkins's Saturday Evening last: Where I have taken a room, and conclude [-] to spend the Winter as retired as may be, and in as close Application as my Health will bear. I doubt not you'll approve the Choice of have made of a Place, and the Resolutions I have taken, to give myself entirely to study 'till the Spring returns. I purpose a ride to Stockbridge, as soon as my Health shall require it. In the Mean Time, please to accept, to yourself & Madam, my humble Duty, and to your family the sincere Regards of

Rev Sir, your dutiful Son & obliged humble Servt. Gideon Hawley

PS. I have wrote this Day to Messrs. Oliver & Hubbard, and have given encouragt to send them my late journal.

Rev Mr. Edwards

## B119. Letter from Edward Wigglesworth (Excerpted), [c. February 1757] B119.E.Wigglesworth-JE c2-57 edited

Edward WigglesworthB19. Edward Wigglesworth to JE, [2/57]. Excerpted in Joseph Clark, *A Historical Sketch of the Congregational Churches of Massachusetts* (Boston, 1858), pp. 182-84. See no. 223, JE to Wigglesworth, 2/11/57.

[Clark comments:]

"Prof. Wigglesworth replies in a long letter, of which the following is an abridgment: 'Among many thing exceptionable in the marginal notes [of Dr. Mayhew's book] I at length met one which seemed to insinuate that the canon of the Old Testament was compiled according to the humor and caprice of the people; that some books were admitted and others left out of the canon, according as the people relished or disrelished the contents of them. I immediately thought that this was the first thing which demanded my attention. For of the divine authority of the books of the Old Testament be once shaken, besides all the other mischiefs (too many to be mentioned) we shall be deprived of the weight of that evidence which might be drawn from them for the true and proper Godhead of our Saviour. I, therefore, at my very next lecture, delivered the inclosed discourse, which I ask your candid acceptance of,'-which discourse, we learn from the same letter, was published at[^378-note1] the 'request of almost every student in the college,' as an antidote to the doctor's heretical views. Harvard College, a hundred years old, vindicating the *true and proper Godhead of our Saviour* against the possible harm that may come to it from a blow aimed at 'the divine authority of the books of the Old Testament!' -and all this through her learned theological professor!! "The writer lets out other secrets which have a deep significance; as that, in the 'Boston Lectures,' during the vacation following the publication of his views, 'the worthy ministers of that town were generally vindicating the divinity of Christ.' 'At length came out a catholic and judicious discourse of Mr. Pemberton upon the subject, prefaced by Dr. Sewall and Mr. Prince, the two oldest ministers of the town. I thought it was now time to have done, and wait in silence till we saw whether any thing would be replied to Mr. Pemberton or to me. And I believe (for more than one reason) that if no further stir had been made, we should have met with no more trouble. But the printers, who live very much by disputes, observing that the people's passions were up, that any thing on that subject would fetch a penny, and that every thing was supposed to be pointed at Dr. Mayhew, continued printing little things with pompous advertisements about them in the newspapers, week after week. If it had not been for these repeated and long continued provocations, I don't think we should ever have seen the "Layman's" new edition of "Emlyn's Inquiry."' The professor hopes this book of Emlyn will not have much of a run; but if it should, he stands ready to 'give the youth of the college the best preservative' in his power against it. He thinks it 'by no means desirable,' however, to 'publish a new answer to a book that hath been answered over and over again on the other side of the water.' This would be to 'encourage hungry printers to pester us with new editions of any pernicious books written in other countries,' and 'set us a writing and sending more grists to their mill.' If any thing in this line is to be done, he[^378-note2] would recommend 'the reprinting the best answer to Mr. Emlyn which hath been written abroad; and perhaps some other "layman" may usher it on to the stage with as much address as Mr. Emlyn hath been introduced with before it. This would serve all the good purposes which would be served by printing a new answer to him. And at the same time it would avoid giving any occasion, which some of the adverse party seem to wish for, of setting the controversy on foot among ourselves; a thing which I would avoid as much as possible consistent with a due concern for such an important truth. For if the gentlemen get to writing one against another upon so interesting a subject, I greatly fear that the debate will be managed with so much acrimony and warmth on one side, and perhaps with such an intermixture of threat and sarcasm on the other, as would be a great disservice to the interests of religion. And if the controversy be once begun, perhaps neither I nor you, sir, who are much younger, will live to see the end of it.' The writer expresses himself much pleased with Mr. Edwards's 'concern for the honor of our blessed Lord,' though differing from him somewhat 'about the most prudent methods to support and vindicate it, at the present conjecture;' and closes his interesting letter with, 'I pray God direct us to what may be most agreeable to his will. We both aim at the same end, though we may not have the same sentiments about the means to compass it.' The uncontroversial 'method' of Professor Wigglesworth prevailed, and its dire consequences have been seen. What the result of President Edwards's plan would have been, we never shall know; but we wish it had been tried."

[^378-note1]: **marginal.** [183]

[^378-note2]: **marginal.** [184]

## B120. Letter from Aaron Burr (Excerpted), February 12, 1757 B120.A.Burr-JE 2-12-57 edited

Aaron BurrB120. Aaron Burr to JE, 2/12/57 and ff. Quoted in Richard Webster, *A History of the Presbyterian Church in America* (Philadelphia, 1857), pp. 262-63, describing college revivals.

Burr[^379-note1] wrote to Edwards, February 12, 1757:-"As I have had more fatigue, so I have had more comfort in my little society this winter than ever. There has been more of a religious concern than I have ever known: some of the most careless and thoughtless are considerably reprouved, and others solemnly concerned." February 14: "Half the students join in the society. Much old experience has taught me to judge of these things more by their fruits than by any accounts of experience for a short season." February 22: "I never saw any thing in the late revival that more evidently discovered the hand of God. Mr. Spencer says the same. Certainly a great and glorious work is going on. For nearly a month, a [^379-note2] religious concern has been universal, not one student excepted. When it began, I called such as were hopefully pious, and laid before them what I thought had obstructed the work of God heretofore. Their conduct has been very prudent. Mr. William Tennent agreed as to the method pursued, and has been very helpful by private applications." March: "I never observed conviction of sin so rational, solemn, and thorough."

[^379-note1]: Webster footnotes “Gillies,” i.e. John Gillies, Historical Collections (Glasgow, 1754), though numerous searches have not found it there.

[^379-note2]: **marginal.** [263]

## B121. Letter from Richard Stockton, September 29, 1757 B121.R.Stockton-JE 9-29-57 edited

Richard StocktonB121. Richard Stockton to JE, 9/29/57. BRBL, f. 1332.

Nassau Hall Septr. 29th: 1757

Revd. Sir-

It has pleased the most High on the 24th. Instant to call to himself the Reverend, truly Pious & Learned Mr. Aaron Burr, whose Death may be Justly esteemed a publick loss to Religion & Learning; but more especially to this Infant Seminary, of which he was President: and We desire sincerely to Condole with you on this Melancholy Occasion, to whom, We believe, he was very dear, considered in a double Relation as a Son & an eminent Christian.

Having Considered the Necessity that the Presidents Chair should without delay be filled; We have this Day, by a very great Majority, Chosen you for that Purpose, and We do hereby desire your acceptance: which you will be pleased to signify by a Letter to our Clerk.

We now write to the Honle: Andrew Oliver Esqr: of Boston to make application, in our Name, to the Comissioners of the Honle: Society for propagating the Gospel amongst the Heathen, for your Dismission as their Missionary: which we doubt not will be granted; & therefore hope you will by no means refuse our Request.

We think it will be proper for you to be here in Six Weeks from this date, to take the Charge of the College & to remove your Family before Winter, [^380-note1] provided it be incovenient to Mrs: Burr; which we have desired her to signify to you - Your speedy Answer

will very much Oblige, By Order of the Trustees, Revd. Sir Your most hÛble Servt. Richd. Stockton, C1k

To the Revd. Jonathan Edwards

[^380-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## B122. Letter from Esther Edwards Burr, November 2, 1757 B122.E.Burr-JE 11-2-57 edited

Esther Edwards BurrB122. Esther Edwards Burr to JE, 11/2/57. ANTS, f. 1756-59B, #1, 3.

To my Ever Hond Father -

Princeton Novr 2. 1757.

Hond Sir

Your most Affectionate comforting Letter by my Brother Parsons was excedingly refreshing to me, altho’ I was Something damped by hearing yt I Should not See you untill Spring but tis my comfort in this disappointment as well as under all my afflictions yt God knows what is best for me & for his own glory - perhaps I lotted too much on the Company & conversation of Such a near & dear affectionate Father & Guide - I cant doubt but all is for the best & I am Sattisfied yt God Should order the affair of your removal as Shall be for his Glory what ever comes of me

Since I wrote my Mothers Letter God has carried me through new tryals & given new Supports - My little Son has been Sick with the Slow Fever ever Since my Brother left us, & has been brought to the Brink of the Grave But I hope in Mercy is bringing off him back again - I was innabled to Resighn the Child (after a Severe Struggle with Nature) with the greatest freedom. God Shewed me yt the Child is not my own but His, & yt he had a right to recall[^381-note1] what he had lent when ever he thought fit, & I had no reason to complain or Say God was hard with me, this Silenced me. But O how good is God! he not only kept me from complaining but comforted me by ennabling me to offer up the Child by Faith I think if ever I acted Faith, I Saw the fullness there was in Christ for little Infants, & his willingness to accept of Such as were offered to him. Suffer little Children to come unto me & forbid them not, are comforting Words - God also Shewed me in Such a lively manner the fullness there was in himsself of all Spiritual Blessings, yt I Said altho all Streams were cut off yet so long as my God lives I have en enough - He enabled me to Say yt altho’ thou Slay me yet will I trust in the - In this time of tryal I was lead to enter into a renewed & explissit Covenant with him again in a more Solemn manner than ever with the greatest freedom & delight, after much Self examminnation & prayer I did give up my Self & Children to God with my whole Heart . never untill now had I a Sense of the privilage we are allowed in Cove[n]anting with God - This act of Soul left my mind [in] a great calm & Steady trust in God. a few days after this one Eve’ in talking of the [^381-note2] glorious State my dear departed Husband must be in, my Soul was carried out in Such longing desires after this glorious State yt I was forced to retire from the Family to conceal my Joy. when alone I was so transported & my Soul carried out in Such Eager desires after Perfection & the full injoyment of God & to Serve him uninterruptedly yt I think my Nature wuld not have borne much more. I think dear Sir I had yt Night a foretaste of Heaven - this frame continued in Some good degree the whole Night; I Slept but little, & when I did my Dreams were all Heavenly & divine things - frequently Si[nce] I have felt the Same in kind tho’ not in degree this was about the time yt God called me to give up my Child. Thus a kind & gracious God h[as] been with me in Six troubles & in Seven -

But O Sir what cause of deep Humiliation [&] abasement of Soul have I on account of Corruption which I See working continually especiall Pride - O how many Shapes does Pride Cloak it Self in - - Satan is also busy Shoting his darts but blessed be God those temptations of his yt used to [^381-note3] overthro’ me, as yet hant touched me - - I will Just hint at one or two if I ant too Tedious in lengt[h] - When I was about to renew my Covenant with God it Seemed as if one Spoak it to me & & Said tis be[tter] yt you Should not renew it then to Break it wh[en] you have, what a dreadfull thing wil it be if you do[nt] keep it - My reply was I did not do it in my own s[trength] then the temptation would return how do you know yt God will help you keep it - but it did not Sha[ke] me in the least - - O to be delivered from the power of Satan as well as Sin! I cant help hopeing the time [is] near - God is Sertainly fiting me for himself, & whe[n] I think it will be Soon the thought is transporting - I am afraid I have tired out your patience & will begg leave only to add my need of the ernest prair[ers] of my Dear & Hond parents & all good people yt I m[ay] [n]ot at last be a castaway, but yt God would constantly grant me now Supplies of divine grace - - I am tenderly concernd for my dear Brother Timo. but I hope his Sickness will not be unto Death but for the Glory of God - Pleas to give my duty to my Hond Mother [& my] love to all my Brothers & Sisters - - [I] am Hond & dear Sir with the greatest respect your [aff]ectionate & Dutifull Daughter E. Burr -

[^381-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^381-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

[^381-note3]: **marginal.** [4]

## B123. Letter from Richard Stockton, November 4, 1757 B123.R.Stockton-JE 11-4-57 edited

Richard StocktonB123. Richard Stockton to JE, 11/4/57. BRBL, f. 1333.

Revd. Sir,

We recd. yours by Mr: Parsons; and after full Consideration of the Contents, beg leave to Inform you; that notwithstanding the Objections therein mentioned against your Acceptance of the Presidentship of the College of New Jersey, we can by no means doubt of your being loudly called by divine Providence to so Important a Work. We think it just & proper that a Regard be had to your outward Comfort; and wou'd by no means lessen but rather increase It: Your Estate in Lands where you now live, we hope will not, by your Removal, be made Worse; especially as we presume some Person will soon be appointed to, & accept the Pastoral Charge of that Church; and the several Inhabitants that now are there will continue to reside in the Town, without leaving it more open to the Incursions of the Enemy than before: and that in some convenient Time you may dispose of it to advantage. Your personal Estate can be easily removed to this Place; and the Expences attendant thereon, we expect to pay. At the Sessions when you were elected President, we voted you £20 - for the Cost of your removal; and if that Sum shall prove insufficient for the Purpose, we shall think it our Duty to reimburse you for the overplus it may Cost you. The President's Salary at present is fixed at £200 procn: Pr Annum; besides the Graduation money Presidents House, Garden, Barn, Out Houses & Fire Wood -

Your bodily Constitution we hope will not be thought a very weighty Objection; more especially as it may reasonably be expected, from a Removal to so good & wholesome an Air, added to that Diversion from a more severe & uniform Course of Study, which your Situation as a President will call you to, that the bodily Inconveniencies you complain of, will in some comfortable [^382-note1] Degree be removed.

We have good reason to believe that you have no such Defects as a Scholar, which incapacitates you to sit in the Presidents Chair with Honour & Usefulness; and altho its most certain your Predecessor was remarkably qualifyed for the Business he was in; yet (we thank the most High) we have not Reason to expect so wide a Difference as your Modesty suggests.

The Publick has long known that you have been engaged in Studies of great Importance to Mankind; and We doubt not, that the several Plans you have laid for the executing the great & excellent Works you mention, if they have your Hand to finish them, will eminently serve the Interest of Christ's Kingdom in the World: Nevertheless we beg leave to observe, first, that your Office as President it is very likely, may leave you so much Time, as to do something in that Way; and further that the Part of your Labour which extends to the Government of a Society so constituted & so immediately calculated to serve the most important & extensive Interests of Mankind, as this, we do not in the least doubt, will be of much more universal Service than if applied in the Way you intended.

We consent & agree that you execute the Office of President in the manner that you purpose: and doubt not that your doing the whole Work of a Professor of Divinity will be of eminent Service to the Society.

You will easily conclude Sir, that this Society must be in a very unhappy Situation without a Head: and We beg leave to inform you that we Concieve Its present Situation will by no means dispense with your absence from it this Winter. Divine Providence has so far smiled on our Election, as that the Comissioners of Boston have consented to your Removal (as you'll see by the [^382-note2] Copy of a Letter from Mr: Oliver enclosed). We cannot but hope your own Conclusions added to the repeated Requests & Reasons herein mentioned, will leave you no Room to doubt of the Way of your Duty. We therefore earnestly request, and Judge it absolutely necessary, that as soon as possible after the Receipt of this, you come to this Place & take upon you the Charge of the College. We suppose the Season is too far advanced to remove your Family before Spring; That, We hope, can be put in such a Situation as not to suffer in your absence: and if you think that your being here this Winter will be made more comfor able by the attendance of Mrs: Edwards, and she can [also][^382-note3] leave the Family; you can both without the rem[oval] of any of your Goods be very comfortable in the Presidents House; as Mrs: Burr with all her house hold Furniture, will continue therein till Spring.

We most heartily pray that it wou'd please a gracious God to remove your Doubts (if any yet remain) in this important affair; and that you may speedily conducted hither in safety.

Signed in the Name of the Trustees Richd. Stockton Clk. Nassau Hall 4th. Novr. 1757.

[^382-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^382-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

[^382-note3]: Conjecture for ms. damage at the end of this line (and the next) where seal was placed.

## C1. Gershom Bulkeley to Timothy Edwards, September 11, 1702 C001. G.Bulkeley-TE 9-11-02

Gideon BulkeleyC001. Gershom Bulkeley to TE, 9/11/02. ANTS, f. 1700-1719A, #16. Addressed on verso to "The Rev d Mr Tim o Edwards."

Wethersf. Sept r: 11. 1702.

Rev d Sr,

I have sent you y e pill & S.C.C.[?] you wrote for. You know yo r occasion for these & not I; & I canot advise much about them: only for y e pill I have two sorts of it; & I supposed you might meane such as yo r father use to have, w ch is y e strongest sort, & y n I shall only caution you to take heed that you do not give too much of it; if you see you have given too little, that is Easily amended by giving some more by & by.

ffor yor Child I have sent you y t w ch I hope will set it up againe. It is in y e Vial wth ye Rag typed over it. You may every morning give it 10 or 12 drops of it in a little good wine or beere; & once or twice in y e day beside if need be. It will be taken w thout any disgust. & be no wayes troublesome but resulting[?]. This is 2 shillings. I have not time now, Sr to [—-] joke w th you about yo r Hon ble Esquire. I thought you had knowne y t he was dead & buryed long agoe: but w th respects to yo r selfe & Mrs Edwards I am Sr Yor humble serv t

G. Bulkeley

## C2. Esther Warham Mather Stoddard to Timothy Edwards, November 3, 1703 C002.EStoddard-TE 11-3-03

Esther Warham Mather StoddardC002. Esther Warham Mather Stoddard to TE, 11/3/03. BRBL, f. 1569. Addressed "These / For ye Reverend / M r Timothy Edwards / in Winzor."

North Novem 3 17 3

dear s r

yours by your neighbour Baker I have Recei ved & Reioyce with you: in gods goodness & tender mercy to you & us in granting safe deliverance to my daughter god grant y t wee may Render to ye Lord according mercies re ceived where much is given much is [-] requir ed: you speak of some ilnes daughter is troubled with from ye hips downward I have known one who was so Lame after she was deliver ed y t she could not go hardly for a pretty while & was helped with this take some rum more or less & put cloves & mace & gincer[?] cinnomon pounded & seeth in ye rum & bath her joynts & Limbs whare ye pain is Let it be done when she is in bed & be Kareful y t she do not get cold: I shod be glad to hear from you by all oppertunities: we are in health through gods goodnes but there is 2 children in ye town dangerosly sick & a great many in hadly very ill many children in some families sik. but I must take Leave & commit you & my daughter & ye little one to god & daughter above all mak sure of an interest in Christ farwel yor Loving mother

Esther Stoddard

daughter

if I should send you sum peises of stuf of ye lining of your father's Koat it may be you make use of it among your children do not despise it also I send 1 yard of lining cloath & [—] apron y t I had by me I thof't you might mak use of it among children

## C3. Esther Warham Mather Stoddard to Esther Stoddard Edwards, December 7, 1705 C003.E.Stoddard-ESE 12-7-05

Esther Warham Mather StoddardC003. Esther Warham Mather Stoddard to Esther Stoddard Edwards, 12/7/03. No MS. Printed in Solomon Clark, *Antiquities, Historicals and Graduates of Northampton* (Northampton, 1889), 23-24; *Proceedings of the Dedication of the Memorial Gateway to Jonathan Edwards at the Old Burying Ground South Windsor* (New Haven, 1929), 18-20.

Northampton, Dec. 7th, 170[^386-note1]. [^386-note2]

Dear Daughter:—-God be thanked for your safe delivery [^386-note3] and raising you up to health again. We are under mixt dispensations. We have a great deal of mercy, and we have smart afflictions. Eliakim is not and Eunice is not, [^386-note4] and it hath pleased God to take away your dear brother Israel also, [^386-note5] who was taken by ye enemy and carried to a place called Brest, in France, and being ready to be transported into England was taken sick of a fever and died there, as we understand by a letter from the crew's master of the ship now in London. [^386-note6] It is a heavy stroak to us added to ye former, and we, David-like, mourn every day. I had not done mourning for the former, but God hath added grief to my sorrow. What shall I say? It becomes me, Aaron-like, to hold my peace. God grant that I may, with Job, come as gold out of the fire, when I have been tried. I hope you and ye rest of my children will learn by these awful stroaks so to number your days as to apply your hearts to wisdom. We see by these instances that our days may be very few here, and when and how we shall be taken out of this world, God only knows. Therefore we had need to be ready, seeing we know not what hour our Lord will come. Ye time is short, and it may be very short to us that remains as was to your sister and brother. One day made a great change in my dear daughter's condition. Son Williams [^386-note7] is satisfied that she is now in glory, as you may see by the letter which I now send you, which, when you have perused, I would have you let your sister Mix [^386-note8] read, and enclose it in a paper and send to my son Warham,[^386-note9] with the news of my grandson, Steven Williams, arriving safe with some other captives, at Boston. [^386-note10] But I must be short least I should miss of an opportunity to send this. I bid you farewell and subscribe myself your sorrowing mother,

ESTHER STODDARD.

P.S.—-I would have sent you half a thousand pins and a porrenger of marmalat if I had an opportunity. If any of your town come up, and would call here, I would send it. Give my love to son Edwards and your children.

[^386-note1]: **marginal.** [5]

[^386-note2]: The text reads "1703," but this is clearly incorrect since the events related in the letter occurred in 1704 and 1705.

[^386-note3]: Esther Stoddard Edwards had given birth to Eunice Edwards on Aug. 20, 1705.

[^386-note4]: Eunice Mather (1664-1704), was the wife of Rev. John Williams of Deerfield, slain in the attack on the town on Feb. 29, 1704. Eliakim was born in 1668 and died in 1669.

[^386-note5]: Israel Williams (1684-17040, taken captive by a French privateer.

[^386-note6]: **marginal.** [24]

[^386-note7]: Rev. William Williams of Hatfield, who married Christian Stoddard in 1699.

[^386-note8]: Mary Stoddard Mix, wife of Rev. Stephen Mix of Wethersfield.

[^386-note9]: Warham Mather, of New Haven

[^386-note10]: Stephen Williams had been carried to Canada by Indians after the attack on Deerfield in 1704. He arrived in Boston on Nov. 21, 1705.
