## C11. Timothy Edwards to Mary Edwards, April 1716 C0011.TE-M.Edwards 4-16

Timothy EdwardsC011. TE to Mary Edwards, 4/16 (with P.S.5/3/16). ANTS, f. 1700-1719A, #5. Addressed on back "To / M rs Mary Edwards / At / Hadley or Hatfield / D.D. / P r Madam Porter / Q.D.C."

Dear Daughter

I am Glad to hear that your are Still in health, and I pray God Grant the Continuance of so Great A mercy. You may hereby be Informed, that we of this family are all in Competent health. It is a time of General health in these parts: Old Goody Grant is Lately dead: The Stirring Amongst us upon Spiritual Accounts Yet Continues at least in good measure, if not as much as ever. your Mother Brother and Sisters do all Remember their Love to you, We could be all Glad to See you, and hope in Good time we Shall so do. Your Mother has receiv'd your Letter, and Intends to as Soon as Conveniently She can to Send you a Letter. I suppose your Brother Jonathan will do so also. [^396-note1] We both of us that are your Parents do daily remember you (both as to Body and Soul) before God in Our prayers. I would have you Send us word as Soon as you Can whether you receive any benefit by Goody Smiths Means or no; [^396-note2] And If you find hither to that you have received any, I would you take advice of your Uncle and Aunt Williams [^396-note3] whether you had not best to cease from any further waiting upon her means, and Return to them, and to act therein as they Shall advise you; to both of whom give my Love and respects with your Mother, and also our Service to Mr Partrigg & M n, and to Mr Chauncy [^396-note4] and M rs & Mr Porter and M rs when you See them, if it be not too Long first. When you have Occation to pass the great River I would have you be very Carefull y t you Dont venture your Self in a boat that is Over Loaden, or in a Sorry Canoe especially when the wind is high & the water very Rough and that you dont venture to Sit Just on the very edge of a boat &c— be Sure in all respects be very Carefull how you pass the River. Benjamin Bancroft was about a Moneth Since Drowned in Going over from this to ye other Side of the Great River, and many others had Like to have Lost their Lives with him, as I suppose you have heard; and I hear that was the Last week drowned also in One of ye upper Towns. I commit you to ye mercifull Care of God in Christ, and that in all respects, and Am Your Affectionate Father Timothy Edwards ——

Windsor April 1716

Postscript

I would have you Send us word whether you desire to come home or no, and if you do (I mean supposing you are not like to Receive any benefit from Goody Smith) I will take Care to Get you brought home as Soon as May be, but If you Meet with any Inconvenience as to the Means you are Now under the use of, You had best Stay a while Longer, but as to that I Leave you (as before) to your uncle and Aunts advice. And am

Yr Loving Father T.E.

May. 3. 1716

[^396-note1]: See JE's letter to Mary of5/10/16.

[^396-note2]: Possibly Mary was being treated by this Goody Smith for her "crooked neck."

[^396-note3]: Rev. William Williams and Christian Stoddard Williams of Hatfield.

[^396-note4]: Possibly William Partridge and Rev. Isaac Chauncy of Hadley.

## C12. Timothy Woodbridge to Timothy Edwards, September 18, 1716 C012.T.Woodbridge-TE 9-18-16

Timothy WoodbridgeC012. Timothy Woodbridge to Timothy Woodbridge,9/18/16. ANTS, f. 1700-19A, #7. Addressed on back "To the Reverend / Mr Timothy Edwards / Minister / in East Windsor." The back of the letter also contains some sermon notes by TE. TE’s memo following the letter indicates that he probably communicated it to his congregation, so that the request could be voted on.

Rev d Sr

I have Received advice from ye Rev d Mr Stephens moderatour of a Council which sate Lately at ye north society in midletown that that Council not Issuing Some differences amongst ye people there agreed to Call in ye north Consociation of this County to assist *in that matter & he by Consent of ye Council* desires me to Inform your self & ye Church with you of their agreement that your self with a messenger from your church would please to be at Mr Smiths house the first Tuesday in october next about ten of ye clock.lb />yours to Serve you

Hartford Sept: 18: 1716

T: Woodbridge

[memo in TE’s hand:]

Rememb: to pp d L t: Ellsw ths wife to full Communion

## C13. Timothy Edwards to Mary Edwards, January 27, 1718 C013.TE-M.Edwards 1-27-18

Timothy EdwardsC013. Timothy Edwards to Mary Edwards,1/27/18. ANTS, f. 1700-19A, #9.

Dear Daughter

It is probably that before this Time you have that Yr Mother has had Another Little Daughter, whom I have Named Martha, who was Just three weeks old the Last Sabbath day Morning. Yr Mother the Great Goodness of God hath had a very Good Comfortable time all along; the Little one hath well ever Since it was born. Yr Mother hath been Several Times already out with us in The dwelling Room, & its for ye present very hopefull that before it be Long she may Safely Leave her Parlour. We are all about house only Some of us are troubled with Colds; I have not heard but your Brother Jonathan also is well: he hath a very Good name at Weathersfield, but [^398-note1] as to his Carriage, and his Learning. Yr Mother and Sisters do all Remember their Love to you; We hope ere Long to See you ere, and When you Come, you will Stay a while with us. I commit you to God, with my earnest Desires and prayers that he would be every way Gracious to you, and above all that he would bless the precious Means that you now enjoy to the Saving, and everlasting Good of your Soul, by making ye Lord Jesus Christ above all precious to you. [^398-note2] Let us hear from you by all Opportunities, and Now and then If ye Occations will permit it, write to Some of us. Yr Mother thinks you don’t write often enough. Yr Sister Betty Sayes She hath Sent you two Letters, and has not receiv’d One from you.

I am y r affectionate Father

Tim o: Edwards.

Windsor Jan ry:27/1717/8

[^398-note1]: MS sic; TE undoubtedly meant "both."

[^398-note2]: Northampton, where Mary was staying, was experiencing one in a string of "harvests" under Solomon Stoddard.

## C14. Esther Edwards to Timothy Edwards, November 20, 1718 C014.E.Edwards-TE 11-20-18

Esther EdwardsC014. Esther Edwards to Timothy Edwards,11/20/18. CHS, Jonathan Trumbull, Sr. Papers, Misc. Letters. MS damaged and badly rubbed in spots.

Hartford November y e 20: th 1718.

Honored father

I Went yesterday over to weathersfield and I understand that the Scholars intend to go to Newhaven next tuesday and if you please to Send my Brother to new haven with them I am of opinion that it will be much [...] than for him to go down alone Because [...] Scholars have hird a man to go with them to bring back all their Horses and ther not being a present oppertunyty for y e conveying of their chests [therto] they do intend to Carry their books and Cloaths in their portmaneau and if you will please to write a letter to my uncle [....................] and in other respects to take care of my brother It is very probable [it] may save you the Labor of going down and [...] [....................] respect it is verry likely that an oppertunyty will present [...] convey thither what he leaves behind him, and I suppose you will come down to Weathersfield with him which will prevent any farther trouble about my going home

Honoured father, from your dutyful

Esther Edwards.

## C15. Timothy Cutler to Timothy Edwards, June 30, 1719 C015.T.Cutler-TE 6-30-19

Timothy CutlerC015. Timothy Cutler to TE,6/30/19. ANTS, f. 1700-1719A, #1.

June 30. 1719

Rev d Sr

Your Letter came to my Hands by your Son. I Congratulate you upon his promising Abilitys and Advances in Learning. He is now under my care, and probably may continue so; and doubtless will so do, if he should remain here, and I Settled in ye Businesse I am now in. I can assure you, Sr, your & ye Ministers of your Parts good affection to me in this affair is no small inducement to me, & if I am prevail’d on thereby, it shall be a Strong Motive to me to improve my poor Abilitys in the Service of such Hopefull Youths as are with us. They may suffer much from my Weaknesse but they shall not from my Neglects. I am no party-man, but shall carry it with an equall hand and Affection to the whole Colledge, and I doubt not but ye Difficulty and Importance of the Businesse will obtain for me your & all good men’s prayers w ch I do much value and desire. The young man whom you have sent down I have examin’d. I find him, Sr, to have made advances but small in Learning, but I look upon them Considerable with respect to the Time he hath had, & Disadvantages he hath lyen under; & look upon his natural parts as not mean. And tho’ I think we may be too lax in admission yet I know not but y t all things consider’d he ought to be encouraged. I look not upon my Self to have power of admission, & did therefore send him to Mr Andrew to know his sentiments. He sent me word he had nothing against favouring such a person. I have therefore ordered this Isaac Stiles to attend Recitations with the freshman under Mr Brown till the Commencement, when we might know the Pleasure of the Trustees, which (I scruple it not,) will [v.] be in his ffavour. Sr I remain under the earnest hopes and Expectation of your prayers.

Service to Mad m Edwards & all my ffriends with you. Your Humble Serv t

T. Cutler

## C16. Timothy Edwards to Timothy Cutler, [c. Late 1719] C016.TE-T.Cutler c.late19

Timothy EdwardsC016. TE to Timothy Cutler[?], n.d. [c. 1719?]. Fragment. BRBL, endpapers of sermon notebook, 1722-23.

[....] I have Recieved your Letter of May [...] I wish I may ever in any Good degree be worthy of the Character that you th[ere give] me, which for ye present I am far from pretending to. You are wellcom to Mr. [Watts’s] Lyrick poems, which I hope may both Gratify and Improve your Poetical [Appetite] and serve to Rouse your apprehensions of the Glorious and adorable Perfections of the Great and Infinite Creator and Former of all Things and of ye most amiable and Transcendent Excellencies of our Blessed Redeemer. I desire that you would send it to me by my son at his next Coming home, and that you would Inform him that we are all [...] in Competent health and that his Parents and sisters do Remember their Love to him. We shall greatly [like to] hear of his wellfare and that he [Behaves] discreetly and soberly in all his [ways] as indeed [through God’s] mercy I have not yet heard anything to the Contrary. I hope he will Consider that how especially the Glass of his Time is Continually Running out (as it were) in Golden sands and his p rsent Opportunity at ye College is (Considering the time that he hath Lost and how Near it is to its end) so Exceeding Precious that Its pity but that every particle of it should be Improv’d to ye best advantage. and pray tell him tis from me, and also that I hope he still bears in mind, and will Continue so to do, the Great Danger he [...] was Lately in, [^401-note1] together with the Never to be forgotten Mercy that (through the sparing Compassion of a most Gracious God) he now enjoys and that he will make it his Great Care dayly to Give him the praise and Glory of it from whose Goodness alone he hath Receiv’d it. I would have him send us word [at the] first opportunity how he is as to his health, and in p rticular the Cough he Lately Left us with. I pray God Bless and that every way [not only] him but You also with ye whole society (I mean the scholars) and Grant that y r friends may be Great Comfort in, and abundant Cause to bless God for you and Make you blessing to his [...]ple in your day and Generation.

I am y r Real Friend & unfeigned [...]

[^401-note1]: Probably a reference to JE’s bout with pleurisy in his senior year (see "Personal Narrative").

## C17. Timothy Edwards to Mary Edwards, March 2, 1720 C017.TE-M.Edwards 3-2-20

Timothy EdwardsC017. TE to Mary Edwards[?],3/2/20. ANTS, f. 1700-19, #3.

Dear Daughter

I hope to See you Sometime This Spring at your Grandfathers; and If then you are dispos’d to Come home with me, I Intend to Bring you home: The Family would Gladly See you about ye time of ye Election, when also I expect your Brother from New Haven. If I do Come to N: Hampton This Spring, I suppose it will be Sometime in April, for I must Send Down ye Horse pretty early in May for Jonathan. We are all now in Competent Health, though Several of us have been very Considerably Amiss, (and Among others My Self) This winter. I understand Yr Mother and Sisters have Remembred their Love to you in your Sister Betty’s Letter. She hath Lately Joyn’d in full Communion with ye Church to very Good Satisfaction. Joseph Coult and Old M rs Morton are Late ly Dead. It is now a Time of General Health Among us here and in these parts of ye Country. I Commit you both in Body and Soul and So for Time and Eternity to ye mercifull Care of a Gracious God in Jesus Christ, whose Grace and favour in him I hope you above all things prize and Seek, and Am your affectionate Father (always mindfull of you in my prayers)

Timothy Edwards

Windsor March 2 d/1719/20

## C18. Timothy Edwards to Stephen Mix (Fragment), [c. November 1720] C018.TE-S.Mix 11-20

Timothy EdwardsC018. TE to Stephen Mix, c. 11/20. Fragment. ANTS, f. 1720-29A, #6.

[...]

from Reason and Common equity

2 dly he that enjoyes a priviledge on ye amount of Service expected from him, and which is a Sufficient Reward of his Service, is Surely Bound in Justice to ye performance of that Service. If a Man Recieve a Benefit from his Neighbour In Consideration of his being helpfull to him in his Business, ye help expected being not greater but rather Considerably Less in value than ye benefit Rec d; he is Certainly Oblig’d in Reason and equity to afford that help, and do the Service which is ye very Condition of that Benefit, which therefore may be Requir’d of, & Challeng’d from him as a debt. and this I think is the present Case.

3 dly By your Own Act who are his Father, and to whose authority he is Bound to be Subject. If I understand ye Case right, this is the true State of it, viz you desir’d My Son to take yours in with him to be his Chambermate: he plainly told you If he did So, your Son Must be helpfull to him in ye business he had to do in ye buttery or to y t effect, to which he readily and freely Consented; whereupon he took him in: So that in Submission and Obedience to his Father, Elisha was bound in duty to be considerably helpfull to Jonathan; Neither doth his Service come under the Consideration of Kindness, or an expression of the ye Ingenuity of a Kind ready willing Chambermate but is to be look’d upon as matter of Duty. and that which be the act and Deed of his Father May be Requir’d of him & Challeng’d from him as a debt.

Thus Sr according to the best of my Light I have truly Stated the Case that is here Insisted on. and Largely (If not more so than Needs) given you My thoughts upon it: how you will Recieve it, whether with offence or Contempt, or both I cant tell. I do not, nor Cannot Say, I dont Care, for your good Acceptance of it will be far more Agreeable and pleasing to me than the Contrary, for I can truly Say I heartily desire that there may be a Good understanding between us, In order whereunto I Intend as Soon as possibly I can get time to write my Mind to you Concerning Somethings that I have Observed in you and Met with from you, that have been not very pleasing, but to speak ye truth <were> Considerably ungratefull & Grievous to me, and I am verily perswaded are n t Justifiable in you; but how Long it will be first I cannot tell. I should have done it Long ago had I not been Much Straitned for Time: Such are my Circumstances that I can well Spare Time for it, and yet Cant Satisfie my Self without it.

My Wife gives her Love to Sister Micks (to whom also may Give my Respects) She hath been Lately <very> Credibly Informed that before three Young women, two of them being Strangers, I Mean not at all Related to our family, She talk’d So Against her Son Jonathan, that She Cant but think it tended not a Little to discredit him and blemish his name. If it be so, She Desires that She would Seriously Consider whether She hath therein done the part of a Near Kinswoman, viz Acted towards him as might well be expected from [————] One So Nearly Related to him as his Mothers Own Sister.

I am

Sr Yr humble Serv t

Timothy Edwards

## C19. Daniel Dwight to Timothy Dwight, April 11, 1721 C019.DDwight-TDwight 4-11-21

Daniel DwightC019. Daniel Dwight to Timothy Dwight,4/11/21. ANTS, f. 1720-29B, #11. Addressed on back "For Mr / Tim o Dwight / Att Northampton / Per Hubbard."

New-haven, April ye 11 th 1721

Lov:

Brother I waited till now, not only for this Convenient oportunity By Hubbard but that I might observe to you Something from the Trustees Meeting, when & where there was nothing more Rremarkable than that they have Chang’d Cap t Munson for a better Steward Scil. John Ponderson The Schoolars were all Strictly Examin’d in order to Detect the Shamfull Crime Laid to their Charge by New haven but all Prov’d unsuccessfull.

Pray improve the first opportunity to Send me word whither you Did any thing att Windsor att your Return hom. If you Did Send word what your agreement was but But in Short Let me have the Sum of your management in y t affair

Dan ll Dwight

## C20. Timothy Edwards to Bolton Church Committe, January 16, 1723 C020.TE-BoltonChh 1-16-23

Timothy EdwardsC020. TE to Bolton Church Committee,1/16/23. CHS, MS 71914. Accompanied JE’s letter of12/20/22.

To the Gent m: of the Committy In ye Town of Bolton

Gent m:

I hae herwith Sent you a Letter that I have Lately receiv’d from my Son, which he Directed to your Selves from New York, as you will See by the date and Contents of it. At the Same Time I Receiv’d one from him to my Self of the Same date with yours, and also Another to his Mother Written Near a Moneth Since viz. Jan: ry 7 th from which I expect (Life permitted, and health Continu ed), in the Spring, and I am apt to think he will be here either in March or Sometime in April Next at furthest. And Considering my Own Mind in the Matter together with what he hath expres’t in his above mentioned Letters to My Self and his Mother, I very Much expect that he will Leave the People with whom he now is at his next Journey home. I have perused my Sons Letter to y rSelves, and find Nothing in it Discouraging as to ye Motion you have made to him.

I am

Gent m: Yr Affectionate friend & Serv t: Tim o: Edwards.

Windsor Jan ry: 16 th/ 1723/2

## C21. Anne Edwards to Mary Edwards, June 17, 1723 C021.A.Edwards-M.Edwards6-17-23

Anne EdwardsC021. Anne Edwards to Mary Edwards, 6/17/23. Amherst College, Special Collections, Uncat. MSS, Box 3, f. 34. Addressed on back "To / Mrs Mary Edwards / att / Northampton / These."

Windsor June [-] 17 1723

Dear Sister

I fear it has been a considerable disapointment to you, as it has to me, that I have not before now been to Visit you; I [-] have waited about a month for an opportunity, but I now hope to be gratified with one as soon as I am ready; for I am more unready in Some Respects than I was a month ago. I am almost alwais thinking of you, and hope I Shall See you in about a fortnight, and therefore Shant Stand to write anny news only the Family is in health, and we lately heard Sister Betty was So. accept of these Scribling lines with abundance of love from your uneasy Sister untill She Sees you —— —— —— —— ——

Anne Edwards

## C22. Timothy Edwards to Paul Dudley, October 18, 1723 C022.TE-P.Dudley 10-18-23

Timothy EdwardsC022. Timothy Edwards to Paul Dudley,10/18/23. HSP, Ferdinand J. Dreer Autograph Collection 126:1, American Clergy, v. III.

Windsor Oct r: 18 th 1723

Sr/

I have ye Hon r: of Y rs of Oct r: 16, wherein You desire to know the truth from me Con cerning two things therein Mentioned. as for ye Latter of them viz ye pigs, it is wholly a Mistake. I never had any thing Extraordinary of that Kind. As for ye pompions w t Yr Hon r: hath heard of them is not beyond, but I think Short of ye Truth. Yesterday by Mr Collings’s Desire I wrote him An Account (the best I then Could) of it, that he might Commu nicate it to Yr Hon r: but in ye Account I Gave him I have Good Reason to Conclude that I Kept much within bounds. I Cant now Give you So full an Account of ye things, as I might do If I had More time, but Intend Sr to Obey Yr Hon rs: Commands in it, by ye first Good oppor tunity to Boston in a Letter which purpose to Direct to y rself as Dwelling in Roxbury (for So I suppose you do) In which Account I shall be More particular and full then I can (so well) be Now: I would Gladly Serve your Hon r: in it Now, but that I Greatly want my time for my Sabbath preparations, my time being every day Much taken up, by teaching of four Grammar Schollars, So y t for want of time I was up Last night I am apt to think till one or two of ye Clock in ye night, and need So to be this night, And besides as I hae already Intimated I Cant do it now with y t Advantage, and So Much to y r Hon rs: Satisfaction as I hope to do hereafter. I shall not further add Sr, but that I Heartily wish you may have ye presence of God with you while you are in these parts of ye Country in any Concerns of weight that may be before you, And you May have ye Conduct and Mercifull Care of his Gracious providences and be Covered with his protection In y r Journey hence, And his blessing may On All accounts Rest upon y rSelf y r Lady and whole house. I Rejoice in Any Opportunity Advantage Good Occation to Serve y r Hon r:

I am Sr Yr Hon rs: Most Obedient & Humble Serv t: Tim o: Edwards

## C23. James Pierpont to Timothy Woodbridge, November 5, 1723 C023.J.Pierpont-T.Woodbr11-5-23

James PierpontC023. James Pierpont to Timothy Woodbridge,11/5/23. *Publications of the Colonial Society of Massachusetts*, Transactions 1899-1900 (Boston, 1904), April 1899, pp. 199-200. Footnotes reproduced from CSM Transactions.

Rev d Sr

I received y rs of Oct 28 and am thankfull to you for ye Information you therein gave me. I have in complyance with your Directions accomodated Kilburn [^408-note1] to his satisfaction.

You are I presume sensible who the Trustees appointed to go to New York. yy all went save Mr Chapman, [^408-note2] the Committe from ye Synod mett them, & after much discourse among them selves & with ye parties Concerned yy broak up without doing any thing to effect, being obliged thereto by ye Scotch parties extravagant terms, which were such y t our [...] Gent: could by no means advise ye English to comply with this affair I conclude is so Sircumstanced that Mr Edwards [^408-note3] will not any more enguage in it & therefore I hope he will have your advise in favour of North haven in as much as it is a much better place than where, he is, & it is both for ye interest of ye Trustees & safety of ye Colledge to have the neighbouring Clergy both able & well principled both which in my account Mr Edwards bids very fair for.

I have nothing Speciall respecting the Colledge therefore shall leave it in your hands to be presented on all occasions to ye throne of Grace. I was verry Sorry you were not here att ye meeting of ye Trustees & y t ye more because you were detained through indisposition; of which I hope this will find you freed. So with dutyfull regards to y r Self & Ma m I conclude who am y r most humble Servant

James Pierpont [^408-note4]

[^408-note1]: Presumably Pelatiah Lilborn (Y.C. 1724). See Dexter’s Yale Biographies and Annals, i. 305.

[^408-note2]: Presumably, the Rev. Daniel Chapman (Y.C. 1707) of West Farms (since the Revolution called Green’s Farms, and now included in the town of Westport), Connecticut, is here referred to. As his parish was not far from the New York border, he would naturally have been thought of in connection with such a mission. See Dexter’s Yale Biographies and Annals, i. 65, 66.

[^408-note3]: Jonathan Edwards is here referred to. In August, 1722, almost immediately after he had been licensed to preach, he began to minister to a small Society of Presbyterians in New York, but left them in April, 1723. On the twenty-eighth of July, 1727, he married Sarah Pierpoint, sister of the writer of the letter in the text (Sprague’s Annals of the American Pulpit, i. 330; and Dexter’s yale Biographies and Annals, i. 218-226.)

[^408-note4]: James Pierpont (Y.C. 1718) was born 21 May, 1699 in New Haven, where he died 18 June, 1776 (Dexter’s Yale Biographies and Annals, i. 189). [. . .]

## C25a. Timothy Edwards to Stephen Williams, November 23, 1724.doc C025a.TE-SWilliams 11-23-24.doc

Timothy EdwardsC025a. Timothy Edwards to Stephen Williams,11/23/24. HSP, Gratz Collection, Case 8, Box 22. Inscribed on verso: "To / The Rev d: Mr Stephen Williams / Minister of the Gospel / In Springfield / These."

Dear Sr

I Rec d: not Long Since a Letter from Mr Hopkins, [^410-note1] wherein he Inform’d Me that he Intended to Go the first of Dec r: next to Windham, and bring my Daugh- ter Esther home, if She came not home before, and also desir’d me If should come home before that time, that I would Inform him of it, that So he might not take Such a Journey to No purpose, I request therefore of y r Self that you would by a Line or two as Soon as you can Inform him that She is now at home, She came home last Wednesday [———] [——————————————————] [^410-note2] Dec r: Comes in early ye next week and m r Hopkins writ me word he had business at N:Hampton (as I Remember) ye Last week in November or ye next Lecture, It will be needful there I Conclude to Send him w d As Speedily as you can. My wife Gives her Love to y r Self and to Cous n to whom also pray Give mine. This with my best wishes for y r Self and y rs is all at pr sent from

Sr Yr affectionate friend & Kinsman

Tim o: Edwards

Windsor Nov r: 23 d/1724

[^410-note1]: Rev. Samuel Hopkins of West Springfield, who would eventually marry Esther Edwards.

[^410-note2]: A lengthy, illegible deletion by TE.

## C26a. Timothy Edwards to Elizabeth Edwards Huntington, June 24, 1725 C026a.TE-EHuntington6-24-25

Timothy EdwardsC026a. Timothy Edwards to Elizabeth Edwards Huntington,6/24/25. Photographically reproduced in William A. Edwards, *Timothy and Rhoda Ogden Edwards of Stockbridge, Mass., and Their Descendants: A Genealogy* (Cincinnati, 1903), p. 5. The back of the letter is addressed, "To / M rs Eliabeth Huntington / In Windham."

Dear Daughter

I have time now but Just (in Great hast) to write a few Lines to you m r Allyn of Lebanon who is quite a Stranger to me, now waiting. I have Intended to write more Largely to you when I have more time, but must only Now Just tell you that through ye Goodness of God we are all about house, & none of ill any otherwise then with Such Indispositions as have commonly attend ed the Great Colds y t have of Late been Common here, & that I Dayly Remember you In my prayers in a very particular Manner. I commit you to ye Mercifull care of o r Gracious God & Father, for So I hope he is and will be, both to me and you; And my earnest prayer is that he May be So to us all. I hope you han’t forgot what I have [^412-note1] you a hint of when I Last Saw you, Concerning y r writing to me, and Giving Some particular acc tt &c —— of w t I y n mentioned. Such a thing would be very Acceptable to me.

Mr Harper Cant Make y r Wheell till after harvest, Yr Mother with all y r Sister Remember yy r Love to you both, Give Mine also to y r husband. [^412-note2] Yr Mother desires that y r husband would Send her ye Cards She Spake to him for by ye first Good Opportunity. I shall n t further add

But y t I am Yr affectionate

Father Timothy Edwards.

Windsor

June 24 th/ 1725

[^412-note1]: MS sic; "gave."

[^412-note2]: Elizabeth Edwards (1697-1733) m. Jabez Huntington of Windham, Conn., on 30 June 1725.

## C27. Timothy Edwards to Esther Stoddard Edwards, October 11, 1725 C027.TE-ESE 10-11-25

Timothy EdwardsC027. Timothy Edwards to Esther Stoddard Edwards,10/11/25. ANTS, f. 1720-29B, #4. Addressed on back "To / M rs Esther Edwards Sen r: / In North-Haven / These."

My Dear [^413-note1]

I have Sent Joseph Elmer with my horse to wait upon from N: Haven home, Concluding that you want to be at home, especially Considering you expect to be Speedily Sent for to Windham, and hoping that by this time Jonathan may be So far recovered as to allow (without any danger or difficulty) of your Return to your Family.

M rs Riply told me at Mr Whitings Funeral at Mr Collings’s (of whose death I conclude you have heard before now) that Betty [^413-note2] expects to Ly in by the Middle of this Moneth, but Sister Backus told me Since, that She told her that She did not expect it till ye Latter end of this Moneth, or the Beginning of November.

If your Sons State will allow you safely and Comfortably to Leave him, I conclude you will gladly Improve this Opportunity by my Neighbour Elmer to Return to us, but if not I chuse rather that you Should Stay Longer with him, for I would by all means have all needfull care taken of him, And had much rather be at ye trouble and Charge of Sending again for you, than he Should be Left under any Circumstances of Danger or Difficulty.

The family is in its usual state of health. At Mr Whitings Funeral, which was the next day after I Left you, M rs Ripley told me that betty was well, in no Bad way in any respect that She knew of, and that Anne was as well as She use to be. James Rockwell was at Father Stoddards and tells me y t Father and Mother and Mary were well. [^413-note3] Serg t: Bissell is Return’d and tells us that Esther [^413-note4] Got well to Boston, and is in good health there, (as I take it) at Uncle Stoddards. I Just now enquir’d of Abigail, [^413-note5] and She Sayes that he expressly told her that She is there. We have Still very great Cause of thankfullness to God for his Goodness. Y e Lord give us Grace Answerable thereunto. Give my Respects to Mr Stiles and M rs and to any of my Kindred that may enquire after me, and in particular to Cous n Todd if you See her. I shall not further add but that I pray God be with you and y r Son in y r absence and in your Journey home, & that the Children all Give their Duty to you.

I am y r affectionate Husband

Timothy Edwards.

P.S. If you do now come home, besure to take all due Care of Jonathan, both by getting what help he may need for him, And Advising him to take Care of himself that So he may not by a Relapse grow ill again.

Windsor Oct: r 11 th/1725 forget not to thank Mr Stiles & Mistress for any kindness yy have Shewed to you & for their Care of him, & put Jonathan in mind to pay Mr Stukes for y r Entertainment. you may Let him read this Letter.

[^413-note1]: JE was at this time convalescing at the home of Isaac and Kezia Taylor Stiles in North Haven, Conn., after collapsing on the way back to East Windsor from New Haven.

[^413-note2]: Elizabeth Edwards, who had married Jabez Huntington of Windham, Conn., June 30, 1724; she gave birth on Nov. 1, 1725, to a daughter named Elizabet

[^413-note3]: I.e. Solomon and Esther Warham Mather Stoddard, and Mary Edwards.

[^413-note4]: Esther Edwards.

[^413-note5]: Abigail Edwards.

## C28. Timothy Edwards to Esther Stoddard Edwards, October 20, 1725 C028.TE-ESE 10-20-25

Timothy EdwardsC028. Timothy Edwards to Esther Stoddard Edwards,10/20/25. ANTS, f. 1720-29B, #5. Addressed on back "To / M rs Esther Edwards Sen r: / In North-Haven / These / P r Maj r: Rog r: Wollcot. Q. D. C."

My Dear

I Rec d: Mr Stiles’s Letter by my Neighbour Elmer and am Glad to hear that Jonathan is mending, and Sorry that he is Still So weak and Low. I hope you will Take utmost Care y t he dont Get cold. I am afraid of y r taking too Great a burden upon y r self in Tending your Son both day and Night, I desire therefore that you would not only take Care of him, but of y r Self also: Accept rather of ye Neighbours Kindness in watching over again then outbid your own Strength (which is but Small) by Overdoing.

I have sent y r Spectacles by Maj r: Wollcot, who came Last night to our house and Express’d himself very ready to be ye Bearer of both this and them to you. I desire y t you would not fail by the first Opportunity to Send me word when you would have me Send for you, And how both you and y r Son are. This day in ye Morning, Young Joseph Porter told me (being Just come home) that he very Lately Saw Esther In Boston at Uncle Stoddards, and that She Seem’d to be very well. We are all through ye wonted and Great Goodness of God, in Ordinary health; ye Children all Give their Duty to you, with their Love to their Brother. We find your absence (especially So Long) makes a great empty place in the house. I Commit you with my Son, with ye rest of our Children to ye mercy of God who has ever be Exceeding Good to us and Ours, and hope that through his grace he will Still be so. I am with Love to Jonathan, y r affectionate Husband

Timothy Edwards

Windsor Oct r: 20 th/1725

P.S. I am now So very busy that I cant without Considerable Inconvenience be from home one day. but yet if my Son Continues still So weak & Low as he has Lately been I think I must go down and See him. I would have thee therefore Send me word very particularly how he is & whether you dont think it needfull that I should do so.

## C29. Timothy Edwards to Esther Stoddard Edwards, November 10, 1725 C029.TE-ESE 11-10-25

Timothy EdwardsC029. Timothy Edwards to Esther Stoddard Edwards,11/10/1725. ANTS, f. 1720-29B, #6. Addressed on back "To / M rs Esther Edwards Sen r / In North Haven / These."

My Dear

I have Sent my Neighbour Elmer to wait upon you home; We shall all (If you can now Safely Leave your Son) Rejoice to See you well come home. I bor a Small vial of M rs Bekcley which I forgot and Left it as I Remember in Mr Stiles’s North Chamber in ye Shelf over ye mentle-tree pray remember and take it with you and Deliver it to ye Owner as you come homeward. I also Ten Single pennies as I Remember, w ch are two pence a piece. Remember to bring them too. Leave My Son under ye best care that possibly you can, and Remember to put him in Mind to pay Mr Stiles both for himself and for y r Keeping at his house, and to thank him for all their kindness. Give my Respects to them both. Yr Children Give their duty to you, we all wish you a Good Journey home. Mercy and the Children had put up a Great more of our thanks-giving fare for Jonathan, but Neighbour Elmer Could [...] [^415-note1] See how he Could carry it, Neither Indeed Could I, he would have been very wellcome to it If we could by any means have Got it Down to him. I and all ye Rest of ye family would Gladly See Jonathan at home or have him here with us a while before he Returns to ye College Again If it may Consist well with his Circumstances.

I shall n t further add but y t I heartily wish thee a Good Journey home And am (In Great haste[)] Thy very affectionate Husband

Tim o: Edw ds

Windsor

Nov r: 10. 1725

at Night ye night after I am for ye present (methinks) very Loth Jonathan Should Return to his work In ye College before he hath been a while at home.

[^415-note1]: TE’s omission.

Esther EdwardsC030. [Esther Edwards,] "On the Soul," n.d. [c. 1726]. Draft. ANTS.

A Mem d : for my Daughter Esther besure Remember to pay m r Green what I am in his Debt for y e News Letters I have had of him, y t you bring with you at y r Return.

Remember also to buy of him for me M r Sims’s Sermon Concerning Ministers Maintenance. with m r Tufts Letter (as its Said to be to Squire Kent on y e Same Subject.

Get y m for me If yy be to be had In Boston. And Enq re : If yy re be any other Book on y e Same Subject Lately printed, and Look on it and If you like it buy it for me except mony fall much Short. [^416-note1]

[verso:]

I am in formed y t you have advanced a notion y y t the Soul is matereal & keeps w th y e body till y e resure[c]tion as I am a profes’t Love of Novelty you must alow me to be much entertain’d by this discovery w ch how ever old in Some parts of y e world is new in this [^416-note2]

I am informed y t you have advanced an Notion y t the Soul is materiall & atends y e body till y e resurection as I am a profest Lover of novelty you must immagin I am very much entertained by this discovery (w ch however in Some parts of y e world is new to us) by but Suffer my Curiostity a Little further I w d know y e manner of y e kingdom before I Swear alegance 1 st I w d know whether this materiall Soul keeps w th in y e Coffin and if so whether it might not be convenient to build a repository for it in order to w ch I w d know w t Shape it is of whether round triangular or fore Square or whethe[r] is it a number of Long fine Strings reaching from y e head to y e foot and whether it dus not Live a very discontented Life I am afraid when y e Coffin Gives way y e earth will fall in and Crush it but if it Should Chuse to Live above Ground and hover about y e Grave how big it is whether it Covers all y e body or is assined to y e head or breast or how if it Covers all y e body w t it dus when another body is Laid upon y t whether y e 1 st first Gives way and if So where is y e place of retreat but Supose y e Souls are not So big but y t 10 or a dozen of y m may be about one body whether yy will not Quar =ril for y e highest place and as I am insist much upon my honnour and property I w d know wher I must Quit my dear head if a Soperior Soul Comes in y e way but above all I am Consearned to know w t they do where a bureing Place has bin filled 20 30 or 100 times if there they are a top of one another y e upper =most will be so far from the body of[f] y t it Can take no Care of y e body I Strongly Susspect they must march of[f] every time there Comes anew Set I hope ther is Some Good place provided for them but dupt [^416-note3] y e undergoing so much hardship & being deprived of y e body at Last will make them ill temper’d I Leve it w th your phisicall Genus to determin whether Some medesinall applications might not be proper in Such Cases and Subscrib your proselite when I Can have Solution of these maters

## C32. Timothy Edwards to Anne Edwards, September 12, 1729 C032.TE-A.Edwards 9-12-29

Timothy EdwardsC032. Timothy Edwards to Anne Edwards,9/12/29. ANTS, 1720-29A, #10. Addressed on back "To / M rs An<n>e Edwards / In Killingworth / These / P r Mr Tourney / Q. D. C."

Dear Daughter

Yr Letter to y r Mother and I we have rec d: and are Sorry for your Going back in y r health you Speak of, but yet Glad that you are So well as you are, and y t you are (as you Say you think) rather better then you us’d to be for ye most part at home. You are very apt to Get Cold, and very Subject to a Cough, you must therefore be very careful in y t respect of y r Self I should be Glad to See you well at home, and So we Should all, but yet I am willing If Mr Eli =ot If Mr Eliot tis probable y t you may thereby Recover y r health, that you Should Still wait upon providence where you are in ye use of means, but yet do much Expect to See you at home before the weather Grows So Cold, as to expose you to a Cough by y r taking Such a Journey. I have Lately heard Directly from y r Brother, and Rec d a Letter from, and by Both his Letter and by Mr Benj: Pierpont understand to my Great Comfort that he is very much better in health, and bears ye Burden of his work (which hath for Some time Lain wholly upon him) that he is Still mending under it, So y t Mr Pierpont tells me he is both in Countenance and voice rather better y n he was before this weakness came upon him; he also tells me that ye People of Northamp ton Seem to have a great Love and respect for him, and that they take Great Content in his Ministry. They Continue their usual Kindness to him, and have built it a Good Large Barn & almost finish’d it, Since he hath been Laid aside by his weakness from his work. I understand y t Sister Mary hath writt to you of y r Sisters, that are married. we are in usual health, y r Mother Remembers her Love to you. I commit you to ye mercy of God, and hope I Shall Still Remember you in my prayers. I am (in Great Haste) y r

very affectionate Father

Tim o: Edwards

Windsor Sept r: 12 th 1729

Give mine & y r Mothers Service to Mr Eliot and M rs and Sutably Remember us to o r Relations as you have Opportunity.

## C33. Timothy Edwards to Anne Edwards, October 6, 1729 C033.TE-A.Edwards 10-6-29

Timothy EdwardsC033. Timothy Edwards to Anne Edwards,10/6/29. ANTS, f. 1720-29A, #9. Addressed on back "To / M rs Anne Edwards / In Killingworth / These."

Dear Daughter

You may hereby be Inform’d That o r family through ye Great Goodness of God to us are all in usual health, only Mercy is pretty amiss, but we hope in No Dangerous way, and rather better that She Lately has been; She keeps about house, Goes out of Doors dayly, and Sometimes does a little in ye house. Mr Russell and M rs came hither to from N: Hampton Last Friday Night, and Give us a very Comfortable Account of y r Brother, Who now hath for a Considerable [time] [^419-note1] preach d both parts of ye day, and Done the whole Work of ye Minis= try, and Mr Russell tells me Seems to him to be quite well, or as well as ever he knew him or to that effect. I desire you would Send us word by Mr Neighbour Rockwell who I hope will deliver this to you, but If he Should fail, by ye first opportunity how it is with you, and when you desire y t I should Send for you home. and If you have rec d any Considerable kindness from Mr Eliot or M rs besides Common Civility Since you have been with them, Mention it In y r Letter. I commit you to ye mercy of God in all respects and Am besure take great care you dont [...] [^419-note2] any New Cold.

Yr affectionate Father

Timothy Edwards

Windsor Oct r: 6 th/1729.

P.S. Yr Mother and Sisters Remember their Love to you We Should all be very Glad to See [...] [^419-note3] well at home. and very Much expect it this Moneth, and hope y r State may be Such as allow of y r re= turn before the Weather Grows Cold. y r Sister Eunice was Married Last Wednesday to Mr Simon Backus, and went with him ye Same day to Newington. Jerusha has been there with her ever Since.

## C34. Matthew Rockwell to Jerusha Edwards, [c. Late 1729] C034.MRockwell-JEdwards late29

Matthew RockwellC034. Matthew Rockwell to Jerusha Edwards, n.d. [late 1729?]. BRBL, f. 1568. Addressed on back "To / M rs Jerusha Edwards / Att / East Windsor."

Madam

My admiration of your excellent Person would be Sufficient to gain you best and most pure Love: were it not so conterary to my nature, to give it to her who hath given hers already to ano= ther than myselfe. wherefore for two substantial reasons, v:i:z: my necessi= ty of restraining my most free affe= tion; and the vanity of hoping for a return of yours; (being already given to another.) I think candid Madam no offence can or will be taken at my delaying to seek such a conver= sation as is most expedient for the ratifying of a happy union between mutual Lover.

I am Madam your faithfull Frien.

## C35. Jonathan Parsons to Jerusha Edwards, December 10, 1729 C035.JParson-JEdwards12-10-29

Jonathan ParsonsC035. Jonathan Parsons to Jerusha Edwards,12/10/29. BRBL, f. 1566. Fragmentary address on back: "For M rs / [. . .] Edwards / [. . .] Mr Bissel These."

Mam

The State of my Mind is at present owing to the unhappy News of your Illness. Tis not an easy thing to conceive of the Damp that is cast upon my Spirits, and the Cloud that hides my usual Temper. Since the most tender Affection I am capable of, inclines me be interested in your tenderest Love, it cannot but be a very Sore Affliction to me to think of having the Hopes of a Sure and lasting Friendship, cut off before the real Enjoyment. My constant and tender Regards for So much goodness, have improved themselves in the Strictest Sympathy. Even while I write, it Seems to me I feel a Strong Pain at my heart, for fear that Life Shou’d be dissolved, and the Springs of Nature broken, before I may Secure to myself So divine a Pleasure, as the Certainty of your Friendship. The Tast of Pleasure is nothing Short of Bitterness to me, while my dearest Friend is broken with Strong Pain. Tho’ I am well Satisfied, by a close Application to the Duties of Religion, you may have a Prospect of a Scene of future Happiness, Since by patient Continuance in well doing, I Steadfastly hope, you have Sought for Honour, & glory, and Immortality; yet I cannot find myself freely willing to have the World, as well as my self, part with so much Virtue and Goodness, I think, we Shou’d loose: But must learn to corres correct my unjust Appetite Desire. If my Wishes had any Influences upon your Will, you would consent to tarry a while longer in this World of Trouble, before you adjoyn your self to the kindred Minds Above. However; may your Virtue and the Grace of God be your exceeding Consolation, to bear up your Spirits in the Agonies of Such a Distemper; and dispel all Fear of being [^421-note1] remov’d out of Such a State as this, to be put into the Possession of Rivers of Pleasure, which flow at God’s right Hand forever. By Such Meditations, a good Frame of Soul will be cultivated; which may be as a kind assisting Hand to releive you of your bodily Infirmities. If you will not upon my Sincere Desire; yet consult your own good So much as to be Steadfastly fixed in the Path of Life; not too much dejected; willing to Stay on this Side the Grave. Consider the Sore Affliction of your best Friend, is nearly in Proportion to the Sense he has of your Groans. Mitigate your Sorrows, that I may receive the chearful News of your Recovery from your own Hand, with all the hast that wings true Friendship to Such a Distance. Till then, the good Wishes and earnest Prayers of him, Shall be employed on your behalf, who is your.

Assured Friend, and devoted Servant, J. Parsons

Y.C. N. Haven.

Dec r 10. 1729.

[^421-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C36. Timothy Edwards to Mary Edwards, [c. 1729] C036.TE-M.Edwards c.1729

Timothy EdwardsC036. Timothy Edwards to Mary Edwards, n.d. frag. [c. 1729?]. ANTS, f. 1720-29A, #7-8.

Daughter Mary

Your Sister Anne Receiv’d a Letter from you Last Week wherein we understand you were then under Some Indisposition by reason of Cold, as I my Self and Severall of the family are At this present Time, but Otherwise through the Goodness of God are in Ordinary health. See y t you be Carefull of your health, and to that end that you keep your Self warm both Day and Night, & Take heed that you Don’t wet your feet, And to prevent that keep your Shoes tight and in good State. And See that you don’t Go too thin to meeting: And if you Should be at any time So ill that It Should be needfull for you to In prove the help of a physician, I would not have you Spare, for I will take Care to defray the Charge you may be at upon that Account.

And as I would have you to take due Care of your health, So I would have you to be very Care full of your Name and Reputation. A Good name is a thing of great worth, a Jewell y t can hardly be Over-valued, or kept With too Much Care, especially in persons of your Sex, therefore See that you prize it, and be very tender of it. Carry your Self respectfully to your Uncle and Aunt, kindly to the Children, & Courteously to ye Servants, and Discreetly towards all; See that you be not unseasonably out a nights. Nor too often or much abroad in the Town at any time: & be very exact in attending family orders: and when you [...] [^422-note1] abroad be rather Sparing then Overfree in Conversation. & that So you may please your Uncle and Aunt, and Get their good will besure mind these three things two of which I have Mentioned already, viz, be kind to the Children, be very Orderly in your walk in ye family with respect to Religious dutys (which you Should be from a higher Motive then that of fearing men, namely ye Consi= deration of y r duty to God) And Shew your Self alwayes very ready and willing to do any thing for them that they desire.

But Above all Other things I would have you duly Carefull of, and Concern’d for the Good of your Soul. See therefore that it be y r dayly Care and prayer that you may be kept from Sinning against God, y t you watch and and [^422-note2] pray that you may not fall by Tempation. & remember that young persons Stand in Slippery places, they that Stand therefore had need to take heed Lest they fall. I might easily Say Much more upon this Subject, but I hope I have Said More then enough already.

See y t you dayly Seek ye Grace of God in Christ by Secret prayer: Rember that you have an Immor tal Soul [. . . . . . . . .] that is Lodged in a frail Mortal Body and it is So precious that all [. . .]

[^422-note1]: TE’s omission.

[^422-note2]: MS sic.

## C37. Jonathan Parsons to Hannah Edwards, January 29, 1730 C037.J.Parsons-H.Edwards1-29-30

Jonathan ParsonsC037. Jonathan Parsons to Hannah Edwards,1/29/30. BRBL, f. 1527. Addressed on back "For M rs / Hannah Edwards / att Windsor / These /P r Mr Stebbins."

Ma m

You will not wonder at the Tenderness & Concern I have expresed for that Dear departed — — - Jerusha, if you was once Sensible of ye inward Sentiments of My Mind about her, while before ye Fair Spirit flew away. There is Such a feeling Sense of Loss, remaining upon my Spirit, when I wou’d Converse with ye Surviving Sisters, that I am at a Stand, least my Passions Shou’d over bear my Actions & So render my whole Conversation undesireable. But yet when I am put into ye Condition of Absence, by ye Strength & exercise of my Mind, roving & longing for ye Releif of Redress of its blasted Hopes; nothing Short of Commencing a Lasting Correspondence with the Sisters that yet Survive her, or at ye Least with her Surviving Companion, is, or can be equal to my Desires. Tis usual to See that Leng of Time Long Absence, takes Men’s tho’ts off from they, by Some intimacy had made ye Object of their Desires; but, ye Longer I reflect upon ye Loss, consider’d in general, or apply’d in particular to my Self, the more am I fill’d with a Sensible Grief. The comely form of her Body, (if my Judgment is not warp’d by my Passion) was but a very faint Resemblance of ye more desireable & pleasing Beaty that naturally adorn’d her Mind: that togeather with her Attainments in Learning especially of a divine Nature, & her Piety & Devotion towards God, added to her Benevolence towards Men, fill’d my Soul with as generous a Friendship for her, as I, under my Circumstances, was capable off. Take it not ill, therefore, if under melancoly thots of a Long eperation, I ask ye Liberty to Settle an Epistolary Correspondence with her agreeable Survivor; which will undoubtedly give a Secret Satisfaction to him, Who is

Your Assured Friend & hum le Se t: Jon a: Parsons

Y.C. N. Haven

Jan y: 29. 1729/30

P.S. Think it not Strange [^423-note1] that I neglected to return you my Thanks for your Trouble in Sending me a Letter. thro’ a mistake I took took it to be Sent by M rs Abigail. I present my due Regards to ye whole Family.

[^423-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C38. Jonathan Parsons to Hannah Edwards, July 29, 1730 C038.J.Parsons-H.Edwards7-29-30

Jonathan ParsonsC038. Jonathan Parsons to Hannah Edwards,7/29/30. BRBL, f. 1527. Addressed on back "For M rs / Hannah Edwards / Att Windsor / These / P r Am m."

Ma m, I cannot but reflect with melancoly Apprehensions, &, Sometimes, little Short of Impatience, when I see my Self hindered sharing my Joys & Sorrows with Such a capacious yet tender Mind, as already has taken her flight to tast Sublimer Pleasures, than we can conceive of, or imagine. Under my Sorrows with [—] a mixture of Joy, as my busy Mind was much upon futurity, or ye world of Spirits, whither ye dear departed was gone, a friend of mine gave me the Such an Entertainment as that I can’t refrain giving you ye Oppertunity of perusing ye more material Points.

’His tho’ts were (he tells me) much upon futurity: Whither, Says he, metho’t ’I flew welcom’d by ye Angels of Light & Love into Paradisaical Pleasures: ’where I found ye most friendly Converse y t Set me into rapturous Devotion. There were many talking over ye grand transactions of ye Almighty. ’they Sung ye Power y t first gave them Being, & afterwards redeem’d them ’from worse than nothing. Charm’d with what I Saw & heard, I could ’not but reflect with a little Impatience Disdain upon my Self, y t ever I ’Shou’d be Shock’d with ye most untoward dificulties, I had ever met with ’withall, ere I reach’d d this happy Place. hearing me vent my tho’ts (says ’ye Author) you thus added, & doe you not well remember, you have some’times felt an internal Joy, not altogether unlike this, Springing from ’ye Consciousness of honesty endeavouring to be what you Shou’d be? - While ’we were in this delightful garden, there entered, accompanied in the Same ’friendly Manner, as we had been, a form altogether Angelical. At the ’first Sight, I cou’d desern ye Same Soft features, y t distinguish from ye rougher ’Sex, y t Part of human kind, we were wont to call ye female. You (says ’my friend) was at Some distance, so y t I had opportunity to take a more ’leasurely view of ye divine Creature, which, had you been present, you had ’certainly prevented. At her Approach among ye Croud of happy Spirits, I cou’d ’See ye kindest Social Affection appearing in their Countenances more ’visibly than I had observ’d on any other Occasion. I with rapturous Pleasure ’for a while, hung on this form, whos beauties were too Transcendent to be ’described; wherefore I attempt not, by words to express her Merits; nor is ’it possible for you So much as to imagine ye more than mortal Joy, I then ’discovered in your Air, your Mein, your Ghesture, when at a distant Sight ’of ye heavenly Charmer, you cried no more, than, O Jerusha! - And with ’open Arms flew & embrac’d as Angels doe - — This had Such an Impression ’on my Mind y t I cried out with an audible Voice, Thrice happy Parsons! ’that has this Superaded to ye other Pleasures of this Place, to meet in the [^424-note1] ’Closer Embraces of ye Mind, & to tast at once in ye immortal State, the ’Unmix’d Delights of Such a friendly Spirit. ——————————— If you feel half the Passion in reading, as I did in writing this, you’l be full both of Tears of Joy & Sorrow: Yet it may, perhaps give you Some Satisfaction, which if it does, I Shall look upon my Self well paid for my Trouble, and ever

Subscribe your Assured friend & Se t:

Jona th Parsons

Lyme July 29. 1730.

[^424-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C39. Abigail Edwards to Mary Edwards, July 25, 1731 C039.AEdwards-MEdwards 7-25-31

Abigail EdwardsC039. Abigail Edwards to Mary Edwards,7/25/31. ANTS, f. 1730-39, #4. Addressed on back "To M rs / Mary Edwards / att / Windsor / These."

Dear Sister

I Can only take Time Just to inform you y t Through ye favor of Heaven I Got well through my Journy & have injoyed my Health as well as usial Since I have been at Newhaven I am at present well content I would intreat you to send by s r Wolcot with ye [faceing?] of my stays some [—] pieces of new [ ] [...] to Bind y m with & my pencels you will find y m in sister Rushas uper drawer in plain sight you will find tow or three [...] in ye Bin in ye Celler ye Thikest of which I desire you to send I should be glad of a Lin from your hand But Can write no more my self with this pen & ink but y t I am your

Efectionate sister

A Edwards

Newhaven July 25 1731
