Aunt Mather gives her harty Regards to my parents. give my duty to y m & Love to ye rest of ye family

## C39a. Benjamin Colman to Edmund Gibson, September 13, 1734 C039a.BColman-EGibson9-13-34

Benjamin ColmanC039a. Benjamin Colmann to Edmund Gibson, Bishop of London,9/13/34. Fulham Papers, Lambeth Palace Library, London, England. This is a cover for the letter to the Bishop from the Hampshire County ministers of Sept. 10, 1734 (A009a).

I am desired to forward & cover the Inclosed to your Lordship, from my Rev d & Hon d Brethren the Associated Pastors of the County of Hampshire in New England; partly because I am now the Senior Pastor in this Sea Port of our Province, & partly because they Suppose my worthless Name may be a little known at London, tho’ not to Person of your Lordships Dignity.

It is now thirty five years since I left the City, where I was not unknown to the Venerable D r Bray, [^426-note1] that Man of God for Apostolic Love & Zeal: Since which I have had the Honour of a long most free Intercourse by Letters with the late Excellent Bishop of Peterborough, D r Kennet, [^426-note2]now with God.

Your Lordships three Pastoral Letters, occationed by some late surprising Writings in favour of Infidelity, have justly honoured your Name to us, & we hear your Character for Moderation & Righteousness with high Esteem & Pleasure. I do therefore ye more willingly joyn my Brethren, who live remote from Boston & hitherto quite out of ye Way of the Missions whereof they write, in their Address to your Lordship; being fully persuaded of their Integrity & Uprightness, & that they aim at nothing but what is just & right in ye Light of God.

The Harvest, my Lord, is plentious from North Carolina to New York, & multitudes are perishing within that long Spread of Virginia, Maryland, Pensylvania & the Jersies; But from New York north-ward Dr. Bray found little Need of Missionarys for the Propagating of Christianity, the Narraganset Country, excepted; And in the Coloniy of Connecticut & Massachusetts none at all, as at the Time I was informed.

Were your Lordship & the pious Trustees here upon the spot, I am sure you could not think the professed End of your Charter, & the Design of your Donours, answered in your supporting Missionary’s at Boston, Brantry, Newbury, Stratford, Bristol, Salem, Groton &c: Or if the seaports of great Trade, Boston, Newport, Marblehead, need to have Minisers of the Church of England, for ye sake both of the Inhabitants & strangers; yet also ar ethey well able to support their own Worship: Or did they want some Assistance, there can be no Pretence for it out of a Fund sacred to God for the sending his Gospel into dark & ignorant Places of ye Earth; but they ought to be provided for ssome other Way, & not by Alienating a devoted confined Charity, which were to run a Danger of Sacrilege & grea t Unfaithfulness.

This my Lord, is our View of the late now laid before you, which is humbly submitted to your Righteous & Impartial Judgment. Yet I fear that I have not preserved all ye Humility & great Modesty, which adorns ye Inclosed from my Brethren. I am ready therefore to humble my Self & beseech your Lordships Candor; While I doubt not but your own Heart wil make some Excuse for a little Zeal & Resentment, from an apprehended Injury to one of the most noble Charities to Souls, & most extensive Services to ye Name of Christ, that has been proposed to ye Workd for Ages past. A Concern on this Principle must be justified, & have your Lordships Approbation. I entreat my Lord your candid Constructiton, Forgiveness, Prayers & Blessing, & your Leave to subscribe my Self

Your Lordships most Humble & Obedient Servant,

Benjamin Colman.

Boston N.E.

Septem. 13. 1734.

[^426-note1]: Thomas Bray (1656-1730), active in the Society for Propagating Christian Knowledge, and late in his life the rector of St. Botolph’s, Aldgate, London.

[^426-note2]: White Kennett, Bp. of Peterborough, 1718-28.

## C40. Timothy Cutler to Zachary Grey, June 5, 1735 C040.T.Cutler-Z.Grey 6-5-35

Timothy CutlerC040. Timothy Cutler to Zachary Grey,6/5/35. *Illustrations of the Literary History of the 18th Century*, ed. John Nichols (London, 1822), 4:297-99.

Boston, New England, June 5, 1735.

Rev. Sir,

It is now a long time that I have promised myself a letter from you; but I will not despair, if Dr. Grey be alive, as long as I know how good a man he is, and how disinterested in his favours.

Mr. Johnson is so modest that he cannot tender his performances to so good a judge as you are, and imposes that work on me, and I the readier do it that I may therewith slide into your hands a worthless sheet of my own, for which I ask pardon and your candour. I would also remember some other friends, but I cannot be so very free with so poor a token.

We hear of the sad progress of Infidelity, and feel too much [...] of its effects with us. God forgive those who think Infidels qualified to be Bishops in a Christian Church. I have heard so many said accounts of Dr. Conyers Middleton, the Proto——s in Cambridge, that I begin to give into a jealousy of him. I know, Sir, you introduced first into an acquaintance with him, and that the gentlemen in Cambridge were the farthest men alive from the principles charged on him. How the case is, and what may have altered him, I beg to be informed by you.

As I said, Infidelity prevails also among us. Chubb’s and Dr. Clarke’s Works, &c. do much mischief among us. One Kent,[^427-note1] a Dissenting Teacher, is now suspended by a Council for Arianism and Arminianism, though the latter is grown so venial that it would have been hushed had it not been for the former. It is expected he will entirely be laid aside; however, that he will find friends enough to make him a new congregation and support him. A French Convert among the Dissenters now resides at our College in Cambridge, to teach the Students French. He is pretty open in avowing Arianism, and withal sets himself up for an inspired dreamer, and says he has in dreams been checked for many miscarriages and errors in his life, but never for this—— *Ergo* .——He with his proselytes (one of whom is a Fellow of the College) is shortly to work Miracles. He expects a Millenium in 1736, and a Messiah Ben Ephraim to appear. How far we may be corrupted, I cannot tell.

The News-Letter will let you into a sad squabble at the Anniversary Meeting of our Teachers. One Fisk,[^427-note2] the subject of it, has a long time teazed his people, by charming some, and exasperating others. At length, after several of our Fanatical Councils appearing against him, a strong party voted him out of his pulpit. He offering to enter it, has been repulsed, and bound over to the Quarter Sessions, where there will be a fine bull-baiting. You will see a great many Teachers take his part, and it is likely to prove a country quarrel; and so indeed do most of our Ecclesiastical Controversies; but this is an eminent one. He, good man, cares to be judged by none but Christ Jesus; but, I believe, he has no reason to be sanguine there.

The Calvinistical scheme is in perfection about 100 miles from this place. Conversions are talked of, *ad nauseam usque*. Sixty in a place undergo the work at once. Sadness and horror seize them, and hold them some days; then they feel an inward joy, and it first shews itself in laughing at Meeting. Others are sad for want of experiencing this work; and this takes up for the present the thoughts and talk of that Country; and the canting question trumped about is, *are you gone through?* i. e. Conversion.

These are too mean things to trouble a gentleman of Cambridge with; but, Sir, you that have given yourself the troubles to look into the whimsies of us will the readier forgive me in these narratives, especially as Fanaticism must overdo itself by the nonsense and confusion it clothes itself in, and thereby pave [...] the way to sobriety, and sound faith, and order; and, indeed, it has this effect upon many, and nothing keeps down the numbers of our Church but want of opportunity, and fear of starving.

You will please to make my compliments to your worthy lady and family, the excellent Dr. Dickins; and if there by any other gentlemen that remember me in Cambridge.

Your prosperity shall ever be a joy to me; and while I live I shall be, dear Sir, your most affectionate friend, and most humble servant,

Timothy Cutler.

[^427-note1]: Benjamin Kent, pastor of Marlborough, dismissed Feb. 4, 1735, after which he became an attorney in Boston.

[^427-note2]: Possibly Samuel Fiske (1689-1770), pastor of Salem First Church from 1718-1735, then of Salem Third Church from 1735-1745

## C41. John Sargeant to Hannah Edwards, July 28, 1735 C041.JSargeant-HEdwards7-28-35

John SargeantC041. John Sargeant,7/28/35. BRBL, f. 1528. Address on cover "To / M rs Hannah Edwards / at / Windsor."

Dear Madam

I am more than ever I was before convinced of the mighty power of Love. One would have tho’t the wildness of this country, the Savage manners of the people, that inhabit it with the sacred & solemn importance of the business I am ingaged in, would have banish’d from my breast the soft & tender passion, the tempting pains *& pleasing anxieties of love. But so* it has happen’d, ever since I Saw you last, a certain uneasiness (which I Suspect is what they call love) has attended me, which I neither can, nor am willing to get rid of. If any faith is to be given to the fables of Poets, Venus & her cruel Boy seem to have had a spite against me; so deep to wound my heart, that I must languish here at so great a distance from the fairest creature in the World, the lovely cause of those gentle pleasing emotions I feel whene’er I think of you. My fancy, or judgment discoverd something in you, undescribable by words, which transports me to all this extravigance of passion, extravigance I call it, (tho just) because I have So little reason to hope for the wish’d returns of love from you. But why not? ————

Love is a foolish passion, full of vain hopes & vain fears: However I am resolved to love you. Nay I cannot but love you. Your beauty I will not [^428-note1] name (tho that alone might charm a Stoic) your Superiour good sense, modesty woman’s peculiar ornament & praise, unaffected wisdom, & Sanctity of manners, with a thosand nameless beauties, attendent upon your every word & action, captivate me with the tenderest sentiment of Love.

Grace is in all your Steps, heaven in your Eye In every gesture dignity & love. - Milton

Dear Mad m I hope your candour will excuse what I have written not with more freedom than Sincerity. A favourable line in answer to this would give me more pleasure than I can express. However if you do not forbid me, I will presume to wait upon you in my return to New-Haven, a little more than a month hence —— In the meantime I beg leave to Subscribe myself

Your great admirer

And passionate lover

Sheffield July 28 1735

John Sargeant

M rs Hannah Edwards

[^428-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C42. William Williams to Joseph Pynchon[?], [c. September 1735] C042.WWilliams-JPynchon c.9-35

William WilliamsC042. William Williams to John Pynchon[?], fragment, n.d. [c. 9/35]. ANTS, Sermon on Matt. 7:15 (Jan. 1743). Regards the conflict over the ordination of Robert Breck at Springfield.

Honoured Sir.

upon ye consideration of yours of 7 ber [^429-note1] 10 wherein you desird a meeting of ye Association at Spring field ye week after next it hath seemd to me to be impractiable (I mean to get those ministers to come to it that allow ye proceedings at your church & favour m r Brecks settlement.) also likely to be unproffita ble we not being desird ye church & Mr Breck tho questionable whether y t will refer ye case to those who shall convene or will at all regard our Judgment. I had thought it would be better ye Association to meet at Deerfield according appointment only a week soon er w c is ye time you wrote that Mr Clap & others and as many of yourselves you think fit would meet ye Association there. but having receivd last night a letter subscribd by ye ministers of Boston viz messieurs Cooper Welsted gee & others w c was ye persons your church upon Mr Brecks motion we hear have sent to whence y y thus express them selfs to me Sr ye chief design of this Letter is to make this motion & request that your Association meeting w c was to be on y t day (viz ye day set for ye ordination at Deerfield) may be ordered [. . .]

[^429-note1]: I.e. September.

## C43. Esther Edwards Hopkins and Samuel Hopkins of Springfield to Hannah Edwards, [Before October 1735] C043.ESHopkins-H.Edwards 10-35

Esther Edwards Hopkins, Samuel Hopkins of SpringfieldC043. Esther Edwards Hopkins to Hannah Edwards, n.d. [before 10.35]. BRBL, f. 1524. Addressed on back "To / M rs Hannah Edwards / at Windsor."

Dear Sister

My mind was fully bent to have Given you A visit this weak if Providence had Permited indeed was So much Set I S d have over Come Considerable defeculties rather than fail’d but yet am Obliged to Stay at home my Little Daughter being very ill brok out into Sores about her faice & much Swell’d in her throat attend at times w th a feavour Pain in the head Sickness at the Stomack &c I had Considerable Opportunity w th unkle Unkele Williams of west =on [^430-note1] & did w th as much Equality & justis as I Could Lay the Case between Mr R—— [^430-note2] & you before him tho’ the one half was not told him he is vehe mently against your haveing anything more to do w th he represented his Confidence of your unhapiness by avariety of Expressions w d have me tell you from him y t you must Cloath your Self w th resolution & must Put an end to it & ye Lik to tedious to relate but one thing I may not omit he Says Let your obbligations be w t they will: ye Liber y t he Gave you at our house desolves y m all. however if you Cannot Resolution & Strength of mind anough to do it, father and Mother must for dg it must be done. but no more of this. I w d iform you y t m r Woodbri is Still very ill he has Still ye relicks of his distemper hanging above him & as he Soposes ye janduce Set in w th it I am my Self much bet =ter in helth than w n you was hear the time appointed for m r Bricks Ord Ordination is the 8 of October. [^430-note3] you must note y t w t Said was up on Soposition y t wat I Said true I think I keept a Great ways w th =in ye bounds of truth. we are Like to have a high time at Sprinfeid I have been very urgent w th Mother to Let me you be w th me a Little while She you w d not be willing these are to Let you know y t you Shall be very wellcome yours

E H

[Postscript by Samuel Hopkins on verso:]

Dear Sister

I am heartily Concerned for you and if you will follow my directions I guess I Can help you for tho your distemper be bad yet abstinence will Cure you. starve it. that is to say, keep up ye resolution you had when you left us y t you will be free: and let not ye best man alive abridge you of it if one Comes sniveling and Crying, tell bid him be gone. if another Comes with all ye fine airs of a pretty spark, tell him you will have nothing to do with him. And if this method dont do, send me word and I will give you further directions yours In hast

S H -

[^430-note1]: Rev. William Williams (1709-1750).

[^430-note2]: Matthew Rockwell of East Windsor, Hannah’s would-be husband.

[^430-note3]: Robert Breck. He was not ordained at Springfield until July 26, 1736, because of opposition from the Hampshire County ministers.

## C43a. Benjamin Colman to Stephen Williams, October 21, 1735 C043a.BColman-SWms 10-21-35

Benjamin ColmanC043a. Benjamin Colman to Stephen Williams,10/21/1735. HSP, Gratz Collection, Case 8, Box 22.

Boston. Oct. 21. 1735.

Rev’d Sir,

Yours of Oct. 9 is before me, for wch I thank you, & pray you not to write to me with so many Respects & Reverences, for I am your Brother, & cannot compare my Self with your Brethren of Hampshire. I have acted as I tho’t my Duty. & have in ye midst of Resolution betrayed fear. & humble my Self that I did not utterly oppose our Churches sending Mr Cooper. [^431-note1] I wish ye Civil Magistrates had not interposed as they did, & you are very much mistaken if you think that you satisfied Mr C— — that you were no wayes accessary to the Measures w ch they took. It wil be as hard also to make him think he knows nothing of ye state of the grieved Brethren. On ye last Lords day he staid ye church to read to em their Result at Springfield, & Mr B——s Confession of Faith. He & ye Deacons came to me ye Lords-day Morning, & told me it would offend ye Brethren if it were not read. Mr B. preached at Mr Gees & Welsteds. And ye Talk is that he is to preach for Mr Cooper ye next Lords day. Just now I received a Line from Mr Cooper, to inform me that ye Springf d Council met that hour by Adjournment to his House: That he knew not what they could do at this time, unless to consider whether it be their Duty to present a Memorial to ye General Court, of what [^431-note2] they met with in ye Affair at Springfield. That he tho’t it his duty to inform me of the Adjournment, that if I pleased I might favour them with my Presence & Advice, w ch he believed would be very acceptable to all ye Brethren concerned as wellas to himself. —— I immediately answered him in Writing, "That as to ye Compliment of my Presence with them on ye Occasion before them, he well knew ye Distance of my Heart from it, and as to ye particular he mention’d to be considered of, whether to present a Memorial, &c, my Advice would be not to do it; because we have had things of late too much carried thither. It w d be eno’, I judged, to speak when called upon that matter, if (as ye Talk is) it be complained of to ye Civil Magistrate. —— But there is one thing I told him they might do well to consider of, How to stop ye Tongues let loose against the worthy Ministers of Hampshire: for in three Visits I had made yesterday, I was obliged at two Places to vindicate those Godly Men, whom God had so remarkably owned, as well in their Order, & Discipline as in their holy Ministry, these last thirty years; & this last year more than ever before. ye I doubt not but their Ministry, & Order of ye Gospel among them, is regular & valid, & not to but [^431-note3] broken in upon, which God has crown’d with so great Success. So asking the Special preventing & directing Presence of Christ with them, I subscribed one among the many of his grieved Brethren.

From what Mr C——r has told me, I fear that your As- [^431-note4] sociation is broken to pieces, & that Mr Chancey, Devotion, Rand, Allin & one more wil never meet you again. What a lamentable Breach is this! But if you grow into two Associations, you may be yet united Brethren, & I hope wil be so. God over-ruled ye parting of Barnabas and Saul for ye promoting ye Gospel. Y e Lord grant it may be so among you, under this Division or separation. The Talk at Cambridge is, I hear, of our Association splitting into two: But I know nothing of it: If they may drop me & Mr Chancy they be are all Congregational; for I look upon Mr Welsted a Convert now: but I forgot Mr Abbot of Charlstown.

I am glad to hear of ye Arrival of ye Letter from y r Society, & long to see it, as do our Brethren here also. We have Country-Pay for our Services abroad & at home; at London & Husstonnek. But I hope are accepted of God.

Mr Appleton has your Letter, & has advised with me about ye use he has to make of it.

We thank God ye Town, & Country near us enjoy a great Health, & ye News from Newbury about the sickness in those parts is very comfortable, in ye Abatement of it.

My Duty to Father Williams. [^431-note5] Let not his quiet spirit be cast down, but fixed, trusting in ye Lord.

There’s talk about Ordaining Mr B- here, but I hope nothing in it. —— I salute ye Brethren with you, ask their Prayers, & am their Brother & Companion in Tribulation, & in ye Kingdom &c—.

Benj a Colman

[^431-note1]: Rev. William Cooper, Colman’s colleague at Boston’s Brattle Street Church, who was involved in the controversial ordination of Robert Breck over Springfield, whose case is discussed in the first two pages of this letter.

[^431-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^431-note3]: MS sic; "be"?

[^431-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

[^431-note5]: Rev. William Williams of Hatfield, senior minister of the Hampshire Association.

## C44. John Sargeant to Hannah Edwards, February 3, 1736 C044.J.Sargeant-H.Edwards2-3-36

John SargeantC044. John Sargeant to Hannah Edwards,2/3/36. BRBL, f. 1528.

Sheffield Feb. 3. 1735/6

Dear Madam.

So long an Intermission of correspondence between passionate Lovers, I confess, looks a little odd. But if you have utterly forgot ten me, I shall not much wonder at it, Since I Seem almost to have forgotten myself. The coldness of this winter Season has pretty much confin’d me to my chamber; and when I venture to look abroad, my eyes are Saluted with a horrid prospect of rocks, mountains & inhospitable woods, that my imagination dare hardly venture over the frightfull impediments, that lie between you & me. But these difficulties, tho’ great, are not the chief; for if I Shoud give my Soul a loose and it surmounting these, Should meet with Some invincible one nearer your person, (which is what I am most afraid of) it would perhaps, being discouraged, not be able to find its way back again. But the returning Sun begins to thaw my frozen passions, & to raise the soft Sentiments of love: love the best blessing of life, the Softener of our cares, & the charm, that chases Sorrow from the heart of man, who, sociable by nature, & finding many wants, that cannot be supplied in a solitary life, rests not, till Heaven gives him a Sharer of his grief & a dear partner of his joys. How ever melancholy I may be alone, methinks, if you were here & would lend your assistence I could deter easily deermine a long disputed point in Geography about the place of the Garden of Heav Eden; for I fancy I Should presently conclude Paradise was here: Which would doubtless be a discovery not less surprising than entertaining to the [^432-note1] Learned world. But whatever the rest of the world world would think of it, I am sure it would be no disagreable discovery to you me, nor I hope, to you neither, Since, I Suppose, you are of an inquisitive & phylosophical in humour. However, if you dont forbid it, I intend to make you an other visit; & I believe with Something more of warmth, than when I say yo Saw you last; when an Ague had almost Shook my frame to pieces, and a feaver had So burnt up my Spirits,that there was almost nothing in me for love to kindle up a flame upon. —

I have been a Stoic all winter, but am out of conceit with that Philosophy, & have a mind to try one of a more agreable kind. However I intend to try one experiment more in tha Philosophy; for I have purposed to try five or Six weeks in the woods with our brown Gentlemen & Ladies. And if that don’t mortify me to the world in a literal Sense, I beg leave once more to breathe my vows into your ears, & tell how much I love you. In the meantime I ask the favour of you to every to allow me to entertain my self with your Idea in the woods; for methinks I guess it will be the best company I Shall find: How I wish the Original would as readily bear me company wherever I go. However I warn you to prepare for a visit from your very humble Servant Sometime in the Spring: Then be coy: put on all your frowns; and if you can, (which I know is impossible) hide all your charms and loveliness: for if you appear as charming as you [^432-note2] used to do, you will hold me your willing captive Still for I am your very great admirer and most humble Servant,

J. Sergeant

M rs H. Edwards

[^432-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^432-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C45. Samuel Hopkins of Springfield to Hannah Edwards, March 9, 1736 C045.S.Hopkins-H.Edwards 3-9-36

Samuel Hopkins of SpringfieldC045. Samuel Hopkins to Hannah Edwards,3/9/36. BRBL, f. 1525.

springfield March 9. 1735/6

Dear sister

were I possesed of half the tenderness to, and Inclination to serve, my fellow Creatures, y t appears in you, it would oblige me to Exert myself for your help in ye present situation of your affairs. and such a degree of it I seal to you, as draws from me this letter; which please to Accept in good part; and as an Evidence of my Concern for you.

I love you dearly as a sister (without flattering as deceit I speak it) And therefore was possesed of no small degree of Joy and satisfaction when I saw you, a little while ago, set at liberty as a Roe from ye hunter, and as a bird from ye hand of ye fowler: and in ye same proportion my sorrow and uneasiness now Arise, to see you again about to be worried and Entangled in ye same snare y t you was in before.

Possibly there there are but few if any who have a fuller understand ing of your Case than I have: And so far as I Can Judge I think you are in duty obliged still to Assert your own liberty: And totally to dismiss ye affair that now perplexes you, let who will say what they will. for you Can’t freely and of Choice proceed to marriage, and it is inconsistant with ye law of Marriage, and of Nature too, y t you should proceed, if it is not freely and of Choice —— y t you Can’t freely and of Choice proceed, is what I know not only from your Conduct, but also from your own mouth: And your own reason will oblige you to Conclude y t it must be of Choice, or not atall. And for y t Reason you ought to put an End to ye affair.

Again to keep ye thing in hand perplexes and kils you, but to dismis it restores you to ye Enjoyment of yourself and friends. for ye truth of all this I refer you to your own Experience: when you have had ye afair in hand, for yours past, has it not been a Constant uneasieness to you, has it not wracked nature, and Exhasted your spirit and life, so y t you have appeared like a fadeing flower? on ye other hand have you not returned to ye vigor and spriteliness of youth, when it has been dismised: therefore ye Law of self preservation obliges you to put an End to it

Again you are obliged In Justice to mr R-[^433-note1]

to do it: for so long as his hopes are kept alive, and not fully Answered, he will be in Constant uneasieness and perplexity; but were the affair Entirely Ended, it would (I am Confident) restore him to himself. Hope defered makes ye heart sick. but hope Cut off, often works ye Cure. And so far as you have made ye Experiment have you not reason to think y t this is ye Case? has he not had ye possession of himself better when he has looked upon ye Case as lost than any other time for years past. In short ye Case seems to be thus, when you are nearest to one another you are most uneasie; when you are furthest apart ye better you Enjoy yourselves. And I think ye Conclusion must be this, part and live, or marry and die.

yea further I think y t God in his providence has made ye way of your duty plain before you, by Continuing in you such a disinclination to the thing, after so many Endeavours to Reconcile yourself to it. is not ye hand of God in this? and ought you not to look upon it as a voice from heaven, forbiding ye thing? Can you go Contrary to it, without running Counter to ye Call of divine providence?

I suppose you will grant y t in ordinary Cases that must govern, [^433-note2] And a person’s inclination or disinclination must determine ye matter but you will say y t yours is an Exempt Case, And make such an Enquiry as this.

Q. What shall a young woman do if she, if she really fears y t a denyal will undo the man? upon which my are I will give you my tho’ts as Clearly as I Can. —— And I will in ye first place suppose the worst, viz. y t ye man is undone if he be denyed. And yet I think it is your duty to deny him: for you are undone if you have him, and there is no Law, divine or humane y t obliges a man to love his Neighbour better than himself. And if one of you must be undone, and you have ye Casting voice in ye Case, I think you ought to free yourself before any other person.

Again you are both undone if you marry, and better one than two. But in ye next place, there is not half ye probability of his being undone by a denyal, as there is of your being undone by a Compliance. for it has often been observed, and I suppose is a Just observation, that those men, who will needs die if they are bagg’d, and will go to ye Ends of ye Earth and never be heard of more &c. make the worst Husbands if they gain their point, and make but little of baggs if they are Cast upon them. — look round you, dear sister, yea Enquire of ye best man you Can find, and give me an instance if you Can of a woman marrying a man to save him from being undone, who has not undone herself by marrying of him. And these reasons may be given why such matches are allways unhappy. (1) the person y t is so unmanly, as to Compel a woman to have him, by such a plea, has not anough of ye man in him to make a good husband. (2) a man who so over values ye Creature will Certainly fail of haveing his Expectations Answered, in ye Enjoyment of ye object he is so much in love with; And therefore his passion will End in ye uneasieness of a disappointment. and Consequently be in an uneasie posture, y t will render them both unhappy. yea (3) he will always be Jelous y t ye woman dont love him after marriage, who he knows did not before. and (4) when the heat of his irregular passion (which cannot last long) is Cooled, and abated, by Enjoyment, it will, very likely, turn into resentment. And then where is ye poor woman? she had better be a slave.

I seriously tell you, my sister, y t I had rather see you marry a man who professes y t he don’t love you above other women, than to see you marry ye same man in such a violent passion. for one who is so Indifferent will find his Expectations vastly more than answered, in ye Enjoyment of such so fine a woman. but he whose Expectations are raised so Exceeding high, will be ye subject of an unhappy disappointment, even tho he marry ye best of women. And to say ye best of it, such violent passion, is a fearful overvaluing ye Creature. And gives Just reason to fear y t a blessing will not attend it.

upon ye whole, is there not ten times the danger of your being both undone by marrying, than there is of his being undone by being denyed, or rather by his being kept off now he is denyed.

but further such persons if they are denyed, bear it as well as other men, and make as little or less of it, as any persons whoever. when did you know a man prove as good as his word, who was so very fond of dying for love?

I grant indeed y t when a man is deeply in love, it is a heavy affliction, to have a bagg forced upon him, this is what Experience as well as observation has taught me. And when such an affliction is fresh and strong upon a person, he may think it will be too hard for him. but as in other afflictions so in this, ye weight of it decreases by length of time, till it is worn off. And such violent passion goes off very Easiely. and ye subjects of it have in pretence, if not really, rejoyced y t they have been denyed. to ye truth of this your Eldest sister Can testifie. for when she [^433-note3] was as much afraid of ruining mr T [^433-note4]

as you be of undoing mr R. it proved otherwise, and he pretended he was glad of it, when they were parted. upon ye whole, I don’t suppose you have any reason to fear y t a bagg would prove mortal in ye Case.

I will allow y t you know more of mr R. than I do. but you must allow y t I am better acquainted with our sex than you be. and I will give you this one direction, to help you in your Conduct towards for ye future. when you see a man about to die for love. you must attribute one half of his mallady to Conceit, and if he be a man y t is inclined to ye spleen, it must be ye largest half. one quarter (if he be a pretty honest man) you must attribute to dissimulation; and the quarter that is left wil never kil him. tho I am Joculer in this passage, yet there is a great deal of truth in it. And I am sensible, by my own Experience, y t men Can’t die by ye bagg half so Easiely as they think for.

possibly you will Enquire further whether your keeping Company so long, is not an obligation upon your’s to which I answer That it is impossible y t this should oblige you to go Contrary to your own Inclinations, as I observed before, but then,

Whose fault is it y t you have kept Company so long? has it not proceeded from his pressing importunely? and Can that be an obligation upon you suppose a man Came to me to buy a farm, and I tell him I will Consider of it a week. at ye weeks End he Comes, and I tell him that I will not sell it don’t intend to sel it. he urges me y t I will Consider of it a month longer, and upon his importunity I do it, At ye End of y t month he urges me to Consider of it a month more, and so on. And I finally tell him, I think it not best to sell my farm. would not you think that man out of his wits if he should urge y t I was under obligations to sel it to him, because ye thing had been so long in hand? when it was by his Importunity only y t I had it under Consideration so long.

if you Enquire, whether you ought not to take still more time to see if you Can reconcile yourself to it. I think you have been much too long upon y t Already, and y t you Can’t be Justified in making any further tryal. it looks to me too much like a degree of self murder, to keep yourself in that uneasie posture any longer.

if you should ask me how you shall put an End to it. my advice would be this. y t you should Cut him off Entirely from haveing any Conversation with you, for this, seems to me to be ye only way y t is left you. for if you give him opportunity of Conversation with you, he will look upon ye thing as yet in hand, say what you will.

if you object, or any other should object and say, you must treat him with Civility, it will not do to be so harsh and severe with him, &c.

I answer. y t if you should break ye broom staff over his head and bid him never say a word to you more of y t matter, you would not deal with him more Injuriously than he does with you. why will you think y t so much tenderness is to be used on your part, while nothing of that nature is used on his? must you be Gentle and kind to him, while he is doging you to death? Contrary to all ye rules of reason and humanity? I dont say this, with any design y t you should treat him ill. but I think you ought to resent his unreasonable treatment of you, and give him no more opportunity to do it.

I hope, dear sister, you may have ye divine Conduct and [^433-note5] direction in this and all your affairs. and y t God who governs all things in infinite wisdom, will bring these things to an happy issue. And what better Course Can you take, than being much at ye throne of grace, with your Earnest requests for divine Conduct? and what Can be more Encouraging hereto, than y t sweet text phil.

4. 6. be Careful for nothing but in every thing — let your requests be made known to God? Commit your ways to him, and he will direct your steps.

we dont know of any body going to Boston at ye time you speak of in your letter. my wife sends you some flax, by mr Bliss. I shall be glad to see you at my house, and will freely Come and fetch you if that will be any kindness to you. if you will send me word when.

we Received your letter lasst night after nine of ye Clock, and I was loth to miss of this opportunity of writing to you, I have therefore been up ye whole night to write this. and it is now almost sun rise. if it will be of any service to you that will be a sufficient reward for watching.

we present our duty to father Edwards and Mother, and love in large measure to yourself and ye rest of our sisters. I am.

your loving Brother And Humble ser t

S. Hopkins.

[^433-note1]: Matthew Rockwell of East Windsor, who claimed that Hannah Edwards was legally bound to marry him.

[^433-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^433-note3]: **marginal.** [3]

[^433-note4]: This could also be a shorthand symbol. Apparently referring to an unsuccessful suitor of Esther’s.

[^433-note5]: **marginal.** [4]

## C46. Hannah Edwards to Sister, August 12, 1736_ C046.H.Edwards-Sister 8-12-36_

Hannah EdwardsC046. Hannah Edwards to "Sister", 8/12/[...]. BRBL, f. 1521.

wind springfeild august the 12

Dear sister

the state of this family having been for some time very defecult and having no oppertunity to send for phillis [^434-note1] by the bootes we are obbliged to send hors and man for her —— hannah has had smart fits of the fever and ague every day above this fortnight and now she has had y m every day five days going her fever is sorest quite of she is also very much excercised with all which makes the Do er not without concern - about her —— m r Hop— s [^434-note2] was taken with a Cold fit on mon day Last and a smart fever follow’d it which was not of till Last sometime Last Night he is still very poor we expect it - will Return again - sister has been so ever since phillis has - t been gone (except two or three Days) that she does but Just Grun de about. they begin to talk of Casting Jonah into the sea —— I conclu it will be said by some the Cours Caus Curse Causless does not Come and y t (as Sr nt stoughton said) we shall Lose all our Caus if we persist in the new way of singing —— I am sincible y t I am as I expected severely sensure’d and Look’d upon at windsor as very vile with Respect to my Concern with m r Rockell [^434-note3] —— neither is it Confind to windsor but Let it be as unconfinded as its every Like to be. I do not disign it shall give me much disqui et as it never has yet one ours - but I Percieve you all - all the family suffers with mine for being unReasonable — defecult twisting a man about from one Business to an another for several year together ocationing of him in such a way to spend his estate and then not being pleasd with any and being fals gals harted or double tongu’d in Carri ing smoth to his face and yet shewing your selves enimies behind his back and now wronging the truth in pretending you are not but have not been against his your sister only because she does not Love him but I hope it will not much disrest you. for there must be a time for all things. a time be spoke ill of [—] any thing aboute this affair —— (which you have carefully avoided ever since I Came away I wo’d be glad you wod write me word and tell me whether my Parents are unesy about me or no for if they be not I dont Care what the brawl of the ignorant mob is — I am in the gratest hurry I fear I shall forget twenty things that I wo’d [^434-note4] say I wo’d intreat you to send my Red skarf and some old [——] Light Coulour’d Caape you find the grate good[?] up in the gar garret if you Cant send nothing else I hope you will write to me very Perticularly of the state of the family and frinds at Newington do send sister sister Backus some maple suggar upon my account give Little Rusha a Convenent quantity tell her her aunt hannah sent it to her I am saving her [ ] and wish her [...] some where els my Duty Love and service to my frinds I Love them all very well but I am Contented here without Phebe your to serve H E

[^434-note1]: Possibly a family servant or slave.

[^434-note2]: Samuel Hopkins of Springfield, Hannah’s brother-in-law, at whose house she is staying.

[^434-note3]: Matthew Rockwell.

[^434-note4]: **marginal.** [2]

## C47. John Sargeant to Hannah Edwards, September 20, 17 C047.J.Sargent-H.Edwards9-20-36

John SargeantC047. John Sargeant to Hannah Edwards,9/20/36. BRBL, f. 1528.

Sheffield Sep t. 20. 1736

Dear Madam,

The tender affection I have for you, & the high regard I always pay to your family make me bear a part in every affliction you Sustain, & share in all your joys. By this agreable, but involuntary Sympathy my heart was touch’d with frief at the melancholy news of your dear Sister’s death; not indeed for her Sake, who is doubtless gone to a happier world than this; but for the Sake of Surviving friends, to whom She is lost; cut off, decay’d and wither’d in her blooming youth. How death has marr’d a beauteous form! Her body made of the finest mould, and the workmanship a divine artificer, the warm abode of an immortal mind, is now a cold lump of clay! Where are those eyes, that used to shoot soft fire, & kindle love! Where is that charming voice, that used to breathe harmony, good sense & virtue? where is the musick of her tongue; that was wont to excite joy & gladness in her aged parents hearts, & chear the whole house! These are no more! Lucy the young, the virtuous, the beautifull & ingenious Lucy is no more! Her name is remember’d no more, but with Sorrow, nor mention’d but with Sighs! But why do I Sooth my own grief, & recall yours dwelling on these melancholy tho’ts? Heaven is wise & providence benign in every event of [^435-note1] time: and perhaps most so, when we think it least. And while I mourn your Sister’s death, I rejoice in your recovery & M rs Nabby’s . Lucy has the start of you, & is gone before to partake of the happiness of that world of Spirits; among whom She found her other Sisters; who congratulated her arrival, & pitied your harder fate: or perhaps they attended her last moments, & catch’d her departing Soul, & were the first tha embraced her; & conducted her Spirit to Paradise. How gladly did her Sisters welcome her to their blisfull Seat! And how joyfully did She return the Salutation! How Surprised & charm’d was she with the glories of that world before unknown! How suddenly & with what pleasure did She contract ion familiar acquaintance with the Strangers there, Spirits humane & angelick, among whom there is nothing but condescention, mutual love & joy, without any mixture of Stiff ceremonious formality, pride, envy or disdain. There the Godhead shines with transcendent beauty & glory. And Jesus the mediatour is seen, loved & adored. The benevolent Strangers, but chiefly her Sister-Spirits enquire of her after those She left behind, & rejoice to hear, that they follow their Steps, in the paths of piety & virtue, which led lead to their happy mansions. Your name was doubtless mention’d amongst them; (or perhaps you are there known by some other name) Lucy carried the tidings of your Sickness; which tho’ melancholy to us, perhaps was joyfull [^435-note2] news to them: and who knows but they were preparing the most agreable entertianments of their world for you & your Sister Nabby , hoping the Sovereign & beneficent disposer of all things design’d now to dismiss you both from the perplexities & troubles of this uneasy world, & to gratify your wishes & theirs in allowing you to join with them and the rest of the happy inhabitants of Paradise. But Heaven Saw meet to disappoint their hopes & yours and our fears. They submit with perfect resignation to the Supreme will of him, who is Lord of both worlds; whose pleasure it was to try your faith & patience a little longer, & to bless the world with your Stay in it: for the world & your Sex need the bright examples of piety, benevolence & every other virtue, the lovely ornaments of life; which add charms to beauty. Virtue is a Solid & Substantial thing, & usefull in itself. Benevolence charms & enag engages the attention & love of all mankind; and with a sweet but almost irresistible force constrains to imitation. It was doubtless with reluctance that, when you was almost within Sight of Paradise, you return’d back again to bear some more of the painfull toils of life. But Heaven order’d it so, & you know how to submit. The prospect beyond death is most delightfull to one prepared to die: to such an one this is the world of darkness & misery that of light & joy, however gloomy the passage to it may appear. Give me leave notwithstanding to congratulate your friends at least, if not you upon your recovery; and allow me to take particular pleasure in it myself; & to wish it might be design’d in special kindness to me. For tho’ I cannot challenge any peculiar right in you, yet am loth to quit all pretentions to you; of whom I always think with the utmost tenderness of affec- [^435-note3] tion & the warmest Sentiments of love. Nor can I help it, while I discern in you every thing, tha is beautifull in womankind: which persuades me, he must needs be the happiest man in the world to whom you give yourself. And tho’ I can hardly Say, I hope to be that happiest man, yet I am bold to Say, that an return of passion from you equall to mine would certainly make me so. Perhaps you will say I am a little extravagant & enthusiastic: but if I am, I am willingly so. I confess my imagination is fill’d with a thousand bright & Sparkling Ideas of pleasure, when I allow my self to think that you are mine. If we were separated almost from all the world I fancy we Should enjoy one anothers love with less interruption from the noise, hurry & jargon of mortals. Our affections having no other objects but one another to center upon would, methinks, be swallow’d up with mutual enjoyment. In the deepest Solitude we should never be alone. In the closest retreat & retirement from com pany, we Should enjoy more pleasure, than the world can afford. And while we were the greatest benefactors to the world (which is the most generous & godlike noble ambition) we should be the happiest pair in it.) Innocence & good deeds Should finish the day & pleasure crown the night. One Soul, methink, would So animate each others body, that we must needs both die together, and neither leave the other behind to mourn: and Death itself should never part us. — — These tho’ts, I know, are meer creatures of the imagination: but I hope you will not envy me the pleasure of enjoying in this romantic way, what perhaps you will never allow me to enjoy in reality. —From my last conversation with you, you will forgive me, if I cherish some slender hopes of you. I am in pain to know my fate, & yet afraid to know it. If you will believe me, my pretensions of kindness to you are most Sincere. And I presume you have evidence eno’ to believe me, when I tell you, that

I am, with the highest respect and tenderest affection yours J. Sargeant.

P.S. If you dare trust a letter you would very much gratify me in writing an answer to this. J.S.

[^435-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^435-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

[^435-note3]: **marginal.** [4]

## C48. Elisha Williams to Stephen Williams, November 9, 1736 C048.E.Wms-S.Wms 11-9-36

Elisha WilliamsC048. Elisha Williams to Stephen Williams,11/9/36. Yale Manuscripts and Archives, Stokes Autograph Collection. Written from New Haven.

D r Sir

Since I failed of Seeing You in my Return - I venture to Write a Line to desire that y t Letter of mine in y r hands w ch has been so abused [^436-note1] may Lye safely w th You w thout any Copies being taken of it (or Seen) and that I sup =pose if y r is no occasion for Mr Edwards to say w t y r is in it in his answer So he will not do it tis error to Say agreably to w t you Wrote to me tis a false Coppy &c for Let ye difference between y r false printed Coppy & ye original be never so great y r is no need to print ye original to Shew it tis w t ye World has no Right to know any thing about. their action is easily Shown to be vile of your unequall know[?] I had thought to have said a Word ab t ye Revisal of w t shall be drawn up but I Refer you to Mr Bull ye Bearer not suffering me to add Save a Desire of Secrecy in y t Matter & hearty Love to you & Cousin & that I am y r Kinsman

& serv t — E Williams

N H Nov r 9 - 1736

[^436-note1]: See WJE, 12:142, 145-47, on Elisha Williams’s letter being broken open by supporters of Breck.

## C49. Abigail Edwards to Hannah Edwards, [Before October 1737] C049.AEdwards-HEdwardsbef10-37

Abigail EdwardsC049. Abigail Edwards to Hannah Edwards, n.d. [before 10/37]. BRBL, f. 1526. Addressed on back "To / Mrs Hannah Edwards / att/ Windam."

Dear Sister // you can’t but conclude y t ye Absense of so dear a Sister as you are Leaves a Large Vacancy in my mind, but notwith= standing I am deprived of ye happiness of your Company and y t of our Dear Relations and Friends at Windsor yet I am surrounded with many new Pleasures and Good things as a more healthful Constitution, plentifull and free Entertainment by my Friends, variety of entertaining Conversation, New Objects &c. upon ye Consideration of which I have determined to remain in New=haven About one month Longer. but ye chief motive to my tar= raying here is ye hopes of having my health more perfected. Be pleasd to present my Love to Brother & Sister and Little cousens and sutable regards to others at discretion.

Your Loving Sister

Abigail Edwards

## C50. Abigail Edwards Metcalf and William Metcalf to Hannah Edwards, November 13, 1737 C050.AMetcalf-HEdwards11-13-37

Abigail Edwards Metcalf, William MetcalfC050. Abigail Edwards Metcalf and William Metcalf to Hannah Edwards,11/13/37. BRBL, f. 1526. Addressed on back "To / M rs Hannah Edwards / Living / att / Windsor."

Dear Sister

I Received yours this very Day and Read as Sone as the Sabath was over with joy & Delight and am answering of it in the Same evening but my oppertun ity is Short & therfore you must accept of my willing Spirit instead of a more particular Letter: But I will familliarly tell you in breif that I am Contented here and find things Equal to my hopes in my brightest & Esteem my Self much indebted to the favourable of a Gracious God for inclining a man So well fitted to make my Life Comfortable to make my S Choice of me I find mr metcalfe a very Religious man and in as well as in many other instances God has been better to me than my fears. I want to hear particularly from you in Regard to your Comfort at home (you will understand me) Sister molly met— e Gives abundance of Love and Service to you She Loves you very much and Cri’d when you w went home if I am Not mistaken we have all been to a very fine weding Since I Came & Rid as far as walldings of windham to meet the bridgroom & bride Seth Johnson waited upon Sister molly & bille Metcalfe upon me. ——— wee all give our abounding Love to you & Sister Elsworth and brother. & Give my Special & most friendly Regards to m r wolcot and mr bissel & m r abot & Love and Service to all friends as you have oppertunity A I am with Sincerity and tender affection your Sister

Abigail Metcalf

Lebanon Nov-13—1737

[verso:] Dear Sister Hannah

I wrote this Line on the backside of your Sisters Letter Just to Let you know that I think of you tho’ I Dont Say how much I Do so, for that wo’d be Difficult. For I have often Told your Sister that I Can’t but be Considerably Touch’d & affected with the Lonesomeness & malen colly which I Cant but think you have felt at your re turn home where you found So great a Gap in the Family as the absence of two So Dear Sisters must needs Make, And what to Say for your Comfort I know Not, If My Tender Sympathy woud Do you the Least Service you have It. for I am Sure I Do (with the greatest Sincerity) wish Your comfort & welfare w ch is all have time at presnt to S To Say [——] Subscribing my Self your Loving & well

Wishing brother & hum le

Serv t W m Metcalfe

Lebanon Nov r. 14. 1737.

P.S. Duty to our hon d. Father & Mother, Service to Sister Patty m r. Woolcot & m r Bissel & all friends

W. M.

## C50a. Sarah Pierpont Edwards[?] to Hannah Morse, December 7, 1737 C050a. _-H.Morse 12-7-37

Sarah Pierpont Edwards[?]C050a. [?] to Hannah Morse, [^439-note1]12/7/37. One leaf, signature cut out. Possibly by Sarah Pierpont Edwards, or by one of Edwards’ daughters or sisters. The presence of this letter with items by or relating to Edwards suggests an Edwardsean provenance. Presbyterian Historical Society, RG 332, f. 4.

Curteous Madam; I Received your paper: and thank you heartily for [...] [^439-note2] I hope your [...] and [...] speak[?] [...] I remember it was the saying of a freind to me: that those helpfull to one another heare in the way shall meet again with the greater Joy another Day I see you Complain much of your Coldness and Deadness in spiritual dutys and am sorry if you have have reason so to Complaine: for I think neiver more need of wa[tc]hfull Lively Christians then in these dul Declineing u Days you say yo[u] have but Little heart to morn for your Coldnes I am sorry for that: yet see Isaiah 40 from ye 27 vers to the end: and O amaesing mercy in God Look Chapter 43 ye 24 and 25 verses; Compare them togather and you will see the bottomles depths of mercy you Complain of the hurries of the world: but I hope you will overcoom that: for every one that is born of God overcometh the world: but allas that is no eassy thing to [do] because ar hearts are Earthly [a]nd in Love with it I think the world is as great a temptation to me as any from without me I Rejoyce to herar you freely acknolidg your mercies: I hope you bitter Complaints against your selfe very shortly be turned into songs of praise to your Blessed saviour

I thank you for your advice to me: but allas I fear I Louse ground Dayly I fear Leest whiles I Recover my helth and eas: my soul fall into a sad relaps of Coldnes and formality which make me think of them psalm 78 ye 34 35 verses I belive tis as Difficult to behave aright under Prospertie as in adversity I remember mr Bolton [^439-note3] says it is one of the Dreadfullest Curses under the sun to prosper in our way and be out of the way of Heaven: and another: said that he Desired riches and honner no more than a weary horse doos a heavy bag or Load I am often Croosed in my desighns and belive tis best for me that I am to for I belive I am more inclinded vanity and pride then many others and therfore have more need of afflictions to humble me and mind me of the nothingnes of the world the fation whereof paseth away O I Desire to be thankfull for mercies I have been in greate afflictions and much discouraged respecting my helth: but am now restored to helth in good measure

well mrs Hannah I wish those promises you mentioned may be fulfild to you I suppose you have Lerned by faith to trust in promises though at presant you find not the blesed friuts of it in your self O Let us Larn to trust in God as we have Laitely been exhorted unto for he is fa faithfull that hath promised see second of Sam 23 5 vers and [-] Ezek. 37. 4 and [...]emiah 31 - 10 and 14 verses and then 33 down to the end 37 and Chapter 32 and 27 vers

but to end: I Desire you to forgive what is amise in these Lines and remember one that needs your prayers; yours in Duty to be Instructed

December ye 7 th 1737 [signature cut out]

[^439-note1]: Hannah Morse (b. 1696) was the daughter of Patrick Faulkner and Hannah Jones [of New Haven?]. She married Deacon Seth Morse, and was 41 at the time of this letter. (Information on Morse taken from notes on transcript made by Mrs. W.H. Hoag of Prattsburg, NY, in PHS collection.)

[^439-note2]: MS damage where the letter was folded results in lacunae here and in the following lines.

[^439-note3]: Possibly Robert Bolton (1572-1631), author of, among other works, *Instructions for Right Comforting Afflicted Consciences*, 2 ed., (London, 1635), a copy of which Timothy Edwards owned.

## C51. Joshua Gee to Joseph Sewall, September 25, 1738 C051.J.Gee-J.Sewall 9-25-38

Joshua GeeC051. Joshua Gee to Joseph Sewall,9/25/38. MHS, Misc. Bound MSS.

Rev d & Hon d Sir,

At your desire I have read over the Papers that you lately rec d. from Windsor; and supposing the representation of facts to be fairly given , I cannot wonder at the dissatisfaction of the Brethren of a Congregational Chh upon such a conduct in their Pastor. For if the Rev d Mr E.[^440-note1] delivered it to them as agreeable to congregational principles, That it belongs to the Pastor of the Chh to judge, & determine what complaints or accusations shall be brot before the Chh and what not — and that the pastor may ex officio hinder complaints from ever being heard by the Chh : I think the Brethren had reason not only to except against the Pastor’s sole power of Judging and determining, but to deny that an Eldership properly constituted have any such power to hinder ye Chh from hearing complaints: For when tis said Platf.[^440-note2]

I can find no reason to justify ye 2 d Article N o.1. and the manner in wch tis express’d: Witnesses (whether y y can write & sign yir Testimony or no) should always be ready to do yir duty, that the Elders may be enabled so to prepare matters in private, that in publick y y may be carried an End with less trouble & more speedy dispatch, as is directed Platf. Ch. 7. #167; 2. part. 3; And that the Elders may be able to act as Guides & Leaders in all matters ptaining to Chh Actions as part. 5: But may yy not do yir Duty, with t being confined to this method?

The refusing to let the Messengers have an equal Voice in Councils, is, I think, another just ground of dissatisfaction: and I can t but approve the Censure past upon it Article ye 3 d. As to the method of Chusing Messengers wch is next spoken of, I canot indeed think any oth r Member as much chosen as the P rson propounded by the Pastor &c: But yet, in y t method it appears to me, y t yre is no fair & free choice.

With reference to the Case of Mr Diggins, [^440-note4] as it is represented in ye Letter, I think ye Rev d Mr. E’s [^440-note5] denying a Chh meeting upon it, will (if he persists in it) expose him to a process for Male-administra- tion: I mean it will render him liable to be justly condemned, if they should enter into such a process upon it. For if as a single Pastor he had an indis- putable right to negative Chh-Acts (which the Brethren have disputed and not without some weigh ty Reason in N o 2.) yet y t is no good & suffici- ent Reason why he should refuse to let the Chh have a Meeting to make use of his power to nega- tive, after the Church had an Opportunity to declare yir Judgment with the reasons of it; wch might possibly give him light & change his sentiments & Conduct upon the Case.

But, upon the whole, what is to be advised? I freely confess myself to be in a state of doubting. And whether Mr Diggins should be advised to consult the peace of the Chh of Windsor by seeking Baptism for his Child in some other Chh? Or Whether the Brethren should not rather be advised respectfully to repeat yir Application to ye Pastor that he may join with ym in calling a Council as a means of Light and peace? And if he refuses, Whether they should not be advised to call a Council of Congregational Chhs ymselves upon a Complaint & Charge of Male-Administration? —— these are Questions wch I must refer to your[^440-note6] much wiser Judgment. I cannot deny, that (all things considered) I incline to think the Brethren sh d be advised to proceed towards such a Process, if the pastor will not prevent it by laying the Matter before his Chh for their consideration and Judgment upon it.

Thus, Rev d & Hon d Sir, I have given you the Sum of my thougts that have arisen upon reading the Papers you left in my hands: And I depend on it, that what has been done at your request, wch has with me the force of a Command, will be received with your usual Candor. —— That you may be long continued a burning & shining Light among the people of God & that I & mine may have a remembrance with you at the Throne of Grace is ye earnest desire of

Rev d. & Hon d. Sir,

Your obliged humble Serv t

Joshua Gee

Boston Sept. 25 th1738.

To ye Rev d. Dr Sewall

[^440-note1]: Timothy Edwards.

[^440-note2]: Cambridge Platform. Ch. 10. #167; 9. It belongs to the Elders to receive them from accusations brot to the Chh & to prepare ym for the Chh’s hearing; - this I can t but look upon to be expressive of their duty as well as of yr power; and their refusing to do what belongs to ym in such a Case would (it seems to me) give the Chh just grounds to charge them with Male=Administration, if it wd for using their power of office in such a way as will not consist with ye Power of Priveledge in the Brotherhood. To say that if the Pastor act thus corruptly, the chh hath no power to rectify it ; is to contradict Platf. ch. 10. #167; 7 - And if the Rev d. Mr E. has preach d to his Chh, that ye Votes of the Brethren to convict or restore an offend- er are of no force or validity with t. the Concurrence of the Pastor ; he has at least challenged for the [2] Pastor all that can be challenged for an Eldership in an Organick Chh & right administration; and I know not how he can support such a Claim. Indeed I think that whatever should be pleaded in behalf of an Eldership from Platf. Ch. 10. #167; 11. but w t may be understood in a manner consistent with what is said of the power granted by Christ to the body of the Chh & brotherhood #167; 5 of ye same Chapt. Compar’d with #167; 2. & Chapt. 5. #167; 2. marginal

[^440-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^440-note4]: Joseph Diggins, whose child Timothy Edwards refused to baptize because Edwards accused Diggins of an offense.

[^440-note5]: **marginal.** [3]

[^440-note6]: **marginal.** [4]

## C52. Benjamin Colman to Isaac Watts, [Before Ocober 11, 1738] C052.B.Colman-I.Watts c.10-38

Benjamin ColmanC052. Benjamin Colman to Isaac Watts, before10/11/38. BRBL, f. 1338. Copy of excerpt.

In a Letter from D r B. Colman of Boston to D r I: Watts of London the Same year.

As to Mr Edwards ’s Narrative I am sorry to see the base treatment offer’d to you & D r Guyse in some of the publick New’s papers, which in Several particulars is not only abusive, but downright ffalsehood & Calumny. I trust, Sir, you have nothing to fear from hence, where all possible Gratitude and Respect is due. I have already wrote to the venerable Mr Williams of Hatfield for the Attestation of the Ministers of the Neighboring towns to the Work of God among them. [^441-note1] We about Boston know so much of the Character of those Ministers, & of the Report made by them at the time of the sur= prizing Work among them that we cannot doubt in the least the Truth of the Account given by Mr Edwards. The Thing was not done in a Corner or managed in Secret, but in ye most open manner made its own way, to the Astonishment of the Inhabitants & those that came among them, and the good Fruits of it remain to this Day in an Abiding gracious Disposition & Conversation becoming the ffaith & Laws of the Gospell among the people of the said Towns. —— If some take offense and Scoff at what you have done, many more I hope both with you and us are giving Thanks and praise to God. ———— ———

[^441-note1]: See William Williams et al to Isaac Watts,10/11/38.

## C53. William Williams and Hampshire County Ministers to Benjamin Colman, October 11, 1738 C053.WmWmsetal-B.Colman10-11-38

William Williams and Hampshire County MinistersC053. William Williams et al to Benjamin Colman,10/11/38. BRBL, f. 1338. Two leaves, with letters on recto of each leaf. Rev d Sr

In Your Letter of August 19. you Inform us, that The Rev d: Doctor Watts, & Doctor Guise desire that some other Mi= nisters who were Eye, & Ear Witnesses to Some of those Numerous Conversions in the Other Towns About Northampton, would draw up an Account in Brief of the like Work of God in those other Towns, at the Same Time, or Attest Unto what The Rev d: Mr Edwards has written of Them. In Answer to which We take this Opportunity to Assure You, y t the Account Mr: Edwards has given in his Narrative of Our Several Towns or Parishes, is True, And that Much More of the like Nature might have been Added with Respect to some of them.

## C54. Samuel Hopkins of Springfield to Hannah Edwards, February 18, 1739 C054.S.Hopkins-H.Edwards 2-18-39

Samuel Hopkins of SpringfieldC054. Samuel Hopkins to Hannah Edwards,2/8/39. BRBL, f. 1525. Addressed on back "To / M rs Hannah Edwards / at Windsor / P r Mr Stoughton."

Springfield feb. 8. 1738/9.

Dear sister.

My wife lately made a visit at Lieu t Mirick’s, where mrs Mirick told her she had lately been at Windsor, and That mrs Woolcot (mr John Woolcots wife) told her that she under- stood y t you had sent several messages to mr Rockwell, [^443-note1]

we make no doubt but this is an artifice of R—l’s, but yet I Chose to let you know it for two reasons. one is y t you may know how to Conduct yourself at Windsor. to Contradict it, if you think fit and shall find occasion. the other is y t you may, when you have a good opportunity, let us know y t it is not true, that we may be able to Contradict it here. for tho we now Can say y t we suppose there is not ye lest truth in it, yet we Cannot so fully assert it, as we Could if we had it from yourself.

Duty love &c as proper to all at home. take you[r Con]tent [^443-note2] in God and follow him as a dear child, thro’ this rest [...]d troublesome world, and how sweet will th the rest [be whe]n you find yourself out of ye reach of all slander, pain and sorrow, y t so much abounds here.

I am with sincere respect your loving Brother &c

S Hopkins.

[^443-note1]: Matthew Rockwell of East Windsor, Hannah Edwards’s suitor.desireing him to releas you from the obligations you are under to him, And that he as often refused to give you a release. and y t people there (at Windsor) Conclude y t ye reason you are do not marry is because you dare not till you have gotten a release: that it is from thence you have refused several good offers &c.
