## C55. Benjamin Doolittle to Benjamin Wright, March 3, 1739 C055.BDoolittle-BWright 3-3-39

Benjamin DoolittleC055. Benjamin Doolittle to Benjamin Wright et al.,3/3/39. Northfield, Mass. Fragment (apparently top of bottom portions only). ANTS, f. 1730-39, #5.

Dear freind. it is mater of great grief & Sorrow to me y t you have caused[?] yourselves & me so much uneasiness & troble & I Earnestly pray y t ye God of peace & love might open your eyes & mine to See w t is amiss in us & unite our hearts in true love and peace by his holy word & Spirit: wich is w t every Christian should Sincerely endeavour after: For ye want of this is very hurtfull to ye intrest of Christ among us: which who is to blame for: let God & every mans own Conscience to judg:

In a paper you Sent me Dated Febr. 24. AD: 1738/9 you Signified to me your uneasiness but (as I understand it) Signifie nothing [. . .] of peace love or reconsciliation [. . .] Seems to me [. . .]

[. . .]

w t y t Christian Sattisfaction Shall be on Either Side which Complied withall Shall be a final Desison of ye Controversie between us; I desire your compliance with those preliminaries or your Answer in writing praying y t ye God of love & peace may Direct both your heart & mine into ye right way for true peace & unity

your loving Pastor Benjn Doolittle

March 3 d 1738/9

To Cap t Benjn Wright

## C56. Benjamin Wright to Benjamin Doolittle, March 12, 1739 C056.BWright-BDoolittle 3-12-39

Benjamin WrightC056. Benjamin Wright et al to Benjamin Doolittle,3/12/39. Northfield, Mass. ANTS, f. 1730-39, #5. Inscribed on back "Our 2 proposal."

Rev nd Sr It is matter of grief and Sorrow to us y t there are So many grounds of unesyness and that you are pleased to Charge us of making you and our Selves uneasy as If there was nothing done by you y t Could be a Just grounds or Even Eany grounds of our unesyness However that be we don’t desire any more then that Impartial & Juditious Divines Should Judge wheither we are unesy without grounds. In a Paper. You Sent us baring Date March 8: 1738,9 You Charge us of having Signified nothing of a desire of peace and love wereas we desire nothing more and ye design of ye paper which we Sent to you was to lay a Just foundation for it you Excepted Against ye proposals which we made in order thereto as being hard & unreasonable and have proposed Something y t you Judge are Easy & reasonable but we have this to Except against your proposals.

what is ye grounds of our uneasyness is our Imagning y t you have often advanced Arminian principles both in Pulput & private Conversation. this you declare you have not done or y t you are not an Arminian & you have never in ye least blamed us for having avirsion from ye Arminian Principles & have In Sted of defending y m as Principles which you love often told us y t you are not a frind to y m Now e Rev nd Sir we Except against you proposals in ye paper which you Sent us bcaus being tryd according to y m your are Safe altho proved to be an Arminian because upon Supposition you are an Arminian we Justly Conclude that you will Choose an Arminian Council & this Council will without doubt think our uneasyness is groundless & advise us to be Still without having any Satisfaction We Sir are willing Sir to Comply with y m proposals which you have made with this alteration.

1 That you will Either oblige your Self o Chouse no Ministers but what are Generally reputed Orthordox or Calvinistical Divines.

2 or if you have ye Power to Choose any Divines Either Arminian or Calvinistical you Shall be obliged upon their hearing you Convicted of Arminianism Either to give us Such Grounds of Easyness as they Shal Judge fit or Cease to be our Pastor & teacher

3 that we will not be obliged to make mention of ye Sermons in which you do Principles are Contained any time before ye Sitting of ye Council or that if we mention y m y m A fortnight before. our Not having pitcht upon ye right Sermons for want of Remembring y m Shall Neither benefit your Case nor prejudice ours we agree y t whatever Sermons we Shall mention Shall be mentioned A fortnight before but if we happen to pitch upon ye wrong It Shall not be u Esteemed an Evidence that our Case is bad or any wise prejudice it

4 we will have ye liberty of Chusing any Minister in ye Council Excepting ABrother or first Couson: Sir we desire your answer to ye above written in writing.

Northfield March 12 AD 1739/9

Benj n Wright

Eliezar Wright

Eleazar Holton

## C57. Benjamin Doolittle to Benjamin Wright, Eliezer Wright, and Eleazar Houlton, March 23, 1739 C057.BDoolittle-BWright 3-23-39

Benjamin DoolittleC057. Benjamin Doolittle to Benjamin Wright et al,3/23/39. Northfield, Mass. ANTS, f. 1730-39, #5. MS damaged; lacunae indicated with bracketed ellipses.

Dear Bretren: In ye paper you Sent me Dated March. 12 AD 1738/9 you Signifie Some thing as tho you desire Love & peace & Sent your first paper to Lay a foundation for it: & desire y t impartial Divines might judge ye grounds of your uneasiness w c you know I Consented to in my answer to your first paper: But tho ye preface of your paper Seems to hold forth Something of your willingness for Love & peace & y t impartial Divines may Judge ye grounds of your uneasiness yet ye Consequent part of your paper dos (to my understanding) Contradict it. for you are not willing y t impartial ones Should be judges but Such as you look upon partial for if you think I will chuse partial ones you do as much manifest [ . . . . . . .] Chuse partial ones. besides you lay no foundation for love & peace [ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .] of ye ministry me[. . . . . . . . . . .] brand me with ye odious name of an arminian & y t if you can by Allegations true or false fasten y t name upon me I must be obliged to Qut ye ministry. for I cannot See y t your paper tends to anything more then this For you very industriously Avoid mentioning ye holy Scriptures as having any hand in Determining ye Controversy between us: but y t this matter must be Desided by mens opinions whether they are right or wrong: But ye word of god must and Shall be ye only rule by which this matter Shall be Decided: or it can never be decided in this world: For this is ye rule by w c you and I must be tried & judged at Last & not by ye odious names of Arminian or Calvinist: I have alway taught you both in publick & private y t the word of God is ye only rule to try all Doctrines by: & not ye opinions of men how great or good soever they were: for I am no papist to make Either Calvin or Arminius my pope to Determine my Articles of faith for for: Nor am I a Quaker to think to have this done by any reavilation or inspiration not Contained in the written word of god for tis in it I find all my Articles of faith: And with your discorses with me for ye most part you have in- sisted only on ye opinions of men: w c has given me just Grounds to fear y t you have left ye standing rule of Gods word to turn aside to ye Doctrines & Commandments of men as ye jews did math. 7. 7. 8. As to my rule of faith Christ has taught me to call no man father upon Earth math 23. 9. You Except against my proposals because (say you) being tried by them I am safe: but have given no good reason why I should not if a Councel judge y t ye Doctrines I have Advanced are agreable to ye word of God: All your Exceptions against my proposals (as far as I can see) are founded entirly upon this Supposition y t all y t an Arminian houlds is Certanly Erronious & all y t a Calvinist holds is infalible true: & therefore without any further dispute if a minister holds any thing y t An Arminian holds he must be condemned as an heritick without more a doe: & thus all ed ye Divines y t Ever have been in this land must be Condemn as heriticks: & thus Calvin must be looked upon as an infa- lible Pope to Determine all Articles of faith for us. So y t a minister must be obliged never to make any farther Enquires into ye Sacred Scripture but only enquire what Calvin holds & finds y t to proceed no further Least if he Should by further Enquiry find Some things y t Calvin held was Erronous & for this be

Condemned as an heretick. [. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .] [^446-note1]

Decreed: for this Supposes Calvin [. . . . . . . . . . . .]

be in ye wrong in any thing: But can [. . . . . . . . . . .]

Article of faith: & if there be any [. . . . . . . . . . .]

this y t Calvin was infalible his a th[. . . . . . . . . . .]

a papist then I am of an arminian [. . . . . . . . . . . .]

would be as fiery a persecuter any [. . . . . . . . . ] if ye [. . .]

God be Layed by & mens opinions trumped up [. . . .] ye rule to try Doctrines by this is a great [. . .] towards turning to Rome again for a jesuit Could not have oposed an[. . .]e ready way to bring us back to Rome then [. . .] I never thout it worth my while to [. . .] concerned [. . .] my opinions were just ye

[. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .]

Contained in ye word of God. for I know y t all men are failible as well as I & as I may be wrong So may they: So y t if you want or expet any other Satisfaction then w t is Contained in or required in ye word of God: I must tell you I cannot give it nor have you any right to demand it: As to what alterations you propose to make in my proposals: ye first is only to restrain me to ye Choice of Such only as you look upon partial in ye Case and there is just as much reason for me to Chuse partial ones as you: & you planly enough say y t you think I will Chuse partial ones: I have as much reason to think you will & y t therefore these you Chuse will condemn me right or wrong as y t you Should think y t those I Chouse will acquit me right or wrong: but Surely for Either of us to Say this is an unreaso nable & unchristian reflection: & yet there is just as much reason for me to Say it as for you: As to your obliging ye Councel to condemn me upon hereing me Convicted of Arminism: According to what you Said before you can mean then y t part of ye Councel which you Chuse for you before Supposed y t part I Chose will be partial in my favour & by ye same rason those you Chuse will be as partial in yours & y t therefore let your Allegations be as false as ye wit and mali- ce of men can invent: I must according to your proposals be obliged to Qut ye ministry or be obliged to make y t Satisfaction y t God for bids So y t w tever pretence you make of Love & peace you plainly indicate by w t you write it Shall be only by my Quitting ye ministry among you: & if this be a foundation for Love & peace let others judge as well as I: As to your 3 d Alteration it tends to ye same thing seeks to Crowd me from ye ministry right or wrong: only by laying a snare for me y t I might have no time to make my defence: for by this you would not oblige your selves to mention w n & where or in w t Sermon or discorse I delievred such Doctrines: & thus you Labour to Lay me under an imposability of making any defence & y t all y t must try ye Ca Case must be your bare Say y t tis so: & then (w c is w t you seme to aim at) you your Selves would be ye only judges: & if so w t need of a Councel. but surely you must have an high oppin ion of your selves own wisdom & knoledge or think y t I am a fool or you would not propose such a thing.

I am glad you are so reasonable as at last to agree y t w t Sermons you do mention Shall be mentioned to me a fortnight before ye Councels sitting: & I am Sure y t you [^446-note2] must Some time or other mention ye night or it must in ye judgment of all reasonable men prejudice to your Cause & let it be when it will y t you mention ye night you agree it Shall be a fortnight before ye Councel sits to judge upon it & tis very reasonable I Should have time to make my defence & for any of you to think to bring in any testimony without mentioning w n & w t Sermon or discorse it was is much ye same as if a man should testifie he saw such a man murther another but give no account when nor where nor who & he must be a very partial judge [. . . . . . . . . . . .] no more Condemn much as you can [. . . . . . . . . . .] an impossability to make any defence & so you are afraid ye truth Should Come to light for if you were not you would be willing y t ye word of God should be ye only rule to try my Doctrin es by & would allow me fair oppertunity & advantage to cleare up ye matter but one y t is afraid ye truth Should come to light is afraid of ye right rule & is not will ing y t another should have ye same Liberty & advan- tage he Claims for himself: I know not w t a Lawyer or a young Skolar may judge of your answer and Exceptions but I am pretty well assured y t no honest Juditious & impartial Divine can judge y m of any great force: your Last alteration I agree to only with this adition (nor y t has given advice in ye Case) & now I cannot but think w t I proposed was reasonable & hope this will Sattisfie you y t twas so & y t we may Come to a mutual agreement in this afair & y t ye Issue may be love & peace y t ye God of peace may Dwell among us w c is what I desire heartily to Seek & pray for

Northf d Your Loving pastor Benj n Doolittle

March 23. 1738/9

Please to let your Answer be in writing

To Cap t Benj n Wright

Lieu t Eliezer Wright & Eleazar Houlton

[^446-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^446-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C58. Timothy Cutler to Edmund Gibson, May 28, 1739 C058.T.Cutler-E.Gibson 5-28-39

Timothy CutlerC058. Timothy Cutler to Bp. Edmund Gibson,5/28/39. *The Church of England in Pre-Revolutionary Connecticut*, ed. Kenneth W. Cameron (Hartford, Transcendental Books, 1976), 53-55. Reproduced as printed; bracketed letters and words are Cameron’s, apparently supplied where the MS is damaged.

My Lord

I am very sorry that I have given so long an Exercise to [...]r Patience as to the Enquiry you were pleased to make of me; but my [...]ost and faithfullest Endeavors laid out in the Case could not command [q]uicker Intelli- gence. Tho’ indeed I have been of late suspended from [my] Business and Care by the most distressing Sorrow that ever God dis[po]sed to me in my whole Life; in the Death of my youngest Son, too dear [to me] and dear enough to all that knew Him, who sail’d into the Mediter- ranean [...] the Recovery of his Health, for which, I am sure from his religious and [...]tuous Life, God has given Him an happy Exchange in a better world, where [I lo]ng to be with Him.

But I shall be tedious enough without such Digres- sions, thinking [it b]etter to be lengthy than slighty in my Narrative. And, my Lord, I am personally [...]uainted with Mr [Jonathan] Edwards of Northampton, [Connecti- cut,] [^447-note1] who is now in Town, and has made [me] a Visit: but as I expected no more light from Him than what his Book [...]tain’d, we kept clear of that Subject. Nor was I an entire Stranger to his [...]ndfather, Mr Solomon Stoddard, his Predecessor there.

That Gentleman was of no great Learning and Read- ing, but of a [stro]ng Brain and Thoughtful, and withal sober and Religious, grave and pru[dent] in Conversa- tion. he was also narrow and odd in his Sentiments, Self-opin[ioned], haughty, assuming, and impatient of Contradiction, and encreased a Stiffness [li]ving remote from those He could improve by, or dared to oppose Him, so [that] He was many years the Oracle of the Country, especially in those parts [wher]e He lived long, had a numerous Family, and where a great number [of] Minis- ters were related to Him by Bloud or affinity. I am an Instance of [...] severity at my first arrival here from England, who then sent me a Letter [of R]eproof for my Departure into the Church of England, which I answered [as m]odestly as I could, and with particular Considera- tion of his age: but He [repli]ed to me with that Indecency, that I thought it best to leave Him the [last] word. But I durst not be so troublesom to your Lordship as to present you [...] Copies of those Letters.

His notions about Conversion were very peculiar: one was, That [...]ry man not culpably careless, knew when He was converted: and according[ly] Edwards in his Book, mentions his Grandfather Stoddard as speaking [of] five Harvest He had among his People in above fifty years of [his d]welling with them, which comes out in Ten or Twelve years, when [...] Generation of young People grows up: and Mr Edwards seems to [have] got into this Period: for the Conversions He speaks of were about Two years after his Settlement in Northampton. But Mr Stoddard was oftentimes [de]ceived about his Converts, and many were known, after a Shew of Piety, [to] relapse into, and persist in grievous Sins.

And his Sence of the Operations of Grace, very much resembles wha[tever] we find in his Grandson’s Book (which I ask your Lordship’s acceptance of) and H[e has] spreaded the same among many in the Country, his Relations par- ticularly who [...]versally adhered to Him. A few years agoe I was credibly informed of an Ins[tance] very much akin to ye Narrative , in one Mr Bulkly Teacher in Col- chester, [^447-note2] and [of] my particular acquaintance, a man of excellent Understanding, and good Imp[rove]ments in Di- vinity and Physick, who languished under great Disorders, that al[most] ended his Life. Under his Illness, there be- ing no Physitian near whom He cared to con[sult] He sends to one Mr Mix, [^447-note3] a Teacher, and Practitioner in Physick, a man of good U[nder]standing, and of his acquaintance, and Son in Law to Mr Stoddard, living 30 or [^447-note4] Miles from Him, desiring to see Him. Mr Mix enquires of the Mes- senger about [...] Condition, and upon the whole concludes, That the work of Conversion was the[n just] beginning in Him, and takes no other care of Him but to send Him a Treatise of Stoddard’s called A Guide to Christ , and so Mr Bulkly, distant, from any agre[eable] Physitian, was left to conflict with his Distemper till it overcame Him.

Mr Edwards was brought up under my care at Yale College, a Person [of] good Abilities, Diligence, and Pro- ficiency in Learning, and continues his Applic[ation] to this time, and in such a degree, that He is very much emaciated, and impair’d in his Hea[...] and it is doubtful to me whether He will attain to the Age of 40. He was Critical, sa[d] and peculiar, but I think not very solid in Disputation. Always a sober Person [he was] withal pretty recluse, austere and rigid. Presently after he left the College, he r[...]ved to Northampton to assist his Grand- father, and was intirely formed by Him, a[nd] now has the care of a People at a great distance from the promiscuous Conve[nticles] and the Infection of our Sea-ports, generally regular and sober, uniform in Le[arning] but remarkably train’d up in self-conceit, to Disputation, and a Fondness for [...] Stoddard’s own School-Divinity.

About the time of this remarkable appearance at Northampton a[nd] the parts adjacent, there was a number of Visionaries at Cambridge, and in [...] College there. It began in one Langloiserie, a Refugee from Canada, [...] dwell’t in Cambridge to teach the Scholars French, and insinuated himsel[f into] the Esteem of many, by a sober Life, and demure Behavior mixed with [some] En- thusiasm, tho’ He refuses to attend any Public Worship, and has privately [...]erred, and laboured to propagate gross Corruptions in Religion. He is [said t]o be an Arian, to believe two Messiahs, Ben David and Ben Ephraim, and [to] have given out that the World would come to an end within a year or two [of] that time. One of the Tutors of the College, with several of His Relatio[ns] who are Teachers, appeared much affected by it, and remarkably careless a[bout] Temporal affairs; at which the College was alarmed, and warned the Se[niors ag]ainst any Con- versation with this Langloiserie, and brought the Tutor of the [Co]llege to some Reflections; and so this matter stopt there. But the Perswasion [th]at the World would soon come to an end got up to Northampton-parts, and wrought [mu]ch on the People’s Spirits, and what engaged the Indians thereabouts I cannot [te]ll, but they are also said to have at that time conversed with the English [mo]re seriously, and to have been more abstemious than was common for them.

The New-England Teachers referr’d to in Mr Ed- wards’s Narrative, tho’ [ma]ny of them, I hope, very honest men, are not sufficient to set it beyond Contra- dictio[n]. [S]o D r Colman to whom the Narrative is di- rected, He is more noted for easy Expres[sions] than for thorough Judgement, and his well known Foible is to en- courage [and c]ourt Public Salutation and Applause, and to be smoothed into a good opinion [by] whatever comes to Him in that manner.

The Four Teachers of Boston who recommend the Narrative, [^447-note5] are men [of t]he lowest Form in Learning and Judgment, contracted in their Thoughts, and [...]y apt to fall in with any thing whimsical and visionary. But for Learning I [ex]cept Mr [Thomas] Prince, tho’ his Oddity has got much the upper hand of it, joyn’d with a [stro]ng Disposition to say every thing that He thinks will give Reputation to his own [...]y, and leave the Church of England much behind it, as appears from his [...] New England Chronology .

I know all the Teachers upon Connecticut River save one who have [give]n their attestation to ye Narrative, and believe them to be honest men, but [easi]ly led away by whimsical appearances and fantastic Shows, and one of [...]m is a Son in Law to Mr Stoddard, and the other a Descendant. [^447-note6]

I also know Twelve of the Teachers referred to in it, Five whereof were rela[...] to Mr Stoddard, all byast by his schemes, all weak men, and some of them in [...] lowest degree: and with such only was Mr Edwards in- dustrious to catch up as [many suc]h as would make up a Book, and I can now find none other that do commend [...] As Mr Edwards takes Stratford into his Reports, I wrote to my Rev d. Brother [John]son about it, who answers me, That the Humor began in his Parish (where [...] Gould, is Teacher) but never prevail’d as He expected. In the North Parish [...]re Mr Mills [^447-note7] is Teacher, it began with an old whimsical Maid, crazed with Love [...] a young man belong to his (Mr Johnson’s) Church , which she assign’d to [a] Courtship, and complain’d of Him to Mr Johnson, who was not able to find [...]thing culpable in the man, and therefore dismissed the woman with some [pi]ous suggestions and Exhortations. And this gave her (who as well as Mr Mills [...]ered upon ye Seat of these Schemes) a turn towards this imaginary Relig[...] and set her to crying for she knew not what, and thereby made others cry for [they] did not know what, especially little Girls .

In Mr Johnson’s Parish the Humor did not take with more than 4 or 5 young women, who in the time of it used [^447-note8] to get together and cry, and they continue p[retty] serious, but two of them married soon after these religious Rap- tures, and h[ad] each of them a Child in 6 or 7 months . Mr Johnson knoweth nothing of th[...] having been remark- ably vicious before or serious since .

And there are many more of whom I have enquired personally, or b[y] assistance of Friends: and some ap- pear very frank in their Narratives, and ot[hers] as shy of giving their sence of Facts, for fear of prejudicing them in that [part] of the Country, by their Contradicting what is there counted very sacred. [...]dry young Gentlemen brought up at Harvard and Yale Colleges, some [of] whom are Candidates for Orders among them, say it is all a Whim: Tho’ a[ll] that I have spoken with give in to the Truth of ye Narrative: but all say [that] it is now over, and generally add, that many are become as bad as ever.

Several inform me, That their Imaginations were much wrou[...], some pretending to have seen very strange Sights, some surprizing Lights[, and] one an Hawk on a Stump of a Tree. A Friend of mine who trav- elled into [those] parts asked a Teacher there, whether He thought the thing was not catching [. He] answered He did. Another Teacher of those parts, and a very worthy sensible [...] told me upon Enquiry formerly, That He thought there was something remarka[...] in it, but it was too much magnify’d and strain’d, and proposed to give me a [book] and to discourse more upon the Subject, but I was disappointed. I have si[...] written to Him upon it, and received no answer, but know not why, unless that H[e is] shy at this juncture, being hotly charged with Arminian- ism. A Prea[cher] said He had two Sisters who had gone through the work (a favourite Phr[...] on the Subject) but they were no better than before. I laboured to gain a Visit fr[om] Him, but that stirred up his Jealousy, and He will not see me. A man of Hatf[ield] says, His Minister Mr W m Williams, (tho’ He is one that attests the Narrative) wi[shes] Mr Edwards had not been so full and forward in the matter, and I have [come t]o doubt it, because such things are frequently hurryed on among us by [in]judicious Zeal, and it is scandalous to be slack and deliberate, and beca[...] good information perswades me He is a very honest man: He also thinks th[at] so much in it as is pre- tended, but is glad He did not see me, as I laid out for [him.] From others I find that Children of about 12 years old would run about [...] Streets, and say, they were bound to Zion , and would enquire the wa[y to]ward , that they would assemble to pray and sing in the Meeting- houses, a[nd] were admitted to Communion, that the Height of this Paroxysm [...] within two months, and as all others say, now for a considerable time entirely o[...] and that the sober Anabaptists in those parts take it for a whim, and so[me] others question the nature and tendency of the thing, but conceal th[...]elves for fear of Dis- pleasure.

It is credibly reported by sundry, That one Mr Hawley han[...] himself at this time, because what He had been seeking for, and had [...] found in fourty years, others had found in a few days, and that another [...] his Throat upon it, but the Wound proved not mortal. [^447-note9]

I employed a Dissenting Friend of mine in this Town to a[ppoint en]quiries; and He finds two Persons who have studiously examin’d the matter; one is a Teacher, who finds it had it’s Rise from a Report that the World would [...]rtly come to an end, strengthened by Mr Whiston’s [^447-note10] Prediction of a Co[met, so] that many of the Converts have relapsed, and He thinks there is no[thing] in it: An- other is a very consciencious discreet Dissenter, greatly reverencing [...] respectful towards his Teachers, and whom I should rather expect to fall [...] the Scheme than not. He, after strict Enquiry cannot find the Rise to be [from] Preaching, or any thing Providential; He thinks there were [valid] Impressions among some, but much chaff among the wheat . And He re[lates] this Story as very credible: A Certain Person in Northampton wanted [to sup]ply his Pile of Firewood which was low, and bad his Son go out into the Woods and [cut s]ome Firewood, who said He could not . Whereupon his Father argued [with] Him, and bad Him observe the need they were under; but He continued saying, [He wo]uld not go . At length his Father told Him that unless He was ill he would [call f]orth his Authority, and make Him go. And then his Son took up his Axe [...] went into the Barn, where He made an hideous Mourning and Noise, that [awak]n’d the Neighbours and they went to Him, and then called his Father. At [last] it was moved to send for Mr Edwards their Minister, before whom He conti[nued] in this man- ner, who thereupon advised the Father to forbear urging his [son,] telling Him that He was under some extraordi- nary Influences of the [Spiri]it, and was getting through ; a Phrase much apply’d to such cases.

Upon the whole, My Lord, I find it to be the sence of People in general [that] in this great Appearance of Re- ligion there is reason to think many were real, [that] others were led by Example, that many remain serious and unblemisht, & [perh]aps as many who were bad have relapsed in to y t former state; and the [peop]le in those parts any thing unbyast by y r popular Schemes, think there was [a gre]at deal fantastical and foolish in those shows, but find it not for their [inter]est to speak dis- paragingly of them; that the meanest of the Teachers, here [& elsew]here, and scarce any other Teachers, fall into them; and that the Talk of these [things] is now generally dropt.

I hope your Lordship will have full satisfaction to your Enqui[ry fr]om this Account, which I fear has been too prolix, if not too triffling, at the [same] time that I chose rather to exceed than to be scanty in my Obedience: but [whate]ver further Service your Lordship shall lay on me in this, or any other affair, none [will] be readyer to undertake it.

And now, My Lord, I do in the humblest manner beg your Pity, and [your] Prayers to God for me, under his hand which presseth me sore, though [most j]ustly, that I may honour Him more in the Bereavement than I have in the [...]ment of his Favours; and I also beg a Portion of your Lordship’s Compassion[ate in]structions to my only Son whenever He has the Honour to come into [your] Lordship’s Presence. I shall ever think your Lordship’s life a [grea]t Blessing to the Church, and be glad of mak- ing full proof that I am / your Lordship’s / most obedient Son & Servant

[...]ton May 28, 1739 Timothy Cutler

[My Lo]rd, your Commands are an entire Secret to [every]body but my Self here, & so will be.

[^447-note1]: Sic.

[^447-note2]: Rev. John Bulkley (1703-31).

[^447-note3]: Rev. Stephen Mix of Wethersfield, Conn.

[^447-note4]: **marginal.** [40]

[^447-note5]: Joseph Sewall, Thomas Prince, John Webb, and William Cooper.

[^447-note6]: William Williams of Hatfield, Ebenezer Devotion of Suffield, Stephen Williams of Longmeadow, Peter Reynolds of Enfield, Nehemiah Bull of Westfield, and Samuel Hopkins of West Springfield. William Williams was the son-in-law of Stoddard, and Stephen Williams a "descendant."

[^447-note7]: Jedidiah Mills.

## C59. George Whitefield to Thomas Foxcroft[?], September 20, 1740 C059.G.Whitefield-_ 9-20-40

George WhitefieldC059. George Whitefield to [Thomas Foxcroft?],9/20/40. BRBL, f. 1337. Overwritten by Foxcroft with sermon notes (dated Nov. 25, 1784).

Sep br 20 th 1740 [^448-note1]

past 9 at night

Rev d Sr.

For many reasons, my Friends disapprove of my preaching for You to morrow in the afternoon. They say it will bring people from other Meeting houses, & as all cannot come in, it will perhaps cre- ate disorder. I therefore think to preach in the field about 4 of clock. [^448-note2]Then servants may hear & also persons from every Meeting.

I am in great haste Rev d Sr Your hum: Ser vt

GWhitefield

[^448-note1]: At this time, Whitefield was in Boston. On that day, Whitefield had preached at "Rev. Dr. Sewall’s meeting-house," then on the common to "about eight thousand," and then "at night, to a thronged company at my lodgings." *George Whitefield’s Journals* (London, Banner of Truth, 1960), p. 460.

[^448-note2]: On Sept. 21, Whitefield recorded that he preached in the afternoon "to a thronged auditory, at the Rev. Mr. Foxcroft’s meeting-house. Immediately after, on the common, to about fifteen thousand." Ibid.

## C59a. Unknown to Unknown ("Sinners"), July 6-7, 1741 C059a._-_ (Sinners) 7-6-41

Unknown (copied by Samuel Savage)C059a. Anonymous to anonymous, 7/6-7/41. Extract from a letter written from Suffield. Samuel P. Savage II Papers, Box 1, Folder 1712-1750, MHS.

Yesterday I got to this Town, where I kept the Sabbath; and had the Joyfull Opportunity of setting down to the sacramt. with about 470 Comuns. 93 of which were admitted by Mr. Edwards of Northampton who preach’d here Yesterday morng The sight was truly glorious: 93 Persons chiefly middle Aged admitted to the Lord’s Table; One Own’d the Covenant and the Infants baptiz’d: Mr. Devotion ye late Minister dyed this Spring, since wh. Mr. Woodbridge has preachd here occasionally; but the Famous Pomroy has been instrumental in this mighty Work; this Mr. Pomroy with Mr. Wheelock, Miles, Bellamy and Some others ride about preaching in many Places, and scarcely any where without remarkable success: They do it on Each day of the week and at ten Miles distant (by the peoples going) I find I am to hear Mr. Pomroy a few hours hence In this place I yesterday saw a dumb <and deaf> man, and in the Evening sent for him and One that could Exche. his thoughts for mine This Person has at this remarkable Time been carryed thro’ great distress to Considerable Joy; his Distress was so great that from his Knees in his Chamber where he was found praying he was heard by an Unusual noise at near a miles distance, not by One only, but by the whole neighborhood within this Space, so as to draw them together, when they found him in the greatest agonies, Sweat ran down in Streams, heaving wh his breast, and panting as if Just Expiring; Since which he has received Comfort, and has embraced the Lord Jesus Christ; My Inquires were about the Compitence of his Knowledge, without wh either the Work might be doubted of, or a miracle must be wrought, & I found he had a Knowledge of three in One; & One in three; I believe he had this Communicated to him by signs instead of sounds, but Cant learn he had any Suteable Knowledge of Xt as the way to the Father: Indeed Signs cannot Convey the necessity of a Propitiation, but if they could be sure they would fail of shewing a God man to be necessary to be [of act]-And yet to be Equal with God. but wn. I see you ’Ile acquaint you more fully of an Affair wh. makes a gt noise here.-

July 7th

Yesterday I reach’d Hartford 17 miles from Suffield the chief of the day being rainy wh gave me Oppo. witht. Loss of Time in ye Afternn. To hear ye fams. Pomroy & Wheelock who both preach’d at Windsor wt. only a sht. Prayr. and a Hymn betwn. ye Serms. Mr. Wheelock in my Judgmt. Exceeds Mr. Whitefield in digested [?], Clearness & beauty of stile, (Yes, and is very correct too, tho he preaches wholly [?], and as much as Mr. Whd. Extempore, in strength of Reason, Gesture & Tone & Accent in the presence of his Mind & ye spirit wth wh he speaks; perhaps he equals him in Fervoar, and it may be doutfull [?] him in Grace, [or comes] short of him in success-This Gentn. <& Mr.> Pomroy <I think> has [...] Mr. Edwards been improv’d & own’d at Suffield where I wrote you in my last I saw 93 admitted last sabbath to the Lords Table & since which Mr. Edwards has corrected my Acct. and says there were 96 most wh. after Strong Convictions and of short Continuance were fill’d wt Peace & Joy. The morning following wh. was Yesterday being detain’d by rain, I thought I would step in & hear what Mr. Edwards had Invited the people to the day before, I was late and lost ye sermon but come just after it and soon enough to see the Effects of it, it was in a private House, where two large Rooms were fill’d wt. Children, Youth and aged persons of both Sexes In No. I Judge abt 200 when I came with in about a Quartr. of a mile of ye house, I met one leading his daughter home, perhaps to put her in bed, imediately after this heard a Confus’d, but very Affecting Noise, wh. as I drew near perceived to Come from different Ages & sexes proceeding wholly from distress, but of different degrees the lowest kind seem’d like Sobs of bereaved Friends, higher then these were Groans & Screeches as of women in ye Pains of Childbirth; but above these were Houlings and Yellings, wh. to Even a Carnal Man might point out Hell, & Convince him yt Concience let loose, sights of a holy Absolute God, and mens vileness, must either lead him to Xt, or Cause Damnation when there is no litterale Fire when I came into the Room the sights did not differ from the sounds but Evidently held forth the same distress in the severall degrees of it, bereavemt, litterall Child birth, and the Torments of Hell, nor were ye Effects of this distress less Surprising. Faintings in the lowest, & [enervation] in the Higher, and ye highest were so intirely embraced that you would have thought there bones all broken, or rather yt they had no bones; so much as to this Extraordinary thing as it offer’d to the Sences.-To ye mind it held forth (to be sure to my mind it did) mens Vileness by his Fall in Adam, a holy jealous God, and ye wonders of his Grace & love in Xt Jesus: Grace & Love indeed <they> thought who were brought from ye higest degree of this distress (as they Exprest it, from the lowest pit of Hell, and had yr Feet plac’d on a Rock. It held about 3 hours in which space Mr. Edwards chose to carry on by Prayer chiefly, and being faint called in the Assistance of 4 or 5 private Xians in so short a space a gt No. perhaps 15-20 or more were brought to different degrees of Peace & Joy, Some to Rapture, all extolling the Lord Jesus Xt all begging & beseeching Each One they could speak to to Come to a Redeemr. who had shew’d them his mercy, and was willing to do it to all <who> could believe, and [desire] his Grace.

I rode wt Mr. Edwards from Suffield to Escantick or East Windsor to hear Mr. Pomroy & Mr. Wheelock -

## C59b. Eleazar Wheelock to Lebanon Crank Church, July 11, 1741 C059b.Wheelock-LebChh8-11-41

Eleazar WheelockC059b.Eleazar Wheelock to Lebanon North Parish Church, July 11, 1741. Wheelock Papers, #743900.1, Dartmouth College Library, Hanover, N.H.

To ye Chh and People of God in Lebanon North Parish

Dearly Beloved

I Came to Winsor [^450-note1] yesterday with a Design to Come to you this Day. ye Lord Bowed ye heavens and Came Down upon ye assembly ye Last night, ye house seamd to be filled with his Great Power, a very Great Number Crying out under a Sence of the wrath of God and ye weight of their Guilt, 13 or 14. we Beleive Converted. My Dear Brother [Benjamin] Pomeroy Came to me this morning from Mr [Jonathan] Ma[r]sh’s Parish [^450-note2] where ye work was allso Great ye Last night. we were Just setting out to Come home but a Number of people were met together and ye Distress among them soon arose to such an heighth y t we think we have a Call of Providence to Continue here over ye Sabbath Several have been Converted already this morning. there is <now> work Enough for 10. Ministers now in this town [&] there is a very Glorious Work att suffield and it was very marvellous in a Great assembly at Enfield Last Wednesday. <ten or twelve Converted there> much of his power was Seen at Long-meadow on thursday, 6 or 7. Converted there and a Great Number wounded. there was Considerable Seen at Springfield old town on thursday Night and much of it again yesterday morning at Long meadow [^450-note3]-people Every where throng together to hear ye word and I do verily beleive these are ye beginning of ye Glorious things that are Spoken Concerning the City of our God in the Latter day I am much Concernd for Some y t Remain yet Stupid and Blind among my Dear flock I Desire your Continual Remembrance of me your poor pastor in your prayers to G d y t I may be Strengthned in ye inward & outward man to all y t ye Lord shall Call me to I hope to be with you at the beginning of next week. I am

Your souls Friend & servant for Chr t

Eleazar Wheelock [^450-note4]

[^450-note1]: Location uncertain: East Windsor?

[^450-note2]: Windsor, First.

[^450-note3]: Stephen Williams reported a "considerably shakeing & trembling before ye revivle was finished" when EW preached from Job 27:8 at Longmeadow on that afternoon of July 9. (DSW, 3:376). Later that evening, he went to Springfield, where he heard EW preach a second sermon from John 7:38. "He was Enlarged & Solemn," Williams noted, and "Some Children cryed" (3:377). The following day, EW returned to Longmeadow and delivered a sermon on Isaiah 8:11. Again, Williams noted, "ye word come with mighty power" (3:378).

[^450-note4]: On verso, written in another (probably later) hand: "to his people at Lebanon, 1743."

## C60. Gilbert Tennent to Unknown, [c. Late 1741] C060.G.Tennent-_ Late ’41

Gilbert TennentC060. Gilbert Tennent to [?], c. late 1741, apparently a copy made for JE. ANTS f. 1743, #1. On back is a memo: "A copy of a Letter from Mr Tennent," and a portion of JE’s draft of a council’s decision against Bathsheba Kingsley of Westfield, Feb. 1743.

Rev d and dear sir

I rejoyce to hear y t my poor labours have been of any service to any in New England. all glory be to ye great and glorious God, when out of ye mouths of babes and sucklings he is pleased sometimes to ordain praise I rejoyce to hear of ye progress of Gods work among you this last summer & y t there are any appearances of its Continuance, blessed by God. Dear Brother as to y t par- ticular you mentioned in yours (viz.) of Laymens being sent out to Exhort and teach, supposing them to be real converts, I Cannot but think if it be encouraged and Continued, it will be of dreadful Consequence to ye Chh’s peace & soundness in ye faith principles. I will not gain say but y t private persons may be of service to ye Chh of God by private, humble, fraternal reproofs and ex hortations, and no dou’t it is y r duty to be faithful in these things. but in ye mean time if Xian prudence & humility do not attend y r Essays, y y are like to be prejudiced to ye Chhs real well being. but for Ignorant young Converts to take upon them authoritatively to Instruct and exhort pub- lickly, tends to Introduce ye grossest Errors, and ye greatest anarchy & Con- fusion. the ministers of X sh d be apt to teach and able to Convince gainsayers, and it is dangerous to ye poor Chh of God when these are novices, whose lips sh d preserve knowledge. it is base presumtion, whatever Zeal be pretended to, notwithstanding for any person to take ye honour to y mselves unless y y be Called of God as Aaron. I know rash heady young Zealots are apt, thro’ Ignorance Inconsideration and pride of heart [to] undertake what they have no proper qualifications for, and thro’ y r imprudences and Enthusiasms ye Chh of God suffers. Dear Brother I think all y t fear God sh d rise up and Crush ye Enthu- siastick Creature in ye Egg. Dear B. ye times are dangerous we live in. perhaps ye reviving of Gods work in divers places is but a prelude to a storm. the Chhs in America and else where are in great Hazard of Enthusiasm. [—] we have need to think of ye maxim principiis obsta. there is a late sect Come unto this part of ye Country Called Moravian Brethren, whose principles are a Confused Medley of Rank Arminian Antinomianism Arminianism & Quakerism, y y are ye most subtil plau- sable sect y t ever I saw, and one like to do much mischief here. pious people, where they go, do generally divide. things this way seem to ri- pen for a storm. faithful ministers are here brought to ye bar, and to be Condemned, tho Inocent. May Zion’s King protect his Chh. I add no more but love, and beg a remembrance in your prayers.

Gilbert Tennent

## C61. Hadley Second Precinct Committee to Ecclesiastical Council, September 18, 1741 C061.HadleyChh-EcclesCncl 9-18-41

Hadley (Mass.) Second Precinct CommitteeC061. Hadley Second Precinct to Ecclesiastical Council,9/18/41. ANTS, f. 1741, #3.

Rev d & Worthy Gentlmen

We being assemled this morning Receivd a paper from your selves Dated 17 th Currant wherin you inform us of being Convend as an Ecclesiastical Council inviting us to lay Greivances before you promising your advice & assistance withal Signifying your Sorow for our unhapy diferences. [^452-note1]

Gentlmen We are not unsensable of ye frown of heaven upon us in permitting Such differences among us which we desire Lament & desire to be humbled under & ask your prayers for our healing Gentlmen we hope we are & Shall be ready to receive whol advice from any of our Christian brethren but canot think it our duty to Submit our Selves to your determination as an Ecclesiastical Council Since we have already had a hearing before a Council mutualy Chosen by ye Difering parties & ye major part of this Chh & Precinct are Satisfied in their determination & those brethren of our Chh which have joind with Mr Rawson [^452-note2] in inviting you hither have never signified their disatisfaction with that result to us other ways than in private Conversation nor nee we ever met together Since that Council to endeavour to bring our difficulties to Some accomodation but they alone without moving to us to join with them have proceeded to call a Council.

The Case being thus Circumstanced it will not be expected that we lay our matters before you & we pray you not to strike at us in ye dark because we don’t give that light which we never promised.

We Still remain well satisfied in ye Result of ye former Council & acquaint you that we have wholly done with Mr Rawson as a minister & if you endeavour to restore him to his place it (instead of promoting our peace) have a tend- ency to end in our [——] disturbance.

We take Leave to Subscribe our selves your Christian Brethren Hadly Second Precinct & humble Serv ts

Septem r 18 th 1741.

[^452-note1]: See Hampshire County Association minutes (Forbes Library), for April 8, 1741, in which the ministers voted to advise the people of "New Hadly" to apply to the churches of the county to "hear their Difficulties." The next day, the Association voted that "Each Party Should Give a Copy of Articles of Charge that they have against Each other."

[^452-note2]: Grindall Rawson, pastor of South Hadley from 1733 to 1741, when he apparently removed from his pulpit. This letter reflects an appeal process on the part of Rawson’s supporters to have him restored, which the writers of the letter oppose. Rawson eventually settled at Hadlyme, Conn.

## C61a. Thomas Clap to Solomon Williams, June 8, 1742 C061a. TClap-SWilliams 6-8-42

Thomas ClapC061a. Thomas Clap to Solomon Williams, June 8, 1742. MS American Colonial Clergy Collection, Gratz Collection, HSP. Printed in Stephen Nissenbaum, ed., *The Great Awakening at Yale College* (Belmont, Cal., Wadsworth Pub., 1972), 169-70.

[New Haven]

For the Revd Mr. Solomon Williams of Lebanon

Revd and Dear Sir

I was very sorry I could have no more Conversation with you at Hartford upon the present perplexed State of Affairs. The Trustees seemed generally to be fixed and determined that order and govern- ment should be Supported in College, and to obviate some objections proposed it as an expedient that sundry of the Trustees should come and preach here each a Sabbath, and if that did not fill up the time till Mr. Burr should come they proposed that you and Mr. Russell should be desired to come and preach. The Committee of the As- sembly, as I heard drew up a Report that it should be recommended to the Governours of the College to take special care to uphold Order and Government in that Society, and to use their utmost endeavors to prevent the Scholars from running into errors, Disorders &c and those who would not be Subject should not enjoy the Priviliges of that Society &c. But I understood that some of the Comtee were not will- ing to come into it [that is, approve the report] unless a Clause was added to Recommend it to the Trustees to nominate some Judicious Divines to come and preach there for the present, and that money be granted out of the Public Treasury to pay a Preacher that should preach in their Room. But I was informed by sundry members of both Houses that the Assembly were not generally pleased with that Clause; and so, tho’ the Report was accepted in the Lump, yet no Bill in form was drawn for granting the money. And so that scheme seems to drop. At present I suppose Mr. Noyes will [ex]change with some of the Trustees and perhaps some others near at hand, and I hope Mr. Burr may be here in about a month. It is probably that you may come here to bring your Sons and if it would Suit you to be here upon the Sabbath I should be glad. The Scholars of late seem to [be] much more cool, submissive and orderly than they were before the Vacancy, and some that I have discoursed with freely acknowledge their fault and promise Reformation. And I should have an agreeable Prospect that all things would go on well, if others would let them alone. And indeed I never tho’t that the fault was originally much in the Scholars, but principally in others who think That Religion is but promoted by Commotions, separations, over- turnings and the like, and who have done their utmost endeavor to bring the Scholars over to their Party. Messrs Devotion, Breck & Woodbridge told me that they read the late N. Hampton result to Mr. Pierpont, [^453-note1] and he declared that it had [been] drawn up in the Cabinet Councel office; it could not have been more calculated to defame the Interest of Religion. Mr. Edwards is Scarce allowed to be a good man. Your Sermon about the 2 Childrens Visions is exceedingly Condemned. It is reported here that Mr. Wheelock is to come next Sabbath and administer the Sacrament to the Separate Party and preach to them a month. I should be very glad to know how you advised him in the affair. In expectation of waiting upon you here in a short time I remain

Your Assured Friend and Humble Servant,

Thomas Clap

P.s. Be pleased to give my service to Majr Fowler, and read to him this Letter if you please because it is in part an answer to his.

[^453-note1]: *A Copy of the Resolves of a Council of Churches, Met at Northampton* (Boston, 1742), the results of a council that met on May 11, 1742, to render its reactions to the revivals. "Mr. Pierpont" is James Pierpont of New Haven, Edwards’s brother-in-law.

## C64. Sarah Noyes to Sarah Pierpont Edwards, October 31, 1742 C064.S.Noyes-SPE 10-31-42

Sarah NoyesC064. Sarah Noyes to Sarah Pierpont Edwards,10/31/42. Two leaves, shorn on left side of first leaf. BRBL, Sermon fragments, f. 1198.

[...] d & Dear Mad m

A dutifull Sence of my obligations to you: will not Suffer me to omit So Convenient an oppor tunity to present my duty to my dear unkle & your Self - & to acquaint you of our wellfare.

it has been a very Sickly time among us many have been Laid in ye grave blessed be God it is abated of Late if I Should atempt to make you a Sharer in our Sorrows as is natural to do when we Converse with a dear freind - I would Some of those many which have died of Late Cap t Munson has buried his Son James ye Stay of his age ye only Son y t Lived with him & his Daughte r[-] [—] Sibel who were married to mr Day - now Lies unburied - this night we have buried Israel Munsons wife - his Second you know: a desirable woman: Leiutenant Dickerman has Lost his wife of his Son Ahbram mr Tod his only Daughter — but a kind providence has dealt tenderly with us when ye arrows of ye almity have been flying by day: we have had but a touch of ye Distemper & y t among ye Servants and therefore have had oportunity to help our [-] neighbours - O magnify ye Lord with me

[. . .] [MS lacuna?]

with us) & tho absent in body ([-] Let[L. 2] joyn in giving praise[-] to our Constant preserver —— I hope you are in good health it is a Long Since we hared from you we have an affectionnate for you all tho at So great a distance we wish for more frequent Communications — ye best news among us is y t mr Birdsy was ordained at westside [^455-note1] y s month to ye Satisfaction of y t people & of those y t wish y m well mr Wodbridge is to be ordained this week at amity [^455-note2] — I wish I Could tell you y t religion hass revived of Late but I Cannot our Neighbours Continue in there unhappy Suparation ye Standing part have given mr Whittlesy [^455-note3] a Call agreable to ye advise of ye association but I Shall weary you with my news untill I Could write better or you had more time my parents Send kind regards to you all as due my Sister Duty & Love to Cousens give my kinndest to Cousens no more at present I remain your Dutifull

Neice

Sarah Noyes

Newhaven oct br 31 1742

[ *written vertically in left margin:*]

PS please to give my Service to mrs Dwight & tell her I think ye time Long Since I heard from her ——

[^455-note1]: Nathan Birdsey of West Haven, ordained Oct. 12, 1742.

[^455-note2]: Benjamin Woodbridge of Woodbridge, ordained nov. 3, 1742.

[^455-note3]: Chauncy Whittelsey, who was a tutor at Yale College from 1739-1745 and not ordained at New Haven First Church till 1758.

## C65. Esther Edwards Hopkins to Sarah Pierpont Edwards[?], [Before January 1743] C065.EEHopkins-Sister bef.1-43

Esther Edwards HopkinsC065. Esther Edwards Hopkins to Sister [Sarah Pierpont Edwards?], n.d. [before 1/43]. ANTS, Sermon on Matt. 7:15 (Jan. 1743).

I recev’d your kind invitation to come & visit You by one of Mr Millar’s family it is not for want of affection or from estrangment y t I have not been before now but have been pro =videntially hindered & y t remarkably w n I have appointed to Goe be sides ye Standing hindrance my haveing no body to take [-] care of my family notwithstanding which I intend to Goe up in a Short time if pro =vidence Give Leive it is & has been in my mind to Spend Some days w th you if I can

I was Last week at Windsor Saw your daughter I [. . . . . . . . . .] Brother & Sisters Says [. . . . . .]n She Sends her [. . . . . . . .] [. . . . . . . . . .]e is ordinary well & thingks She Shall be contented to Stay till Spring

Consearning Spirituals. ## C066. Stephen Williams to Eleazar Wheelock, February 16 1743 C066.S.Wms-E.Wheelock 2-16-43

Stephen WilliamsC066. Stephen Williams to Eleazar Wheelock,2/16/43. Dartmouth Univ. Lib.

L. M. Feb ry: 16 1742/3

Rev d And dear Sr

I take this method to ask your Excuse for not comeing again to your House, & preaching for you - as you de sir d I had Something of a cold, and remember d ye pain, I had Lately had after a cold I thôt therefore I had best take ye advantage of Good weather to Get Home - assoon - as I could, & thrô the Good Hand of God, upon me, I got to Mr Raynolds [^457-note1] on monday night, & ye next day Got Home in safety, & found my family, under comfortable circumstances, I desire to ascribe praise to God; I hope providence may allow me an opportunity to preach for you - if you & your dear people should desire it - &c -. I am in pain to know, what was done at Hebron &c. [^457-note2] patiance should have its p per work , and o r master has told us that we shall have tribulation in the world, but we may be of Good cheer for he has overcome the world. I pity ignorant Souls, y t strain at Gnats, & Swallow Camells &c, I fear God may be provok d to leave a poor back-slideing people - y t talk about religion, & are ready to Quarrell about it, and yet be not�� [^457-note3] Concern d to be conform d to God or to have implant d in them a divine principle Springing up unto Everlasting life &c - but I must leave my thot &c - for ye pre sent for just now - I am told y t ye Rev d m r Edwards, is this day at Westfield - upon m rs Kinsley s Case [^457-note4] - he & m r Ballantine, [^457-note5] with some others. spent ye forenoon in prayer - & were this afternoon to hear her case - & Give y r judgmt upon it - & she has promis d to abide by it &c the Lord direct them, and help ye woman &c. I ask your prayers for me & my family & flock & - let me hear from you assoon as my be; I and my wife Salute you & yours &c ——the Lord make me humble & Holy - meek and prudent - I am Dear Sr your affectionate

B r & Fellow-Serv t

Steph n: Williams

PS I am for plainness & uprightness — the Land dont need jesuiticall tricks &c I cant but recomend anew to you, my advice found d upon prov. 22. 24. 25. please to Salute the my B r & sister at Co- ventry, & Excuse my not going thither &c ye Season is now Such, y t I rejoyce, I am at Home &c

## C67. Charles Chauncy to Nathaniel Chauncy, March 16, 1743 C067.C.Chauncy-N.Chauncy3-16-43

Charles ChauncyC067. Charles Chauncy to Nathaniel Chauncy,3/16/43. *New England Historical and Genealogical Register*10 (Oct. 1856), 332-33.

Reven d Dear Sir,—The person by whom you sent your last, went out of town so unexpectedly, that I mist that opportunity of writing to you, for which I was sorry: For I would willingly improve all opportunities of letting you know the regard I have for you, and the sense I maintain of your past kindnesses to me. The affair of Mr. Cooper and Mr. Ashley has been the most observable of any thing that has lately past among us. I suppose you have seen the publication in the newspapers upon this head. Some other things were wrote more nettling to the good Gentleman, which, if I can procure, I will send by this conveyance. An answer has lately ap- peared to Mr. Edwards’ "trial of the spirits;" [^458-note1] and I think it to be a well done thing, epsecially the preface. Another piece is in the press; Gil- bert against Tennent, which is well calculated to do service. It exposes Mr. Tennent’s principles and conduct exceedingly. He is made to appear so inconsistent and contradictory to hismelf, that the most vulgar eye can’t help discerning it. Mr. Edwards’ book of 378 pages upon the *good work* is at last come forth; And I believe will do much hurt; and I am the rather inclined to think so, because there are some good things in it. Error is much more likely to be propagated, when it is mixed with truth. This hides its deformity and makes it go down the more easily. I may again trouble myself and the world upon the appearance of this book. I am preparing an antidote, and if the world should see cause to encourage it, it may in time come to light. The Weekly Christian history, by Mr. Prince’s son, or rather by the *father* of the son, I suppose you have seen an account of in the public prints. Few among us like it. Many of Mr. [^458-note2] Prince’s parishioners are much troubled at it. I believe tis not much en- couraged, and I hope will drop off itself: Otherwise it may produce another paper; and this may be the means to perpetuate a spirit of bitter- ness. Mr. Whitfield is strongly expected over this spring by his friends. I’m satisfied his vanity was never so well pleased as with the Hosannas of ministers and parishioners in these parts of the earth; and it would not be strange to me, if he should incline to have his vanity gratified again in the same way: Though if he comes with any such expectation, I hope he will meet with disappointment. I trust there are some who will think it proper if he should again appear among us, to magnify themselves and their office. I hope the ministers in the country (I can’t be bound for the ministers in Boston, all of them) will let him know that they look upon him but as a man, and a man of smaller talents than many among themselves; and will properly testify against his Itinerating practice, which, in my opinion is the source of all our other disorder; nor will they be satisfied till this way of conduct has an end put to it. I shall be always glad to hear from you, and hope you wont forget to write an account of any *remarkables* , if they happen. Our regards to your good spouse, to your son and his spouse, and the whole family.

I am your friend and kinsman,

Charles Chauncy.

Boston, March 16, 1742-3.

[^458-note1]: William Rand, *The Late Religious Commotions in New England Considered* (Boston, 1743).

[^458-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

## C68. Sarah Pierpont Edwards to Northampton Constable, March 26, 1744 C068.SPE-Constable 3-26-44

Sarah Pierpont EdwardsC068. Sarah Edwards to "Sir" (Constable),3/26/44. BRBL, Sermon fragments, f. 1158. William Bartlett and Benjamin Alvord were the constables at this time.

Northampton March ye 26 1744.

Sir

Mr Shelden just now informs me that you that you cannot Send all the money at the time Mr Edwards is Rid out and therefore I write to Desire you to Send Some as much as you can Possibly can for Mr Edwards is under Such obligations that he cant Possibly do without it and therefore must use all possible Pains to procure it this from your friend and Serv t

Sarah Edwards.

PS I and my Children give our Love to Leah [^459-note1]

SE

[^459-note1]: Possibly the Edwardses’ slave, whom they may have sold or hired out to one of the constables. There were no Alvord or Bartlett family members named Leah, as far as could be ascertained.

## C69. Thomas Clap to A Friend, December 10, 1744 C069.T.Clap-Friend 12-10-44

Thomas ClapC069. Thomas Clap to "A Friend in Boston,"12/10/44. Printed as *A Letter from the Rev. Thomas Clap . . . to a Friend in Boston* (1745).

A L E T T E R FROM The Rev. Mr. *Thomas Clap*, &c.

*Sir*,

IAm informed by sundry Persons, that the Report of *Contradiction* between the Rev. Mr. *Edwards*of *Northampton* and *my self,* has occasioned much Talk, and various Reflections in the *Country*, and especially in the Town of *Bo-* *ston*; and that he has wrote a *Letter* to *Boston*, which is to be *printed*, in which, it is said, there is a *Denial* of some Things which I reported.

This is very unexpected to me; especially con- sidering the *Letters* which have passed between us upon that Subject. And since it may be some Time before I shall see what he has wrote, I think it may be proper, in the mean Time, to give you this brief Information.

About two Months ago, when I heard the Report [^460-note1] that Mr. *Edwards* had *denied* some Things which I had said, I wrote a *Letter* to him, wherein I put him in Mind, that when we rode together toward *Boston*, in *May*,**1743. we had a long Dis- course about Mr. *Whitefield*, and the *State* of *Reli-* *gion*, and that both of us seem’d to be well agreed to *condemn sundry Errors*and *Disorders*, which some had fallen into and practised: And among other Things, I said, that it appeared to me, that there had been a *Design* to turn the *generality of Ministers in the Country out of their* *Places*, and where they could not make the Party strong enough to do to that at once, they would, in the mean Time, set up a *Separation*, hoping in Time to bring over the *Major Part*: Upon which Mr. *Edwards* said, *Mr.* Whitefield *told me, that he designed to turn the generality* *of Ministers in the Country out of their Places,* *and bring over Ministers from* England, Scotland *and*Ireland, *and place them in their Room.* I also informed him of what he farther said up- on it, the *Substance* of which was, that *he* told Mr. *Whitefield*, that he disliked that, and some other Things; after which he did not seem willing to have much Discourse about it.

Now I am *very clear*and *positive*, that Mr. *Edwards* said to me the *Words above recited*, not only as to the *Sense* and *Substance* of them, but even as to *most*of the *Principal* ** *Terms:*And though I am sensible of the Im- [^460-note2] perfection of humane Nature, that a Man may sometimes be mistaken, tho’ he seems very positive; yet in this Case I can’t at present think, that I was under any Mistake, for these three *Reasons*.

1. Because I took *very good Notice of the* *Words*, and *laid them up in my Mind*, and *soon related them to others*; and that, because I never before had any direct Information, but only conjectured about that part of the Design relating to the bringing over of *Foreigners*, &c;———tho’ as to the *other* Part, which respects the *turning out*, or *separating*from *Un-* *converted*Ministers, it was no News to me at all.

2. Because it was notorious to the World, that Mr. *Whitefield*, and *other Itinerants* did endeavour to perswade People, that the *gene-* *rality* of the Ministers were *Unconverted*, *Pha-* *risee Teachers*, &c. and that all *unconverted*Per- sons were *half Beasts*and *half Devils*, and could no more be the *Means* of any Man’s *Conversion*, than *a dead Man could beget a living* *Child*; from whence it necessarily followed, that People ought to *discard* them, or *separate* from them, as accordingly they did, in a short Time, in a multitude of Places in the *Country*; especially in *Connecticut*, and that with the *Ap-* *probation*of the*Itinerants,*witness *Mr. Ten-* ** *nant’s Sermon upon the Danger of an uncon-* [^460-note3] *verted Ministry*, Pag. 18. *&c*.

3. Because Mr. *Edwards*himself is, in the main, of the same Opinion with me, and the generality of others, in this Point, as appears by sundry fair and ingenuous Concessions in his *Letters* to me on this Subject, some Clauses of which I shall transcribe *verbatim*. "I have also (says he) on some Occasions, mention’d it as my Opinion, that Mr. *Whitefield* was formerly in the Opinion and SCHEME of People’s *forsaking unconverted Ministers,* which possibly you might hear of from others."——— "I heard Mr.*Whitefield* say, that he had Thoughts of bringing over a Number of young Men from *England*into the *Jerseys*, and *Pennsylvania*, that he intended should be ordained by the *Tennants*."———Indeed Mr. *Edwards,* in his *Letter,* seems not willing to allow that he mentioned *Ireland*, because he never heard of any Interest Mr. *Whitefield* had there, *&c.* But I remember I had hearD he had, and thought of it when Mr. *Edwards* mention’d *Ireland*; and it is well known, that the *Tennants,* and the generality of those whom they have ordain’d, came originally from *that* *Country;* and it is most probable they would chuse to Ordain such as they had done, and that Mr. *Whitefield* should chuse to gratify them in *some, at least,*of those whom he should send over. But Mr. *Edwards*, in his [^460-note4] *Letter*, says, that Mr. *Whitefield* did not say that the Persons thus ordained in the *Jerseys*, were to be sent into *New England*. I think it no ways material whether he said so or no, since the constant Practice of the *Tennants*, and their *Presbytery*, makes it evident to the World, that *that*was their *Design*; for they sent Mr. *Finley*, Mr.*Sacket*, and sundry others to preach to the *Separations*in *New-Haven*, *Milford*, and other Places in *New England*; and I have often heard it said, *that the*Tennant’s*and their* *Presbytery assumed as much Authority to send* *Missionaries into*New-England, *as the Bishop of* London: And if so many have come from thence heretofore, we may presume that a greater Number would come, when they had a new Supply of *Foreigners*. But to go on. Mr.*Ed-* *wards*, in a *second Letter*, says "I have some- times said to others, as I inform’d you in my late *Letter*to you, that I supposed Mr. *Whitefield*was formerly of the Opinion, that *unconverted* *Ministers ought not* *to* *continue in* *the Ministry*; and I do suppose, that he *en-* *deavour’d to propogate this Opinion*, *and a* *Practice agreeable to it*. It is also true, that I talked with Mr. *Whitefield* about judging other Persons to be unconverted. Tho’, as I said, I remember no Conversation about Mr. *Whitefield*at that Time; yet ’tis possible I "might say to you, that I believed Mr. *Whitefield did* [^460-note5] *aim at People’s forsaking unconverted Ministers, and to* *endeavour that there should be a Supply of converted* *Ministers as fas as in him lay*, or something to that Purpose. In the same Discourse, it is possible I might mention what Mr. *Whitefield*told me of *his Design* of bringing over some young Men from *England*to be *ordained* by the*Tennants* in the *Jerseys*; and might say, that I thought I had dealt more plainly with Mr. *Whitefield* about his *Errors* than any other Mi- nister; and when I talk’d with him about *Impulses*, he did not seem to like to have much Discourse about it." And I think it is reAsonable to presume, as I understood Mr. *Edwards* at first, that he had this Knowledge of Mr. *White-* *field’s* SCHEME *of People’s forsaking unconverted Ministers*, &c*.* from Mr. *Whitefield’s own Mouth.*

Thus, it appears that Mr. *Edwards* and I are, in *Sub-* *stance*, of the same Opinion in this Point: and tho’ he has not, in the above *Letters*, us’d exactly the same Terms, yet he has used a variety of those which are *equally full*and *strong*; and if we still differ, it is only about some particular Terms, and inconsiderable Circum- stantials, which are not worthy of any Dispute.

I desire you would send me what he has *printed*, and in the mean Time you may make what Improvement of this *Letter* you think proper.

I am, *Sir*,

Your humble Servant,

*New Haven, Dec* 10 1744

*Thomas Clap.*

## C70. Stephen Williams to Eleazar Wheelock, February 18, 1745 C070.EWheelock-SWilliams2-18-45

Stephen WilliamsC070. Eleazar Wheelock to Stephen Williams,2/18/45. Dartmouth University Library, Special Collections.

Rev d Sr & very Dear Brother

I’ve had no opportunity Since I Came home to Convey a Line to You Nor do I know of any Now, however hope it may fall into Some hand y t will Convey it. I Got home Safe, and Seasonably ye day I Left you, and found my family much as I Left it, & So they Still Continue. Sarah yet Lives to ye wonder of all who have known her State, has ye free use of her Reason and often a Sweet frame and Calm in her Soul, Sweet Resignation to ye will of God, I think She is a happy proficient in Christs School. O! y t Go wo d Sanctify his mixed Case to me and mine, and make us holy humble thankfull, & fruitfull. ye Confusions at Windham [^461-note1] &c yet Continue I preachd there ye Sabath before Last but ye Separatists would Not Come to hear me, I See no appearance of ye Like Difficulties yet among my own people, but hear we are threatn d With a visit spedily from them Whether they will have any Encourag among us or not I Cant tell. I wish y t Mr Edwards or some other Gentle- man y t has an intrest in Mr Whitefield would give him a faithfull account of ye State of things in these parts before he Comes Among us. I have done it in short already, & I Cant but think it wo d be of service if Some Good Friend of his at some Distance sho d do ye Same, he has Doubtless heard many reports and what his apprehensions are I Cant ttell, but we Dread ye Con- -sequences of his Coming here and not Discounte -nancing & Discouraging these things. We salute you & yours most Affectionately. pray for us

Your Affectionate tho’ unworthy

Brother Eleaz r Wheelock

Leb. Feb. 18. AD 1744,5.

[^461-note1]: During the Great Awakening, many members of the Windham, Conn., First Church withdrew because of the antirevival attitude of ministers Thomas Clap and Stephen White. In 1747 they formed a Separate church under Elihu Morse. Also, in the Third Church (Scotland), disaffected members had withdrawn in 1741. They too formed a Separate Church led by lay exhorter John Palmer.

## C71. William Metcalf and Abigail Edwards Metcalf to Hannah Edwards, March 25, 1745 C071.WAMetcalf-HEdwards3-25-45

William Metcalf, Abigail Edwards MetcalfC071. William and Abigail Edwards Metcalf to Hannah Edwards,3/25/45. ANTS, f. 1744-46, #6. Addressed on back "To / M rs / Hannah Edwards / Att / Windsor / P r Mr Warner."

Dear Sister.

We have Just Rec’d Your Letter (But when, or where it was writ we know not or By whome Sent, but Conclude by what was in In it, it was Of Late date,) And are very thak Thankfull to you for writing for we very much Wanted to hear from you & our hon d Parents not hav- ing had any particular News for Some time to be Depend- ed upon. And we Cant but be Sensibly Touched With our hon d Mother’s [^462-note1] repeated Misfortune and Affliction & hope that Providence may Restore Her beyond what by your Letter you are Ready To Fear. And I Conclude by what you write That you have Never heard of the Affliction we have met with by the Sickness & Distress of our Youngest Son, [^462-note2] (in whome we have reason to fear we have placed too much of our Delight) which hath ben Exercised with Convulsion Fitts It had three fits one a Day Succesively & y n mis’d It’s fits About a fortnit & y n had two more in 2 Days & y n about 10 days after had another which was Last Wednesday but has had none Since But has been Seemingly very near it Diverse Times Since, & is in a Very week & Low State & we are in Continual fears of ye Returns of its fits And Suppose it is Owing to ye Continual use of means to prevent them that they are kept off & we want That Our hon d Parents & friends Shou’d Know of our Affliction - Depending if they Did we Shou’d have Their good prayers for us which we Earnestly De- sire — Were it not for the Sickness of our Child we Shou’d hope to Visit Our Parents this Spring But it is very Uncertain how it will be with [^462-note3] Us & whether we Can Come or no; Our Maid Lydia Thacher Left us Last Jan r Being under Such Bodily Infirmities as that She was not able to serve us as we tho t wou’d be profitable or Comfortable To us. but have had Some help f m Cous: Sarah Metcalf who is a boarder in the house when She does not work Abroad in whome we Can put Confidence in ye Care of our Child. Your Sister is oblidged to undergo hardship from the Sickness of ye Child w ch keeps her Low Otherwise might probably be as well as She Ordinarily Has ben — As to News I think of but Little that may in ye Least Affect you, I Suppose You know that Bro r W ms & Sister are Removed To Sharon which was Last fall ——— we had a Letter from them Lately which Inform’d us that She was Then Lately delivered of a Lusty Son & Like to do well. —— Bro r John Huntington is Engaged in the Expedition to Cape Briton having an En- sign’s Commission Given him. —— But per- haps I Shall write what you will think of Little Consequence to you to know, I Shall therefore not Trouble you further by taking up y r Time to Read, But only Inform you y t we & our friends here Are Generally well, & y t we Give all Dutifull regards to Our hon d Parents, & much Love to you & our Sisters & beg y r Continual Remembrance of us. & Subscribe

Yr Loving Bro r & Sister

W. & A. Metcalf

Lebanon March 25.1745.

P. S: Our Mother Sends her Regards To Your [^462-note4] Father & mother & to you & ye Rest of ye family, as Also Cousen Sarah Metcalfe Sends her Dutifull Ser- vice & Remembers y r kindness to her. I have Sent you what I guess will be agreea- y d able to you for Cuffing ye Price is 15/6 w ch is much Cheeper than it Can be had now if bo t now.

W m Metcalfe

P. S.: 2. I had Like to have forgot your mention of our apprehension of a fledg[l]ing out of ye Nest of Old maids for my own part I must Confess I was So farr from Supposing that the Birds Left not their Nest before Now because Not fledged before tho’ I Shou’d rather Im put situte [^462-note5] it to y r Being fledged So Long As that by reason of Age their Wings were Grown So week that they were not able to Carry them from their Nests.

But however Let it be from the weekness of y r Plumes or brains I know not how To help it, but must Leave it till they have Strength, or Skill or Disposition to see what power they have, but Eno’ of y s. [^462-note6]

[^462-note1]: Esther Stoddard Edwards

[^462-note2]: Eliphalet Metcalf, b. July 10, 1744, d. May 1745.

[^462-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^462-note4]: **marginal.** [3]

[^462-note5]: Conjectural; apparently Metcalf meant "Impute."

[^462-note6]: This playful postscript probably refers to Hannah Edwards’s continuing unmarried state, though she would soon wed Seth Wetmore of Middletown.
