## C73. Timothy Edwards to Abigail Edwards Metcalf and William Metcalf, July 11, 1745 C073.TE-A & WMetcalfe 7-11-45

Timothy EdwardsC073. TE to William & Abigail Edwards Metcalfe,7/11/45. BRBL, f. 1552. Fragment.

Windsor July 11 th, 1745.

Dear Son & Daughter

By a Letter I receiv’d from your Sometime Since, wherein you Inform me that God has Taken from you your Dear Little Son by Death, [^464-note1] which Information I receiv’d with Sorrow. I question not but that you will both readily Own, that God both actually and rightfully Governs the workd as an Absolute Sovereign, and That is the perfection, and Glorious Excellenccy of his Nature, that he is Righteous in all his wayes, and holy In all his works and that he never did, Or possibly can, do the Least wrong to any of his Creatures, and that as he is Infinitely not only the highest but also the best of Beings, so it is most fit that in all his dispensations to= wards Mankind his Glory Should be his Great end. and as God only knows what is most for his Glory, and So What is best to be done, So it most agreeable to Religion and Reason, that the most Should do with all the works of his hand whatsoever he pleases. Now if you receive these things as true and in the Love of them, you do that which is pleasing to God. We have Many, yea very many passages in Gods holy word very agreeable to what I have now written Concerning the ab= solute Sovereignty and Glorious Excellency of God, Some of which (and but a few) I Shall now Mention, viz. Dan ll: 4. 35 and All the Inhabitants of the world are Reputed as Nothing; and he doth According to his will &c — Among the Inhabitants of ye Earth, and none can Stay his hand or Say unto him what doest thou? Hab: 2. 20. But the Lord is in his holy Temple, Let all The Earth keep Silence before him. 1. Sam ll: 3. 18. and he Said, it is the Lord, Let him do what Seemeth him Good. Zach: 2. 13. Be Silent O all Flesh before the Lord. Psal. 39. 9. I was dumb, I Opened not My Mouth, because thou didst it. Lam: 3. 28. 29. he Sitteth alone, and keepeth Silence, because he hath born it upon him, he putteth his Mouth in the dust. —— These Texts and Many others hold forth to us, the Infinite Greatness, Majesty, Absolute Sovereignty, Spot less Righteousness, and Glorious Excellency of God. If therefore from the high thoughts and Apprehensions of him they are therefore pleasing to you, and your Souls close with them, as God is honoured and Exalted by them, you give to God In Some Good measure the Glory that is due to his Name. heartily and practically to acknowledge the Sovereignty of God, to ascribe Righteousness to our Maker to entertain high and honourable thoughts of him, in a time of Great and Sore affliction, and So with humble Silence and Submission, patiently to bear his afflicting hand, acknowledging that he afflicts us far Less that we deserve, and that we have Still great cause to bless his Name, with Much of a Spirit of Love and thankfullness, for the Mercies that we yet enjoy, this is to put Singular honour upon God, and to Shine like Gold brightly when Lying in the Furnace. In a due manner Acknowledge God, as the Great King and So- vereign of the world, and So to walk humbly with him, and to have Exalting, and Adoring thoughts of him, and that when he dispenses things that are very Grievous and Bitter to us, If these things be the things that we Love, if we delight in them after the Inward man, and that because God is hereby honoured, and Glory is given to him, and the Contrary to them even in the Least degree, as it is against God, and to his dishonour is the evil, or are the things that we hate, our Souls with in us So acknowledging the Glorious Perfection, and Infinite Exellency of the Blessed God, that the Least mean Low thought of him, is that which we abhor; This is Surely pleasing and Acceptable to God. Such a Spirit as I have now in Some measure describing, I have comfortable hopes God hath Given to both of you to whom I am now writing, and that he hath enabled, and will enable you, humbly to walk before [...] [^464-note2] under that Bereaving stroke of his holy hand wherewith he hath Lately Sorely afflicted you: and If it be So you have Great cause to be thankful to God, for this is a mercy Greater, yea Much greater, then your affliction in the final departure (as to the Life that now is) of your Dear Child, though that be very great: for So to do is to act graciously, and So an Evidence, not only of Grace in Truth, but also of Grace in Exercise, as realy, as believing in Christ, and Mourning for Sin with Godly Sorrow, or of the Souls Going out after God or the Lord Jesus Christ in Desires, from a Spirit or principle of Divine Love is So And that you may See that what I have here Last written is Agreeable to the Judgment not only of ministers of a more Com= mon and ordinary Rank, but also of them that have been Esteem’d very Eminent both of New-England and Old, as may appear by what I shall next write, which is but a Small part of what I have had for many years Lying by me, chiefly Transcribed from the Printed Works of Several of the Ministers I have Respect to in what is Just above written; Some thing of it I receiv’d from two of them in Discourse, with which I shall begin what I here Intend.

"I once heard the Renowned Mr Samuel Willard Say thus or to this effect, viz, That a humble acknowledgement of, and "Submission to the Sovereignty of God, was a Sign or Mark of a mans being truly Converted, or an act and Evidence "of true Grace. Old Mr Woodbridge of Hartford, a Faithful Minister of Christ, and one of Great wisdom and Knowledge, once as we were Riding together as I Remember between Hartford, and Farmington, told me, or Said to me in Discourse, "that for "A Christian quietly to Submit himself under the hand of an afflicting God was a Great Act of Grace, and a Great At= "tainment in Christianity, or to that effect; he also Said to the Same purpose Lately when we were Sitting together at "his house also in his Last Lecture which was Feb: — 1718/19 — from Prov. 16. 7. when a mans wayes please "The Lord, — he Said that for a Christian to acknowledge the Glorious Atributes of God &c— to acknowledge him "In his Government of the world [...] [^464-note3] things pleasing to God - and that Submission and Resignation to God under "his afflicting hand So as not to Murmur &c— is thatwhich is very pleasing to God.

"When the Saints patiently bear affliction as coming from God, they Exercise Grace and holiness, they actually Submit "to Gods hand Subject themselves to him, and So are made more meet to enjoy him; when we patiently bear afflictions we "Subject our Selves, and this is the way to Live, and to Live Eternally with God. Our Patient Suffering is acceptable to God. Pres: t Wadsworth in his Resignation to God under afflictions p. 72. ††

†† under -"Thy Sutable Carriage under affliction, is one Good medium to know thou art of Child of God; this is a Good way to Evi= "dence thy Sonship. —— The more meek, humble, patient, and Long Suffering you are under troubles, So much the more you "have of your being Gods Children. ———— In So doing we greatly Glorify God &c ——— by our Submission and re "signation, we practically do our utmost to Set God on the Throne of his Sovereignty, we Glorify him by Obeying that pre= "cept, Psal. 46. 10. be Still and know that I am God. - We Glorify Gods Justice and Righteousness, we practically Justify "God in all he does, Saying his throne is Guiltless, no fault is to be found with any of his proceedings &c — [^464-note4] "God in all he does, Saying his Throne is Guiltless, no fault is to be found with any of his proceedings &c- "Mr Wadsworth in his Resignation to Gods will under afflictions. 91. 92. 93 &c ——

"The Sea when it is calm is as Still and quiet as any River, but Let the winds Once Rise and you Shall See a difference; "Then you Shall See Nothing but Raging, and Storming, out mire and Dirt. In peace wicked mens Corruptions Ly hid, then "they will carry themselves to God and Man More Moderately: but Let God Lay affliction on them, and then (as Satan falsely Charged Job) See if they will not Spit the very poyson of their blasphemy, in the face of God himself. ——— "———— Therefore doth James Call afflictions Temptations, because they Serve to try us &c— how was the tryal of Abra= "hams Sound heart, when God Laid that Cross upon him, that Grievous Command, &c —— now I have Given thee a thorow "Tryal of the Integrity of thine own heart. here was also the tryal of Jobs Good heart &c - —— how meek and patient was "he? No Murmuring, No Gruding, how meek and patient was he. the Lord hath Given and taken, blessed be his Name.

Mr Daniel Dyke of the Deceitfulness of Mans heart; Concerning the discovery of the heart by affliction. 328. 329. 330. ‡ vide marg t [^464-note5]/p>

"A Holy Silence is that Excellent precious Grace, that Lends a hand of Support to every Grace: Silence is the keeper of all "other vertues; it Lends a hand to faith, hope, Love, humility, and Self denyal. A holy Silence hath its Influence upon all other "Graces that be in the Soul: it causes the Rose-buds of Grace to Blossom and bud forth. Silence is a Grace that keps a man "Gracious in all Conditions: Silence is a Christians Right hand. ——— It bears up the Soul in Adversity. A quiet Silent Spirit is "of Great Esteem with God. &c —— 1. Pet. 3. 4. even the Ornament of a meek and quiet Spirit, which is in the Sight of God of great "price. It is a Spark of the Divine Nature, a Beam of Glory, it is a Heav’n born Spirit. —— This is a Flower of Paradice; it is "a precious Gem that God makes Great Reckoning of. Mercy is nearest, Deliverance, and Salvation is at hand, when a "Christian Stands Still, when he Sits quiet and Silent, under his greatest troubles, and Sorest tryals. No man honours God, "Nor No man Justifies God at So high a Rate, as he who Lays his hand upon his Mouth, when the Rod of God is upon "his Back. Mr Brooks his Mute Christian under the Smarting Rod, p. 123. 124. 125 &c ————

———— "But then the Last thing to be Inculcated upon us is this, my Brethren, Let us be very Studious to "follow the Blessed Jesus; ——— to Conform to that Glorious Example which our Lord hath Given us of a pati "ent Submission to the will of God in every thing being a mighty Article in our Conformity to our Saviour.

"Take pains with your own hearts, Renounce your own will, cry to the Glorious One, that he would Subdue the Re= "bellion of your own will &c —— Give not Over till you can Say, &c — O my God If this be the Cup, which thou hast ap= "pointed for me, I wil Strive to Submit unto it, thy will, thy will Shall be Mine O my God! Make Choice of Spiritual "Blessings, which Shall be an Abundent Compensation for the Loss of the Temporal ones of which your Sufferings may de "prive you; and then Say If the Lord, and Such Blessings of the Lord, may be the portion of my Cup, I have a Goodly he= "ritage. It will be Impossible for you to Gratify Heaven More then by Such a Devotion.

"Doct r: Cotton Mather in his Sermon, of the will of the Father Submitted to, from Jn o: 18. 11. the cup that my Father "hath Given me to Drink, Shall I not Drink it? p. 25.—27.-

"We cannot Glorify the Great God more then by Submission to his holy providence. There are Some who read [...][^464-note6] Silence is praise to thee O God. Wenever parise our God, So Significantly, So Effectually "So acceptably as in Silence under his afflictive dispensations. Let us with an humble Resignation Sweetly Submit "unto the will of God in the Death of our friends, and Let us as the Genuine Children of Abraham, offer up unto God, "The very Isaacs of our Tenderest Love. ——— The Angels of Heaven will be the Glad Spectators, of this our hum "ble Resignation, and Say, Gen: 22. 14. Now I know that thou fearest God.

"Doct r: Cotton in his Piety quickned at a Funeral, from Eccl. 7. 2.

"I am to tell you over and over again, that you never gratify the Glorious God So by any thing as by this Resig= "nation unto him. No Devotions of a Godly Life do more Glorify God then this one Article of it.

Doct r: Cotton Mather in his Sermon of the Divine Sovereignty displayed and Adored, from Job 9. 12. behold he Taketh away, and who can hinder him.

"If I Take with a patient Submission the Cup that is appointed for me, tis as Good, as Rich, as Bright a Token for "Good as can be found upon me. t’will be aToken of thy Sincerity to Take it Sutably. perhaps t’is the Cup of "A funeral. that which was the Desire of thine eyes, the Delight, the Darling of thy Family must have its fu= "neral, to part with thy Isaac is the Cup that is Given thee, take it, and hear those acclamations of Heaven over "thee, —— Now know I that thou fearest God. ——— We Read 2. Tim: 2. 12 If we Suffer with him we Shall "Also Reign with him. If we Take our Cup as the blessed Jesus took it, and if we tread in the Steps of his patient "Submission to the Condition appointed for him, then we Shall be with him, and Sit with him and Sup with him, and "and Drink of the fruit of the vine in his Kingdom, with him, and that Lamb of God will feed us, and Lead us "to Fountains of Living Water for evermore.

Doct r: Cotton Mather, in his Sermon, The will of a Father Submitted to, from Jn o: 18. 11. the Cup which my Father [hath given me, Shall] [^464-note7] I not Drink it.

" — When Aaron had his Sons taken from him after an awful manner tis Said Aaron held his peace, Levit: 10. 3. — he "did not Murmur against God. When Eli was Informed by Samuel &c—— how humbly and Graciously did he Ex= "press himself, Submitting to the will and providence of God. 1. Sam ll: 3. 18 he said it is the Lord, Let him do what Seemeth him "Good. If God Shall Withhold from us those things which our hearts are most Set upon, we must humbly Submit to his holy provi= "dence. So did David, when he knew not whether ever he Should See the ark of God again, which he much desired; with what re= signation to the will of God doth he Express himself. ——— Behold here am I, Let him do to me, as Seemeth Good unto him. "———— Passive Obedience is the most difficult: If the Lord will take from our Estates, and bring us to penury, or If the "Lord will take from us our health, and afflict us with painful diseases; to Say the will of the Lord be done, is a hard Lesson; If the "Lessons in the School of Christ, &c. — Doct r: Increase Mather in his Sermon Occationed by the Death of his wife from that text, Mat: 6. 10. thy will be done. p. 13. 14. 15. &c. —— 36. 37.

"Concerning Crosses afflictions, Troubles &c— A patient Submission unto, and fruitful Exercise under [^464-note8] "Gods visiting hand is an Infallible demonstration that thou art a Son, and not a Bastard. again he Speaks thus, or to s "This purpose that Such a Submission unto God will, and Exercise under his afflicting hand are evident Marks of a persons "being in the right way to Heaven. Mr Robert Bolton in his Book of a Comfortable walking with God. p. 368. 369.

"To be above the Stroke of passion is a Condition equal to Angels; to be in a State of Sorrow, without the Sense of "Sorrow is a disposition beneath beasts; but duly to Regulate our Sorrows, and Bound our Passions under the Rod, "Is the wisdom, duty, and Excellency of a Christian. he that is without Natural affections is deservedly Ranked among "The worst of Heathen, and he that able rightly to Manage them, deserves to be numbred with the best of Christians. "Though when we are Sanctified we put on the Divine Nature, yet till we are Glorified we put not off the Infirmities "of the humane Nature. whilest we are within the reach of troubles, we cannot be without the Danger, Nor ought we "to be without the fear of Sin. how apt are we to transgress the Bounds of Reason and Religion under a Sharp afflic= "tion, appears in most mens Experience.

"Whatever God doth with us or ours, Still we Should maintain Good thoughts of him. A Gracious heart cleaves near= "er and Nearer to God in affliction, and can Justify God in his Severest Strokes, acknowledging them all to be Just and "holy, Psal: 119. 75. and hereby the Soul may comfortably Evidence to it Self its own uprightness, and Sincere Love to God; "yea it hath been of Singular use to Some Souls to take right measures of their Love to God in Such tryals: to have "Lovely, and well pleased thoughts of God, even when he Smites us in our Nearest and dearest Comforts, argues plain "ly that we Love him for himself, and not for his Gifts only, and that his Interest in the heart is deeper then Crea= "ture Interest is. And he observes that very great hath been the Comfort that hath Resulted to Some from Such dis= "coveries of their own hearts by close Smarting afflictions.

"The more Lovely and Engaging your Relation was, the more Excellent will your patience and Contentment with "the will of God in its death be: the more Loveliness, the more Self-denyal, and th emore Self denyal, the more grace. "It may turn to you for a Testimony of the Truth and Strength of Grace, that you can like Abraham part with a Child, "whom you So dearly Lovein Obedience to the will of God.

"Mr Flavel in his Token for Mourners, 1. 2. — 34. 35. 122. 123.

I have Comfortable hopes (as I think I have already Said) that you have both of you that in your hearts that is very agreeable to what is above-written, of the Judgment of Several Ministers of Christ, of a Superiour Character, (Some of which were men of fame and Renown in their day, above most of their order,) Concerning a patient Bearing of† [^464-note9] Affliction as the hand of a Sovereign God, and a humble Submission to his will therein.

Now if Such a Question Should Arise, viz Suppose we have hope from as it Seems to us we find and feel in our hearts That we have (and do experience) this patient hearing of affliction as the hand of a Sovereign God, and that from the high apprehensions we have of him we can freely Justify him in it, and humbly Submit to his will in it as is above Expressed [...] [^464-note10] but that we therein act Sincerely, and with the Excercise of True Grace.

[ . . .]

Blood and there be with him, and receive from him, the most Endearing Expression of his Love for evermore, and there [^464-note11] as our portion we Shall See God as our Father, and fully and everlastingly enjoy him in the [———————] brightest displays of the Glorious Excellencies and perfections of his‡ [^464-note12] Blessed Nature, and of his Love to us as Some of his Dear Children, and in a State of perfect holiness, and with most high and Glorious actings of Grace towards Our God and Redeemer, and tha forever And ever.

If we Esteem these things the Chief Good, the highest happiness that we can enjoy or desire, and So Set our hearts upon y m, to prize and Seek them above all other things whatsoever, we certainly Act Graciously. This is an act and Evidence of Grace † [^464-note13] viz. Supream, and So of Sincere Love to God and our Lord Jesus Christ.

It is very clear from Gods own word, that none but them that are truly Gracious, being Inwardly Renewed and Sanctified by the ho= ly Spirit in their Regeneration, can have Such high thoughts and Apprehensions of the Glorious Excellency of that Infinitely Glorious and Excellent being, the Blessed God, Being One God in three Divine persons, the Father Son and holy Spirit, as freely, and with their whole Souls to Chuse him to be their God, and accordingly to Serve and Glorify him as God and their God while thy are in this world, and to place their highest happiness in the full Enjoyment of him as their portion for ever in the Life to come. 6. and Lastly If we humbly hope in the Mercy of God in Christ for pardon and Salvation, and this hope be Accompanied with Such a fear of God that we are careful in all things to Avoid Sin, that So we may not Offend and dishonour him; In a word If it be much our Desire, delight and Care, dayly So to walk before God that we may please and honour him, and humbly acknowledging our great unworthiness as Sinners, and yet taking Encouragement from the Greatness and Riches of Gods mercy to Sinners in through the great Mediator, hope and trust in the Mercy of God in Christ for forgiveness of Sin and Eternal Salvation, this is truly to fear God, and truly to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. To fear God, and not to hope in his Mercy in Christ, is to be either a dispairing Sinner, or but a Self-Righteous Pharisee. Again to hope (after a Sort) in Gods mercy in Christ, and not to Sanctify him in his heart and to make him his fear and his Dread, So as carefully to avoid Sinning against him, or so as to allow himself in any Course or way of known Sin, is to be a presumptuous Sinner, and one whose hope is but the hope of the Hypocrite; but So to fear God, and humbly to hope in his mercy in Christ, &c- as is above expressed, is to be a True believer, a Sound Christian, And So one that God Loves and takes plea= sure in. Psal. 147. 11. The Lord taketh pleasure in Them that fear him, in those that hopein his Mercy.

I am Sensible that I have been very Long, in If not too Long in this Letter; when I first begun it, I Intended it Should have been very Much Shorter then Now it is, but as it is, it is my hearts desire that God would make it not only profita= ble, but also comfortable to you both in this Day of your Mourning. I am also very Sensible that at Such a time as this you might well have Expected a Letter from me Some weeks ago, and Indeed I Intended to have Sent you one Long before now And I have been for Some time under considerable uneasiness that it has not been done, but by reason of the more then ordina= ry business that has ddayly Lain upon Me, that I am far from being able to as I would. Neither have I written this Letter without Considerable Difficulty, by resaon of Dayly want of Time. for many moneths together, (I am very apt to think) my work, every week, has been very near, if not full as Much again as the ordinary Work of my ministry in preparing and preaching two Sermons, Constantly every Sabbath &c— would Amount to. Before I conclude, or finish what I have further to Say in what I am Now writing, I would Say Something for your Comfort concerning your dear departed Little Son, and it is this viz that by what I have heard and Read, I am Inclin’d to think that Such Parents that have Good hopes Concerning themselves Respect their Eternal State may upon Scripture Grounds have the Same hopes for their Chil= dren that die in Infancy, Especially if they die Baptiz’d; and this by what I have met with in Discourse and Reading of the great est and most Judicious of our Divines, yea I have no Reason to question but that it is So of Divines in General, which I think

## C73a. Hannah Edwards to Unknown, [Before January 15, 1746] C073a.HEdwards-_ bef.1-15-46

Hannah EdwardsC073a. Hannah Edwards to [?], n.d. [before Jan. 15, 1746]. BRBL, f. 1522. Two drafts of same letter, incomplete at end, each two leaves, torn lengthwise.

[1. Transcribed version]

[Draft 2[?], p. 1.]

I understand that A our Late Conversation up the rites and obbligations of Husbands and wives has given disgust and I am Call’d a bold and arrogant old maid for Setting up my openion in oposition to the general openion of mankind and to the wisest divines and not only So but to many plain texts of Scripture —— and that you wonder what I think of Ephe V th 22 - 23 - 24 &C

I Conclude my arrogance appear’d in declairing my openion that a wife was no proper Subject of Correction or private government but that the only proper time of Life was over for Tuition and further that there was no propriety in a Husbands Commanding his wife but d if he took it upon him She was under no absolute obligation to Comply but if She thought obedience was Like to procure greater evil than his displeasure of the two evils the ought to Chuse the Less and further that it was a 5 more agre vated heinous breach of peace tending more to Confution and every evil work and theref [-] vastly greater Crime for a man to whip or any way to distress his wife than it wo’ d be so to distress his neighbour. now s r by way of apology for my Self I wo d remind you that I did not peremtorily asert that these things were So but only that they appear’d so to me now I hope s r if it is impro per for a wife to any openion of her own it is not out of Character for an old maid Modestly to tell how things appear to her is it not the way to gain Light if She is in an error that she may receive Light and allowing my openion differs from the Common openion - perhaps it will not appear so very bold if you consider the great —— depravity of all mankind and their universal proneness to err through their thirst for dominion the narrowness of their veiws and great partiallity to themselves which gives rise to a maxim that no man must be a judg where he is a party - 5 and in this Case the wisest must be Considerd as a party and forthly 5 as for my venting an openion that is differing from the wisest divines or divines in general I am not Convinct it is so but be that as it will if I am obbliged to beleive as divines beleive I hope till they are universally universally united in Sentiment I may Chuse on whose Sleve to pin my openion and there does fail to Some approve’d - divines that not only think but print there openions that a Husband has no rite of Compultion over his wife and as to what I uttered respecting a mans Commanding his wife perhaps I must ask your pardon for Speaking

[Draft 1[?], p. 2]

very well know what determinate idea to affix to the word Com mand 5 if it but means that I Cant be Intitled except you doubt I am Sincible that the Law of Self preservation and revelation by reason of a womans Dpendent state Requires it as for my openion being contrary to many texts of Scripture - I do not take it to be so I should not have vented it you have particularize but are I Sopose were I capable it wo’ d be arrogance for me to pretend to expound Scripture a woman must believe as the man beleive but as to that perticular you mention 5 perhaps I of y t and many other places where wives Submission is mentiond Sho d be better able to tell you m openion if you wo d please to [^465-note1] give your Sentiments on the VI of first of Corinthians 15 and 16

 verses or if I were a wife I wo d be Content ot accept the Apostles own exposition of himsel fin the Last verse of the Chapter I think it wo’ d be very proper for them to examine the Conduct of the holy women of old whose example is Set before them I am Sincible there is many texts injoin Conformable behavour from a wife to her husband but neither precept nor exmple of a husbands Commanding or Compelling, his wife and perhaps it Cannot be more Strongly infer’ d than the poor mans right to take of the rich mans estate because he thinks there is many precepts requireing him to bestow it.-but the rich man thinks it is the disposition that is absolutel requir’d and that it is Left to his Rea- son and discretion to determine when almsgiving will interfear with other duties and when not and So Says the wife and Sho d the poor be the Strongest party they wo ed without doubt with as good Countenance make pray of goods of the rich and if need be of their Liberty to and bring many places of Scripture to brace themselves as we now see many of the vagrants by this time I Sopose you as the Husband does of the Liberty of the wife [2. Edited version]

I understand that our late conversation up[on] the rights and obligations of husbands and wives has given disgust, and I am called a bold and arrogant old maid for setting up my opinion in opposition to the general opinion of mankind and to the wisest divines; and not only so, but to many plain texts of Scripture, and that you in particular wonder what I think of Eph. 5:22-24, etc.

I conclude my arrogance appeared in declaring my opinion that a wife was no proper subject of correction or private government, but that the only proper time of life for tuition was past, and further, that there was no propriety in a husband’s commanding his wife; if he took it upon him, she was under no absolute obligation to comply, but if she thought obedience was like to procure greater evil than his displeasure, or than neglect of the two evils, she ought to choose the less. And further, that it was a more aggravated, heinous, greater breach of peace, tending more to confusion and every evil work, and theref[...] a vastly greater and more aggravated crime for a man to whip or any way to distress or pretend to punish his wife than it would be so to distress his neighbor. Now, sir, by way of apology for myself, I would remind you, in the first place, that I did not peremptorily assert that these things were so, but only that they appeared so to me. Now I hope, sir, if it is improper for a wife to have any opinion of her own, it is not out of character for an old maid to have an opinion, and modestly to tell how things appear to her. Is it not the likeliest way to gain light, if she is in an error, that she may receive light?

And allowing my opinion differs from the common opinion: for one to differ from a number that are all in one common interest, perhaps it will not appear so very bold if you consider the great depravity of all mankind for dominion, and their universal proneness to err through the narrowness of their views and great partiality to themselves; which gives rise to a maxim amongst you, that no man must be a judge where he is a party. And in this case, the wisest of you must be considered as of a party. As for my having an opinion that is differing from the wisest divines or divines in general, I am not convinced it is so; but be that as it will, if I am obliged to believe as divines believe, I hope, till they are universally united in sentiment, I may choose on whose sleeve to pin my opinion: and there does not fail to [be] some approved divines, that not only think, but print, their opinions that a husband has no right of compulsion over his wife. And as to what I uttered respecting a man’s commanding his wife, perhaps I must ask you pardon for speaking my sentiments on that which I did not understand: for I must confess, I do not very well know what determinate idea to affix to the word command; but, however, I still think, were I a wife, I should think myself far more obliged to compliance by a mild manifestation of my husband’s will or choice than by any imperious, threatening dictates he could use.

And in the last place, as for my opinions being contrary to many texts of Scripture. If it is so, I confess it bold with a witness; but had I thought it so, I should not have vented it. I suppose it would be arrogant in me to pretend to tell my sense of Scripture, and were I a wife, perhaps I should fear to have any sentiments, much [more] to broach them, if in any respect differing from my husband—a woman must believe as her husband believes. I am sensible that the woman’s inferiority of strength brings her into some degree of dependence, so that the law of self-preservation, as well as many texts of Scripture, enjoin a great care to please and fear to offend, and so, in a good degree, a respectful, conformable behavior from a wife to her husband; but there is in Scripture neither precept nor example of a husband’s by any means compelling his wife. And perhaps his right to it cannot be more strongly inferred than the poor man’s right forcibly to take of the rich man’s estate, if he was but once the strongest party, because there is many precepts requiring the rich man to bestow it. But the rich man thinks it is the disposition that is absolutely required, and that it is left to his reason and discretion to determine when alms-giving will interfere with other duties, and when not; and so says the wife with respect to the obedience you talk of. And were the poor the strongest party [...]

[^465-note1]: In the left margin at this point, written perpendicularly, Hannah Edwards wrote: "source of subjection / submission obedience / Command obedience &C"

## C74. Hannah Edwards Wetmore to Esther Stoddard Edwards, November 5, 1746 C074.HWetmore-EEdwards 11-5-46

Hannah Edwards WetmoreC074. Hannah Edwards Wetmore to Esther Stoddard Edwards,11/5/46. BRBL, f. 1520. Addressed on back "To / M rs Esther Edwards / Att / Windsor / The[se]."

Honour’d Mad m / This may acquaint you though I am not quite so well now as when at windsor Last yet I have had as much health (and now) as I Cou’d Reasonably expect want very much to hear from my parents have heard nothing Since I Saw them — have had great hopes of Seeing them at my own House this fall but it grows So Late in the year I fear a disapointment —— this Comes Mad m as a Token of my duty to and fillial Respect (which I wo’d in all proper ways express) and to desire that if may not See — yet I may be Remember’d by my Parents and have an Interest in there most ernest addresses at the throne of grace — that they would Espetially Request for me that I may be in every Respect fitted for and Resined to Gods will and Disposal — and that if God is pleased to Continue my Life it may be in mercy to me and others that I may be assisted to perform the Dutyes ( and withstand the temptations) of the Place and Relations I Stand in I hope I am not alltogether insincible of and Desire to be Suteably thank for the great mercy I have injoy’d in my Parents and that they are Still Continued and Capa ble of Praying for me —— I am Honoured Mad m on many accounts under I now injoy many Comforts and as much Calmness of mind as Can be expected and I am Ready to Say as Can be desired under my Circumstances except I were better prepared to meet with Danger —— but it Seems Something Mallancholy to me not to have the Company of any of my natural Relations — and if it is not Like to be injurious to the Comfort of my father nor you I wo’d Request that Sister Molly might tarry with me before She goes home ——————————

Honoured Mad m the above was [——] written before Sister Molly Came from Killingsworth She is [^466-note1] now here and it wo’d be a great Comfort to me and I think She is willing with our Parents Consent to tarry with me a month Longer — but wo’d neither of us urg it at all if it is Contrary their wills your minds in this Regard we Sho’d be glad to know you wo’d please manifest to Mr Wetmore who will be at Hartford this week and Next and designs if Sister insists upon going home to Carry her Next Monday this Mad m with our Duty to my father and you and Love to sister Patty is from your Dutifull Daughter

H: Wetmore

Middleton November 5 th 1746

[^466-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C78. Sarah Edwards to Elihu Spencer, [c. January 1748] C078.SEJr.-E.Spencer c.1-48

Sarah EdwardsC078. Sarah Edwards (daughter) to Elihu Spencer, c. 1/48. BRBL, sermons on Job 36:26 (6/48) and Hos. 3:1-3 (6/48). Fragment; opening portion of letter missing. Extant text is cut into three parts: pts. 1 & 3 in Sermon on Job 36:26, pt. 2 in Sermon on Hos. 3:1-3. Addressed on back "To Mr Elihu Spencer / In / Newjersey." According to the biographies of Elihu Spencer, *DAB*, he and Job Strong past the winter of 1747/48 with John Brainerd at Bethel, New Jersey, and the following summer with JE, preparing for their work. This would seem to pinpoint the letter some time in that winter. However, Dexter ( *Yale Biographies*) states that they were then with John Brainerd among the Christian Indians of New Jersey.

[. . .] many reproaches on this account. My Father has therefore this Winter in= sisted upon it that they Should pitch upon a certain Sum and agree to give give him so much Yearly, but they forsooth Say they have promised to main= [tain] him Honoarably, and why cannot he trust to that and that they would promise to Maintain as large a Family as his is with not more than Half so much as he has; which conduct in this People has caused in both my Parrents much grief of Mind and has been very discouraging to my Fa= ther For they have never Maintaind him in any Measure, the Straits and difficulties he has been put to Since he has been their Minister have been almost innumerable and he has drawn up in writing what the wants of Fa= mily are in one year without any extraordinary Charge and has shown it to Some to of his People and the wants of Family in one year for Victuals and Cloaths only just to be Carried Comfortably through the year Comes [^470-note1]to Several Hundreds more than they give and the People that Saw this will them

Selves allow that he wants these things all of them, and yet are unwilling

to give him that which in any Measure keep him above Board, but are like

those who Say be ye Depart in peace be ye warmed, and filled, Notwithstanding he give him not those things which are needfull to the Body. these things I am sinsable

have done much toward making my Father willing to leave his if a Conveni-

ent Opportunity Present.

Our Family through mercy, are all Preservd alive as yet but we are not

well our youngest Sister [^470-note2] has been afflicted with a grevious sore all Winter and the

Doctor is afforaid what it will prove at Last. My Father had a Fall from a Horse the last week and has complaind ever since of a bad pain in his Breast.

Sister Jerusha has been much better in health this Winter Since you was here than She was then till now about a Fortnight has been Somwhat indisposed and [^470-note3] this Day was taken very much out of order but we hope it will prove but a Short Turn. I am not So well my Self as I was when you was here and as was all the Last Fall and the forepart of Winter. the returns of the Sun

I find makes a great alteration with respect to Health.

Sir I must ask many Pardons for Lengthening out this Letter thus, but your I Perswade my Self your Candour will excuse it, for I have felt the greatest freedom in writeing to one whom I esteem So Cordial a Friend. The defects in write ing Inditeing and Spelling I am sure your Cloak of Friendship I am Sure your will cover.

We all with one accord Present our best regards to both you and Mr Strong and assure yourselves you have our sincere good wishes.

From Sir your true Friend and Humble Serv t.

S. E

Mr Elihu Spencer

[^470-note1]: First part ends here.

[^470-note2]: Probably Elizabeth, b. 1747.

[^470-note3]: End of second part.

## C79. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, February 16, 1748 C079.JHawley-EHawley 2-16-48

Joseph HawleyC079. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,2/16/48. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #6.

Northampton Feb ry 16 th 1747/8

Sr

I received yours of ye 8 th Instant by Serg t Foster, in which you inform me y t you Arrived at ye Fort ye thursday before in good health, at which I rejoice and desire to be thankfull. You desire in yours y t I would let you know how Tim o Wright disposed of ye leather - he returned last week on Wednesday and gives but a dull account, he went a little round about to Rhode Island, and was not able (as he Says) to Mar- ket any leather; heard to people’s talk y t ye Country was glutted with leather, got discouraged, left 70 ll of leather at Rhode Island with one Bennet, brought about 20 ll home with him, having Sold but 4 Skins. We have Sent out Doct r King from Hatfield with a good pack[?]. Se Josiah Searl is to Set out this day with about 10 ll to market it if Can, then to go to Rhode Island, take what Wright left there and market that. As to ye Affair y t I was to manage I tried for an agreement before Court, they insisted on £150 down which I thought was too much, Consider ing what risque there is of ye Ch ds life, I therefore thought best to tarry a while longer before I concluded ye Affair, and till I could have Some Account of y r Mind, Not doubting but I could Obtain a Continuance of y r [-] Recog- nizance, which Accordingly I did tho’ with Some difficulty, I hope before Next Session I Shall[^471-note1] accomodate ye affair upon easier Terms than they Seem at present to insist upon, if not I Should think it best to Abide ye Order of Court but I believe I Shall have oppertunity to inform you further of ye affair ere long Serg t Foster being in a Considerable hurry. M rs Jerusha Edwards died last Sabbath in ye morning of a Pluretick disorder of about five days Continuance A very Sudden Death and a Most awakening and Mo- nitory providence, is to be interrd this day. Through Din e goodness we are in health.

Pray let y r Conversation and behav r be religious towards God, Steady and Manly towards Men, And one thing I d mind you of viz. y t you evermore give intelligence of ye State and provision of ye Garrison with respect to Eatables and warlike Stores to those whose business it is to provide, y t So ye blame may Never be devolved on you if Mischief Should happen through defect of these Take heed you be not Surprized through Carlessness which is a very ignoble Cause of Mischief. Yr brother and hu le Ser t

Joseph Hawley

To Mr Elisha Hawley

[^471-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C81. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, December 23, 1748 C081.JHawley-EHawley 12-23-48

Joseph HalweyC081. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,12/23/48. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #12. Addressed on back "To / L t Elisha Hawley / at / Fort Massachusetts / P r Sam ll Colhoon."

Northampton Dec br 23 d 1748

D r Sr.

I this Instant receiv’d y rs of the 9 th of this Month but a few minutes before Colhoon was going away: I went to Kate Wright immediately for y r Shirts I find She has finished but one; which I Send to you p r Colh n together with 3 ll of butter Mother Sends, which he is to Carry to ye halves. I believe its best for you to Come down assoon as you Can with any Convenience. I have thought a great deal of your aff r, am abund= =antly Clear in it, y t no Church on earth Can by their Censures inforce a Match in Such Case, untill ye two points viz Absolute virgin ty and the enticement on ye mans Side are fully prov’d; And were I in y r Case I Should have no regard to any thing they pretended to do Authoritatively in ye particular of Matrimony, nor would I Attempt or labour to prove any thing against her Since the burden of proof, beyond all dispute lies wholly on either ye woman or the Church as they are respectively Considered, as Acting. But more than all this the woman declares against taking you, in ye form ye Church talk of as also her father and Mother; So that if they proceed, they would impose more than the Jewish Yoke which S t Peter declares Neither the Jews in his time Nor their fathers were Able to bear.

All therefore that I at prsent would do (let the Church take what Course they would) Should be, to offer them a proper Confess n and rest ye Matter. As to Matrim y I would Do what I knew God was right in Conscience and before God, by if there was any thing [y t I] [^473-note1] knew of, that was particularly binding that, No body else knew of.

Freinds are all well. Selah Wrig[ht is i]n a drooping State, in Some degrees as he was at Louisb ge

Grant Complim ts to Capt t W ms —— I am Sr. Yr Most aff tte

Brother Joseph Hawley

[^473-note1]: MS damage in the middle of the paper affects this and the following lines.

## C82. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, January 16, 1749 C082.JHawley-EHawley 1-16-49

Joseph HawleyC082. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,1/16/49. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #14.

Dear Brother,

I have known of no oppertunity of Conveyance to you till now, Since you went from home, which has been ye rason you have not had a line from me. I am very glad of ye present oppertunity by Roberts and Harvey. But I conclude you are not so excusable in not writing to me for oppertunitys therefor there have been I understand, and you have are certainly knowing to all there be, but you have omitted to improve even that which there was by these men by whom I send to you, and tho’ I can’t say certainly there has been none Advantageous for me before yet this I can say I have carefully sought em and have known of none till now, therefore I have apology and you have none. But however I am glad at length to hear from you (for this is ye first time ever have So much as heard any thing by which we could certainly deter= =mine y t you had ever arrived At ye fort) and y t through ye Good= =ness of our bountifull preserver, of whom we receive every thing you were well last week.

Mother and I are in health. Mother Sends you ab t five pounds of butter by ye Aboves d soldiers, you’l take notice of their service, if they convey it to you honestly. Freinds are generally well.

As to News I have very little. People are generally in health in Town. But Deac n Clark is dangerously sick of ye long fever & M rs Esther Edwards is very wea and low with ye Rheuma= =tism. Mr The dispute between Mr Edwards, and ye Church is very much unsettled, tho’ peoples’s minds Seem to be calmer y n they were before ye Council which lately sat here to advise us what course to take under our present difficultys and disord rs who advised us to peace charity and moderation and to attend ye ordinance of ye Lord’s supper, which had been for some time o= mitted pursuant to a vote of ye Church passed severall times N.B. the vote had been repeated by reason y t divers were dissatisfied at ye neglect thereof and had prevail’d to have ye matter reconsidered, which advise of ye council was last sabbath complied with. They advised for ye present to suspend all publick agitations of ye aff r both in Church and precinct. Amongst other things the Church Church particularly desired ye advise of ye Council whether[^474-note1] (if finally there must be a council to determine whether Mr Edwards should be dismiss’d his pastoral office here) such a Councl ought to be mutall any part of them to come from parts out of ye County, or without ye vicinity or Neighbour= =hood, the resolution of which point ye council deferred to ye last first tuesday in feb ry next, to which time they adjourn d

The Council consisted of the Churches of Hatfield, Hadley, Sunderland Coldspring and ye second church in this Town. But before I conclude I must add one word to you upon that head in which you and I and every Mortall Creature with an immortall Spirit, is infinitely concerned.

True Religion, My Dear Brother, and thorough Religion, is ye plesantest of everything this side heaven. [—]

It is the most resonable of All things, Our happiness so consists in it, y t without it we can’t be happy. It is a fountain of continual peace and Sweetness to ye reasonable Mind and every deviation therefrom is a wandring from happiness. It Don’t consist in Abstruse Nice Notions and speculations, But in that which ye unprejudiced reason and sense of all Mankind says is right, and acquiesces in as best as soon as proposed, and always acknowledges in therey.

The Most Material Doctrines thereof are Subjects most wor= =thy of co[n]templation and Admiration and Minister meet Satisfaction to a thinking mind, Its precepts are as I indeed[?] said before in all respects right.

We are thereby required to believe Nothing but what is supported by good evidence, and in No other Manner than the evidence will avouch. But to say what I at present have in my mind on ye subject will exceed ye bounds of a letter and perhaps trespass on y r patience, therefore I conclude in a word The Christ Religion is in all respects adapted to the Necessitious state of the humane race and ministers every thing to Which he wants in order to his compleat Blessednes, and whoever looks impar= =tially into the Bible, which contains ye System thereof will find it it to be so, I therefore in ye most earnest manner recommend [^474-note2] religion to you in Both ye parts thereof viz faith and prac tice and that universally. And the Bible as the best Book in ye world, And of that The Book of Job, of Psalms, The works of Solomon and the New Testament, and Indeed the whole (as it is was given by inspiration of God) so it is profitable for Doctrine for reproof, for Correction i.e. qui= =dance and direction, and instruction in righteousness.

Mother presents her love to you And I am y r Most

Affectionate Broth r and Humble

Ser tJoseph Hawley

L t Elisha Hawley.

[^474-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^474-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C83. Andrew Croswell to Eleazar Wheelock, May 3, 1749 C083.ACroswell-EWheelock 5-3-49

Andrew CroswellC083. Andrew Croswell to Eleazar Wheelock,5/3/49. Darmouth University Library, Wheelock Papers, #742303.

Groton, May 3. 1749

Dear Brother,

Having perused the letter you Sent me, I could not help Saying within my Self what meaneth the heat of all this Anger ? You Seem to labour,and that not without a bitter zeal,to prove that I have been very faulty in my conversation, both before God was pleased to quicken me, and ever Since; when alass! I Know a thousand times as much Against my Self, as you have charg’d me with. Ever Since I have been at Groton,till last Spring I have given way too much to a Spirit of Jesting and Disputing. Thô I can truly Say it, that if ever I happen’d to find a man that could talk experimentally about Jesus Christ, my heart always burned within me,and my Spirits were Solemnized for Some time after. If men would but have talked about the Dear Redeemer, in those times, I could have talked about him Night and Day, for I loved him even then with all my heart, and with all my Soul; and the thoughts of what he had Done and Suffer’d for my Soul, gave me habitually more pleasure, than all the world besides. How ever, I would not lay the fault So much upon the times, as not to be Sensi ble of my own vileness, and to loath and Abhorr my Self therfor in Dust and Ashes! Lord Jesus! that this tongue which Should have been employd in uttering the Memory of thy Goodness,and in Inviting others to taste and See that the Lord was Good,Should be So Debas’d by perverse Disputings,and A of [^475-note1] foolish Jestings,as to make others question whither I had ever any true Love to thee in my own Soul! Dear Sir, pray that I may Devote this unruly member, for the future Entirely to the Glory of him who loved me, and Gave himself for me ; that I may have a tender heart,and a conscience that will check me for any Sort of conversation which tends to Deaden the Spiritual life. For this twelvemonths past, more Especially Some few months, my thoughts have (thrô mercy) been So Strongly turned another way, that I have been comparativly Deliver’d from a Vain conversation,(thô Still a Righteous God hath much very much Against me, I shou would be Strict to mark Iniquity . ————— Your Saying that Mr Dorrance was formerly more like a converted man,than I; and what Mr Owen Reported the other Day, (which I Suppose is now gone abroad) that you had Seven times as much Reason to think Mr Dorrance converted, as you had to think me converted,have Done me much Good, and I bless God heartily that I have had the Opportunity to hear and read what thoughts you had of me. To hear, what is to our praise, hurts,but to hear what Disparages us, is health to the Soul ! Wherfore If you and I ever get acquaint -ed enough to write letters to Each other, let us write not what will Sooth,but what will pull down that wretched pride which is So Natural to us both. ————— As for Mr Dorrance,for Several Reasons which you know Nothing of, I can’t look upon him as a converted man, (thô I never Declared him to be Unconverted) And if Deacon Snow Speaks true; and if Godly men in Voluntown Speak true, you Your Self, are much at a loss about him, to Say the least; now how you could Carry one with you to preach X t, that you was So much at a loss about whither he was Christ’s friend or Enemy,is what I cant comprehend: I fear, that in this thing, you walked not uprightly, According to the truth of the Gospel, and when I See you I will withstand you to the face, because you are proud of, and call’d your Brethren, that I can by no means Acknowledge as Such: and perhaps, I may be put to the great Difficulty of having You and Some thousands of them, Set against me, with Regard to one of them. but Sufficient for the Day is the Evil therof : when my conscience forces me upon any Duty which flesh and bloud Start at; my God will Stand by me, and Strengthen me . When God Gives me a Sense of the worth of Souls, then I See the Danger of unconverted Ministers, and Should Sin Against my own Soul, If I Did not bear Testimony Against them; and If all men, even my Dear Brethren Pomroy and Davenport should forsake me ; I Dare not be Dumb, and Muzzle my mouth in this Glorious cause. As to what you Say, about my backwardness to Speak comfort to private Christians I Endeavour to Act conscience in this matter —— tis very probable that I Should not think one half of your converts,converted : It may be Mr Davenport would Reject more of them than I should. who then must be the Standard? you,or he,or I,neither of us; we must Each of us have only the word of God, and our own conscience for our Rule ———— ————————

Mr. Edwards is a Gentleman I have no personal Knowledge of; but yet I love him Dearly, and never can think of him (Scarcely) without blessing God for him: however I make no Doubt at the Same time but that he is too timerous, or Cowardly in the Cause of X t, and that t’was Owing to this Infirmity and a Culpable Desire of pleasing both Sides, that led him into a Gross, and Important Selfcontradiction in the latter End of his late Treatise, [^475-note2] which Mr Cooper of Boston told me he Observed, before I mention’d it to him. As to his Spirit -ual life, twas Natural to make Some Estimation of it, by his writings: and besides, Mr Buel lately gave me Such an Account of it, As [^475-note3] perfectly Agreed with the Idea I had of it before: The Lord increase it to him, and make him to exceed even Mr Davenport,himself. In the meantime I am fuly persuaded that thô he and Such Others as Connive at Unconverted Ministers may have more Spiritual life than Some of us, who bare Testi mony Against them, they have much less, than they would have had, If they would come out more fairly in the Cause of Christ.

To Draw to a close my long letter; I am Afraid my Dear Brother, the Devil oftentimes makes fools of us both, by making our hearts Swell; and putting us upon Setting up for great men ; for when we try to make our Selves great men ; we allways make our Selves little Christians. Oh that Instead of Striving who Shall be the Greatest we may Strive who may be the least; And be heartily willing (if God Sees fit) that every one of X ts faithfull Ministers Should in honour be preferred, before us ——May Each of us be a Worm and No Man in Our own Eyes. May we be perfectly Joyned together in One Mind, and Speak the Same things; or however lovingly,and tenderly differ from one Another. May we not only Save our own Souls, but the Souls of them that hear us; and be Instrumental in Carrying thousands to heaven with us; is the Earnest prayer,

of your affectionate brother,

Andrew Croswell.

[^475-note1]: MS sic.

[^475-note2]: Apparently he means *Religious Affections*, particularly the 12 th sign, on the importance of Christian behavior.

[^475-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

## C84. Joseph Bellamy to Thomas Foxcroft, May 6, 1749 C084.Bellamy-Foxcroft 5-6-49

Joseph BellamyC084. Joseph Bellamy to Thomas Foxcroft,5/6/49. Harvard, American Mss. 1427.1.

Northampton May 6. 1749.

Revd. Sir

I Understand that Mr. Edwards has lately Sent a Peice to the Press, upon a subject that begins to be much discoursed of in the Country. Mr. Stoddards being against it & the seperates for it, will tend mightily to prejudice many against it as NEW and HETERODOX . I am Glad to see the letter you have sent to Mr. Edwards upon the Subject, & still more glad to hear that you are like to write an apendix to it. for I can’t but think that if the Country are informed of the true State of the Case, that it is a Doctrine which has been so generally maintained by protestant divines, that it will mightily remove their prejudices, & dispose them to read the peice with impartiality & candor. When the book is printed I wish it might be advertised 5 or 6 weeks going in the publick prints. (To this day I believe not half the Country have ever so much as heard of Mr. Edwards peice upon the Scotland Concert .) if the News effectually gets thro’ the Country I doubt not they will Sell. there are yet a pretty many, among ministers & people, in Connecticut & else where, that I know of, who are inclined to the right side of the Question, notwithstanding what has happened to prejudice them to the Contrary. &[?] Some will buy the book for the sake of the author, and some out of Curiosity. & besides there is already appeared five men who will take off 250 books , if need be, rather than it should be dropt. I wish sir the printer might be hastened that it may be publisht without delay. as to Mr. edwards Excellent Treatise upon religious affections, I hear that there are yet many books not Sold. The subscribers got a notion there were not books enough printed for them all. at first, & that presently they were all sold, & none to be had, & so were discouraged & hence many never sent.

As to the present State of this Town, where I have been for several days, according to the best accounts I can get, I am of the opinion that when the book comes out, the people will generally be brought over . Many of the more thinking men, notwithstanding the prejudices of education, seem disposed impartially to reconsider the point. & before all is done, I guess , it will make its way thro the country, & do much towards recovering of it to the principles of its first settlers

I am Sir your Dutifull son and Humble servant

Joseph Bellamy

P. S. Very many books will be wanted if the Country in general should get engaged in the affair. I am afraid not enough will be printed. J.B.

## C85. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, August 11, 1749 C085.JHawley-EHawley 8-11-49

Joseph HawleyC085. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,8/11/49. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #16.

Northampton 11 th Auguest. 1749

Dear Brother

I just now receiv’d your letter by Hooker I am very glad to hear y t Cap t Williams is likely to re= -cover, I had a great deal of concern what ye event of his Sick= =ness would be and the rather because, I concluded ye Accommo= -dations at ye forth were but ill for a Sick man.

As to your coming to Northampton I only Say in gen ll it will be best you Should come as Soon as you can with conveni= =ence and consistence with wi your duty at ye fort. I fear with you, y t ye remaining part of ye year will produce Sickness which may prove mortall and epidemick, but ye God of life and health hath hitherto continued gen ll health with us, as well as with you. And we wought Still to hope in his Good= =ness, tho’ it is of ye last consequence to us y t we be prepar’d for all events, and always to remember y t human life is a va= =pour, and y t man at his best estate is altogether vanity. You have, Brother, a great deal of time for consideration, I know I had, when in Garrison, I hope and earnestly desire you would improve it.

You Signify your desire to hear whether the people are very uneasy at ye Councill’s determination. At first there was a pretty deal of talk about it, and many manifested a great deal s of disatisfaction thereat, but latterly ye conversation has almost (as far as I can observe) entirely Subsided. I did hear, Soon after you went from hence y t Phelps [^477-note1] was resolute for another Council but I hear nothing of it latterly, I believe he has quite given it over. I have not heard y t Mr Edwards Says much of ye Aff r Since he came home; [^477-note2] The dispute between him and [^477-note3] ye people on his late Sentiments engrosses Most of ye Conversation. And I belive ye event will be a Separation be ween him and ye people.

Serg t Nath ll Courtis lately cut his Ancle Slightly with his hoe at hoeing which being ill managed at first has increas’d to a Mortification of nigh half his legg, And the Chirurg ns have but little hope of his life. Noah Lyman’s disorder has lately prevail’d upon him, he is now almost entirely confin’d thereby. Means used (tho’ I believe they are very thorough) appear to have little or No effect. I believe his prevailing thought is y t it will prove fatal, And I believe he has a great deal of reason to fear it.

Since you went away, we have had a certain acc t by a letter from Mr Birdsey, y t Our kinswoman M rs Abigail Lockwood, once Hawley is dead, Since ye death of our other freinds there. All these instances of Sickness and death Speak out loudly how frail we are. There is but one way of Absolute Safety, And, Blessed be God, there is one, ta which we may all take.

Give My humble Ser ce to Cap t Will s, and tell him I wish him well with all my heart. Mother Mentions her regards to you, We are all well.

I am SrYr am y r most Affectionate Broth r

Joseph Hawley

Mr Elisha Hawley

[^477-note1]: Possibly Charles Phelps, a Northampton native who moved to Hadley in the mid-1740s, who was a mason and a self-educated lawyer who later helped construct the Northampton jail

[^477-note2]: During the latter part of June and into early July, JE had been in Portsmouth, N.H., at the ordination of Job Strong, and then at Boston.

[^477-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

## C85a. Samuel Kneeland to Joseph Bellamy, September 4, 1749 C085a.SKneeland-Bellamy 9-4-49

Samuel KneelandC085a. Samuel Kneeland to Joseph Bellamy,9\4\49. MS 81179, Hartford Seminary Foundation. One folio leaf, addressed "For the Reverend / Mr Joseph Bellamy / at / Bethlehem."

Boston, Sept. 4 th: 1749.

Rev. Sir,

On my receiving the Proposals for printing the Piece you have in Hand, [^478-note1] I readily comply’d with your Desire in doing the same, and have sent some of them to Mr. Edward’s, which per- haps you may have received; but not knowing how that may be, I have now enclosed and sent you a few more of them; and herewith would acquaint you of my rea- diness to engage in the proposed Work, and am earnestly desirous it may go on, seperate from any ex- pected Interest thereby; and shall be very willing to undertake the same on the most reasonable Con- ditions; and on obtaining a Number of about 6 or 700 Hundred, or if it be something Less, the Work may go on as soon as you are ready with the Copy of the same; and shall expect to hear further from you as soon as conveniently may be, that there may be Paper &c. prepared. ——

I have lately printed Mr. Edwards Enquiry &c. [^478-note2] which perhaps you may have seen. When I first undertook the doing the same, I had determined [^478-note3] the printing off such a Number, but on Mr. Henchman’s [^478-note4] receiving a Let- ter from you, offering, as he informs me, to take off 250 of said Books, I added that Number to [—] what I first proposed; and hope you would be so good to me, as to en- deavour the taking as many of them as you possibly can procure; the Work exceeds very much what was at first proposed; and I have but very few who have subscribed for them. —— I should be glad to hear speedily from you. ——

I write in my own Name, as Mr. Green, [^478-note5] and I, now act seperately, and are about to finish all our Affairs in Partnership; and I am in hourly expectation of new Types of several Sorts, a Specimen of which, if I am not dis- appointed, you will have an Opportunity of seeing.

I am, Sir, your humble Servant

Sam ll: Kneeland.

[^478-note1]: Probably *True Religion Delineated* (Boston, 1750).

[^478-note2]: *An Humble Inquiry* .

[^478-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^478-note4]: Daniel Henchman (1725-1775), Boston printer.

[^478-note5]: Timothy Green (1703-1763), Boston printer, later of New London

## C85b. Samuel Kneeland to Joseph Bellamy, October 2, 1749 C085b.SKneeland-Bellamy 10-2-49

Samuel KneelandC085b. Samuel Kneeland to Joseph Bellamy,10\2\49. MS 81180, Hartford Seminary Foundation. One folio leaf, addressed "To the Reverend / Mr Joseph Bellamy / at / Bethlem / in / Connecticut / Q.D.C.

Boston, Octob. 2. 1749.

Rev. Sir,

Your Letter by Mr Jones, [^479-note1] I received, and have at your Desire, readily sent you the 50 Books of Mr Edwards’s, [^479-note2] and 200 more for the other Subscribers you mention, thinking it would be best they should be with you before the Spring, lest the Sale of them should be hinderd. The Book, as you will find, contains 20 Sheets, in Quarto, and according to the printed Pro- posals are 12 d a Sheet, the Subscribers have one gratis in every half doz. but as the Num- ber sent you is something considerable, I would propose you, and the other Subscribes for the 200, should have 15 to the Doz. which will considerably lessen the Price; and should be glad you wou’d promote the disposing of as many of them as you can, there being but few Subscribers among us, tho’ I doubt not but as the Book comes to be known, they will be in Demand. I would desire you Sir, to take a Note of Hand, or otherwise as you think best, pay- able to your self or me, for what those Sub- scribers take of them, and are willing to engage for, on the foregoing Terms; and if any of the Books remain undisposed of, I will take them again in the Spring, or sooner, if you please; and should be glad to hear [^479-note3] from you as to this, as soon as you may have an Opportunity of sending to me; Mr. Jones has kindly offer’d me his good Offices as to the disposing of a Number of the Books, if you think it proper. If there should be any Defect in the Number of Books, or any torn or defac’d, I will allow for them. [^479-note4]

I hope and trust, the Providence of God, will so order it, that the Volume you propose to publish, [^479-note5] will be seasonably accomplished, and I shall stand ready to engage in the same, if Life permit it, and am looking out for a suitable Paper on which to do it. ——— The Letters I daily expect are not yet arrived, but the Gentleman is, [—] who had the Care of procuring them, and informs me, that they would be certainly ready to ship in a Day or two after he left London, and I may depend upon them in the next Vessel; ———

I am, Rev. Sir, your sincere Friend and humble Servant

Sam ll: Kneeland

[^479-note1]: Probably Isaac Jones (1717-1784), minister of Warren, Mas

[^479-note2]: I.e. copies of An Humble Inquiry

[^479-note3]: **marginal.** [2

[^479-note4]: This sentence is written perpendicularly in the left margin

[^479-note5]: Kneeland did indeed publish Bellamy’s *True religion delineated; or, Experimental religion, as distinguished from formality on the one hand, and enthusiasm on the other, set in a scriptural and rational light* (Boston, 1750), with a preface by JE

"Northampton Oct 16 th 1749."

[Dwight ed.:]

To the Precinct Committee for the first Precinct in Northampton:

We, the subscribers, desire that there may be a precinct meet- ing as quick as may be, for the Precinct to take into consideration Mr. Edwards’ doctrine, with respect to the admission of members into full communion into the church.

1. We desire that Mr. Edwards, by the Precinct, or by a com- mittee which the Precinct shall appoint, may be friendlily and in a christian manner treated with, and entreated to recede or come back [...] from his principles, which he has pretended to maintain in his late book, against his own practice, and Mr. Stoddard’s practice and principles, with respect to the admission of church members: which, if he refuses,

2. To see if the Precinct will come into his notions or prin- ciples, about the admission of church members: which, if the town refuse,

3. Then to determine whether the Precinct do not think that it will be more for the honour of God, and more likely to promote the interests of religion, and peace and comfort in the Precinct, to endeavour after a separation, or any thing else, which the Precinct shall see cause to come into: which we desire may be done in the most friendly and christian manner possible.

John Hunt, Gad Lyman, Ephraim Wright, Josiah Pomeroy, Jonathan Strong, Jr., John Lyman, James Lyman, Jonathan Hunt, Joseph Wright, Gideon Lyman, Seth Pomeroy.

*Northampton*, Oct 16, 1749.

## C88. Chester Williams to the Hampshire Association of Ministers, February 20, 1750 C088.CWilliams-HampAssn2-20-50

Chester WilliamsC088. Chester Williams to Hampshire Association,2/20/50. ANTS, "Narrative of Communion Controversy," Dwight MS copy, p. 125 (also printed in Dwight ed., 1:390-91).

The Northampton people are desirous of having some minister preach on the opposite side of the controversy to Mr. Edwards. They have brought an application to the Association for ad= vice & lodged it with & at their desire & at the advice of some of our brethren in the ministry I have written to the ministers to desire them to meet at my house on Thursday, early in the morning. I hope you will come for you cannot easily think what posture they [^482-note1]are in. And unless we do concert some measures we are in danger of being overrun; & Northampton will proceed to extreme measures being conducted by some gentlemen not over tender of ministers or churches; which may prove of pernicious con= sequence to us & all our churches. I have the promise of some gentlemen to come & hope you will not fail.

From your brother, &c.

Chester Williams

Hadley Feb. 20 1750
