## C89. Peter Clark to Ebenezer Pomeroy, April 4, 1750 C089.Clark-Pomeroy 4-4-50

Peter ClarkC089. Peter Clark to Ebenezer Pomeroy (copy),4/4/50. BRBL, f. 1327.

Hon d Sr

Yours of the 12 th of last March came to my hand on the 25 th wherein you repeat your request to me at the motion or by a Vote of your Precinct About my writing an answer to Mr Edwards’ his late Book which was a little Surprising to me Considering what I had written in A former letter, which I thôt might have induced You to Lay aside All further Expectation of my being Engaged in that Affair & indeed Sr I must confess it Unhappily falls out yt I am in no better Capacity of returning a more Satisfactory answer to Your request than when You wrote Your first letter for want of a Sight of y t book which I have not as Yet been Able to Obtain having been under bodily Indisposition ye latter part of last Winter, I have gone but little abroad Yet I have taken Some Considerable pains in making Enquiry after the book among my neighbour Minist rs & Others whom I thôt it most like ly to meet with it but find it very Scarce in our parts; none that I have discoursed with About it in Salem or Marblehead either before or since Yo r last letter having as Yet Seen it the Contents & design of which book have been differently represented to me, So that being left to Conjecture I could not hitherto You may be Sure form any distint thôts upon it nor can I easily recollect what the Expressions were that Occur’d in my letter which might give Encouragem t to my good friends in Yo r parts to Ex- pect that I might be prevailed with to answer that piece of Mr Edwards’s unless it were my Saying that as Mr Edwards his Oppinion was repre sented to me it was Easily Answered by being reduced to an Absurdity but this (as I remember I Signified to you) was Said upon A Gen ll representation of it in private Conversation & that Some Considerable time before the book Came out of the press the Comon report then was to this Effect as I remember that Mr Edwards was About new Modeling of his Church designing to have A pure Church consisting only of true Converts & that he had written & was About printing in defence of his Oppinion; now there needs not many words, or any long Controversie to shew the Absurdity of Such an Oppinion or pur= pose in any man for it takes away that Comonly received & well grounded Distinction of the Church into visible & Invisible it Supposes A thing Contrary to the declaration of our Lord in Several of his parables that his Church in the world According to the Instituted Course of its Administration being Committ ed to fallible men would consist of A mixture of Good & Bad Sound & unsound Christians till the great Day of discrimination it Supposes those that have the power of Admitting numbers into the church infallible discoverers of the State of mens hearts to Judge of their Sincerity All which are Openly Absurd but I have Always Esteem’d Mr Edwards A Gentleman of moral sense & modesty & pi ety than to make Such pretentions & therefore can Scarce perswade my Self that that is the Subject & Scope of his Book ——— However You See s r how much at A loss I am & how unprepared to Engage in a Controversie on a Sub ject I have so little & distinct knowledge of out & possibly upon the Sight & peru sal of that book I may not have the Same Apprehensions with your People of the Necessity, or Expediency of an Answer to it & to Deal plainly & Ingeniously with you I must so far declare my Opinion About the Qualifications of Chh Members as to let you know that tho’ I think it not necessary to constitute the [^483-note1] Visible Chh of Christ that all the members of it should be Sincere Converts but that a Visible Saintship or in other words a Credible Profession of Faith & repentance (I call that a Credible Profession which is founded on a Competent Measure of Christian knowledge together with a good Conversation Joined to a Serious & Solemn Consent to Cov t of the Gospels) gives a Gospel right to all Sacred ordinances in the Chh. in which all that have Power of Admitting members into its Comunion ought by the Gospel rule of Charity to Acquiesce & leave the Judgment of the State of their hearts to God Alone to whom it belongs; Yet I cannot in all Points fall in with the Sentiments of Venerable Mr Stoddard your former worthy Pastor thô I pay a great Deference to his Judgm t & can easily Apprehend in what Sense his Opinion upon this Subject where in he differed from others may in the main be reconciled to that of those with whom he had a Controversy in his Day, Setting Aside a few Tolerable Differences, Particularly I have no clearness to give my Assent to that Position which he has Maintained, that the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper (or indeed any other Sacraments which as seals of the Covenant presuppose Conversion especially in the Adult) is a Converting Ordinance & some other Points depending thereon, for reasons not here to be mentioned or insisted on, Thô I agree it is the Duty of unconverted Professours to come to the Lord’s Table but in a right Maner i.e. with the Gospel Qualifications of Repentance & faith in Christ, it is equally their Duty to repent & pray (Acts 8:22[)] & so to repent & partake of the Sacram ts, or Attend any other divine Institution, but that the Latter is not to be urged without the former, and it is a Gospel Profession of this, as I have explained it that must Satisfy Ministers & Churches in order to their Admission & warrants them to receive Such as make this Profession, & carry it toward them as true Converts as Saints & Brethren in Christ tho at the Same Time it be granted that many who pass under this Character are really & in heart unconverted, known only to God & to their own Conscience. but Ministers & Christians being but fallible men & keeping within the bounds of reason their own faculties are in reality (whatever may be pretended) capable of no higher Evidence of their Sincerity, than Such a Profession taken in its proper Latitude includes in it. How far my Principles relating to this Subject (which I have thus briefly open’d) agree or disagree to those which Mr Edwards has maintained in his late book, I know not; but by them perhaps you may be Able to Judge whether or how far I shall be obliged by the Princi= ples I have laid down to Oppose any Tenets Advanced in the s d Book. But forasmuch as I perceive a Speedy Answer is tho’t necessary & general ly desired among you & the Premises considered, you will See how remote I am at present from a Capacity to gratify Such a desire. I must therefore intreat my Christian friends as Brethren of your Precinct to dismiss all further Expectations of my writing an Answer to the S d Book; and I can’t but think, there are Gentlemen in you Parts of the Countrey or Much nearer to you, who have had Time to Digest their Thôts upon the Subject [^483-note2] & may have greater Leisure & Capacity for that undertaking if that be found Adviseable & Necessary, as it Seems it is. I am greatly obliged to you Sir, & to the rest of the Good Brethren of the Precinct for your respect to me as Also to the rev d Gentlemen ye Ministers in your Neighbourhood for the good Opinion they have conceived of my Abilities & Influence in Such a Case which is far higher than what I dare Assume to Myself. Yea which humbles & shames me, when I consider how litle I am able to make it good who best know my own Infirmity. writing is Tedious to me more than what is Comon & I have no Inclination to Controversy further than plain Duty makes it necessary However if upon reading the Book (when it shall fall into my hands) I think it proper & Adviseable & if it shall please God to give Leisure & Ability I may write my Thôts upon it & Send them to you (which you will not understand as a promise Especially of any Such Thing as an answer) but this may require Considerable Space of Time Considering the Stated Duty of my Charge Attended with too frequent Avocations —— I am Sorry to hear of the Threatning Aspect of the present Controversy upon you Chh & Town.

I heartily wish you may be led into healing Methods, or to the Proper Means of preventing the Evils feared — and tho’ it be very desireable that both Ministers & People shou’d be of the Same mind & Judgm t yet it may deserve the Serious Considerations of Yourselves & of your rev d Pastor whether retaining your Several Sentiments in the present Case you may not con= sistently therewith Accord & unite in Affection & Practice & in all the holy administrations of the house of God, as has been usual? Especially considering what an eminent Branch of Gospel Holiness that Charity is which is directed to express itself in a Condescention to the Infirmities of the weak & in a Mutual forbearance in Love, under different Apprehensions among Christians, against the mischievous Consequences whereof there is no remedy but this Charity & how earnestly it is recomended in the evangelical writings as a means to prevent the violation of unity in Christian Churches Rom: 14:1.2.3.4.5. & 15:1.2.3 Eph: 4:1.2.3.15 16. Col: 3:12.13.14.15. Phil. 3:15.16. Joh: 13:34. 35 & 17.21. Tho most of you are Strangers to me yet not only the Bonds of our Comon Christianity oblige but Christian Charity also teaches & inclines me to desire your welfare & prosperity & to Stand ready to Serve you & the Cause of Truth holiness & peace Among you So far as God Shall Call & enable me & to Lament the present Difficulty & Temptations you are under which call for much prayer & watchfullness Humiliation & dependance on God to overrule them for Good & prevent the unhappy Effect of them. So beseeching Almighty God the Father of Lights to afford you Direction & Assistance in all your Difficulties & to pour out a spirit of Love Light & Love of Holiness & peace on y r Pastor & all the Members of the flock & Comending you with them to the Care & Influence of their great Shepherd of the Sheep I remain Hon d Sr y r sincere & Affectionate Friend

& Serv t in the Gospell

Peter Clark

Salem Village Ap l 4 th 1750

To the Hon d Eben r Pomroy in Northampton to be Communicated

PS. I had no prospect of an opportunity of Sending before now else I shou’d have written Sooner —— Tuesday April 17 th 1750 read the Original of which this is a true Coppy throughout in A precinct Meeting in Northampton T Dw t Sen r

[^483-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^483-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C90. Stephen Williams (for Hampshire Association of Ministers) to Northampton Church Committee, April 4, 1750 C090.Williams-N’tonCom4-5-50

Stephen Williams (for Hampshire Association of Ministers)C090. Stephen Williams to N’ton Committee,4/5/50. BRBL, f. 1335.

Springfield Apr. 5 th. 1750.

Gentlemen

We have yours by Mr. Pomroy, are heartily grieved at the unhappy Situation of your Affairs, and wou’d gladly contribute any thing in our Power for the Bettering your State. ——

Your Question to us is, whether you Shall agree to what the Rev d. Mr Edwards insists upon of Chusing two or three Ministers or Churches out of the County or no?

We are Sensible that the Chh [^484-note1]Northampton Church, in ye Rev d Mr Stoddard’s Days, voted "that what Difficulties might arise among them, Shou’d be issued by a Council of Churches within the County," or to that Purpose. We See no Reason for your Departing from that Vote, except in Some Special Case in which there may be weighty Reasons why you shou’d receed from it. ——

We are not acquainted with the Reasons your Rev d. Pastor may have to offer why you Shou’d go out of the County; perhaps therefore we Shou’d be too rash if we Shou’d advise you not to agree with him; and, on the other Hand, no less rash, if we shou’d advise you to agree with him in the Case. —— We are indeed too much unacquainted with your State and what may be Said pro & con in your Case to be positive in our Advice.

We understand that a Council, to which the Rev d. Mr Edwards & the Chh referred the Question, were equally divided upon it; But, Gentlemen, cannot there be further Steps taken to determine that Matter? either by adding Some other Churches to the Council, or by refferring of it to one or both the Associations of ye County, or in Some other Method, that your Rev d. Pastor and the Church may agree upon in a friendly manner; and we Shou’d heartily desire you to act Jointly in the Affair, if possible, and advise you to put on all Christian Condescension; But if this cannot be obtain’d by any Means, we dont know but you will be reduc’d to a Necessity of calling in the Assistance and Advice of the Churches of the County. Wishing to you and your Rev d. Pastor the Divine Direction and Blessing, we are your hearty Friends

Stephen Williams Moderator

in the name & by the order of the Association

A True Copy

John Ballantine

Scribe

[^484-note1]: These words, faintly visible, were scratched out, leaving a blank space on the line.

## C91. Thomas Prince to Timothy Dwight and Northampton Minority, [c. April 1750] C091.TPrince-TDwight c.4-50

Thomas PrinceC091. Thomas Prince to Timothy Dwight and Northampton Minority, n.d. [c. 4/50]. NYPL, Hawley Papers, 339.

Dear Brethren

Being informed y t there is [. . .] [^485-note1]

Congregation of Northampton [. . .]

falter, if not sink, if ye Rev M[. . .]

from y m, & earnestly desire [. . .]

their minister to give my advice with others to ye s d adheren[...] what method is best for them to take under their presen[t] Difficulties ? & in Particular to consider whether there may n[ot] consistent with ye gospel Rule be an accomodation, & y t Mr E[d] wards & those who hold to ye Practice of ye late Rev Mr Stoddard subsist together as Pastor & Church .

In Compliance with w c Desire I can only at Present answer, That tho I am uncertain what was ye late Rev Mr Stoddard’s Practice ; yet if his Practice was agreable to his published Principle y t visible saintship is a requisite Qualification for admission to ye Lord’s Table ; and if ye Church are of ye same Principle & will agree to Practice accordingly, I apprehend y t This is all Mr Edwards Desires, & I see no Reason for their separation, or that should hinder their Re-union. And on this comon Principle I would therefore earnestly in ye 1 st place urge you to labour an ac- comodation. Or if ye word saintship may be apprehended by ye church as being rather too strict, as seeming to imply some eminent or very strong appearance or signs of Holiness; & see not but that both Parties may be reconciled upon Mr Stod- dard’s Definition of saint & of an instituted Church , in his Doc trine of instituted Churches , Chap II, exactly in ye following words; a Church is a society of saints joined together, according to ye appointment of Christ for ye constant carrying on of his Publick Worship. 1. Cor. 12. 27. Yee are ye Body of Christ, & members in particular. It is a society of saints: ye members of a Church are saints by calling. 1. Cor. 11. 12. To ye Church of God w c is at Corinth, to them Quest: w c are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints. Who are visible saints ? Answer, Visible saints are such as make a serious Profession of ye true Religion, together with those who descend from them, till rejected of God .’ Taking Mr Stoddard ’s words in their comon [^485-note2] And having seen a Letter of ye Rev Mr Clark ’s of Salem Village to ye Church on this Affair dated ye 4th Instant,[^485-note3]

Solliciting an accommodadation; I would likewise heartily concurr with him

[. . .] labour in ye 1 st place to[^485-note4]

[. . .]ween ye Church & Mr Edwards .

[. . .] mutual Concessions only in Gen-

[. . .] articular; To expedite & whether

[. . .]uest ye following Medium or

[. . .]ion between both Particip- [ants] in order to come into ye Church & so to Baptism & ye Lord’s [S]upper, every adult Person shall Present themself a Disciple of Christ , there being nothing known compares to this Profession, such Profession shall entitle Him to an Admission. And if you ask — what is meant by a Disciple of Christ ? To this I Reply, tis one y t declares he is determined, as far as He knows hos own Heart Henceforward to Deny himself, take up his Cross & follow Christ as long as He lives.

If the Church wont concede to such a scriptural, & most reasonable Term as This; Then it seems as if they wou’d not have ye Churches of Christ to [-] consist of ye Disciples of Christ , & they separate in this General article from all other Protestant Churches I know of in ye world and I see not [how they can] [^485-note5]be very easy [——] with so licencious a Princple; so it will seem as if ye Church refusing such a Term as This, will have a mind to necessitate ye Dividing into Two Churches, y t each Party may uninterrup- tedly enjoy their several Principles. But I have a better opinion of ye Holiness & Judgment of that Church, & their Love to Christ & Zeal for ye Purity of his Churches, than to imagin y t they wou’d refuse so great & plain a Principle, or admit any other than ye Professing disciples of Christ to their [——] communion.

And as for any further advice I am at present unprepared in my own Judgment till I know ye Issue of your Endeavours for an accomodation & Re-union. and so humbly comitting you to ye Grace & Care of Christ ye Great & universal shepard, I rest

Your affection t Friend & servant

Thomas Prince

To Timothy Dwight Esq & ye Rest of ye Brethren of ye Church in Northampton adhering to ye Rev Mr Edwards

## C92. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, June 11, 1750 C092.JHawley-EHawley 6-11-50

Joseph Hawley116e. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,6/15/50. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #19.

Northampton 15 th June 1750.

Dear Brother,

I receiv’d yours of the 17 th of May be quick Conveyance in which you inform y t you was arrived at the fort in good health, which I was glad to hear, and Indeed It always rejoices me to hear of your health, and prosperity in all respects, and I can truly say my affection to and Concern for you sensibly increases daily and above all things relating to you am I concerned for y t which is truly y r greatest, and Main Interest, the spiritual health of y r Soul, and therefore Can’t forbear recommending to you the right ways of god or true religion which is no other than a reconciliation and Consent of heart with and to the way of Salvation as to the procurement of It by Jesus Christ, and a Choice, & pleasedness of the heart with universall purity and Holiness of Practice, and although such is a Temper is what a person Can’t begat in himself Merely by his own power (as In= =deed is ye Case for ought I know, with respect to all tempers and Af= =fections of the mind) for who is there that can alter ye Mode in w h he stands affected to this or that object, while he veiws in the same light, of himself) yet this is Certain, that God is ready, by his spirit to begat and work in us all those good and amiable af= =fections and dispositions which it is our Dut to exercise, If We sincerely, and earnestly Seek to and rely upon him therefor.

And how Sweet, My brother, is an entire and universal Devotedness to God, If We have a Single eye to our Duty, in all things, (which is ye same with the Divine will) If we are steadfast therein and will not be moved, either allured by the flashy, Shadowy and full= =some pleasures of sin, which always Baulk ye expectation, and and leave the soul emty and disappointed, besides the bitterness, vexation to the Mind even in this world; which is always almost infinitely more than a Counterpoise to the pleasure, and if we are not Intimadated therefrom by what the world Can threaten, We never need Concern our selves ab t the event, for God, who governs all, will Certainly order all things accord= =ing to the trite but true saying for thte best, and tho’ at present per= =haps we may n’t be able to see it, yet we may rest assured y t it is so and most generally sooner or later in this world, but if His way should be so much in the deep here yet we shall never ye satisfaction of Seeing and Admiring It forever hereafter. [^486-note1]

One thing, Brother, which I beleive you have heard Mr Edwards urge, with great reason in preaching, I would hint to you viz. Seriously and Solemnly Consider whether upon Counting the Cost and a due ballance of things It is not absolutely necessary, yea whether It wont prove Infinitely Advantageous to be thoroughly religious, even as the Gospell requires, If reason answers In the Affirmative, Resolve immediately to be so, that is, to be as reli= gious, and to do as much for y r Salvation, as Conscience enlightened by the Word of God says will ever be necessary, or as ever you de= =sign to do, for If a person will delay and defer it for the present Notwithstanding all he has to Admonish of ye Absolute Uncertainty of life, and of a future oppertunity, he Can have No rational ground to Judge y t he ever shall, Yea has good reason to Con= clude y t he never shall, And Be Advised also to Carry this same Method of reasoning into the performance of every duty par= =ticularly secret prayer, that is, Never by any means hurry over that duty, Nor perform it in a Careless, Cold inattentive manner secretly promising yourself y t you will perform some future duty or duties of that nature with more Attention engagedness and importunity. But seriously Consider y t you have no sort of Assurance y t you shall ever have an other oppertunity at the throne of grace other than ye present, and y t It would be no strange thing if you Never Should, and if you should, It is likely y t if you won’t be thorough in the Duty at present tis a vain thing, And a Cheating and imposing on yourself of To promise or flatter your self y t you ever shall, I be= =lieve every man’s experience will more or less afford matter of Convic= =tion of ye truth hereof, if he reflects - Therefore in every prayer be as Importunate for saving Mercys, and pray for as many things as you want, I don’t Mean hereby y t there may be no occasions y t may make it reasonable and indeed a duty to be shorter in Devotion y n at other times, but what, Dear Brother, is y t you take infinite care not to improve on y r Self, for Self-De= =ceivings are most fatal, and they are Inexcusable.

These Advises you’ll take as from a most affectionate Brother, and one who, I hope, has some true acquaintance with his own heart, and has greatly at heart y r Eternal Wellbeing.

An Ecclesiastical Council is to sit here ye 19 th of this Instant June with Power if they think fit to Issue our religious Disputes. Deacon Pomroy [^486-note2] Is gone Representative, and they say The Deac n enjoys Much health at Court, And it seems y t the Pleasing event of his Choice has filed off sveral years of his Acc t gave a start to his Blood and spirits, and ushered new vigor into his very Soul, tho’ I must Confess the Deacon be= =haved very modestly upon ye occasion.

I Can’t learn y t you have let out y r grass at middle-meadow and it’s almost time It was Cut, I shall therefore rent if If I can to good Advantage, Otherwise let it for such part of the hay as I do my Own.

Mr Elihu Parsons and M rs Sally were Alias ye Widdow were Married last Monday.

Mother gives her love to you, would have you be prudent and wise in all matters, and if you should have ye Cold w h is Epidemick In the Country take Medicines that tend to defend ye vitals and Drive out.

Friends are generally well excepting Colds.

I am Sr Yr very loving Brother, and one Always ready to serve you Joseph Hawley.

L t Elisha Hawley

P.S. I wrote sent to Cap t Ephraim by all means to procure ye Mending y r Compass and to bring it up with him.

J H

## C93. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, July 31, 1750 C093.JHawley-EHawley 7-31-50

Joseph HawleyC093. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,7/31/50. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #20.

Northampton July 31 st 1750.

Dear Brother

I have but a minutes time to write you. Mr Edwards is desirous to make a partition of the land he and Mother hold in Common at Pelham - You know mother has a design y t you should have it, and she is desirous you should be at ye Dividing of it. I should be very glad you would Come down assoon as you Can, for Mr Ed= =wards is de set to have it divided very soon. L t Will m Lyman designs to Contract Matrimony within a week or fortnight. Freinds are well.

Hope Root, and Ithamar Clark’s wife are dead lately.

I am y r Affectionate Broth r & Ser t

Joseph Hawley

L t Elisha Hawley

P.S. I believe ye land must be surveyed and I believe twill be well for you to do It.

## C94. Joseph Hawley to Martha Root, August 8, 1750 C094.JHawley-MRoot 8-8-50

Joseph HawleyC094. Joseph Hawley to Martha Root,8/8/50. Joseph Hawley Papers, NYPL.

Northampton August 8 th 1750.

When I was before the Ecclesiastical Council which sat at Northampton on ye 17 th day of June 1749. to determine a dispute between the first Church of s d Northampton and my Brother res= =pecting his Obligation to marry you, In giving an Evidence to s d Council to prove y t you had been industrious in seeking my brothers Company for some time before you charged him with being unlawfully familiar with you, Among other things I said, y t within About ye space of half a year during ye time of y r Acquaintance together, I had seen you in our street (as I Judged) forty several times, putting a Certain number for an uncertain, and y t I did not doubt, but that, besure it was so often.

And further y t I had seen you in almost all parts of our street, and at Corners or where ye Paths met particularly at ye Corner by the Bridge and Near the school house. Now so far as this Acc t represented ye Mat= =ter beyond ye truth, so far I injured you. And to the first particular (Although I then spoke my Judgm t) yet on Cool consideration I must say that I suppose y t I represented ye matter beyond ye truth and reality, for tho It is true y t I may frequently saw you in our street, within ye space of half a year, and more fre= =quently than any other of y r fathers family. Yet I don’t suppose that I saw you once every week, and twice every other week or so often take one time with another, which must been If my Judgment, delivered, before the Council had been right. And as to the Other particular viz that I had seen you at ye Above mentioned Corners, or places where the ways met. I acknow= =ledge y t I said it precipitantly and presumptuously. And tho I remember other places in particular where I have seen you in our street, yet I have no particular remembrance y t I ever before that time saw you at those Above= mentioned places. and I said it through want of due Consideration, and pre= =suming it, because I had seen you very frequently our way. Now wherein the Above representation was beyond what was true in fact, so far I in really reality and fact injured you, and so far as it was beyond, what I had Cer= tain knowledge was true (wherein I spoke positively) so far I acted pre= =sumptuously. For which I am heartily sorry, and in Observance of the Di= =vine rule James 5. 16 v I Confess this to you, And do freely and humbly ask y r pardon and forgiveness. and shall be always ready to Own what is Above written.

Joseph Hawley

For Martha Root

## C95. Timothy Dwight to Spencer Phips, August 16, 1750 C095.TDwight to SPhips 8-16-50

Timothy DwightC095. Timothy Dwight to "Hon’d Sir,"8/16/50. Mass. Archives, v. 53: 519-20. Possibly to Spencer Phips?

Northampton Aug t 16 th: 1750

Hon rd Sr

I rec d Your letter of the 14 th: of May last, & took Immediate care to make the Amendm t in the Coppy of the Order of Council on Courtis’s Appeal, Althô I knew it was Submitted to an ar bitration, but had Opportunity to Inform of it, because I was going directly to Stockbridge by order of the Gen ll Court to Call a proprietors meeting, & Settle a Propriety Among the Ind n In dian Inhabitants there, & to Survey their lots, which I per form’d with great fatigue & Dificulty, there was but two or three days in the whole time charg’d but what I Spent in Service Abroad & of those, two was of the meeting. I lay in the wilderness at nights had very little but (brook) water to drink during, the whole of my Service, I never Spent a penny for any Sort of Strong drink during the whole time, I was carefull of my time & money as if it had been my own & hastned the Accomplishment of the Business as much as possible, from Whence I have reason to hope the Hon ble Com ttee of Council for Allowing & Ordering the payment of Acco ts, will please to Allow & Order the Paym t of mine, I have Charg’d 6/ Lawfull money P r Day, last year in Oct r I was at Hoosuck Laying out Two Townships not half So difficult & Hard a Service as this & the Com ttee Charg’d 60/ P r diem & rec d 50/ finally, in this Case I was Obliged to be Master & Serv t & to take Care as Master that their proprietors Meeting was Called & Mannaged & the pro =priety Settled According to Law & then as a Servant to pursue the votes in Laying out the Lands among Swarms of Gnats & Muskeetoes I Should be glad the Hon rble Comm ttee would please to do the business as Soon as Conveniently they Can that Mad m Edwards who bring my Acco t to Co l Wendell may have Some of the money All means of that good Gentleman & his families Support are Cut of & I durst not Say what I think is really true with respect to the Spirit & Temp er of the people of his Church & Congregation towards him we are in a most lamentable condition with respect[^489-note1] to our Ecclesiastical Affairs it is become almost Crimi =nal to Appear in his favour or to Say any thing in his behalf what will be the Sorrowfull Event God only knows. I En =treat You Sr to remember our pitious Circumstances at the throne of Grace. I am Sr with great respect Yo r Hon rs most Humb le & Obed t Serv t

Timothy Dwight

[^489-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C96. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, September 27, 1750 C096.JHawley-EHawley 9-27-50

Joseph HawleyC096. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,9/27/50. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #21.

Springfield Septemb r 27 th 1750

My Brother

The Day before yesterday I came from N. H. left mother in usual health as also Uncle. But his Wife is sick of the Long fever in a low degree, taken last Week, I hope will not prove fatal, nor of long Continuance. There is no Candidate as yet come to Northampton But Mr Russel is daily expected.

We have lately had News of new Troubles at the Eastward viz. Killed some and Captivated others of w h Cap t Williams will give you a more particular acc t —— I desire you would be very prudent & Carefull as becomes a resonable and prudent man and expecially as one in y r Station. — But Dear Brother Consider of what vast Importance it is y t you be ready for all events. What Satisfaction and peace of mind will It all ways minister to you to Consider y t y r Case is such y t Nothing Can harm you. I have killed y r steer and disposed him @/11 s old Ten r p nce

I am y r Brother & Ser t

Joseph Hawley

L t Elisha Hawley

## C97. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft, October 13, 1750 C097.Dwight-Foxcroft 10-13-50

Timothy DwightC097. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft,10/13/50. Yale, Sterling Lib., Archives and Manuscripts, Dwight Family Papers, B. 1, f. 1, #1.

Northampton Oct r: 13 th: 1750

Rev rd Sr

Mr Edwards being Obliged to go to Stockbridge to take care of Some Lands he has there & having no Opportuni =ty himself desired me to inform that there are Some great misrepresentations in A pamphlet lately printed by the Hampshire Ministers in Vindication of their Con= =duct respecting his dismission which will Evidently Appear by Sundry things well Attested & not knowing but Mr Hobby might be inclined to publish Some answer to it thinks it might be well for him to delay till he might be in =form’d of Some things he is not now Acquainted with which when Mr Edwards comes back from his Journey he’l Send & knowing no better way to get Mr Hobby Noti =fied desires You’d please to Undertake it—— & being now Writing think it not amiss further to in= =form that Coldspring Church the forepart of this week made choice of A Council for haveing & finishing y r persecuting design & Mr Billings Opposers have Chosen ye Rev rd; Mr W ms, of Lebanon, Mr Hopkins of Springfield, W ms of Hadley, Woodbridge of Hatfield, & Campbell of Oxford, & Con =ditionally D r Chauncy. & Mr Billing himself has Chosen the Rev rd; Mess rs Peter Clark, W m Hobby, Parkman, Hall, & Eaton, the three last in Worcester County, & in case D r. Chauncy comes tis hoped You will come Since we cant have Your help without him, Sundry Others are chosen in case of disappointm t of any of the first in Nomination I Earnestly intreat Sr that You’d Use Your influence with Mr Clark & Mr Hobby to come; I cant but think their com= =ing & the determination of Coldsprings Cause will have a great Influence into our’s at N Hampton, the time Appointed is five weeks this week (viz) about the 20 th of Nov r. it’s like the Season May be difficult & Mr Clarks age may make him shrink, but ministers frequently go long & tedious Journeys for their health & I cant but hope many of em think the health of Christs Church [^491-note1] of as much Consequence as their own if Mr Clark Should come to Coldspring & Exert himself as he is Able to do by what I have heard of him it would be more likely to Serve one of his unhappy fellowlabourers in the Gospel =ministry & A miserable & vastly more unhappy, delud =ed people than All that ever has been done yet I mean the Rev rd Mr Edw ds & the distracted people of this Town if minis[ters] of the Gospell who are to spend & be spent in the Service of God & Souls of his people for the Sake of A little Ease will flinch in So great & weighty a Case & and let one of their brethren Sink under the burthen of it Alone I cannot think they’l be Able to Excuse themselves great numbers of the Ablest of them being convinced of the truth of it & Able to come to the help of the Lord at the Same Time I have nothing nothing further to add but that I am with great respect Rev rd Sr

Yo r most Humb le & Obed t Serv t

Tim o Dwight

Mr Foxcroft

[^491-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C098. Robert Breck et al to a "Friend," C098.Brecketal-Friendc.late50

Robert BreckC098. Robert Breck et al to a "Friend," n.d. (late 1750), printed Boston, 1750.

An ACCOUNT

Of the Conduct of the *Council* which dis- Missed the Rev. Mr. *Edwards* from the *Pastoral Care* of the first Church at *Northampton* ; with Reflections on the *Protestation* accompanying the *Printed* *Result of that Council* , and the *Letter* *Published* relating to that Affair. In a Letter to a Friend.

*Sir* ,

IN Compliance with your Desire, "of a more parti- "cular Account of the Conduct of the *Council* that "dismissed the Rev. Mr. *Edwards* from his Charge "of the first Church of *Northampton*, than you have "been able yet to obtain from the sight of the *Result*of "that *Council*, and the *Protestation* accompanying that " *Result*, and the *Letter* published by a Gentleman in " *Boston* from his Friend in the Country," we will in a few Words give you an impartial and just Rela- tion of that Affair, though a Regard to those protest- ing Gentlemen would have forbid us, had not the Publi- cation of that Protestation &c,— rendered it necessary.

We conclude, we need not inform you that the Church Of *Northampton* have for many Years been fully established In those Principles mentioned as theirs in the *Result*, and that Mr. *Edwards*, when he settled there, and for many Years after, acted agreeable thereto, though of late Years He has embraced the Principles mentioned in his Treatise upon the *Qualifications* *for full Communion in the Church*, —— [^492-note1] and could no longer proceed in his former Method of Admission to *Baptism*and the *Lord’s Supper*: —— And ac- cordingly *refused* some Persons who offered themselves to Admission, and whom the Church thought qualified for them ; and after a considerable Tract of Time, the Con- troversy being as the Church thought sufficiently agitated, Mr. *Edwards* having used his Endeavours to lead his People to Embrace **what he apprehended was Truth—— and they having examined the Scriptures and other Trea- tises on the Subject and still retaining their former Sen- timents, the *Ecclesiastical Council* before-mentioned was mutually chosen by Mr. *Edwards* and his Church ; and accordingly Letters were sent to the several Churches chosen, desiring their Presence by their Rev. Elders and Deligates, " *to give their best Advice for a Remedy from* *"the present unsettled broken State of the Church by Reason* *"of this Controversy ; and if they upon the whole of what* *"they found in their Circumstances judged it requisite, to* *"proceed immediately to dissolve the Relation between Pastor* *" and People* , as expressed in their Letters Missive——

The *Council*, being convened at *Northampton*, had the Matter in Controversy laid before them, when it appeared the Pastor and the Church stedfastly adhered to their Prin- ciples in Opposition to each other, but desired the *Council* to find out some Method wherein the Pastor and Brethren might consistently unite in the Admission of Persons to special Ordinances, and yet retain their different Sentiments, if such an one could be found :——— When the Rev. Mr. *Edwards* let the Council know *he could not with a good* *Conscience be active in admitting Persons to Sacraments, or* *in administering Sacraments to them, who are without those* *visible Qualifications*, mentioned in his Treatise upon Qua- lifications for full Communion, and delivered his Reasons therefore in Writing; and the Church also, let the *Council* know, that they could not in Conscience bar all such as were without those Qualifications, Mr. *Edwards* insisted on. Hereupon the *Council* retired and consulted about [^492-note2] some Method wherein the Rev. Mr. *Edwards*and his Church might unite, consistent with their different Sen- timents, in the Admission of Persons to Gospel Ordinances, and after a large Debate upon one Method and another, the *Council* at last came to the following Resolve, " That "after maturely weighing and deliberating the Case in "all its Circumstances, we have as yet been able to find "no proper Expedient to reconcile Pastor and People, "and therefore are ready to proceed to an hearing upon "the other Point; viz a Seperation of Mr. *Edwards* "from his People." This passed, *Nemine Contradicente.*

And now the Council repaired to the Meeting-House and published the fore-mentioned Resolve, and proceeded to hear the Church Committee upon the Reasonableness and Necessity of a Separation. After this the Moderator asked Mr. *Edwards* if he had anything to offer in Reply to the Committee, and he answered, *he had no Disposition* *to enter into that Controversy, though he had no Inclination* *to leave his People if he could continue peaceably with them* : then Col. *Dwight* and others who adhered to Mr. *Ed-* *wards* , were asked, whether they had any Thing to offer, and they were silent——The hearing of the Case being now finished, the Council retired and considered of the Rea- sons offered by the Church Committe for a Dismission of the Rev. Mr. *Edwards* ; and after fully discussing the Matter, the following Questions were put, *viz*.

1. Whether it be the Opinion of this Council that the Rev. Mr. *Edwards*, persisting in his Principles, and the Church in theirs in Opposition to Mr. *Edwards*, and insist- ing on a Seperation, it is necessary that the Relation between Pastor and People be dissolved? Passed in the Affirmative.

We would only observe here, that all the Members of the Council said yes, to the Question, except the Rev. Messirs. *Billing* and *Abercrombie*, and Mr. *Gray*, who said they had nothing to say to the Question, and the Rev. Mr. *Raynolds* and his Delegate who said yes, if no Remedy can be found ; which as yet they could not conceive of ——

2. Whether it be expedient that this Relation be immediately [^492-note3] dissolved?

Resolved in the Affirmative by the Majority of one Voice only.

Then a *Result*was drawn up, and publickly read, and after that the Protestation was publickly read also : and the Church voted their Content to the *Result* and Advice of the *Council* —— and the Rev. Mr. *Edwards* was dis- missed by a great Majority ; the Number that appeared against his Dismission being but twenty, though it was said by them there were three or four more against his Dis- mission, that were not present ; whereas the Number of Male Members as certified by Mr. *Edwards*, was *two* Hundred twenty nine ——

Having given this Relation of Facts, we cannot but make a few Remarks on the Conduct of those Gentlemen that *protested* against the Dismission——

You doubtless observe, that they say they cannot agree to a Dismission, at least for the present. 1. "Because that in the Nature of the Thing there is "no just Cause therefor : Mr *Edwards*, his Sentiments "being perfectly harmonious with the Mind of our "LORD JESUS CHRIST, &c."

And what if they did apprehend so, and what if they really were so? Are the Church and Congregation of *North-* *ampton* obliged therefore to receive those Principles, and act agreeable to them, though they in their Consciences are really persuaded that they are contrary to the Mind of our LORD JESUS CHRIST?——Have they not a Right of private Judgment? and are they not bound to act agreeable Thereto as well as others? And if they judge Mr. *Edwards* alters the Conditions on which CHRIST the great Author of the Gospel Charter has granted them the Liberty and Priviledge of attending the Ordinances he has instituted for the conveying the Graces of the Spirit to their Souls, to fit them for the Enjoyment of him in Glory, yea, has made it their Duty to attend for this Purpose, have they not an indisputable Right to oppose Mr. *Edwards* and seek his Dismission from them? We think this is what [^492-note4] all must grant upon *Protestant Principles* ; and if so, how could the Gentlemen refuse to vote his Dismission? And of what Force and Efficacy is this Reason, and is not the refusing to grant such a Seperation, a downright Invasion of the Rights of others Consciences? But whether Mr. *Edwards* his Sentiments are perfectly harmonious, &c. we shall not at present dispute ; However, That the Reason here assigned by the Gentlemen who could not agree to a Seperation, was not perfectly *harmonious* with what they both voted and said in Council, we think none will Dispute. The Gentlemen will not pretend to deny, that they voted a Seperation to be necessary, Mr. *Edwards* continuing of his Principles, and the Church of theirs ; and how could they then consistently say, they could not agree to a Seperation at present because Mr. *Edwards* his Sentiments were perfectly harmonious &c : if this was a Reason against a Seperation for the *present*, it would have been equally forcible in Time to come.

But they say, 2dly, "Upon Supposition that Mr. " *Edwards*were in the wrong in the present Contro- "versy ; yet there is, as we apprehend, no Proportion, "between the Importance of the Controversy, and that "of hisDismission"——But how could theGentlemen assign this as a Reason, and say, the Importance of the Controversy bears no Proportion to the Importance of his Dismission, when they themselves could find no Method wherein Pastor and People, differing so widely in Sentiments, could unite in the Admission of Persons to special Ordinances, and (some of them) judged a Seperation necessary: When it is evident the Controversy was of such Importance, that the Doors of the Church has been shut for some Years past, and must have continued so, unless one or other of the Parties had altered their Sentiments, or sacrificed their Consciences?

And as to the third Reason assigned by the Gentlemen why they could not agree to a Seperation of Mr. *Edwards* from his People, *viz.* " it appeared to them there had "been no proper Essays in the Way of fair Reasoning��[^492-note5] "with or before the Parties, to convince either of them of "the Truth or Falseness of their Principles, which Love "to the Truth and their Souls requires"——How could these Gentlemen say that no proper Essays had been made, when nothing is more obvious, that that the Rev. Mr. *Edwards* had calmly reasoned with his People, both from the Pulpit and the Prefs, as well as in Conversation with many of them? Can these Gentlemen have the Vanity to imagine, that they could in a short Time convince that People by Reasoning with them, when Mr. *Edwards* by all his Preaching, Printing and Reasoning with them could not convince them, although under the Advantage of his People’s having an high Opinion of, and endeared Affection to him——which those Gentlemen could not pre- tend to——And when the neighbouring Ministers has spent considerable Time in endeavouring to convince Mr. *Ed-* *wards* ; and Mr. *Billing*, one of the Protestors, had with special Zeal attempted to reclaim him from what he ap- prehended at that Time was an Error in Mr. *Edwards*?

As to the last Reason the Gentlemen assign, *viz*. "the "Church, or at least its Committe, whilst they offer to "us Reasons for seperating them from their Pastor, yet "will not suffer us so to enter into the Grounds of the "Reasons as to offer them that Light which the Word "of God affords, which we esteem an Imposition on "our Consciences, and doth but tend to keep them in "the Dark ;——

It is certain that neither Mr. *Edwards*, nor the Church of *Northampton*, determined to refer the Point in Contro- versy to the Decision of the Council : but how these Gentlemen can judge this to be an Imposition *on their* *Consciences* we cannot conceive. Had not Mr. *Edwards* and the Church of *Northampton* a Right to determine whether they would refer that Matter to them or not? or was it necessary that the Council should settle the Point in Controversy between Mr. *Edwards* and the Church ; in order to their determining whether there could be an Accommodation, or that a Seperation was necessary ? As [^492-note6] to the first, we cannot suppose the Gentlemen themselves will pretend it to be necessary, nor even the latter, when they consider that they themselves voted that Mr. *Ed-* *wards* persisting in his Principles, and the Church in theirs, a Seperation was necessary.

But what renders the Protestation more surprising is, that when these Things lay with so much Weight on their Minds, they should never so much as mention them when Matters were debated in Council before they had come to a *Result* ; which we suppose we might reasonably have ex- pected from them, but cannot remember they ever did. In- deed of Pathos urged, that Mr. *Edwards*his Dismission might not immediately take Place, but be deferred for some Months, that his Salary might be continued, till he had Time to turn to himself, and make Provision for his Family ; but of this we find no mention made in the Protestation, and therefore conclude, it afterwards lost its Weight with them.———Another Thing also diverse Times urged as a Motive to defer the Dismission for a few Months was, that if done, there might be an Union among the Members of the *Council*——And it was offered by some of those gen- tlemen, that the *Council* should immediately vote a Sepa- ration, and that nothing should be deferred but only lead- ing the Church to the Vote and the formality of declar- ing the Relation between Mr. *Edwards* and his Church Dissolved.

But although we were very desirous of acting unitedly, and although we had the Interest of Mr. *Edwards* and his Family very near our Hearts, yet when they were in Conpetition with the Peace of *Northampton* Church and the Interest of Religion there, we were at no Loss, which ought to have the Preference. And therefore we thought it our Duty to give our Voices for Mr. *Edwards* his Dis- mission.——

Thus Sir, we have given you some brief Account of[^492-note7] the Conduct of the *Ecclesiastical Council* at *Northampton*, and have added some Remarks upon the *Protestation* offered by some of the Members against Mr. *Edwards* his Dismission, we hope without any just Grounds of Offence to any. And are,

Your humble Servants,

Robert Breck

Joseph Ashley

Timothy Woodbridge

Chester Williams.

## C99. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft, February 17, 1751 C099.Dwight-Foxcroft 2-17-51

Timothy DwightC099. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft,2/17/51. Yale, Sterling Lib., Archives and Manuscripts, Dwight Family Papers, B. 1, f. 1, #2. Addressed on back "[T]o the Rev d / Mr. Thomas Foxcroft Pastor of a Chh / In Boston."

Northampton Feb ry 17 th 1750/1

Rev rd: Sr

I have given the Rev rd Mr Clarks letter to Maj r. Pomroy I also gave him the Rev rd. Mr Princes & Yours with A promise that I should have their Connection & Dependance & Mr Clarks being so Enforced by them I thôt it might so Serviceable. I told Majo r Pomroy y t considering they were to have a Fast this week that it was their duty after the people were Generally Assembled to read all the letters before they proceeded in the Publick worship & that it would be A good preparatory for the duties of the day which is Appointed by the Advice of the Association to Look to God for direction & Success in Quest of A minister All Attempts having hitherto failed Mr Arthur as well as Others. I a little Expect the Com ttee who Sit this day on the Affair will incline to pre= =vent a Publick Reading I have provided to be read thrô the Town as Opportunity presents which I hope will Serve my proposed End (viz) to Reconcile more people to Mr Edwards Mr Edwards is not returnd home Yet & the People having no bait for their Ill Will & Resentment (Mr Edwards being out of their way) & they having a Stock laying Idle they have Turnd it over to me & now threaten to dismiss me from my Offices I have not heard what they Object Against me I am Sensible they will do me what Injury they can mans pride inclines him to be impatient with all Superiours in Office & privilidges I should be glad Sr. if I might have an Intrest in your favour & that You’d please to use your Influence with His Hon r; the Lieu t, Gov r. & with Yr Hon ble. Brother that I may not be displaced only out [of] prejudice & because I am friendly to A faithful Gospell minist[er] that has been Abused in A very high degree however if that must be the Consequence I had Rather let All go than persecute the Messengers & dearest Members of Christ I am with due

Regards Rev rd. Sr Your Most Humb le Serv t

Tim o. Dwight

Mr Foxcroft——

## C100. Timothy Edwards to Hannah Edwards Wetmore, March 8, 1751 C100.TE-H.Wetmore 3-8-51

Timothy EdwardsC100. Timothy Edwards to Hannah Edwards Wetmore,3/8/51. BRBL, f. 1523. Addressed on back "To / M rs Hannah Wetmore / In Middle-Town / These."

Dear Daughter

Yr Mother and I have Lately been Informed by a Letter from y r Huband, and Another from your Self, of the Death of your Dear and only Son, Elisha, for which we Mourn with you, and for you, being very Sensible of, and heartily, Sorry and Grieved for, your Great Loss, and Sore affliction therein.

I have Great hopes that though your Child can no longer be here with Its Parents, yet that its Soul is now with Christ in Heaven, who himself hath told us that the Kingdom of Heaven (that is the Multitude or Great Number of blessed Souls that are, and will be in it for ever) doth very Much Consist of those of Little Children. Mat. 19. 14. Mark. 10. Luke. 18. 15. 16. for the hopes of the present and Eternal blessed State of your dear Little departed Son I have Several Reasons which with me are, and I think Ought to be of Weight, and which by what I have met with with, I have reason to think are So with some Eminently holy and Judicious Divines. Neither have I heard or Read of any other wise minded. the particular Reasons of my hopes which I have, and desire you may have concerning the Dear Child, which God hath Lately taken from you, I have not now time to mention, for I want time for the work of the ministry, the whole burden whereof Lyes upon me, at an age that wants but two moneths and Something Less than Seven dayes of fourscore and two years. but If God be Graciously please to Give me opportunity to See you here once more, (which I desire and hope for and Should be Glad that it my be as Soon as your Circumstances will Comfortably allow of it) then I shall If you de= sire freely and particularly Mention to you the Reasons of that hope that I desire you may to your Support and Comfort entertain Concerning your Dear Child. and Shall here further Concerning it, that I am well Satisfied that your So do ing is Agreeable to the word, and So to the will of God, and realy that which is your duty.

Remember in Love to Husband. I consider that ass in the Death of this pleasant and Dear Child, as it was very near, so I make no question that it was very dear to you both, and by taking it from you as God hath done, the Almighty hath dealt bitterly with you, both & put you both into deep mourning; and that the affliction of you both herein, is attended with a heightning and agravating Circumstance, God calls him to Mourning in, and by the Removal, and Such a Removal of a dear little Son, and not only So, but therein also by a repreated Bereaving Stroke of his afflicting hand, having taken from not Long Since a pleasant and dear Little Daughter; and hereby calls you to Mourn ing not only for the final Departure of a very pleasant and dear little Son, but to mourn as one mourneth for an only Son. My desire and prayer ot God therefore you both is, that you may walk humbly, and closely with God, ascri= bing Righteousness to y r Maker in the affliction he hath according to his holy and Sovereign will brought upon you, with humble Submission to him therein, according to Jn o. 18. 11 the Cup that my Father hath Given me, Shall I not drink it? & Mat: 26. 42. and he went away again the Second time & prayed, Saying, O my Father, If this cup may not pass away from me except I drink it, they will be done. and that you may with holy Job honour God, and Give Glory to him by being thankful to him for the mercies you Still enjoy; according to that in Job, 1. 21. The Lord Gave, the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the Name of the Lord. I Remember you dayly in my prayers: The Lod Lord Grant you both all all that Grace and mercy, help and Comfort that he Sees needful for you in your affliction, and though your Loss be great, make you on Spiritual accounts Gainers by it, by bringing you Nearer to himself, and Granting more of his Own Gracious, and Soul-comforting presence. It is also my desire and prayer that God would mercifully preserve your Dear little Lucy and make her a great comfort and blesssing to her Parents.

I am y r Affectionate Father Timothy Edwards.

Windsor. March 8 th / 1750/1

## C101. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley, March 11, 1751 C101.JHawley-EHawley 3-11-51

Joseph HawleyC101. Joseph Hawley to Elisha Hawley,3/11/50. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #18.

Northampton March 11 th 1750

Dear Sr

I have an opportunity to Wri ght you by Cap t Williams who is Now in Town. You desire in your last (viz. of ye 16 th of last month) to be informed of our ministe= =real Concerns and I hardly know what to say to you upon it. I believe y re is no prospect of Mr Edwards’s resettlement in this Town for reasons too lengthy to insert here, We have no Candidate here, Nor have we ever had any yet. Mr Frink preached with us two months, to great satisfaction, but he was not with us on probation ——— Cap t Wright made ye journey to the Jerseys for Mr Arthur, [^495-note1] of w h I wrote you in my last found Mr Arthur sick or rather leart it of Mr Burr at Newark so that he did not go to New Brunswick. Mr Arthur’s wife died while Cap t Wright was in the Jerseys, and in Ab t a month after he deceased, himself to the gen ll grief and sorrow of the people in those parts, but had he liv’d he would not Come hither having determined not to leave his people before his sickness. But Cap t Wright while in those parts got intelligence of a young Gent n Namely one Mr Farrand [^495-note2] graduated at ye Jersey Colledge last Commencem t. He was highly recommended by President Burr but mus[t] be very fresh Not being licenced when Wright was in ye Jerseys. Mr Burr recommended him very highly to the Our Association and the people I believe are in expectation of him in Aprill or May. Our state is very Malancholly who= =ever is in the Mistake either Mr Edwards or ye people yet surely s our loss of him and ye difficulty y t we meet with in endeavour ing for a Candidate are tokens of the great Displeasure of the Almighty.

May God be Mercifull unto us.

Noah Lyman is highly Oblidged to you he says for y r letter to you him and would write to you were he Able, but I be= =leive he is truly unable, he has little hope of livign long and I believe has little grounds to think otherwise of his Case than he does, he presents very g t regards to you.

As to my Matrimonials I can’t say a great deal ab t it in this Epis= -tle, I have visited M--y [^495-note3] several times ye winter past, and have within a month since been to Brookfield, and Come off as Ebenez r Searl did from Mr Stoddard’s, what another visit may determine I can’t say - But I design if Providence permit, to make another visit Shortly as as Consists with good Judgm t and policy. [^495-note4]

Mad m Dwight is not like to Continue long being Confinded to her bed. The Col o is I hope, gaining health, having subject= =ed himself to a strict regimen in diet.

I want very Much to see you and hope Providence will give us oppertunity therefor - but when we are apat it’s always un= =certain whether we shall ever Meet, May God prepare us both for a final parting as to this life that we may meet happily in the other better state D r Brother let us make it our whole Concern to secure God for our portion who is the only Adquate portion for the soul. So much religion as we have so much true happiness and No More. I assure you Brother religion has all sweetness in it. Christ is a good master His yoke is easy and his Burden light It is the Dignity of our Nature It enobles the soul; Nothing is Worthy a Wise Man or rather a Man Can’t be Wise Unless religious — —

Friends are Well at N.H. - May God Bless you in soul and Body, Be y r guide and Portion which is my most sin= =cere prayer —— I rest y r Most affectionate Brother

and ser t

Joseph Hawley

L t Elisha Hawley

P.S. If you don’t design to be down soon you will write to me how you would have y r land disposed of also what disposition you would have made of y r oats

Old Neighbour Strong is dead and Job is to be here this spring to whom ye homestead is Mainly descended I conclude he will make some disposition thereof perhaps set it up to sale and I apprehended you might be willing to know it.

[^495-note1]: Thomas Arthur (b. 1723), pastor of New Brunswick, N.J., from 1746 till his death in Feb. 1751.

[^495-note2]: Daniel Farrand (1722-1803), pastor of South Canaan, Conn., from 1752 till his death.

[^495-note3]: Mercy Lyman, daughter of Joseph Lyman, a prominent citizen of Northampton. She and Joseph were married in 1752.

[^495-note4]: **marginal.** [2]

## C102. Northampton Minority to William Hobby, [c. April 1751] C102.N’tonMinority-WHobby 4-51

Northampton MinorityC102. Northampton Minority to William Hobby, n.d. draft [c. 4/51]. ANTS, f. 1751, #14. Written in JE’s hand.

To the Rev. Mr. William Hobby, Pastor of the Church of Christ in Reading, to be communicated.

Reverend, honoured and beloved.

We the subscribers, Members of the first Church in Northampton, being in der very difficult & distress’d Circumstances State, by Reason of the following Things relating to our Circumstances. viz. that we are deprived of the Ministry of Him who for many years has been our faithful Pastor, whom the Council that led to his dismission acknowledged to be eminently qualified for the work on the ministry, & whom the greater Part of that have heretofore esteemed as the Instrument of the greatest Good to Them that it is possible one Creature should be of to another, and whom most of us think our selves obliged to esteem & Love as our spiritual Father: He having the last year been separ separated from his People, meerly because that none ought to be admitted to full Communion in the Christian Church but such as make a credible Profession of real Chrisianity; therein agreeing, as we suppose, with the common sentiments & Practice of reformed Churches, and with the original Constitution of this Church, and the Principles on which it was founded in its first Establishment; as plainly appears by our Church Records: which Constitution was never altered by any publick vote or Act of the Church; tho’ They gradually swerved from it in Principle and Practice.

This Controversy with our Pastor, which has Issued in his being publickly renounced by this Church, has apparently, all along from the Beginning, been managed with such degrees of unchristian Heat & vehemence of spirit as appear to us quite inconsistent with that Calm & impartial Consideration which an Affair of such vast Conquence [^496-note1] ought to be proceeded in. The Consequences of which are manifestly very awful: The Congregation is left as sheep without a shepherd, in & without any Prospect reasonable Prospect (as appears to us) of of obtaining any settled Pastor; remaining in a state of great Confusion, and in deplorable Circumstances (as appears to us,) out of the way of God’s Blessing & in the way to Ruin.

The Church and Congregation have lately earnestly advised by some old of the elder Ministers, & of mo & of most eminent Character in the Land, "to reconsider the Controversy and to refer the matters "in Controversy to the Judgment and Advice of a number of wise, mo"derate and disinterested men, Ministers & others, who should be "mutually chosen, in Order to an Accommodation (if possible.) between "Them & their late Pastor, that He might be restored and resettled "in his Pastoral office." This Advice has, by those ministers who gave it, been largely urged, & pressed by many moving Arguments, in Letters sent to that End. we on our Part, have taken much Pains that this Advice might be complied with; but the Church has refused so much so much as to take it into Consideration, and have publickly rejected it, once and again, with great Testimonies of disregard.

we are far from approving the Conduct of many enthusiastical People of late, who have suddenly & rashly broke off & separated from the Churches they belonged to, without proper Advice, and (as we suppose) without sufficient Grounds . But yet it seems hard to us forever to confine our selves & our Children to the Stated Communion [^496-note2] of a Church which most is confirmed in a Method of publick Administrations, which most of us are fully perswaded is contrary to Christs Institution, In admitting Members to sacred Ordinances, & the most special Priviledges in Christs House, without any Pretence to any cordial Friendship to Christ, or real Compliance with the Terms of the Covenant of Grace, or any intentional Profession of that Faith & Repentance which are the great Conditions of that Covenant; & who continue with so great & inflexible a Resolution to go on in this Practice, after so great & long continued Means have been used with Them to enlighten Them; & who on this Foot have proceeded to the utmost Extremities. we cannot Satisfie our selves or make our selves easy in our thoughts of forever denying our selves & our Posterity, the Comfort and Benefit of an attendance Communion in special Ordinances in a purer manner, with a society of the visible and professed Friends of our blessed Redeemer, as he hath appointed. nor can we be willing (if it be possible to be avoided) to be henceforward totally deprived of the Enjoyment of the ministry of our Pastor, which we so much value; for no other Cause, but only because He insists on such a w an Administration: we are willing rather to part with much of our worldly substance than to continue in such lamentable Circumstances with Regard to the spiritual well-fare of our selves & Families.

we desire to humble our selves before God for our Misimprovement of past Priviledges, in this day of God’s awful Frowns, which we are sensible & earnestly to seek his Compassion & direction. And also think our selves obliged to ask Counsel of our Christian Fathers & Brethren in other Churches. And besides some of our neighbour Churches, which we now apply our selves to, we think our selves called to seek the assistance of some at a distance; most of the neighbouring ministers & Churches having interested Themselves in the Controversy, & being Zealously engaged in Opposition to the Principles of our late Pastor. we therefore desire the Presence of your Reverend & honoured Pastor, & a Messenger or Messengers, to meet with in this Town, on Thursday the 16 sixteenth day of May next; at that time to, lo particularly to look into our Circumstances, & to give our us your Judgment, whether it be re adviseable & requisite that we should be embodied, with others that are willing to join with us, as a distinct Church; and accordingly to incorporate us, if you think it best, and to appoint over us the Rev. Mr. Edwards to be our Pastor; who is willing to submit to the Advice and direction of a Council as to that matter. But if this ben’t thought expedient, we desire you would direct us what to do in our extremely difficult Circumstances. for in this Case we shall greatly need Advice how to conduct our selves in many Respects.

we hope you will take our lementable Case into your serious & Compassionate Consideration, & that you will not refuse your Charitable Assistance, to Those who, we trust, you must needs be sensible exceedingly need Advice & Help, & who are willing to have the best Advice they can obtain. we desire not that any of our Representations of our Circumstances or of the state of the Town should be taken without thorough Enquiry, [^496-note3] and therefore desire that our Advisers should be on the spot, & under the best Advantages for Information.

This with a Request of your Prayers to God for us is from your distressed Brethren & servants in Christ, [^496-note4]

[^496-note1]: MS sic; "Consequence."

[^496-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^496-note3]: **marginal.** [3]

[^496-note4]: From the Reading Church Records for May 1751: "Having Rec d Letters from a Number of ye Breth n of ye Chh of Northampton adhering to y r. Late Pastor ye Rev d Mr Edwards Signifying y r. Desires y t. we w d Incorporate y m. & Install y r. Late Pastor over y m if we Saw meet, or Otherwise give Such Advice as y r. Circumstances Calld for; having also Rec d Letters from ye Rev d: Mr. Edwards, desiring y t. he might have an Opportunity to lay his Case before a Councill, & have y r advice, I Read ye Letters to ye Chh who Voted to Send according to ye Desire of ye. Petitioners — N B. Cap t: Brown & Sam ll. Bancroft Jun r. Deleg." *The Colonial Church Records of the First Church of Reading (Wakefield) and the First Church of Rumney Marsh (Revere)*, ed. James F. Cooper and Kenneth P. Minkema (Boston, Colonial Society of Massachusetts, 2006), 194.

## C104. Edward Billing to Timothy Dwight, [Before May 1751] C104.EBilling-TDwight bef.5-51

Edward BillingC104. [Edward Billing] to Timothy Dwight, n.d. [before 5/51]. ANTS, f. ND1, #8[?]. Unsigned, but definitely in Billing’s hand.

To ye Hon rable Col Dwight

I think it is not only adviseable but duty to invite mr Edwards to take ye pastoral care of yr Souls at N H Reasons. NorthHampton is large enough for two parishes, and the people can without difficulty support two ministers.

And to invite mr Edwards is a proper declaration of repentance for sending Him away without grounds. you and it may be making restitution for ye wrong [——] have done to Him and a means of support of his family: I we am perswaded ye Town is oblieged to support Him, because you under promises to give Him maintenance during his continuing a faithfull minister of Christ and you are perswaded ye ground of his seperation from you is an[——] Instance of his Faithfulness.

But further divine providence has been far from smiling upon your Attempts to settle a minister. you have not had ye opportunity of hearing a Candidate for ye ministry since mr Edwards was dismissed.

altho’ you have much sought for it. and it seems that you have been under a frown of providence, in that respect, or that no Candidates are [—] to be obtained But If you should obtain a Candidate there is but little prospect of your settling Him without difficulty.

For either he will be of mr Stoddards principle, or mr Edwards. If of mr Stoddards then a Considerable number will oppose his settlement. his opinion being Contrary to your opinion. and it seams yt no likely Man will settle upon ye terms proposed by ye greater part of ye town. which are that He must resign his settlement or quit N H If He should dissent from mr Stoddards opinion.

And If He should profess Himself to be of mr Edwards opin= ye [——] greater part would oppose his settlement for ye same reason for which they sent off mr Edwards. there is but little prospect of settling a Candiate at [^498-note1] N H yt will please ye Town and subserve ye Interest of religion . for none will please them but superficial[?] preachers of experimental religion, or ye vital power of Godlyness. and such preachers are exceeding scarce: And it is probable that in one years time a greater Number would rejoice in mr Edwards ministry. than in ye ministry of any other you have a prospect of obtaining. If He should now[?] be Installed by a number of judicious Godly ministers.

—— farther more it is likely North: will be a contentious quarrelsome place If mr Edwards should not be settled there. for your principles are so diverse that If you have but one minister He must be a means of & scheme[?] contention till He can bring you all into one sentiment and y it is as probable yt mr Edwards would do that If you should chose Him as another.

—— further more to settle Him at N H is but a proper testimony to ye cause of God, for there dont appear a [——] good reason why you should not chose Him for your pastor seing you are able and will ing to afford Him maintenance. surely those who are convinced mr Edwards principles are right. ought to manifest their esteam of them by chosing Him for their pastor seeing each part of ye Town is able to grant a minister an honourable support

—— further ye cause of God is likely to suffer much by not settling mr Edwards It is well known He has been a successfull preacher of ye Gospel, and perhaps no ministers have laboured more to promote heart vital religion than He. but now He is despised by many and some secretly rejoice at ye afflicted Circumstan= =ces mr Edwards is under.

they readily think what He has preached is not to be [^498-note2] so much regarded, since He is deposed, or not esteamed fit for ye Gospel minstry, that He who has appeared so erroneous as to be dismissed may be mistaken in many things which He has delievered from ye pulpit.

But If mr Edwards should be Installed at N H by an honourable counsel it would not only be an honour to Him but to that religion which He has preached.

And many would regard Him as a good and great divine tho’ they now despise Him.

—— if He should not be restored to N H then ye devil would be buzy in driving away all other ministers that are or may be [-] mr Edwards sentiment.

but If He should be restored. other ministers might of his principles might be easy with their people. and those Chh members who have an awfull Enmity against Godlyness at present would think it best to lie still, forbearing to afflict and ye ministers, and endeavour yr sepera= tion. I can think of nothing yt can be done by men so conducive to make ye devil and his Instruments lie still and to continue other ministers easy in yr relation to their flock. But surely If it should not be done, Every minister yt is or may be of mr Edwards sentiment must move of ye stage. and seek some other place for refuge and rest than ye County of Hampshire.

I never saw people [——] so angry and raving mad against ministers of mr Edwards entiment as they were [————] After mr Edwards was dismissed.

that they and If mr Edwards shold be resettled, other ministers and chhs yt are of his sentiments might peaceably continue their relation to one another.

—— But further from a fear that Arminianism will grow[^498-note3] amongst us, some that belong not to N H desire mr Edwards would set up and continue public Lectures yt to suppress that [...] to preach down yt dangerous error, and would willingly make contributions to Encourage mr Edwards to preach.

And least any Gentlemen in ye ministry at Boston or else where, should refuse to travail so far into ye Country [——] Meerly to Install mr Edwards, I would propose this other important buisness to induce them, namely to sit in Counsel at Cold Spring after they shall have Installed mr Edwards. tho I believe our ye Chh at Cold Spring will not desire ye advise of a Counsel after they have had[?] so good work at N H.

But If those Gentlemen will [...][^498-note4]

affair they must come to Counsel at Cold Spring, but I believe there would be no need of a Counsel If that should be done.

thus I think you are not only bound in point of your own Interest but in point of ye Interest of your Neighbours to call a Counsel to resettle mr Edwards. thus Sir I have Just made a few marks without order or method. [——————————————]

propose [————————]

## C105. Ephraim Williams to Jonathan Ashley, May 2, 1751 C105.EphWilliams-JAshley 5-2-51

Ephraim WilliamsC105. Col. Ephraim Williams to Rev. Jonathan Ashley,5/2/51. In Wyllis E. Wright, *Colonel Ephraim Williams: A Documentary Life* (Pittsfield, Mass., Berksire County Hist. Soc., 1970), 61-62. The footnotes are Wright’s.

Fort Massachusetts, May 2, 1751

Rev. Sir:

I this minute received your long letter. Shall endeavour to remem- ber you (first having christened my own child) but you must keep it an entire secret, lest I should give offence, there being several which have spoken before you, though I am not under an obligation that I remem- ber to any of them. Please to let me know how much he owes you, his debt to me is large, all cash lent.

Sir, I should be glad to know what subject you preached from at N. Hampton, & whether it will bear printing. It seems some gentle- men look upon it as a mean performance. I have heard one compared you to your brother [^499-note1] at Stockbridge, which every person knows, dont understand divinity, any better than mine that is there understands botany. I assure you it raised my welch blood.

Mr. Edwards has lately wrote to Mr. Woodbridge at Stockbridge, who informs him he has not heard from them, dont know whether they desire he should come among them, and that he hears I have done all I can to prevent his coming. I am sorry that a head so full of divinity should be so empty of politics. I would not have him fail of going for 500 pounds, since they are so set for him, not that I think he will ever do so much more good than an other, but on account of raising the price of my land. Its true when they first talked of settling him I was against it, gave my reasons, & sent them to him like an honest fellow, when to my certain knowledge some in the place could say as much against him behind his back, but darent open their mouths in any shape to his face, a method I despise in my soul. Perhaps you have heard the reasons I had to object to his coming which if you have not I will let you know them.

1. That he was not sociable, the consequence of which was he was not apt to teach.

2. He was a very great bigot, for he would not admit any person into heaven, but those that agreed fully to his sentiments, a doctrine deeply tinged with that of the Romish church.

3. That he was an old man, & that it was not possible for him to learn the Indian tongues therefore it was not likely he could be serviceable to the Indians as a young man that would learned the tongue. Why no more pains should be taken with the old Indians to save them, [^499-note2] that as it were they must be under the necessity of being d——d I knew not. [^499-note3]

4. His principles were such, if I had been rightly informed, I could by no means agree to, that I taken pains to read his book, but could not understand it, that I had heard almost every gentleman in the county say the same, & that upon the whole I believed he did not know them himself.

The above reasons I sent him by Lt. Brown, who has since told me he delivered to him verbatim, which I believe did not suit him.

I am Sir your most humble servant,

Eph Williams Jun

P. S. I send proper salutations to Mrs. Ashley with all friends. E W

[^499-note1]: Benjamin Ashley was employed by the mission at Stockbridge, apparently largely in order to secure the services of his wife as an interpreter. He had married Rebecca Kellogg, a sister of Martin Kellogg who had, like him, been taken captive at Deerfield and learned Mohawk while a captive.

[^499-note2]: **marginal.** [62]

[^499-note3]: Many of those interested in the Stockbridge mission seem to have been at least as much concerned with keeping the Indians friendly to the English and opposed to the French as with their religious instruction. Gideon Hawley wrote in his diary for 1757, when he had been driven from his mission in New York by the outbreak of war and was being urged to return, "I wont go among Indians in the character of a Christian missionary except I can go upon Christian principals . . . But why do I talk of Christian zeal in this case tis a *political* affair. Those who talk about the propagation of Christianity among the Indians, don’t much care whether any of them go to Heaven . . . Mr. Edwards . . . has blind notions about things and no wonder seeing he knows nothing but by hearsay and the half has never been told him. If he would endeavour to excite me go engage in my mission and use only the motives which are suggested in Christianity I should like it better." Mr. Edwards is a very good man but capable of being biased." -Quoted by Clifford K. Shipton in *Biographical Sketches of Graduates of Harvard University* (Cambridge: C. W. Sever, 1873-), XII:399.
