## C107. Samuel Davies to Joseph Bellamy, July 4, 1751 C107.S.Davies-Bellamy 7-4-51

Samuel DaviesC107. Samuel Davies to Joseph Bellamy,7/4/51. MS 81192, Hartford Seminary. Two folio sheets, addressed, "To / The Rev d. Mr. Joseph Bellamy, Minister / of / Bethlem / in / Connecticut / New=England." Printed in *Presbyterian Magazine* 4 (Nov. 1854), 512-15.

[Hanover, Va.]

Rev d. & very dear B r.

I never received an Information of the Kind in my Life, that afforded me so many anxious Tho’ts as yours concerning the great Mr. Ed= =wards: It has employ’d my waking Hours, & even mingled with my midnight Dreams. The main Cause of my Anxiety was the Delay of your Letter, which I did not receive till about 3 Weeks ago, when I was in Lunenburg a= =bout 130 Miles from Home. This made me afraid lest Mr. Edwards had s has settled somewhere else, being weary of waiting for an Invitation from Virginia. Should be the unhappy Case, & should the Obligation to his new People be deemed undissolvable, I shall look upon it as a severe Judgement from incensed Heaven on this wretched Colony — What shall I say? I am lost in Perplexities at the Tho’t.

I assure myself, Dear Sir, of your most zealous Concurrence to per= =suade him to Virginia; [-] Do not send him a cold paper Messenger; but go to him yourself in Person. If he be not as yet engaged to any Place, I depend upon your Word, & "make no Doubt but he will come." If he is engaged, I hope he may be regularly dismissed upon a Call of so great Importance — Of all the Men I know in America he appears to me the most fit for this Place; & if he could be obtained on no other Condi= =tion, I would cheerfully resign him my Place, & cast myself into the wide World once more. Fiery [——] superficial Ministers will never due in these Parts; they might do good, but they would do much more Harm: we need the deep Judgement & calm Temper of Mr. Edwards among us — Even the Dissenters here have the nicest Taste of almost any Congregation I know, & cannot put up with even the Truths of the Gospel in an in= =judicious Form. The Enemies are watchful, & some of them crafty; & raise a prodigious Clamour about the raving injudicious Preaching. Mr. Edwards would suit both — Our Liberties are precarious, & Methods are used to restrain them; There’s no Body here who is known in great Britain, whose Representation might have some Weight to counterballance of the Council; & on this Account we extreamly need Mr. Edwards, whose Cha= =racter there, especially in Scotland, would have considerable Influence. He might also, as y o. observe, do much good by keeping an Acadmey; & which is of greater Importance all, might be the happy Instruments of turning many to Righteousness.

Assoon as I returned from Lunenburg, I wrote to the Elders in the upper Part of my Congregation, (which I want to cast off, when they have Opportunity of obtaining a Minister,) urging them to take Pains with the People in their respective Quarters to obtain Subscription for Mr. Edwards’s Maintenance; and tho’ they had no Knowledge of Mr Ed= him but my Recommendation, they have made up about 80 £ of our Currency, which is about 60 or 65 Sterling; & tis the general Opinion of the People, that if Mr. Edwards does in any Measure answer the Character I have given him (& I doubt not but he will) they can easily afford him 100 £ per An. Sundry of them did actually plead their Want of Acquaint= [^501-note1] =ance with him as the Reason of their Backwardness; & I could not ex= =pect it would be otherwise; others might have that as a Reaso secret Reason, who did not publickly mention The people about the lower Meeting=house, which is my more immediate Charge, assure they will contribute something towards the expences of this first Year’s Settle= =ment; & the People in Lunenburg told me they would cheerfully subscribe towards his Maintenance the first Year, should he settle any where in Virginia; & I doubt not but all the dissenting Congregations in Virginia will do the same: So that I believe Mr. Edwards may safely depend on 30 or 40 £ the first Year besides his annual Salary. This, however, I am certain of, he has the Prospect of a comfortable Livelihood; & indeed should I ensnare him into Poverty designedly, I should censure myself as the basest of Mankind — My Salary at present is about 100 £; & not withstanding 20 or 30 £ peculiar Expences, I find I can make a Shift to live upon it.

I could not content myself with following your Advice, & only writing to Mr. Edwards; & therefore the People have sent the Bearer, a worthy youth [^501-note2] who has been under my Tuition for some Time, to wait on him with their Invitation. He has lived so long here, & is so perfectly acquainted with Affairs, that he can inform you & Mr. Edwards of them, as well as myself.

And now Sir, I shall answer the other Parts of your Letter. I send you herewith a Narrative of Religion here. As I have no [—] Correspondence with any of the Boston Ministers, I have been obliged to impose upon you the Trouble of sending it to the Press, if you think it worthwhile. I beseech you, dear Sr. to make such Corrections as you & Mr. Edwards shall think fit; & be not afraid of offending me by so doing; for I was designedly careless in writing it, as I [—] knew it would pass thro’ your Hands. I would have you particularly consider the Ex= =pediency of publishing the P. S. & the poetical Lines on Mr. Blair. [^501-note3]

I am impatient Sir, to see your Books; & am impatient wish you could inform me of which Way I shall send the money Price of them to the Printer, & order them to be conveyed by Water to the Care of Mr. John Holt Merch t. in Williamsburg, or of Col. John Hunter Merch t. in Hamp= =ton, as may be most convenient.

I have dropt the Tho’t of my intended Treatise on Morality & Gospel=Holiness, till I have more Leisure, & have a larger Acquaintance with Divinity; but am now & then collecting Materials for it.

I believe the weakest of the Congregations in this Colony could afford a Min r. 60 or 70 £ yearly Salary; & as to Itinerants the usual Rule 20 or 30 s [^501-note4]a Sunday. As far as I know them, the Paianies [^501-note5] here are in general pretty generous.

This Colony is very healthy, except on River’s Sides, & "will suit very well with the Constitution of New England Men."

Dear Sir, if Mr. Edwards fails, shall I prevail with you to come y r. self, at least to pay us a transient Visit? O! how would re= =joice my Soul to see you?

Whenever I write to you, I am in such a hurry, that I am appre= =hensive my Letters afford you a very mean Idea of my intellectual Ability; but as you don’t wrong me in it, I shall be quite easy, unless you think I make you such wretched Returns, as that my Correspondence is insufferable.

Pray for me, Dear Sr. & write to me as often as you can. If you have another Half, present my Respects to her. I am Sr, [^501-note6]

Y rs. in the tenderest Bonds.

Sam l. Davies

July 4th —51

P.S. You may insert or omit the marginal Note in p. 28 of the Nar= =rative as your Prudence directs; the Contents are undoubtedly true; but I am afraid will seem incredible.

[^501-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^501-note2]: The "worthy youth" is not further identified.

[^501-note3]: The Narrative was indeed published, as *The state of religion among the Protestant dissenters in Virginia; in a letter to the Rev. Mr. Joseph Bellamy, of Bethlem, in New-England: from the Reverend Mr. Samuel Davies, V.D.M. in Hanover County, Virginia* (Boston, 1751), including the "P.S." (as an appendix) and the "poetical Lines on Mr. Blair" (p. 35). Samuel Blair (1712-1751), a 1735 graduate of the Log College, served Prebyterian churches in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.

[^501-note4]: I.e. shillings.

[^501-note5]: I.e. pagans, or Indians.

[^501-note6]: Conjectural reading where the MS is damaged.

## C107a. Samuel Davies to Joseph Bellamy, July 13, 1751 C107a.SDavies-Bellamy 7-13-51

Samuel DaviesC107a. Samuel Davies to Joseph Bellamy,7\13\51. MS 81193, Hartford Seminary Foundation. One leaf, inscribed on back, "To / The Rev d / Mr. Joseph Bellamy."

Rev d. dear B r.

I did not receive [the co]mpleat [^502-note1] Subscription for Mr. Edwards till yesterday, which happily exceeds my Expectation: It amounts to about 97 £, which is near 80 £ Sterling. This will undoubtedly be a very sufficient Maintenance. You’ll see by the Subscription=Paper [^502-note2] how many dissenting Families there are in ye least half of my Congregation; for the Subscribers are chiefly Heads of Families - O! dear Sir; let me renew my Importunities with you to exert all your Influence in our behalf with Mr. Edwards —— Tho’ the People seem eager for him above all Men on Earth, yet they request you by me, in Case this Attemp fails, to endeavour to send some other to settle among [...]m [^502-note3] (for they have no Prospect of Relief these sundry years fro[m Newcast]le P by [^502-note4] ) but let him be a popular Praecher, of ready Utterance, good Judg Delivery, solid Judgm t., free from enthusiastical Freaks of ardent Zeal; for I am assured they will accept of none other. & I would not have any sent here that might be unacceptable. You or Mr. Edwards are the only Men they could make an implicit Venture upon ——— I am with the warmest Emotions of Heart,

D r. Sir,

Yr. most affectionate B r. &c

S. D.

July 13 - 51.

## C107b. Samuel Finley to Joseph Bellamy, August 1, 1751 C107b.SFinley-Bellamy 8-1-51

Samuel FinleyC107b. Samuel Finlay to Joseph Bellamy,8\1\51. MS 81194, Hartford Seminary Foundation. One folio sheet, addressed, "To / The Rev d: Joseph Bellamy / at Bethlehem, Fairfield County / In / Connecticut."

White-clay-creek. Aug t: 1. 1751.

my Dear & Rev d: Sir,

Being abroad I have not y e: Oppertunity of laying before your last acceptable Letter for my Direction in this; & being in haste I can only give you a few hin imperfect Hints; y e: Opportunity of this Bearer was quite unexpected, [——] but very acceptable. You will Learn from him & M r: Davies’s Letter y e: full State of Things. Our Presbytry was providentially Sitting when M r: Harris Came along, from Virginia — & we Sent a Letter to M r Edwards to [—] Manifest our hearty Concurrence with our Brethren in Virginia in their Address to M r: Edwards him. I was much griev’d in hearing of the Treatment

 he reced from y e: People of Northampton, & tho’t it very Strange ——— but all-governing-Wis- dom has an infinite Reach; & Incidents y t: we cannot Now Understand, we shall hereafter clearly See their Necessity in order to Some important Event. my d r B r, I hope you will Second y e: present

 Applicaon to m r Edwards; & also encourage some other hopeful Candidates to come to our Assistance, if you find any such so dispos’d. S r Mitchell [^503-note1]

 is well, & has been Studying Divinity in Intervalls since he has been with me. m r: Whitlesey [^503-note2]

designs to go to New-England this ffall, when I hope to write more fully to you; & express More of y e: Kindness of my Heart. M r Rodgers, one of my dear Brethren gives his Love to you - I tho’t to have Sent you a Sermon preach’d at this Ordination, but have none with me; however [-] I Shall endeavour to get one convey’d. Give my Sincere Respects to your Dear Spouse — & accept as much Afection as you can desire, from yourS. ffinly

P.S. my thrice dear Br S: Blair, [^503-note3] is lately departed this Life, & [—] went off y e: Stage with Triumph.

[^503-note1]: Possibly Alexander Mitchell (1731-1812), who graduated from Princeton in 1765 and preached at various Presbyterian churches in Pennsylvania.

[^503-note2]: Eleazar Whittelsey (d. 1752), born in Bethlehem, Conn., Princeton, 1749, preached in Presbyterian churches in Maryland and Pennsylvania

[^503-note3]: Samuel Blair (1712-1751), a 1735 graduate of the Log College, served Prebyterian churches in New Jersey and Pennsylvania

## C108. John Rogers to Joseph Bellamy, August 3, 1751 C108.J.Rogers-J.Bellamy 8-3-51

John RogersC108. John Rogers to Joseph Bellamy,8/3/51. BRBL, f. 1537.

Rev d & D Sir

Tis perhaps quite neces= sary I shou’d begin this hasty Scribble with an Apology for my troubling you at this Time. It is, Sir, in Complyance with ye Request of my worthy & Dear Brother Davies, with others of my Friends in Virginia, earnestly solliciting me to forward, to ye utmost of my Power, ye truly de= sirable Attempt in ye Bearer, Mr Harris, is en= gaged — As ye Motion was originally Yours, Sir, as I perceive from ye Mr Davies’s Letter to myself & some of my Brn — I doubt not but you will lay your Self out to ye utmost of your Power & In= terest to promote it — How truly invaluable wo’d the Favour be to ye Interests of our Dear Redeemer in thoese Parts, according to present Appearances, shou’d God direct Mr Edwards’s way to Virginia — My Soul exults at ye distant Prospect of his being determined thither — tho’ not without considerable Fears least[^504-note1] his being allready engag’d to some Place — The Cir= cumstances of his numerous Family — The Manner of his living in a Town, different doubtless from y at that can be expected, in an ordinary Way, in a Coun= try Place — The Distance of Virginia from N: England — or some other Circumstance may disconcert ye present Attempt — But shou’d this be ye discouraging Case I can’t but hope ye present Attempt will engage Mr Edwards more particularly to lay himself out for the Promotion of our Redeemer’s Interests in those Parts — Sr I can Nor can I perswade my self you will be wanting in this, Sir — It wou’d be Arrogance, not to be pardon’d, for Me to direct you in your Choice of Persons, suitable for Labouring in y t important Branch of our Ld’s Vineyard — Your Prudence Lea no doubt, suggests ye Necessity of particularly Prudence, Judgment, Learning & Popularity in those y t are sent thither — Mr Finley has no dobt inform’d you of ye truely great & eminently useful Mr Blair’s Death - My Father, My Father, the Chariots of Is= rael & ye Horsemen thereof - The Fall of so great a Man in our Israel is lamented by ye Friends & Enemies of true Piety — Religion & has a discouraging Aspect on ye Interests [^504-note2] of Religoin with us - But the Residue of the Sp t is with ye Ld — I have herewith sent you Mr Finley’s Sermon at my Ordination, which please to accept as a Token, tho’ small, of my worthless Regards. May our Dearest Ld long continue in his Vineyard, make you very to be ver faithful, & bundantly suc= sessful in all your Attempts; which is ye sincere Desire & earnest Prayer of

Rev d & D Sir,

Your younger, unworthy

Brother & Serv t in our dearest Ld

Jn o Rodgers

S t Georges

August 3 d 1751

## C109. Josiah Willard to Stockbridge Inhabitants, October 19, 1751 C109.Willard-Stkbr. 10-19-51

Boston Oct. 19. 1751

Gentlemen & Friends

In Answer to a Petition of the Rev d. Mr. Jon a. Edwards your Minister, to the Gen l. Assembly of this. Praying for Liberty to purchase of the Indians of Stockbridge an Hundred Acres of Woodland for his necessary Use of Fire Wood & Timber, I am directed in the Name of the said Court strongly to recommend to you the Proprietors of Lands (both English Indians & English) in said Township to appropriate such a suitable Quantity of Land therein as shall be suffi- cient to supply the Said Mr. Edwards with Firewood &c during his Abode with you in the Work of the Ministry & for his Successors therein: Which Thing I do recommend to you accordingly, desiring your Answer when you have considered acted upon this matter. ## C110. John McLaurin to William Hogg, November 8, 1751 C110.McLaurin-Hogg 11-8-51

John McLaurinC110. John McLaurin to William Hogg,11/8/51. Princeton Univ., Firestone Lib.

Glasgow November 8. 1751

Dr Sir

While the other leaf of this Letter is perhaps fitter to be shown to other good acquaintances who may be willing to hear such accounts, I have reserved this leaf for things proper more peculiarly to be told to yourself & our most intimate friends. By Mr. Prince’s Letter I find there is a pacquet at this time sent by Mr. Edwards tho not yet come up from the seaport. But in a letter from Mr. Abiel [?] Walley, Merchant, who was a Justice of Peace in Governour Belchers time, there is the following passage. "I received the goods both parcels of them; and have sent them to Mr. Edwards, seen both him & Spouse who received the account thereof with most wonderful Thankfullness; Looking up to God & Blessing his name for so remarkable Appearance in his Providence in moving the hearts of gentlemen, Strangers and at Such a Distance; And desire me to return all possible Thanks & Gratitude to their Benefactors. According to your Desire I have prevailed with Mr. Edwards & his wife to have their pictures drawn; Letting them know that some friends with you ordered me to get them done at their Charge. And they are done to the Life have a very exact resemblance; they are pact in a box on board Capt. McCunn marked EML. The cost is five pounds sterling which the Gentlemen may remit to me in a parcel of fine Tartan Stuff. In the Box I have put up a Pacquet from Mr Williams of Lebanon, another from Mr Edwards with some of his farewell Sermons" (which I intend to send soon to Edinburgh for your perusal)

Whereas you had proposed in one of your letters that the drawing might be sent here to be engraven here, it seems to me this is what they have complied with. I take it for granted you have by much the better engravers in your Town. If several hundred prints were cast off, some of which perhaps might be sold elsewhere, chiefly at London, which it might be fit to compliment Several of the Contributors at Edinburgh & here gratis, probably several of others, with whom more freedom may be used, will cheerfully give so much for their copies of the prints, as may in some measure lessen the Charges of the drawing & engraving. It seems to me you have the best right to the property of the pictures, as seven prints will serve me by which I would by no means be understood to lessen my share of the charges of the drawing as well as engraving: perhaps several will join us in both. I have upon the matter sent two messages to good Capt. McCunn about sending up the Box & intend to tell you when it comes. I had written to Mr P_[?] Mr Edwards your liking to see his picture. I am not sure if I wrote to him about [...] [frag missing c] to send you my copy: I think I wrote to him another thing viz: that I [_] who was to send for other things from Boston to send for another Copy of [...] [frag missing] some other pictures; Mr Princes writes to me he has now sent a copy of his pict[...] [frag missing] carefully to send to you. McLaurin [word undecipherable]

Summary of the few accounts in Boston Letters of last September, which came to Glasgow on Novem b 7 1751.

1. As to Mr Edwards after his Dismission from Northampton he had three Invitations to other Settlements; two large churches of New England people much pleasanter as to worldly accommodations than the settlement at Stockbridge of which the Revd Mr Prince says that it is an Indian town above 160 miles right out in the wilderness west of Boston: that the church there consists both of English & Indians but chiefly of Indians, there being but about 12 or 14 English families yet in the place, but Mr Prince says he expects that Mr Edwards will soon draw many more to it. Those who invited Him to this settlement are called the Commissioners for Propagating Christian Knowledge among the Indians. He was installed there by a Number of Ministers. The present maintenace is 70L Sterl. per annum. He had not much more at Northampton. But that which seems to show a distinguished regard to him on the part of the Managers is that one of the Letters says there is a promise of more if the present salary shall be found not to be enough.

2. As to Mr Pemberton president of the Correspondents of the Honll Scots Society for propag. Xian Knowledge, Minister at New York & a chief promoter of the Interest of the New Jersey College, Mr Prince writes that "he was under promise to him to employ that day (Sept. 6) & to move us in writing Letters in favour of his Design for new Jersey College to his Correspondents in London." & /Adds/ As to Mr Pemberton (who was in Boston at the time) "This worthy Gentlemen having lately lost his consort & having a Colleague settled with him; the Honourable & Revd Trustees of the said College have earnestly entreated him to take a voyage both to South & North Britain to solicit Help for that important Interest; & he has kindly complied & intends, with Submission to Providence, to sail this fall for London. And he is now come hither partly to see & take leave of his friends & relations here, where he was born & educated & partly to request our Recommendation of his great Design. The Boston Association had appointed me to draw up a brief Recommendation of the same; at his Desire: and the Association were at my house in consideration of my Draught yesterday afternoon - [longer dash] & the Revd Mr Pemberton is to set sail on Monday morning for New York; in order to meet the New Jersey Synod Some time this month before he sails for England."

3. Mr Cooper writes to Mr Erskine that he heard lately from one who had been at Nova Scotia that there were about 12 or 13 hundred dwelling houses in Halifax, where a year or two ago there was almost nothing but an uncultivated wilderness; that besides the Episcopal Church there was a Church for the Dissenters the minister of which, Mr Cleaveland from New England, is a very good character.

[Back cover says; to Mr. William Hogg/ Merchant in the Castlehill/ Edr.]

## C111. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft, December 25, 1751 C111.Dwight-Foxcroft 12-25-51

Timothy DwightC111. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft,12/25/51. Fragment. Yale, Sterling Library, Dwight Family Papers, B. 1, f. 1, #3. End of letter missing.

Northampton Dec r 25 th 1751

Rev rd, Sr

Supposeing the Rev rd Mr Hobby of Reading often comes to Boston I cant think of any place so likely to meet with him as at your house I beg the favour Sr of You to desire him on my behalf to imploy Some Scriv e to draw a Coppy of the Remonstrance our church Exhibited to the Rev rd Council in May last Against the Rev rd Mr Edwards & those that Adhered to him of the first Church in Northampton if Mr Hobby think proper after he has compared & Attested it to leave the original at your house for me I will send for it the[re] [^507-note1] but if it be thôt Improper to part w th the original then to let me have the Coppy attested &c & minut the Cost in the margin or on the bottom & I will leave the money at Yo r house for him I would Send it now but cant give any guess what the Sum must be but I will take Effectual care what Mr Hobby demands shall be left at yo r house for him within a Convenient time after I’m inform’d

We are in Utmost Confusion in our Ecclessiastick Affairs we had a church meeting Yesterday & Some of the C hh Committee Said it was to see if the Church would give One Mr Farrand a young Gen tn from the Jersey Colledge a Call & others of the Comittee Said not. We are left to blind Guides in the Mannagem t of th[e] [^507-note2] business & no doubt are like to succeed [. . .]

[^507-note1]: Hole in MS

[^507-note2]: Hole in MS.

## C112. Thomas Foxcroft to Timothy Dwight, March 31, 1752 C112.TFoxcroft-TDwight 3-31-52

Thomas FoxcroftC112. Thomas Foxcroft to Timothy Dwight,3/31/52. ANTS, f. 1752B, #1. Addressed on back "For / Timothy Dwight Esq / In / Northampton."

Boston Mar. 31. 1752.

H d Sr

I take the first Opportunity to acknowledge your Favours of Feb y 10 th & Mar. 16 th. It grieves me to hear that Things are in such an unhappy State among you; and so likely to remain in ye same. Your Situation must needs be very uneasy to you; and I doubt will be more so still, if the Controversy you mention, as beginning, be- tween you and the Chh (or the Committee, or Agents for it) shou’d go on. I hope, Sr, you study the things that make for Peace, and are willing, if possible, to live peaceably with all Men, especially with your Christian Brethren. I pray God direct you to all wise Mea- sures for that End. The Beginning of Strife is as the letting forth of Water —— The Contentions of Brethren are as the Bars of a Castle. —— The Fruit of the Spirit is in all Goodness, and Righteousness, and Truth. For Peace-Sake, Mr Hobby (I believe) will bury in Silence his Reply to Mr Breck [^508-note1] ——I am apt to think, Mr Parsons & Asheley’s Opinion about Mr Williams’s Book is founded in good Reason, if that be indeed as you say you’ve heard it is. Mr Edwards’s Answer to it will (I doubt not) make this appear abundantly evident.

I am exceeding sorry at what you write me concerning the State of Things at Stockbr e — We have rec d shocking Accounts of some Troubles — However, if things are as they’ve been represented, I am persuaded the Commissioners for Indian Affairs will not let him be abused, &c.

I have deliver’d the Cash you sent to Mr Hobby, for the young Gent n, that transcrib’d the Copy you desired. By a Mistake of Mr Bromfield’s, [^508-note2] the Pac Superscription of my Packet for you was alter’d; and so it went to Mr Edw ds. But I suppose you have receiv’d it before now, by what I see of an Extract from it in your Lett r to Mr Clark [^508-note3] - which I’ve seal’d & forwarded to him already. I at first pleased myself with the Thôt of Col o D- s going to dwell at Stockb.- but unless the Case has been misrepresented to me, I have seen Reason to alter my Mind.

Please to communicate to me in your next what further occurs in Relation to Stockbr. North n & Cold Spring — I hear nothing yet of Mr Edw.’s Reply to Mr W ms [^508-note4] nor whether ye old Rector be arriv’d home [^508-note5] - With my Salutes to your Family, I conclude this hasty Scroll from Sr yr very humble Serv t

Tho s Foxcroft

[^508-note1]: Rev. William Hobby of Reading and Rev. Robert Breck of Springfield, who were on opposite sides in the council that dismissed Edwards from Northampton. Apparently Hobby had prepared a tract defending the views of the minority that supported Edwards.

[^508-note2]: Edward Bromfield of Boston.

[^508-note3]: Rev. Peter Clark of Danvers.

[^508-note4]: I.e. *Misrepresentations Corrected, and Truth Vindicated* (1752).

[^508-note5]: Elisha Williams.

## C113. Peter Clark to Timothy Dwight[?], April 16, 1752 C113.P.Clark-T.Dwight 4-16-52

Peter ClarkC113. Peter Clark to Timothy Dwight[?],4/16/52. ANTS, f. 1752A, #3.

Danvers, alias, Salem Village. April. 16. 1752.

Hon rd Sir,

Yours of ye 16 th of last moneth, I receiv’d a- about a Week ago, and I take this first opportunity, that has Since occurr’d of making a Return. I am great oblig’d to you, Sir, for your kind offer once, & again of being assisting to me in Settling my interest in Stafford, & I Receiv’d a Letter from you to that purpose the Last Summer, & the Reason why I have not since written to you about it, was partly my Distance, & want of opportunity for Sending, & partly because I waited for a man in those parts whom I had trusted with some part of my business, to inform me how matters Stood at Stafford, who came not down till Late in the Fall, & from the Account I have receiv’d, I don’t apprehend at present, that my incumber’d with any such dif interest in the Lands of that Town are incumber’d with Such difficulties, as to require your Going thither to take Care of them, that I hope the trouble may be Spared, if it Shou’d prove otherwise, I will either send, or come my Self. & accept your kind assistance. Pray Sir, Let it be no matter of Concern or uneasiness, that I have not Given you the opportunity of doing the Service you design’d in Consideration of My Coming to the Council at Northampton, the I desire no other re- compence than the Continuance of your friendship, & Goodwill, and the Repeated expressions of your readiness to serve me, are more than Sufficient.

I Greatly Lament the unhappy Condition of the Church of Northampton continuing Still, I hear, in a Broken & unsettled State; I very much feared, & do still fear the consequences of their Refusal of the Chari table pacifick measures, the Council would, by Repeated attempts have Led them into; whether this their Refusal was the Result of their own inclination, & Choice, I cannot Say, or whether it pro ceeded from the overbearing influence of others, out of Jea[...] [^509-note1] sy for ye Punctilio’s of order, which doubtless in all ordinary Cases ought to take place, but when the Case is extraordinary, as whe[reby] the Constitution of a people is nigh broken, or Greatly threat[ened,] to refuse help from whatever kind hand offers it, under [pre-] tence of Zeal for any humane order, or Constitution, is quite unseasonable, & indiscreet, & perhaps the people in Northampton may be Convinced by experience, that their Conduct in O[ppo-] sition to the Council was not Acting for the Best, However[?] pressed[?] to heal the Breach in your Church, & unite you Again; under a pious, Learned, & faithful pastor. - Tho’ the Council fail’d of that most desired End in Coming to you, ye reestablishing ye Rev d Mr Edwards in his pastoral Charge, thro’ insuperable Difficultys, & Discouragem ts (as they Appear’d) thrown in the Way; yet I hope there was this Good Effect of their Determination, & advice, that thereby Divine providence made the way of their Duty more Clear, whatever to Mr Edwards, & his Adherents, whatever Acts of Selfdenial [^509-note2] & Resignation, they might be Called unto on that occasion. Sir, I am Sorry to hear that you & others, Mr Edwards’s Adherents do Still meet with trouble from your Brethren. I have made Enquiry into that Article of Charge Contain’d in the paragraph you transcrib’d to me, from the papers bro’t to me in y t Council from your church; (the papers I have not Seen Since ye Council, they being in Mr Hobby’s keeping, but I now Remember the passage you Refer to) & I fear Mr Edwards Opposers go too far upon Surmises. I have Ask’d my Son Hobart at your desire what it was he Said to Cap t Barnard About the Church at Northampton their Dismissing Mr Edwards. he Remembers he was at Cap t Barnard’s about a year Ago, (when you Came with Mr Edward’s to bring Letters to the Churches,) having Some business with him: And as the Council that was Call’d was the Subject of peoples talk he fell into Some Discourse with my Son about it. The particular words he Spake to that Gentleman he can’t Readily Call to mind, but in general, As near as he Can remember, they were to this Ef- fect, That it was tho’t it would be most for the Advantage of Re ligion if Mr Edwards was Establish’d again in his pastoral office, & that if this was once done by a Council, A Gr it was thought a Great part (he might Say the Greatest part) of his people would in time Come over to him; but he is positive that he Never Said those words in the Paragraph above mention’d; And the circumstances of caution he was under in talking with Cap t Barnard mad which he Call’d to mind, make me believe that he did not Say those words. However he went immediately to Salem to talk with Cap t Bernard about that matter. And I Sent An Extract of about 3. or 4 lines from y t Paragraph in your Letter, which contains ye Charge Exhibited against A Cer tain Gentleman, & others, & Shews the Evidence they have to Support it Comes from him. The Gentleman Seem’d Surpriz’d, & Readily Clear’d my Son, declaring he never heard him Say Any thing Like it to his Remembrance, and in a Short Le[tter] to me upon it, he has these Words viz . "As to the Paragr[...] Said to be in Coll Dwights Letter, I can only Say, I never [have] heard that particular asserted by any Person that I can re- member . . ." This, Sir, is the best Account I can Send you [on the] Particular you Desir’d information about. - I could add mu[ch] in Reference to your Affairs, & those of Mr Edwards, but you know, Sir t[...] is peculiarly tedious to me. Remember me in the Kindest terms to Mr Edwars when you See him (whom I highly Esteem from ye Little Acquain- tance I have had with him, & Pray God to bless him in all his Services for his Kingdom,) & also to his Dear Spouse & family, if residing yet at North hampton. I Sympathize with you all in your Late trial on parting.

May the God of peace & Love make your way plain, & Lead you into union & Communion with all your brethren, by removing all obstacles. I wish you, & your Family ye best of blessings. My Wife, & Daughter Send their Salutes & Respects to you, We all greatly desire to see you since we had ye happiness of a Visit from you & Mr Edwards a year ago. in the meantime,

I Rest your Sincere Friend & Humble Serv t Peter Clark.

[^509-note1]: MS damage at the end of this line and several lines following.

[^509-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

## C114. Aaron Burr to Joseph Dwight (Draft), June 26, 1752 C114.A.Burr-J.Dwight 6-26-52

Aaron BurrC114. Aaron Burr to Joseph Dwight,6/26/52. ANTS, Burr Letterbook.

New k June 26. 1752

Hon rd & dear Sr

A Line from one with whom you have So Small Acquaintance, will doubtless be unexpected, but I persuade my Self not unexceptable.

Twas no Small Disappointment to me y t I miss’d Seeing youo when at Stockbridge. And the more So as I Should have been glad to have discours’d with you on ye Situation on ye Indian Affairs there, which Seemed to be in an undesirable Situation - Twould be impertinent and altogether improper for me to attempt to give my Advice - You will allow me however to express my earnest Desire y t there Should be a Reconciliation between Mr Edwards & you. - Tis I think of very Great Importance to ye Interest of Religion especialy among the Indians. - The any Sound of your Difference does a great Deal of Hurt Abroad. The great Esteem I have for Mr Edwards, ye Prospect of being nearly related to him, And the good Opinion I have of you, from the your establish’t Character and ye Small Acquaintance I have been favoured with; Make me very desirous there Should be a cordial Friendship between you: but a Sense how much the Spreading the Gospel among ye poor Heathen depends upon it, makes me much more So.

Mrs Sergeant has given her Friends here a good Deal of Pleasure with a Short Visit, as her Departure gives em a good Deal of uneasiness. [^510-note1]

I congratulate on ye Prospect of your Alliance with So excellent a Person So Well qualified to communicate and Share the Days of a refined & virtuous Friendship. - She is high in my Esteem and has long been among the N o of my perticular Friends — I rejoice y t She has made So Wise a Choice and y t there is Such a Prospect of her being So happy and usefull in the World.

May ye best of Heavens Blessings attend you both. May your Days be Many and be filled up with much Comfort and Usefullness

I am with unfeined Respect Yr most Hu b Serv t

ABurr

[^510-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C116. Joseph Paice to Thomas Secker, July 18, 1752 C116.J.Paice-T.Secker 7-18-52

Joseph PaiceC116. Joseph Paice to Archbishop Secker,7/18/52. Lambeth Palace, London, Lambeth 1123, #61.

Sir

Last Monday I received from Mr Jonathan Edwards (who succeeds Mr Sergeant deceas’d in the Mission & School master-ship to the Indians at Stockbridge) a Letter relating to the Education of Indian Children. I have taken the freedom to inclose a Copy of it for Your perusal; & must ask Pardon for Troubling You with so Long a peice, which I should not have done, did it not appear to contain some particulars of Importance I would have sent the original, but it is wrote in a hand hardly Legible —— as I have the Original I beg you will not take the trouble to return the inclosed —— Permit me Sir farther to mention, that I do not Patronise his observation on the Episcopal Missionaries in New England; but, as that is part of his Letter, I could not avoid transcribing it with the rest.

I remain with Great Respect

Sir

Your most obedt humble Servt

Josh Paice

Cloak Lane 18th July 1752

## C117. Timothy Foxcroft to Timothy Dwight, August 4, 1752 C117.T.Foxcroft-T.Dwight 8-4-52

Timothy FoxcroftC117. Thomas Foxcroft to Timothy Dwight,8/4/52. ANTS, f. 1752A, #1. Addressed on back "For / Timothy Esq / In / Northampton."

Bost. Aug t 4. 1752.

Hon d Sr

Your acceptable Favour of May 22 d I sometime since own’d the Receit of in a short Line in the Cover to my Lett r to Mr Edwards; and your last in Company with his Packet (including the Copy for ye Press &c) is also come to hand, w ch demands new Acknow- edgements from me. But as I am obliged this Morn g to go out of Town, I have Time only for a Line; which I was not willing [-] to omit, as I understood there’s an Opport ty now for its Con- veryance. I must content my self at present with saying in a Word, —— I pity your sad Situation amidst so much Con tention & Opposition —— and I pity poor bleeding Northampton — But I hope a compassionate Saviour has Mercy in Reserve, and will yet gloriously appear, to assert his own Cause, and vindicate his own faithful Serv ts

Mr Edw ds in his last writes me nothing ab t Stockbr e Affairs. I wish they may have a taken a new Turn, to his Satisfaction -

I have dipt into his Manuscr t - and I find Mr W ms Book has appear’d to him just in ye same Light, as it did to me, full of Inconsistencies, both with Mr Stoddard’s known Principles w ch he undertook to defend, and with his own Principles as asserted in this Book of his & in other of his writings —— I truly think, the Man must be an Arminian , or very near akin to one, that will thorowly embrace some of Mr W ms Tenets in this Book, and pursue em in their just Conseq s —— And I always said pretty nigh as much of Mr Stod.’s Scheme - I remember about 10 years ago I made some such Observation to Mr Edwards, and told him how I c d make it out - To which the Answer he made, I remember, was shew shrewd, but not satisfying.

I shall take the best Care I can about the Subscription papers - I have done as Mr Edw. directed me - and now send you a Dozen - with my best Service to you & yours, and to Mr Edw. when you write to him

I am (in Haste)

Sr Yours sincere Friend

Tho. Foxcroft

## C118. Report of Committee for Managing the Affairs of the Six Nations to Spencer Phips and General Court, November 22, 1752 C118.JDwight-Phips 11-22-52

Joseph Dwight and John AshleyC118. Joseph Dwight and John Ashley to Spencer Phips,11/22/52. Mass. Archives.

To his Hon r Spencer Phips Esq r L t Governour and Commander In Cheife In & over his Majesty’s Province of the Massachusetts Bay In New England, The Hon ble his Majesty’s Councill & House of Rep tives In Gen l Court assembled Nov r 22d Anno Donum 1752 Court

The Com tee apointed by the Hon ble on the 11th Day of Octo r 1751 for Managing the Affairs of the Six Nations &c: & for carrying into Exec n the Votes and orders of this Court of the 9 th of the Same Octo r humbly beg leave to Report, That In obedience thereto, They have caused to be Erected on the School Lands in Stockbridge, accommodable to the free borading School there, [———] a Convenient School House for the Indian Boys Dimensi ons 22 —— 38 feet and 8 feet Studs, which is now well boarded and shingled & filled with Window Frames and Sashes, a good Stone Chimny with three fire places In the Same Erected and the Rafters[?] of the House Ceiled.

That they have cased Two Rooms in the S d Board =ing School to be Ceiled, Cabbins for Lodging for the Boys to be made, Stairs built, & other Accommmodations for Stores of Provisions &c &c.

That they have caused to be provided a Frame for another School house for Indian females & Children, which is now going on a Spot of Land belonging to the Heirs of the late Rev. Mr John Sergeant in Stockbridge [...] [^514-note1] [^514-note2] the Com tee were of opinion [copy poor] that a Spot [...] a Garden &c: ought first to be Purchased and one of the Com tee was of opinion that th eCourt had not expressly or impli citly authorised the Com tee to purchase such a Spot. another of the Com tee [...] not proper so [ ] that Matter [...] of the Governm nt Boards, [...] & Nails are provided towards [...] of the Same.

The Com tee [...] Report that [...] the latter End of [...] 1751 [...] from Day to Day appeared, & Desired to be Supported & Instructed in The School, about forty Mohawk Children & Youths male & female including seven Stockbridge Indian Boys, That Att that Time Capt. Martyn Kellogg had the Care & Instruction of the S d Children & Youth till About ye first Day of Feb y last, and because of some peculiar Discouragemnts That have attended the S d School and that They may appear in their True Light, The Com tee beg leave in Justice to the Cause and That Gentleman to say, That at the Desire of the S d Mr Sergeant, for Mr Holliss He first took the Care & Instruction of [...] Indian Boys at Newington, & kept them there for one year, Shut[?] In Aprill 1749, he [...] to Stockbridge with his S d Boys, had them examined as to their Profi ciency in Learning the English Language, their Reading, Catechising &c: & to Mr Sergeants great Satisfaction they were found proficient beyond his Expectation as appears by original [—] Letter which the Com tee have seen under his own hand to Mr Holliss and The Com tee are Credibly Informed That on his Death [^514-note3] Bed, & in his last Hours, he desired the S d Kellogg by no Means to Desert or leave the s d Hollisian Boys, but to continue with them at the S d Boarding School for their Instruction &c. and which he accordingly Did and supported & Instructed them for all most Two Years on his own acc tt & Risque, except a part which Col o Williams of Stockbridge, engaged for, the S d Kellogg however hoping that The s d Holliss or some other Charitable Person or Per sons would in Time appear to take off this Charge, (or at least a part thereof, which otherwise he thought would be a Burthen too heavy for him) and which the S d Holliss afterwards Did; and In the mean While as the S d Kellogg was anquainted with the Six Nations of Indians, and the Valuableness of their Country, their Ascendency & general Influence upon & over other Tribes, & was strongly perswaded of the great Advantage of Securing them in his Majesty’s Interest, & so gaining a Possession of their Country to the Crown, as a faithfull Subject of the King, & a true Lover of his Country. It appears to us That on these Principles he acted & from Time to Time took much pains by writing (and otherwise) to Col o Johnson, Hendrick & others to be com municated to the several Tribes of the S d Six nations, to perswade them If possible by many & Strong Argu ments to Continue their former Union with one another & faithfullness to the Crown of great brittain, inviting Them to bring their Children to the free Charity School of which he Now had the only Care, That by his unwearied Attention to this Affair amongst many Sufferings & Difficul ties he att length prevailed by the small help of a few others In February last upon the Mind of so many of these Tribes as That There was now at the School fifty or Upwards, &[^514-note4] several Families were come with Design to Settle There for the Advantage of their Children, And Others came to see & know the Circumstances of the School, That They might carry good News to their Tribes, All This Since there were about one hundred In All, and so It happened That Capt. Nicholas a Restless & uneasy tempered person of The Coniwage[?] Tribe, made Mis chiefe, met with & turn’d Back Hendrick with several Other Cheifes with a Number of Boys who were within Seventy Miles on their Road from their own Country coming to the School; and among those who came he Also made great uneasinesses, which when they came to be treated with by one of the Com tee and the s d Kellogg were not removed without Difficulty and probably would not have been removed att All but by the Help of the S d Kellogg, who being much Ac quainted with their peculiar Temper & Manners, was the better Able with prudence to Obviate their multiplied Objections, and reduce their minds to that State, That with abundant pleasantness, & seeming Satisfaction they gave up their Children not only to the Instruction but Correction & Discipline of the School, and expressed in the fullest manner and very particularly their Thankfulness to this Government to Mr Holliss & to Every person they knew of as con cerned to promote their Good in the Matter of the School: and Altho the Com tee Thinks the s d Kellogg has omitted some things which he might have done for the Encouragement of the School, and for ought [^514-note5] we know (for we can’t absolutely determine considering the peculiar Temper of the Indians has been to A Fault Remiss in his Government: Yet The Com tee are of Opinion consider ing the Many Difficulty’s Attending this Affair he had done att least as well as any person and perhaps better than any person less acquainted with these People could have done, and That It was prudent and reasonable for him to tarry Att the Boarding School after Mr Hawley the Master provided by the Commissioners arrived there in order faithfully to Discharge his Duty to Mr Holliss, and we were especially well pleased with his Story there as he appear d: to us to be of a genius and Temper peculiarly adapted & of a much more than common Capacity Disposition and hearty good Will in this Cause to serve the Interest of the Crown and this Province in particular —— yet so It has happened from Causes to us unknown and un -accountable, That from a Strong Disaffection in the minds of Diverse persons in publick Employment in that Town & some in the School, That he has met with Violent Opposition, Affronts & Abuses —— and particularly on thte Lords Day the 19 th of Aprill last, the Minister after Divine Service publickly said to the Indians, That He had something of Consequence to say to sa to them and Desired They would meet him the next Day at The School House, and Then said That If any of the English People desired to be present They might.

They accordingly met and at the Opening of the s d [^514-note6] Meeting the Minister Said to The Indians to this purpose —— "That He understood That many of Them at The Time of Wheat Harvest went into the Dutch Country to labour, That That was a place of Temptation to them Especiall, to drink to Excess & advised them not to go and he further Said That he had heard That some of their Young Men talked of going to Oswego & he advised them to the Contrary, for the Same Reason: [—————————] [————————————————————] [——————————] Mr Hawley the Master of the Mohawk Schook Then stood up and said to the Indians & the Parents of a Number of Youths & Children under the Care of Capt Kellogg Att The Charge of Mr Holliss to be supported and Educated That he Thought their Children were not well governed nor Instructed and advised Them to them their Children from the School & Then One Benjamin Ashley stood and said to them to the same pur -port, & L t Woodbridge an Open & avowed Enemy (If we may believe him) to the S d Kellogg and to whom the Indians are apt to give Ear said, That If Things were as the said Hawley & Ashley had reported, he Also advised the Parents to take away their Children from the School

This we have from his own mouth and thing advised[^514-note7] to was immediately put in practice Seven of the Boys within a few days wholly deserted the School and Several of them have told the Com tee that they did it upon this advise

Now these measures the Com tee are humbly of oppinion were premiditated & Concerted by all the affore named per- sons with design So far as they tho: t proper to break up the Said Hollisian Schook and by the Same rule if their Judgmetns were for it they might at their pleasure as rightfully break up the whole School and far this and other like practices which have been done there have a tendency to defeat Mr Hollis ’s Charity and both the Charity and political views of this Government in their measures to Support a School there we leave

The Com tee beg leave further to report that In ye latter End of January last there being then fifty or more Indian Children and Youths male & female at the Board- ing School & no regular School as yet Set up for want of a master tho Capt Kellogg was there affording them what instruction he Could which were but few & in a poor manner by reason of his many avocations to other matters relating to ye Indians one of the Com tee was at the expence of a Journey of his Son of Two hundred & Sixty miles out & home to procure the Said Hawley for a master for the Boys & about ye Begin of [———] February he arrived at Stockbridge & on the next day or two after the Rev d Mr Edwards tho: he might reasonably Expect the Com tee there that day; as thte Com tee are fully informed he introduced the Said master in the School and placed the Said Ashley as an assistant Instructor in ye School a person in the Service & pay of the Government for other purposes bt never thot of by any one of the Com tee that we know of for this Service & in the opinion of the Com tee a person very unsuitable for it being by many accounted in principle what is Called at this day a Separatist, & great Enthusiast, & has lattely as the Com tee are informed Called one or more religious Indian meetings & placed himself at the head thereof as an Instructor and for reasons too many to be enumerated the Com tee have not employed [^514-note8] him for Several months past but were loath to use forcable means to drive him away least Some of the Indians Zealously affected to him Should perhaps for no good reasons Should take Umbradge a it and a general uneasiness be Created among them by this Instance of the ministers Conduct and Several Circumstances that attended it the Com tee apprehend Several mischiefs have arose

Suitable lodgings & provisions for the master of every kind were Seasonably provided & he was told by the Com tee that if at any time things for his Comfort (as he Said he was much of an Invalid) were wanting he might Send the Said Ashley who was in the pay of the Province among any of the neighbours in Stockbridge or Elsewhere as far as Sheffield for Supplys & the Com tee would See the expence paid & tho: he Seemed Satisfied with this provision made for him & was desired to take up his Lodgings at the Boarding School agreeable to the vote of the Court yet the Com tee Cant learn that he has ever done it for more than two or three nights from the first of his Coming in February last to this day by this means the Indian Children & English Houghs were left intirely at a loss from that regular & orderly family Government which was originally designed in the founding of that School: & which the Com tee apprehend was agreeable to the Intention of the Court to have put in practice hereby diverse advantages to s d Childrren have been lost, & ye Parents f the English youths after an Expence to get them there finding themeselves disappointed & the youths discouraged for want of a ead & Governour to protext (as well as direct) them among So Great a number of ungoverned Indian Boys they were oblidged to take them from the School & the Com tee apprehend that by the absence of the master and English youths and the want of that orderly family which the Master Should have kept the Indian Boys made no progress in their learning of the English lan- -guage & Customs & in their Morals in proportion to what might otherwise have reasonably been Expected from this and other Conduct of the Master it appears Evident to the Com tee that he has not only neglected & Slighted their advice to him but has also disregarded the mind & Sence of the Court with which he was acquainted in this & oher matters relating to [^514-note9] the School evidently Submitting himself from his first entrance there to the Gent: n who introduced him who (as the Said master Said) thought he had the direction of the School as wel as the Courts Com tee tho: the Com tee don’t find by the orders & votes of the Court which they have taken for the rule of their Conduct & which expressly authorise them to instruct & regulate that School, and manage all the prudentials thereof Subject to Such direc- tions & instructions as they Should from time to time receive from this Court that that person or any other is Joyn d to act with them, much less are they able to discern that he or any other particular person or persons are authorised to Criminate, Contradict oppose & Counter- act the measures reasonably persued by the Com tee in Conformity and obedience to ye general Courts orders which however has been frequently done & particularly have Endeavours been used with workmen Employed by the Com tee to desist their Labours pretending that what they are Employed about was not agreeable to the mind of the Government & that they would never be paid for it

Now the Com tee are humbly of oppinion that by multiplied managements of this Kind & by evil surmisings & Such tatlings as well as violent & open opposition against the Com tee & more Especially against Capt Kellogg that School which appeared in the most fair prosperous & desirable Circumstances till Such a temper & practice appeared has from that time in the general Sensibly decayed & Tens have been reduced to Units yet the Com tee don’t think, that the low state of this School is to be imputed altogether to these things but partly to a new & profitable business of Gathering the root Called Ginseng to which the Indians were invited early in [^514-note10] thte Sumer & partly to a general Sickness which prevailed among them at Stockbridge in the Course & more Especially in the Latter End of thte Summer

And the Com tee further report that in Obedience to the order of Court they in December last made an d agreement & parole for a Considerable part of the Lands Called the hop-lands for which they were to give Equivalents in Poovine[?] Lands but as thet Season would not admit of Completing that agreement till the Spring of the year & the Difficultys & Discouragements before hinted at appearing in the latter End of winter & Continuing occasioned Still a delay Yet as the Indians in the Spring manifested a desire & forwardness to go upon the Said lands at their desire the Com tee Caused about nine or ten acres of the Said lands to be fenced & Brok up most of which the Indians planted but late whereby it was exposed to Early frosts So that tho: the Corn was flourishing & good yet perhaps not more than one half Came to maturity Yet what Corn the people raisd at this place and on the Boarding School lands the Com tee are of opinion may be near a Sufficiency for the year fo rthose now there which are thirty Eight in number but as the Indians have Since Said nothing of going there and there appearing to the Com tee So man Curcum stances rendering the Success of the Affair in general Doubtfull they thot it advisable not to persue the Said purchase for he present The Com tee have further to say That as They under took [^514-note11] this Service with views to serve the publick Good so they have according to the best of their Discretion and prudence faithfully pursued It, and The Discourage ments attending the Affair have been their constant Griefe however the can’t but humbly hope that The Wisdom of this Court will find Ways under the Divine Conduct to remove The Discouragements & Difficulties suggested And If nothing of that Nature can be effected They shall utterly Dispair of being any further Serviceable in this Cause and pray That They may be excused accordingly. Yet in Case of any New and fair Prospect of that Advantage to the Crown & Plantations and this Province In particular & the poor Ignorant & Hea- then Nations which They wish for and apprehend may yet be obtained, by well concerted Measures vigorously pursued may still Cheerfully obey the Courts further Orders and as in Duty Bound will ever pray

Joseph Dwight

John Ashley

[Notation in different hand:]

In Council December 13. 1752

Read & Ordered that Joseph Wilder, John Otis & Jabez Fox Esq rs with such as the hon ble House shall appoint be a Committee to take into Consideration this Report & Report as soon as may be to this Court what [-] Proper to be done thereon

Sent down for Concurrence

Tho s Clark Dp ty Secry

## C119. Memorial of Stockbridge Inhabitants to Spencer Phips and General Court, [After November 1752] C119.Woodbridge-Phips aft11-52htm

Timothy Woodbridge, Stockbridge InhabitantsC119. Timothy Woodbridge & Inhabitants of Stockbridge to Spencer Phips, n.d. [after 11/52]. Mass. Archives. In hand of Timothy Woodbridge, with original signatures of English and Indian inhabitants.

To his Honour Spencer Phips Esqr. Lieut Governour, & commander

in chief, in & over his Majesys Province, of the Massachusetts Bay in New-

England. And to the Honrbl his Majesties council, & house of Repretes

in general court convened at Boston.

The memorial of the inhabitants of Stockbridge, Humbly sheweth that about

Sixteen years ago, the great & general court of his province, made a grant of land

in this wilderness to us; of about twenty three thousand acres, two thousand & four

hundred of Sd land was allow'd for the english Settlements; and four hundred more

was purchased of a proprietor of upper housatonnock, whose right fell in that part

of Said Upper housatonnock, (viz) the north part that was taken of from Sd Town-

ship, to make part of the Township of Stockbridge, this quantity of land was original-

ly granted to Six english Settlrs, which are now augmented to twelve, exclu-

sive of the present ministers family, near one half of Stockbridge belonged the

proprietors of upper Housatonnock, about three Square miles of Said half, the

Indians procured by exchanging their lands, which they reserv'd in the

Township formerly called the lower Housatonnock, on which they liv'd in the

time Stockbridge was granted. The other half, (viz) the north part of

the Town was claimed by several Indians, by a native right, whom to

make easy the Indians, and english, in order to bring the whole into

a common propriety, was obliged to advance a Sum of money ---

Sixty pounds our old Tenr., to satisfy these original claimers, So that

about two thirds of the Town was procured, by the Inhabitants by the

exchange of land, & the payment of money, before we could peacably

possess the grant made us by the great & general court.-------

These things being amicably settled, among us with considerable cost &

pains, we hop'd a foundation was laid for future peace, being sensible that

our Situation & circumstances in a peculiar manner obliges us

hereto. And as we have been Sedulous & carefull, to promote peace,

and harmony, among ourselves, so we could with ease & pleasure

maintain it, if we were not in a very extraordinary manner broken

in upon, by some persons who have of late taken up their residence in this

Town. When the Late Revrd Mr. Sergeant propos'd to us, who are the chief

proprietors of this Town, his scheme of setting up a free boarding school

in this place, and his desire tha twe would provide a tract of Land ac-

comadable for the Same, his arguments to obtain so valuable and large

a tract of our land was, that our children should have the benefit

of it, and that Mr Hollis would Support & educate a number of our

children. On such a Proposal, we yielded up the land The Said Mr Sergeant

unhappily for the peace & comfort of this Town, introduced one Mr

martin Kellogg to be the School master, in Said boarding school.

Both Mr Sergeant, & we, were at the first introduction of Said Kellogg[^515-note1]

unacquainted with his qualifications, temper & disposition, tho we

have had opportunity Since, to determine that he is not a Suitable

person for the business he is employ'd in any of the before men-

tioned respects: and we have good evidence that Mr Sergeant viewed

him in the same light, for Some of us know very well, that

he was looking out for another master, a little before his

death, and had actually had conversation with a young Gen-

tleman, of a liberal education, to undertake the school.

Several of your memorialists put their children into this New school

upon Mr Sergeants desire, but not we apprehend to their advantage

Especially since Mr Sergeants death, those few of our children that

have been at Mr Kelloggs school at turns sometimes having

five or six, sometimes two or three, & Sometimes none; have

been left at very loose ends as to their education they have

neither been dieted, clothed, or instructed, in industry or any

other usefull knowledge, as we espected when And as we had

assurances of when we deliver'd our children to be instruct-

ed by Sd Kellogg. Excepting two or three that have had

considerable part of their instruction in the Town school; that

have made some proficiency in reading only there is but little

effected by the large sum Mr Hollis has remitted here from

year to year. The children that have been instructed at the boarding

school, have appear'd to make no progress, in civility & vertue

but have rather declin'd, living an idle life, and much without

government, has tended much to their being more [---------]

uncivil and mischievous in their conduct, & behaviour. we have found[^515-note2]

this to be the case with our children & the Mohawks begin loudly to

complain of he increase of unrulyness in their children.

And we cant but express our wonder, at the odd measures that are gone

into by Sd Kellogg, in order, we must think, to impose on mak-

kind; which is when any persons of distinction, come into the Town

to set these two three young men to read a lesson, pretending that

others that have been instructed for Sixteen, or Seventeen, years are

equal in their proficiency to these, whereas many ten years

ago as forward as they be now. But this being the produce, of thousands

of pounds; the best must be made of altho the world be impos'd

upon thereby. And we begg leave further, to express our Surprize, at

## the

Strange report, prefer'd to the great and general respecting the affairs [^515-note3]

and people, of, Stockbridge, by Coll Dwight and Capt Ashley which

they prefer'd to the great & general court, at their Session in Novem-

ber last. These gentleman have often express'd their sense of Capt

Kelloggs conduct, in a very different manner, from what they

have done in the Said report. When and by what means these gen-

tlemen, made the discovery, of Capt Kelloggs great knowledge,

of the value of the country of the western tribes of Indians; his

extraordinary talents, & prudence, in the management of Indian

affairs, his Zeal for the crown, and the good of this province.

We must confess ourselves at an intire loss: and must remain so

till Something appears to manifest this late to others, as well as to

them. Tis manifest that both these Gentlemen have view'd Mr Hollis's

cause in a suffering condition, and have often expressed their dissatisfac-

tion with the Sd Kelloggs conduct, relating hereto. Indeed Coll

Dwight of late has chang'd his voice; but in as much as Capt

Ashley has ever Since he has had concern at the boarding school,

from time to time declar'd himself dissatisfied both with the cond

conduct, & accomps, of Sd Kellogg, we must charitably beleave

that he remains so still. And it is certain that Capt Ashely; has

manifested his disapprobation of setling the female boarding

school, on Mrs Dwights land, repeatedly and long since Coll

Dwight has carried the materials for building the same to that

place. The representation made to the great & general court as if the

inhabitants of this town, or any of them, had been guilty of crimi

nizing, contradicting, counteracting, and violently opposing the gene-

ral courts Committee: especially Capt Kellogg; That endeavours

have been us'd with workmen to desist from their labour, that by

multiplied managements of this kind, together with tattlings and evil

surmisings, which have tended to defeat the charitable designs of Mr

Hollis, & the political views of the government. These [-----] are

very harsh, they sound very ill, And we apprehend no manner of

foundation for such a representation, but we satisfied it was done

with an intent to Stir up the resentment of the court, without cause against

us: which we look upon as the most injurious treatment; Since it

is manifest to us us that these Gentlemen endeavoured to palm these

and many other things upon the great and general court, that have

no foundation, in truth; to gain the courts interposition that they might

## the

The better, and more Successfully, carry on their personal, & intrigu[?][^515-note4]

ed Schemes. Their representing a design premidat[at]ed, & concerted,

by certain parsons, to break up the Hollisian school, is a Mere

fiction: much like the school itself. The account they gave the court

of a hundred Mohocks, residing here, and fifty children in

the school, is a mere chimera; a thing that we never had any

reason to believe existed. Thare was in the beginning of Mr

Hawleys Setting up the school, for a little space something more

than thirty, including several grown persons that attended

the school: but this appearance was soon ended: but not as is

unjustly represented, by means of an opposition by the people

of this Town, to the Comtee & Capt Kellogg. And their tens was

never reduced to units by any such methods. But if it ever came

to pass; it was by other means. If the gentlemen have not mistook

in their calculation, it is most like, their number was reduced

by the impolitick and rangling conduct, of the managers: for

we affirm it as a truth, that we have not oppos'd the Comtee in

any thing, respecting their business as Such, neither is thare one

Mohock the less here by means of any thing that we have done

nor has our conduct had, (that we know of,) the least tendency to lessen

their number. [----] we have reason to fear, the conduct of these

Gentlemen, will prove a reason, why thare will not be any here

in a little time. We hope we are not behind hand with the Comtee

themselves, and Capt too. in revering honouring and obeying

the supreme authority of this province. We, esteem their protection

a high and valuable previledge, and their resentment a very

great calamity, and we never intend justly to deserve it:

and we cant but account them our enemies, who would

bring this misery upon us. We confess our ignorance to be such

respecting Capt Kellogggs being here, we did not know that

thare was any order of government relating to him:

and Still apprehend thare is not; but conclude Mr Hollis to be

his principal & Sole improver, and on whose account only

he resides here. And we being so Scituate, as continually

to observe the state and condition of his affairs: And it has ap-

pear'd to us for some years pass'd it has been under such poor

cir

circumstances, so miseraly managed, that there has been a great mis-[^515-note5]

applycation of that Gentlemens money, and his Noble and generous

designs almost, if not quite defeated; thereby we under this view of things,

veryly tho't it our duty, as friends to that Gentleman, who is at so extraordina-

ry a charge, to promote Christian knowledge in these parts, to give him

some notice of what we knew of the bad condition of his affairs, which

we did in the following words. -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- --

'Revd & Honoured Sr. Considering the right you have to proper information

'of the State of your affairs, in this place, for the support of which, you are

'with so extraordinary a charity & generosity, at so great expence, and that

'it is impossible you should have any information, but what must come

'originally from some tha live on the spot. We the subscribers who have

'been a long time inhabitants of the Town of Stockbridge, have thought our-

'selves called in providence, to inform you, that it has been very manifestly

'our observation, that your money that has been expended at the boarding

'school here, since Mr Sergeants death, has not in any good measure answer-

'ed your generous, & pious, intentions, of promoting knowledge, religion,

'civility, & industry among the ignorant, & barbarous Heathen: and we have

'reason to think from what has been very observable, of late, that it has been

'so improved, as rather to be a great hindrance to those good designs, and even

'to the great wrong, of the religious interests, of this place in general; And the

'affair of Capt Kelloggs continuance here, at your charge, since Mr Hawleys

'coming, which has been without any visible, Stated, employment, which

'Has to our observation, been matter of great offence to good people in gene

'ral, in these parts of New England, wo have occasion to observe it.

'And tis very manifest many ways, that you cannot be safe in the ex-

'pence of your moneys here, without committing them to the care

'of the Commisrs in Boston, who are wise & faithfull men, and not

'interested in the misunderstandings that subsist between some per-

'sons of distinction in this western part of New England, about our

'affairs. Or in committing them to some other faithfull trustees.

'We say these things with much regret, having no disposition to injure

'any perticular persons Character, either as to their prudence or fidelity,

'our giving this information, we assure you, Sr, is not from any such

'disposition, but as we hope from a regard to the honour of God,

'& justice to you, and from regard to the interest of the important

'affair of the instruction of the Indians in this place, which di-

'vine providence has of late given the most fair, and happy oppor-

'tunities for And which we hope might still be gloriously ad-

'vanced, if proper measures were taken.

We give the honourable court the trouble of this transcript, because we

understand that some of the Honrble members appear dissatisfied

at this conduct of ours. In this we had no design of intermeddling

in the affairs of government, or doing any thing that should prove [^515-note6]

a disadvantage to the design of the instruction of the Indians

for that is a thing we have a disposition from our hearts, to promote

And as none can tax us with a conduct contrary to such a pretence,

it was mere clamour to represent us, the people of this Town as

being any ways instrumental, of confounding the affair of Set

Settling the Mohocks in this government. But on the contrary, we

have on all occations manifested, a forwardness to promote it, we

have Shewn ourselves friendly, to the strangers that come among

us, nor have we endeavoured to disaffect them to any, and if they

are so, it is from their own observations. And notwithstanding

we aprehend, we have a just & legal title to the fee of the land in

this Town, we have been willing to suffer Several inconvenien-

ces, in opening a way to receive the Mohocks, till the govern-

ment should provide for them, they have had the use of the

School lands, for two years, that we & our children fitted for

cultivation, and other lands we have provided Since their com-

ing among us, that they have had the use of, and we have

often assisted them in labour, to get something for their sup-

port. But still we must be traduc'd as the authors of ruining

the design; we think this treatment very ill & Severe, and impos'd

on us, the better to answer anotherr design, those gentlemen have

in view. For we can as well account, for their Threatning to give us

a blow on one side, when they intend to strike us on the other, as

we can conceive, how Coll Dwight, & Capt Ashley, have occation to

change their Sentiments about men & things so Suddenly; one while

applauding The Revrd Mr Edwards, as the most Suitable, & capable

person, that could be found for the business he is employed in.

And Capt Kellogg as utterly unfit for the service that he is

employ'd If these gentlemen, pass'd this judgment before they

were acquainted with the merit of the men, this proves that

they were at least too hasty, & precipitant in their judg-

ment. But if it be as Coll Dwight has declar'd, that his high

opinion of Mr Edwards, was founded on a twenty years

acquaintance, we are left at an utter loss to know, why all at

once, he Shifts sides, and becomes an enemy to Mr Edwards.

And now he is an unfit person of no service, nor like to be

Serviceable, here in the work of the Ministry in this place.

Nor any pains, or representations, must be spar'd now, to render

him of a character unsuitable for this service, representing him very[^515-note7]

unjustly: without any reasonable foundation that we can imagine as

a troublesome person, a busibody in other mens matters, one whom

the Indians disaffect, whose preaching is Short, and unintelligible,

and that the Indians are not like to gain much knowledge from

his instructions. Altho he stands approv'd by the Honrble & Revrd

Commisrs whose, approbation, of the qualifications of their

missionaries, have ever been esteem'd Sufficient till now.

And is esteem'd by the inhabitants of the Town, both english, and

Indians, as a faithfull and good minister, in whom we take in-

tire satisfaction. And we think it a very extradinary piece of

conduct, in Coll Dwight, Capts Williams, & Kellogg, that they

should so resolutly undetake to deprive us of a minister, that

we have the highest value of.

Two of these Gentlemen have no real esate in the Town, and

are but just inhabitants among us, and Neither of them have

been at cost or pains, in procuring or Settling the Minister.

And it looks very ill to us, that Coll Dwight, and Capt Kellogg,

should take so much upon them, respecting this church and

congregation, as to determine against our choice of a minister,

seeing, they don't properly belong to either. We think this is an

unreasonable, and violent breaking in upon our previledges

ecclesiastical previledges, and has a great tendency to per-

petuate our disturbances, and to bring us into a broken,

and miserable circumstances. And we have great and just rea-

son to complain to the Honourable court, of the conduct of these Gentle

men, whose restless haughty and Selfish conduct, we veryly think to be

the foundation of all our difference, and the calamity we Suffer thereby.

They are offended, because we don't view them in the same light that they view

themselves: proper persons to lord it over us, whose conduct must never be tho't

amiss by any of us; and like lame dupes not only quietly to suffer them

to break this church in pieces, & to thro' this Town & church into the

utmost Confusion, by removing the Minister; which we have so

lattely Settled to the Satisfaction of the whole Town, but would

have us yield up our judgments in the same manner.

We have no controversy with those Gentlemen with respect to the business

that they are employ'd in, but only as they trouble the Society in taking

upon them to act those things that don't belong to them, as e

know of in any capacity at all. Indeed they are the men that are

medlers, in other mens matters, tho they endeavour unjustly to render us

odious by charging this upon us, allowing themselves in that, which they

condemn in another. Indeed we judge, and as things appear to us, & we [^515-note8]

cant judge otherways, that with all the great expence of the province;

and [--] what Mr Hollis has been at too, thare is very little effected

in carrying into execution the designs of either. We who gave the lands

for the encouragement of the school, have yet seen no appear-

ance, of any thing that was promised us, when we were apply'd

to for Said lands, but has hitherto serv'd rather for a retreat of

persons that set themselves against the good of the Inhabitants

of the Town, some commanding it as the agents of the Govern-

ment, and others as Mr Holliss. Tho we never heard of its being ap-

propriated in either of these ways. Nor ever gave the Lands on

other conditions then that if we did not find matters conducted

as was promised, the Land should revert to us again, which

Mr Sergeant gave us his promise. Mr Woodbridge has propos'd

to us the governments expectations of Sd lands being se-

cur'd for the use of the school, we are willing to comply with

this, provided it be not a place of contention, & confusion, as it

has hitherto been, and is like to be, So long as the persons that

are upon retain their dispositions. which are we apprehend to

deprive us of our liberty, and priviledges, as free Subjects of the

government, and rather than not bow & buckle us to their schemes,

would overturn & bring to an end, all the designs of promoting

christian knowledge among us. We don't pretend to any right to

order in the affair that belong to these Gentlemen, much less would

we do any thing that should hinder the good design intended. They

are accountable to their principals, and we only think we have

a right to inform them, and to defend ourselves against any

ill contrivance, they may be carrying on against us.

We are tired with contention, and the calamities that attend it

we waited on Coll Dwight soon after his return from Boston,

desir'd him to give His reasons for engaging to Zealously

to remove the minister we are he has no right to do and that

it cant be effected without injuring his Character, & usefull

ness in the world more than would be done conistent with

justice, we propos'd to him if he had reasons that were Sufficient

we would attend to them, but if he had not we hop'd to convince

him, that he was acting an unreasonable part, but he

treated us with contempt; and told us that we came in an odd

manner, and upon an errand as odd, that he was not oblig'd to give

us his reasons, but let us know, that he did not think Mr Edwards

would be usefull among us, Tho he might have been he told

If we had perswaded our minister, (not his) timely to have fallen[^515-note9]

in with his Schemes, which if he had have been perswaded into, we en-

tertaining the same opinion of that Gentlemans Schemes, that

we have hitherto done, we Should be as willing for his dismission

as he is. We know not how Coll Dwight, would make him more usefull,

he gift of tongues or any other miraculous power, he has not to be-

stow. And he stands in no need of his assistance, to be an able, faith-

full, & painfull minister: for he justly Sustains that Character already.

But we think the Gentleman must mean if anything, that if Mr

Edwards had but have prostituted his judgment, at all perad-

ventures to that Gentlemans, & Capt Kelloggs Schemes, he

would have given him a different to the world, then what he

has lately done. Thus we have as truly and plainly as we can

laid before the Honourable Court, the miserable State and Con-

dition of the Town by reason of these unhappy contentions.

Humbly praying that the great & general Court would

be pleas'd according to their great wisdom & goodness to in-

terpose for our relief, that we may with peace & quietness,

enjoy our rights, & previledges, both civil and religious,

according to our Excellent constitutions; And your

memorialist Shall as in duty bound Ever pray &c

Timothy Woodbridge enKaukewenaknaunt[^515-note10]
