## C121a. Gideon Hawley to Joseph Bellamy, April 14, 1753 C121a.GHawley-Bellamy 4-14-53

Gideon HawleyC121a. Gideon Hawley to Joseph Bellamy,4/14/53. MS 81528a, Hartford Seminary Foundation. Two folio leaves.

Stockbridge Munday 14 th Ap l 1753

Rev d & very dear Sir (a private Letter)

Tis very crossing to undergoe the disappointment of not seing y o this Spring; I have been pleasing myself for Mounths past with y e Prospect of it; There is no man in the World y t I want to see half so much. I have a great many private tho’ts y t I can’t disclose to any Body in y e World but you; I want to see y o y t I may open my Difficulties and tell y o my whole Heart for I can’t trust (at least) I can’t feel free to trust any but y o. M r Ed ws & Mad m act y e part of Frnds & parents to me but I don’t feel free to tell’em all my Sentiments & all y e burdens of my Mind. I could give you my reasons for it but I’ll not trouble y o with those things —— I am about to Leave my Native Country & my dear Frnds, & going to a barbarous ignorant uncultivated Nation. I expected a Companion but he fails. M r Breinard [^518-note1] talks of going but I believe it will End in talk —— ’tis a sinking thing y t no body is willing to engage in this aff r but I must undertake it alone, and I am almost worn out already riding & fatuaging about, I have very little Time to Study & make improvemts —— very dear Sir y o helped to introduce me to this Business and I don’t know but I Shall petition for y r assistance to get me out of it again tho’ I heartily Love y e Indians & wish well to y r precious Souls, and if I could have a prospect of great & extraordinary Servicable- ness among ’em I will gladly encounter all difficulties, but then I must have an honourable Support. I must have more than 70 £ Sterling or I can’t make it do among ’em which M r Edwards says y e Commis rs will not give. I must also have a good Companion, such a one as would be a Comfort to me in every respect, for if y e aff r dies with me (which will be in a few years time I Live here alone) it will not be worth while for me to to Sacrifice my Life for y e little good y t is like to be done among ’em —— I find y t my Constitution is not made with brass tho’ my resolution will carry me prodegious lenghths, yet I now want a recruit —— I wish M r Edwards could take in these things, I wish you would urge y e need y t I Shall Stand in of a Companion &c. and if upon y e whole you Judge y t I am not like to live Comfortably & usefully, I must intreat y o to use y r influenced to settle me some where else —— or at least declare y r Sentimts to ——— who may influence in this aff r - I am not now in a malon- choly mode these are my Sentimts in my Brightest moments - I ask y r prayers for me, y t y e Divine Blessing & presents may attend me in this very Difficult Business & give me Strenght of Body & mind.

If [^518-note2] alive & well hope to see you next fall and tell you my Sentiments about a great many Things, in the mean Time let w t I have suggested in this rest in y r own Breast: between y o & I let it be just hinted y t tis very possible y t I shall never settle among y e Indians and I act upon certain maxims some of which I learnt of you and which I look upon to be agreable to reason: however I desire you’ld enquire of M r Edwards w t y e State of things is like to be so far as he is capible of informing [-] y o (for he does not know so much about many Difficulties y t will attend y e aff r as I do) and prepare his mind if you to [—] have me decline the Service if I am not like to be settled usefully & Comfortably; I must in= treat y o to insist upon it as not a prudential thing for me to settle among y e Indians without some great good is like to be answer’d and I can be settled comfortably ; you know w t Difficulties M r Breinard [^518-note3] under went, & how it wore him out - my Constitution is not so good as his was. I leave it all with you - I remember y r many favours with the Sincerest gratitude to y r self & Mad m I don’t [know] [^518-note4] whether ever I Shall see y o this Side Heaven — farewell

———— Rev d & very dear Sir I am y rs affectionably & cordially-

G. Hawley

M r Edwards & Mad m are cordial & disinterestly Frndly I would not by any thing I have s d suggest any thing otherwise

[^518-note1]: John Brainerd.

[^518-note2]: Here begins the text on the verso; Hawley skipped half of the page before commencing.

[^518-note3]: David Brainerd.

[^518-note4]: Hawley’s omission.

## C122. Timothy Dwight to Timothy Foxcroft, June 6, 1753 C122.Dwight-Foxcroft 6-6-53

Timothy DwightC122. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft,6/6/53. Yale Manuscripts and Archives, Dwight Family Papers, B. 1, f. 1, #4. Addressed on back "To the Rev, rd / Mr Thomas Foxcroft / In / Boston." Underlining by Foxcroft.

Northampton June 6 th: 1753

Rev rd Sr

I Rec d Yours of the 7 th of May last, for which I thank You, have nothing new to write, we are govern'd by the Old Spirit of Anarchy still, we have now one Mr Hooker [^519-note1] in view, have pass'd a vote to hear him as A probationer, & am apt to think Utmost Efforts will be used to Obtain him, I Esteem him to be Superior to any we have had before him, he is a descend t from the famous Hooker of Hartford, he is Sought by Pomfret people & has promis'd I hear to preach there, if he has Opportunity its likely will Settle there, I cant think it will be Safe for him to Settle here, till Providence has taken us in hand & given us A new Apprehension of our State, & the means of our being brought into it, Mr Edw ds. is now here, A few of us obtain'd his consent to preach tomor

row at 5:o th Clock P M in A private A Sort of Neuter one. C. Hunt

mov'd & Accomplish'd his going to preach at the meeting house in publick, what number of hearers he will have is yet unknown, it's likely he may preach All or part of the day next Sabbath, & has already consented to preach A publick Lecture next Wednesday what Effect these things may have I cant tell I am Con

=stantly looking out for Some new things I desire Yo r prayers

for this people, & for me, I pretty much Expect to move down the river out of the Govern t (viz) to Enf d, or Suffield, am not yet fully determined, Mr Edwards will no doubt write to You at this time our case Appears awfull to me being as I Esteeme it in a State of ruin & no proper Sense of it I am Rev rd Sr Yo r most Humb le & obed t

Serv t Tim o Dwight

To the Rev rd Mr Foxcroft——

[^519-note1]: John Hooker, who was ordained at Northampton on Dec. 5, 1753.

## C123. Aaron Burr to Abigail Williams Sargeant Dwight (Draft), [c. Fall 1753] C123.A.Burr-A.Dwight Fall53

Aaron BurrC123. Aaron Burr to Abigail Williams Sargeant Dwight, n.d. draft [c. fall 1753?]. ANTS, Aaron Burr Letterbook. Note that in the fall of 1753 the Stockbridge Church ordered Abigail Dwight and members of her family to appear for a hearing.

Mad m

I am Suprized to hear y t ye Story ab t ye Letter I writ you wrote Me is revived again. And much more So to hear you endeavor to fix ye Imput n of Falsehood on Mad m Ed: & my Wife - And to persuade People they were the Authors of Inventors of y t Story - —— The Charge is utterly unjust —— — I think my Self bound in Justice to them which I Should if they were Stranger to me . to declare y t I was the Author of y t Report —— I cant pretend to recollect ye Words, but it was to this Purpose viz -

I did indeed apprehend it to be So from y r Lett r Tho upon a Review I did not find So much in y r Lett r to Support Such a Thoug t as I Have imagind there was —— I now[?] far from Justifying my Self in what I Said —— I can only Say with gr t Sincerity I had no Desire or though t of doing ye least Injury to y r Ch r - I can but think you bound in Justice to Mad m & my Wife to take of ye Aspersion from broug t on y r Ch rs and to let the World know they were not ye Authors of y t rep t.

And Since you have Made free in sharing y t Lett r, I desire you would Share it or a

Copy of it to Mr Edw ds.

## C124. Esther Edwards Burr to Mary Edwards Dwight, December 2, 1753 C124.EEBurr-MEDwight 12-2-53

Esther Edwards BurrC124. Esther Edwards Burr to Mary Edwards Dwight,12/2/53. ANTS, f. 1753A, #1. Addressed on back "To / M rs Mary Dwight / at / Northampton."

Newark Decem ber th 2. 1753.

Dear Sister

I much wonder that we never have any Letters from you. I am Sure you have Some oppertunities if you were disposed to improve them.- if it is but one line Just to tell whether you are dead or alive, it would be much better than nothing. but perhaps you don’t think any thing abot us - tho I cant think So of you in ernest. —— I am throu the goodness of God in a very comforttable State of helth - I Suppose more Fleshy an Fresh than ever you Saw me in your life. [^521-note1] tho Just now I have a very bad cold and cough - You don’t know nor cant think how much I want to See you - so pray Send me word whether you don’t think of coming into the Jersys next Spring —— I want to hear what you are a doing at Northampton - I hear you are about to Settle Mr Hooker, [^521-note2] but I don’t know how true it is I wonder you cant Send a body word what you are about —— you might go to England and back again before we Should hear one word of it - I wonder if your House is finished, and a hundred other Shuch things -- M rs Sarah Prince is come to winter with me, tho now She is in Newyork —— they are in a Sad Jumble there, I Suppose you have heard before this time that Mr Commins is dismised and Mr Pem- berton [^521-note3] is like to leve them for Boston —— I have not much news to tell you but I tell all I can think of ——— M rs Brainerd [^521-note4] has got a fine Daughter —— I have been to Princeton this fall and am much pleased with the place — I wish Mr Dwight had a good Settlement there instead of Northampton - O I had like to have forgot it - I hear Mr Dwight is made Colonel - I wish him Joy ——— Mr Burr is well Joyns me in Affectinate regards to you and Brother, and Humble Service to Colo’ Dwight and his Wife —— Wishing you all the Comforts of this Life, and the blessings of another

I remain your ever affectionate and Loving Sister.

Esther Burr

P S Luch and Timo’ Send their Love. pleas to give my Service to Mr Mather. [^521-note5] and to all other friends that enquire after me - Adeu —E B.

[^521-note1]: She was to give birth to a daughter, Sarah, on May 3, 1754.

[^521-note2]: John Hooker was settled at Northampton on Dec. 5, 1753.

[^521-note3]: Alexander Cummings and Ebenezer Pemberton were colleague pastors of the First Presbyterian Church in New York City, both dismissed in Oct. 1753, Cumming having served there since 1750 and Pemberton since 1727. After preaching in Brunswick, N.J. from 1753-1761, Cummings went to the Old South Church in Boston till his death in 1763, while Pemberton was settled at the New Brick Church in Boston from 1754 till his death in 1777.

[^521-note4]: The daughter’s name was Sophia Brainerd, who lived to the age of five.

[^521-note5]: Samuel Mather of Northampton.

## C125. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft, December 7, 1753 C125.Dwight-Foxcroft 12-7-53

Timothy DwightC125. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft,12/7/53. Yale, Sterling Lib., Archives and Manuscripts, Dwight Family Papers, B. 1, f. 1, #5.

Northampton Dec r: 7 th: 1753

Rev rd: & D r Sr.

The 5 th Curr t Mr John Hooker I suppose Great Grand Son to the famous Minister of that name formerly of Hartford was ordained here Mr Reynolds made the first prayer, Mr Parsons of Hadley preach'd Mr W ms of Longmeddow gave the Charge, Mr Hopkins made the Last pray r Mr Breck the right hand of fellowship, [^522-note1] a Vast Concourse of people attended I really hope there is A foundation laid in him by his powers to make a Usefull & Serviceable man in the Gospell ministry, but I am really afraid his mind is drawn Aside from the Simplicity of the Gospell Salvation & has a lurch towards the new prevailing way of mens Invent ing I am really please'd with his performances considering his Short Ex =perience & am not Certain of his being Erronious in the main & prin =cipal points but fear it because he has never given me Satisfaction at Such times as I thôt he would have been constrain'd if his conceptions would have permited, It was Earnestly Urg'd that Mr Edwards might be one of the Council by Cap t Wright [^522-note2] who was one of Mr Edwards's Resolute opposers, but it was Opposed by Majo r Hawley [^522-note3] & forbidden by a great Majority in Such a manner as Evidently to show that the Old leaven Abides, he has been here a Considerable time but never been at my house I suppose he is convinced by his friends & my Enemies that its dangerous for him to visit me, At the time of the Choice of the Council in a very publick

Manner by Cap Wright Aforesaid that Mr Hooker was an Arminian & the Informer a particular Acquaintance of Mr Hookers named & I have heard of it too credibly Otherwise, but Allow e must be made for false reports these Awfull times, & I cant pretend to determine Yet that which length of time must make manifest. with Sincere Reg ds to Yo r Self family & all friends, I am Sr Yo r most Humb le Serv t

Tim o Dwight

I am Obliged to be Short for the Sake of a Safe transportation under Cover by A letter to Cap t Wendell [^522-note4] Notes

[^522-note1]: Peter Reynolds, David Parsons, Stephen Williams, Samuel Hopkins of Springfield, Robert Breck.

[^522-note2]: Probably Noah Wright.

[^522-note3]: Joseph Hawley.

[^522-note4]: Jacob Wendell, a Boston merchant.

## C126. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft, February 22, 1754 C126.Dwight-Foxcroft 2-22-54

Timothy DwightC126. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft,2/22/54. Yale Manuscripts and Archives, Dwight Family Papers, B. 1, f. 1, #6.

Northampton Feb ry. 22 d: 1754

Rev rd Sr

This day I recd; Yo rs of the 1 st Ins t which by Accid t I sent to Stock =bridge & have a further renew'd Acco t of Mr Edw ds's; & families wel =fare I remember not a word of What I wrote You last I keep no Coppies. But respecting Mr Hooker I really hope by the best Judgm t I can make principally & Indeed altogether by his pray =ers there is some Good thing in him towards his Maker, I cant be satisfied with his Method of Preaching, no Experimental re =ligion no rules of Examination a constant dwelling on Works & I am really afraid he Lurches towards an Arminian Justificati =on, & there is lately a pretty deal of Murmering in the Camp

which Seems dayly to increace, what will be Issue is unknown Its probable its may Arise to an Open & publick Opposition in time if he dont Alter his Method, numbers of those that was against Mr Edwards are as Uneasy with Mr Hooker & I am apt to think more So than they was with Mr Edwards One of em A man of Substance [^523-note1] lately confes'd that he voted Mr Edwards away, but now would be glad to be one of thirty that Should be obliged to Support him. I cant but think this people have Something to Suffer for their Abominable Treatment of that faithfull messenger of Christ, & I have thot it likely they may. be punish'd as Multitudes of Others have been by being permitted to go on in that Idolatrous Sin of Ecclessiastical contention till

they are a byword, a Hissing, & Gazing Stock of Others. How ever Gods ways are not as ours &c a I verily believe our people are Endeavouring to find a broader way to Heaven than heretofore we have been Taught, they are not Endeavouring to Enter by the door but Climbing up Some Other Way, I desire Sr Your fervent prayers for us at the throne of Grace for this distracted Compa that know not what they have done. Please to give my best regards to the Rev rd; Mr Hobby of Reading I am well pleas'd with his rueles of Self Examination have much Satisfaction in reading of it lately. He lives out of my reach & I can have no correspond with him I believe I have almost tired You therefore finish with my best regards Sr Yo r Most Humb le Serv t

Timothy Dwight

To the Rev rd Mr Foxcroft

Mr Edwards & Mr Hopkins his neighbour have Agreed to assist at the Installment of Mr Billing [^523-note2] on the last Thurs

day of March the Greenfield You have heard before

[^523-note1]: In all probability, Joseph Hawley

[^523-note2]: Edward Billing, who was installed at Greenfield on March 28, 1754.

## C127. Joseph Dwight to William Shirley, March 25, 1754 C127.J.Dwight-W.Shirley 3-25-54

Joseph DwightC127. Joseph Dwight to William Shirley,3/25/54. Mass. Archives. Addressed on back "To / His Exc y / William Shirley Esq r / Gov r In Cheife &c," with the notation, "P r Fav r of Capt Ashley."

Stockbridge March 25 th 1754

Sr

On The 25 th of Feb y last The Rev d Mr Edwards of This Town Informed me by his L r Inclosing Coppy of A Paragraph or more of Mr Isaac Holliss’s L r to him of the 23 d of Sept r last That He had orders to take upon himself The Care of Mr Holliss’s Charity School here, which consisted of Mohawk Children & Youths, all except one Stockbridge Boy: & desired me to give him seasonable Notice when I wo’d resign the School to him; I Immediately wrote him in answer That I was ready to do It That Day or any Day he pleased, but told him That at his Desire & to sute his Convenience till he could provide for The School, I was willing to continue It in the Shape It was now in, with The present Master & Mistress of the Family for about Ten Days, pro- vided he wo’d pay The Expence from The Day he rec d Mr Holliss’s orders; after some Hesitation of a Day or Two he concluded, & Desired me to continue the School as I had pro- -posed to him, & engaged to Defray The Expence from the Day he rec d his Orders, But The next Day as I remember he gave me to understand That he had heard a report That All The Mohawks Design d: to Leave the Town as soon as their Season for making their maple Sugar was over - & said he wo’d have a Conference with Them the next Day and If he sho’d find It So He w’d be at no further Ex- pence for Their Children after the Conference: This Conference he had, & The Result was That he w’d Take no further Care of The Children because as he supposed They Design’d soon to return home one and All of y m but This I presently found to be a Mistake made by himself or his Interpreter: for parents & Children both wept at least some of Them

The Parents That They were now Disappointed of the Instructi [^524-note1] on w ch They had hoped for, for their Children; and the Children at part The Tho’t of Parting with Their Master I found my Self at The utmost Loss whither to Continue the School till the Courts pleasure sho’d be further known upon the present Circumstances, & being undetermin’d did not Dismiss The Master for Several Days when The Parents & Children seem’d Discouraged with the Broken Measures; & the Children withdrawing their usual Attendance I Dismiss’d The Master After having fully Informed The Parents of the State of the Affair They appeared easy in their Minds towards the Government but seemed to be at a Loss what to do with Themselves & Families for Subsistance till the Season was more sutable for so long a Jour ney as They must Take homewards: I Tho’t It not prudence to Deny Them all Subsistance & Told Them I w’d for The present be kind to them In that Regard. They still hope to be supported for ano ther Month till the high Waters are down and they may have better Travelling for themselves & Children Thus I have conducted in this Matter hitherto which I Tho’t was A point of prudence as accounting ye Expence for so long a Time as They proposed to tarry a Triffle compared with the Disadvantage That might arise from the Families returning home Disgusted: as Things are now They take All well and are thankfull.

I hope your Exc y will move to the Court to pass their order for my future Conduct in this matter and in Case They do not I shall take It for Granted They Disapprove of any Thing further to be done for them and shall as soon as I know It withhold of further Support [^524-note2]

I am heartily Sorry That so good Advantage as It seems to me might have been made by the propoer manage ment of This School, which laterly has certainly been in a flourishing Condition should be wholly lost —— I wish That our Enemies the French may not Improve the Throw- ing of It up to our Disadvantage

I am y r Exc ys most Ob t & most h ble Serv t

Joseph Dwight

[^524-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^524-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C128. Lucy Edwards to Mary Edwards Dwight, August 20, 1754 C128.L.Edwards-M.Dwight 8-20-54

Lucy EdwardsC128. Lucy Edwards to Mary Edwards Dwight,8/20/54. ANTS, f. 1754, #1. Addressed on back "For / M rs Mary Dwight / In / Northampton / P r Mr Nash."

Dear Sister

Your kind Letter I receiv’d by my Brother Parsons, which was very acceptable to me. It is true I did think it something hard y t you wrote so [ ], & I began to think y t I was quite burdensome to you with my Letters. But Since you let me know they are not so you may be sure of having them very often as heretofore.

We none of us thot y t you would willingly be ye cause of uneasiness between Sister Burr & any of us; but we didn’t know but you might ignorant ly by not knowing how Little able she was to have any body say anything as tho they didn’t like her way of marrying. you know she never could bear pestering very well, but I think she grows worse about it if that be posssible than ever so we must take care what we say —— We never till last week heard of your Circumstances, which is that you are like to increase your family. As to my coming to N. hampton this winter, my mother says she shall leave it to your choice, (as she concludes you will want some of us this winter) whether She comes or I. She says that you know she cant stay a great while if She should [^525-note1] come, for my father will not be wiling, And she Says if I go I shall be with you as long before hand as you please & Sometime afterwards. Now my mother says if you choose she should come under those Circumstan ces rather than I, she will come, for she knows, father will be willing she should go if she don’t stay too long. mother would be Glad if you would snd word as soon as you which of us you would have come, And how long before you think you shall want any of us.

You desire to know who sister Burrs Child looks like, My mother says She never was a judge who babies look like when they are so young, but people at Newark She Says Some of them said that it looked one part of the face like ye father and tother part like the mother. & some that it look’d very much like me. Mother says She believes it will have black eyes for it had such Coloured eyes as her Children us’d to have when so young. She says also that was not handsome when it was born but began to grow handsomer before she came away. I intend the next time that I write to sister Burr ask her all about her little Sally, & then I will tell you. We are all thro’ the goodness of God moving about tho my mother is not quite so well as Common, And father has not had any fit of the feaver & ague since I wrote to you last, [^525-note2] but is weak yet & gains strength very Slowly.

Sister Parsons’s Little Esther is better tho she is very weak yet. We are very sorry to hear of your beeing so troubled with the tooth ach and other Difficulties as you say you have been. Mr Searle is gone from us & has been for above a fortnight & is goin upon Long Island for his health.

I hope you will write by the bearer of this if you have any time to write a few lines if no more. My Father & mother & all of us join in Love to Mr Dwight & your self.

From your Affectionate

Sister

Lucy Edwards

Stockbridge Aug t ye 20 th 1754.

P. S. mother says she would not have you be discouraged, but hope in a good God who is able to carry you thro all that is before you. my parents send it as a [...] to the Co l & his wife. L. E.

M rs Dwight

[^525-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^525-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C129. Timothy Cutler to Thomas Secker, August 28, 1754 C129.TCutler-TSecker 8-28-54

Timothy CutlerC129. Timothy Cutler to Bp. Thomas Secker,8/28/54. Printed in *Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New-York* (Albany, 1855), 6:906-908.

My Lord

Your very good and condescending letter came to hand July 28.

Had any important charge risen from the pamphlets I sent Your Lordship, I had presumed to lay it before: but I thought it too minute to mention, and myself happy enough in Your Lordship’s acceptance; now Your Lordship’s Command, must determine me; who think it my duty to obey, and not dispute. D r Mayhew’s Sermon cost 9 d sterling. The price of his Election Sermon now enclosed has 5 s written on it, and charged by the bookseller and is but equal to 6 d sterling. What else I enclosed has unhappily slipped my memory: but the cost was in the same proportion. The whole impression of Hobart’s Sermon is now disposed of; nor could I procure a single copy upon any consideration. Some time ago, by great chance, I got one Copy for the Secretary of the Society, and it is now in his hands. It looks odd to us, that Mayhew should be appointed to preach the Election Sermon in that place where the regular teachers of the town, disliking his sentiments in religion, would not take him to bear a part in their weekly lecture: but for this service, he must thank friends he had in our general Assembly. I understand, my Lord, that some other books, no small Octavos, are now in the press. One is a Vol. of D r Mayhew’s sermons. Another is the second Vol. of Mr Prince’s Chronology of New England. He is justly counted a fanciful, credulous man, of the same spirit, without the boldness of D r Mayhew. The 3 d is a treatise of Mr Jonathan Edwards, a new light, famous both among us and in Scotland, upon the doctrines of Election and Reprobation, which he would place upon the same footing with the H. Scriptures. I have known the man for many years, and think to be superior to Mayhew or Prince, a man of much sobriety and gravity, and of more decent language than they; but odd in his principles, haughty and stiff and morose. There an an hundred subscriptions to the impression, from Scotland. I hesitate about sending these books to Your Lordship, but am ready to observe any hint of Your Lordship’s pleasure about them.

The good circumstances of the Society are a comfort to us, and give us hope towards the success of our applications to them in behalf of places where churchmen are in a body, but too weak to support that interest, of themselves. I say not this to weaken Your Lordship’s just remarks on the prudence requisite to conduct the Charity towards us: but am sure that as the wisdom of the Society is on the one hand too great to give an handle to the licentious speech of Dissenters, so it is on the other hand to be controul’d on proper occasions to do good.

Your Lordship’s good inclination towards resident bishops among us does highly gratify and oblige us. And if that blessing must yet be suspended, we trust in the wisdom and goodness of our superior to be thoughtful of us in the *interim*, and in God over all to succeed and reward their charitable concerns for us in due time. No wonder the dissenters oppose it: they are consistent in principle and interest. Interest of their cause, I mean, and not of their persons. The truth would brighten, and it would be a credit to be a Churchman.

Your Lordship’s representation of the state of religion is very melancholy, but comfortably qualified. We share in the unhappiness of the times. There is scarce any bad book that does not cross the water: and but few good ones follow them: nor are our Clergy furnished with learning or leisure to yield antidotes. I acknowledge Your Lordship’s great goodness that is disposed to help us in this unhappy state.

The Undeserved kindnesses of the late excellent bishop of Cloyne [^526-note1] to me will not suffer me to forget him or his, and your Lordship has much obliged me by the account of his lady, promising Son, and daughter; and this gives me hopes, that when opportunity serves Your Lordship will present my honourable regards and best wishes to them. Perhaps the lady does not know the death of Mr Smibert who was in the Dean’s Company in his travels in Europe, and came over with him to New England. He was a man of an honest, amiable easy temper, but an inflexible Dissenter.

May God continue Your Lordship for many years as a blessing to the Church: Your Lordship’s happiness will be an article in my prayers and joy. I trust for the benefit of Your Lordship’s Compassions toward, myself, and my only son now Curate to the Rev d Dean of Bocking, and am, as obliged,

Your Lordship’s most thankful and dutiful Son & Servant

TIMOTHY CUTLER

Boston New England

August 28 1754

[^526-note1]: George Berkeley.

## C130. Esther Edwards Burr to Lucy Edwards, November 4, 1754 C130.EEBurr-LEdwards 11-4-54

Esther Edwards BurrC130. Esther Edwards Burr to Lucy Edwards,11/4/54. Princeton. *Journal of Esther Edwards Burr*, pp. 291-93.

Newark Novbr, 4. 1754.

Dear Lucy

I received yours No 8 by Mr Burr. I am very glad you are with Sister Dwight at this time (I think more glad than if you had come here, which I had some hopes of when I heard of the rupture at Stockbridge) [^527-note1] for I realy believe she wants you more than I do tho’ I have nobody with me nor have had since Commencement, tho’ throu mercy I have my helth as well as ever I had in my life or I could not possibly get a long in any shape. But you know there is nobody to have. Girls are very scarce for all are Ladys now a days.

I wrote you a letter whiles Mr Burr was gon which I suppose you have not yet received. I enclosed it in one to my Mother and sent it to Stockbridge, and when I wrote it I had forgot that I had wrote by Mr Badger, [^527-note2] and I beleive the bigger part of it is for substance the same with that Mr Badger carried. Only this I remember, I wrote somthing about the Chince which I have not yet got for the reasons there mentioned, but I shall get it soon, that it may be ready to go by Pomroy. Mr Murry could not carry it if I had it.

I wish you would send me word whether you have received all my No or not. Timo’ went to Princeton last week, he will write you about it I suppose. He is going out of the house I this Morn perceive, tho he has said nothing about it to me, but only in general when Mr Burr was gon, what if he should, what should I think of it, should I be displeased, and so on. I hope he has a good desighn in it and wish it may be for his good, but indeed tiss very hard . I can hardly bare it, but I must for I promised my Mother when she was here that I would not oppose it if he desire it again. She said she thought twas best I should not. But only think of it, No Brother! No Sister! but he not <. . .> live with me, is it not hard! I beleive I should not consent if I had not given my word. I expect it will set all the Town a talking. Tis a pety, for now they are prety still.

It is for no dislike he says to anybody, or anything, but purely for his own advantage. He proposes to live with Mr Duffield at Justis Ogdens. You will not wonder if you see many blunders for I write Rocking the Cradle. By the way people say Sally looks much like you, dont you want to see her?

I have no news to tell you, I think. O yes I have! Miss Elizabeth Eaton is like to be married at RoadIsland, ant you glad? Now I think of another pice of News. Joseph Woodruffs Wife has got a fine Son. [^527-note3] One thing brings another, I thought I had no news. Mrs Sergent is like to have a Child, pray what do you think of this? I know you will laugh.

Now I write with Sally in my arms for I am resolved to write. Loyer Ogdens Wife latel Layin with Twins, two Daughters and lost em both.

Perhaps you may loose that Letter I sent by the way of Stockbridge so I will tell you what Mrs Cuming said about the Chince. She says the Brown Chinces wash all out in a little time. Kittys and Pollys did so and they were sorry they got such. [^527-note4] Now if I could hear from you before I get it I should feel easyer.

I am exceeding glad to hear that Pinty and Betty [^527-note5] are at Northampton. I hope they will not go to Stockbridge till the dainger is quite over. I wish I had some of em here with me. Give my very kind love to em, tell em I think a great deal about them, and long to see them.

I can add no more, but my very kind regards to all enquiring friends, and a deal of Love to your self.

From your dear Sister, your most affectionate,

Esther Burr

I find you are still of the mind not to come to see us till we get to Princeton. In my Letter by Stockbridge I tell you not to shew my Letters to Mr Dwight, [^527-note6] and you must tell me that you will not.

As soon as Sister Dwight is abed contrive I should know it for I feel much concernd about it. I hope Mother will be with her.

We have had a very warm fall. We had string Beans till the middle of last week and of the same vines that were planted last May. A few days ago I had six sorts of flours in the garden and court-yard that it looked like sumer. And in two days more should have pinks blown the second time. The bigest part of people go to meeting without their Clokes yet.

Why did not you write to me by Murry. You cant write two often, nor two long.

Sir Hait is got a preaching. [^527-note7] You dont know how smart Timo’ looks with his gound and New Coat. I think there is not one in College looks so smart and genteel.

[^527-note1]: Referring to the raids by Schagticoke Indians after one of their tribe was killed by two Englishmen in the spring of 1753. In 1754, the Edwards parsonage was turned into a fort with a palisade around it.

[^527-note2]: Jonathan Badger (1729-57), a tutor at New Jersey College.

[^527-note3]: Ann Hunloke Woodruff gave birth to Hunloke Woodruff on Oct. 23, 1754.

[^527-note4]: Kitty Bradley and Polly Banks.

[^527-note5]: Elizabeth and Pierpont Edwards.

[^527-note6]: Timothy Dwight, husband of Mary Edwards Dwight.

[^527-note7]: Bejamin Hait, recently graduated from New Jersey College and assigned to the Forks of the Delaware.

## C131. Samuel Hopkins to Joseph Bellamy, February 20, 1755 C131.Hopkins-Bellamy 2-20-55

Samuel HopkinsC131. Samuel Hopkins to Joseph Bellamy,2/20/55. Yale, SML, Manuscripts & Archives, Bellamy Papers.

Sheffield, Feb. 20. 1755

Rev. & Dear Sir,

From what Mr. Edwards said to me of your Intention, I have been expecting you here every Week this Month. And because a Visit would be so welcome to me, and I trust to Mr. Edwards , I will not yet give up my Expectations. Trusting you will come, and perhaps set out before you receive this, I will not at present undertake by Pen & Ink to communi- cate what I want to say to you. I have not seen Mr. Edwards for some Time, putting off my Visit till I should have the Favour of accompanying one of his best Friends. I hear this Week that [he] [^528-note1] is considerably bloated, and is under considerable appre- [hensions] of a Dropsy. It may be a kind visit from some of his Friends might so raise his spirits as to be the means of altering the Tone of his Blood.

I find three of my Neighbouring Ministers have a great Esteem of Mr. Ashley’s sermons on Churches consisting of saints , [^528-note2] and I believe it is generally thought by those that oppose Mr. Edwards to be the best thing that has been published, and even unanswerable. Mr. Williams’s piece is wholly done with, and this is Trumped up. Now, if Mr. Ashley’s scheme is built upon a non-entity . (alias, upon a few of his peremtory Assertions) and contains a number of palpable Contradictions, would it not answer a Good End to have this well made out before the World? I think it may easily be done, if undertaken by one equal to the Task; and since Mr. Edwards will not deign to so much as to read A-ly’s Performance, if I had the Ordering of the matter, I would allot this Burden to you .

A Sermon upon the same Text, and in much the same Method with Mr. Ashley’s , with a few particular Observations upon Mr. Ashley’s, in an Appendix, might perhaps answer the End well. If this is not the best method then Set Paulinus & Agrippa to Dialoguing. - The whole of this is submitted to your better Judgment, by

your Friend & humble servant,

Samuel Hopkins.

[^528-note1]: MS damage to the beginning of this and the following line.

[^528-note2]: Jonathan Ashley, *An humble attempt to give a clear account from Scripture, how the Jewish and Christian churches were constituted, and what sort of saintship is necessary in order to be a communicant at the Lord’s table. : Endeavoured in two sermons preached at Deerfield, on the Lord’s Day, June 24. 1753* (Boston, 1753).

## C132. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft, April 1, 1755 C132.Dwight-Foxcroft 4-1-55

Timothy DwightC132. Timothy Dwight to Thomas Foxcroft,4/1/55. Yale Manuscripts and Archives, Dwight Family Papers, B. 1, f. 1, #6. Addressed on back "To The Rev rd / Mr Thomas Foxcroft one of The Pastors of the first Church / In / Boston."

Rev rd Sr,

I have not rec d; any answer to my letter sent you P r Mr Alvord & having lately heard that Deacon Woodbridge [^529-note1] with Cap t Conkopot &

some Other Stockbridge are gone to Boston conclude it is to Inform the Commiss rs. of the difficulties that arise from the Indians being made so dependant on Brigad r; Dwight. [^529-note2] & if any new prospect shou[ld] open of a Probability of his leaving Stockbridge I should be glad if you'd please to hint it to me & also write a letter to him to En =courage him to return to Northampton if the people, Enô of them, will unite to call him & provide him a Comfortable Support. He is at present & I dont see but he is like to Abide so (viz) as a Sheep &c

He has a very considerable number of close friends here that I hope if he comes will rejoyce in his light but there he is like a can dle set under a bush ll, & the Minist rs now in Service are many of them making the way to Heaven so broad that his & his Lord & Mast ers Strait & narrow way, is not Acceptable. In short many people are not directed to Enter at the Door of the Sheepfold but to climb up some other way. I Esteem him a Gent n of great Powers & I verily believe he Suff rs from many on that very Acco t they cant Endure he should so much Exceed them, that is the real thô very unjust foundation of the W ms's Hatred of him I am now of necessity Calld on & can't add but am Rev rd, Sr Your Sincere friend & Humb e Serv t;

Tim o Dwight

Rev rd Mr Foxcroft

April 1: 1755

[^529-note1]: Timothy Woodbridge, Stockbridge teacher.

[^529-note2]: Joseph Dwight.

## C133. Aaron Burr to William Hogg, May 10, 1755 (Excerpt) C133.A.Burr-W.Hogg 5-10-55

Aaron BurrC133. Aaron Burr to William Hogg,5/10/55. Princeton Univ., Princeton Papers, 1749-56. Excerpt.

[Newark or Princeton]

"I have had the pleasure of reading some of your pious & excellent Letters to my Worthy Fathr in Law Mr. Edwards, which (have) given you no small Room in my Esteem Affections. His situation at Stockbridge has of late been exceeding difficult by Reason of frequent Alarms & constant Fears of ye Enemy. And his Indians of late have not behaved so well as heretofore. But I suppose you will have a particular acct of these Affairs from him."

## C134. Gideon Hawley to Joseph Bellamy, September 18, 1755 C134.G.Hawley-J.Bellamy 9-18-55

Gideon HawleyC134. Gideon Hawley to Joseph Bellamy,9/18/55. BRBL, f. 1535. Addressed on verso "To / The Rev / Mr Joseph Bellamy / at / Bethlem."

Stockbridge 18 th Ap l 55 —

Rev Sir

I delivered your Letter to Kneeland — As to Mr M'Gregory I can only say that I heard y t Presi- dent Burr was about to come up for Him, upon the Account of New York —— I was so full of Business at Boston that I attended to no other Aff rs but my own ——— The Commis rs make ye same allow- ance to provide a Companion — Mr Edwards they allow 20£ Y. C. [^531-note1]

for the encouragement of his son Jon th who is to set out with me next Monday for the Indian Country. I have hired a man to do my secular aff rs & another I expect to take from Cherry Valley —— It begins to be perilous times I am impatient to be gone from these parts —— I design to be at Comm t next fall, if alive & will - Pray for me & my poor people ——— my Service to M rs Bellamy & Mr Waddams &c—

From Sr, their & your cordial Friend & Serv t

G Hawley -

Rev Mr Bellamy

[^531-note1]: York currency.

## C135. Lucy Edwards to Mary Edwards Dwight, August 16, 1756 C135.L.Edwards-M.Dwight 8-16-56

Lucy EdwardsC135. Lucy Edwards to Mary Edwards Dwight,8/16/56. ANTS. Addressed on back "For M rs Mary Dwight / In / Northampton."

D r Sr

I don’t dout he likes me at all, there is no reason to dout it, I went to his ware house [^532-note1] once it was ye first time tho and he could’nt tell read from brown while I was there, and he could’nt would’nt know how Many y ds he had measured off till he had counted over half a doz’ times. What you do think of that now do let a body know hant I good reason to say as I do, if I hant do tell me if it . ———

I heard of Col l Dwight cortship at spring field, and also hear that Mr Lotrop was courting Miss Hannah, am glad to hear Esther Stoddard is at Bos’n You had a mighty genteel wedding ont the other day wish I had been at it for there never be any wedding here, unless I marry my Self and that I cant do if I would. You don’t tell me whether Sally Dwight is with you or not . ————— As to y r Cloak I was’nt there in the season to see em, but inquired and was told they did’nt [...] so much as they did [...][^532-note2] so, but your is made ought I know, I did not have my Cloak made with a head to it, because it was crimson for I remembered you told me it made people look black and I need nothing to make me look black I am sure. I will send you a piece of my cloak, it is a very fine piece, and what makes it better it came out of Mr Tomys ware house. ————

my mother will indeavour to be with you by the [time] you set, [^532-note4] pray write me word by Cap n Sheldon next time how much you have done to y r house —— I put on fan mounts by doz s here I got a number of ye prettyest mounts in B—— [^532-note5] that ever you saw and very cheap, if you want to have a fan done in the best manner pray send it up here and it shall cost you nothing. Well now I am Sleepy. My Duty over the brook, Love to Mr D. and Timmy & your pretty Seno, [^532-note6] and buss him hard for me, Love to Molly, & accept a large portion y r Self from one that prays you may be carry’d safe Thro all that is before you, & is y r truly Affect.

Sister and Hum be Serv’t

L. Edwards

Stockbridge August 16. 1756.

[^532-note1]: The words "ware house" appear above, apparently in a different hand.

[^532-note2]: **marginal.** [2] marginal

[^532-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^532-note4]: "Time" is inserted as an apparent omission; "you set" is a conjectural reading, perhaps referring to Mary Dwight’s impending delivery of Erastus on Sept. 13, 1756.

[^532-note5]: I.e. Boston.

[^532-note6]: Mary’s children Timothy, then four years old, and Sereno, then nearly two.

## C135a. Gideon Hawley to Joseph Bellamy, February 14, 1757 C135a.Hawley-Bellamy2-14-57

Gideon HawleyC135a. Gideon Hawley to Joseph Bellamy,2/14/57. Hartford Seminary Foundation, MS 81576. Two folio sheets.

Sheff d 14 Feb. 57 ——

Rev & very dear Sir

The Commissioners not being sufficiented [^533-note1] with

ye Situation of Indian affairs, and thro’ a tender Regard to my Mission can’t bear to dismiss me from ye Ser- vice - I am loth to do any Thing y t shall disoblige them or injure so good a Cause as y t I have been en- gaged in could I do any Thing y t would probably be-

nefit & do Service ye Indians souls — My Conscience is tender

and I know possibly ye Difficulties & hardships of my Mission may sway me too much. And I want your advice; You [are] [^533-note2] an unbiased person —— are quite friendly to ye affair [kn]ow me better than any Man on ye Globe beside —— you are capible of advising me - you have conversed with me frequently upon ye affair - you know how long I pro- secuted it with unfainting resolution. I should never have engaged in it had I not expected Mr. Brianard [^533-note3] for a Companion and Fellow Missionary. He disappointed me & ye Correspondent of Scotland Society sent me Mr. Gordon [^533-note4] who was with me part of ye first Summer. But was so dispirited poor Gentleman, that ye chief Service he did me

was to keep up my Spirits & ware a cheerful Air that

He might not be discouraged — But in ye Fall he left me. I advised ye Com ` is rs of ye disappointment and y t I could not prosecute my Mission without a Companion - No Young Gentleman of lib’ral Education was to be found willing to engage in ye affair. And I consented to take such a one as I could get. You advised me to Israel Holly, [^533-note5] and He consented to go with me, but before we arrived near my people his Spirits sunk - when we came to Onoh- guage he bursted in a flood of Tears. I soothed him, and he proved while he was with me a very great Comfort - After little more than a year, He, tho’ loth to leave me, could stand it no longer but forsook me not as Demas did Paul for ye World [^533-note6] but thro’ Discouragements - I was again deserted & alone, but loth to quited ye Mission en gaged in it with double resolution - I now took with me Mr. Edwards his Young Son & a lad [^533-note7] y t I could engage for no certain Time to help in my secular affairs, and now had no person that I could properly call a Companion — I never was more determined than now support my Mission - While these Persons were with Gen l. Brad- dock was defeated and our first Expedition against Crown Point proved abortive. In the Fall I came down with Mr. Edwards his Son and tho’ I was suffi ciently aware of ye great Probability of a disaffection among ye Southern Indians, if not among ye Six Nations, [^533-note8]

However I returned to my Mission and young

Mr. Edwards & the other Lad with Difficulty were

perswade[d] to accompany - I soon found by y r timorous-

ness y t I had better been without them. In the Depth of Winter the Indians advised me to come off having for several Weeks lived in constant fear, and my boys almost scared to Death - were constantly pressing me to bring them off - I came off and bro’t them home. And returned to a Gen l. Treaty with ye Six Nations held in February last at Mount-Johnson. [^533-note9] - My Indians after ye Treat[y] [^533-note10]

advised me return for a few Weeks into Ne[w]

England and meet them at y t Place again af[ter] they had been home. I punctual observed the Appointment, but when I came back, I did not meet them, but had advise from them that it was not safe for me to be at Onoh’quage - However I ran ye risk of it - When I arrived to them they advised me to turn back immediately, and that it was unsafe for any English Persons to be there — They told me, y t M rs Ashly, [^533-note11] my Interpreter was in Danger, and desired me, as she was loth to go, to be present when they delivered y r Sentiments, y t I might tell her Friends in New England, y t if any Misfortune came to her by staying, it was her own falt - and y t they would not bear the Blame - Her Husband [^533-note12] not being at home, she suspended her determination, till his return - So I left her there, where she & Her Husband are determined at all Events to live and die - It is my Opinion, by all Accounts I have had from others,

as well as by Acquaintance that being alone with

the Indians they are in Danger of doing hurt and afraid as well as others that he has done a great deal of hurt —— There is also a Gun Smith there who came off last Spring but for fear of ye Press ran back to ye Indians - And Mr. Ashley owned to me that he mended Guns, made hatchets &c. for animy Indians as well as any. And Ashley has supplyed ye Dioga Indians who are our profes sed Enimies with Corn and indeed how can they do otherwise if they live there - For if If they don’t the Indians will killed them. For there [^533-note13]

is no living there but being Friends to all ——

And it is not very likely that will protect them long —— But to return to myself - I made faith- ful Representation to ye Com ` is rs of ye Situation of their & my affairs - They as well as myself were desirous of having me continued a candidate for ye Business till Fall, not knowing how affairs mi ` t be altered in our favour at ye close of a Cam- -paign. But has our success ye Summer past been such as put any more favourable aspect upon my Mission? Is there ye least Probability of things being in better Situation? Is it my duty to return to my Mission? Must I at this Time of Life wait to have providence determine my duty plainer than it has? - Let me have you tho’ts —— I should also be much obliged to you if you would write to Mr. Foxcroft from whom a few Days ago

I recieved strongly urges me not to give up my

Mission.

If must sacrifice my Life, I will - yet I have fortitude enough to do it, without a spark of Grace —— I can desire Dangers, — yet I dismiss them - But can I do it conscienciously without answering some valuable End — ?

Your Friend, Sir, is in Danger, - I wish I had more of ye Christian - I have enough of ye Roman - Did I ever yeild yet in any affair I ever under took. No, you & every body acquainted with me can

testifie ye Contrary - I conscienciously advissed the

Commissioners to dismiss me, because was sensible it would answer no valuable End to continue me -

Was there not apparent reason for my so doing — is not Oswego gone — ? the Six Nations, generally gone over to ye French — ? And my people sensible of ye Danger I shold be exposed have not advised my return to them - But I have told you how I found things in my late Tour.

I am exceedingly pressed in my Mind - Friday [^533-note14] Night I slept but very little - Saturday had ye most darking Exercises - Saturday Night slept not a Wink till just brake of Day - Lords Day in ye Morning & all Day was in ye utmost dis- tress. Last night had little more rest than for two Nights past, this Morning rose calm pati- ent & resigned. I have examined my heart & made appeals to Conscience. And can’t find y t I have violated its Dictates. In Conscience I must say y t I have done my utmost to support my Mission - I verily believe I have done if any Thing more than God required of me - And now I should think, did not others, who can’t be so good judges as I, think I ought to wait further upon Providence, that I ought to give it up ——— must I resign myself implicitely to others - If I must I will.

I have been so exercised y t my Nerves are all relaxed [^533-note15] - I shall now have my constitution flung into ye utmost disorder too -

I am mistaken if the Commissioners don’t blame me in y r minds for not going to my Indians this Winter and y t they would think that I did my Duty if I set out immediately for Onoh’quage - This grieves & vexes me. If I must die & sacrifice my Life, you my Friend, the Commiss rs. & ye whole World shall see that I can do it — I disdain to yeild - My Temptations are exceeding strong - pray for me. If I am pressed the Consequences will be very unhappy.

Pray write to me a long letter very soon - do write to Mr. Foxcroft upon my affairs - I think I must go to Boston - I can’t study & I had bet-

be ter be riding than stay her & go into a hectic as I am in great Danger of ——

I am sensible this is a long unconnected Letter - if you knew how I felt you’ll readily pardon ye incorrectness of it —

Pray for your Friend &

Gid n. Hawley

P.S. Mr. Edwards is my Friend but must be esteemed a partial Judge in my affairs

[^533-note1]: MS sic; "sufficiently."

[^533-note2]: This and the beginning of the next line affected by MS damage.

[^533-note3]: John Brainerd (1720-1781), brother of David, missionary to Indians in New Jersey.

[^533-note4]: Alexander Gordon (d. 1754), 1751 graduate of College of New Jersey, and tutor, 1752-54.

[^533-note5]: Israel Holley would later become pastor of the Separatist church in Suffield, Conn.

[^533-note6]: II Tim. 4:10

[^533-note7]: Jonathan Edwards, Jr. (b. 1745). The "lad" is not further identified.

[^533-note8]: **marginal.** [2]

[^533-note9]: The home of Sir William Johnson, Colonel of the Six Nations, in New York.

[^533-note10]: This and the end of the following two lines are affected by MS damage.

[^533-note11]: Rebecca Kellogg Ashley (1695-1757), former captive of Deerfield raid of 1704; she died at Onohquage, N.Y.

[^533-note12]: Benjamin Ashley (1715-c.1758), formerly Indian schoolmaster at Stockbridge.

[^533-note13]: **marginal.** [3]

[^533-note14]: **marginal.** [4]

[^533-note15]: In the archaic sense of being deprived of usual firmness.

## C136. Gideon Hawley to Timothy Dwight, June 11, 1757 C136.G.Hawley-T.Dwight 6-11-57

Gideon HawleyC136. Gideon Hawley to Timothy Dwight, 6/11/57. ANTS, f. 1756-59B, #2.

Sheffield 11 June 57.

My Friend,

Not long after I wrote you last, had such advice from my Indians, y t I was upon y e Point of seting out for Onohoquaga —— But my Friends & at Albany advised me, as y e Small-Pox was rife all over y e Dutch Country & had spread among y e Indians, at least to postpone y t journey, were there no other Ob- jections against it —— I confess, if it is my duty to continue in, & prosecute my Mission to y e Six Nations, I need a great Deal more Zeal, but am conscientious, and hope never to quit a good Design, merely because of y e hardships attending it. That Being who knows all Things only knows one half y e Anxiety, I have felt on Account of that perplexed affair ———— In my most serious moments I think it my duty to resign it, but am not satisfied with all y e motives I have to enduce me, Some of them, at least, are such as I question, whether they ought to have much weight: and y t perplexes me —— But then I think, I can’t help being flesh & Blood, A burnt Child will dread the Fire.

A few Days ago, I had a letter from Gunn, w ch informs me, y t My Interpreter, he thinks, has for sometime been in a deep Consumption, and of many things which add to my former discourage- ments. He thinks not but for me to come to them. The ensuing summer, my Friend, is big with the most important Events. I am surprized at myself y t I am so taken up with my own private affairs, when our all is at Stake - I wish affairs may turn better than our reasonable Fears. - What is y e Matter no Fleet has arrived? The Sea- son is advanced, and we have not yet taken y e Field. We hear y e French have advice of our design upon Quebec.

I want to see you, but am obliged to meet Mr Edwards at Springfield Monday next, so can’t come come your Way. The Pocket handkercheif I wrote [^534-note1] about last, if you have not sent it this Way you’ll be so kind as to wrap it in a paper & send it by some hand to me at Boston - Let it be left with M rs Hubbard. May be you’ll see me sometime next Fall, tho as you design into y e Jersie New-Jersey, 'tis not so likely you will ——

My sincere regards to you all; let me always have a share in your special Friendship, as I doubt not I shall. —— Our Friends at Stockbridge are all well, ex- cept poor Joseph Barnard who is in y e last stages of an incurable Consumption. - Tis really affecting to see one who so much desires to live cut off in y e flower of Life - The Lord prepare him for his ap- proaching Change -

I am, dear Sir, very sincerely your affectionate Friend

Gid n Hawley

Nothing lately from y e Jersey -

Sheffield -

P.S. Monday 6 o’Clock Mane I this morning transmit Mad m Edwards y e News we had last Evening of Miss Lucys having y e Small Pox ————

P.P.S. Springfield Tuesday 6 Clock Mane - Last Even g arrived here - Seen[?] Col o Williams at Westfield who says Miss Lucy was broke[?] and [——] y t it was of y e worse sort —— I assure you y t I have rising hopes to hear news[?] y t she is upon recovery. And from y e last Account notwithstand ing for if she had been dead we should have had it [perpendicular in right margin:] Miss Susa. [^534-note2] I hear is gone up but have not seen her, so y t if you sent any thing to Me by her I have not rec d it —— adieu - forgive blunders

Mr Dwight

[^534-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^534-note2]: Conjectural reading; i.e. Susanna Edwards?

## C138. Esther Edwards Burr to Sarah Pierpont Edwards, October 7, 1757 C138.EEBurr-SPE 10-7-57

Esther Edwards BurrC138. Esther Edwards Burr to Sarah Pierpont Edwards,10/7/57. Extract. Printed in Hopkins, *Life and Character of the Late Rev. Mr. Jonathan Edwards* (1765), 89-90.

N O doubt dear Madam, it will be some comfort to you, to hear that GOD has not utterly forsaken, altho’ he has cast down. I would speak it to the glory of God’s name, that I think he has in an uncommon degree discovered himself to be an all-sufficient GOD, a full fountain of all good. Altho’ all streams were cut off, yet the fountain is left full.

I think I have been enabled to cast my care upon him, and have found great peace and calm in my mind, such as this world cannot give, or take.

I have had uncommon freedom, and nearness to the throne of grace. GOD has seemed sensibly near in such a supporting and comforting manner, that I think I have never experienced the like.

GOD has helped me to review my past and present mercies, with some heart-affecting degree of thank- fulness.

I think GOD has given me such a sense of the vanity of the world, and uncertainty of all sublunary enjoy- ments, as I never had before. The world vanishes out of my sight. Heavenly and eternal things appear much more real and important than ever before. I feel my self to be under much greater obligations to be the Lord’s, than before this sore affliction.

T he way of salvation by faith in Jesus Christ has appeared more clear and excellent; and I have been constrained to venture my All upon Him ; and have found great peace of soul, in what I hope has been actings of faith.-Some parts of the Psalms have been very comforting and refreshing to my soul.

I hope GOD has helped me to eye his hand in this [^535-note1] awful dispensation ; and to see the infinite right he has to his own, and to dispose of them as he pleases.

T hus , dear Madam, I have given you some broken hints of the exercises and supports of my mind, since the D eath of H im , whose memory and example, will ever be precious to me as my own life.

O dear Madam! I doubt not but I have your, and my honored father’s prayers daily for me ; but give me leave to intreat you both to request earnestly of the Lord, that I may never despise his chastenings, nor faint un- der this his severe stroke ; which I am sensible there is great danger of, if GOD should only deny me the sup- ports, that he has hitherto graciously granted.

O, I am afraid I shall conduct so as to bring dishonor on my GOD, and the religion which I profess! —— No, rather let me die this moment, than be left to bring dishonor on GOD’s holy name. ——— I am overcome —— I must conclude with once more begging, that as my dear parents remember themselves, they would not for- get their greatly aflicted daughter, (now a lonely widow) nor her fatherless children.

M y duty to my ever dear and honored parents, love to my brothers and sisters.

From, dear Madam, your dutiful and affectionate daughter,

*ESTHER BURR.*

[^535-note1]: **marginal.** [90]

## C139. Gilbert Tennent to John Guyse, November 15, 1757 C139.Tennent-Guyse 11-15-57

Gilbert TennentC139. Gilbert Tennent to John Guyse,11/15/57. Princeton Univ., Princeton Papers, 1757-63.

[Philadelphia?]

The valuable President Rev d. Mr. Aaron Burr has been lately removed by Death; W c: is justly & generaly [...] Lamented: - [longer dash] in the mean tyme Providence has mercifully interposed in the choice of a Successor, the Rev d: Mr Jonathan Edwards formerely of North-Hampton, now of Stokbridge, whose praise who for superior acumen, orthodoxy, Learning, Piety, & courage in the cause of God is in all the Churches: -[longer] Here give me leave to observe, that there is a great resemblence between this seat of Learning, and that of Hall[e] in Saxony, began by Pious D r: Frank in repect of their rise, progress, & influence , especialy in respect of vital Piety : & there is reason to it will be in respect of continuance; when the kind, unmerited & indeed unexpected interposures of divine Providence, in favour of it, in tyme past in many instances, to[o] tedi[o]us here to enumerate & particularly in [when; substitute for "in"] those before mentioned are considered.

(The best information he has is that Chief Justice Morris expects to succeed Governour Belcher; he fears Morris will be prejudiced against the dissenters in genl & college of New Jersey in particular.)

## C140. Esther Edwards Burr to William Hogg, December 22, 1757 C140.E.Burr-W.Hogg 12-22-57

Esther Edwards BurrC140. Esther Edwards Burr to William Hogg,12/22/57. ANTS, f. 1756-59B, #4. Apparently a copy by Esther Burr.

Letter to Mr Hogg — Decr. 22. 1757. by E B

Hon d Sir

I flatter my Self I Shall not be thought im- pertinent by a gentleman of your Carracter if I acknowledge in a few lines the receipt of your Letter dated in August to my late dear Husband which fell into my hands near three Months after he was beyound the reach of all mortal things. The affect. regard you express for one y t was dearer to me than my own life was extreamly affecting to me, nor can I forgive my Self if I neglect to acknowledge it in terms of the greatest re- spect. You Sir had a large Share with me in y t dear good Mans Heart which he often expressed with the warmest affection. - I thought it might not be improper to lay your Letter before the Trustees as they were then conven’d & it cheifly concerned the College & then I sent to my Hon d Father the Rev d Mr Edwards who is Chose to Succed my dear companion which I hope will be grateful to the friends of this College in Scotland - I here inclose you Sir the Last attempt my dear Husband made to serve God in publick & do good to his fellow-Creatures a Sermon y t he preached at our late Excellent Governor [^537-note1] — You will not think Strang of its imperfections when I tell you y t all he wrote on the Subject was done one afternoon & eve when he had a fit of the Intermiting Fever upon him & the whole night after was irrational

Give me leve to beg an intrest in your praires at the throne of Grace for a poor disconsolate Widdow & two fatherless Orphans —Please to Present with great respect my kindest regard to your Lady & dau Daughters ——————

I am Hon d Sir

[^537-note1]: Jonathan Belcher.

## C141. Ecclesiastical Council Met at Stockbridge to Trustees of the College of New Jersey, January 4, 1758 C141.Council-Trustees 1-4-58

Ecclesiastical Council Met at StockbridgeC141. Council of Churches Convened at Stockbridge to Trustees of College of New Jersey,1/4/58. ANTS, in Sermon on Heb. 13:7-8 (Jan. 58).

To the Honour’d and Rev d the Trustees of the College in New-jersy; We the Council Conven’d at Stockbridge January ye 4. 1758 to Consult and Advise in Relation to ye Rev d Mr Edwards’s his Removal from his Mission and Labours here to take upon him the Trust to which you have seen fit to Call him, being Tenderly Concerned for the poor People of this place being now made destitute in Consequence of sd Call, and being desired by the Chh in this place to have them all the Assistance we can in Relation to ye Resetlement, have in Conse Compliance with their Earnest desire writ to ye honourable Commissioners in Boston, in their Favour. and particularly that the Rev d Mr John Brainerd, might be applied to, Come and Labour among them, as a Proper Person, to Serve likely to Serve the good Ends Prop proposed in Erecting a Mission here; as he has lately been among them and given them sone teast of his Minister- ial Labours, to the good Satisfaction of both English and Indians who earnestly desire y t he might be obtained for them.

And moreover In Compliance with their Earnest desire we beg leave to Signify to your venerable Body; y t as it has been Intimated here y t Mr Brainerd, would still be suited with an Indian mission under hopeful & promising Circumstances, and y t he was himself had Intimated y t he was perswaded if the Remainder of his late Indians would be Pers prevailed upon to Remove to Stockbridge Provided they Could be accommodated with Land here; we have The hope of his being obtained, has and the Remove of those Indians hither, has had some Consideration in the minds of this Council; while we have been Consulting that Interest, the Service of which has now pro made this vacancy ————

We would beg leave to observe to your venerable Body y t the hope of his being obtained has had some Consideration, while we have been Consulting that Interest, for the service of which a vacancy is now made. and we do hereby in the behalf of this People and the Common Cause of our Lord among the natives, earnestly beg th your Assistance, either as a Body or of your Members according to y r Respective Provinces[?]; that ye said Mr Brainerd may be obtained to Labour In this place, in Case he should be ob applied to by thte honourable Commissioners.

## C141a. Samuel Hopkins to Joseph Bellamy, January 19, 1758 C141a.Hopkins-Bellamy 1-19-58

Samuel HopkinsC141a. Samuel Hopkins to Joseph Bellamy,1/19/58. MS 81580, Hartford Seminary Foundation. One folio leaf, inscribed on back, "To / The Rev. Joseph Bellamy / at Bethlem / P r Favour of m r. John Hamlin."

Rev & Dear Sir,

You will with this, I expect, receive your Saddle. It was done when m r. Brinsmade was here. I told m r. Brinsmade it was not done, not knowing what passed between you and the Sadler, after you went from my House. I have enclos’d to you the Answer to J. G. [^539-note1] partly because agreed to take it, and get it printed, but forgot it. but especially, because Mentor [^539-note2] has lately been here, and advises by all Means to have it published, and that as Soon as may be. - I leave it with you, either to Send it to m r. Leavenworth , with what Instructions you think best; or Send it your Self to the Printer, or Suppress it, and write Something better in its Room. I am suspicious the Printer would be loth to publish any Such thing, as I suppose him to be a Friend to J. G. and may probably object against its Length. on that Account, that which you took with you, has the preference. — The Answer that has been published, I suppose makes it evident to all considerate persons, what the Design of J. G. was, as he doubtless answers himself.

I have not yet quite finished the Remarks upon the Winter Evening; [^539-note3] but I am grown qite quite proud about — MENTOR has heard it and commends it, and offerd to be the first Subscriber, if I would draw up proposals for printing them. I am zealous to finish them, and Send them to you; but Time passes away, and little is done.

Mr. Edwards left my House yesterday Morning in his Way to Prince Ton Princeton . Exepcts not to return till next May. Alass! his Mantle is gone with him, for all that I have Seen of it. - I have Some of his long Papers [^539-note4] tho’; and have Liberty to Go to his Manuscript Ser- mons and take what I please. I had need make this Winter as long as I can, and be a good Husband of every Hour.

A Line from you by the first Opportunity would oblige,

your unworthy Friend & Brother,

Sheffield, 19 th Jan ry. 1758.

Samuel Hopkins.

[^539-note1]: This MS may not have been printed, nor did Bellamy take up Hopkins’ invitation to write one of his own. Hopkins did publish *A Bold push, in a letter to the author of a late pamphlet, intitled, Fair play, &c.*(Boston, 1758), but that was an answer to Alexander Cumming’s *A Bold push, in a letter to the author of a late pamphlet, intitled, Fair play, &c.: In which it is inquired, whether what he says in opposition to the doctrine of election, is not in direct contradiction to St. Paul . . . : Also, a brief vindication of the doctrine of God's decrees. Being the substance of a letter from a minister, to one of his neighbours, in answer to a letter sent to him on that subject* (Boston, 1758). The identity of "J. G." is uncertain. One of the printers of Cumming’s pamphlet was John Gill (1732-1785). Alternatively, in his copy of Hopkins’ letter made during the 19 th century, Richard Webster identifies "J. G." as "D r Gale of Killingworth author of the Saucy[?] piece mentioned by Mr. [Thomas] Robbins"; however, no information on this person or publication has been found. (Thomas Robbins [1777-1856] was minister of East Windsor, Conn., and founder of the Connecticut Historical Society.) Webster, MS, " Letters to Joseph Bellamy from Aaron Burr, David Brainerd, etc., and other papers concerning Mr. Bellamy, 1739-1787," 2 vols., Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia, 1:139.

[^539-note2]: I.e. JE.

[^539-note3]: Actually, it was Joseph Bellamy who published *A letter to the reverend author of The winter-evening conversation on original sin, from one of his candid neighbors* (Boston, 1758), a response to Samuel Webster, *A winter evening's conversation upon the doctrine of the original sin between a minister and three of his neighbours accidentally met together* (Boston, 1757). Perhaps Hopkins turned over his remarks to Bellamy for him to finish

[^539-note4]: Probably some of the "Miscellanies" notebooks

## C142. Esther Edwards Burr to Unknown, January 1758 C142.E.Burr-_ 1-58

Esther Edwards BurrC142. Esther Edwards Burr to [?], 1/58. ANTS, f. 1756-59C, #3. A copy apparently by Esther Burr.

Princeton Jan y. 1758.

Sir

Your most agreable favour of November last I return my most hearty thanks —it gave me inex- pressable pleasure & at the Same time afresh Set open all the avenues of Greif & again Probes the deep Wound Death has given me. —— My loss —— Shall I attempt to Say how great my loss is? —— God only can know & to him would I carry my Complaint! - Indeed Sir I have lost all y t was or could be desire- able in a Creature! I have lost all y t ever I Sat my Heart on in this World! —I need not in- large on his innumerable amicable quallities to one y t was so well acquainted with him as you was however pleasing it is to me to dwell on them

Had not God have Supported me by these consider ations first by Shewing the right he has to his own Creatures & to dispose of them when & in what manner he pleases & Secondly by innabling me to follow him beyound the Grave into the Eternal World & there viewing of him in unspeakable glory & happiness freed from all Sin & Sorrow I Should have before this have been Sunk amongst the dead & covered with the Clods of the vally

God has wise ends in all y t he doth this things don’t come by chance & rejoice y t I am in the hands of Such of God ——

My brother is not here but I have Sent your Sons Chest to Mr [^540-note1] with a line to desire him to take pertecu- lar care of it & here inclose your Sons acc ts Since May 7 last. most of these acc ts I had received & paid before I received your Letter as I had been been informed he was not to return . it gives me great pleasure y t I have it in my power to do the least Service for you if you would pleas to deliver the Money to Miss Prince who will come here Soon in the Spring I Shall be further obliged to you —I hear inclose you a Sermon preached at Governor Belchers Funderal the last attempt y t ever my dear Husband made to Serve God & do good to his fellow Mortals. I need not apoligise for its imperfections when you have read the prefeas and especually when I tell you y t all y t was wrote was part of one afternoon when he had a violent fever on him also an Elegum your acceptance of which will greatly oblige me

[^540-note1]: Burr left a blank to fill in the remainder of the name.

## C142a. Nathaniel Hazard to Joseph Bellamy, March 20, 1758 C142a.NHazard-Bellamy 3-20-58

Nathaniel HazardC142a. Nathaniel Hazard to Joseph Bellamy,3/20/58. MS copy, Richard Webster (c. 19 th century), in "Letters to Joseph Bellamy," 2 vols., Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia, 1:141. [Original at Hartford Seminary?]

New York March 20 th 1758

Rev d & Dear Sir,

I rec d yours of 2 d Feb y about 10 days past & y rs without date I rec d this day, for both which I am obliged to you & particularly for y r friendly reproof, which I trust will be of use to me. I also rec d the note of the alteration you would have made in the sermon which I have put to the press. [^541-note1] Mr. Finley’s I have got done already. [^541-note2] In regard to your Book on the Wisdom of God in the Permission of Sin &c, [^541-note3] I cannot say what number of Subscribers can be got, but I shall be very glad to have proposals sent me as soon as possible. I shall be glad to have them spread & intend to take pains for it. I suppose you have heard Mr Edwards is innocu- ated & has the Small Pox. He was past the worst stage of it last week & had it favorably as I am informed, & Mrs Burr also.

There is nothing remarkable with us more than is public with you. I suppose Gen l Webb sailed for England last week in the packett. The raising so great a number of men I expect will fill the country with concern & some places I conceive with distress. May the Lord sanctify affliction & judgment to works repentance & reformation. The affairs of the King of Prussia may have a very different aspect from what it has now a twelve month hence. I know people in general take great Encouragement from his late victories. But for my part I cannot but imagine the Lord intends to humble our nation & make us feel more concern & distress that we may acknowledge his hand in our deliverance; for my part I can see very little that looks like deliverance, turn which way I will to Church or State.

I am respectfully, Yrs

Nath l Hazard

[^541-note1]: *Sermons upon the following subjects, viz. The divinity of Jesus Christ. The millenium [...]. The wisdom of God, in the permission of sin* (Boston, 1758).

[^541-note2]: Samuel Finley, *The madness of mankind, represented in a sermon, preached in the New Presbyterian Church in Philadelphia. On the ninth day of June, M,DCC,LIV* (New York, 1758).

[^541-note3]: *The wisdom of God in the permission of sin, vindicated* *in answer to a late pamphlet, intitled, an attempt, &c (Boston, 1760* ); a reply to Samuel Moody, *An attempt to point out the fatal and pernicious consequences of the Rev. Mr. Joseph Bellamy’s doctrines,* *respecting moral evil . . .* (Boston, 1759)

## C143. William Shippen to Sarah Pierpont Edwards, March 22, 1758 C143.W.Shippen-S.Edwards3-22-58

William ShippenC143. William Shippen to Sarah Pierpont Edwards,3/22/58. ANTS, f. 1756-59C, #1-2. Addressed on back to "M rs Sarah Edwards / at / Stockbridge."

Princeton March 22 d 1758

Most dear & most worthy Madam

I am heartily sorry for the Occasion of my writing to you by this Express, but I know you have been informed by a Line from your Excellent, Lovely & pious Husband, that I was brought here to Inoculate him your dear Daughter Esther, & her children for the small Pox which was then spreading fast in Princeton; and that after the most deliberate & serious Consultation with his nearest & most religious Friends - he was accordingly Inoculated with them ye 23 d Day of last month & althô he has had the Small Pox favourably, yet having a number of them in the Roof of his Mouth & throat he could not possibly Swallow a Sufficient quantity of Drink to keep off a Secondary Fever, which hias proved to many for his feeble Frame, and this after- noon between two & three o’clock it pleased God to let him sleep in that dear Lord Jesus, whose Kingdom & Interest he has been faithfully & painfully Serving all his Life & never did any Mortal Man more fully & clearly evidence the Sincerity of all his Profession, by one continued universal calm, chearful resignation & patient submission to the [^542-note1] Divine Will through every Stage of his Disease than he not so much as one discontented Expression nor the least appearance of murmuring thrô ye whole —— and never did any Person expire with more perfect freedom from pain, not so much as one distorted hair but in ye most proper sense of the Words, he really fell asleep - for Death had certainly lost its Sting, as to him; and a very short time before he expired, he Spoke to Lucy to ye following purpose dear Lucy it seems to me to be the Will of God that I must shortly leave you & therefore give my kindest Love to my dear Wife & tell her, that the uncommon Union that has so long subsisted between us has been of such a Nature as I trust is Spiritual and therefore will continue forever: and I hope she will be suppor- ted under so great a trial & submit chearfully to the Will of God; And as to my Children you are now like to be left Fatherless which I hope will be an Inducement to you all to seek a Father who will never fail you; & as to my Funeral I would have it be like unto Mr Burrs, and any additional Sum of Money that might be expected to be laid out that way, I would have it disposed of to charitable uses ————— [^542-note2]

Your Daughter Burr & her children through the Mercy of God are Safely over the Disease & she desires me to send her Duty to you the best of Mothers, she has had the Small pox the heaviest of all that I have Inoculated & little Sally [far the] [^542-note3] lightest she has but 3 in her face - I am [sure] it will prove serviceable to her future Health. She thinks it will be highly Necessary th[at her] Brother Timothy comes here directly to look after & settle his Fathers affairs ———— I conclude with my hearty prayer that [...] may be enabled to look to that God, whose L[ove &] Goodness, you have experienced a thousand [times] for direction & help under this most afflictive Dispensation of his providence; & every other Diffi- culty you may meet with here; in order to your more perfectly fitted for ye joys of heaven hereafte.

I am dear Madam Your most Sympathizing affectionate F d & very h le Serv

W m Shippen

[^542-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^542-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

[^542-note3]: Margin of letter damaged; words in brackets supplied from Dwight transcript (ANTS).
