## C145. John Ballentine to Esther Edwards Hopkins, March 29, 1758 C145.Ballantine-Hopkins 3-29-58

John BallentineC145. John Ballantine to Esther Hopkins,3/29/58. ANTS, f. 1756-59C, #5. Addressed on back "To / M rs Esther Hopkins / at / Springfield."

Westfield Mar. 29. 1758

Madam,

These Lines, wrote at the Desire of Madam Edwards, bring you the sorrowful Tidings of the Death of your Rev d. and Hon d Brother President Edwards. He departed this Life, last Wednesday, about two.

In the progress of his Distemper, there was g t hope of his recovery, but after the turn of the Distemper, his Throat was so fill'd, that they could not get enough into Him to keep of the Secondary Fever, which prov'd fatal to Him. ——— He very calmly submitted to Death, holding fast hs confidence to the End, knowing in whom he believed.

You have a great Share in the general Mourning that the Death of so good and great a man occasions, I wish you a abundant Consolation from the God of Com- [^544-note1] fort under It hath pleasd the Sovereign God to put Lover and Friend far from you, but Gods presence will infinitely make up all losses. and the prospect, of meeting him & others dear to you in another & better world, will I doubt not mitigate your trou- ble in being bereav'd of them ——

We have all reason to put up Davids prayer help, Lord, for the God ly man ceaseth, & the faithful fail - He is Safe arriv'd, I trust, to the peaceful regions while we are yet tossd on the boisterous Ocean -

Mr Edwards submitted to innoculation because it was judg'd his infection was in evitable in the Situation he was in. he

did with the advice of those of his friends he had opportunity to consult, and also with the advice of the Trustees.

M rs Edwards purpos'd to have waited on [^544-note2] you, & to have gone to Windsor, but this dispensation of Providence makes Ne- cessary that She Should be with her Chil- dren at Stockbridge as soon as possible She desires you to send an Acco t to Windsor, as soon as possible —

I am, Madam. Your Sincere Friend and humble Servant

John Ballantine

[^544-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^544-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C146. Sarah Pierpont Edwards to Esther Edwards Burr, April 3, 1758 C146.SPE-E.Burr 4-3-58

Sarah Pierpont EdwardsC146. Sarah Pierpont Edwards to Esther Edwards Burr,4/3/58. ANTS, f. 1756-59C, #9, C, #4. Appended is Susanna Edwards to Esther Edwards Burr, same date.

O my very Dear Child

What Shall I Say. A holy and Good God has Cover’d with Dark Cloud. O that we may all kiss the rod and Lay our hands on our mouthes. the Lord heas Done it. he heas made me adore his Goodness that we had him So Long. but my god Lives. and he heas my heart. O what A Legacy my Husband and your Father heas Left us. we are given unto God. and their I am and Love to be

Sarah Edwards

## C147. Susannah Edwards to Esther Edwards Burr, April 3, 1758 C147.S.Edwards-E.Burr 4-3-58

Susannah EdwardsC147. Susanna Edwards to Esther Edwards Burr,4/3/58. ANTS, f. 1756-59B, #9, C, #4. Appended to Sarah Pierpont Edwards to Esther Edwards Burr, same date.

Dear Sister

My Mother wrote this with a great deal of pain in her neck which disennabl- ed her from writeing any more. she thoughtt you would be glad of these few lines from her own hand

O Sister how many Calls we have won uppo the back of annother O I beg your Praiers that we that are yong in this fammly might be awakend & Stir up to Call more earnest uppon God that he would our father and frind forever [^546-note1]

My father took leve of all his people & fammely as affectionately as if he knew he should not com again he Preahed from those words We have no Continnuing City therefore let us Seke own to Com the Chapter that red was Acts ye 20 O how proper what could he don more —— when had got out of dooers he turnd about I commit you all to god Said he I doubt not but god will tak a farherly Care of us if we forfit i.

so I rest yor ever Affectionate and simpethiseing Sister

Susanna Edwards

Stockbridge Aprel 3 d 1758

[^546-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

## C148. Timothy Dwight to Gideon Hawley, April 5, 1758 C148.Dwight-G.Hawley 4-5-58

Timothy DwightC148. Timothy Dwight, Jr. to Gideon Hawley,4/5/58. Hartford Seminary, A.C. Thompson Papers, Doc. Box 216, f. 3155, item 85173. Addressed on back "To the Rev d / Gideon Hawley Missionary to the / Indians at Mashpee / To the Care of Thom s Hubbard Esq / Boston." Hubbard’s note: "Rec d & forwarded by / Sir / y r most humb: Serv t / Tho s Hubbard."

Northampton 5 th April 1758

Rev’d & D r Sr

You will doubtless e’er this reaches you, by Some other means hear of the heavy Affliction God in his Providence has bro’t upon us in taking from us to him- -self one So near & dear to us as our rev d & Hon d father Edwards on the 22 d of March last the Circum- -stances of whose death as collected from Letters Sent to mother Edwards who with Tim o Jon a & Betsey were at my house when the Sorrowfull Tidings Arrived by Woodb—e from Princeton to Stockbridge & here by Cooper & poor I So full of Grief as to make it visible must communicate it the Shock you will easily was great to us all but Madam endured the Trial with a truly Christian firmness being Supported & comforted as I trust by the Spirit of God who can change Darkness to light & bring Joy out of Sorrow —

He finding it altogether unsafe at this Time to live in the Jerseys not having gone thro with the small Pox (having been much exposed in his Journey down) by Advice of the Trustees & Doct r Shippen who was coming up to Innoculate at Princeton consented to undergo the Danger s & painfull Disease & take the Infection to prepare for future Services without fear of it in the Natural way, & Accordingly on the 23 d of Feb y last after proper preparation rec d the Distemper & was quite easy And Chearfull About it (as Appeared by a line from him a day or two before he broke out,) as having Suitably conducted to know his Duty & contented to have [^547-note1] done it; Doct r Shippen was constantly by him as Physician & nurse, he Says (in his letter) he had it very favourably but the Pox coming out full in the roof of his Mouth & throat prevented a possibility of his Taking Suitable Nourishment or Medicines to prevent a secondary fever which carried him we Trust from Gods Service below to more Sublime Serv c & Joys, o how great his Happiness, how great our Loss: he departed with an entirely calm unruffled mind in the clear possession of himself & his reason - expecting Soon to be with Christ whose will as to all the Events of his removal from Stockbridge & what was Consequent upon it he faithfully endeavour’d to know & obey, the Doct r writes "in his Sickness he never "Manifested the least concern as to the Event or the least "Complaint or Murmuring & at his Death Suffer’d not "the least Distortion of body not of a hair but in the Most "proper Sense of the words He fell asleep" Such Composure of mind Such a peacefull Death is Surely worth 54 Years Self denial & faithfull Service of him who has & can Again ordain it So, but the Joys that Shall Succeed Such a Change are infinitely more than a ballance always growing Always encreasing & never at end, may we all who by this Dispensation are deprived of a Husband a father or a friend be excited to prepare for the Same Transition that "we may die the Death of the righteous & our Latter end be like his."

God seems to have a Controversy with this land in Gen l with the College of N Jersey & with us of the bereaved family in particular. That College has Since my Graduation (who am not quite 32 years old[)] [^547-note2] been erected, had three the greatest men for knowledge in general especially Divine for its heads & Presidents & been their Grave how greatly they have been frownd upon & how greatly they have increased tis Gods Strange work as to us, his calling So many of his faithfull Servants from his Service here, the Pillars of our Sinking land Seems to portend Some grievous heavy Judgments to be bro’t upon us which are Only to be prevented by repentance & Turning to God which I pray God we may all do & the Tokens of his Displeasure be Averted.

I have rec d two letters from you of late respecting Pitkins horse know not whether he yet keeps him but Shall take the first opportunity to know & purchase him if to be had & Advise you am Sorry to hear of your Ill State of health hope you’l be like us in our way for the recovery of it, had pleased myself much with a Scheme for your removal to Stockbridge & Some things consequent upon it had form’d Invincible Arguments as I conceived for it but alas Some pleasant part of the Scene is changd & I begin to fear the other will not be Effected, The building of our weak minds are easily demolished by him that knoweth all things, my wife Joins with me in Cordial Salutations desiring your prayers we may Suitably behave under this divine Correction & rebuke.

I am Sr with hearty Affection your obliged Friend & Hum e Servant

T. Dwight Jun r

P.S. I almost forgot to tell you M rs Burr & her two Children were Inoculated at the Same time & are well thro it out of Danger ——

Rev d Gid n: Hawley

[^547-note1]: **marginal.** [2]

[^547-note2]: **marginal.** [3]

## C149. Sarah Edwards Parsons to Mary Edwards Dwight, April 18, 1758 C149.S.Parsons-M.Dwight 4-18-58

Sarah Edwards ParsonsC149. Sarah Edwards Parsons to Mary Edwards Dwight,4/18/58. ANTS, f. 1756-59B, #6. In composing, Parsons dropped a number of words.

Stockbridge April 18 th 1758

D r Sister

I received your kind Letter by my Husband for which return you my hearty thanks - but what or how to write or speak I know not. Last Saturday we had another Express from Princeton which brought us the Sorrowfull Tidings that Dear Sister Burr was dead and buried yesterday was week wh and no doubt have joind the Company of our dear dear Friends lately deceased and who have all got safe home to their heavenly Fathers House, are come to the New Jerusalem the City of the living God and to the innummerable Company of Angels, and to Jesus the Medi- ator of the new Covenant, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spi- rits of just Men made perfect - O how loud the the call to us that Survive that of this Family, be ye also ready. how much does it concern to be as servants with their Loins girt and their Lamps trimmed and burning waiting now we are so plainly taught not only in Gods word but by his Providence, that we know not what hour our Lord will come . God is now Chatizing us may he not only Cor- rect but teach us what he would have to do we ever are now loudly Called upon to Search our hearts and try our ways and turn our feet into God testimonies - Sister I hope your are in a much better under than these tryals than I am I find Im far from being in Such a tender Humble frame as I ought to be in - It is what has with great weight on my Heart and has ever since the Moment I heard of my Fa- thers [^548-note1] death that Gods dealings might be sanctified. O! my Heart trem- bles at the thought of disposing these Chastizings of the Lord [-] God grant these Corrections may be in Covenant love and faithfullness

The residue of the Spirit is with God may we all Cry mightily that his gracious Presence and may not be buried with our Friends but that he would grant that a double portion of the Spirit of Christ y t was in them might rest on us - but in order to this as you observe we had need to Stir our Selves to every duty

My Brother Tim o Set out this Day from here to go to Princeton. I cant but feel much Concerned about him but twas judged by all his call was clear - poor Lucy Im greivd for her may she get much Spiritual liquor in this Furnace of Affliction. And O the Dear Little babes my heart overflows with Pity and Compassion towards them, Tim o expects to bring them up with him but is not Certain Sister Burr made a Will but we don’t know the [^548-note2] Contents as to that Matter fully - Mr Cummins [^548-note3] was to Preach her Funeral Sermon upon her desire - She died of an acute fe Feavour by Lucys was much like the Feavour that Carried my Sister Jerusha out of the World; lived but Just a Week after She was taken apprehended She Should die from her being first taken her ill ness appearred not at all threatneing till Tuesday (She was taken on Friday Night) She was then taken with a violent Headake and soon delerious and So remained till She died on Friday the 7 Instant - Oh how fast has She been ripening for that world She is now gone what a mercy that God Should take those out of [. . .] [^548-note4] that were ready to die and is warning us hereby and yet giving further Opportu- nity to prepare may we have hearts to improve the Same

my Mother and Sisters and Brothers join with me in kind to you and Brother and your Little ones

From your very affec t and Sympathizing Sister

Sarah Parsons

P.S. Should be very glad if youd get me at Hez Wrights 3 yards and 1/2 of good Cypress and send a Scain of black Silk y r there was an unhappy Mistake about the Silk that was Carried down. please to send them by the first Fast conveyance I return you thanks for the Apples you Sent me

Your [. . .] [^548-note5] S. P.

[^548-note1]: This and the following lines are damaged where there is a fold in the MS. Text follows *Journal of Esther Edwards Burr*, p. 303.

[^548-note2]: **marginal.** [2]

[^548-note3]: Alexander Cumming, pastor of the New Brunswick, N.J. church.

[^548-note4]: MS damage

[^548-note5]: MS damage.

## C150. Sarah Edwards Parsons to Mary Edwards Dwight, April 26, 1758 C150.S.Parsons-M.Dwight 4-26-58

Sarah Edwards ParsonsC150. Sarah Edwards Parsons to Mary Edwards Dwight,4/26/58. ANTS, f. 1756-59B, #8. Addressed on back "To / M rs Mary Dwight / At / Northampton."

Stockbridge April 26 1758

D r Sister

In the greatest hast I write by this Con= veyance only of a few errands - My Mother Spake to Mr Pomroy when here the to let her have a pair of Cart boxes and to send them by the first Opportunity as far as N o. One and there left but She’s Since heard that She cant have a Cart made therefore Let him know that they must not be left there but brought heither My Mother Pleas desire you to get for my Mo- ther and me 1/4 of a pound of Quicksilver [...] of Doctor Mather she is in a present great want of it. also a considerable quantity of Onion seed for us. please to send me if you can get it some [^549-note1] seed. And get me an Ounce of [...] [^549-note2] and two Ounces of Orange Peel - two of the Children in our Family (viz my Little Negro Girl and my Youngest Son) have had the Feavour and Ague a long time, the Girl was taken some days before my Husband went to Northampton. had the First Fit that Day he went from us they are brought low with it. Mr Dwight told [^549-note3] Brother Tim o that he intends to come up this Spring and bring you with him I hope you wont fail of coming, I long greatly to see you; youl send me the Cypress I hope without fail and 3/4 f a y d of very dark Coloured Calico [-] if you can get that which is worth having.

From D r Sis r, your ever Affect t tho’ Afflicted Sister

Sarah Parsons

M rs Mary Dwight

## C153. Thomas Foxcroft to Joseph Bellamy, January 1, 1759 C153.Foxcroft-Bellamy 1-1-59

Thomas FoxcroftC153. Thomas Foxcroft to Joseph Bellamy,1/1/59. BRBL, f. 1534. On back, envelope cover is addressed to the Rev d. Mr. Joseph Bellamy, pastor at Bethlehem, care of Rev. Mr. Hopkins at Sheffield, and is noted, Sheffield, Jan. 14, 1759, that it was received and forwarded by Samuel Hopkins.

Bost. Jan ry. 1. 1759.

Rev d & D r. Sir,

I have to acknowledge ye. fav r. of oct o. 25th. which came to hand in Season: and I must rely on your Goodness to excuse my Delay of writing to you, as not owing in the least Measure to Ingratitude or Unmindfulness ——

The inclosed Letter from our Friend, Mr Erskine, fully expresses my Opinion with Relation to Mr. Presid t. Edwards’s Character, and my Desire respecting his M.S.S. — Please to let me know, as soon as may be, what Return I am to make to Mr Ersk. ——

I’m glad, M rs. Edwards left her Desire to have the Presid t’s. Life written, and hope Mr Hopk s., by this time, has made considerable Progress therein. If it ben’t too lengthy, it may be put before his Remains, which I pre- sume you are collecting — I don’t doubt, one way & another, Sufficient Encouragement may be procur’d for the Publication y rof.

I don’t find, as yet, but the Minister, intends to let his 2 d Nei r turn Calvinist. For I hear of no Reply to the Letter &c. But the Vindication of Wint. Ev g. is now at last in the Press - [^552-note1]

As to Mr. C——k’s Answer to the Opinion &c. it seems to me to have better clear’d up the Difficulties objected to him, than I expected — [^552-note2]

Query. May not a Law mean one Thing, and the Lawgiver intend something different? —— Might not the Cov t. with Adam , in it self, refer to Posterity , and yet they be included in the Purpose of God? —— In Case Adam had stood, was he not to have a Posterity , who in Consequence of their Interest in him, were to be happy? — Was it not the primary Design of the original Cov t. with Adam , to secure Happiness to him & his Posterity ? — Might it not be the true Meaning of the Covenant, that in Case he sinned, he sh d. be liable to immediate Death ; and so in the Nature of Things, cou’d have no Posterity ? But notwithstanding this was the Meaning of the Law, might not the Lawgiver consistently exercise his prerogative in reprieving determining to reprieve the Offender, and to give him a Posterity , but they to share in his Punishm t?

Do’s not the Event demonstrate this to have been God’s Design; thô the true Sense of the Threatning , view’d in it self, might look another Way? — But I have no Zeal to expend in this Dispute; nor indeed Time, at present, to lay out much Thôt upon it.

What if the general Opinion be groundless, which considers the threatned Punishment as extending to Death in all its Notions and m[o]re especially respecting [^552-note3] the Death of ye Body ? — May not we safely, wi[th]out going into any of Dr Taylor’s dangerous Errors, suppose, y t the Sentence of Temporal Death, which undoubtedly was pronounced after the great Promise of a Saviour, is properly to be refer’d to the Covenant of Grace ? Might it not be an Absolute Gospel-Threatning ? — And as to the Law-Threatning denounced originally, might it not, in its true Meaning, refer immedi- ately to Death spiritual , the Death of the Soul , — The most important Notion of Death , and frequently the Scripture-Sense of the Word - And but Consequentially refer to Death eternal , in case of going out of the World under the power of Death spiritual?

But this is only mention’d as a problematical Point. I shall but add, if the first Threatning included bodily Punishment, must it not be supposed to be confined to what is Temporal ; and not to extend to that which is Eternal? If it included bodily Death , did it also a bodily resurrection ? — And if the Body was not to rise again, how do’s it appear, from Scripture or Reason, that the dead Soul wou’d not have been annihilated, when separated from ye Body?

Dr Watts scruples not to suppose, the Souls of Infants, dying without Christ, are annihilated: and why mayn’t Annihilation be supposed the final & utmost Punishment of original Sin? You can’t, I believe, account for the future Existence of the Body , but upon the Plan of Chris Christianity. And can you acc o. for the fut. Exist. of ye Soul on any other Plan?

But I have only Time to add———(besides that - BOLD PUSH, [^552-note4] is going to appear) — that I desire your Prayers for

Sr.Your Bro r. & Serv t.

Tho s Foxcroft

P.S. The old South have nominated Mr. Cummings, Mr Jackson, and Mr Lock, [^552-note5] to preach for some Months to come, each 6 Weeks &c.

[^552-note1]: Referring to a pamphlet exchange on original sin between Samuel Webster (writing anonyomously) and Peter Clark. Webster, *A Winter Evening’s Conversation upon the Doctrine of Original Sin, between a minister and three of his neighbours accidentally met together: Wherein the notion of our having sinned in Adam, and being on that account only liable to eternal damnatin, is proved to beunscriptural, irrational, and of dangerous tendency* (Boston, 1757); Clark, *The Scripture-doctrine of original sin, stated and defended: in a summer-morning’s conversation, between a minister and a neighbour. Containing remarks on a late anonymous pamphlet, intitled, "A Winter-Evening’s Conversation. . ."* (Boston, 1758); Webster, *The Winter Evening Conversation Vindicated* (Boston, 1758); Clark, *A Defence of the principles of the "Summer-morning’s conversation - concerning the doctrine of original sin." Agains the exceptions of the author of the "Winter evening’s conversation vindicated" . . .* (Boston, 1760).

[^552-note2]: Charles Chauncy, *The opinion of one that has perused the Summer morning’s conversation, concerning original sin . . .* (Boston, 1758). Clark, *Remarks on a late pamphlet, intitled, "The opinion of one that has perused the Summer-morning’s conversation . . .* (Boston, 1758).

[^552-note3]: **marginal.** [2]

[^552-note4]: Samuel Hopkins, *A Bold push: in a letter to the author of a late pamphlet, intitled, Fair play, &c. . . .* (Boston, 1758). Edmund March, *Fair play! or, A needful word, to temper the tract, entitled, A summer morning’s conversation, &c. Being a letter to the Rev. Dr. Sewall, the Rev. Mess. Thomas Prince, Samuel Phillips, Thomas Foxcrift, and E. Pemberton; on occasion of their putting a recommendatory preface to Mr. Clark’s tract. . .* (Portsmouth, 1758)

[^552-note5]: The associate pastor of Old South Church, Boston, Thomas Prince, died Oct. 22, 1758. The three candidates were Alexander Cumming, then pastor of the First Presbyterian Church in New York City; Joseph Jackson, tutor at Harvard College; and Samuel Locke, who would become the president of Harvard in 1770. Of the three, Cumming was selected and ordained in 1761, though he died only two years later.

## C155. Joseph Hawley to David Hall, May 9, 1760 C155.JHawley-DHall 5-9-60

Joseph HawleyC155. Joseph Hawley to David Hall,5/9/60. MS fragment. BRBL, f. 1557; printed, *Boston Evening-Post*, May 19, 1760.

Northampton May 9 th 1760

Rev d Sr

I have often Wished that Every member of the Two Ecclesiastical Councils (that formerly Sat in Northampton upon the unhappy difference between our former most worthy and Rev d Pastor Mr Jonathan Edwards and the Church here) whereof you was a member, I say Sr I have often wished that every of them truly knew my real Sense of My own Conduct in the affairs that the one and the other of s d Councils are privy to —— And as I have long apprehended it to be My Duty Not only to humble my self before God for what was unchristian and Sinful in My Conduct before s d Councils, But also to Confess My faults to them and take Shame to myself therein before them — I have often Studied with myself [in what manner] [^554-note1] It was practicable for me to do It — and when I understood that you Sr and Mr Eaton were to be at Coldspring at ye time of their late Council, I resolved to improve the oppertunity fully to open my mind there to you and him therein, and thought that probably Some method might be then thought of in which my reflections on myself touching the matters above hinted at might be Communicated to Most if not all the Gentlemen afores d who do not reside in this County — But you know Sr how difficult it was for us to Converse together by ourselves when at Coldspring without giving umbrage to that people —— I therefore proposed writing to you upon the matters which I had then oppertunity only most Summarily to Suggest, which you Sr Signified would be agreeable to you —— I therefore now undertake what I then proposed: In which I humbly ask ye Divine Aid, and that I may be Made most freely willing fully to Confess my Sin and guilt to you and the world in those Instances which I have reason to Suppose fell under your Notice as they were publick and Notorious transactions, and on account whereof therefore you Sr and all others who had knowledge thereof had Just cause to be offended at me

And in the first place Sr I apprehend That with the church and People of Northampton I Sinned and erred exceedingly in Consenting and labouring that there Should be so Early a Dis= mission of Mr Edwards from his Pastoral Relation to us, even upon the Supposition that he was really in a mistake [in the disputed point: not only because the dispute was upon matters] [^554-note2] so very disputable in themselves and at the greatest remove from fundamental; but because Mr Edwards had So long proved himself a most faithful and painful Pastor to s d church and also changed his Sentiments in that Point wholly from a tender regard to what appeared to him to be truth, and had made known his Sentiments with great moderation and upon great deliberation, against all worldly motives, and from mere fidelity to his great Master, and a tender regard to the Souls of his flock, as We had the highest reason to Judge — which Considerations now Seem to me Sufficient and would (if we had been of a right Spirit) have greatly endeared him to his people, and made us to the last degree reluctant to part= ing with him, and disposed us to the exercise of the greatest Candour gentleness and Mode= ration — how much of the reverse whereof appeared in us I need not tell you Sr who was an Eye-Witness of our temper and Conduct

And Altho' It does not become me to pronounce decisively on a Point so disputable as what was then in dispute - Yet I begg leave to Say that I really apprehend that it is of the highest Moment to the body of this church and to me in partiuclar most Solicitously to enquire whether like the Pharisees and Lawyers in John Baptists time We did not reject the Counsel of God against ourselves in rejecting Mr Edwards and his doctrine which was the ground of his dismission - and I humbly concieve that It highly Imports us all of this church most Seriously and impartially to examine what that most Worthy and Able Divine about that time published in Support of the Same whereby he being dead yet Speaketh

But there were three things Sr Especially in my own Particular Conduct before the first Council which have been Justly matter of great grief and much trouble to me almost ever since, To wit, In the first place I Confess Sr that I acted very immodestly and Abusively to you as well as Injuriously to the church and myself when with much Zeal and unbecomeing assurance I moved the Council y t they would Interpose to Silence and Stop you in an address you was making one morning to the people wherein you was, if I don't misremember briefly exhorting them to a tender remembrance of the former affection and harmony that had Subsisted between them and their rev d Pastor, and the great Comfort and profit which they had apprehended that they had recieved from his ministry - For which Sr I heartily ask your forgiveness and I think that we all ought instead of opposing an exhortation of that nature to have receiv d it with all thankfullness

Another particular of my Conduct before that Council which I now apprehend was Criminal & was owing to the want of that tender affection and rev d respect & esteem for Mr Edwards which he had highly merited of me, was my Strenuously opposing ye adjournment of the matters Submitted to that Council for about two months for which I declare myself unfeignedly Sorry and I with Shame remember that I did it in a peremtory derisive vehement and very Immodest manner But Sr the most Criminal part of my Conduct at that time that I am Conscious of was my [^554-note3] Exhibiting to that Council a Set of Arguments in Writing the Drift whereof was to prove the reasonableness and Necessity of Mr Edwards's dismission in Case No accommodation was then effected, with mutual Consent which tract by Clear Implication Contained Some Severe uncharitable and (if I don't misremember) groundless and Slanderous Imputa= tions on Mr Edwards and Expressed in bitter language — and altho' the original draft thereof was not done by me yet I foolishly and Sinfully Consented to Copy it and as agent for the Church to read it, and deliver it to the Council, which I could never have done [if I] [^554-note4] had not had a wicked relish for perverse things — which Conduct of mine I Confess [...] very Sinful, am perswaded was highly provoking to God, and for which I am ashamed [...] founded and Nothing to answer.

As to the Churches Remonstrance (as It was called) which their Com tee preferred [to the] last of s d Councils, to all which I was Consenting, and in the Composing whereof I was [very active] as also in bringing the church to their Vote upon it, I would in the first place [only ob] serve that I don't remember anything in that Small part of It which was plain[ly] discursive of the Expediency of Mr Edwards's resettlement there as Pastor to a part of the Church which was very Exceptionable — But as to all the residue, which was much the greatest part thereof (and I am not Certain that any part was wholly free) It was every where Larded with unchristian bitterness, Sarcastical and unmannerly Insinuations, Contained diverse direct grievous and Criminal charges and allegations against Mr Edwards, which I have Since good reason to Suppose were all founded on Jealous and uncharitable mistakes & so were really gross Slanders - Also many heavy and reproachful charges upon diverse of Mr Edwards's adherents, and Some Severe Censures of them all indiscriminately, all of which (if not wholly false and groundless) yet were altogether unnecessary and therefore highly Criminal — Indeed I am fully Convinced that the whole of that Composure, excepting ye Small part thereof abovementioned was totally unchristian a Scandalous abusive and Injurious Libel against Mr Edwards and his particular friends, especially the former, and highly provoking and detestable in the Sight of God — for which I am heartily Sorry and Ashamed and Pray I may remember it with deep abasement and penitence all my days.

Nor Do I now think that the Churches Conduct in refusing to appear and attend before that [Council to support] the charges and Allegations in s d remonstrance against Mr Edwards and s d Brethren, which they demanded, [was ever] Vindicated by all the Subtile Answers that were given to s d demand - Nor do I think that our Conduct in that Instance was Capable of a defence, for it appears to me that by making charges of Scandalous matters against them before s d Council We Necessarily so far gave that Council Jurisdiction — And I own with Sorrow and regret that I zealously endeavoured that the church Should perseveringly refuse to appear before s d Council for ye purpose Aboves d, which I humbly Pray God to forgive

Another part of my Conduct Sr of which I have long repented and for which I hereby declare my hearty Sorrow was my Obstinate opposition to the last Councils having any Conference with the church, which s d Council earnestly and repeatedly moved for and which the Church finally denied (as you know) I think It discovered a great deal of pride and vain Selfsufficiency in the Church, and Shewed them to be very opionative especially the Chief Sticklers, one of whom I own I was - and I think it was running a most presumptuous risk, and Acting ye part of proud Sinners for us to refuse hearing and candidly and Seriously considering what that Council could Say or propose to us among whom there were diverse Justly in great reputation for grace and Wisdom.

In these Instances Sr of my Conduct and others (to which you was not privy) in the Course of that most Melancholy Contention with Mr Edwards, wherein I now See that I was very much Influenced by Vast pride Selfsufficiency, ambition and Vanity, I appear to myself Vile, and doubtless much more so to others who [...] [^554-note5] ** more Impartial - and do In ye review thereof abhor myself and repent Sorely —— and, if my own heart Condemns me, It [behoves me solemnly to] remember that God is greater and knoweth all things —— And I hereby own Sr that Such Treatment of Mr Edwards as is herein before Mentioned wherein I was so deeply Concerned and Active was particularly and very aggravatedly Sinful and ungrateful in me Because I was not only under ye Common obligations of each Individual of the Society to him as to a most able diligent and faithful Pastor But I had also rec d many Instances of his tenderness goodness and generosity to me as a young kinsman whom he was disposed to treat in a most friendly manner ————— I indeed Sr I must own that by my Conduct in Consulting and Acting against Mr Edwards within the Time of our most unhappy disputes with him and especially in and about that abominable remonstrance remonstrance I have So far Sym= bolized with Balaam, Ahithophel and Judas that I am Confounded and filled with Terror oftentimes when I attend to ye most Painful Similitude — and I freely Confess that on account of my Conduct abovementioned I have the greatest reason to tremble at those most Solemn and awful words our Saviour Mat. 18. 6. and those in Luke 10 th at ye 16 th — and I am most Sorely Sensible that Nothing but that Infinite grace and Mercy which Saved Some of the Betrayers and Murderers of our Blessed Lord and the Persecutors of his Martyrs can Pardon me — In which alone I hope for Pardon for ye Sake of Christ, Whose Blood (Blessed by God) cleanseth from all Sin ————

On the whole Sr I am Convinced that I have the greatest reason to Say, as David "Have mercy

[Printed version: *The Boston Evening-Post*, May 19, 1760, pp. 1-2.]

*To the Publishers of the BOSTON EVENING POST.* *Please to insert the following Copy of my Letter to Mr.* **HALL, *in your next Paper, and you’ll oblige,* **

*Your humble Servant.*

JOSEPH HAWLEY,

*To the Rev. Mr.*HALL *of* Sutton.

Northampton May 9 1760.

*Rev. Sir,*

I HAVE often wished that Every Member of the two Ecclesiastical councils (that formerly sat in *Northampton* upon the unhappy differences be- tween our former most worthy and reverend pastor Mr. *Jonathan Edwards* and the Church here) whereof you was a member: I say Sir, I have often wish’d that every of them truly knew my real sense of my own conduct in the affairs that the one and the other of said councils are privy to; and as I have long apprehended it to be my duty not only to hum- ble myself before God for what was unchristian and sinful in my conduct before said councils, but also to confess my faults to them, and take shame to myself therefor [^554-note6] before them, I have often studied with my- self in what manner it was practicable for me to do it; and when I understood that you, *Sir*, and Mr. *Eaton* were to be at *Cold Spring* at the time of their late council, I resolved to improve the opportunity fully to open my mind there to you and him thereon, and thought that probably some method might be then thought of in which my reflections on myself touch- ing the matters above hinted at, might be communi- cated to most if not all the gentlemen aforesaid who do not reside in this county; but you know, *Sir*, how difficult it was for us to converse together by ourselves when at *Cold Spring*, without giving umbrage to that people; I therefore proposed writing to you upon the matters which I had then opportunity only most sum- marily to suggest, which you *Sir*, signified would be agreeable to you: I therefore now undertake what I then proposed, in which I humbly ask the divine aid; and that I may be made most freely willing fully to confess my Sin and guilt to you and the world in those instances which I have reason to suppose fell under your notice, as they were publick and notorious transactions, and on account whereof, therefore, you *Sir*, and all others who had knowledge thereof, had just cause to be offended at me.

And in the first place Sir, I apprehend that with the Church and People of *Northampton*, I sinned and erred exceedingly in consenting and labouring that there Should be so early a dismission of Mr. *Edwards* from his pastoral relation to us, even upon the sup- position that he was really in a mistake in the disputed point; not only because the dispute was upon matters so very disputable in themselves and at the greatest remove from fundamental, but because Mr. *Edwards* had so long proved himself a most faithful and pain- ful pastor to said church, and also changed his senti- ments in that point wholly from a tender regard to what appeared to him to be truth, and had made known his sentiments with great moderation and upon great deliberation, against all worldly motives and from mere fidelity to his great master, and a tender regard to the souls of his flock, as we had the highest reason to judge, which considerations now seem to me sufficient and would (if we had been of a right spirit) have greatly endeared him to his people and made us to the last degree reluctant to parting with him, and disposed us to the exercise of the greatest candour, gentleness and moderation; how much of the reverse whereof appeared in us, I need not tell you *Sir*, who was an eye witness of our temper and conduct.

And altho' it does not become me to pronounce de- cisively on a point so disputable as what was then in dispute, yet I beg leave to Say that I really appre- hend that it is of the highest moment to the body of this church, and to me in particular, most sollicitously to enquire whether like the Pharisees and Lawyers in John Baptist’s time, we did not reject the council of God against ourselves, in rejecting Mr. *Edwards* and his doctrine, which was the ground of his dismission. And I humbly conceive that it highly imports us all of this church most seriously and impartially to examine what that most worthy and able divine about that time published in support of the same, whereby he being dead yet speaketh.

But there were three things *Sir*, especially in my own particular conduct before the first council which have been justly matter of great grief and much trou- ble to me almost ever since, to wit.

In the first place I confess *Sir*, that I acted very immodestly and abusively to you as well as injuriously to the church and myself, when with much zeal and unbecoming assurance I moved the council that they would interpose to silence and stop you in an address you was making one morning to the people, wherein you was, if I don't misremember, briefly exhorting them to a tender remembrance of the former affection and harmony that had subsisted between them and their reverend pastor, and the great comfort and pro- fit which they had apprehended that they had receiv- ed from his ministry, for which Sir, I heartily ask your forgiveness, and I think that we all ought in- stead of opposing an exhortation of that nature to have received it with all thankfulness.

Another particular of my conduct before that coun- cil which I now apprehend was criminal, and was owing to the want of that tender affection and reve- rend respect & esteem for Mr. *Edwards* which he had highly merited of me, was my strenuously oppo- sing the adjournment of the matters submitted to that council for about two months, for which I declare myself unfeignedly sorry, and I with shame remem- ber, that I did it in a peremtory, decisive, [^554-note7] vehement and very immodest manner.

But *Sir*, the most criminal part of my conduct at that time, that I am conscious of, was my exhibiting to that council a set of arguments in writing, the drift whereof was to prove the reasonableness and necessi- ty of Mr. *Edwards*'s dismission in case no accommo- dation was then effected with mutual consent; which tract by clear implication contained some severe, un- charitable and (if I don't misremember) groundless and slanderous imputations on Mr. *Edwards*, and ex- pressed in bitter language; and altho' the original draft thereof was not done by me, yet I foolishly and sinfully consented to copy it, and as agent for the church to read it and deliver it to the council, which I could never have done, if I had not had a wicked relish for perverse things, which conduct of mine, I confess was very sinful, am persuaded was highly provoking to God, and for which I am ashamed, confounded, and have nothing to answer.

As to the Church’s remonstrance (as it was called) which their committee preferr’d to the last of said councils, to all which I was consenting, and in the composing whereof I was very active, as also in bring- ing the church to their vote upon it: I would in the first place only observe, that I don't remember any thing in that small part of it which was plainly dis- cursive of the expediency of Mr. *Edwards*'s re-settle- ment there as pastor to a part of the church, which was very exceptionable; but as to all the residue, which was much the greatest part thereof (and I am not certain that any part was wholly free) It was eve- ry where larded with unchristian bitterness, sarcasti- cal and unmannerly insinuations, contained divers di- rect, grievous and criminal charges and allegations against Mr. *Edwards*, which I have since good reason to suppose were all founded on jealous and uncha- ritable mistakes, and so were really gross slanders, al- so many heavy and reproachful charges upon divers of Mr. *Edwards*'s adherents, and some severe censures of them all indiscriminately, all of which (if not wholly false and groundless) yet were altogether un- necessary and therefore highly criminal. Indeed I am fully convinced that the whole of that composure, excepting the small part thereof abovementioned, was totally unchristian, a scandalous, abusive, and in- jurious libel against Mr. *Edwards* and his particular friends, especially the former, and highly provoking and detestable in the sight of God, for which I am heartily sorry and ashamed, and pray I may remem- ber it with deep abasement and penitence all my days. Nor do I now think that the Church’s con- duct in refusing to appear and attend before that council to support the charges and allegations in said remonstrance against Mr. *Edwards* and said brethren, which they demanded, was ever vindicated by all the subtile answers that were given to said demand, nor do I think that our conduct in that instance was ca- pable of a defence, for it appears to me that by mak- ing charges of scandalous matters against them before said council, we necessarily so far gave that council jurisdiction, and I own with sorrow and regret, that I zealously endeavoured that the Church should per- severingly refuse to appear before said council for the purpose abovesaid, which I humbly pray God to forgive.

Another part of my conduct, *Sir*, of which I have long repented, and for which I hereby declare my hearty sorrow, was my obstinate opposition to the last council’s having any conference with the church, which said council earnestly and repeatedly moved for, and which the church finally denied (as you know.) I think it discovered a great deal of pride and vain self-sufficiency in the church, and shewed them to be very opiniative especially the chief sticklers, one of whom I own I was, and think it was running a most presumptuous risk, and acting the part of proud scorners, [^554-note8] for us to refuse hearing and can- didly and seriously considering what that council could say or propose to us, among whom there were divers justly in great reputation for grace and wisdom.

In these instances, Sir, of my conduct and others (to which you was not privy) in the course of that most melancholy contention with Mr. *Edwards*, where- in I now see that I was very much influenced by vast pride, self-sufficiency, ambition and vanity, I appear to myself vile, and doubtless much more so to others who are more impartial, and do in the review there- of abhor myself and repent sorely, and if my own heart condemns me it behoves me solemnly to re- member that God is greater and knoweth all things; and I hereby own, Sir, that such treatment of Mr. *Edwards* as is herein before mentioned, wherein I was so deeply concerned and active, was particularly and very aggravatedly sinful and ungrateful in me, because I was not only under the common obligations of each individual of the society to him, as to a most able, diligent and faithful pastor; but I had also received many instances of his tenderness, goodness, and ge- nerosity to me, as a young kinsman whom he was disposed to treat in a most friendly manner. Indeed, Sir, I must own, that by my conduct in consult- ing and acting against Mr. *Edwards* within the time of our most unhappy disputes with him, and especially in and about that abominable remonstrance, I have so far symbolized with *Balaam, Ahithophel* and *Judas* that I am Confounded and filled with terror oftentimes when I attend to the most painful similitude.

And I freely confess that on account of my Conduct above-mentioned, I have the greatest reason to trem- ble at those most solemn and awful words our Saviour, *Matth*. 18, 6. and those in *Luke* 10 th, at the 16 th; and I am most sorely sensible that nothing but that infinite grace and mercy which saved some of the betrayers and murderers of our blessed Lord, and the persecutors of his Martyrs, can pardon me; in which alone I hope for pardon for the sake of Christ, whose blood (blessed by God) cleanseth from all sin. On the whole, Sir, I am convinced that I have the greatest reason to say as *David*, "Have "mercy upon me O God according to thy loving "kindness, according to the multitude of thy tender "mercies blot out my transgressions, wash me thorough- "ly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin, "for I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is "ever before me; hide thy face from my sins and "blot out all mine iniquities; create in me a clean "heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me, "cast me not away from thy presence, and take not "thy holy spirit from me. Restore unto me the joy "of thy Salvation, and uphold me with thy free "spirit."

And I humbly apprehend that it greatly concerns the church of *Northampton* most seriously to examine whether the many hard speeches, spoken by many particular members against their former pastor, some of which the church really countenanced, and especial- ly those spoken by the church as a body in that most vile remonstrance, are not so impious and ungodly as to be utterly uncapable of defence, and whether said church were not guilty of great sin in being so willing and disposed for so slight a cause to part with so faith- ful and godly a minister as Mr. *Edwards* was. And whether God will ever hold us guiltless till we cry to him for Christ’s sake to pardon and save us from that judgment which such ungodly deeds deserve, and publickly humble and take shame to ourselves therefor. And I most heartily wish and pray that the town and church of *Northampton* would seriously and carefully examine whether they have not abun- dant cause to judge that they are now lying under great guilt in the sigh of God, and whether those of us who were concerned in that most awful con- tention with Mr. *Edwards* can ever more reasonably expect God’s favour and blessing, till our eyes are opened and we become thoroughly convinced that we have greatly provoked the Most High, and been injurious to one of the best of men, and until we shall be thoroughly convinced that we have dread- fully persecuted Christ by persecuting and vexing that just man and servant of Christ, until we shall be humbled as in the dust therefor, and till we openly [^554-note9] in full terms, and without baulking the matter, con- fess the same before the world, and most humbly and earnestly seek forgiveness of God, and do what we can to honour the memory of Mr. *Edwards* and clear it of all the aspersions which we unjustly cast upon him, since God has been pleased to put it beyond our power to ask his forgiveness. Such terms I am persuaded the great and righteous God will hold us to, and that it will be in vain for us to hope to escape with Impunity in any other way. This I am con- vinced of with regard to myself, and this way I most solemnly purpose to take myself (if God in his mercy shall give me opportunity) that so by making free confession to God and man of my sin and guilt, and publickly taking shame to myself therefor, I may give glory to the Lord God of Israel, and do what in me lies to clear the memory of that venerable man from the wrongs and injuries I was so active in bringing on his reputation and character, and I thank God that he has been pleased to spare my life and oppor- tunity therefor to this time, and am sorry that I have delayed the affair so long.

Altho’ I made the substance of almost all the fore- going reflections in writing, but not exactly in the same manner, to Mr. *Edwards* and the brethren who adhered to him, in Mr. *Edwards*’s life, and be- fore he removed from *Stockbridge*, and I have reason to believe that he from his great candour and charity, heartily forgave me and pray’d for me, yet because that was not generally known I look on myself obliged to take further steps, for while I kept silence my bones waxed old, &c. [^554-note10]

For all these my great sins therefore, in the first place, I humbly and most earnestly ask forgiveness of God; nextly, of the relatives and near friends of Mr. *Edwards*. I also heartily ask the forgiveness of all those who were called Mr. *Edwards*’s adherents, and of all the members of the ecclesiastical councils abovementioned; and lastly, of all christian people who have had any knowledge of the matters above- said or any of them.

I have no desire, Sir, that you should make any secret of this letter, but desire you would communi- cate the same to whom you shall judge proper, and I purpose (if God shall give me opportunity) to procure it to be published in some one of the public news- papers, for I can’t devise any other way of making known my sentiments of the foregoing matters to all who ought to be acquainted therewith, and therefore I think I ought to do it, whatever remarks I may foresee will be made thereon.

Probably when it comes out some of my acquain- tance will pronounce me quite over-run with vapours, others will be furnished with matter for mirth and pleasantry; others will cursorily pass it over, as re- lating to matters quite stale, but some I am persuaded will rejoice to see me brought to a sense of my sin and duty; and I myself shall be conscious that I have done something of what the nature of the case admits towards undoing what is, and long has been, to my greatest remorse and trouble that it was ever done.

*Sir*, I desire that no one would entertain a thought from my having herein spoken respectfully of Mr. *Edwards*, that I am disaffected to our present pastor, for the very reverse is true, and I have a reverend esteem, real value, and hearty affection for him, and bless God, that he has, notwithstanding all our un- worthiness, given us one to succeed Mr. *Edwards*, who (as I have reason to hope) is truly faithful.

I conclude this long letter by heartily desiring your prayers that my repentance of my sins above- mentioned may be unfeigned and genuine, and such as God in infinite mercy for Christ’s sake will accept, and I beg leave to subscribe myself,

*Sir, your real, tho’ very unworthy friend* *and obedient servant,*

JOSEPH HAWLEY.

## C157. Hannah Edwards Wetmore to Esther Stoddard Edwards, October 11, 1760 C157.HWetmore-EEdwards 10-11-60

Hannah Edwards WetmoreC157. Hannah Edwards Wetmore to Esther Stoddard Edwards,10/11/60. BRBL, f. 1520. No address.

Honour'd and very Dear Mother / Last Night before I went to bed I had prepared every thing for my Journey to windsor - meaning to Set out very early this morning in hopes of by that means to have had an oppertunity of Seeing and Conversing with — and of expressing Some part of the gratitude I owe to the best of mothers —— but this Comfort is Providentially deny'd me at present —— after I had been abed but two Hours I was obblig'd to rise to to my Little son was taken with a Stopage and Horsness and fever - and was obblig'd to be up god good part of the Night — he is Somewhat better this morning but I am afraid to Leave him and am also not well my Self — design if possable to Set out monday morning — this with —— Mr Wetmores and Cousin Bettys and our Childrens dutifull Respects together with mine is from your dutyfull and very affectionate Daughter

H: Wetmore

Middleton Oct r - 11 th 1760

## C159. Samuel Hopkins to Joseph Hawley, March 21, 1761 C159.SHopkins-JHawley 3-21-61

Samuel HopkinsC159. Samuel Hopkins to Joseph Hawley,3/21/61. Joseph Hawley Papers, NYPL.

Sheffield, 21 Mark, 1761.

Honoured Sir.

I have been not a little affected and pleas’d with your letter to the Rev. Mr Hall, published in a Boston newspaper. I hope and trust, God has given you to view the treatment Mr Edwards met with in that sorrowful affair, in a true light; and has led you to a repentance, never to be repented of.

A brief history of Mr Edwards’s life is drawn up, which perhaps will be published: and tis thought nes necessary that some account should be given of the occation and manner of his dismission from North- ampton. And as the above mention’d letter of yours to Mr Hall, will serve to illustrate and confirm what may be related of that matter; tis thought pro- -per, and of importance that it should be inserted. This is therefore to ask your consent that it shold should be thus published; and to desire you to give any particular directions about it, that you shall think fit, in a line by the Bearer, (Mr Parsons,) to

your humble Servant,

Samuel Hopkins.

Jos. Hawley Esq r.

## C160. Joseph Hawley to Samuel Hopkins, April 11, 1761 C160.JHawley-SHopkins 4-11-61

Joseph HawleyC160. Joseph Hawley to Samuel Hopkins,4/11/61. NYPL, Hawley Papers, #76.

Northampton 11 t April 1761

Rev d Sr

I rec d yours of ye 21 st of March by Cap t Dwight wherein you inform me y t there is a design of publishing a brief history of Mr Edwards’s life and that it is thought that my letter to the Rev d Mr Hall will Serve to illustrate and Confirm Some things which that History is to Contain and therefore you are pleased to ask my Consent that my s d letter Should be inserted in that piece and also to propose y t I Should give Some directions About ye manner of doing it, if I think proper.

In answer I have to Say, That as I wrote and Published that letter with ye full Consent of my heart and after much deliberation So I never yet at repented of my Conduct therein (am chiefly Solici- tous that my repentance may be of ye right kind) and am quite free that any use Should be made of it, which may Serve to do Justice to the dead or living or promote the Welfare of Mankind Temporal or eternal —— By publishing it in the manner I have done, I have fully Submitted it to others to determine what Improvem t thereof will Serve those ends, and am entirely Satisfied in having done so - I have therefore only to pray in reference thereto that they may be directed in their use of it As to the manner of Inserting it in any piece I only desire that propoer care may be Taken y t there by no error in transcribing it and that the whole of the letter be inserted if any part

I am Sr your unworthy Friend & Humble Ser t

Joseph Hawley

To the Rev d Mr Sam l Hopkins
